Handled seriously does not zero this out the way the earlier note assumed - the corrected axis prices what is actually depicted on its own terms, not only how crude the prose register is, and a child's seduction by an adult carries real weight there even told in restrained, literary prose. What already capped this below Artemis 69 - a flatter, duller lead than Weir's - is compounded rather than relieved by this axis.

t: Muzi, kteri nemaji zeny (Men Without Women)
why: The collection's shared subject is men shaped by the absence or unknowability of women in their lives, not a sexual relationship as such, so filter 6 does not apply. But that subject is a mood, not a worked premise with consequences the way the ideas this reader rewards work (Project Hail Mary 92 on astrophage's second-order effects, Red Rising 95 on its interiority-driven plot) - a short story collection in literary fiction with a diffuse theme rather than a nameable, worked-out idea tends to settle in the low-to-mid 60s for this reader rather than climb into the A band. The sexual content itself is light in volume and restrained in explicitness, so it is a minor risk rather than what carries the number.

t: Prvni osoba jednotneho cisla (First Person Singular)
why: Eight first-person stories, mostly nostalgic reminiscence with one or two swerving into the fabulist (a talking monkey who steals women's names; an old man's riddle about a circle with no circumference). No hard filter fires: each story is single-narrator and legible from its first page, unlike the simultaneous-thread failures that scored 30; nothing on the page is real-world occultism, only invented strangeness; there is no investigation plot. On the heaviest axis Murakami sits outside the usual test rather than failing it: he never undertakes to explain the strange things he declares, and per the rule 'nothing obliges an author to explain anything,' an author who states up front that an event 'can't be explained, defies logic' is not reneging on a promise the way Mortal Engines or 2001 did - he never made one. That is a genuine difference from Chiang's Top-pick-candidate method of declaring one premise and rigorously working out its consequences: Murakami is close to the opposite of that discipline, so the worldbuilding axis gives him neither the Chiang-style credit nor a Mortal-Engines-style penalty - it is close to neutral here, not a driver of the score either way. What actually has to carry the number is whether the ideas left behind are good ones, per the short-idea-driven rule that the suspension of character/plot penalties never adds points by itself. Some stories clear that bar with a genuinely nameable idea - Cream's meditation on disturbing, unresolved experience losing its sting yet still shaping you; the title story and the memoir-blurring Yakult Swallows piece both worry at how solid a first-person self even is. But this is graded against real risk, not a clean pass: multiple reviews (Harvard Review's 'confusingly drawn map that means more to the creator than reader,' NPR's 'a few missteps... the payoff doesn't always satisfy') describe exactly the failure mode that downgraded Alice Munro - technique in search of a payoff that doesn't arrive - and Confessions of a Shinagawa Monkey is explicitly self-aware that it has no stated theme at all. That keeps this well short of Animal Farm 78 or The Little Prince 82, where the idea is sharp and singular, and lands it closer to the competent-but-uneven B band such as Les Miserables 71. Field fix 2026-08-26: axis:ideas appeared in both leanedOn and risks, which makes both fields useless; it is kept as the axis carrying the number and the range already expresses the uncertainty. No number changed. Re-derived 2026-09-03 under the new collection axis: a multi-story book is read from the front and put down on its weakest early pieces, not averaged and not skipped past. Ja, robot 55 is the anchor - the reader stopped after three stories, on the first story's cast and the third story's implausible behaviour, and never reached the pieces the prediction was built on. Eight first-person pieces with no connecting arc, and the sexual-content risk already recorded on this line sits inside individual stories rather than across the book - which under the new axis means it can land on page one as easily as on page two hundred.

t: Oci modreho psa (Ojos de perro azul)
why: Positive case: these eleven apprentice stories (written 1947-1955, collected 1974) run almost entirely on interior consciousness rather than event -- a boy narrates his own living burial from inside a coffin diagnosed as a 'living death', a woman narrates her wish to shed a hereditary curse of beauty by willing her soul into her cat -- which is the motives-over-action register that ranks Speaker for the Dead 90 and Mockingjay 91 above their more event-driven counterparts. Each story checked opens on one concrete, legible situation and stays there rather than fanning into several threads, the exact clarity that Gunslinger 30, Colour of Magic 30 and Guards! Guards! 30 all failed on. Deductions: this is an anthology, and per the anthology reasoning already on file, a collection has no single idea to name and averages toward its middle rather than being predictable up the way a single-premise work is. Critics treat these apprentice pieces as valuable mainly as a seed of the author's later style rather than as well-realized stories on their own, which is the heavy-description/thin-story shape that cost nothing in LOTR 84 but capped it at 84 rather than higher, and that is closer still to Unfinished Tales 69, 'fragmented and not aligned' -- eleven standalone, unconnected early pieces is nearer that shape than to one worked-through premise. Leaned on the anthology/ideas axis and the structural (fragmentation) face of worldbuilding, not on protagonist or opening clarity, both of which check out fine here and are not what caps this one. Field fix 2026-08-26: axis:worldbuilding appeared in both leanedOn and risks, which makes both fields useless; it is kept as the axis carrying the number and the range already expresses the uncertainty. No number changed.

The whole text is the narrator's own examination of what she wants and why, with almost no external action until the final page - a purer case of the axis that separates Mockingjay 91 from Catching Fire 83 and PHM 92 from The Martian 82, since here the ratio of interiority to event is even more extreme than either. The idea is nameable: seventeen sleepless days strip away a stereotyped, outwardly content marriage and let her see her own routine from outside, in the same short-idea-driven register as Animal Farm 78 (bleak, but leaves something to think about rather than immersing in misery) rather than the plain-warm register of The Little Prince 82. Two deductions keep it off the top: the ending leaves her alone in her car at night, unable to move, as two shadowy men rock the vehicle - unresolved and frightening rather than a settled resolution, so bleakness and the passive, uncertain final beat both cost a few points, the same way Artemis 69's flat-but-competent lead capped Weir's range even with the world-logic fine throughout. Leaned on motives-over-action first and the named idea second; not leaned on worldbuilding, since Murakami declares the anomaly (no sleep, no decline, if anything she looks younger) but never undertakes to explain its mechanism - the same protection that let Silmarillion 80 and Little Prince 82 carry unexplained strangeness with no penalty. Re-derived 2026-09-03 under the new collection axis: a multi-story book is read from the front and put down on its weakest early pieces, not averaged and not skipped past. Ja, robot 55 is the anchor - the reader stopped after three stories, on the first story's cast and the third story's implausible behaviour, and never reached the pieces the prediction was built on. NO MOVEMENT, and the reason is worth recording: this is catalogued as short fiction but it is one continuous text with one narrator, so a collection axis has nothing to grade here. The axis is added as a dep rather than applied, so that a later cataloguing correction does not read as an unexamined clearance.

Reversalism - an inverted economy where workers pay their employer and shops pay customers - is nameable in a sentence, so it clears the bar the short-idea-driven rule sets before crediting a short book at all. But naming the gimmick is not the same as it holding up: reviewers report that once Reversalism is defined the novella stalls rather than working out its consequences with the rigor Project Hail Mary 92 (astrophage's second-order effects) or Golden Son 92 (earned reveals) show, and flag internal inconsistencies McEwan never resolves - a cockroach hive-mind remembering a human pop song, and a transformation that reads as an accident on the opening pages but a deliberate hivemind plan by the close. That is the heaviest-axis failure this reader's own rule names: the author must follow the rules he lays down, and here the premise does not survive its own book. Jim Sams is also not a protagonist worth rooting for - a satire vehicle standing in for a Boris Johnson figure, driven by cockroach appetite rather than any want-and-why - the same unrootable-lead problem that cost The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 22 points against Sunrise on the Reaping, and the protagonist axis outranks worldbuilding when the two conflict. With the idea failing to hold under its own logic and no lead to invest in, there is no positive case here beyond having cleared the filters, which the rules explicitly say is not a case at all. That places it with Divergent 58 and Mortal Engines 55 - thin premise, no rootable lead - rather than with the short books that actually earned their score, Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82. Field fix 2026-08-26: axis:ideas appeared in both leanedOn and risks, which makes both fields useless; it is kept as the axis carrying the number and the range already expresses the uncertainty. No number changed.

The Czech title tracks this book's spine more than the English 'Vagabond' does: Thomas is captured and interrogated by a Dominican inquisitor pursuing the Vexille heresy, which puts his stated Christian faith under real pressure instead of leaving it as backstory - the same 'does the book examine what is actually true' test that made Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus (91) the strongest testimony in the log, though here it is one thread inside an adventure plot, not the whole book, so it earns less than that memoir does. His friendship with the Scottish noble Robbie Douglas gives the loyalty-under-pressure axis Red Rising and Golden Son both score well on. Risk: this is the middle volume of an unresolved trilogy, so the Grail's declared power and the Vexille conspiracy's coherence cannot be graded yet, and Cornwell's usual thin-secondary-character problem still applies to the cast around the siege of La Roche-Derrien.

Unusually for the series, this entry is not built around a battle: Sharpe investigates why his depleted regiment's replacements never arrived and uncovers a recruiting-fraud ring reaching into Whitehall, trading the series' usual set-piece for exactly the axis the log rewards most - what people want and why, worked out in scheme and consequence. Reviewers single this book out for its 'clever detail' and its departure from formula. Sharpe stays a rootable underdog defending his men against institutional betrayal, a milder version of the class-conflict idea, and the strongest positive case this series offers on the axis the log weights most. Risk: the antagonists (Lord Fenner and the London 'nest of vipers') are reviewer-described in the same single-dimensional-villain terms that recur across the series, so this does not reach the tighter causal payoff of Golden Son's reveals (92).

A hundred-year-old man joins a flight to a comet and a second ship comes down on an ice moon: the sights are the point and the story is not. Reviewers converge on no path and no purpose, on long stretches of recycled text padding the length, and on the stranded crew never being in real danger - which removes the one thing that kept a survival story moving for this reader (The Martian 82 ran on problem-solving under threat). A thin story spread over pages is the penalty term in this log, the reason LOTR 84 could not pull clear of The Hobbit 84. Characterisation is the recurring complaint, and interiority is the axis that makes the difference at the top here - Red Rising 95 above Golden Son 92 on nothing else. Ideas belong in the risks, not the case for the book: the central mystery is barely advanced and reviewers report learning nothing new, so the one thing that could have carried a plotless book is the thing least likely to hold. A sequel as well, and sequels are not safe bets here - Hitchhiker's fell 83 to 70. Decided at the low-line gate on form, genre and one search.

t: 3001: posledni vesmirna odysea (3001: The Final Odyssey)
why: The premise is a good one and it is delivered on for a while: an astronaut left for dead is revived a thousand years later, and the first stretch is a guided tour of what changed, told through one man learning it. What sinks the number is exactly what this log punishes hardest. Reviewers agree on the shape - the tour is the strong part, the story after it is thinner still, and the resolution arrives in about a chapter. A thin story spread over pages is the standing penalty: LOTR 84 was held level with The Hobbit 84 because the story was very thin for the number of pages, and The Martian 82 was docked for an ending that dragged. The people are described as glossed over, and page time on what characters want and why is the axis that puts Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 at the top. Ideas go in the risks rather than the leanedOn on purpose: the long-running mystery is finally answered by turning the mysterious thing into a machine that can be handed a computer virus, and a payoff like that leaves nothing behind. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets here - Hitchhiker's fell 83 to 70. Decided at the low-line gate on form, genre and one search; no deeper research would move it above 68.

t: A zrodi se Nadace (Forward the Foundation)
why: One man's life from forty to eighty-one, with the page time going to what he wants and what it costs him rather than to events: the wife destroyed defending him, the adopted son killed, the funding stripped year by year, the work continued anyway. That is the axis Speaker for the Dead 90 and Mockingjay 91 both top, and it is unusual for this author to hand a book one figure to follow for its whole length. It also opens on a single legible situation with nothing running alongside it. Trimmed 2026-09-03 on this author's first real score - Ja, robot 55, abandoned three stories in on a cast nobody could root for - because the structural deduction here is the same one in miniature: four self-contained sections a decade apart, and Unfinished Tales 69 is what disconnected parts cost even when the material is good.

t: Alcatraz versus dabelsti knihovnici (Alcatraz Versus the Evil Librarians)
why: A comic middle-grade fantasy narrated by its own hero, who interrupts himself, taunts the reader and cheerfully admits he is not to be trusted. Chapter one is one legible situation, not a fan-out: a stranger at the door claiming to be his grandfather, a stolen bag of sand, and a Librarian pointing a gun at him in the kitchen, so the failure that scored 30 three times over does not apply. The voice is the asset and it is well made, which is what holds the number in the 60s rather than lower. What the book does not do is leave an idea behind: the premise is a running gag about libraries hiding the truth, and Kirkus finds the joke tiresome by repetition with the similes stopping the narrative flow. That is precisely what stalled Narnia at 67, marked down for lacking higher things to think about, and Ranger's Apprentice at 74, easy to read but not much to think about. Comic invention can reach much higher - Hitchhiker's 83 - but that book has a real premise under the jokes. A thirteen-year-old lead is a further small pushback of the kind that cost Ender's Game points on re-reading. Leaned on the narrator rather than on the invented magic, which is played for silliness and is never asked to carry weight.

t: Alcatraz versus legie Zakladatelovych kosti (The Scrivener's Bones)
why: The engine is the same self-mocking first-person voice, and it is a real asset: one boy telling his own story, one situation at a time, no fan-out to be confused by. But this is a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log - Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70, the steepest series decline recorded, and even Collins dropped from 89 to 83 when a sequel repeated a set piece for its own sake. The book widens the invented furniture rather than the thinking: a hidden city the family comes from, a library that takes your soul in exchange for a book, a part-metal antagonist. That is fun and it is consistent, but it is not an idea a reader carries away, and this reader's most common reason for a competent book to stall in the 60s is exactly that: Narnia 67 lacked higher things to think about, Ranger's Apprentice 74 was easy to read with little to think about. The metafictional joke also has to work a second time on a reader who has already met it, and the reported cost of that joke is broken momentum. A thirteen-year-old lead is a small further pushback. Leaned on the narrator, deliberately not on the worldbuilding, which is comic by design and never asked to hold up under thought.

One premise stated precisely - a pump that trades matter with a neighbouring universe, giving everyone free energy while making the Sun certain to explode - and the whole book is that premise's consequences, including the political one, that nobody who benefits wants the calculation checked. That is the form the reader named as a positive in Old Man's War 87 and rewarded at 92 in Project Hail Mary. Trimmed 2026-09-03 on this author's first real score. Ja, robot 55 was abandoned on two things this book also carries: a cast nobody could root for, and behaviour that did not read as plausible given the rules the author had declared - and the middle section here is written from inside an invented three-sexed species, which is exactly where a plausibility objection would land if it lands anywhere. Three separate settings with three separate casts is the structure risk on top.

t: Anna na krku a jine povidky (Anna na krku a jine povidky)
why: The positive case is as strong as the form allows: this is a writer whose entire method is page time on what a person wants and why, with the incident cut to almost nothing - a provincial girl marries an old official for money and discovers what it makes of her - and that is exactly the axis that puts Red Rising 95, Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 at the top of this log, delivered in clean prose of the kind that helped Ender's Game 87. Also in its favour: each story opens on one concrete situation, which is the opposite of the failure that ended The Gunslinger 30. What holds it under the line is the shape of this particular object. It is a career-spanning editor's selection of roughly forty-seven pieces across 399 pages, mixing early comic sketches with the mature work, so there is no one to follow and nothing accumulates - the complaint that put Unfinished Tales 69 at the bottom of the Tolkien range. And this author's declared position is to pose the question and refuse the answer, so what a reader carries away is a diagnosis of a life rather than an idea he can restate, which is the usual reason a good book stops in the 60s. I leaned on motives, not on ideas, for that reason. Re-derived 2026-09-03 under the new collection axis: a multi-story book is read from the front and put down on its weakest early pieces, not averaged and not skipped past. Ja, robot 55 is the anchor - the reader stopped after three stories, on the first story's cast and the third story's implausible behaviour, and never reached the pieces the prediction was built on. A selection rather than an authored book, so the order is an editor's and the strongest pieces are not reliably first. What the line leans on - page time on what people want - is real in the best of these and thin in the anecdotal ones, and the reader meets both in whatever order the selection imposes.

Short stories, so the character and emotion rules are suspended - but the profile is explicit that the suspension removes penalties and never adds points, and there is nothing here to add them back. The positive case is the talk: ordinary men on the Prague periphery whose whole substance is what they want and how they narrate it, which is the axis behind Red Rising 95. Against that, the register is death sitting inside the banal - the title story opens on a girl's body found hanged in a suburban snack-bar arcade and then simply carries on with the afternoon - and sustained bleakness is a recorded discount: 1984 60 was too depressing, though Animal Farm 78 shows bleakness costs little when it leaves an idea behind. That is where the doubt sits. An editor's selection reshuffled across printings has no single premise to work out, so I would put ideas under risks, which is why I leaned on the short-form suspension and on motives instead.

The engine of the plot is four siblings concealing their mother's death and improvising a family structure once all adult authority disappears - a real, nameable idea about what a household regresses into without structure - and the incest is the endpoint of that regression rather than the reason the book exists, so filter 6 does not fire. That puts it near the territory of Promena 58, a book with a real idea undercut by a hard-to-root-for lead and bleakness that arrives from the start rather than gradually - Jack here is similarly controlling and unsympathetic, harassing his younger brother throughout. Unlike Promena, this book also carries a real sexual-content cost: moderate volume, explicit depiction at the climax, and a coarse register several reviewers flagged directly, which compounds further below that anchor.

The book is a manoeuvre: run a warship past a blockade, hold an alliance of convenience together, get a stranded colony fed. Those are problems, not ideas, and I would put ideas in the risk column rather than the support column, which is what usually decides whether a book of this kind clears the 65 line here - Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68 are both competent novels whose scores were not carried by anything they left behind. It does not fall further because the shape is safe: one narrator, one concrete objective at a time, no confusing fan-out of the kind that ended three books at 30, no occult, no investigation, and sexual content that is understated rather than crude. Against that, it is a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70 and Unfinished Tales 69 is the lowest Tolkien. The set-piece emphasis is the other drag - set-piece action with no character revelation reads as dead weight for this reader, which is why Golden Son 92 sits under Red Rising 95 despite the same author and cast.

It does start clean: four years of peace, one ship, one reconnaissance objective, and a reader who knows within a page what the situation is and what is wanted from it. A single concrete starting situation is the strongest positive available in this log, since the three books that ended at 30 all failed on exactly its absence. What I cannot do is name an idea beyond 'the enemy was not finished after all', which is a plot turn rather than something to think about, so ideas go in the risk column - and that is the most common reason a perfectly readable book settles in the 60s here, as with Narnia 67 and Ranger's Apprentice 74. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70 and Unfinished Tales 69 is the lowest Tolkien. No filter fires - one first-person narrator throughout, no occult, no investigation, and sexual content handled without crudeness.

Reviewers agree the draw is the politics and not the fighting - one warns outright that a reader after non-stop bloodshed will not find it here - and that the friction between an honourable hot-head and a self-made climber is the vehicle for what a voting city could and could not bear. That is page time on what men want and why, the axis Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 both score on, and it leaves one idea nameable in a phrase: a free city will vote out the man who saved it. Both leads are interesting and worth rooting for, the pairing whose failure cost The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 22 points against Sunrise on the Reaping 87. It opens on one concrete situation, the field at Marathon, so the several-plot-lines-at-once start that put Guards Guards and The Gunslinger on 30 is not the danger here. Capped in the high 70s because historical fiction has not cleared The Count of Monte Cristo 75 in this log, and because three to five rotating viewpoints dilute the tight single narration praised in The Hunger Games 89. One review reports the Delphic oracle prophesying Leonidas' fate appearing in the text; divination enacted on the page is a hard filter, and the Greek pantheon is what held Percy Jackson to 57, so that is a risk that could sink the number rather than trim it. Leaned on motives and ideas rather than on the battle writing, because set-piece action with no character revelation is what docked Catching Fire 83. Re-examined against the occult ruling of 2026-08-26 (failing EITHER test is a veto, and a rite enacted on the page fails even when the system is invented): the record does not settle it, so the number is unchanged but axis:occult is now a priced risk rather than a cleared question - this range is void if the check below fails. Outstanding check: the Delphic oracle prophesying Leonidas' fate - enacted in a scene, or reported?

The structure is a sequence of standalone nighttime-Tokyo character vignettes whose fates barely intersect, using sex and violence as the connective texture for a critique of consumer alienation and loneliness rather than the plot itself being a sexual relationship, so it clears the sex-as-the-plot filter, if narrowly. Held on 2026-08-28 with the comparator corrected. Ruled 2026-08-28: The Witcher 53 is a CONFOUNDED row and cannot be cited as a sexual-axis floor - the reader named two independent causes, 'both magic (witches) and the sex was through out the series', and the magic is the occult filter, the most severe objection in the log. The clean crudeness anchor is Ready Player One 55 - 'it was the kind of sex that reduced it that much', the kind and not the amount - with Artemis 69 confirming crudeness costs even in small doses. VOLUME IS UNANCHORED and must not be priced as cheap: Red Rising 95 and Valka stareho muze 87 are BOTH low volume on the reader's own account ('mostly one chapter of a book'), so neither shows what sustained non-crude content costs, and the log's only high-volume row is the confounded one. Note also that VSM's single chapter was still enough to become his one named complaint, so light volume is not free. The correction changes nothing here: graphic explicitness plus a crude, joyless treatment is the Ready Player One charge at sustained length, so the sinking dimension is present at full strength and volume compounds it. The episodic structure also gives no single protagonist to invest in, unlike the mythic scope that let The Silmarillion score 80 despite lacking one; here nothing offsets it.

Catalogued as povidky and as autobiography, and the printed contents list is a run of destinations - Marianske Lazne and Sumava, the Cote d'Azur, the Loire chateaux, Britain - which makes it a travel-anecdote collection rather than a book with a subject. There is no premise whose consequences could be worked out and no plot to hold together, so the whole weight falls on what the observations leave behind, and the stated message that attitude matters more than age is a sentiment rather than an idea. The memoir and testimony form earns nothing by itself in this log - the same form produced Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus at 91 and The Diary of a Young Girl at 40 - and what earned the 91 was rigorously examining what is actually true plus real insight into how another group experiences the world. A sequence of holidays attempts neither. Description with little story is a named penalty term for this reader, and a chapter per destination is mostly description. For scale: The Chronicles of Narnia stalled at 67 for lacking higher things to think about while still having a plot and an invented world; this has neither, so it sits under that. I leaned on the form rather than on ideas because ideas is the axis I would list as the risk.

There is a real question at the centre and it is a declared price with consequences: crossing the place outside space costs memory, so the heroine spends the self she is trying to defend in order to defend it, and the same journey is how the book finally answers what the enemy actually is. Working a stated cost through to its second-order effects is the thing that put Project Hail Mary at 92, and the first-person voice that carries it is the tight single-POV shape of The Hunger Games 89. The shape of the book is the risk, and it is a well-documented one: reviewers consistently report a slow first half, a quest that reads as a detour from the war framing the story, and the familiar cast replaced almost wholesale by new faces. This log punishes that combination specifically - Lord of the Rings 84 was docked because the story is thin for the number of pages, Catching Fire 83 because the second set piece existed for its own sake rather than to reveal anyone, and Unfinished Tales 69 because the pieces did not connect to each other. A sequel is also not a safe bet here: Hitchhiker's 83 to 70. Leaned on the memory premise and the narrator rather than on the worldbuilding, which is inventive but is mostly new scenery rather than a consequence of anything declared earlier. Discovery (axis:discovery, 2026-10-24): the memory price and the answer to what the enemy is, argued above, are the shape the reader named in Project Hail Mary 92, his own memories and an unknown place at once; central with a lead who is not in doubt, so +4.

Nine short pieces about children and adolescents keeping hold of their dignity in the transports and the camps, written out of the author's own years in Terezin, Auschwitz and a Buchenwald satellite. What is genuinely there is moral seriousness: the stories are built on borderline situations and refuse the consolation that the right choice always wins, and examining what is actually true is what earned the Qureshi memoir 91 rather than the form it was written in. Three things cap it below the line. Short fiction has the character and emotion rules suspended, but the suspension only removes penalties and never adds points - and separate stories with no single premise leave no worked-out idea to lean on, only glimpses, which is the most common reason a competent book stalls in the 60s here. The protagonists are children observed from inside, and that pairing produced the log's lowest entry of all, a first-person child testimony abandoned at 40, and dropped Narnia to 67 partly for the same reason. And it is unrelieved: sustained bleakness is the mildest recorded objection but a real one, 1984 at 60 for being too depressing, with none of the companionship that lifts a grim book. Leaned on the dignity-and-motive thread rather than on the historical weight of the subject, because weight of subject has never by itself scored well for this reader.

t: Den, kdy padla noc (A Day of Fallen Night)
why: The declared question is a good one and the book is genuinely built on it: an order of warrior sisters has trained for five hundred years against an enemy that never came, the younger ones have started saying out loud that their whole institution is pointless - and then the enemy wakes. Set beside a princess whose only recognised function is to bear an heir she did not choose, it leaves behind the thought that institutions and dynasties outlive their reasons and go on collecting the same sacrifices anyway. That is a premise with consequences rather than a backdrop. The stronger asset is the lead: a woman of about fifty, the kind of character normally parked in a mentor's chair to hand a sword to somebody younger, carried here as the actual heroine, and reviewers consistently name her the standout of the book. Interesting and worth rooting for is what separated Sunrise on the Reaping 87 from The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 by twenty-two points, and it lands on the right side here, which is why the number leans on her rather than on the setting. The deductions are structural. It is 868 pages and there is broad agreement that the central plot only properly starts after a long stretch of buildup - thin story for the page count is the penalty that held The Lord of the Rings to 84 and Les Miserables to 71, and it bites harder in a book that is slower still. One of the four viewpoints is reported as the weak one, spread across four separate continents. Two life-phase pushbacks, a woman of fifty and a girl of fifteen, are worth a couple of points between them and nothing more, since The Little Prince 82 shows the rule bends when the ideas carry. Magic is invented, drawn from a tree and from the stars, and the gods prayed to are the book's own inventions, so the occult filter does not engage. Not leaned on worldbuilding: the world is inherited rather than newly worked out, and Artemis 69 is what leaning that way costs. Re-examined against the occult ruling of 2026-08-26 (failing EITHER test is a veto, and a rite enacted on the page fails even when the system is invented): the record does not settle it, so the number is unchanged but axis:occult is now a priced risk rather than a cleared question - since the 2026-10-24 re-ruling a prayer or offering to these invented gods shown in a scene costs a graded deduction rather than voiding this range. Outstanding check: prayer to the book's invented gods - is a prayer or offering shown in a scene?

One premise declared precisely and then followed: take a species whose cognition is nothing like ours, uplift it, and work out what it actually builds. The answer here is a civilisation of octopuses whose thought is distributed through their arms and which therefore settles disagreements by broadcasting emotional state rather than by argument, set against an alien on a neighbouring world that cannot be negotiated with at all because it has no concept of a separate self. Second-order consequences genuinely explored is exactly what put Project Hail Mary 92 eight points above The Martian 82 by the reader's own account, and coming to understand an alien culture from the inside is what put Speaker for the Dead 90 above Ender's Game 87; this book is built on both at once, which is why the range sits in the A band. Structure is legible rather than confusing. Two strands - a terraforming crew in the past, a joint expedition in the present - kept apart by tense as well as by heading, each opening on one concrete situation, and reviewers describe the interleaving as tension-driven rather than withholding. That is not the several-plot-lines-at-once failure that ended Guards! Guards! and The Colour of Magic at 30, though three protagonist groups is more than the tight single narration praised in The Hunger Games 89. The ceiling is set by the lead. Attention is split across humans, spiders and octopuses with no one person to root for, and while The Silmarillion 80 proves that can survive, Artemis 69 is the recorded failure of predicting a book up on its world while the lead was visibly thin - so the high is deliberately capped rather than pushed into the high eighties. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy 83 fell to 70 for the ones that followed, the steepest decline recorded. Bleakness arrives as dread rather than sustained misery, closer to Animal Farm 78 than 1984 60, and a stretch of roughly sixty pages without dialogue is the density risk. No occult and no investigation. Discovery (axis:discovery, 2026-10-24): an expedition following a signal to worlds nobody understands, whose survival depends on working out what lives there, the shape the reader named in Project Hail Mary 92; central, one step lower because the lead is the open doubt, so +2.

Naming the idea is the problem: rebuilding a fleet and training replacements is a situation, not something the book leaves behind, and I would list ideas as a risk here rather than as what carries the number. That is the usual reason a readable book settles in the 60s for this reader, as with Narnia 67. Worse, the specific complaint reviewers make is the one this reader has actually walked out on a book for: a chase whose stated scarcities - fuel, food, exhaustion - are announced but never felt. Mortal Engines 55 was abandoned in its first chapters purely because a declared resource did not behave like a scarce one, so a book that names its constraints and then ignores them is exposed at exactly the point where this log is least forgiving. It stays in the 60s rather than lower because the narration is a single legible first-person line with no confusing opening, no occult, no investigation and no crude sexual treatment - the same clean profile that keeps Exodus 68 comfortably above the C band.

Two brothers meet over the mountain house their father left behind when he killed himself. One never left the valley and wants to raise a child in that house; the other has been felling timber in Canada for years and wants his share in cash; and a concealed ski-lift project makes the land suddenly worth a fortune. That is a declared premise whose consequences actually play out, and the book spends itself on what each brother wants rather than on what happens, the axis that lifts Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90. Two things hold it down. It is 123 pages for a subject - inherited land, drink, fraternal violence - that Italian reviewers split hard over, one calling it short and forgettable and too slight for what it takes on. And it is unrelieved: a poacher father dead by his own hand, two sons who cannot stop once they start drinking, and someone shooting dogs along the river. Sustained bleakness is this reader's mildest recorded objection, but it is still the one that took 1984 to 60. I leaned on motives rather than on ideas because the fraternal motive is the thing the book demonstrably does, while whether the theme lands in that space is precisely what the reviews disagree about.

It opens on one concrete situation - a girl and her father waiting in a petrol station car park in early 1957 for the dragon they have hired - which is exactly the legible start this reader asks for and the opposite of the several-lines-at-once opening that ended Guards! Guards! 30 and The Colour of Magic 30 in their first pages. It also has something to think about, and the fantasy is doing the thinking: a Japanese American family still not accepted after internment, a racist deputy, and an argument over whether dragons have souls all run on the same rails, so the premise earns its keep rather than decorating. Three deductions hold it here. The narration is spread over four perspectives, one of them a goddess, and reviewers report the point of view switching at unexpected places inside chapters - not the confusion filter, since the first chapters are grounded, but a legibility cost that runs the whole length. The prophecy is the engine rather than a background detail, which by itself no longer costs - Licanius 92-96 carries more prophecy than anything read, and the reader praised how it was handled - so what remains on that axis is handling: a worshipping cult acting on divine instruction, its tone unverified. One point back from the 2026-10-24 rewording, not more, because that question is still open. Heaviest: the book declares its alternate 1957 in detail - a treaty, dragons as ordinary as cats, a Cold War - and then pivots to a parallel world where dragons never existed. This reader verifies declared worlds, and Divergent 58 sits in the C band precisely for a premise assembled from borrowed pieces that does not cohere. Leaned on ideas and motives rather than worldbuilding, because worldbuilding is the axis most likely to take this below the range, not above it. Re-examined against the occult ruling of 2026-08-26 (failing EITHER test is a veto, and a rite enacted on the page fails even when the system is invented): the record does not settle it, so the number is unchanged but axis:occult is now a priced risk rather than a cleared question - this range is void only if the goddess is a real-world deity; a petition to an invented one staged in a scene now costs a graded deduction instead. Outstanding check: one of four POVs is a goddess - is she petitioned in a scene? REVISED 2026-09-02 for the new axis:same-sex-romance (prominence light-middle), was [64, 74]. Carried by the assassin, one of four viewpoint characters, as a storyline rather than the book's subject. Light-to-middle end of the graded range. Magnitude is not separable from the single data point: Caropisci 67 lost about thirteen points to this, the hierofant rite and the portrayal warning together, so this dock states a direction and a prominence tier, not a measured size.

The engine is whether history can be steered at all once there are people who can read and quietly rewrite minds, and both halves lay the reveal in fairly before it lands - Golden Son 92 is scored up for exactly that quality, a reveal logical and consistent with what came before rather than sprung. Each half also opens on one legible situation. Dropped 2026-09-03 on this author's first real score: Ja, robot 55 ended three stories in on a cast nobody could root for, and this book is two long sections sixty years apart that share no cast at all - the same objection at novel length, with Unfinished Tales 69 already recording what unconnected parts cost.

Literary fiction and a short-story collection at the same time, which is where this reader's returns are measurably thinnest: fifteen small episodes from the everyday lives of a city's inhabitants, most of them deliberately withheld from resolution. Short work has the character and emotion rules suspended, but the suspension only removes penalties and adds nothing. There is one idea and it can be named - lives that cannot move, stagnation taken for ordinary life - but it is atmospheric rather than a premise declared and then worked out, and the declared-and-worked-out kind is what earns the high scores here, so it belongs in risks rather than carrying the number. The closest read comparison is Unfinished Tales 69, marked down explicitly because the pieces are not logically connected to each other; fifteen unrelated casts with no continuous plot is more fragmented still. Sustained gloom costs a little on top - 1984 60 was too depressing. On the credit side the prose is legible, each story opens on one concrete situation, and nothing trips a hard filter. Leaned on the collection form and the mood rather than on the ideas, and did no further research.

Blocked on the occult filter, by what the book stages rather than by its lore. Twice a human sacrifice is on the page: the princess follows the king into the sewers and finds him naked and bloodied at an altar, knife raised, a servant girl cut open and tied to it as an offering to spirits; and at the climax the villains' monastic order travels by burning one of its own monks as fuel. Čaropisci 67 lost heavily to a sacrifice kept as lore; staged, the rule vetoes, and a villain holding the knife does not change that. The heroes' magic is clean: drawn characters with declared rules, a fall traced to the land's shape and mended by one added line, a curse that falls at random with no rite. The screening's opening risk dissolves on reading: one man in one concrete situation, each new viewpoint a chapter later with its conflict in its first line. Without the rites it would sit in the high 70s or low 80s, on motives as Speaker for the Dead 90 and a priest's serious doubt of the kind Světlo věcí konečných 96 was praised for, less a slow first half (Počítání hvězd 85 shows what low drive costs) and two leads their own author calls static. Standalone. If the reader rules a villain's single staged rite gradable, re-price this rather than drop it.

I cannot name an idea this book puts on the table. The war, the enemy and the narrator are all already standing, and what is added is a campaign, a famine on an ice moon and a standoff between human fleets - events rather than something left behind. That is the most common way a competent book stalls in the 60s for this reader: Narnia 67 was marked down for lacking higher things to think about and Ranger's Apprentice 74 for being easy with little to think about. It should stay out of the 50s, because one first-person narrator on one assignment at a time keeps the opening legible - the axis that ended three books at 30 - and there is no occult, no investigation and no crude sexual treatment to dock. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70, and Catching Fire 83 was docked specifically for an arena that existed for its own sake, which is the risk when a war continues for its own sake. Leaned on the legible opening and the momentum; the ideas are the risk, not the support.

A gothic standalone that is mostly atmosphere. A girl with no voice inherits a house with a wall she is forbidden to cross, and roughly the first two thirds are her walking the corridors and reading her mother's journal while very little happens; reviewers put that stretch at a handful of story days. That is precisely the log's penalty term - a thin story spread over pages, plus description and digression - and it is what cost The Lord of the Rings 84 the tier its ideas would otherwise have reached, and what left Les Miserables 71 below The Count of Monte Cristo 75. Here there is less to offset it. The communication thread is real and is the best thing in the book, a mute protagonist whose signing and drawing are how she is known at all; but the central proposition amounts to choosing the living over the dead, which is nearer a mood than something left behind, and Quo Vadis 66 and The Chronicles of Narnia 67 are where well-made books without higher ground settle in this log. Reviewers also report the resolution arriving in a rush after that long build and the cousin relationship never developing, either of which would pull it under the range. No hard filter fires: the opening is one legible situation, a girls' school and then one house, and the death figure, the ghouls and the bone shards are the author's invention rather than anything drawn from real occultism. Leaned on story density and the shortage of ideas rather than on the prose, because beautiful writing is not an idea and this log has never paid for it.

t: Gentleman v Moskve (A Gentleman in Moscow)
why: One premise declared with complete precision - a man is sentenced in 1922 to spend the rest of his life inside a single hotel, and will be shot if he steps outside - and the whole book is its consequences. That is the shape Project Hail Mary 92 is praised for: a declared condition whose second-order effects actually get explored. It opens on one concrete legible situation, a tribunal transcript and then an attic room, so the confusion that put The Gunslinger and The Colour of Magic on 30 is absent. One protagonist, a third person extending only from him, and nearly all the page time on what he wants and why rather than on what he does - the axis Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 both top. It leaves an idea that can be stated in a phrase: how a person keeps purpose and dignity when his circumstances are fixed for good. The deductions are real but bounded. It is historical fiction, and historical fiction in this log settles between Quo Vadis 66 and The Count of Monte Cristo 75, chiefly where sprawl and digression cost - and the middle of this book leaps across three decades in widening episodes, which is thin story over many pages, the objection that cancelled the extra ideas in The Lord of the Rings 84. The Soviet backdrop adds mild bleakness, though the treatment is warm rather than grim. No occult, no crudeness, no investigation. Held under the high 80s on density rather than on protagonist, because the lead is the part of this book least in doubt.

The setup is worth something: two friends put on opposite sides of a siege with a captured sister between them, so allegiance and loyalty are in genuine conflict, and friendship is the thing that carried The Hobbit to 84 and The Lord of the Rings to 84 in this log. Against that, the mode is battle-forward military adventure whose outcome history has already fixed, and reviewers of this author's Punic-war writing praise the descriptive combat while granting the plot holds no real surprises. Page time goes to how a siege is fought rather than to what the men want, which is the axis Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 win on, and easy well-researched adventure with little to think about is what left Ranger's Apprentice at 74. I lean on the two leads and their competing loyalties, because that is the only thing here that can push the number toward the top of the range; I do not lean on an idea left behind, because I doubt there is one past the cost of war, and that doubt is what caps it. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70.

An orphaned, lame girl kept alive only because her hands are useful, in a village that discards the weak, set to embroider the robe on which the village's own history and future are stitched. The idea is nameable in a phrase - whoever holds the picture of the past owns what a people believe about itself - and that is the axis that carries short work in this log, since Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 both scored on ideas rather than on plot. The lead is worth rooting for and interesting with it, the pairing that separated Sunrise on the Reaping 87 from The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 by 22 points. It opens on one concrete situation, a girl about to be judged for existing, which is the opposite of the several-plot-lines-at-once start that put The Colour of Magic on 30. Nothing occult: the gift is invented, and an invented system is explicitly fine however elaborate. Held under the high 70s because the prose is spare and functional rather than a pleasure in itself, the lead is a teenager and that is a standing small pushback, and the society is the part most likely to break under thought - a village that culls the weak yet feeds and lies to three gifted orphans has to cohere, and an engineered society that does not is exactly what put Divergent at 58. Leaned on the idea and the protagonist rather than on the worldbuilding, because the world is the part I would not bet on.

The idea can be named in a phrase and it is actually worked out rather than gestured at: feed the world by herding whales like cattle, then let a religious leader argue that killing creatures of that order is murder, and make the man who runs the farms answer him - which he does, by changing his mind and losing the argument he was paid to win. A book that leaves an idea behind is what lifts a modest story in this log; that is how a short allegory reached Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 with no other advantage. Two further things fit this reader: the ending turns on going down for other people rather than on solo survival, which is the difference he named between Project Hail Mary 92 and The Martian 82, and the belief question is a thread inside the story rather than the subject of it. Deductions are real. Reviewers call the lead thin with only the religious leader standing out, and a flat protagonist is the whole 16-point gap from Project Hail Mary 92 to Artemis 69. The book is episodic in three parts with a mentor's death dividing it, so momentum breaks in the middle - the same objection that put Catching Fire 83 below The Hunger Games 89. The opening is a single clear thread, a man waking from a nightmare about space, so the failure that ended three books at 30 does not apply. Leaned on the idea and put the protagonist in the risks deliberately, since that is the axis that has misfired before.

The case for this one is payoff: long-built arcs close and characters who parted far back cross paths again, which is the kind of earned reveal that put Golden Son at 92 - consistent with what came before rather than sprung. The lead ends as someone worth rooting for rather than a figure in slow moral decline, and that single axis is worth 22 points here, the gap between Sunrise on the Reaping 87 and The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65. The deductions are large and specific. Reviewers describe near-continuous duels, showdowns and battles across 717 pages, and action with no character revelation is dead weight for this reader: Mockingjay took the top of its trilogy at 91 for showing the most motive and the least arena, and this is that trade run backwards. A book that is mostly battle is also a thin story over many pages, which is the named penalty term, not length. A sequel besides, and sequels are not safe bets in this log - Hitchhiker's fell 83 to 70. I leaned on the lead rather than on momentum, because relentless fighting produces pace whether or not anything is at stake in it. Re-examined against the occult ruling of 2026-08-26 (failing EITHER test is a veto, and a rite enacted on the page fails even when the system is invented): the record does not settle it, so the number is unchanged but axis:occult is now a priced risk rather than a cleared question - this range is void if the check below finds a Source failure; a rite of the invented pantheon shown in a scene now costs a graded deduction instead. Outstanding check: Hebrew-derived pantheon - Source question, plus is any rite shown in a scene?

t: Inzerat na dum, ve kterem uz nechci bydlet (Inzerat na dum, ve kterem uz nechci bydlet)
why: Seven stories about people the 1950s pushed to the bottom - tradesmen, lawyers and philosophers shovelling ingots at the Kladno steelworks - and the strongest thing in its favour is the kind of understanding it offers: what it is like to be inside a group the state has written off. That is the axis that earned Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75, and here it comes with the wants and the talk foregrounded over the events, the axis behind Mockingjay 91. Two deductions. The tone is unrelieved - forced labour, discarded lives, and the author deliberately declines to turn it into criticism, so the misery is on the page without a conclusion drawn from it, and 1984 60 is the log's warning about exactly that. And two of the seven are described as barely narrative at all, closer to lyric bands than stories, so a reader wanting one legible starting situation gets prose poetry instead. I leaned on motives rather than on the testimony axis because this is fiction and the profile is clear that the memoir form earns nothing by itself.

t: Jak byt zenou (How to Be a Woman)
why: This is a broad-topic feminist memoir, not a book built around a sexual relationship or behaviour, so filter 6 does not apply. On the memoir-form axis, what earns points for this reader is examining what is actually true and giving insight into how another group experiences the world - the standard Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75 set, against the counter-example of Anne Frank 40, the same form that failed to work. This book gives real insight into a woman's experience of body and work, but reads more as personal opinion and manifesto than the rigorous examination of truth that carried Qureshi, capping it well under the S band. Moderate volume and explicit content on the sexual-content axis (masturbation and body chapters) cost further, though the crude-humor register itself is not the objection per this reader's own rule, and reviewers largely call the treatment frank rather than crude.

t: Jak stvorit divku (How to Build a Girl)
why: The plot is Johanna's self-reinvention as Dolly Wilde across several threads at once - family poverty, a music-criticism career, class identity, and sexual exploration - so sex is one thread among several rather than the reason the book exists, and filter 6 does not fire. The protagonist is repeatedly described as witty, self-aware and sympathetic, and this reader's rule ranks a rootable lead above worldbuilding or plot mechanics whenever they compete - the clearest case in the log is Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65, docked 22 points from Sunrise on the Reaping 87 purely on an unrootable lead, so a genuinely likeable teenage lead here is a real positive. Moderate volume and explicit content cost on the sexual-content axis, but the treatment is repeatedly described as comedic and self-aware rather than crude, which keeps the deduction from compounding as hard as it otherwise would.

t: Jasno lepo podstin zhyna (Spill Simmer Falter Wither)
why: A fifty-seven-year-old recluse adopts a one-eyed dog bred for badger baiting and talks to it through four seasons. The interiority is real and it is the whole book, which is the axis the log rewards most - Red Rising 95 tops it for spending more time on thoughts and motives than on action - and that is why this is the low 60s rather than the 50s. The problem is what the book leaves behind. Named honestly, the idea is loneliness rendered beautifully: a mood, not a thought, and reviewers agree the first half is close to plotless before an aimless road trip that slows again. A thin story spread over many pages is the standing penalty, the sparseness that held The Lord of the Rings 84 to a tie despite far greater ideas, and sustained bleakness is a mild further discount, as 1984 60 records. Because the idea is the part I would not bet on, no further research was done.

t: Jiskra v popelu (An Ember in the Ashes)
why: The opening is a genuine strength and worth saying first: one concrete legible situation from page one - a night raid on a house, grandparents killed, a brother dragged away - and two first-person narrators who each want one nameable thing. Tight narration and constant momentum is what makes The Hunger Games 89 the baseline favourite here, and both leads are interesting and rootable, which is the axis that separated Sunrise on the Reaping 87 from Ballad 65 by 22 points. What decides the number is the supernatural furniture. The author says in two interviews that the jinn, efrits and ghuls come from the Middle Eastern folklore her mother told her, and that the order of seers is modelled on the Pythia at Delphi; that is borrowed real-world material rather than an invented system, and it is the most expensive thing in this log - Percy Jackson 57, marked down because the Greek pantheon counts and not just witchcraft, and Harry Potter 51 for magic drawn from historical witchcraft. On top of that the themes stop at resistance and complicity with nothing worked out past them, and events with nothing to think about is what put Narnia at 67. Leaned on the occult axis rather than on the protagonist axis, because the protagonists are the part that would argue this number upward. Re-examined against the occult ruling of 2026-08-26 (failing EITHER test is a veto, and a rite enacted on the page fails even when the system is invented): the record does not settle it, so the number is unchanged but axis:occult is now a priced risk rather than a cleared question - this range is void if the check below fails. Outstanding check: jinn and efrits from Middle Eastern folklore, Augurs modelled on the Pythia at Delphi - is the borrowed material enough to fail Source?

A curated selection of Bradbury's 1950-1964 stories, and what carries the number is the ideas: each piece declares one situation - a man who becomes afraid of his own skeleton, a house that goes on serving breakfast after its family is gone - and spends its length on the consequence rather than on plot. That is the axis Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 score on, and it is why this sits in the 70s rather than the 60s. Two deductions hold it there. Seventy separate stories cannot pay the reader's heaviest axis at all: there is nobody to want anything for longer than twenty pages, and the log has already priced a book of disconnected pieces at Unfinished Tales 69, whose stated fault was that the parts are not logically connected to each other. Bradbury is also atmospheric by method, and description carrying little story is a standing penalty. Leaning on ideas rather than on the protagonist axis is deliberate, because the protagonist axis has nothing to grip here, and The Silmarillion 80 is the log's proof that a book with no continuous lead and dense prose can still land well when the ideas are large. Re-examined against the occult ruling of 2026-08-26 (failing EITHER test is a veto, and a rite enacted on the page fails even when the system is invented): the record does not settle it, so the number is unchanged but axis:occult is now a priced risk rather than a cleared question - this range is void if the check below fails. Outstanding check: seventy stories, not verified one by one; does any piece enact a real-world rite? Re-derived 2026-09-03 under the new collection axis: a multi-story book is read from the front and put down on its weakest early pieces, not averaged and not skipped past. Ja, robot 55 is the anchor - the reader stopped after three stories, on the first story's cast and the third story's implausible behaviour, and never reached the pieces the prediction was built on. Seventy stories in one volume is the largest count on the shelf and the most exposed case there is. The line already said that seventy separate pieces cannot pay the heaviest axis at all, with Unfinished Tales 69 the price of parts that do not connect; with the front of the book now deciding the outcome, a curated seventy is a lottery rather than a breadth argument.

t: Klara a Slunce (Klara and the Sun)
why: Opens in a shop window with one narrator who never leaves the frame, and the case rests on her: a machine whose entire motive is another person's good, who spends herself for a sick child with nothing to gain. That is precisely what this log rewarded in Project Hail Mary 92 - companionship instead of isolation, and self-sacrifice to save others rather than personal survival - and the narration is nothing but motive and inference, the axis behind Red Rising 95 and Speaker for the Dead 90. There is a real idea to carry away: whether a person is an irreplaceable centre or a learnable set of behaviours, put to the one narrator who has to answer it in practice. Two things hold the range down. The world is asserted rather than worked out - gene-edited children and displaced workers are foregrounded as the subject and the society is never reorganised around them, the same breach that cost Harry Potter 51 its worldbuilding. And the narrator builds a private devotion to the sun, addresses pleas to it and destroys a machine as an offering, on the page; it is her own invention with no root in real occult practice, so the hard filter does not fire, but Percy Jackson 57 shows that a devotional frame aimed at a real object of worship costs points here. The plot is also quiet and thin for its length, the charge that held The Lord of the Rings to 84. Leaned on protagonist and ideas and deliberately not on the world, since the one recorded prediction failure in this log came from leaning up on worldbuilding.

Stopping early because the idea is the thing I would list as the risk, and that is the sharpest separator available. What the book is: a dying-Earth novel told as a written testament by a prisoner in a swamp penal colony below the last human city, working backwards through how he got there, episodic and non-linear. The Clarke Award shortlist assessment is that it is a series of events rather than an overarching concept, and that it reproduces the furniture of the subgenre without extending it. Measured against real scores that reading is unforgiving. A competent book with nothing to leave behind stalls in the sixties - The Chronicles of Narnia 67 was marked down in almost those words, for lacking higher things to think about - and an episodic story stretched over great length is the named penalty that held The Lord of the Rings to 84 and Les Miserables to 71. Sustained bleakness adds a smaller deduction on top: a swelling sun, a prison, and an ending reviewers describe as fizzling out, with solo endurance rather than companionship, and 1984 60 is what unrelieved gloom costs here. The memoir frame earns nothing by itself either - the same first-person testament form produced Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and a DNF at 40, so the form is neutral and only the examination inside it pays. What could lift it is invention and prose, and the range is set where it is because prose alone has never moved a number in this log. The number leans on length against a thin plot and on the bleakness, not on the idea, which is precisely the thing in doubt.

The reason this cannot be estimated high is its construction, not its author. The book is a montage that interleaves excerpts from two earlier prose texts, alternating chapter by chapter - the author himself described zipping them into each other by the pattern of an acacia leaf - so from the first pages a reader is tracking two unrelated strands, one a philosophising monologue that drifts and one a story about an artist. That is the log's single most reliable negative: Guards! Guards! 30, The Colour of Magic 30 and The Gunslinger 30 were all abandoned in their first chapters for several things starting at once with none of them legible, and this is that shape by design. The second deduction is that it was cleared for publication under normalisation and the philosophical, erotic and grotesque passages were cut, which removes the part that would have left an idea behind and leaves the mood. I leaned on motives - the artist strand does have a man with clear wants, and that is the axis behind Speaker for the Dead 90 - rather than on ideas, which the censorship is precisely what damaged.

t: Kocka a cert (The Cat and the Devil)
why: Graded, not excluded: the children's filter was retired on 2026-08-26 and this is now a question of how far toward a children's book it sits, which here is as far as it goes. Joyce wrote it on 10 August 1936 as a letter in deliberately simple language to his four-year-old grandson, retelling the folk legend of the bridge at Beaugency, and it has only ever been printed as an illustrated picture book; the Czech edition follows that form with a named illustrator. The positive case is real but small - a devil outwitted by a literal reading of his own bargain is an idea nameable in a phrase, and the short-form rule suspends the character and emotion tests. But that suspension removes penalties and never adds points, and The Little Prince 82 is the measure of what a children's book has to carry to score: an idea a grown reader keeps turning over. A ten-minute nursery anecdote carries nothing of that weight, which puts it below Anne Frank 40, the lowest completed score in the log, on reading experience rather than on subject. Leaned on axis:childrens rather than axis:ideas because the idea is present and simply too slight to lift the number, and the register is what decides it.

Read after volume one, which it continues directly. The opening is one concrete scene with the context volume one supplied: the apostate actor watching Geder on the steps of the goddess's new temple, a high priest preparing the low rites, a call to prayer. That is the occult content, and it is light, -2 on both ends: the devotions do nothing, because the priests' power is spiders living in their blood, passed by infection, not granted by a rite. The lean is motives. Dawson's coup against Geder sets two men with legible wants against each other, and reviewers give them equal sympathy - the page time on what people want that Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 top the log on. Five main viewpoints rotate one per chapter, the staggered shape Golden Son 92 handled, each thinking differently. The idea is real: priests who hear certainty and take it for truth, and the world keeps to that declared rule instead of bending it. It asks a new question, what the priests do to a nation, so it is the Mockingjay 91 kind of sequel, not the Catching Fire 83 kind. Main risk: Geder, whose chapters are a man sliding into tyranny, the failure that sank The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65, held to under a fifth of the chapters by leads worth rooting for. Second: density, with the start reported slow before it picks up. No strand is an investigation.

BLOCKED on the occult filter 2026-08-26, when the reader ruled that failing EITHER test is a veto. Same cosmology: human sacrifice to Abaddon, a demon taken from Revelation, fails the Source test outright. Failing either test is now a veto.

Close third person anchored on one young man learning his trade under an older commander whose respect he wants: that is page time on what a character wants and why, the axis Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 both score on, and it is far nearer the tight single narration praised in The Hunger Games 89 than a rotating cast. The idea is stated by reviewers rather than invented by me - a generation that inherited a famous victory has to work out who it is now, personally and as a people - and the middle of the book deliberately is not battle: a marriage, an assembly, a man paying for a tragedy at a city festival. The lead is both interesting and worth rooting for, the pairing that separated Sunrise on the Reaping 87 from The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 by 22 points on the protagonist alone, and his status is earned on the page rather than granted, so unearned competence does not bite. Held down by two complaints reviewers actually make: the cultural and military exposition is called explanatory even by the standards of the genre, and the middle is called slow - a thin stretch spread over many pages is what cancelled The Lord of the Rings 84 against The Hobbit 84 despite the larger ideas. A sequel too, and sequels are not safe bets here: Hitchhiker's fell 83 to 70. Leaned on the lead and his motives rather than on the campaigns, because predicting a book up on spectacle while the interior is thin is the error that put Artemis at 80 against a real 76.
