Outstanding check: the Delphic oracle and Greek sacrifice - is divination or sacrifice enacted in a scene?

Chapter one is one concrete situation - an eighteen-year-old driven home from a work farm to a foreclosed farm, a plan to take his small brother west, and then two stowaways in the trunk who send him east instead - so the confusing-opening failure that put The Gunslinger and The Colour of Magic on 30 does not fire. The substance is motive: each perspective exists to say what that person wants and why, which is the page time this reader values above action, and the ten-day frame keeps events moving. The deductions are structural and specific. The book runs on eight perspectives, two in first person and six in third, with sections as short as three pages across nearly six hundred pages, and reviewers report the shifts reading as obtrusive and the whole as disjointed - that is the multi-POV cost plus a thin story spread wide, the objection that held The Lord of the Rings 84 down and that separates Les Miserables 71 from the tighter Monte Cristo 75. Worse for this reader, the one character kept at third-person distance is the central one, and reviewers say he is the hardest of the cast to feel connected to; a lead who is not interesting is the entire 16-point gap between Artemis 69 and Project Hail Mary 92. Leaned on multi-POV and protagonist rather than on ideas, because the journey-as-heroic-quest thread does leave something behind and is not what limits the number.

t: Mapa a uzemi (La carte et le territoire)
why: An artist photographs Michelin road maps and finds the map more alive than the land it stands for, and around that runs a quiet thread about work, fame and an aging father. There is a real idea in it - what a representation is worth against the thing represented, and what a life of work amounts to - and this reader rewards a book that leaves something behind, which is what puts Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 where they are. The cap is the lead. Reviewers describe Jed Martin as an emotional vacuum with almost no inner life outside his studio and his supermarket runs, and Artemis was docked to 76 purely because the protagonist was not interesting while the world logic was fine. Then the final third drops the artist novel for a police investigation with a new cast, which is the shape this reader avoids on principle, and several reviewers say the book never recovers from it. I leaned on protagonist rather than on ideas because ideas are the axis that shows up on both sides of this reader's line while a flat or unlovable lead has never been forgiven: 22 points separated Sunrise on the Reaping 87 from The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 on rootability alone. The melancholy is priced in mildly, and the sexual material is clinical rather than juvenile, which the log says costs little.

Written and published for readers of eight to twelve, and it reads that way: a single twelve-year-old narrator, a haunting-of-the-week shape, and an idea I cannot state in a sentence beyond 'the dead linger and someone has to send them on'. The log is explicit that a competent book with nothing higher to think about stalls in the 60s, and The Chronicles of Narnia 67 is docked for exactly that combination - a child lead plus no higher ground - which is the closest thing in this reader's record to what is on offer here. Reviewers describe the narrator herself as flat, with the ghost sidekick carrying the personality, and that matters more than the world does: the rules of the spirit realm are reported as carefully built and consistently kept, but the recorded Artemis 69 miss came from predicting a book up on a solid world while the lead was thin, and the profile puts protagonist above worldbuilding when the two compete. There is also an occult deduction to price in. The mechanism is invented - a curtain between living and dead, a mirror pendant, a spoken phrase that releases a spirit - and no witchcraft, seance or divination is performed on the page, so no hard filter fires on the evidence I found. But the frame is real-world paranormal investigation at real haunted sites, and Percy Jackson 57 records how far this reader marks a book down when the supernatural is taken from what people actually believe rather than invented whole. Leaned on the thin idea and the flat lead rather than on the world; the range is kept wide low because that occult deduction could take it under.

Family, loyalty and honour are the declared subject here rather than decoration, and that is the axis The Lord of the Rings 84 scored on for this reader - with Tolkien's own drag removed, because 661 pages here carry a thick plot rather than the thin story that cancelled out those ideas. Roughly half the book sits with a blacksmith's son whose wants are legible and who is easy to root for: interesting and rootable at once, which is what put Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 at the top of the log. Deductions: the ideas are conventional good against evil, and thin ideas are what held The Chronicles of Narnia to 67 and Ranger's Apprentice to 74; the escalation into set-piece battle is the same drag that cost Golden Son 92 its three points against Red Rising 95. Sexual treatment costs nothing - what is reported is implicit rather than crude, and Red Rising 95 shows presence is not the objection. I leaned on motives and the lead rather than on the invented angelology, because predicting up on worldbuilding over a thin lead is the recorded mistake that put Artemis at 80 when it scored 76. The number is conditional on one thing: seven points of view spread over a continent are running by the early chapters, and a confusing opening is the only cause in this log that has ever produced a 30. Re-examined against the occult ruling of 2026-08-26 (failing EITHER test is a veto, and a rite enacted on the page fails even when the system is invented): the record does not settle it, so the number is unchanged but axis:occult is now a priced risk rather than a cleared question - this range is void if the check below finds a Source failure; a rite of the invented pantheon shown in a scene now costs a graded deduction instead. Outstanding check: Hebrew-derived names (Elyon, Asroth, Ben-Elim, Kadoshim) on an invented pantheon - does that make the Source real-world, and is any rite shown?

A collection of newspaper columns and interviews, so there is no premise to work out and nothing whose consequences can be followed; the axis that most often decides a number here is missing by construction. The form earns nothing by itself in this log - first-person non-fiction produced both a 91 and a walked-away 40 - and what earned the 91 was sustained examination of what is actually true, which weekly pieces on caffeine, celebrities, Twitter and a royal wedding do not attempt. Short pieces have the character and emotion rules suspended, but that suspension only removes penalties and never adds points, so what is left is a witty book with nothing to leave behind: the stall that put The Chronicles of Narnia at 67 for lacking higher things to think about, plus the fragmentation charge that took Unfinished Tales to 69 for pieces not logically connected to each other. Recorded rather than rejected, because nothing here trips a hard filter.

A ghost story written and published for readers of eight to twelve, and its idea is about as nameable as the form allows here: a girl who nearly drowned is hunted by an emissary of death, and the real question is what she owes the dead friend who only exists because she did not die. That is want-and-why material, and companionship plus self-sacrifice over solo survival is the axis that puts Project Hail Mary 92 above The Martian 82. But it is carried by a twelve-year-old narrator in a book built to the same city-plus-a-haunting template as the ones before it, and The Chronicles of Narnia 67 records what a child lead and limited higher ground cost together. The occult is the reason the range does not go higher and could go lower. The core mechanism is invented and no ritual drawn from real occultism appears in the chapter recaps I could reach, so no hard filter fires on the evidence I have; but the book states outright that voodoo is real, and where the plot goes for help is a secret society of practitioners with a medium, warded premises, protective amulets and an evil-eye pouch. Percy Jackson 57 is the log's record of what happens when the supernatural is taken from what people actually believe instead of invented whole, and that alone could put this under the range. It is also a sequel, which is not a safe bet here - the Hitchhiker's sequels fell to 70 from 83. Leaned on the idea and the motive thread rather than on the world, which is the same one each time and which has never rescued a book in this log, as Artemis 69 shows. Re-examined against the occult ruling of 2026-08-26 (failing EITHER test is a veto, and a rite enacted on the page fails even when the system is invented): the record does not settle it, so the number is unchanged but axis:occult is now a priced risk rather than a cleared question - this range is void if the check below fails. Outstanding check: the text states voodoo is real and the plot runs through a voodoo shop and a society of practitioners - voodoo is real-world occultism, so Source may already fail; is any rite shown?

t: My ostatni tu proste zijem (The Rest of Us Just Live Here)
why: The ceiling is the lead and where the pages go. Mikey's OCD is written from inside - counting, loops, hands washed until they crack - and a reviewer with the condition calls it the first time she met her own symptoms in a book; nearly every page goes to what four friends want and fear before graduation, the axis behind Mockingjay 91 and Red Rising 95. Jared's healing is set up early, given a limit and honoured, so the world costs nothing. That earns the domestic shape of Male zeny 79 with a better lead. The floor comes from what the screening never looked at. Jared's secret relationship with Nathan is a late thread with a real falling-out, and Mikey's own past with him is mentioned: below premise and lighter than the protagonist's relationship that helped hold Caropisci at 67, but a recurring cost. Sexual content is light but teenage-frank - an erection, masturbation, crabs from a past partner - and Valka stareho muze 87 shows a little still registers. Readers widely report that little happens, the one fault Pocitani hvezd 85 carried. The cat-god and an off-stage possession ceremony stay a joke and a header sentence; the chosen-one parody is mostly affectionate. Prom-and-crush interiority costs a point or two. Standalone.

One question declared precisely and then paid for: may a court override a seventeen-year-old's religiously grounded refusal of the transfusion that would save him, and what does the court owe him afterwards. The book does not merely pose it - it settles the legal question at the halfway mark and spends the second half on the consequences, which is the premise-worked-out pattern that earns the top scores here. It is also the same rigour the reader singled out in Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91: an honest examination of what is actually plausible and believable inside a belief, neither mocking it nor conceding it. Faith runs as a thread inside a story rather than as a subject in its own right, so no deduction falls there. The opening is one concrete situation in one voice - a judge alone in her flat, her husband asking permission for an affair - the structure The Hitchhiker's Guide 83 is credited with and the opposite of the several-plot-lines-at-once start that ended three books at 30. Deductions: a boy dies and the close is sour rather than redemptive; sustained gloom is a real if mild cost, and 1984 sits at 60 on it. The lead is a judge near sixty absorbed in her work, so life-phase distance costs a couple of points, and her coldness towards the boy is the plot rather than a flaw the book resolves, which withholds part of the rooting interest. Leaned on the ideas for exactly that reason rather than on the protagonist.

A continuous novel rather than assembled stories, and its engine is motive: a councilman who believes he is being used, a mayor who is in fact using him, and a mentalist who believes a third power is steering both. Almost all the page time goes to who wants what and why, the axis Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 top, and the question underneath - whether a plan that predicts you leaves you anything to decide - is a real idea rather than a mood. Deducted because two plot lines start in parallel and run separately for roughly half the book, and a confusing opening is the reader's one absolute filter. Trimmed further 2026-09-03 on this author's first real score: Ja, robot 55 was abandoned on a cast nobody could root for, so his characters are now a priced deduction here rather than a worry.

Held low because the book declares a question and then does not answer it. The declared question is whether a galaxy merged into one shared mind is the right future, and the answer arrives as assertion: Kirkus calls the fade-out illogical and the finale artificial, and reviewers describe the argument between individual and collective as repeated rather than developed, across a planet-by-planet travelogue they call frightfully padded. A thin story spread over many pages is what cancelled LOTR 84's advantage and cost Les Miserables 71 its tightness. Dropped 2026-09-03 on this author's first real score, Ja, robot 55: undertaking to explain and then not explaining is the same breach the reader named when the robots' behaviour stopped being plausible, and it lands here on the book's whole ending.

t: Najdi odpoved (The Ask and the Answer)
why: The whole book is built on the axis this reader scores highest: page time on what people want and why they consent to what they do. Two young narrators are held apart under rival powers, one a tyrant and one a resistance, and the drama is which of them each will become and what each will agree to - a branding, an interrogation, a bomb - to survive and reach the other. That is what Mockingjay 91 does best, the most of what people's motives are and the least of the arena, and it is why Speaker for the Dead 90 sits above Ender's Game 87. The idea is nameable and load-bearing rather than decorative: there is no clean line between a terrorist and a freedom fighter, and complicity is arrived at in small agreements. It opens on one legible situation - arrival at the city that was supposed to be safe, already taken - so the confusing-start filter that ended Guards! Guards! 30 does not apply here. Deductions: sustained oppression with very little relief, and 1984 60 is the recorded price of a book that is simply depressing, though the profile weights bleakness only mildly and there is companionship rather than solitude, which The Martian 82 shows this reader prefers. Two alternating first-person voices cost some legibility, reviewers report the story marking time against a high page count, which is the story-density penalty that cost The Lord of the Rings 84 a tier, and it is a sequel - not a safe bet in this log, where the Hitchhiker's sequels fell to 70 from 83. Leaned on motives and ideas rather than on the protagonist, because Ender's Game 87 shows a teenage voice read from the inside is a small pushback and not the engine.

One day of a ceasefire, one airfield above Jerusalem, one pilot deciding on his own authority to avenge two comrades who did not come back: a concrete starting situation, and 246 pages spent on what a man wants and why rather than on what he does. That is the axis this reader rewards above all others, and revenge as a subject carried Monte Cristo to 75. The closest read anchor for the setting is a historical novel of Israel's founding at 68, Exodus, and that is where the ceiling sits. Two things stop it climbing past that. Czech readers report the dialogue in the first half is hard to follow - who is speaking, and about what - which touches the single most reliable negative predictor in the log, the confusing opening that ended three books in their first chapters. And the idea is deliberately withheld rather than delivered: the narrator is praised precisely for almost never giving a direct answer, and one line of criticism is that the material is nearly squandered. A competent literary novel that does not land an idea stalls in the 60s, and unrelieved gloom costs a little more on top - 1984 scored 60 as too depressing. Leaned on motive rather than on the testimony value of the material, because the form earns nothing by itself here: the same first-person shape produced both 91 and a 40 abandoned in its first pages.

RETRACTED AND RESET 2026-08-28, third pass. Raised earlier today, and too far: part of that move was the withdrawn volume-is-cheap claim. The part that survives is real - the old text asserted 'Ready Player One 55 and The Witcher 53 were both sunk mainly on volume', which is wrong on both counts - so a three-point correction stands, not six. Kundera's late novel braids an essayistic meditation on the self as image with a fictional strand, and the ideas are real and nameable - what it costs to be looked at, and whether a self survives being curated. That is the axis that carries Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82, but the delivery here is discursive rather than dramatised, so it does not reach them. RAISED 2026-08-28 from [50, 60], and the old reasoning is retracted outright: it read 'Ready Player One 55 and The Witcher 53 were both sunk mainly on volume' and priced a band-sized deduction off it. Ruled 2026-08-28: The Witcher 53 is a CONFOUNDED row and cannot be cited as a sexual-axis floor - the reader named two independent causes, 'both magic (witches) and the sex was through out the series', and the magic is the occult filter, the most severe objection in the log. The clean crudeness anchor is Ready Player One 55 - 'it was the kind of sex that reduced it that much', the kind and not the amount - with Artemis 69 confirming crudeness costs even in small doses. VOLUME IS UNANCHORED and must not be priced as cheap: Red Rising 95 and Valka stareho muze 87 are BOTH low volume on the reader's own account ('mostly one chapter of a book'), so neither shows what sustained non-crude content costs, and the log's only high-volume row is the confounded one. Note also that VSM's single chapter was still enough to become his one named complaint, so light volume is not free. This book is moderate in volume, explicit but literary, and not crude at all, which is the cheap corner of the axis. The remaining deductions are the ones that were always real: essay displacing story, which is the density penalty that capped Les Miserables at 71, and no single figure to follow through.

t: Nikdy nevystoupat na vrchol (Senza mai arrivare in cima)
why: A 112-page record of a walking journey into the Himalaya, alternating geography and sketches of local life with the author's own reflections on friendship and his spiritual development. For this reader the memoir and testimony form earns nothing by itself: the same form produced both the highest non-fiction score in the log, Seeking Allah Finding Jesus 91, and an outright DNF at 40 for The Diary of a Young Girl. What separated them was whether the book genuinely examines what is plausible and true, and whether it gives real understanding of how another group of people experiences the world. There is one flash of the second thing here - the locals' polite incomprehension that a westerner would trade comfort for hardship at altitude - but a short impressionistic travel diary is not a sustained examination of anything, and Son of Hamas 75 shows that a strong first-person account without that rigour settles in the A band at best. I leaned on the memoir form rather than on ideas because the form is the thing I could establish, while the idea is exactly what I would list as the risk. No hard filter is in play and the print route is verified, but clearing filters is not a reason to score.

t: Nokturna (Nocturnes: Five Stories of Music and Nightfall)
why: Five loosely linked stories rather than one premise worked out, so the axis that most often carries a number here is absent by construction. Short work has the character and emotion rules suspended, but the suspension only removes penalties and never adds points: The Little Prince 82 and Animal Farm 78 are the short books that scored well, and both scored for a single idea pressed all the way through. What is on offer instead is a recurring theme - self-delusion about one's own talent, and hopes dimming with age - which is a mood rather than something whose consequences get followed, and reviewers split precisely on whether the restraint reads as depth or as thinness. Nothing in the material trips a filter and nothing in the log objects to it, so this is not a low number for content; it is where a well-made book with nothing to leave behind lands, the stall that put The Chronicles of Narnia at 67 for lacking higher things to think about.

t: Oblazek na obloze (Pebble in the Sky)
why: Opens on exactly one concrete situation and one man: a retired tailor walking through Chicago, a laboratory accident, then waking on an Earth thousands of years older. Nothing fans out, so the filter that ended Guards! Guards! 30 and The Colour of Magic 30 is not in play. The positive case is a single idea followed in both directions - Earth despised as a radioactive backwater, and its own people answering with a plan to poison the galaxy - so contempt and fanaticism feed each other rather than one side simply being wronged, and Animal Farm 78 shows what a short book earns for leaving one idea behind. Trimmed 2026-09-03 on this author's first real score: reviewers agree the people are underdeveloped, and Ja, robot 55 turns that from a general reputation into this reader's own recorded objection to this author. Discovery (axis:discovery, 2026-10-24): a man thrown thousands of years ahead into a world he knows nothing about, who must understand it to survive, the arrival case the reader named beside Project Hail Mary 92; central, one step lower because the lead is the open risk, so +2.

A sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log - Hitchhiker's fell 83 to 70 and Catching Fire settled at 83 under The Hunger Games 89. What this one has going for it is the thing the reader rewards most directly: the prophecy stops being scenery and resolves into a concrete opposition between two named men, one of whom is convinced he is the promised saviour and is in fact being handled. That is page time on what a man wants and why he is wrong about it, the axis Speaker for the Dead 90 and Mockingjay 91 were both praised for, and the prophecy is played straight and questioned on the page rather than recited, which is what the reader singled out in Licanius 92-96, where the characters question fate in a way that makes sense to the world and is not forced or mocking. Since 2026-10-24 that earns on the ideas axis rather than merely not costing, which is the two points this gained. Pace also tightens, and constant momentum is the stated reason The Hunger Games sits at 89. Deductions: the point-of-view roster widens across a continent instead of narrowing, more chapters sit with the villains, and the book turns markedly more gruesome - sustained grimness is a real if mild dislike, and 1984 60 is the floor that objection produced. I leaned on momentum and the prophecy handling rather than on motives because the widened villain-side roster is exactly what could crowd motive out; if several stories run with none of them legible, this drops toward the 30s that confusing structure has produced three times. This is a campaign novel: an invasion goes in, the plan does not survive contact, and the fighting is the content. Reviewers rate the combat writing highly, and that is genuinely worth something here because momentum is a thing this reader rewards - The Hunger Games 89 and The Count of Monte Cristo 75 are both credited to it. But sustained battle is also the exact weight that costs points: page time on what characters do rather than on what they want and why is the deduction that put Golden Son 92 under Red Rising 95, with chapters skimmed to get to the next event, and Mockingjay 91 is the reader's favourite Collins precisely for showing the least of the arena. I cannot name an idea the book leaves behind beyond the cost of retaking ground, so ideas belong in the risk column, which is what caps this in the 60s. Nothing here trips a filter: one first-person narrator, a legible opening situation, no occult, no investigation, no crude sexual treatment.

The case is the idea, and it is stated plainly enough to name: a country taught to want everything on too grand a scale breeds men who chase vastness until it kills them, and a woman can spend a whole life tethered to one of them and still refuse him. Ideas of that size are what carried Animal Farm to 78 and what The Lord of the Rings 84 was loved for. The opening is legible - one woman's life told in order from her birth - so the confusion filter does not fire. The deductions are structural. The first stretch is deliberately distanced third person that withholds who is telling it, then the book hands over to a first-person narrator, then to letters; the reader who scored Unfinished Tales 69 for pieces that are not logically connected to each other is a poor bet for a hand-off like that, even though here the parts do join up. And the man's Arctic and African escapades take page time away from the woman the book is named for, which is the opposite of the interiority that put Red Rising at 95. Two wars, bereavement and deafness earn the mild bleakness discount 1984 60 measures. Leaned on ideas rather than protagonist, because she is admirable but held at arm's length for a long stretch, and this log records one prediction that failed by leaning on the wrong side of exactly that pairing.

t: Orlove v bouri (Eagles in the Storm)
why: What the book has going for it is a single legible objective - recover the last of the stolen legionary standards - which keeps one concrete goal in front of the reader instead of fanning out, and momentum of that kind is what The Count of Monte Cristo 75 was credited with over hundreds of pages. It also keeps a German viewpoint alongside the Roman one, so the enemy has motives rather than just numbers. Against that, this is a campaign novel: marches, ambushes and set-piece battles whose result is fixed by history, and set-piece action with no character revelation is dead weight in this log. I cannot name a thought it leaves behind, and that is the finding rather than a gap in my research - it is the same stall that held Ranger's Apprentice to 74 for being easy and having little to think about, with historical fiction here settling around Exodus 68 and Quo Vadis 66. It is a sequel resting on events narrated elsewhere, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's went from 83 to 70. I lean on momentum rather than on the leads, because I have no source on how much interior life they get here.

Reads standalone: same year, its own leads and premise, and reviewers who started here say it works alone. The case is motives. Garreth, heir to a merchant house going under, is set against a match his parents need; Elaine, the prince's daughter, works out what has changed her father. Duty against desire is the axis that tops the log, and romance as the subject costs nothing, as Pýcha a předsudek 75 shows. Both leads are flawed and rootable, if young, a small life-phase pushback. The city is praised, and its declared theology, gods made real by belief, has to hold. Occult is priced heavy, minus ten: the secret Elaine uncovers is a god that has ruled for centuries by taking royal bodies through a Daris Brotherhood blade rite that consumes each host, lore graded by the Čaropisci 67 precedent. One open risk. The finale, where the leads are thrust into that conflict, is unchecked; if it stages the rite, the book is vetoed. Garreth is betrothed by his parents to a foreign woman when the central romance begins, which the reader ruled on 2026-10-24 is not infidelity: an arranged betrothal is not an engagement. Also against it: a slow burn, the Počítání hvězd 85 drive problem, and a last stretch one reviewer found hard to follow alone. The opening is legible: a funeral prologue, then one heir and one unwanted match. Elaine's inquiry and a hunt for Aunt Thorn are flagged.

t: Ozveny velke pisne (Echoes of the Great Song)
why: There is an idea here and it is the spine of the book: an immortal ruling caste whose immortality turns out to be a decaying technology, and the page time goes to what the rulers and the ruled want from each other rather than to the battles - the axis that puts Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 at the top of this log. The power source is invented crystal, declared to be running out and then behaved as if it were, which is the self-consistency the reader rewards and the opposite of the premise collapse that sank Divergent 58. Heroism and loyalty inside a small band is what he said he loved in LOTR 84 and The Hobbit 84. Deductions: a short book carries five viewpoint figures, and characters who do not think and want differently is the separator between Golden Son 92, where three leads each want something distinct, and Divergent 58; reviewers also complain the scope is compressed into too few pages. The opening is one legible strand - a warrior on a mission to re-energise crystals with two companions - so the failure that ended three books at 30 does not apply here. Leaned on motives and the idea rather than on the invented world, because predicting up on worldbuilding while the lead may be thin is the recorded Artemis 69 error. Read after the four volumes before it; it picks up where the last one stopped. The opening is one scene inside a breakaway priest, legible to a reader who saw that schism begin: his service in a frozen swamp, pulpit, altar and call and response, new initiates still dazed from receiving the spiders, until the high priest kills him and the narration notes the goddess was not there to receive him. That is the most rite on the page in the series and still light, -2 on both ends: the rites do nothing, the power is a parasite, and the climax that burns the priests in one room with dragon fire is a killing by the heroes, not an offering. The lean is ideas and motives: how to end a war without seeding the next, and who answers for a nation talked into atrocity, settled without a battle, the Mockingjay 91 shape. Geder learns he may disagree with the priests and stays in the doomed room so the plan works, the turn the reader liked in Caeden (Svetlo veci konecnych 96), though here he also orders children killed and reviewers doubt the turn is earned. No strand is an investigation. Risks: the heaviest axis, as several reviewers call the ending pat and its last twists unearned, the convenience Valka stareho muze 87 was praised for refusing; and drive, with readers reporting the momentum lost. Its question is how to stop, not how to win, so it is not more of the same.

Short pieces carried by voice and by ordinary people's motives - the axis that tops this log - with the character rules suspended by the short-form rule, which removes penalties but adds nothing. Two things could drag it under: the vulgarity, and description standing in for story. On the first, the language itself is no objection at all; what would cost is the bawdy anecdotes turning crude *about sex*. Held on 2026-08-28 with the comparator corrected. Re-derived 2026-09-03 under the new collection axis: a multi-story book is read from the front and put down on its weakest early pieces, not averaged and not skipped past. Anecdote and voice rather than premise and consequence was already the objection to this author's story work, and it is the least transferable thing on this reader's axes. A collection of anecdotes has no arc to reward waiting.

What carries the number is the family material: four siblings and a mother who each want something nameable - a missing father found, a reputation matched, a way out of the dunes - and page time on wants and why is this reader's heaviest axis, the one Mockingjay 91 tops its trilogy on. But the buried world stays a setting rather than a proposition. Nothing in the book accounts for how a mile of sand arrived or what ended the old one; the cause is deliberately withheld and never picked up, so there is no idea to take away beyond the image. A competent book with events and nothing to think about stalls in the sixties here, which is what Narnia 67 was marked down for in those words and what put Ranger's Apprentice at 74. The larger exposure is the world logic: this reader abandoned a book in its first chapters, scoring it 55, over machines whose energy cost was never accounted for, and a diving technology declared as precisely as this one invites the same audit - rules add obligation, not credit. That doubt about the idea is why this stops here rather than going further.

Filter 6 asks whether the plot is mainly sexual behaviour or a sexual relationship, tested by whether removing the sex leaves a book. Here both halves of the plot are built directly on sex: the personal relationship (S&M, public sex, partner swapping) and the business plot (a chain of sex-tourism clubs conceived from that relationship). Nothing remains of the story without it, so this is the clean filter case rather than a graded one, and books-read.md scores do not enter into it.

The centre of the book is a market where people hand over parts of who they are for what they want, and a community founded on welcome quietly voting itself a wall. That is one premise declared plainly and then followed to its consequences, and it leaves something behind, which is what Animal Farm 78 scored on - a short allegory that gives you something to think about instead of immersing you in the misery. It ends on the lead choosing to spend himself to undo the damage, and self-sacrifice to save others rather than solo survival is the stated reason Project Hail Mary 92 beat The Martian 82. One close viewpoint and one concrete starting situation, so the confusing start that put The Gunslinger on 30 is not in play. Everything supernatural is invented - a healing gift, a blind seer, a forest that answers intent - so the real-world occult filter that held Percy Jackson to 57 does not fire, and the Christ-figure shape of the ending is a parallel rather than an objection. Capped in the 70s because the prose is functional rather than good, reviewers who like it still call the allegory heavy-handed and the story flat in stretches, the lead is fourteen and life-phase distance is a standing small pushback, and a sequel is not a safe bet here: Hitchhiker's fell 83 to 70. Leaned on the idea and the lead rather than on the worldbuilding, because predicting up on a world while the lead is thin is the error that put Artemis at 80 against a real 76. The nearest thing to an idea is the discovery that an enemy fought for years as a mindless swarm is aware and keeping secrets - which would reframe the whole war if the book paid it off. Reviewers say it does not: the marooned premise barely bites, several threads go nowhere, and the ending arrives by rescue rather than resolution. That puts ideas in the risk column, which is the most common reason a readable book settles in the 60s for this reader, and an ending that drags or fizzles is a separate documented deduction - The Martian 82 was docked for exactly that. Starvation and dwindling fuel far from home also make it the bleakest stretch of this story, and sustained bleakness is a mild but real objection here: 1984 60 was 'too depressing', while companionship beats solo survival, and a crew rather than one man is at least on the right side of that line. Held out of the 50s by a legible single-narrator opening, steady forward motion, and no occult, investigation or crude sexual treatment.

t: Pozdni zivot (Das spate Leben (The Late Life))
why: A man of seventy-six with a young wife and a six-year-old son is told he has about twelve weeks left: one concrete starting situation, one point of view, nothing to disentangle, so the filter that ended The Colour of Magic at 30 does not come near it. The positive case is real and nameable - what a father can hand to a child he will not see grow up, and what a life adds up to once the accounting is forced - and the book is almost wholly interior, the axis Speaker for the Dead 90 and Mockingjay 91 score on. Against that, reviewers agree the tension never builds and the manner stays deliberately dry and stereotyped in places, and this log punishes exactly that: The Martian 82 was docked for an ending that dragged, and The Lord of the Rings 84 for a story too thin for the number of pages even where it loved the themes. A dying narrator carries the mild bleakness discount 1984 60 records, and a protagonist five decades older than the reader is the small life-phase pushback, a couple of points and never a tier. Leaned on motives and ideas rather than protagonist: the man is drawn sympathetically, and it is the flatness of the narrative line, not him, that decides where this lands.

The positive case is the ending it commits to: a man chooses to destroy the installation he helped build, and himself with it, so that other people he will never meet get to live. Self-sacrifice to save others rather than solo endurance is a difference this reader has priced explicitly - Project Hail Mary 92 over The Martian 82 - and the premise the whole series runs on is closed here rather than deferred again. What holds it down is the people. Review consensus is that the secondary cast is interchangeable and the partings land flat because the relationships were never built, and distinct characters who each think and want different things is exactly what earned Golden Son 92 its praise; the inverse costs the same amount. Reviewers also report the remaining mysteries being resolved by exposition and long stretches of two characters sitting and thinking, which is thin story spread over pages - the deduction that keeps The Lord of the Rings at 84. Leaned on character differentiation rather than on the payoff of the premise, because the one recorded prediction failure in this log came from leaning up on a world while the people in it read thin.

One premise declared in the first few pages and then escalated: a high-school lineman makes a tackle and comes up in a world where the stop signs are blue, and every subsequent hit moves him further out - a rich father, himself as the school dealer, then a world where segregation never ended. A premise whose consequences are actually worked out is the axis Project Hail Mary 92 scores on, and this opens on one concrete situation in a single first-person voice, which is what The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy 83 was credited for. It also leaves something behind: what a life owes to the accidents that arranged it. One deduction keeps it out of the 80s. The shape is one issue per jump, and reviewers split over whether that reads as argument or as lecture; borrowed ideas assembled without cohering is what cost Divergent 58. The lead is a deliberately unremarkable everyman, and since 2026-10-24 that is no longer a deduction: ordinary is not flat, as Valka stareho muze 87 showed by scoring eleven above a range built on an everyman narrator. The book is built so that a straight white male footballer's default worldview is the thing to be corrected, and the racism, sexism and homophobia he meets are largely carried by male characters, one of whom assaults his girlfriend; Kirkus calls its messages of empathy and equality short in execution. The substance is what people want and why - who wants to take the family west and out of the survival routine, who needs to be the diver a vanished sister was, what a girl owes an alcoholic father set on revenge - and that is this reader's heaviest axis, the one Mockingjay 91 wins on. t: Prevorstvi u pomerancovniku (The Priory of the Orange Tree)
why: The positive case is a doctrine declared precisely and then taken apart over the whole length. A kingdom's state religion holds that the unbroken bloodline of its queens is the only thing keeping the world's destroyer bound, the book follows what that belief costs the women who have to embody it, and then shows the claim was manufactured - the uncanny resemblance between the queens was a glamour, and the actual binding was a pair of jewels with a fixed thousand-year expiry that nobody had counted. That is a premise whose consequences are worked out rather than asserted, and it leaves an idea behind: the victor writes the history, and a state can rest for a millennium on a lie nobody alive is able to check. Rival accounts of one event, each partly self-serving, is the axis The Silmarillion 80 and Speaker for the Dead 90 both score on. The court plotting also spends real page time on what people want and why rather than on set pieces, and the lead is competent and easy to root for, which is the combination behind Mockingjay 91. Two deductions. It runs past eight hundred pages and two of its four viewpoints do very little for the first few hundred - a thin story spread over many pages is the named penalty that held The Lord of the Rings to 84 despite ideas the reader rated far above The Hobbit's, and that cost Les Miserables its digressions down to 71. And one viewpoint belongs to a self-pitying, resentful exile nobody roots for; that is the exact failure that put The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 twenty-two points under Sunrise on the Reaping 87, discounted here because he is a quarter of the book rather than the whole of it. Magic is invented - power drawn up through a tree and down from the stars - so the occult filter does not engage, and the romance between two women is treated seriously rather than crudely, which costs nothing in a log topped by Red Rising 95. Leaned on the idea and on motive-heavy politics rather than on worldbuilding, because the world here is wide rather than deep and Artemis 69 is the recorded price of predicting a book up on its setting. Re-examined against the occult ruling of 2026-08-26 (failing EITHER test is a veto, and a rite enacted on the page fails even when the system is invented): the record does not settle it, so the number is unchanged but axis:occult is now a priced risk rather than a cleared question - since the 2026-10-24 re-ruling, drawing it as a performed rite of this invented system costs a graded deduction rather than voiding this range. Three first-person narrators who genuinely want different things - a boy, a girl, and the branded survivor of the massacre committed against his own people - and the question the book is actually about is whether any of them can avoid becoming what they are fighting. Golden Son 92 stands high in this log precisely because its characters each think and want differently, and giving the wronged non-human species its own interiority is the Speaker for the Dead 90 move: an alien culture understood from inside by motive rather than observed from outside, which is the single axis that separates those two Card entries, 90 against 87. The idea states itself in a phrase - war makes monsters of men, and the live question is whether that is a description or an excuse - and the log is clear that having something like that to leave behind is what lifts a competent book out of the 60s, where The Chronicles of Narnia 67 stalled for lacking it. Deductions: three narrators who share most of their scenes means the same events arrive twice, and reviewers report exactly that repetition, which is a legibility and density cost rather than a filter. It is total war from early on with little relief, and 1984 60 records what unrelieved grimness costs, though the weighting is mild and the self-sacrifice that puts Project Hail Mary 92 above The Martian 82 is here in quantity. And it is a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log - the Hitchhiker's sequels fell to 70 from 83. Leaned on the differentiated cast and the idea rather than on worldbuilding, because the recorded Artemis 69 miss came from predicting up on a world while the lead was thin, and what carries this book is the people.

The positive case is narrow but real: a narrator who is established, competent and easy to root for, carrying command responsibility for people other than himself - and self-sacrifice for others over personal survival is the axis that lifted Project Hail Mary 92 above The Martian 82. That is what keeps the number off the floor. Against it, I cannot name an idea the book adds; reviewers describe a long stretch of a tedious posting and a transfer, with little new ground covered. Ideas as a risk rather than a support is what puts a readable book in the 60s here, and a thin story spread over pages is a penalty in its own right - The Lord of the Rings 84 was held down by sparseness for its length and The Martian 82 by an ending that dragged. No filter is touched: a single legible first-person line, no occult, no investigation, no crude sexual treatment.

Both leads are introduced on the first page by what they want and then made to pay for it: one is desperate to be allowed to fight and cannot get anyone to let her, the other is strong enough to fight and has no heart for killing. That is page time on what characters want and why, the axis that put Red Rising at 95 and Mockingjay at 91 at the top of this log, and both are people to root for rather than a slide into ruin - the failure that held The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes to 65 against 87 for the reader's favourite of that author's prequels. There is a nameable idea as well: a minister who uses people as righteous tools, and what being a tool costs the person. The world is honest about itself - what the characters call elf-magic is salvaged technology and the gods are invented, so nothing is asserted that the book then has to fudge, and no real-world occult is practised. Deductions: two viewpoints instead of the tight single narration The Hunger Games got 89 for, an emphasis on romance that reviewers found slackened the tension, teenage leads as a small pushback, and it is a sequel - not a safe bet here, since Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. I lean on motive and protagonist rather than on the worldbuilding, because Artemis at 76 is this log's warning against predicting a book up on a consistent world.

The argument of the book is stated out loud - a minister tells his apprentice that a blade in the right hands can be a righteous tool and the apprentice asks who decides whose hands are right - and the plot then tests that to destruction through three characters who have all sworn vengeance. Leaving an idea behind is what separates the top of this log from its competent middle, and vengeance and its price get real page time here, the axis Mockingjay 91 wins on. It opens on one concrete situation, a hall burned in the night with a single royal survivor, so there is something to be invested in immediately instead of the several-lines-at-once confusion that ended Guards! Guards! at 30. Magic is salvaged technology and the pantheon invented, so nothing on the occult axis. Deductions are real: three narrators are introduced early, and reviewers report they are overshadowed by returning power-players who make the actual decisions, which is the thin-lead failure that cost Artemis its whole gap to Project Hail Mary 92; one of the three thinks about little beyond fighting and killing, pushing on rootability the way The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes did at 65; and it is a sequel, never a safe bet here given the fall from 83 to 70 across Hitchhiker's. The band is set by the historical novels actually read: Quo Vadis 66, Exodus 68, The Count of Monte Cristo 75. Leaned on the interior time given to a cunning politician rather than on the fighting, because the fighting is the part this reader skims. Re-examined against the occult ruling of 2026-08-26 (failing EITHER test is a veto, and a rite enacted on the page fails even when the system is invented): the record does not settle it, so the number is unchanged but axis:occult is now a priced risk rather than a cleared question - this range is void if the check below fails. Outstanding check: Greek civic religion - is sacrifice or omen-reading shown in a scene?

Single first-person narration with one concrete opening situation - an attack, an alien ship defecting mid-battle, and the pilot who takes its passenger's place undercover - which is the shape of this reader's baseline favourite, The Hunger Games 89, tight single POV and constant momentum. The premise is a real idea and it is worked out instead of asserted: a galactic society that congratulates itself on being peaceful has in fact bred aggression out of itself, hires the fighting it disowns, and keeps its monopoly on faster-than-light travel as the lever that holds the species it calls lesser in dependence. Most of the page time goes on the heroine discovering from inside that the enemy is not what she was told, which is exactly the axis Speaker for the Dead 90 scores on - understanding an alien culture rather than defeating it - and the axis that made Mockingjay 91 the best of its trilogy, motives shown and set pieces withheld. Three deductions, all graded. A teen lead is a couple of points here, never a tier. Competence is partly given rather than earned: she arrives an ace and the disguise is a convenient piece of equipment, the failure mode that sank Divergent 58 when carried too far. And a sequel is not a safe bet in this log - Hitchhiker's 83 to 70. Leaned on motive and premise rather than on the flying, because dogfights are the part Golden Son 92 was actually docked for. Discovery (axis:discovery, 2026-10-24): finding out from inside what the enemy really is, with her cover and her people's survival depending on it, is the shape the reader named in Project Hail Mary 92; partly credited above as understanding an alien culture, so priced as partial, +2.

t: Vyslapana cara (A Line Made by Walking)
why: A twenty-five-year-old artist retreats to her dead grandmother's bungalow after a breakdown, photographs the dead animals she finds and quizzes herself on works of art. Reviewers agree it almost entirely eschews plot in favour of contemplative vignettes moving between the present, the city she fled and a rural childhood. Asked whether the idea holds, the honest answer is that the subject is a state rather than a proposition, and that is exactly what leaves a competent literary novel in the 60s. Two further discounts: pieces that are not logically connected to each other is the stated reason Unfinished Tales 69 is the lowest of its author by a clear margin, and sustained depression is bleakness, which 1984 60 prices as real but mild. It earns back a little for giving genuine page time to what the narrator wants and why - the axis Red Rising 95 tops - and for an inner life close to the reader's own phase, which is why the range is the low 60s and not lower.

t: Vzdycky budeme mit Pariz (We'll Always Have Paris: Stories)
why: Twenty-one previously unpublished late stories, and the reason for a low-60s range is that there is no idea here to lean on. Reviewers converge on short sketches with a truncated sense of incompleteness, several reading as reworked material that had been set aside, and the author's own introduction tells the reader to enjoy the stories rather than think about them - the exact opposite of what earns points in this log. Short work has the character and emotion rules suspended, but the suspension only removes penalties: Animal Farm 78 scores because its one idea is sharp, not because it is short. Without that, what is left is lyrical mood with no continuous character to invest in, and disconnected fragments are what put Unfinished Tales 69 at the bottom of its author's range. Nothing trips a hard filter, and clearing the filters is not a case for reading.

Catalogued as povidky and as autobiography: a humorous run of episodes from the author's own life - looking for a partner, her marriages, absorbing the partners her children brought home, a son's wedding, trips with her mother. The one structural thing in its favour is a through-line, one life told in rough order, so it is not a heap of unconnected pieces - and unconnected pieces is exactly the complaint that made Unfinished Tales the lowest Tolkien at 69. The memoir and testimony form earns nothing by itself in this log - the same form produced Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus at 91 and The Diary of a Young Girl at 40 - and what earned the 91 was rigorously examining what is actually true plus real insight into how another group experiences the world. Light domestic comedy attempts neither, and 'not much to think about' is what held Ranger's Apprentice to 74 and The Chronicles of Narnia to 67, both with far more plot behind them than this has. Short work has the character and emotion rules suspended, but that suspension only removes penalties; it never adds points, so there is nothing to lift it back over the line. I leaned on the form rather than on ideas because ideas is the axis I would list as the risk here.

A young poet is raised by an adoring mother into the Stalinism of 1948, and his lyricism curdles until he denounces his girlfriend's brother and sends her to prison. The idea is named precisely and the whole book is its consequences: that the lyrical age, adolescence itself, is the psychology that makes a young man useful to terror. This reader explicitly wants that kind of leftover thought, and nearly all the page time here is motive rather than incident, the axis that puts Mockingjay 91 at the top of its trilogy. The cap is the lead. He is a mother's boy who slides into complicity, and criticism converges on him being a type rather than a person - both failure modes of the protagonist axis at once, neither interesting nor worth rooting for. That combination is what cost The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 22 points against Sunrise on the Reaping 87, and the log says this axis beats whatever competes with it. The narrator also breaks off repeatedly into essays on Rimbaud, Shelley and Mayakovsky, which is the digression cost that separates Les Miserables 71 from The Count of Monte Cristo 75. I leaned on protagonist alongside ideas rather than on ideas alone because the ideas here are strong enough to clear the line by themselves and the lead is the thing that will not let them. The opening is a single legible thread, the mother's youth and the conception, so the confusion filter is not in play.

The scattered threads converge here on a single objective - who assembles seven artefacts first - and one legible objective is what this reader wants; The Hunger Games 89 and The Hitchhiker's Guide 83 are both credited with fixing on one concrete situation instead of fanning out. At 782 pages it takes no length penalty either: the complaint recorded against The Lord of the Rings 84 was a thin story spread thin, not length, and this is densely plotted. Deductions: reviewers describe the book as fully plot-driven where the earlier material was character-driven, and set-piece action that reveals nothing about what people want is dead weight for this reader - that is the precise drag that cost Golden Son 92 its three points against Red Rising 95 and had chapters skimmed. It also stops on a cliff-hanger rather than a resting point. A sequel too, and sequels are not safe bets here. I leaned on momentum rather than on motives deliberately, because motive is what this book's plot machinery is most likely to crowd out, and that is the risk that would drop it below the range. Re-examined against the occult ruling of 2026-08-26 (failing EITHER test is a veto, and a rite enacted on the page fails even when the system is invented): the record does not settle it, so the number is unchanged but axis:occult is now a priced risk rather than a cleared question - this range is void if the check below finds a Source failure; a rite of the invented pantheon shown in a scene now costs a graded deduction instead. Outstanding check: Hebrew-derived pantheon - Source question, plus is any rite shown in a scene?

A 2027 France where sophisticated attacks hit the symbols of the West, and a ministry adviser whose father collapses and who is then handed a fatal cancer diagnosis. The book still leaves a thought behind - that a civilisation and a body are annihilated the same way and neither can read the signs - so it is not a thin book, and the occult and bleakness deductions already priced (Wicca goddess worship as the marriage's one source of comfort, and 500-plus pages of decline against 1984's 60 for being too depressing) still stand. Re-examined under the corrected sexual-content axis (2026-08-27, volume, explicitness and crudeness all cost and compound): this was not priced at all before, and it should have been. The marriage-repair thread is written with graphic, anatomical explicitness rather than being implied, and a separate subplot has the protagonist attempt to hire a sex worker who turns out to be his own niece - a scene that is crude on its own terms whatever its narrative point. That combination of real explicitness and a genuinely crude turn is the same shape of cost that took Artemis from 76 down to 69 for crude sexual treatment, and it is not a small addition on top of two deductions already near the floor of this reader's range. I now lean on occult, bleakness and sexual-content together, since no single one of the three was doing all the work before and the previous estimate undercounted by leaving the third out entirely.

Catalogued as povidky and as autobiography: humorous episodes and observations from the author's own life during the coronavirus period. A shared recent upheaval is the nearest this comes to the thing that earns on the memoir axis - insight into how other people experienced something - but the subject is her own comfortable domestic routine under restrictions, not another group's world. The memoir and testimony form earns nothing by itself in this log - the same form produced Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus at 91 and The Diary of a Young Girl at 40 - and what earned the 91 was rigorously examining what is actually true plus real insight into how another group experiences the world. Topical comedy attempts neither, and it carries the extra hazard that pandemic anecdote dates fast, leaving even less behind. There is no premise to work out and no plot, so nothing can accumulate across the pieces; unconnected pieces is what made Unfinished Tales the lowest Tolkien at 69, and that book at least had Tolkien's material. 'Lacks higher things to think about' held The Chronicles of Narnia to 67 with a plot behind it. I leaned on the form rather than on ideas because ideas is the axis I would list as the risk.

t: Plamen v temnote (A Torch Against the Night)
why: One objective drives the whole book - get north, break into the Empire's worst prison, get a brother out - and the two who go do it together rather than alone. Companionship over solo endurance is a preference this reader has stated in numbers, Project Hail Mary 92 over The Martian 82, and the strongest thread by review consensus is a soldier bound by an oath she is starting to hate, torn between her Emperor and her family: page time on what she wants and why, which is the axis Mockingjay 91 tops its trilogy on. The number is set elsewhere. The supernatural apparatus moves to the foreground here as a purgatory between the living and the dead with a keeper who passes souls through it, alongside jinn and efrits that the author says in interviews she took from Middle Eastern folklore, and a seer order she modelled on the Pythia at Delphi. Borrowed real-world supernatural material is the most expensive axis in this log - Percy Jackson 57 because the Greek pantheon counts, Harry Potter 51 for magic drawn from historical witchcraft. Deduct again for sustained grimness, since a torture prison, a sadistic warden and a slow poisoning are most of the setting and 1984 60 shows what unrelieved bleakness costs; and note that a continuation is not a safe bet here, Hitchhiker's Guide falling from 83 to 70. Leaned on the occult axis rather than on momentum, because momentum is the book's strength and would argue the number up. Re-examined against the occult ruling of 2026-08-26 (failing EITHER test is a veto, and a rite enacted on the page fails even when the system is invented): the record does not settle it, so the number is unchanged but axis:occult is now a priced risk rather than a cleared question - this range is void if the check below fails. Outstanding check: same borrowed folkloric apparatus - Source question.

It clears the occult test on mechanism rather than on being invented. Orogeny is a bodily sense operated on declared rules - it draws heat and motion out of its surroundings, and the obelisks work as amplifiers that must be linked - and although this book renames the underlying force magic, a silver thread running through living things and the planet, nothing is invoked, worshipped or ritualised on the page and there is no priesthood; even the Guardians' power is sited in a physical implant. That puts it with the systems already accepted as engineering rather than with the real-world witchcraft that sank Harry Potter 51 and the pantheon that sank Percy Jackson 57. The positive case is that the premise is worked out instead of decorated: a world with recurring extinction seasons has its lore, its castes, its architecture and its underground geode cities all following from that one fact, which is the second-order thinking he credited in Project Hail Mary 92. It also spends its pages on motive - a mother and a daughter who want incompatible things and are each being taught by someone with an agenda - over incident. Now the deductions, and there are four. It is a sequel, and sequels fall in this log: Hitchhiker's 83 to 70, Speaker for the Dead 90 to 81 for the books after it. The narration is second person and alternates between two leads, and reviewers report stretches where it is not clear who is speaking, which is the neighbourhood of the failure that produced his three scores of 30. Bleakness is heavy and unrelieved, and 1984 60 is what that costs. And Essun is interesting without being easy to root for - the interesting-versus-rootable split that put twenty-two points between two Collins books, Sunrise on the Reaping 87 and The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65. Leaned on ideas and motive rather than on worldbuilding, because the lesson of Artemis 69 is not to predict a book up on its world when the lead is the open question. Discovery (axis:discovery, 2026-10-24) is partial here, the world's secret continued rather than opened, and the lead is the open doubt, so it prices at nothing; the number holds.

The conceit is legible and disciplined - the same April day in three consecutive years, before, during and after the pandemic, one morning, one midday, one evening - and the book is entirely about what its people want and fear rather than what they do, which is the axis this reader rates above everything else. That is the positive case and it is not trivial. Against it: the point of view is distributed across an extended family rather than held inside one person, and the log is unambiguous that the tight single-POV narration is what makes these books work - The Hunger Games 89 was scored a baseline favourite for exactly that, and Red Rising 95 tops the log on interiority sustained in one head. Reviewers also put the obstacle in the characters themselves, whose trouble is late-thirties disappointment that life has not met expectations, and a flat lead is the whole gap that left Artemis at 76. Naming the idea is where it fails the gate: love under a pandemic is a subject, not a premise whose consequences get worked out, so axis:ideas belongs in risks. A roving ensemble opening carries some of the confusion risk that ended three books at 30, though one family on one day is a long way from several plot lines at once. Leaned on protagonist and distributed POV rather than on bleakness, which is the mildest objection in the log and not what decides this. Exited at gate 2 at one source; the occult question is unexamined and nothing suggests it.

One search decides it. A 72-page illustrated story for children from five, in which a personified water droplet goes to droplet school and is carried through the water cycle - a treatment plant, a reservoir, pipes, sewers - so that the young reader learns how water moves and how it is cleaned. Children's register is graded, never vetoed, and it is graded by how juvenile the telling is: The Little Prince 82 costs nothing because an adult reads it for what it says about people, while the picture-book end of the scale is a 30s-to-40s book, and this is squarely at that end. The educational spine is also the problem for the one axis that could rescue a short book: the personification is a teaching device, not a premise whose consequences get worked out, and at least one reader called the text plotless and brochure-like. So the idea I can name is a school-syllabus fact, axis:ideas goes in risks, and no nameable idea plus a form that suspends the character tests is the lower band. Occult status is unexamined at this exit; a personified droplet is not a rite.

There is something here: one short monologue for each year of a life that ran from 1928 to 2022, each followed by a terse note on where the writer stood, so a century of Czech history is measured against one person year by year. But the memoir form earns nothing by itself in this log - Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 earned its score by actually examining what is plausible and what is not, and The Diary of a Young Girl 40 is the same form failing outright, so the form is evidence of nothing and the content has to carry it. The structure is deliberately fragmentary, and fragmentation is precisely what put Unfinished Tales 69 at the bottom of the Tolkien scores: pieces that are not logically connected to each other. A chronological frame is not a worked-out idea, and with no continuous narrative there is no protagonist or motive to gain points back, so axis:ideas goes in risks. Anchoring on how non-fiction and twentieth-century-history books have actually landed - Son of Hamas 75 and Exodus 68 - a competent, well-regarded set of reflections without a single argument sits just under the line. Leaned on memoir-form rather than density because the book is short; the risk is not length but that the fragments do not add up. Exited at gate 2 at one source, so the occult question is unexamined; nothing in the description points that way.

The idea is as strong as anything in this log and it is genuinely worked out rather than gestured at: one question - whether a man forced to be good is still a man - is declared inside the book itself, tested by conditioning the narrator against his own will, and then answered when he is left to choose for himself at the end. That is the kind of book that earned Animal Farm 78, short and idea-driven and leaving something behind. The opening is also exactly what this reader wants: one first-person voice, one concrete situation, four boys in a milk bar deciding what to do with the evening, no fanning out at all. But the protagonist is the whole problem and it is the heaviest axis there is. The narrator is a gleeful perpetrator for the first third and there is nobody else to be with, and a lead who cannot be rooted for cost The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 twenty-two points against Sunrise on the Reaping 87 on that alone - and this lead is a far harder case than a slow descent into evil, since he starts at the bottom and enjoys it. Deductions stack from there: rape and assault are narrated from inside by their perpetrator, and while the invented slang is a deliberate distancing device rather than titillation, which keeps this well short of the crude-for-laughs problem that hurt Ready Player One 55, it is still crude about the thing it is crude about. The relentlessness is its own cost - 1984 scored 60 for being too depressing, and this immerses the reader in the misery in a way Animal Farm pointedly did not. The invented slang also has to be learned before the prose is legible, a friction Tolkien's densest book never quite paid for. I leaned on protagonist plus ideas rather than on bleakness, because bleakness is the mildest recorded objection and would not by itself pull a book of this quality under the line; the unrootable narrator would.

Filter 6 asks what the book is for: remove the sexual scheme from any of these four stories and there is no story left. 'The Great Switcheroo' has no plot beyond a husband sneaking into a friend's bed in the dark to compare a sexual experience; 'Bitch' has no plot beyond an aphrodisiac perfume and its effects; the two Oswald Cornelius pieces are diary entries of sexual conquest with nothing else driving them. That is a different shape from Pride and Prejudice (75), where romance and courtship - what characters want and why - is the entire subject and costs nothing, because courtship there is motive and relationship, not a sexual deception scheme standing in for plot. This collection fails the new hard filter rather than landing on the graded axis at all, so no range is produced.

t: Modra planeta (Modra planeta: Pribehy deti z ruznych koutu sveta)
why: One search settles the form and with it the exit. This is a 68-page illustrated book for beginning readers from age six: twelve very short stories about twelve children in different countries, all set at the same moment of one day, each followed by factual notes to read with a parent. Children's register is graded rather than vetoed, but it is graded by how far toward a children's book it actually sits, and this sits all the way there - The Little Prince 82 and The Hobbit 84 pay nothing because they are books an adult reads for the ideas, while the picture-book end of the scale lands in the 30s and 40s. The short form also suspends the character rules, and that suspension only removes penalties, so nothing is left to lean on: with a few pages per child there is no room for what anyone wants and why, the axis that carries the reader's whole top band. I can name no idea whose consequences are worked out, only the intention that the world is various, so axis:ideas belongs in risks, and no-idea plus a form that suspends the character tests is the lower band. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

t: Muz v cervenem kabate (The Man in the Red Coat)
why: The detective signal in the annotation is about real trials and the Dreyfus affair inside a work of non-fiction, not about a whodunnit, so filter one did not fire. It exits below the line on the idea. Every review agrees on the form: not a biography running A to B but a circuitous, digressive stroll through Belle Epoque names, with titled tangents and questions the author leaves unresolved on purpose. That is the shape the reader has already scored twice - Unfinished Tales 69 for pieces not logically connected to each other, and Les Miserables 71 for famous digressions - and heavy description with little story is a standing deduction. The non-fiction form earns nothing by itself here: what earned Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 was examining what is actually plausible, and a gossipy period portrait undertakes no such examination. An idea can be named - cross-Channel curiosity against chauvinism - but I would list axis:ideas under risks, which is the exit condition, so one source is where this stops. Occult status is unexamined by design at this exit.

It is short, precise and stays in one place, and there is a nameable observation in it: people moored between land and water who have committed to neither, and the restlessness that follows from that. Short books with something to think about do very well here - The Little Prince 82 and Animal Farm 78 both score on ideas alone with no plot to speak of - so length is not a deduction. What holds the number down is that the observation is a mood rather than a premise whose consequences are worked out; the drama is one woman failing to decide about a marriage, and thin story is the penalty term in this log, the same objection that cancelled The Lord of the Rings 84 down to a tie with The Hobbit. Reviewers also report being dropped in as though they already knew everyone, and several found nobody to be with, and a lead who is not worth rooting for is what separated Sunrise on the Reaping 87 from The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 by 22 points. Leaned on density and protagonist rather than on bleakness: the book is melancholy, but that is the mildest objection recorded and not what decides this one. Exited at gate 2 on axis:ideas at one source, so the occult question is unexamined; nothing in a Thames houseboat novel suggests it.

t: Noc nic nezadrzi (Rien ne s'oppose a la nuit)
why: An autobiographical novel that reconstructs the author's mother's life after finding her dead. The form earns nothing by itself: Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 earned its score by genuinely testing what is plausible, while The Diary of a Young Girl 40 is the same first-person testimony that did not work, so the number has to come from what the book examines rather than from its sincerity. It does examine one real thing - that a family's account of a life is unreliable, and the reconstruction says so about itself - but the payload is a case history of illness and suicide rather than a premise worked out to its consequences, which is why axis:ideas belongs in risks and why this lands under the line. Sustained gloom is the log's mildest recorded objection, so it is the second deduction rather than the first, though 1984 60 shows it costs even where the ideas are strong. Leaned on axis:memoir-form rather than axis:motives: there is ample page time on what people wanted, but it comes from interviews with real relatives, and the one high score in this form came from argument, not access. Exited at the below-the-line gate, so the occult question was deliberately not examined.

t: Obraz Doriana Graye (The Picture of Dorian Gray)
why: The positive case is a genuine idea, statable in a phrase: a life bought on credit, with the bill kept in another room, and what it costs to make beauty the only value. That is the axis that carries Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 - a book that leaves something behind rather than only events - and it is the reason this does not exit below the line. The opening also does what the log's most reliable predictor wants: two men in one room looking at one portrait, one concrete situation, nothing fanned out, no second plot line running. Against that stand two deductions. The lead is the log's most expensive single fault - a knowing descent into evil with nobody to root for, which is what separates The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 from the same author's other prequel at 87 on the protagonist alone, and Dorian is less interesting than the talker who corrupts him. And the story is thin for its pages, with a long catalogue of jewels, perfumes and tapestries standing in where plot should be, the same digression cost that holds Les Miserables 71 below Monte Cristo 75. The decadence is implication rather than depiction and never crude, so it costs nothing by the Red Rising 95 precedent, and the transformation is never explained or enacted as a rite, so the occult filter does not touch it. Leaned on ideas and the protagonist rather than on prose or period colour, because prose has never moved a score in this log and both recorded prediction failures came from leaning on an axis that was not doing the work.

t: Otec Vanoce a ja (Father Christmas and Me)
why: Pitched at nine-to-eleven-year-olds and illustrated throughout, and the praise reviewers converge on is for messages of hope, kindness and believing. That is a moral, not an idea a book leaves behind, so axis:ideas goes in risks and the below-the-line exit is decided right there. The nearest real anchor is The Chronicles of Narnia 67 - not bad, children as the main characters, and lacking higher things to think about - and this sits noticeably further toward a children's book than Narnia does, so axis:childrens takes more off again; the reader's own scale puts an outright picture book in the thirties and forties. What keeps it from the lower band is that the register is not the whole book: there is a real protagonist with her own narrating voice and a genuine want - an adopted human girl who does not fit where she has been put - and Ranger's Apprentice 74 shows an easy children's read with nothing much to think about can still land in the B band on likeable company alone. A sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log, Hitchhiker's 83 down to 70. Reviewers also report the advertised threat barely appearing until past page 200, which is thin story stretched out. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

t: Pikova dama a jine povidky (The Queen of Spades and other tales)
why: A short volume of prose tales: a card-table novella plus a set of ironic anecdotes of provincial Russian life. The prose is deliberately spare and outward - incident, coincidence and a turn of fortune, narrated at a distance from what anyone wants - and that is the exact inverse of the axis carrying the top of this log, where Mockingjay 91 was preferred for showing the most of people's motives and the least of the events. A set of brief tales has no single premise to lean on instead, so there is no route above the line even where each piece is well made. I can name an idea in one of them, an obsession that converts a man's whole life into a single wager, but not one the volume as a whole works out, which is why axis:ideas is a risk rather than something leaned on. This is a recorded, revisable number taken at the below-the-line gate: the occult question was deliberately not examined and is a live one here.

Both C conditions fire together, which is where this stops. One source settles form and genre: realist literary fiction, and a collection of a dozen or so separate stories with different casts and no single premise carrying through, only a shared setting and a framing pair. The idea is nameable but slight - disillusion, the small vanities and meannesses under the quiet surface of one neighbourhood - and it is restated across separate stories rather than worked out once, so axis:short-idea-driven suspends the character and emotion tests without putting anything in their place, which is a removal of penalties and never an addition of points. The log has the matching case: Unfinished Tales 69 is the lowest Tolkien by a clear margin precisely because the pieces are not connected to each other, and the cost here is the same structural one. The default band just under the line is right rather than the low one, because the observation is sharp, the register adult and the satire pointed - nothing suggests the 40s or low 50s. Occult status is deliberately unexamined at this exit, since nothing under 68 is proposed either way.

The positive case is the axis the reader ranks first and this book is built almost entirely out of it.
