Everything arrives through one man's mind - what he wants, what he is calculating, whom he cannot forgive - and the court exists only as he reads it, which is the same tight single-consciousness narration that made The Hunger Games 89 a baseline favourite and the interiority that put Red Rising 95 at the top. Two supporting points, both sourced. The opening is one concrete legible situation, a morning hawking with the king, continuous with what came before and single-POV, so the confusing-opening filter that produced the three 30s in the log is not in play. And the compression is real: five months of 1536, densely plotted, with interrogation scenes driving it, and a critic openly hostile to the earlier work for having no plot called this one full of narrative suspense. Length itself is never a deduction and dense plotting over many pages carries none. The deduction and the risk are the same man. He needs guilty men, so he finds men who are guilty, and he manufactures the case that kills them - and the log's cleanest controlled result is The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 against Sunrise on the Reaping 87 - same author, same world, same form, 22 points apart on a lead who is not worth rooting for. He is more sympathetic than that, self-made against inherited rank, and the descent is not framed as the arc, which is why this is a risk rather than a subtraction, but it is the axis that could collapse the range. A sequel that assumes prior knowledge is also not a safe bet in this log, which fell from 83 to 70 across one series. Reformation theology is a subject here but as politics inside a story rather than apologetics, so faith costs little. I leaned on motives and momentum, not on the protagonist, because Artemis 69 is the recorded failure of predicting up while the lead is the doubtful part.

t: Pribehy z konce predmesti (Tales from Outer Suburbia)
why: Fifteen very short illustrated pieces about strange things turning up in an ordinary suburb, in a picture-book format where the artwork carries part of the telling rather than decorating it. The reader's own scale prices a picture book in the 30s and 40s - Hobbit 84 and The Little Prince 82 pay nothing for a simple register, Narnia 67 pays a little, a picture book much more - and that register is the single thing setting this range. It does not land at the bottom of that scale, because there is a stated subject: how ordinary people react to something inexplicable and how its significance gets missed or ignored, and The Little Prince 82 proves short allegory can be carried entirely by its thoughts. But that is one thought distributed over fifteen sketches rather than a premise worked out, and pieces of two or three pages cannot pay the axis this log weights heaviest, page time on what people want and why, which is why the lower of the two bands is the honest one. Leaned on axis:childrens and axis:short-idea-driven; axis:ideas is the risk, not the support. Exited at the below-the-line gate, so occult status is unexamined.

Form and genre settle in one source - a near-future science-fiction novel, not a mystery - and then the below-the-line question answers itself. I can name the idea, agency itself: whether a person or a machine can bend a timeline that is already running down. What I doubt is that it holds up, which is exactly what puts axis:ideas in risks and ends the research here. Professional and reader criticism converge on the same two things: an intelligence that carries the premise and then disappears from the book for long stretches, and stakes that stay flat while a nuclear war is pending, described as movement signifying not very much toward a predetermined outcome. The lead is the part the log prices precisely - she is repeatedly called a cipher who is told where to go and asks what is happening, and a lead who is not interesting is the entire gap between Artemis 69 and the same author's better-liked books, with no worldbuilding rescue available because interest in the lead beats worldbuilding when they compete. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's 83 falling to 70. The default band just under the line is right rather than the low one, because the prose and the world are competent and there is a real idea to point at. Occult status is deliberately unexamined at this exit, since nothing under 68 gets proposed either way.

Literary fiction and a short-story collection at once, which is where the below-the-line exit is decided: thirteen minimalist pieces held together by a mood rather than by a premise. The form suspends his character rules and adds nothing in return, and I cannot name an idea in a phrase - a longing for love, acceptance and quiet is a subject, not something a book leaves behind - so axis:ideas goes in risks. Two further pulls put this in the lower band rather than the default one. Sustained sadness is announced in the title and is the stated organising principle, and 1984 60 is what that costs him even when the book itself is good. And readers report endings that do not follow from what precedes them and pieces they could not make sense of, which is the neighbourhood of the one failure that has actually stopped him reading - Guards! Guards! and The Colour of Magic both at 30. His nearest real anchor for the form is Unfinished Tales 69, docked because the pieces are not logically connected to each other, and this has less connective tissue than that. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

REVERTED 2026-08-28, third pass, to the pre-today range, for the same reason as the other volume-driven raises: the premise behind them was withdrawn by the reader. The coarse register carries the deduction here and is anchored on Ready Player One 55, so the Witcher withdrawal buys this book nothing. A modernist glass house in 1930s Czechoslovakia as the fixed point while the century moves through it - the building declared as an idea about rationality and light, then tested by what happens to the people in it. Real ideas and a genuine motive structure, the axis that carries this log. RAISED 2026-08-28 from [52, 62]. The old range stacked a volume deduction on top of a crudeness deduction and justified the stack by calling Ready Player One and The Witcher volume cases. Ruled 2026-08-28: The Witcher 53 is a CONFOUNDED row and cannot be cited as a sexual-axis floor - the reader named two independent causes, 'both magic (witches) and the sex was through out the series', and the magic is the occult filter, the most severe objection in the log. The clean crudeness anchor is Ready Player One 55 - 'it was the kind of sex that reduced it that much', the kind and not the amount - with Artemis 69 confirming crudeness costs even in small doses. VOLUME IS UNANCHORED and must not be priced as cheap: Red Rising 95 and Valka stareho muze 87 are BOTH low volume on the reader's own account ('mostly one chapter of a book'), so neither shows what sustained non-crude content costs, and the log's only high-volume row is the confounded one. Note also that VSM's single chapter was still enough to become his one named complaint, so light volume is not free. The coarse register here is real and keeps most of the deduction; the volume stack on top of it does not survive. Still well short of the historical band's better showings because the house, not a person, is the throughline, and the cast turns over around it.

t: Takovy pekny par a jine povidky (Selected short stories)
why: Literary fiction and a short-story collection at once, which is the below-the-line exit: twenty-four magazine pieces an editor arranged into a chronological cycle. The form suspends the reader's character rules and adds nothing in return - there is no single premise whose consequences get worked out, and that working-out is what earns his high scores. A subject is nameable, money's hold on love and self-invention in the jazz age, but a recurring subject across two dozen separate stories is not an idea a book leaves behind, so axis:ideas belongs in risks. His nearest real anchor for this shape is Unfinished Tales 69, docked because the pieces are not logically connected to each other. The craft is genuine and the pieces turn on what people want rather than on incident, which is what keeps the range at the line rather than below it. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

t: Tisice planoucich slunci (A Thousand Splendid Suns)
why: Nearly all the page time goes on what two women want and why - Marjam's inherited shame, Lajla's ambition and then her survival - which is the axis Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 both score on, and the reason those two sit above books by the same authors that lean on incident. It opens on one concrete situation, a five-year-old and her mother in a hut outside Herat, in a single third-person limited line, so the confusion filter that produced his three scores of 30 does not fire; the four parts hand the lead from one woman to the other in sequence rather than starting several threads at once. Both leads are interesting and worth rooting for, and the ending turns on one of them destroying herself to save the other - self-sacrifice over solo survival is exactly the difference he named between Project Hail Mary 92 and The Martian 82. It also gives real insight into how another group experiences the world, the thing he credited in Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91, and it leaves an idea behind: shame handed down as an inheritance, and what makes it bearable. Held out of the top band by sustained bleakness - domestic violence, war and loss with little relief, and 1984 60 shows what that costs him - though companionship blunts it here rather than isolation compounding it. Leaned on motive and protagonist, not on worldbuilding, since the setting is the real Afghanistan and does no work for the number.

t: Usmev lorda Ickenhama (Service with a Smile)
why: The positive case is real: comic prose that reads very easily, one concrete country-house situation rather than a fan-out, and a scheming protagonist who is both competent and likeable - and comedy is not a handicap in this log, since The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy scored 83. What holds the number down is what the pages are spent on. A farce allocates its page time to who is deceiving whom and which impostor is unmasked next, not to what anyone wants and why, and motives over action is the axis Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 both win on. Nothing is left behind to think about afterwards, which is the exact reason competent, pleasant books stall in the 60s here - Ranger's Apprentice 74 was easy to read with not much to think about, and Narnia 67 was marked down for lacking higher things. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's fell 83 to 70. I leaned on motives rather than on protagonist, because the lead is genuinely likeable and interesting; the gap is not who he is but that the book asks nothing of him beyond the scheme. Exited at gate 2 on axis:ideas after one source, so the occult question was deliberately not examined - nothing in an English country-house farce suggests it.

t: Valka svetu (The War of the Worlds)
why: A genuinely idea-bearing book, and the idea is stated outright in the first chapter rather than left to be inferred: before judging the invaders, remember what our own species did to the dodo and to the Tasmanians. Imperial conquest turned around on the conquerors, and human pre-eminence withdrawn - that is something left behind, which is the thing he says a competent book most often lacks, and it is why Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 score where they do on very few pages. It opens on one concrete situation, astronomers watching flares on Mars and then a cylinder in a sandpit at Horsell Common, in a single first-person voice and a lucid, almost documentary register, so the confusion filter does not fire; The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy 83 scores partly on that same virtue of starting somewhere specific. The world also holds up: the invaders' capabilities, the collapse of order and the biological ending all follow from what the book sets up, and nothing is asserted and then dropped. Two deductions, both on his heaviest axis. The narrator is unnamed and, on the consistent critical reading, deliberately flat - he reports his experience objectively and the book does not ask you to identify with him - and a lead who is not interesting is precisely the gap that put Artemis 69 six points under The Martian 82 by the same author. And three chapters hand the story to the narrator's brother, related as though witnessed, which loosens the single-viewpoint grip he prefers. Bleakness is real but bounded and the collapse is followed by restoration, so it costs little. Leaned on ideas and the opening rather than on the protagonist, which is the term pulling the number down.

t: Vynalezci zazraku. Sebrane povidky H. G. Wellse. Svazek I (The Stolen Bacillus and Other Incidents; The Plattner Story and Others)
why: Thirty-three early magazine pieces from the 1890s, gathered by which periodical collection they came from rather than around any one premise, so there is no single worked-out idea for the book to leave behind - and giving him nothing higher to think about is exactly what stalls competent work for this reader (Narnia 67, marked down for lacking higher things to think about). The best pieces do carry a real conceit - displaced sight, a stolen body, a runaway culture in a test tube - and that is the positive case; but they sit among comic incidents and slight magazine trifles, and an unconnected assemblage is where he has been hardest on writing he otherwise admires: Unfinished Tales 69 fell twelve points under The Silmarillion 80 purely because the pieces were not logically connected to each other. The short idea-driven form suspends the character and motive tests, which is why this is not lower, but that suspension only removes penalties: Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 both earn their scores from one idea carried the whole way, which a mixed thirty-three-story gathering cannot do. Leaned on form and density rather than on ideas, because the ideas here are real story by story and unprovable for the book as a whole. Occult status left unexamined - stopped at the below-the-line gate.

Eight pieces of science fiction set around the edges of an existing future history: origin stories for characters, one invention story, one crime story. The invention piece is the best case for it - a single engineering premise followed to what it does to the solar system, which is the Project Hail Mary 92 axis - but reviewers agree the pieces are interstitial by design and that nothing in them is load-bearing, and material that does not connect to itself is exactly what put Unfinished Tales 69 at the bottom of an author whose other work scored 80 and above. With no single premise for the volume to lean on, axis:ideas is a risk rather than an asset. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's 83 to 70 is the steepest recorded fall and it happened on that axis alone. Leaned on axis:sequels and axis:momentum rather than axis:worldbuilding, which is probably strong here and still cannot rescue a book by itself - Artemis 69 is the recorded proof, where consistent worldbuilding saved nothing. Exited at the below-the-line gate, so occult was not examined; nothing in the material suggests it is a question.

t: Zrcadlo a svetlo (The Mirror and the Light)
why: There is a real positive case and it is the reader's first axis: the whole book is one man's interior weather - service, debt, what he wants from a king who is the only source of everything he has - and it leaves an idea behind, that a regime consumes the servant who built it. That is the kind of thing the reader means by higher things to think about, and it is why this is not an exit at the cheaper gate. The number is nonetheless carried downward by density, which is the reader's explicit penalty term. At roughly 900 pages the reviews converge on a slack middle: it bogs down in portentous conversations, remodelling plans, protocol and costings, and one critic calls the pacing dangerously uneven. That is precisely the charge that cost The Lord of the Rings 84 its advantage - a thin stretch of story spread over many pages - and it is what dropped Les Miserables 71 below The Count of Monte Cristo 75 on digressions alone. Length alone is never the objection; the uneven middle is. The protagonist risk is at its sharpest here. He is read as a Faust figure much closer to damnation, his sins no longer deniable, and a lead descending into evil is the log's most expensive protagonist failure - The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 against Sunrise on the Reaping 87, 22 points on that alone. The ending is his destruction, so bleakness adds a mild further discount, the objection that took 1984 to 60. Being a sequel also matters more than usual here, since it assumes a long prior acquaintance with its cast. On the occult question: he hears a dead patron's voice and speaks with the ghosts he sees in the Tower, but that is a haunting rendered as memory and conscience, with no rite performed, no invocation and no medium, so the filter does not fire - the distinction is enactment, not the presence of the dead. I leaned on density rather than on motives alone because the interiority is not in doubt and the pacing is.

Reachable cold: the opening, read from the Czech sample, is one boy in one shop. Bastian, ten or eleven, bullied, mother dead, father silent, steals the book and hides in the school attic to read it, so the context is in place before Fantastica starts. Ideas and motives carry the number. Gmork explains how a dying imagination turns into lies that make people easier to rule. AURYN's motto becomes a search for what Bastian truly wants, at one memory per wish, until his last wish is to be able to love. Ideas worked out inside the world's own rules are what Svetlo veci konecnych 96 was praised for. The rules hold: the memory price is counted down, and the humans who crossed and stayed are shown. Against it, critical readers agree that the second half is episodic and slow, and many stop at the midpoint. That is the thin-story cost of The Lord of the Rings 84 plus the missing drive of Pocitani hvezd 85. Every episode spends a memory on one arc, so it is not the fragmenting of Unfinished Tales 69. Bastian's arrogant stretch is staged on the page, not uncovered from a past. It ends in shame, a wish to love and a confession, the direction he rewards rather than the slide in The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65, but it is the most named complaint. Small costs for the children's register and a ten-year-old's inner life. Standalone. Flag: AURYN's motto echoes Crowley; no rite is staged. Discovery (axis:discovery, 2026-10-24, not part of the dive and priced the screening way): a boy pulled into a world he knows only from a book, who must understand it to save it and to get home, the arrival case the reader named beside Project Hail Mary 92; its rules are already credited above, so partial, +2.

The idea states in one phrase and is the whole book: time saved is life lost, and the grey gentlemen literally live off the hours people economise. It is The Little Prince 82 written at novel length and with an economic argument underneath, and Animal Farm 78 is the precedent for allegory scoring on its ideas without needing anything else. Where the book asserts precisely - the time-savings bank, the accounting of stolen hours - it holds together as satire; Master Hora and the hour-lilies are left numinous, and the scaling rule says vague magic owes little, so the exemption Narnia 67 got applies here too. The pushback is the lead: Momo's whole characterisation is that she listens, which makes her about as passive as a lead can be, and a flat lead beat strong worldbuilding outright in Artemis 69.

Nothing in this catalogue carries more of the stated earner - higher things to think about - per page: it is the history of Western philosophy delivered inside a novel, and the novel then turns on the discovery that Sofie is a character in a book being written for someone else's daughter, so the idea is enacted rather than only lectured. That turn is what separates it from a textbook. Two honest costs. First, a large share of the pages are Alberto's lectures with the plot suspended, and a thin story spread over many pages is exactly the penalty term that capped LOTR 84 and docked Les Miserables 71 - the length is not the problem, the ratio is. Second, philosophy is the subject in its own right, which brushes the same line that rules out apologetics: the log wants ideas carried inside a story, and here the story is partly a delivery mechanism.

Standalone, 152 pages. The book says its own idea: courage is what you do while frightened, because there are things you have to do or you are not a person but a bit of dirt. Narnia 67 lacked exactly that, and it is the read book closest in shape (children in a land under a tyrant, a sacrifice, an ending that dies into somewhere brighter), so the ideas and Karl carry the number. Karl is the ordinary lead the protagonist rule protects: frightened, sure he is ugly and stupid, and he gets past it. The opening was read: one voice, one dying boy, Nangijala explained before he arrives. Three known costs. He is ten and reads as ten from the inside, crying and running himself down, the small markdown Ender's Game 87 took. It is a 9+ book with a real adult layer, so it pays between The Hobbit 84 and Narnia 67. And grief arrives at once, as in Promena 58, though it lifts by chapter 3 and the book is about companionship and self-sacrifice, the PHM 92 side of the bleakness rule, not 1984 60. The double death at the end is the point of the book. Adults object to it on moral grounds ('instructions for suicide'), which no read book measures; it is priced at the mild bleakness weight and sets the floor. No god, no rite, no religion mocked: occult and faith are clear. It sits under The Little Prince 82 for the time spent inside a child's voice.

t: Ronja, dcera loupeznika (Ronia, the Robber's Daughter)
why: Page time goes on what people want and why, which is the axis with the widest evidence in the log - two robber clans forced to share one fortress, two children who refuse to inherit the feud, and a father who disowns his daughter and then has to climb down from it. Mattis wanting his daughter and his pride at once is the kind of motive conflict that put Mockingjay 91 above Catching Fire 83. Ronja is competent because she is taught and tested, not because the book says she is, which avoids the Divergent 58 unearned-competence turn-off. Against it: the ideas are ordinary compared with the Ende and Lindgren entries above, and the register is squarely children's - the same combination that put Narnia 67 in the B band rather than lower. SCREENED 2026-09-02 on axis:sex-portrayal, verdict mild, was [74, 82]. Mattis is the volatile, blustering chieftain whose temper drives the feud and who ends the book shrugging sheepishly, with Lovis as the explicit voice of reason whose deadpan zingers are aimed at him, and the rival clan repeats the pattern with Borka. Held to mild because Ronja and Birk are written as exact equals in courage and wit, and Undis is as belligerent as the men. The dock is the profile's stated convention (mild -2, moderate -5), not a measured magnitude - the axis has no high-contrast anchor yet.

The one genuinely affecting thing in it is the frame: a fostered, unwanted boy in Stockholm gets the father and the country he has been longing for, and the reader is left to decide how much of it he is inventing. That is a nameable idea. Everything inside the frame is generic though - a prophesied boy, a black knight, a sword forged for him - and the log's own warning is that clearing the filters is not a reason to propose. Prophecy is present and leaned into and played straight, which costs nothing - the axis grades handling, not prominence. Lands where Narnia 67 lands and for the same two reasons: child register, not much to think about afterwards.

t: Chlapci z Pavelske ulice (The Paul Street Boys)
why: The idea is that children's play is not play: two gangs run a war over a lumber yard with courts, ranks, oaths and a traitor's trial, and the smallest boy in it dies of an illness he caught doing his duty. The book takes its own premise seriously to the end instead of retreating from it, which is the self-consistency the heaviest axis asks for. Nemecsek is as clear a case as this shelf offers of a lead who is both interesting and worth rooting for - he is despised, he keeps going anyway, and the honours arrive too late. Adult-canonical in Hungary rather than a curiosity. Pushbacks: it ends on a death, and the surrounding register is a boys' adventure story of 1907, so some of the cost of Narnia 67 applies.

t: Ostrov v Ptaci ulici (The Island on Bird Street)
why: One concrete starting situation and immediate investment, which is what the clarity filter actually asks for: Alex is left alone in a ruined house in the Warsaw ghetto and stays there for months because his father said he would come back. He runs it as a survival-engineering problem - water, heat, food, a rope strung to the next building - so the practical work is the text, which is the shape that made The Martian 82 work. The idea is what a promise is worth when nothing supports it. Written by a man who was in the ghetto and then in Bergen-Belsen, so the fact face of the heaviest axis is safe. Two pushbacks: sustained isolation is the specific thing docked in The Martian 82, and a child's inner life inside a testimony frame is the Anne Frank 40 shape - the defence is that this is a novel with a concrete situation and momentum, which is exactly what that diary lacked.

Four boarding-school teenagers walk out into a state that killed their parents for resisting it, and the book spends its pages on why each of them goes and what each is willing to lose - motives over action, the axis four different authors in the log agree on. Two of the strongest strands are an arena fighter who is bred and owned, and a singer whose voice can turn a crowd, so the argument the book makes is about what actually moves people. Told as staggered strands rather than simultaneous ones, which is the configuration confirmed acceptable by LOTR 84 and Golden Son 92 rather than the Guards! Guards! 30 failure. The risk is the one that matters most: this takes a society as its subject, and a subject society must cohere - Divergent 58 is what happens when it does not. The Phalange's politics and economics are sketched impressionistically, and that is unverified.

t: Tim Tolar, aneb, Prodany smich (Timm Thaler)
why: A contract with exact terms and a book that is nothing but its consequences: a poor boy trades his laughter for winning every bet he makes, becomes rich, and discovers that a person who cannot laugh cannot be with anyone. Declaring a resource and then making it behave that way is the form of the heaviest axis the log states most plainly, and the currency here is priced in every scene. The idea states in a sentence, which is what the sharpened short-form rule demands. The cost of the wish is emotional rather than magical, so it earns its allegory the way Animal Farm 78 does. The named risk is the occult one and it is a judgement call rather than a finding: Lefuet is a devil figure, so a reader who treats a devil-pact as occult by source will veto it - but nothing is invoked, no ceremony happens, and no real-world practice is depicted, which is why it is recorded as a risk and not as a block.

The idea is mortality told to children without softening it: a spider spends the only summer she has keeping a pig alive, then dies alone in an empty fairground while the pig lives. Friendship and self-sacrifice beating solo survival is the exact preference that separates Project Hail Mary 92 from The Martian 82, and here it is the whole plot. Male zeny 79 is the new measure of what this register can reach - a childrens-adjacent classic with no premise to work out, clearing the line on character alone - so the top of the range is anchored, not hopeful. The floor drops on re-derivation: Wilbur is passive and Charlotte carries every decision, so the lead the reader spends most time with is not the interesting one, and Artemis 69 now prices that failure mode a band lower than it did. Barnyard register throughout, with the childrens deduction that implies.

Published as adult fiction here, and the idea is stated by its narrator: Death is tired of collecting, and the same words that built the Reich are what saves one girl. Liesel learning to read stolen books while her foster family hides a Jew in the basement is a story where the motives are the content, and Hans, Rosa and Rudy each want different things in different registers - the character differentiation that earned Golden Son 92. The narration is the tell either way: Death interrupts constantly with bulletins and asides, which is a real opening risk in a profile where three books scored 30 for confusion - but the interruptions annotate a single legible thread rather than starting six of them, and the difference between multiplicity and simultaneity is the thing the log already settled. Bleakness is heavy and the ending is announced in advance.

Petr Ginz, the Prague boy who edited the Vedem magazine in Terezin, drew Moon Landscape and was murdered at sixteen - and the reason it belongs on this list is that the book is about a person who kept making things. What earned Seeking Allah 91 and Son of Hamas 75 was insight into how another group experiences the world plus a real examination of what is true, and this is that in Czech and about Czechs. Baobab is a serious literary imprint, not a schools publisher, and the fact face of the heaviest axis is documented history rather than invention. The risks are the obvious ones: it ends in Auschwitz, and it is written for teenage readers, so both the bleakness discount and the childrens-register deduction apply. Neither is a bar.

The single best idea in this whole screen and it is dramatised, not stated: Huck believes helping Jim escape is a sin he will go to hell for, decides all right then, I'll go to hell, and does it anyway. A book whose central act is a boy's conscience being wrong and his instinct being right leaves exactly the kind of thing behind that the log rates highest - and it is the reason this is read as an adult novel with a boy in it rather than a children's book, so the register deduction is near zero. First person, one concrete situation, and the raft keeps it moving. The known cost is structural: the last quarter hands the book back to Tom Sawyer for an elaborate fake rescue that undoes what came before, which is the thin-story-over-many-pages penalty that capped LOTR 84 and the dragged ending docked in The Martian 82.

The ancestor of every book in this log that scores on worked-out consequences: a man with a wrecked ship's inventory rebuilds shelter, agriculture, pottery and defence, and the book keeps the ledger honest - which is what the reader means by an author following the rules he lays down, and why both Weir novels are described as awesome on that axis. Nothing is declared that then fails to behave. Two costs, both large enough to keep it out of the A band's top. Long stretches are inventory and spiritual accounting with nothing happening, which is the digression penalty that docked Les Miserables 71; and it is twenty-eight years of one man alone, where sustained isolation was explicitly the thing docked in The Martian 82. Providence is theology carried inside the narrative rather than argued, so it stays on the right side of the no-apologetics line.

A precisely declared mechanism carrying a real argument: a tree that must be fed a lie to bear fruit, and the bigger the lie has spread the more truth the fruit gives back - and Faith, a girl in 1868 who is not allowed to be a naturalist, works it like an instrument. Declared rules add obligation rather than bonus, and this one is kept: the escalating cost of the lies is the plot. Won the Costa Book of the Year against the adult field, which is what crossover means. The risk has to be led with rather than mentioned: the spine of the book is Faith investigating her father's death, so a hard-filtered genre is not a subplot here but the structure - the rule is to watch for investigation-shaped plots inside otherwise eligible books and flag rather than drop, and this is one. Occult passes narrowly; the tree is used, never worshipped. SCREENED 2026-09-02 on axis:sex-portrayal, verdict mild, was [70, 80]. One reviewer states the novel insists women are stronger, cleverer, braver and better managers than any of the men in it, and the men on offer are a fraudulent naturalist father, a skull-measuring doctor and the pompous would-be MP Lambent. Mitigating: the Victorian setting is an explicit in-world reason for women's intellect being hidden, the father is genuinely learned rather than stupid, and Paul is a sympathetic male ally, so the contrast is real but light. The dock is the profile's stated convention (mild -2, moderate -5), not a measured magnitude - the axis has no high-contrast anchor yet.

t: Alenka v kraji divu a za zrcadlem (Alice)
why: Recorded with the risk in front of the case, because the downside here is a landing in the 30s rather than a merely mediocre one. The ideas are genuine and adults have argued about them for a century - logic and language taken literally until they break, identity questioned by everything Alice meets, and Looking-Glass built on a chess problem that actually resolves. But the profile's most reliable predictor is the confusing-opening filter, and part of its definition is a long stretch without knowing what the real story is or where it leads: after the fall down the hole there is no goal, no threat and no destination for most of the book, only a sequence of encounters. That is the diagnosis on The Gunslinger 30 and The Colour of Magic 30 almost word for word. Every individual scene is legible, which is why this is a wide range and not a block - but legibility scene by scene is not the test, since Caropisci 30 was legible scene by scene too and was dropped in chapter one for offering nothing the reader could attach to.

t: Dopis pro krale (The Letter for the King)
why: One decision drives 456 pages: Tiuri leaves the chapel on the night of his knighting vigil to answer a stranger's call, and can then tell nobody why, so the whole book is a boy carrying a duty he cannot explain and losing the thing he wanted most in order to keep it. Page time goes on that choice rather than on fights, which is the motives-over-action axis. Fast start, single clean thread, no magic in it at all - so nothing supernatural is declared and nothing binds, and the occult filter has nothing to fire on. Two pushbacks: it is a chivalric adventure for young readers and reads like one, and at 456 pages a single-errand plot risks the thin-story-spread-thin penalty rather than length itself, which was never the objection.

A 160-page novel with one device doing all the work: Felix explains everything he sees in occupied Poland as a story, because stories are what he has, and the reader understands what is happening several pages before he does. The idea is what stories are for and what they cost when they are wrong, and it states in a sentence, which is the test the sharpened short-form rule sets. He is worth rooting for without being noble, and every chapter opens on him wanting something concrete. Bleakness is real and the sequence gets bleaker, but this is bleak-with-an-idea rather than immersion in misery, the Animal Farm 78 distinction. The child's-eye Holocaust narration is also the Anne Frank 40 shape, so that is named rather than waved away; the difference is that this has a plot and momentum.

t: Orel Devate legie (The Eagle of the Ninth)
why: Historical fiction lands in the high 60s to mid 70s in this log - Exodus 68, Quo Vadis 66, Monte Cristo 75 - and this is the better-written end of that band. A crippled centurion goes north out of uniform to recover his father's legionary eagle, and the substance is his friendship with Esca, a freed slave who does not owe him it: two men with genuinely different reasons for the same journey, which is the differentiation axis. Research is solid, so the fact face of the heaviest axis is safe, and the reader has already been docked once for false history presented as fact in Ranger's Apprentice 74. What holds it under the A band is that the ideas are modest - loyalty and lost honour, well done rather than new - and Sutcliff's prose slows for landscape, which is where the description penalty sits.

t: Vitr ve vrbach (The Wind in the Willows)
why: Two books stapled together, and only one of them is for adults. The Toad farce is a comic set piece repeated four times; the Mole and Rat chapters are about the pull of home against the pull of the road, and the Piper chapter is a genuine attempt at awe. The problem is structural rather than moral: the parts do not connect to each other, which is exactly the objection that made Unfinished Tales 69 the lowest Tolkien and cost the Hitchhiker's sequels 70 their thirteen points. Nothing here is filtered - the Pan scene is awe, not a rite, and there is nothing to object to on content - it simply does not pay much on the axes this reader weights. Lands where Narnia 67 lands: pleasant, animal-nursery register, not enough to think about afterwards.

The thing worth taking away is not in the plot, because there is barely a plot: Petr Bajza narrates his small-town boyhood in a Czech mangled out of newspaper cliche, shop-sign formality and schoolbook grammar, and the comedy is what that language reveals about the adults who taught it to him. Written in 1943 by a Jewish author who was murdered in Auschwitz the next year, and read in Czech that fact is inseparable from the innocence on the page - which is the idea, and it is not one a translation could carry. Comic prose that works is not the risk here; the Pratchett Fs were never about humour, and Hitchhiker's 83 shows comic writing scoring well. The risk is that it is episodic with no story to build, which is the density penalty in its purest form.

t: Chlapec v pruhovanem pyzamu (The Boy in the Striped Pyjamas)
why: Recorded rather than proposed, and recorded low, so that the most famous title in this whole shelf stops resurfacing in every sweep. The failure is on the heaviest axis and it is at the centre of the book, not the edges: a nine-year-old who has lived in Berlin under the Reich does not know what a Jew is, cannot read the word Auschwitz, is unsupervised for a year, and finds an unwatched gap in the wire of an extermination camp he can crawl through repeatedly. Where nothing is declared, reality binds - and here reality is documented history, which the Auschwitz Memorial itself has publicly said this book misrepresents. That is the Ranger's Apprentice 74 objection, false claims stated as fact, except moved from the decoration to the load-bearing premise, and premise implausibility is one of only two things that has ended a book unfinished in the first chapters, at Mortal Engines 55. The prose and the ending are effective; they are effective on top of something that does not stand up.

t: Anna ze Zeleneho domu (Anne of Green Gables)
why: Carried entirely by its lead, which is the axis that beats worldbuilding when they compete: an orphan who talks too much arrives at a farm that wanted a boy, and the book is her wanting to be kept. Anne is interesting rather than merely likeable - the distinction that separates Speaker 90 from Artemis 69 - and Marilla's slow, unstated change is the best-motivated thing in it. Against that, there is very little to think about afterwards: no premise, no consequences, nothing declared, so the heaviest axis has nothing to grade, and the log's most common reason a competent book stalls in the 60s is exactly that. The register is a girls' classic of 1908. Sits where Narnia 67 sits, a couple of points higher on the strength of the protagonist alone.

The most-read Czech boys' book there is, and what it actually delivers is momentum and place: the Rychle sipy go into Stinadla, a hostile quarter with its own laws, and every chapter ends on a hook. Fast start and constant momentum is a stated preference with three S-band books behind it. Two things hold it down. First, the engine is a puzzle and a concealed society - a hidden Vont order, a coded manuscript, an object to be found - which is investigation-shaped, and while it is not a detective novel it is close enough that the filter has to be named. Second, there is not much to think about: the appeal is atmosphere and a boys' code of conduct, and the didactic layer Foglar built in has aged into moralising. This is a competent, atmospheric read rather than a book that leaves an idea behind.

t: Kde roste cervene kapradi (Where the Red Fern Grows)
why: The competence is earned, which is the specific thing the log says it wants and Divergent 58 failed: Billy works two years and saves fifty dollars in coins before he gets the two hound pups, and the book shows the work. After that it is a boy, two dogs and the Ozarks, with the training and the night hunts described in enough detail to be the substance rather than the backdrop. The idea is a plain one about what you owe an animal that gives you everything, and the ending is the grief that follows from it - bleak, but purposeful rather than immersive. Two pushbacks: the emotional register is straightforwardly sentimental in a way none of the log's higher scores are, and there is little to think about beyond the loss itself, which is where competent books stall.

One clean declared premise in the middle of Prague: a district where electricity simply does not work, so the block has been abandoned by the modern city and has grown its own economy, its own routes and its own people. That is a capability declared and the society visibly reorganised around it, which is the first and most-cited form of the heaviest axis, and the Czech setting is used properly rather than as scenery. But the same axis is the risk: the book does not explain why the anomaly exists, and the explanation is held back for later volumes - explained later in the same book is a valid defence, a sequel is explicitly not. So the central assertion is left standing on nothing for the length of this volume. Middle-grade register, two children as leads, and the plot is a hunt for a missing person, which is worth naming even though it is not a mystery novel.

Storch was an archaeologist writing to show how people actually lived in the Czech lands before history, and the value is that the material is real: tools, hunts, seasons, a clan's survival economics, illustrated by Burian. Where nothing is declared reality binds, and reality here is the archaeological record the author worked in, so the fact face of the heaviest axis is as safe as it gets. What limits it is the same thing that limits Ranger's Apprentice 74 - it is easy to read and there is not much to think about, and here the didactic purpose is openly the point, so scenes exist to demonstrate rather than to happen. Episodic by design, with a clan rather than a protagonist to follow.

The lowest-confidence line written in this screen, and the range is wide because of that rather than because the book itself is uncertain. What is known is real: a Czech original from Baobab, a serious literary children's imprint rather than a schools publisher, catalogued as an anti-utopian novel at 323 pages - so a society taken as the subject, which is the form the log grades hardest and where Divergent 58 collapsed. A Czech-original dystopia for teenage readers with the consequences worked out would sit in the Hunger Games 89 shape; one that borrows its furniture would sit in the Divergent 58 one, and nothing available here distinguishes the two. Recorded so the title sits in the database with its uncertainty visible rather than being found again by the next sweep; the occult check was not run either.

Recorded rather than proposed. The wit really is aimed over the child's head - Eeyore's self-pity, Owl's fake erudition, Rabbit's officiousness are adult jokes about adult types, and the prose is precise in a way almost nothing else on this shelf is. But that is a register, not an idea: nothing is at stake, nothing is declared, nobody wants anything that costs, and the thing the log rates highest is what a book leaves you thinking about. Narnia 67 was marked down for child leads and not enough to think about while at least having a plot and a war; this has neither. It is also episodic sketches rather than a story, which is the density objection. Two hundred pages of nursery register with excellent jokes in it lands below the B band, not in it. Re-derived 2026-09-03 under the new collection axis: a multi-story book is read from the front and put down on its weakest early pieces, not averaged and not skipped past. Ja, robot 55 is the anchor - the reader stopped after three stories, on the first story's cast and the third story's implausible behaviour, and never reached the pieces the prediction was built on. Already recorded rather than proposed, on excellent prose in a nursery register with nothing declared and nothing at stake. Episodes rather than a story is exactly what the new axis prices, and there is no arc here to earn a second sitting.

A declared constraint with a clock on it, and the whole book is the consequences: two brothers find a bag holding 229,370 pounds by the railway embankment seventeen days before sterling is withdrawn for the euro, so the money must be spent or it turns into paper. That is the form of the heaviest axis the log states most plainly - declare a resource and make it behave that way - and it is worked out honestly, including what happens when a nine-year-old tries to give money to the poor and discovers he has no idea who they are. Under the plot, Damian collects the lives of martyrs because his mother has just died, so the page time goes on what he wants and why rather than on the money, which is the motives-over-action axis with the widest evidence in the log. Carnegie Medal, published here by Argo rather than a children's imprint. Three named risks: the narrating voice is a nine-year-old's throughout, which is where the register deduction bites; the saints appear and speak to him, which needs the reader's own ruling; and faith is a thread rather than a subject, which is the stated preference but sits close to the line.

Recorded rather than proposed, and recorded with its uncertainty visible. A seventeen-year-old Czech boy has school, parents, friends and a girlfriend all going fine and is drowning anyway, with the depression written as water rising around him - hence the title. What is genuinely in its favour: a single legible first-person situation, a contemporary Czech voice, and a lead who is rootable without being admirable. What holds it in the C-to-B band is the axis this reader weights most: a state of mind is not an idea you can name in a phrase, and there is no premise whose consequences get worked out - the same reasoning that screens down mood-driven books elsewhere in the log. Sustained low spirits is the 1984 60 objection, which is mild but real, and the lead is close to the reader's own life phase without being it. Stated plainly: this entered the queue on a cheap-model score where the model did not know the book and was reading the library's own blurb, so the range is a flag rather than a finding.

The six leads are individually distinct - a naturalist, a telepath, an illusionist, an empath - which is the positive case reviewers keep giving it credit for even when panning everything else. But 'everything else' is exactly axis:ideas: the recurring, specific complaint across reviews is not that the magic-academy premise is thin but that it is never worked through - 'no plot, barely,' 'no world building, no plot, no tension beyond the sexual/romantic one,' 'there is sadly no story to tell.' That is the C-low question answered directly by sources rather than inferred, so I stopped there. A who-to-trust elimination dynamic runs through the year, which is an investigation-shaped subplot worth flagging rather than a whodunnit the book is actually about, so gate 1 clears. The five abilities read as invented categories (elemental, telepathic, empathic) rather than real-world occult practice, but I did not chase the Depiction question - axis:occult stays open rather than cleared.

t: Buh malickosti (The God of Small Things)
why: A real, examined idea survives contact with the plot: caste as a rule that crushes a forbidden love and the family around it, not a background setting. Ammu is divorced from her husband before the affair with Velutha, so the relationship never crosses a marriage or engagement - axis:infidelity does not fire and is not graded. Two risks pull it toward the line. Chapter one deliberately opens past the ending and jumps as far back as 1876 before the present-day thread is clear; several readers report real disorientation even though most settle in - closer to Anne Frank's testimony-form risk than to the multi-POV chaos of the Gunslinger/Discworld DNFs, but genuinely unresolved rather than dismissible. The bleakness is not the mild, occasional kind the profile mostly discounts - it is sustained and immersive for the whole book, closer to 1984 60 ('too depressing') than to Animal Farm 78, which delivers its bleak idea in short, efficient form. The signals field flagged 'childrens' off the phrase 'detske nevinnosti' (childhood innocence) in the annotation; this is adult literary fiction with graphic violence and caste politics, not a children's book, and axis:childrens should grade near zero.

t: Eleanor se ma vazne skvele (Eleanor Oliphant Is Completely Fine)
why: Single first-person narrator with a clear starting situation (Eleanor's rigid solitary routine, then the concert) - no confusing multi-thread opening, no detective frame, no occult. The 'infidelity' impression from the annotation is a one-sided imaginary infatuation with an unmarried man, not a marriage betrayal, so that axis does not apply. The book is built almost entirely on the axis this reader rates highest - what a damaged but sympathetic protagonist wants and why - with a friendship (Raymond) at the center rather than solo survival, similar in shape to how companionship over isolation lifted Project Hail Mary over The Martian. It resolves toward recovery rather than collapse, unlike the bleak DNFs in the log. Some risk from the childhood-trauma backstory, but it is disclosed rather than dwelt on at length.

The opening is a single concrete situation done well - a Kurdish genocide survivor meets a wounded alien in Central Park - and reviewers single out this stretch as 'extraordinary,' 'witty,' and 'thought-provoking,' carried by what she wants from the bond rather than by spectacle, the axis that also topped Red Rising and Mockingjay. The book earns its ideas rather than gesturing at them - consciousness, game theory and the ethics of empire are the actual subject, close in spirit to the hard-science rigor that made Project Hail Mary score 92. It does not reach that range because multiple reviews, including the New York Times, describe the back half as 'impenetrable,' technobabble-heavy, with a 'shakily-defined' supporting cast diluting the character focus that made the opening work, and an ending the Times itself calls 'dizzyingly unsatisfying.' No occult content surfaced - this is hard SF, not a system drawn from real-world magic.

t: Kniha Noveho Slunce (The Book of the New Sun)
why: Single protagonist (Severian) with one concrete starting situation - expulsion from the Torturers' Guild for mercy shown to a prisoner - so shape one of the opening filter, several plot lines starting at once, does not fire. Shape two is the exposure, and 2026-08-28 promoted it from a vague different-flavour-of-difficulty note to the named thing: the reputation, confirmed across multiple reviews, is for deliberately engineered confusion - a non-linear, omission-heavy unreliable narrator and dense archaic prose full of unglossed invented and revived vocabulary, where the first time through may confuse. Having a situation is not enough if the reader lacks the context to read it, which is what Caropisci 30 established: a heist in progress, perfectly followable, dropped in chapter one because the terms and the stakes meant nothing yet. The range is unchanged and is conditional on that risk not firing; if it fires this is a 30, not a 55. Ideas are strong enough that they are not what would stop it - memory, guilt, a torturer as a genuinely sympathetic lead - which is why it is priced rather than blocked, with real deduction for opacity and heavy description.

Single legible narrator investigating one family for a book about the atomic bomb, so the opening filter is clear, and the invented religion passes both occult tests - it is founded on the page as a deliberate sham by its own characters, and its central rite is a mutual-affection ceremony rather than spellcasting or divination. Dropped 2026-09-03 on the faith axis, which acquired its first anchor today. Ja, robot 55 was abandoned in part because a story in which robots invent a god read to the reader as satire on the main religions and on blind faith, and he said plainly that he did not like it. A religion founded on lies its own prophet admits are lies, and knowingly believed anyway, is that same treatment as the book's comic engine rather than as one thread in it. The technological-hubris idea is real and is what keeps this graded rather than rejected - Animal Farm 78 is the tone comparison and stands - but the narrator is an observer more than an agent for much of the book, so there is nothing to set against the deduction.

t: Kral byvaly a kral budouci (The Once and Future King)
why: The Lancelot-Guinevere affair is prominent - the spine of two of the four books - but the whole work's subject is wider than the affair (Arthur's education and the Round Table's founding happen without it), so this is subplot rather than premise. It is framed as a tragedy that helps destroy the kingdom, not as liberation or a romance to root for, so it lands as subplot+condemned - a few points off, not a reject. Merlyn's magic is invented Arthurian-legend whimsy (animal transformations used to educate a child), not real-world occultism, and no rite is performed as ritual. The book carries the kind of large, examined idea (might versus right, justice, the cost of chivalry) this reader consistently rewards, similar in scope to Tolkien's mythic fantasy (LOTR 84, Silmarillion 80), and Arthur is a broadly rootable protagonist across the arc. Discounted a little for the affair subplot, the whimsical children's-book tone of the opening third (a small cost, per Ranger's Apprentice 74), and the tragic ending.

t: Moby Dick: Bila velryba (Moby Dick: The Graphic Novel (Campfire Graphic Novels))
why: The catalogue record is not Moby-Dick itself: this is the Campfire Graphic Novels comic adaptation (script by Lance Stahlberg, art by Lalit Kumar Singh), 88 pages, aimed at students as an educational classics-in-comics product. Compressing the whole novel to 88 illustrated pages leaves no room for Ahab's monomania to be worked out on the page the way the profile rewards - I would list axis:ideas under risks - and the format (picture-book pacing, all-ages abridgment) matches the picture-book/slight-adaptation band rather than the default C-low band. One source is the C-low budget and this is a decisive, not a close, call.

Kay's Tang-dynasty-inspired setting is researched and richly written - reviewers call it 'complexity and beauty' - which is the positive case. But the same reviewers flag what this reader marks down elsewhere: the magic 'exists on the margins,' one critical review says Kay 'hints at magic... without ever giving real information' and leans on 'magical seeming coincidences' rather than worked-through consequences, and the plot 'meandered' with characters that 'didn't feel as real or developed' as his other work. That is the axis:ideas doubt the C-low gate asks about, so I stopped there. I overspent the 1-source C budget to 2, because the second search (on a shaman-ritual subplot) turned up occult-relevant material before the gate closed the question: a wolf-spirit transformation rite is performed on-page on a named character, which reads closer to real-world shamanism than to a declared mechanical system, so axis:occult is genuinely open rather than merely unexamined by default.

The unicorn's quest costs her something real and irreversible: living briefly as a human under the name Amalthea, she learns love and regret, and the book's own closing line is that she is now different from every other unicorn because of it - a premise whose consequence is carried through to the end, not just declared, which is the axis this reader rewards most. The task line's 'detective' signal is a false positive; there is no mystery to solve, just a quest. Magic here reads closer to fairy-tale convention than to invoked occultism: Schmendrick's power is an innate, unpredictable gift rather than ritual, and Mommy Fortuna's 'witch' carnival is mostly staged illusion, with only the harpy established as genuinely real - I did not find an on-page invocation or ritual scene, but I also did not find a source describing the magic system in mechanical, declared-rules terms the way Sanderson's is documented, so axis:occult is a residual, not a cleared, risk. It is a beloved fantasy for 'youth and adults both' per the Czech annotation, which pushes toward some axis:childrens cost the way Narnia paid a little at 67.

Opens on one concrete situation - a bomb kills a minister, and the same night a fellow student turns up in Razumov's room confessing to it and begging for help - not the several-plot-lines-at-once problem that sank the Gunslinger and Discworld. What follows is almost entirely interior: why Razumov betrays Haldin for a safe, ordinary life, and what the guilt then does to him, which is the axis Speaker for the Dead 90 and Mockingjay 91 both score on. The risk is that Razumov's defining act, unlike theirs, is a betrayal of a friend for self-interest - closer to a flawed anti-hero than a hero, though the book spends its second half on him seeking out and confessing to the sister of the man he betrayed, which is a real redemptive arc rather than a Coriolanus-style descent. Since 2026-10-24 that direction of travel is a positive rather than merely not disqualifying: a lead who understands what he was and decides not to be that man is what the reader named as the best thing in Licanius 92-96, so the range rose two points. Bleakness is present (Razumov ends deaf and crippled) but resolves into a quiet, cared-for exile rather than sustained misery, closer to Les Miserables 71 than to 1984 60.

Single first-person narrator (Offred) from a deliberately disorienting start ('we slept in what had once been the gymnasium') that withholds information gradually rather than juggling several plot lines at once - a hard opening but a legible one. No occult content (no magic or divination in any synopsis) and no detective/mystery frame; the coerced Ceremony and the secret Nick relationship are not marriage-scope infidelity (Offred's own marriage predates and is voided by Gilead). The book leans hard on interiority - what Offred wants, remembers and fears - the axis that topped the log in Mockingjay (91) and Speaker for the Dead (90). But this reader marked 1984 (60, 'too depressing') down specifically for sustained totalitarian bleakness, and Gilead is at least as oppressive; Offred's fragments of memory, love for her daughter, and small acts of resistance give a bit more warmth than Winston Smith gets, so this sits a shade above 1984 rather than well above it.

Anne Elliot broke off an engagement to Wentworth years before the book opens under family pressure, and the whole novel is her living with that regret while he re-enters her world - motives and what a character wants are again the entire book, the axis Pride and Prejudice 75 scored on ('the entire book, the axis that tops the log'). No marriage exists at any point the plot turns on, so axis:infidelity does not apply - this is a broken engagement, not a betrayal within one. The risk against Pride and Prejudice's precedent is momentum: there is less social maneuvering and comic incident driving events forward, and more sustained internal waiting, so it could land either side of Pride and Prejudice depending on how much that quietness reads as thin versus deliberate. Opens on a single concrete situation - the Elliot family's vanity-driven finances - not a multi-thread start.

Gurnah names a real, sustained idea and follows it: colonialism reaches Yusuf through trade and debt long before any European appears on the page, and the 'paradise' of the title curdles the deeper he travels - a worked consequence, not just a mood, which is why I did not treat axis:ideas as a risk at the C-low gate. What holds the score down is that Yusuf spends most of the book as property being moved and traded rather than choosing - the acted-upon pattern that capped Oliver Twist at 57 - with only a late, partial turn toward taking control of his own fate, plus a slavery-and-servitude bleakness with no companionship payoff to offset it the way Project Hail Mary's Rocky does. The novel deliberately echoes the Quranic Yusuf-and-Zulekha story (Yusuf is desired by his master's young wife Amina), but this is a literary parallel folded into a coming-of-age journey, not the engine of the plot - remove it and the debt-bondage, trade-caravan story Gurnah is actually telling still stands, so it grades as a subplot, not a premise, and the tale it echoes ends in resistance rather than consummation.

t: Skoricove kramy (Cinnamon Shops (The Street of Crocodiles))
why: A 1934 collection of interlinked short prose pieces, not a novel, and squarely literary fiction - the exact combination the ladder flags as usually landing under 68. The pieces are unified by voice and a recurring father figure but have no single throughline premise to name as an idea, unlike Silmarillion (80), which succeeded without a protagonist because it had mythic scope to lean on; Schulz's stories are mood- and memory-driven rather than idea-driven. Default C-low band, one source, no further research per the ladder.

Glory tells the same kind of story that made Animal Farm work for this reader - a fable of how a dictatorship actually functions, using animal stand-ins to make the mechanism visible - and the political idea itself is clear and well-sourced (the 2017 Mugabe coup, point for point). Animal Farm scored 78 partly by doing this in under 150 pages; Glory runs to a full novel and multiple reviews say the length works against it, not for it - the Irish Times calls the animal device 'awkward and distracting' that 'obstructs the reader's emotional connection to characters,' and other readers report the book 'wordy,' 'hammering its point home,' with animal characters that are 'ciphers,' not three-dimensional. That is close to the opposite of what this reader wants (a protagonist that is both interesting and worth rooting for) stretched over more pages than the idea needs, which is why I did not stop at C-low - the idea itself is sound, it is the execution at length that costs it.

The Promise names a real idea and sustains it across three decades - a broken promise to a Black servant tracks the country's own unkept promises from apartheid through Mandela to Zuma - and critics single this out as the book's actual achievement rather than incidental backdrop, so axis:ideas is the lean, not a risk. It does not clear higher because none of the three Swart siblings is easy to root for: Anton is 'cynical and self-destructive,' Astrid is drawn as entitled and self-serving, and Amor, the most sympathetic, is largely passive and guilt-driven rather than acting. The family's decline across four funerals is sustained bleakness with little relief. Astrid also has two marital affairs (leaving her first husband for the man she was cheating with, then cheating again in her second marriage) - real axis:infidelity content, but it is one sibling's subplot inside a larger family saga, not what the book is about, and it is framed critically, her hypocrisy and entitlement being the point, so per the subplot-condemned cell this costs a few points rather than triggering a reject.

Mariko's affair with Blackthorne is a subplot, not the premise - the book is built around Toranaga's political rise and Blackthorne's adaptation to Japan, and would still be a substantial book without the romance. But the framing is squarely approving: Mariko is trapped in a loveless, abusive marriage to Buntaro, her feelings for Blackthorne are treated as her true love, Blackthorne formally asks Toranaga to let her divorce her husband, and her death is a heroic political sacrifice rather than any consequence of the affair - simply unpunished. Per this axis's own grading, subplot plus approving framing lands at 30-40 regardless of the book's other real strengths (strong political intrigue, a rootable protagonist in Blackthorne, genuine culture-clash ideas). This is not a judgment on the whole book by reputation - historical epics have done fine in this log (Count of Monte Cristo 75) - it is this specific axis, graded as the rules direct, capping it well below where the rest of the book would otherwise sit.

t: Soumrak dne (The Remains of the Day)
why: A single first-person narrator (the butler Stevens) framed by a clear situation - a motoring trip taken while reflecting on his career - not a multi-thread opening. No occult, no detective frame, no marriage-level infidelity (the unspoken longing for Miss Kenton is never acted on and she is unmarried at the time it matters). The book is almost purely built on the axis this reader rates highest: what a character wants and why, examined with total rigor against Stevens's own chosen definition of dignity - the same kind of interiority that topped the log in Speaker for the Dead (90) and Mockingjay (91). The risk is the protagonist himself: Stevens is passive and self-deceiving by design, closer to Gregor Samsa's un-rootable passivity (Promena, 58) than to an active lead, and the tone is a quiet, sustained regret rather than dystopian despair, so bleakness costs a little but less than it did in 1984 (60).

Opens on a single thread (Billy Williams, 13, starting work in a Welsh coal mine in 1911) before widening quickly to a large ensemble at an aristocratic party - not the multi-thread confusion of the Discworld/Gunslinger DNFs in this log, since each character is introduced with a clear identity rather than left ambiguous, but the sheer size of the cast (seven narrators, told out of chronological order) is a real risk for a reader who has DNF'd before on exactly this shape of opening. Historical family sagas have landed consistently in the high-60s in this log without much held against them beyond scale - Quo Vadis (66), Exodus (68), Les Miserables (71) - and this sits in that same cluster: broad historical scope and readable momentum, not a strong single idea to lean on beyond 'WWI touches everyone.'

t: Tess z d'Urbervillu (Tess of the d'Urbervilles)
why: Hardy names one real idea and works it through completely: the sexual double standard punishes Tess for a rape while Angel's own premarital affair is forgiven, and Hardy states this as the point, not a subplot the reader has to infer - that clears the axis:ideas bar the way Animal Farm 78 and 1984 60 both do. But 1984 was marked 'too depressing' at 60 with a lighter bleakness load than this: a child's death, a rape, desertion, and a hanging stacked without relief, plus Tess is repeatedly acted on rather than acting (rape, abandonment, poverty, execution), the same passivity pattern that held Oliver Twist to 57 and Gregor Samsa to 58. A late reunion with Alec happens while Tess is technically still married to Angel, but it follows her desperation after he deserts her, not a courted affair, and Hardy frames it as her being cornered, not as romance - a subplot point, not the premise, so it does not reject.

The book states its idea plainly and follows it through two braided timelines: people who wall themselves off from a crisis to wait it out, instead of living through it, lose more than the adults who chose it as a shortcut realize - Kirkus specifically praises that the message 'animates' rather than 'overpowers' the story, and it was shortlisted for a translated-fantasy award against Le Guin and Mitchell, suggesting it holds up past the children's shelf. It is marketed and reviewed as a children's book, which this reader's log does not penalize much on its own - Little Prince scored 82 and Hobbit 84 on ideas plus lightness of touch - but one Icelandic reviewer's 'dark, funny and grim' suggests real stakes rather than a purely soft register, which is why I did not push this toward the Little Prince end of the band. Discovery (axis:discovery, 2026-10-24): a girl wakes early into a world gone wild and has to learn what happened, the arrival case the reader named beside Project Hail Mary 92; partial, because the legend rather than the world is the spine, so +2.

t: Ines, ma draha (Ines of My Soul)
why: Ines Suarez's long relationship with conquistador Pedro de Valdivia, who remained married in Spain throughout it, is described by multiple reviewers as the book's central love story, not a subplot mentioned in passing - genuine doubt on premise versus subplot, recorded rather than resolved into a reject, since removing it would not remove the conquest-of-Chile narrative or Ines's own arc entirely, which argues subplot rather than premise. Framing leans approving rather than condemned: reviews call it a 'fiery love affair' and a 'passionate love,' Time praises the book's 'expansive definition of romance,' and Ines is not narratively punished for it - which puts it in the subplot-and-approving cell of the infidelity rule rather than the subplot-and-neutral one, so the band is widened up from that lower floor rather than down from the neutral band. Kirkus separately flagged the prose as overloaded with historical exposition ('a voice more suited to an encyclopedia... overwhelms the story'), which is the axis:density risk that could pull this toward the low end even further.

t: Superman (Superman: Whatever Happened to the Man of Tomorrow?)
why: A short, single-story graphic novel (two 1986 comic issues), so axis:short-idea-driven applies: no penalty for length, but the positive case rests entirely on the idea, and there is a real one - Superman breaks his own code and kills a villain to save everyone he loves, then voluntarily gives up his powers forever as penance, which the story and its critics consistently frame as the actual point rather than as a twist. That is the axis a single-premise short work earns credit on, and it is the same thing that makes Animal Farm 78 work despite being short. The villain, Mister Mxyzptlk, is an invented fifth-dimensional imp with no invocation, priesthood or resemblance to real-world witchcraft, so axis:occult clears on both tests. The risk is tone: several critics single out the Silver Age trappings - Bizarro, a comic Toyman and Prankster, a villain literally 'wearing Brainiac as a hat' - as broad and campy rather than adult, closer to Ranger's Apprentice 74's register than to anything darker, which caps how high the idea alone can carry it.

t: Alone on a mountaintop (Alone on a Mountaintop)
why: The title piece is a real, reflective memoir essay about solitude during a stint as a fire lookout, where the narrator reaches an honest, examined realization that solitude is a state of mind rather than a place - the kind of testimony insight that earned Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 its score, not mere first-person reportage. But this is a slight, three-piece bilingual sampler rather than a sustained memoir, and nothing establishes that the other two pieces carry comparable weight - unlike the sustained self-examination that made the Qureshi memoir land, a short assembled sampler risks being built to show range rather than to carry one idea through. Using the default band pending whether the other two pieces hold up as well as the title one.

t: Amalie Zubata a jednorozci pani (Amelia Fang and the Unicorn Lords)
why: Same calibration as Ranger's Apprentice 74 and Narnia 67: childrens fantasy clears the line only when it carries some idea or edge past its young audience. This is a friendship rescue-quest for ages 6-10 (find and save a friend's mother) with invented gothic-monster worldbuilding (vampires, yeti, a grim-reaper-style character) but no idea beyond the quest itself found in sourced summaries, so axis:ideas is doubtful the way it is for the thinner end of that comparison band.

The book is a mosaic built from Mawer's own family records, giving named wants to an orphan who longs to go to sea, a seamstress dreaming of London and a soldier marrying before the Crimean War - that is motives carrying the page time the way Red Rising 95 and Mockingjay 91 reward. But it is fragments of real ancestry rather than one worked premise, closer to Unfinished Tales 69 (pieces not logically connected) than to Silmarillion 80, which earned its no-protagonist structure through dense mythic material this domestic mosaic does not have. No single idea to name, so per gate 3 I put axis:ideas under risks and stop here; occult is unexamined at this exit.

A memoir of Irish immigrant poverty told with unflinching honesty about hunger, alcoholism and child death, which is exactly what earns points on this axis in the log rather than the form itself -- Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75 both rest on genuine examination of what is true and insight into how another group lived, and reviewers single out McCourt's balance of humor with tragedy in the same register that made tragicomic Saturnin 78 work. It is narrated throughout in a child's present-tense voice, the same small pushback that marked Ender's Game down to 87 without keeping it out of the top tier, and the sustained hardship is the mild, discount-only bleakness objection, mitigated by family and community rather than solitary suffering the way companionship beat isolation in Project Hail Mary 92. SCREENED 2026-09-02 on axis:sex-portrayal, verdict mild, was [76, 86]. The pattern repeats rather than being one man: Malachy Sr drinks the wages and finally deserts, Peter Molloy is Limerick's champion drinker with Nora Molloy left worrying about food, Laman Griffin is cruel, and McCourt has described the book as a hymn to the exaltation of women. Held to mild because critics note Angela herself proves ineffectual and is drawn unflatteringly, Aunt Aggie is unpleasant, Frank the clever narrator is male, and Pa Keating, Mr O'Halloran and Mr Timoney are redemptive men - so a blanket incompetent-men reading is not supported. The dock is the profile's stated convention (mild -2, moderate -5), not a measured magnitude - the axis has no high-contrast anchor yet.

t: Armenska genocida (Armenska genocida: priciny, prubeh a osobni svedectvi udalosti z let 1915-1922)
why: The book pairs a causal history of the genocide - modernisation and rising nationalism turning an ethnic minority into a target for two collapsing empires - with a dedicated section of eyewitness testimony, and reviewers specifically note the author keeps perspective by including Turks who tried to help rather than flattening the story into collective blame. That is the 'examining what is actually true, plus insight into how another group experiences the world' that made Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75 work, not the flat first-person account that stalled on The Diary of a Young Girl 40. Risk: one critical review calls parts of the book a tangent-heavy assembly of loosely connected chapters, the same fragmentation problem that capped Unfinished Tales at 69, and genocide testimony is far bleaker than the mild-penalty bleakness the reader otherwise tolerates, so I keep the range modest rather than lean up on the strong testimony angle alone. Occult and opening-structure do not meaningfully apply to this genre, so confidence is medium rather than high despite this being a full pass.

t: Artur a zlate lano (Arthur and the Golden Rope)
why: Gate 3 exit at the low band -- this is a 56-page illustrated picture book for roughly ages 5-9, the exact form the rule names as landing in the low band. There is no idea beyond a straightforward hero's-quest structure to put under axis:ideas. Norse-myth trappings (Thor, Fenrir) are noted but occult status is left unexamined per the ladder, since nothing under 68 is ever proposed regardless of the answer.

A sequel, and the log shows sequels are not a uniformly safe bet - Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70, though Mockingjay rose to 91 on this reader's other trilogy. The founding-law premise's under-explained grounding carries over unresolved, and a documented complaint that one lead's character arc loses focus to another's across the series echoes the protagonist-thinness pattern that cost Artemis 69 against Project Hail Mary 92 by the same author. A new character built entirely from other people's transplanted parts, wrestling with what makes him himself, is the motive-and-identity material Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 both score well on, which keeps this from falling further. C-low, occult unexamined per the ladder.

Names an idea easily - a law that lets parents retroactively end a teen through organ-harvesting 'unwinding' - and the book dramatizes a consequence directly (a recipient explaining his graft came from an unwound boy). But research turned up a real doubt on axis:ideas: multiple reviewers found the founding compromise underexplained (how the war produced exactly this law, how parents so readily sign) and the three leads reduced to an action-story surface, criticism close in kind to what dropped Divergent 58 on premise logic that never fully worked under thought. Splitting attention across three teens also dilutes the single-thread momentum that carried The Hunger Games 89 and Ender's Game 87. Landing under the line; the author's series share research so this overspent the one-source C-low budget.

t: Biblicke pribehy pro neverici deti (Biblicke pribehy pro neverici deti)
why: This is a didactic retelling and commentary on the whole Old and New Testament, written to argue that Europeans need to know the Bible to understand their own civilisation - a real thesis, but theology and apologetics as the entire subject of a book is exactly what earns nothing on its own by the reader's rule; Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 worked because it was a personal testimony that examined what was actually plausible, not a reference-style survey of scripture. This book is explicitly marketed to and read as a children's book (a national bestseller in the kids' category), which pulls further from what has scored well here. There is a nameable thesis, so this is the default band rather than the no-idea band, but axis:faith as the whole subject is a real ceiling.

Gate 3 exit.
