Multiple reviews independently call the book 'empty,' 'forgettable,' and short of a real thought-provoking dilemma despite an inventive virtual-reality premise, with characters that fit common archetypes rather than being distinctive. That is a real doubt on axis:ideas, established from sources rather than assumed, so this exits at the C-low default per the measured base rate.

On the corrected sexual axis, explicitness and crudeness both cost regardless of moderate volume, and a depicted rape-fantasy passage is the crude end of the treatment dimension rather than coarse language. Held on 2026-08-28 with the comparator corrected. Ruled 2026-08-28: The Witcher 53 is a CONFOUNDED row and cannot be cited as a sexual-axis floor - the reader named two independent causes, 'both magic (witches) and the sex was through out the series', and the magic is the occult filter, the most severe objection in the log. The clean crudeness anchor is Ready Player One 55 - 'it was the kind of sex that reduced it that much', the kind and not the amount - with Artemis 69 confirming crudeness costs even in small doses. VOLUME IS UNANCHORED and must not be priced as cheap: Red Rising 95 and Valka stareho muze 87 are BOTH low volume on the reader's own account ('mostly one chapter of a book'), so neither shows what sustained non-crude content costs, and the log's only high-volume row is the confounded one. Note also that VSM's single chapter was still enough to become his one named complaint, so light volume is not free. The old wording described 'the crude language that alone put The Witcher at 53', which was wrong twice over - the magic was the larger cause there, and language is not this axis at all. Measured against Ready Player One 55 instead, a depicted rape fantasy is worse than the orgasm-chair phase, so the range holds. Bleakness compounds it.

Full research. Pawel's refusal to sign a collaboration pledge and his slow disintegration under Sovietization is a motives-driven account -- the axis that carries Speaker for the Dead 90 and Ender's Game 87 -- and multiple independent reviews name the same worked-out idea, the birth of homo sovieticus under omnipresent fear, which clears the axis:ideas doubt test at gate 3 rather than triggering it. Single-protagonist structure with a concrete starting situation, not the multiple-plot-line confusion that sank Guards! Guards! and The Colour of Magic to 30. Risk is the sustained bleakness of an occupation narrative, discounted the way 1984's misery cost it points off a strong premise at 60, plus the length/density typical of a documentary-grounded historical novel.

Opens on one concrete situation -- Hai about to jump from a bridge, stopped by an elderly widow calling out -- rather than several threads at once, the pattern this log rewards (Hitchhiker's Guide 83). Reviewers consistently describe Hai as sympathetic despite his passivity and self-loathing, driven by legible motives (guilt toward his immigrant mother, shame over addiction) rather than by incident, the same emphasis that tops this log in Red Rising 95 and Mockingjay 91. The main risk is density: multiple reviewers call the prose 'flowery,' and heavy description with comparatively little plot is a recorded penalty distinct from the protagonist axis it does not touch.

A nameable idea - survivors outside a protective Dome were physically fused to whatever was near them when the bombs went off - but reviews describe the execution as better in concept than in follow-through, with plot and characters feeling shallow and action sequences substituting for logic getting from one point to the next. That pattern of a striking premise the book does not fully work out is exactly what cost Mortal Engines 55 and Divergent 58, both of which the reader liked less for the setup not holding up under thought than for anything else. Exiting at the below-the-line gate rather than doing full research.

t: Citanka Neila Gaimana (The Neil Gaiman Reader)
why: Reader-curated from close to six thousand reader votes and reviewed positively (one professional review singles out a revenge-fantasy novella for the strength of its single-minded focus), so the pieces included are not weak by outside consensus. But the book is explicitly assembled as an introduction and survey rather than a single work - nearly fifty stories across decades of tone plus five short novel excerpts chosen to represent rather than complete a longer work - so there is no one throughline idea the way a finished novel offers, the same reasoning that keeps any story collection out of the higher bands here regardless of the quality of its parts. Landing under the line.

The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings both score 84 partly on heroism and friendship themes, the calibration for a brother-bond story scoring well on relationship and motive grounds; five brothers raising each other and one of them building a literal bridge for the family's redemption fits that pattern. Les Miserables 71 and Unfinished Tales 69 are the calibration for dense or fragmented prose costing points even when the underlying material is strong: one sourced review reports the non-linear, heavily figurative prose genuinely obscured two major plot beats, so this sits between the two ends rather than at either.

A Booker-winning novel about a retired judge, his orphaned granddaughter and a cook's son navigating a Himalayan insurgency and New York City immigrant life, weighed against colonialism and class. One widely quoted review states plainly that 'it is a rare novel that succeeds when every supposedly good idea in it fails,' crediting the prose rather than the ideas for carrying the book -- exactly the case this log treats as a warning sign, since being beautifully written is not itself an idea and claiming one that does not hold is the surest way to a wrong estimate.

Reception is genuinely split rather than settling either way: some critics list this among a small handful of essential Kerouac titles, others single it out as one of his worst. Its blend of childhood memoir with an invented pulp-adventure myth (a caped figure battling a hidden evil beneath the narrator's hometown) gives it more of a nameable idea than the straight travelogues - a boy's imagination as armor against real fear - but the dense, surreal prose that divides critics matches the heavy-description-over-story pattern the log discounts in Les Miserables 71 and Unfinished Tales 69. No settled case either way, so it is treated as a competent book that likely sits just under the line.

t: Dva roky, osm mesicu a osmadvacet noci (Two Years Eight Months and Twenty-Eight Nights)
why: Divergent 58 ('ideas borrowed from other books and assembled without cohering') and Mortal Engines 55 (abandoned on premise logic) are the calibration for ambitious premises that do not hold together under thought. Sourced reviews of this book split the same way: several praise the imaginative scope, but multiple others reduce the sprawling jinn-war plot to 'the bare outline for a superheroes movie' and call it preachy or overextended despite the ambition, the same coherence doubt that put Divergent below the line. That doubt is enough to exit here without deciding whether the underlying reason-versus-unreason idea would otherwise have carried it.

t: Dve mista na slunci (A Closed and Common Orbit)
why: Full research. Two character studies -- an AI adjusting to an illegal body, and her friend's escape from indentured clone labor -- converge on a shared question of what makes someone a person, told through relationship and interiority rather than event. That is the same territory that put Project Hail Mary at 92, here built on found-family and mentorship instead of solo survival, matching the reader's noted preference for companionship over isolation. Risk: more than one review calls the plot meandering, the thin-story-spread-thin cost the reader dislikes even in a book he otherwise likes. The two threads are clearly divided and converge late, not the several-plot-lines-at-once confusion that sank Guards! Guards! and The Colour of Magic. Leaned on protagonist and motives.

A family saga about siblings fixated on the house their father's fortune bought and their stepmother took from them; reviews are split on whether it earns its length, one calling it 'not a beautiful story, but... beautifully written' and another noting it 'starts out strong, but then ultimately doesn't go anywhere.' That is closer to a mood or a well-turned sentence than a premise whose consequences the book works out, the distinction that separates a book like Animal Farm 78 -- an idea worth thinking about -- from one that merely reads well.

A close third-person account of what goes on inside Shostakovich's head across three moments under Stalin and Khrushchev - the reader consistently scores highest on interiority over event, from Red Rising 95 down through Speaker for the Dead 90, and reviewers describe this book as almost entirely that: an intimate narrative of the composer's mind rather than a plotted biography. The idea it leaves behind is nameable and squarely the reader's kind - what courage and cowardice actually look like under sustained pressure, the same territory Animal Farm 78 covers through allegory. It is docked for the same mild bleakness discount that applies across the totalitarian-setting books, and for secondary characters, especially the women around Shostakovich, being reported as thin ciphers rather than differentiated people.

REVERTED 2026-08-28, third pass, to the pre-today range. The two-point raise rested on the withdrawn claim that Valka stareho muze 87 showed volume to be cheap; the reader corrected that book to low volume. Nothing else here moves: the deduction is carried by the coarse, objectifying register, which is the crudeness dimension, and Ready Player One 55 anchors that directly without needing the withdrawn comparator. Reviews describe the sex scenes as pervasive across the whole book and across several relationships, rendered in direct rather than euphemistic terms, with more than one reviewer calling one lead's approach to sex transactional and objectifying rather than revealing - high volume with a coarse edge, not the light case that left Red Rising 95 untouched. RAISED to this range earlier on 2026-08-28 from [60, 70]; held here on the second pass. Ruled 2026-08-28: The Witcher 53 is a CONFOUNDED row and cannot be cited as a sexual-axis floor - the reader named two independent causes, 'both magic (witches) and the sex was through out the series', and the magic is the occult filter, the most severe objection in the log. The clean crudeness anchor is Ready Player One 55 - 'it was the kind of sex that reduced it that much', the kind and not the amount - with Artemis 69 confirming crudeness costs even in small doses. VOLUME IS UNANCHORED and must not be priced as cheap: Red Rising 95 and Valka stareho muze 87 are BOTH low volume on the reader's own account ('mostly one chapter of a book'), so neither shows what sustained non-crude content costs, and the log's only high-volume row is the confounded one. Note also that VSM's single chapter was still enough to become his one named complaint, so light volume is not free. The volume share of the deduction is already discounted in this range and the coarse, objectifying register is what remains, which the correction does not touch. The grief-and-brothers, motives-driven engine is the strength, the same axis that carries Pride and Prejudice 75 and Mockingjay 91, but Pride and Prejudice earns 75 with essentially none of this content, so this cannot sit above that anchor.

t: Jak uchvatit draci klenot (How to Seize a Dragon's Jewel)
why: BLOCKED 2026-08-31 by inheritance. An earlier volume of this same series is rejected on the occult filter, and a middle-grade series read out of order is not a route. Prior assessment, kept for the audit trail: Book ten of a long-running middle-grade quest series, with Hiccup an outcast hunting a magic jewel to save his people - a formula-driven fetch-quest rather than a worked idea, in the vein of Ranger's Apprentice 74 (easy to read, not much to think about) but without that book's clean action momentum, since this instalment is described as heavier and grimmer than the one before it. Sequels are not a safe bet in this log - Hitchhiker's fell 13 points into its sequels - which is the same direction a tenth entry in a franchise points. Exiting at the below-the-line gate rather than researching further; this specific volume's occult status was not established (the witch Excellinor is central to the series but this summary shows her scheming and negotiating rather than performing a rite on the page), so axis:occult stays unexamined and kept in deps.

Full research. The linked-twin-death mechanic is a premise whose political consequences are actually worked out -- killing one twin kills the other, so a political rival can be reached by proxy -- the kind of consequence-following-from-premise the reader rewards in Project Hail Mary 92 and docks Divergent 58 for lacking. Cass's motive, wanting equality for a caste she was excluded from by chance, is a clear want, not a passive role. Risk: more than one review calls the later revelations shallow, a worldbuilding-depth concern, and the apartheid-under-catastrophe setting carries the kind of sustained bleakness that cost 1984 points off a strong premise. Leaned on ideas and protagonist.

t: Kdo me vzal prvne za ruku (The Hand That First Held Mine)
why: Dual-timeline novel alternating a 1950s art-world romance with a present-day story about new parents; the historical thread centers on Lexie's affair with her unhappily-separated but still-married employer Innes Kent, a subplot rather than the premise since a second, unconnected present-day thread carries equal weight, so it is graded rather than rejected. The affair is framed sympathetically rather than condemned -- their love is described as enduring -- which this log's infidelity rule treats as a real drag even at subplot level. Beyond that the book reads as a well-executed but familiar exploration of motherhood and identity without a distinct premise worked out the way Animal Farm 78 or Labyrint sveta a raj srdce 70 work theirs out.

Names a clear idea - a child raised outside the world of the living who must eventually choose to rejoin it - and it won major awards, but a close read of reviews turns up the same kind of underexplained-mechanics doubt that has cost other books here: readers and at least one academic piece describe the novel as closer to a linked story collection than a worked plot, the antagonist organisation's motives and a key supernatural creature's nature are repeatedly called thin or unresolved, and the ending is repeatedly called rushed. That is the axis:ideas doubt the ladder asks about, close in kind to what kept Unfinished Tales at 69, the lowest-scoring Tolkien in the log, on pieces not fitting together. A child protagonist costs little on its own - The Little Prince 82 shows the life-phase rule barely applies to a well-carried short work - so the number is driven by the plotting doubt, not the lead's age.

Gate 1 checked and cleared: despite the detective signal, the plot is a revived-soldier redemption arc against an alien occupation, not an investigation, so the whodunit filter does not apply. Gate 3: no source discusses a worked-out idea beyond the isekai-style revival hook -- a soldier killed by his own side and given a second chance by a mysterious stranger -- so axis:ideas goes to risk and this exits at the C-low default per the ladder. One primary source, spent across both checks.

Project Hail Mary 92 beats The Martian 82 partly because of a companion in isolation rather than solo survival. This book's alien presence, deliberately left ambiguous as real-or-hallucination, plays a similar companionship-in-isolation role, and the real engine of the book is the protagonist's dawning realization of what he sacrificed for ambition, a motives-driven arc close to what tops this log. Checked axis:infidelity: reviews describe the marriage failing from distance and neglect during the mission rather than from an affair on either side, so it does not fire and is set aside. Kept below the Project Hail Mary band because the isolation itself, and a marriage that ends rather than a bond that is actively chosen, carries real bleakness risk.

Mortal Engines 55 ('DNF on the worldbuilding alone') and Harry Potter 51 ('the worldbuilding itself doesn't hold up') are the calibration for when a magic or tech system is declared but not carried through. Independent reviews of this book describe the spellbook magic as deliberately minimal, explicitly noting curious readers 'won't be fully satisfied about how magic works,' alongside a predictable plot and thin side characters - the same shortfall pattern, though gentler in degree since nothing here is asserted and then broken, it is simply left vague throughout.

Trade critics gave this strong marks individually - Kirkus and Booklist both starred it, and reviewers compare the best pieces to M.R. James and Poe - so this is not a weak collection by outside consensus. But an anthology of thirty-one pieces in different registers has no single premise the way a novel does, and the axis that rewards a worked idea has nothing to lean on across a book this varied even when individual stories land well; one review's own verdict that the author is strongest in 'the sustained continuous sweep of long fiction' and that the short pieces are 'sketches of unequal merit' matches exactly why a collection is graded on the ideas axis and comes up short structurally rather than on quality. Landing under the line despite the good reviews.

t: Krev kristaloveho kvetu (To Bleed a Crystal Bloom)
why: Gate 3 exit. No idea to name beyond a captivity-romance premise -- a survivor kept safe behind a boundary by a protector who could also execute her. Reviews describe one lead as constantly dark and distant and the other as alternating between distraught and irritating, the same protagonist failure that separated Artemis 69 from Project Hail Mary 92 by 23 points. No axis:ideas to lean on, so this sits under the line at the C-low default. One source spent, within budget.

A single-thread satire, easily nameable in a phrase - a bureaucrat swallowed by a crocodile keeps discussing his salary and official duties from inside it, embracing his entrapment as a path to fame rather than despairing - in the same idea-driven-short-work register Animal Farm scores 78 in and Saturnin scores 78 in on comic voice. Unlike Metamorphosis 58, whose protagonist Gregor is passive and whose bleakness arrives all at once, Ivan here stays comically, absurdly active about his own predicament, so the two risks that sank Metamorphosis do not obviously apply. It is docked because Dostoevsky left the story unfinished, so it has no real resolution - a real cost under story density even though the prose itself is short.

The premise, gods overthrown eighty years ago and a magic-poisoned world that ends in a small way every seven days as a direct consequence, is a nameable idea the author is reported to follow through on: contaminated soil, mutation and scarcity are all shown as the world's actual response to that founding act, the same declared-capability-has-consequences discipline that pushed Project Hail Mary to 92 over The Martian. Magic in this world behaves as an ambient environmental force rather than a rite performed by anyone, which passes the mechanism escape the way an engineered system would, though no source confirms directly that no character performs an invocation on the page. Risk: several independent reviewers report a name- and place-heavy start that took roughly 100 pages to settle before the world made sense, the kind of multi-thread opening that has hurt books before, though those same reviewers rated the book highly once it did.

t: Kudy do kamkoli (Which Way to Anywhere)
why: A blended-family adventure where two sets of stepsiblings who dislike each other must cooperate after their baby half-sister is kidnapped into a world reached through the protagonist's map-drawing gift - a nameable idea (a fractured family forced to actually become one, tied to an environmental-stewardship subplot about a species humans nearly destroyed), closer to what Little Women 79 and The Hobbit 84 do with friendship and family than to a plot-only adventure. Professional reviews single out pacing and momentum as strengths rather than confusion, which matters given how heavily this reader penalises an unclear multi-thread opening. The protagonist's ability is an inherited cartography gift, not invocation or ritual, so it reads as the mechanism escape rather than real-world-mould magic. Four child leads plus several antagonists (a bounty hunter, a robot, a pirate) introduced quickly is a genuine multi-pov risk, so this is not pushed toward the top of its band.

Opens on one clear situation, a father agreeing to take in his disabled older son for the summer, and Brian, the 13-year-old left to actually do the caretaking, is reported as rootable: overwhelmed but trying, with a growing bond to his brother that reviewers single out. That earns the protagonist lean. But reported content stacks up hard against it: a scene of neglect that kills a family dog, ongoing poverty and squalor, and a 19-year-old resident encouraging the 13-year-old protagonist to sexually experiment, the kind of crude-register content that cost Artemis 69 even in small doses, compounded by reviewers describing the whole book as a 'knife edge' toward an unhappy ending, closer to 1984's sustained-misery register (60) than to a book that earns its sadness gradually. Estimating low up front given how concretely these risks are already documented rather than waiting to be surprised by them.

t: Mag & Satori v Parizi (Satori in Paris)
why: Even by the author's usual standard this is judged a minor entry: reviewers call it slapdash and thin on incident, and note it lacks a strong secondary character to pull the narrative forward, leaving a solitary, melancholy travelogue. There is a nameable conceit - a trip taken in search of enlightenment that never quite delivers one - but critics agree the execution does not carry it off, which matches the short-idea-driven axis at its weakest: a slight, occasional piece rather than a worked short book. Using the lower band.

t: Maruska Pulnocni a Zahada Mesice (Marnie Midnight and the Moon Mystery)
why: Ranger's Apprentice 74 and the Chronicles of Narnia 67 show childrens fiction clearing the line only when some idea or friction survives the young audience. This is a lighter illustrated chapter book for ages 7-9 built on a single hook (why moon-magic lessons got cancelled) resolved through an adventure quest, with no idea beyond that hook found in sourced summaries, so axis:ideas is doubtful the way it is for the thinner end of that comparison band. Gate 1 checked: the mystery framing is a plot device for a school adventure aimed at young children, not a whodunit the reader is meant to solve, so not rejected on axis:detective.

Les Miserables 71 ('solid but less tight... famous lengthy digressions') and the sequel pattern already in this log, Hitchhiker's dropping 13 points from its first book to its later ones (83 to 70), both point the same way here. Multiple independent reviews describe this entry as much slower than the book before it in its trilogy, wandering into 'ultimately pointless tangents' and leaning on philosophical monologue over plot. That digression-over-story pattern is enough doubt about axis:ideas holding up to exit here.

A literary review of this book describes its sexual violence as excess, with passages that could have profited from being left as subtext, and describes the threat of sexual violence toward the lead as inescapable throughout the book rather than confined to a single incident. Under the corrected sexual-content grading, explicitness and volume both cost on their own regardless of how seriously the material is handled, which is the exact exemption this axis no longer grants. Artemis 69 shows that crude or excessive sexual-treatment content costs even when the rest of a book is otherwise capable, and 1984's 60 'too depressing' mark is the reference point this log uses for sustained heavy content. Recurring, graphically-described sexual violence running through the whole book, on top of the sectarian violence already flagged, is heavier than the old estimate priced in. The protagonist-and-motives case for the lead himself, wanting to be accepted, the same axis behind Sunrise on the Reaping 87 and Mockingjay 91, remains the strength, but the ceiling needs to come down to reflect how much of the bleakness here is specifically sexual content rather than general misery.

t: Muj bratr ocean (The Sea Is My Brother)
why: Kerouac himself rejected this manuscript as 'a crock' and refused to publish it, and professional reviews largely agree it is minor: 'a boring book, all proclamation and no plot,' 'too brainy for its own good,' of interest mainly to scholars and devotees rather than general readers. That is a harder verdict than the digressive, thin-plot criticism of the author's better-known travel writing, and no outside review nor the author's own later judgment credits it with a landed idea. A short, occasional early work, so the lower band applies.

t: Muz v labyrintu (The Man in the Maze)
why: Full research. The book is a three-way moral study of whether a wronged, self-exiled man should help the people who cast him out, the same motives-over-action territory that put Speaker for the Dead at 90 and Ender's Game at 87 -- interiority and moral consequence carrying the book rather than event. Risk comes from two established problems, not hypothetical ones: reviewers uniformly describe the female characters as sex objects with no depth, the same crude-treatment failure that cost Artemis 69 even with a coherent world, and the ending is called abrupt with the maze's own internal logic left unresolved, a hold-up-under-thought gap. Leaned on ideas and motives; discounted for the sexual-treatment and worldbuilding gaps.

The book's own reputation is as a document of restlessness and freedom rather than a worked idea with traced consequences - it is described as prioritizing raw experience over narrative structure, with long uninterrupted stream-of-consciousness sentences and episodic road-trip vignettes. That is close to the failure mode Les Miserables 71 and Unfinished Tales 69 were marked down for - thin story spread over many pages, digression standing in for plot - and there is no single idea here as clean as the ones that carried Animal Farm 78 or Labyrint sveta 70. A companion character's repeated infidelities within his marriages are incidental to a friendship-and-travel plot rather than its premise, so they do not drive the score either way. Landing under the line on axis:ideas.

t: Nez potkala me (Before She Met Me)
why: Sustained interiority into one man's mind is the axis this reader responds to most - Red Rising 95, Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 all lead on it - and this book is close to nothing but that: Graham's jealousy over his second wife's life before they met is tracked obsessively from the inside. But the same interiority tracks a slide into paranoid, eventually violent obsession, and that specific pattern - a protagonist the reader is asked to keep following as he curdles - is what cost The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 22 points against Sunrise on the Reaping, the two books otherwise matched on author, world and form. Graham is not rootable by the book's end, which caps this below the interiority axis alone would predict.

The population-math doubt already identified for this premise carries forward, since the mechanism at its centre was never fixed, only built on further. The bureaucratic satire around the order of killers (audits, quotas) is the kind of worked-out institutional consequence the log rewards when an author follows his own declared rules, but it sits alongside protagonist criticism - a lead operating alone and turning grim - that recalls how a slide toward a harder, less rootable character cost The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 against Sunrise on the Reaping 87 by twenty-two points on that same axis. C-low, occult unexamined per the ladder.

The premise is a closed society that lies about having left Earth, walling itself off instead - a nameable idea in the Divergent 58 / Mortal Engines 55 mould, where a social or physical setup is asserted but the reader is asked not to press on it. Published reviews of this book flag exactly that: the ending resolves through what one reviewer called a shaky chain of coincidences, and readers report dull, uninteresting stretches in the early chapters describing life inside the walled society. That is the same failure Divergent scored 58 for - a premise assembled rather than followed through - so axis:ideas is a real risk here, not a formality. Exiting at the below-the-line gate rather than doing full research.

t: Nuz (Knife: Meditations After an Attempted Murder)
why: Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 ('genuinely examines what is plausible and believable') and The Diary of a Young Girl 40 ('testimony that did not work') are the two poles this log's memoir axis swings between. Sourced reviews of this memoir split toward the weaker pole more than the stronger one: the Washington Post calls it 'meandering and frequently trite,' and another review flags repeated sermonizing in the second half, even though other reviewers and a National Book Award nomination found real value in it. That split is enough doubt to exit here rather than assume it lands on the Qureshi side of the axis.

t: O dusi a divce (O dusi a divce)
why: Fourteen short illustrated fables set in a mountain range, where talking animals and personified elements (Death, Life, water) each carry a small parable about human life - closer to a slight, whimsical collection than to a single worked-out premise. The Little Prince 82 and Animal Farm 78 show short allegory can score well, but only when one idea is developed at length; here the ideas are scattered one per short tale rather than sustained. Illustrated, aimed at ages 9+, and the character/emotion rules that short idea-driven work suspends do not add points on their own, so this lands in the low band rather than the default one.

Concludes the same fused-survivors trilogy, with Partridge now ruling the Dome he once fled and discovering that power does not make good on his promise to expose his father's lies. The premise-versus-execution gap noted by reviewers across this trilogy - imaginative concept, thinner plotting - matches the pattern that kept Mortal Engines at 55 and Divergent at 58. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not a safe bet in this log: Hitchhiker's fell 13 points from its opener into its sequels. Exiting at the below-the-line gate rather than doing full research.

t: Plavec ve tme (Swimming in the Dark)
why: Opens on a single concrete situation -- a university agricultural work camp where Ludwik meets Janusz -- rather than several threads at once, the pattern this log rewards (Hitchhiker's Guide 83). The book is narrated as a direct address explaining what Ludwik wants and why throughout, and its central conflict -- naming other homosexuals to the state in exchange for a passport, or staying with Janusz -- is the kind of premise whose consequences get worked out that this log values (Animal Farm 78, Labyrint sveta a raj srdce 70). The ending is bleak but reviewers describe it as bittersweet with real hope rather than despairing, which keeps it at the mild bleakness discount rather than the sharper penalty that held down 1984 to 60.

t: Pod septajicimi dvermi (Under the Whispering Door)
why: Wallace's arc from a self-centered lawyer to someone who sacrifices for others tracks the motives-over-action axis that tops the log in Red Rising 95, and runs the opposite direction to the unrootable case in Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65, where the lead's slow descent into evil cost 22 points against the same author's Sunrise on the Reaping 87. The afterlife system (reapers, a Manager, ferrypeople) is invented and run like an office - manila folders and rules of engagement rather than invocation, devotion or a priesthood - so it passes the occult test the way Sanderson's Allomancy does, unlike the real Greek-pantheon veto behind Percy Jackson 57. Risk: several reviewers call it a slow read carried by tea-shop scenes more than plot, closer to the thin momentum that held back Unfinished Tales 69 than to a tightly-driven book, so I lean on protagonist and motives rather than the loosely-explained afterlife rules.

t: Posledni dny Rabbit Hayesove (The Last Days of Rabbit Hayes)
why: Opens on one clear situation, Rabbit being moved into hospice, and stays close to what she wants in her remaining days: to make things right for her daughter and family. That is the motives-over-action axis that tops the log, carried by a protagonist reviewers consistently call rootable and full of life rather than passive. Reviewers describe the tone as balancing heartbreak with humor and call the ending pitch-perfect rather than merely sad, which is closer to Mockingjay 91's family-and-love-focused register than to 1984's sustained misery, though a minority of reviewers did find the terminal-illness material too heavy, the same discount that capped 1984 at 60. Leaned on protagonist and motives, with bleakness flagged as the axis that could pull the number down if the sadness reads as more sustained than reviewers suggest.

Gate 3 exit, mandated: literary fiction and an explicit short-story collection (ten stories plus an epilogue). The short-idea-driven suspension removes the character-arc penalty but adds nothing on its own, and there is no single premise to hang axis:ideas on across a collection of discrete lives. One source used, within the gate-3 budget.

Full research. Enoch Wallace's century of isolation, kept apart from humanity by the very secret that connects him to a wider galactic community, is close cousin to the interiority-over-action, cross-culture-understanding axis that put Speaker for the Dead at 90. Risk is two soft, reviewer-noted costs: an ending called too neat, and a theological/political stance reviewers call preachy in places, further than the reader's faith-as-a-thread-only rule wants. Leaned on motives and protagonist; risk on faith and on density from the more digressive passages reviewers flag.

t: Previtem snadno a rychle (Little Sod's Next Step)
why: Gate 3 exit. This is adult satire narrated from an infant's point of view -- a voice conceit, not a worked idea with consequences -- so there is nothing to put under axis:ideas. Saturnin 78 shows Czech comic voice can carry a book on character alone, but that is an already-read comp, not evidence for exempting an unread book by a different author; the mechanical gate-3 test still calls for exit. Default band, one source.

Sibling co-leads Biran and Sanda are driven throughout by loyalty, political conviction and stewardship of their people rather than by set-piece action alone, which is the axis that tops the log in Red Rising 95 and Golden Son 92. Reviewers repeatedly single out the sibling relationship and character payoff as the strongest thread, matching what worked in Mockingjay 91 (least arena, most motive). Risk: it is a sequel, and sequels are not a safe bet in this log - Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70 across its sequels - so I keep the range modest rather than lean up on the strong reviews alone.

t: Rozum proti vire (Rozum proti vire: Velka turecka valka 1683-1699)
why: This is a narrow military-history chronicle of one campaign, the Great Turkish War of 1683-1699, part of the author's wider series on Ottoman-era wars, and even a sympathetic reviewer calls it a 'rough diamond' that leaves out whole theatres - the Venetian naval war, the Poland/Moldavia front - rather than synthesising the war into a thesis. Absent a stated idea beyond narrating the campaign, per gate 3 I put axis:ideas under risks the way a chronicle-only nonfiction book has nothing to lean on the way Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 does with its examined, first-person thesis about faith, so this exits at the below-the-line band on one source; occult is unexamined at this exit.

The Booker-winning novel about a woman collecting her alcoholic brother's body after his suicide and revisiting a buried family memory; critics note the book may be 'lacking in plot' and one review calls it 'overwrought and pretentious,' the same profile as a book that reads well sentence by sentence without a premise it works out, unlike an idea-driven short work like Labyrint sveta a raj srdce 70 or Animal Farm 78. The narrator Veronica admits to inventing some of her own memories, which raises doubt about whether she is a rootable center rather than merely a voice. The catalogue's detective signal was checked and does not apply: the plot concerns grief and memory, not an investigation.

Mockingjay 91 and Sunrise on the Reaping 87 both score on interiority and motive over event, with a lead worth caring about carrying the book. Shuggie's devotion to his alcoholic mother and his wish to be seen as normal are the entire engine here, the same structure. Reviewers describe the book as unremittingly bleak, including graphic sexual assault and repeated suicide attempts, well past 1984's 60 'too depressing' mark, which is the discount risk weighed against the strong protagonist case; the Booker Prize recognition and reviewer consensus on genuine emotional truth keep it above that floor.

t: Sirotcinec slecny Peregrinove (Miss Peregrine's Home for Peculiar Children)
why: Full research on the actual book behind this key. Jacob's single-POV search for what happened to his grandfather opens on one concrete situation, the legible start the reader rewards -- the standard that sank Guards! Guards! and The Colour of Magic to 30 for multiple plot lines starting at once. The invented peculiar-power system (time loops, shapeshifting) is mechanism, not real-world occultism, so it clears the occult test. Risk: reviewers flag a romantic subplot bordering on incest given the age gap and time-loop mechanics, a content problem in its own right, and a pacing shift partway through from mystery to adventure. Leaned on worldbuilding and ideas, discounted for content and momentum.

Names a real idea - a world without death solves overpopulation by licensing sanctioned killers - but it does not fully hold up under thought: a critical read flags that the stated glean quota is mathematically far too small to check population growth at the scale the book describes, which is the institution's stated purpose, the same kind of unaddressed-consequence gap that sank Mortal Engines 55 on its energy economics. Reviews also repeatedly call the two apprentice leads flat and forgettable against the vivid setting, echoing the exact failure mode that cost Artemis 69 against Project Hail Mary 92 - strong worldbuilding did not rescue a thin lead there either. Landing under the line.

Same fused-survivors premise as the trilogy opener, with Partridge now outside the Dome he escaped and the wretches he meets trying to survive among the smoke and ash. The premise-versus-execution gap noted by reviewers for this trilogy - a striking concept that leans on action to cover thin plotting - is the same pattern that kept Mortal Engines at 55 and Divergent at 58. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not a safe bet in this log: Hitchhiker's fell 13 points from its opener into its sequels. Exiting at the below-the-line gate rather than doing full research.

A steampunk adventure collection following gunslinger Fastynger van Houten; Czech reader reviews call it light entertainment ('oddechovka') that undersells its own premise -- one reviewer states the author 'did not use the potential of an otherwise very interesting theme' and found the connective thread between the stories weak. That is the ideas-doubt pattern rather than an idea-driven allegory or a book that carries the A band on voice and character the way the comic Czech classic Saturnin 78 does. Occult status (the setting's 'cruel mages') is left unexamined per the C-low rule.

t: Strucna historie vecneho zivota (A Brief History of Living Forever)
why: The immortality-and-digital-consciousness premise, with an authoritarian biotech state built out of its consequences, is a real worked-through idea in the mould of Project Hail Mary 92, where second-order consequences of a speculative technology are actually explored, which is why this does not exit at the cheap gate. The risk is structural: a detailed critical review reports the book split across a dead narrator and two estranged adult children in different countries, with the disembodied framing eating narrative momentum, closer to the fragmentation that cost Unfinished Tales 69 ('pieces aren't logically connected') than to the density that did not cost The Silmarillion 80.

A legend-styled parable about a man who wanted only to save himself but is forced into the role of messiah for an entire society; the premise -- predestination and an imposed identity escapable only through self-destruction -- is a real, nameable idea, but it mirrors the exact pattern that held Kafka's Promena (The Metamorphosis) to 58 despite a real idea: axis:bleakness and axis:protagonist both fired there because Gregor is passive and the misery arrives without relief, and this book's publisher description names the same outcome, escape 'only at the cost of self-destruction.' Occult risk is real but unresolved: the false messiah gains 'magic power over the lives of others,' which could fail the source test if enacted on the page.

The premise is a first-contact puzzle - colonists on Asgardia must work out why the planet never evolved sound communication before it kills them - which is the kind of consistency question Project Hail Mary 92 rewards when it is actually followed through. But this is Novakova's early novel and Czech reader ratings place it well below her later, more acclaimed work rather than confirming the puzzle pays off, closer to how Mortal Engines 55 was marked down for a premise whose logic was not actually worked out. Per gate 3 I put axis:ideas under risks on that gap and stop; occult is unexamined at this exit.

The clean crudeness anchor is Ready Player One 55 - 'it was the kind of sex that reduced it that much', the kind and not the amount - with Artemis 69 confirming crudeness costs even in small doses. t: V zakulisi srdce (Behind the Scenes of the Heart)
why: Professional memoir of a Czech cardiologist recounting career milestones ('world firsts') interleaved with short literary vignettes; reader reception is mixed, with several reviewers noting it reads as a flood of names and procedures aimed at insiders. That falls short of what earns points on the memoir axis in this log -- Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75 both rest on genuinely examining what is true and giving insight into how another group experiences the world, not on cataloguing professional achievement.

Full research -- the premise (a supernova kills everyone over thirteen, leaving children to run civilization) is a clearly worked-out idea, so gate 3 does not fire on it alone. But multiple reviews converge on the same failure that dragged Divergent to 58: characters that read as stereotypes rather than people, decisions that critics call arbitrary, and solutions called implausibly grand -- one reviewer says it reads more like an outline than a finished novel. Golden Son scored 92 in part because Darrow, Sevro and Mustang each think and want visibly different things, the opposite of interchangeable archetypes reacting predictably. Leaned on protagonist and motives as the capping axes; risk on worldbuilding for the implausible plotting. The child-run setting is graded on axis:childrens as content, not vetoed.

Critics single this out as the most significant of the author's posthumously published books, valuable for what it shows about his development as a writer - but that is praise for its place in literary history, not for a worked idea a reader can follow. The style is described as fragmented and non-linear even by the author's own already-loose standard, built from tape transcriptions and jazz-influenced improvisation rather than a traceable throughline. That is the same trait that made Unfinished Tales 69 the lowest-scoring Tolkien in the log, twelve points under The Silmarillion, on pieces not being logically connected to each other. Landing under the line.

t: Vyhodme ho z kola ven (One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest)
why: Opens on one concrete situation, a single ward on a single morning through one narrator (Chief Bromden), the same legible-start pattern that scored well for Hitchhiker's Guide 83. McMurphy is a protagonist worth rooting for who rallies the other patients and ultimately sacrifices himself for them, the same self-sacrifice-over-solo-survival trait that pushed Project Hail Mary to 92 over The Martian's 82. Heavy page time on why McMurphy pushes back against Ratched and why the other patients follow him fits the motives-over-action axis that tops the log. Leaned on protagonist and motives rather than the individual-vs-institution idea alone, because the ending (McMurphy lobotomized, then mercy-killed) carries real sustained-bleakness risk of the kind that capped 1984 at 60, even though most of the book balances that tragedy with rebellion and dark humor rather than unrelieved misery.

Gate 3 exit. This is literary fiction whose own reviewers are split on whether its central conceit (cars as allegory for a fetishized, privatized world) actually works -- one professional review explicitly doubts the allegory holds up and states the author is no Komensky, an unfavorable comparison to an author the reader has read and scored 70 for Labyrint sveta a raj srdce on a nameable idea; a reader review separately calls it 'zero narrative credibility.' That doubt is exactly the gate-3 test, so this exits at the default band rather than paying more to confirm a low score.

t: Z Mitfordu do stare vlasti (In the Company of Others)
why: Gate 3 exit. This is a faith-centred family-secrets story, eleventh in a long-running series, resolved mostly through the reading of an old journal, a structure some of its own reviewers found dragged. Reviewers frame its payoff as the love of God dissolving old resentment, closer to theology as the subject than the reader's faith-as-a-thread-only rule allows, and there is no idea beyond the family-secret reveal to anchor axis:ideas against that risk. A minor mystery subplot (a stolen painting) is present but reviewers' praise centers on the emotional/spiritual payoff, not on solving the theft, so the detective filter is flagged rather than triggered. Exits at the default band; this used two sources against a one-source budget, spent establishing both the plot and its reception before the call was clear.

Built on the same central mechanism - a killing quota meant to check population growth - which outside review flagged as not adding up at the stated scale, a doubt inherited rather than resolved. Sequels are not a uniformly safe bet in the log: Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70 while Mockingjay rose to 91 on the same author's other trilogy, so no assumption of improvement is made here without evidence the execution changes the underlying math. C-low, occult unexamined per the ladder.

A sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's 83 to 70. This book's world rests on the same compromise-law premise a reviewer found underexplained, and that doubt on axis:ideas does not go away with time. The storyline of a character built from other people's parts working out what makes him himself is the motive-and-identity material the log rewards - Speaker for the Dead 90 and Mockingjay 91 both score on exactly that focus - which keeps this from dropping into the bottom band. C-low, occult unexamined per the ladder.

Independent reviews of this prequel describe its human cast as fixed types marching from plot point to plot point ('the Virtuous Woman Done Wrong', 'the Self-Serving Rabblerouser') and its machine antagonists as shallow and cartoonish, the reverse of what made Golden Son 92 work, where reveals felt earned because Darrow, Sevro and Mustang each visibly wanted different things. Multiple fan reviews describe the prequel series overall as a decline from the original. I would list axis:ideas under risks given the reported thinness, and take the default band per the ladder.

t: Jak vysoko klesneme (How High We Go in the Dark)
why: This is explicitly a novel-in-stories - most chapters first published as standalone short stories about a plague unearthed in the Arctic permafrost - rather than a continuous narrative, so it lands on the litfic-plus-collection rule: axis:short-idea-driven suspends the character tests but adds nothing, and with no sustained protagonist there is no single throughline idea to lean on the way Animal Farm 78 does, a short work that lands on one worked-out idea. Instead the fragmented, many-strand shape is closer to what capped Unfinished Tales at 69, pieces that are not logically connected to each other. Reviewers note nearly every story is essentially about bereavement, closer to the sustained-bleakness discount that cost 1984 60 than to a book meant to be enjoyed sitting inside. Per gate 3 I stop here rather than research each linked story; occult is unexamined at this exit.

t: Mapa Jinozemi Emily Wildove (Emily Wilde's Map of the Otherlands)
why: Reviewers describe the fae magic here as deliberately confusing, to the point that 'even the exceptions to the rules have exceptions', which the book embraces rather than resolves. That is close to the opposite of the self-consistency the reader has rewarded (Project Hail Mary 92) and penalized the absence of (Divergent 58, Harry Potter 51). It is also a sequel, and the log's one measured sequel comparison shows a real fall-off (The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy 83 down to the Hitchhiker's sequels 70). A missing-scholar subplot is investigation-shaped but a flag rather than a veto, since the book's core satisfaction is the fae world and romance, not solving a case. Leaning on axis:worldbuilding and axis:sequels rather than a specific idea.

t: Misto na svete (A Place in the World: Finding the Meaning of Home)
why: Reviewers describe this as an eclectic assemblage of essay fragments on home, mixing lyricism, recipes, gardening tips and travel description rather than a single examined thesis. The memoir form the reader has rewarded before needed either genuine examination of what is true (Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91) or documented insight into a group's lived experience (Son of Hamas 75); this reads closer to descriptive reminiscence about the author's own homes, without either. Named idea, 'place is fate', is real but stays a mood rather than something worked out, so I would list axis:ideas under risks. Exiting at the default band per the ladder rather than researching further.

t: My vsichni neradi (All of Us Villains)
why: A multi-POV tournament-to-the-death premise praised by reviewers for developed characters, but critical reviews also flag a predictable plot and a death-tournament that delivers surprisingly little death on the page, a declared stake the book does not carry through, the same kind of broken commitment that cost Divergent 58 and, on a plausibility basis, Mortal Engines 55. I would list axis:ideas under risks and take the default band. The occult question is left unexamined at this exit, though the tournament runs on family curses and blood-bound spellcasting, vocabulary close enough to real-world occultism to warrant a real look if revisited.

The annotation's premise, Shadowhunters being murdered while Clary and Jace are bound together by a rival, matches the Mortal Instruments arc where an investigation-shaped subplot (who is behind the killings) runs alongside a romance plot; that is a flag under the detective filter, not a veto, since the reader's satisfaction is the romance and world, not solving the murders. Beyond that the series leans on YA romantic melodrama and plot incident rather than the examined motive that carried Ender's Game to 87 or Speaker for the Dead to 90, so I would list axis:ideas under risks. Default band per the ladder.

t: O cem se nemluvi (Behind a Closed Door)
why: The plot is a couple forced by a gamified app into escalating illegal tasks and then a run from the law, not a sexual relationship, so filter 6 does not fire, and the satisfaction is not a whodunit either, so the detective filter does not fire. Under the corrected axis, most reviewers describe the sexual content as concentrated early and mostly implied - genuine mitigation on the volume dimension, the same shape as Red Rising (95) staying largely undocked because there was little to affect - but a minority of reviewers flag actual explicit passages and degrading treatment of women, which is a real, if smaller, echo of the crudeness that held Artemis to 69 despite consistent worldbuilding. Nothing in the sources establishes strong interiority or motive-driven characters, so this reads as a plot-mechanics thriller rather than one built on what characters want and why - the axis that tops the log - which caps it below the 'nice read' band even with reviewers praising a coherent, twist-heavy plot. Leaned on sexual-content because that is the axis the new rule changes; motives is a risk because the sources say little about character depth one way or the other.

An epic-fantasy trilogy of political intrigue, revolution and war between empires; reviews describe strong characters and a mechanical-construct magic system but no single premise whose consequences the book is built around, unlike the friendship and ideas that carry The Lord of the Rings 84 despite a plot the reader found thin. It is a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's 83 to 70. Occult status is left unexamined per the C-low rule, since the setting includes a goddess's sword, dark magic and a malevolent being that could fail the source test.

An espionage MacGuffin quest: a prison rescue, a friend's dying words, then a hunt for a lost Tsarist library to stop a dormant Soviet satellite weapon. This is plot-mechanics and globe-trotting incident rather than page time on why characters want what they want, the same imbalance that made even chapters of Golden Son 92 get skimmed when it leaned toward action. Not a whodunit (there is no central puzzle to solve, only a chase), so it clears the detective filter, but I would list axis:ideas under risks: there is no standalone idea beyond the chase itself. Default band per the ladder.

t: Sip a vitr, dyka a more (Opowiesci z meekhanskiego pogranicza (tom 2))
why: The annotation itself describes this as woven from individual stories across the world's regions rather than a single followed plot, matching the series' known linked-story-collection format; the one book in the log that succeeded without a single protagonist did so as a short, dense mythic work (The Silmarillion 80), not a multi-region ensemble serial. It is also a sequel, and the log's one measured sequel comparison shows a real fall-off (The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy 83 down to the Hitchhiker's sequels 70). Short-story format suspends the character-and-emotion rules but adds nothing on its own, so leaning on axis:multi-pov and axis:sequels rather than a specific idea. The occult question is left unexamined at this exit, despite the setting's explicit mix of magic, politics and religion/cults.

Senk is an established Czech genre short-fiction writer with fifteen-plus stories published in Ikarie, and this is a themed collection unified loosely by 'gods' across different SF settings rather than a single novel. Reader comments on his other collection describe stories that develop well and then end abruptly on one page, or are barely science fiction at all, an uneven-execution pattern that argues for treating axis:ideas as a risk: a themed collection unified only by a loose motif has nothing to lean on the way Animal Farm 78 does with one idea followed all the way through, and the multi-strand, uneven-quality shape resembles what capped Unfinished Tales at 69 more than a book with a single premise worth trusting. That, plus axis:short-idea-driven suspending rather than earning points, is enough to exit at the below-the-line band without reading each story; occult is unexamined at this exit.

A middle-grade adventure entry praised by reviewers for humor, pacing and friendship, but one reviewer flags that its problems keep getting solved by convenient magical items introduced on the spot (a magic submarine, an enchanted survival kit, a spell-cure for an injured dragon) rather than earned consequences within the world's own declared rules, the kind of shortcut that cost Divergent 58 and Mortal Engines 55. No idea comparable to what carried The Hobbit to 84 on friendship plus real ideas; here the friendship is present but I would list axis:ideas under risks. Default band per the ladder.

Reviews describe the noir plot explicitly as skipping slow investigation for on-the-fly problem-solving, so this clears the detective filter as a flag rather than a veto. But the same reviews describe the lead, a bodyguard-for-hire in a corporate dystopia, as not particularly charismatic and fairly generic, with little room left for character or psychological development next to the book's descriptive prose. That is the same description-over-character imbalance that kept Artemis at 69 despite consistent worldbuilding, except the lead here is reported thinner still, so I would list axis:ideas and axis:protagonist under risks and take the default band.

Direct sequel to 2001, built on a real, worked-out SF idea - what happened to Bowman, why HAL turned homicidal, and first contact via the monolith and Jupiter's transformation - in the vein of what this reader rewards. Docked because multiple reviews flag flat characterization: Metaphorosis calls the cast 'none of whom are interesting' and the plot 'purposeless' relative to the ambition of the premise, and even the sympathetic Goodreads/Time-praised readings focus on plot over people. That is the same weak-lead problem that sank Artemis to 69 below Project Hail Mary 92 for this reader, so the estimate does not lean up on the strength of the idea alone. Discovery (axis:discovery, 2026-10-24): an expedition sent to learn what happened to a lost ship and its missing astronaut, with an answer delivered, the shape of Project Hail Mary 92; central, one step lower because the lead is the open risk, so +2.

A blind ten-year-old girl steps through a painting and can suddenly see - one clear concrete starting situation, the same trait that carried Hitchhiker's Guide 83. From there she is thrown a century back into interwar Prague and has to track down the painter who caused it, giving the book a real idea to hold onto (what changed and what stayed the same across a century, seen through a girl who only just regained her sight) rather than pure incident. Reviews are consistently enthusiastic about the protagonist specifically, not just the premise, which is what separates this from a book that merely clears the filters. Male zeny 79 sets a ceiling for how far pure character-and-friendship without a worked premise can go; this book adds a genuine idea on top, so it is placed a shade above that.

Opens on one concrete inciting incident - a routine clock repair accidentally triggers a decades-old doomsday device - rather than several unresolved threads at once, the structural trait behind this log's strongest openings. The engine of the book is Joe Spork reckoning with his gangster father's legacy - what he wants and why, not just what he does - the axis this log rewards most. It is billed partly as a detective story, but the pull is a slow-unfolding conspiracy and spy plot rather than a whodunit, so this is a flag under gate 1 rather than a filter. Reviewers repeatedly flag uneven, digressive pacing (dense wit 'occasionally to a fault,' one abandoned-read review comparing the opening to disjointed vignettes), a real risk against momentum. The doomsday device and clockwork automata are mechanical/technological, not occult in the ritual sense.

Literary fiction and a short-story collection together - the combination that sits below the line 81% of the time in this log. Ten stories are united only by a loose mood (the surreal breaking into the everyday) rather than one premise whose consequences are worked out, so there is no axis:ideas to lean on, and the short-idea-driven suspension removes penalties without adding points. Reviews are positive on craft (individual stories compared to Poe at his best) but even the coverage of it notes it is not considered the author's strongest work.

Memoirs of an internationally celebrated Czech opera singer's career from the 1920s to 1950s. Available descriptions read as warm anecdote - rehearsal-break sausages at Zofin, career milestones - rather than the truth-examining rigor that made Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 work for this reader. I would put axis:ideas under risks here, which is the test that exits at C rather than going to full research.

t: Cerveny trpaslik (Red Dwarf: Infinity Welcomes Careful Drivers)
why: Reviewers single out Rimmer as an unusually well-realized comic character - 'the eternal under-achiever... a very sad man' - alongside a sympathetic, believably flawed Lister; that is the axis Hitchhiker's Guide 83 topped the comic-SF slot on, character and want over spectacle. The book opens on one concrete situation (Lister stranded and broke on Mimas, then signing aboard Red Dwarf) rather than fanning out into several threads at once, the same structural trait behind Hitchhiker's Guide's score and behind the DNFs (Gunslinger, Discworld) that lacked it. One review flags the novel cramming in several TV-episode plotlines without a fully solid through-line, a mild density risk, but nothing like the outright incoherence that sank those DNFs.

t: Daleko v srdci (Nobody's Son: A Memoir)
why: A multi-generational family memoir - WWII resistance, escape from Communist Czechoslovakia, a difficult immigrant life in Queens - so infidelity is not the premise (the book survives without it) and does not trigger the reject at gate 2. But it is a real subplot, not incidental: the parents' 1945 marriage is described as one born of desperation rather than love, and the mother's decades-long love for another man, resumed years later and lost again, structures a large share of the book and precipitates the eventual divorce. The framing reads as sympathetic to the mother's one real love rather than condemning it, closer to neutral-to-approving than condemned, which caps the estimate in the mid-40s to mid-50s regardless of the memoir's other real strengths. The same examining-what-is-actually-true quality that carried Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus to 91 is present here too (one reviewer calls it 'astounding'), but it cannot lift the number out of the infidelity axis's range.

Reviewers are explicit that this is not a fast-paced whodunit - the killer's reveal is 'swift, almost an afterthought' next to the three interwoven character studies - so axis:detective does not fire. That matches the reader's favorite axis, motives over action: three narrators (an obsessive classmate, a girl who hated the victim, and a cop investigating) are given real interiority instead of clue-dropping, the way Speaker for the Dead 90 and the Collins trilogy score on understanding people over events. Risk: Cameron is an unsettling protagonist (a longtime, secret watcher of the victim), which could cost the way an unrootable lead did elsewhere, and reviewers flag the pacing as slow/overstuffed with flashback, a momentum cost. Leaned on motives and the multi-pov structure, which is not confusing at the chapter-one level - the book opens right after the murder is discovered, one concrete situation, not several unclear plot lines.

t: Dost dobre nenormalni (Nicht normal aber das richtig gut)
why: A first-person humor memoir about living with Asperger's (diagnosed at 22) and ADHD (three years later), covering sensory overload, social misunderstanding and prejudice. It has real insight into a lived, misunderstood experience - the closest analogue to what made Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 work - but the material reads as a loose sequence of 'curious incidents' commented on with perspective and humor rather than a single thesis worked through. I would put axis:ideas under risks, which is the test that exits at C rather than going to full research.

Multiple reviewers of this YA debut say the lizard-people (not the dragons the title implies) read as vampire lore with the names changed, and the central romance feels forced rather than earned - the same doubt-the-idea test that sent Divergent 58 down (ideas borrowed from other books and assembled without cohering). One reviewer found the protagonist actively unsympathetic. Other readers enjoyed the pace and action, so this is a competent-but-derivative genre entry rather than a clear miss, hence the default under-the-line band.

t: Dum v blankytne modrem mori (The House in the Cerulean Sea)
why: Linus's arc from a lonely, by-the-book bureaucrat into a found-family advocate who challenges the institution he served is a clear want-driven protagonist arc, the pattern that carries Male zeny (79) and Animal Farm (78) here; the systemic-prejudice allegory gives a real idea to leave with, even though one reviewer flags its handling of the acknowledged residential-schools inspiration as oversimplified. Magic here is confirmed across multiple reviews to be ambient trait/identity (a were-Pomeranian, a sprite, a gnome) rather than spells or rites performed on the page, so it clears the occult test the same way a mechanical system would, just via absence rather than mechanism. Docked lightly for its whimsical, YA-adjacent register and for a magic system reviewers call more a 'nod to canon' than internally worked out, the way Ranger's Apprentice (74) and Narnia (67) were docked.

A short, single-idea SF piece in the same shape as Animal Farm 78 and the [66, 76]-predicted-and-70-landed Labyrint sveta - short-idea-driven work is only ever as good as the idea, and this one is a canonical, frequently-anthologized concept: 'semiotic ghosts,' the idea that a discarded era's imagined future can haunt the present, and that the shiny 1930s retro-futurism being documented turns out to share an uncomfortable aesthetic kinship with fascist propaganda. No occult content (no magic, no ritual) and no protagonist arc to speak of, but the short-idea-driven suspension means that is not a penalty here the way it would be in a novel. Re-derived 2026-09-03 under the new collection axis: a multi-story book is read from the front and put down on its weakest early pieces, not averaged and not skipped past. Ja, robot 55 is the anchor - the reader stopped after three stories, on the first story's cast and the third story's implausible behaviour, and never reached the pieces the prediction was built on. The title piece is the argument and it is famous for one idea cleanly stated; the rest of the selection is not. That is precisely the reasoning the new axis forbids - a range set by the best piece in a book the reader may never reach the middle of.

t: Gradiva (Gradiva (with Freud's Delusion and Dream in Jensen's Gradiva))
why: The novella's idea -- a repressed love returning as delusion, resolved through recognition and 'cure by love' -- is real, nameable, and is literally the foundational case study of psychoanalysis; unlike Metamorphosis's bleak dead end (58), it resolves warmly, closer to the romance-as-central-subject pattern that costs nothing in Pride and Prejudice (75). Docked because roughly half the published book is Freud's analytical essay rather than story -- heavy exposition, thin narrative event, the same description-over-story penalty the reader profile flags -- and Hanold is passive and deluded for most of the novella before the late resolution, unlike an actively rootable protagonist.

Teenage Sofie wakes alone in a desert and must find a butterfly for a strange girl she meets, a single concrete starting situation close to what worked for Hitchhiker's Guide 83 (opens on one situation, not several plot lines at once). Reviewers repeatedly compare it to The Little Prince and to Maeterlinck's The Blue Bird - both allegorical growing-up quests - and The Little Prince 82 already shows this reader that a short allegory with a real idea (here: things and beings are not what they first look like, and that realization is what growing up is) clears the line despite a child lead. Docked toward the low end of A for the YA register (12+, illustrated), the same modest discount Ranger's Apprentice 74 and Male zeny 79 carry for audience rather than for any specific flaw.

A WWI love story between two schoolboys that spends its pages on what the leads want and fear rather than on battle set-pieces, the axis that also tops Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90. Reviewers describe a real, nameable idea - the gap between the sanitized official record of the dead (school 'in memoriam' notices, many lifted from real WWI papers) and the lived horror behind them. Risk: the romance is 'open door' with sexual content warnings for assault as well, which costs the way Artemis 69 was docked, and sustained wartime trauma costs mildly the way 1984 did. Leaned on ideas and motives rather than plot mechanics, since the book is explicitly interiority-driven and not a war-action novel.

Three widely separated timelines (an 18th-century frontier, a near-future corporate climate dystopia, a far-future ice age) share a symbol - the apple seed - and a manifest-destiny theme, but the library annotation and multiple reviews describe it as a 'meditation' on climate change and responsibility rather than naming one premise whose consequences are worked out; the genre-blending and lyrical prose are praised, but I would put axis:ideas under risks rather than name a single idea I am confident holds up under this reader's rules, so this exits at gate 4.

t: Jak Hitler ukradl ruzoveho kralicka (When Hitler Stole Pink Rabbit)
why: A semi-autobiographical account of a nine-year-old Jewish girl's family fleeing Berlin for Switzerland, France and England, built around family solidarity and Anna's own growing agency rather than passive suffering - closer to Male zeny 79, a domestic story that clears on character alone, than to Diary of a Young Girl 40, which failed as testimony rather than as a shaped narrative. It is squarely a children's book, age 9-12 per multiple sources, but treats real historical persecution with more substance than Narnia 67, so it is not graded down as hard as pure fantasy-children's fare. Small pushback for the child protagonist's age, per the standard life-phase discount.

t: Jak jsme v Teheranu cetly Lolitu (Reading Lolita in Tehran: A Memoir in Books)
why: Examines what is actually true about life under a theocracy and gives real insight into how a specific group - women in post-revolutionary Iran - experiences the world, the same combination that made Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 the top non-fiction score in this log. It is structured around four literary touchstones and opens in medias res on two photographs of her students, not several unresolved plotlines at once, so the opening filter is clean. The main risk is that a large share of the book is literary criticism of Nabokov, Fitzgerald, James and Austen interleaved with the memoir - denser and more academic than Qureshi's book, which could read as digression rather than lived insight depending on how much a given chapter leans on analysis over testimony.

t: Je matka mrtva (Er mor død (Is Mother Dead))
why: A middle-aged artist returns to Oslo after thirty years and becomes consumed with understanding, then surveilling, the mother she is estranged from. The entire novel is interiority - what Johanna wants, why, and whether her own account can be trusted - the axis that tops this reader's log (Mockingjay 91, Speaker for the Dead 90). Docked because Johanna is genuinely hard to root for at points: reviewers describe an 'ugly aggressiveness' and escalating boundary-crossing (hiding in her mother's building, going through her trash) that several critics say erodes reader sympathy as the book goes on - not the flat unrootability of a villain lead like Coriolanus Snow (The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65), but a real risk in the same family.

Two divorced, lonely people are pushed onto a long walking trip by a mutual friend and the book alternates their POV as they slowly choose to re-engage with each other - the wanting-and-why axis that tops Pyc-a-predsudek 75 and Mockingjay 91, with no infidelity in play since both marriages already ended before the story starts. The opening is one concrete situation, a group walking holiday, rather than several competing lines. Risk: it is a 190-mile walk rendered scene by scene, which is the kind of drawn-out structure that cost Les Miserables 71 against Monte Cristo 75 - terrain description could thin the story if it runs long.

t: Kdo tanci s vodou (The Water Dancer)
why: Conduction is declared precisely -- activated by memory, triggered by loss, tied to a maternal lineage -- and the book follows through on that declaration to its climax (Hiram unlocking full power only after confronting the buried memory of his mother's sale), the same self-consistency that rewards Project Hail Mary (92) and Red Rising (95). It clears axis:occult on the mechanism test: no invocation, ritual or real-world esoteric source, just an internal ability keyed to memory. The central idea -- that memory of what was lost is literally the mechanism of liberation -- is nameable and well-executed, reviewed as the novel's organizing metaphor throughout. Slavery is the backdrop, so bleakness is a real risk, but the throughline is family reconnection and purposeful agency (joining the Underground) rather than sustained despair, closer to Project Hail Mary's companionship discount than to 1984's flat misery.

t: Kdyz neni kral (When There Is No King (selected stories))
why: A curated best-of selection of Thiep's stories -- family sagas, historical vignettes, village folktales, and social satire of post-war communist Vietnam. Literary fiction plus short-story collection triggers gate 4's mechanical exit; the anthology spans too many disparate settings and forms for a single worked idea to carry it, whatever its historical importance to Vietnamese letters.

A solid, well-liked entry in a Czech medieval-set fantasy series (82% on Legie), praised for a relatable, developing squire protagonist and strong atmosphere - but the reviewer who covers it professionally singles out that the book under-develops the supernatural threat at its center, and it is told in four episodic parts that each introduce new characters, closer to a competent genre read than one with a worked idea behind it. That is the doubt gate 4 asks about (I would put axis:ideas under risks), so it lands in the default under-the-line band rather than being pushed lower - readers do not report it as confusing, just modest in ambition.

t: Kniha silenstvi a lecby (The Book of Madness and Cures)
why: A Renaissance quest novel that several reviewers call heavy on invented medical/alchemical detail and light on story - 'revels in alliteration,' 'never met an adjective she didn't like' - the same heavy-description-little-story pattern that cost Les Miserables and Unfinished Tales points in this log. More damaging: the book spends its length establishing Gabriella as an unconventional, independent female physician and then resolves her arc into a conventional marriage-and-childbirth ending that multiple reviewers say the character herself doesn't support - a declared trait the book doesn't carry through, the kind of self-consistency breach that sinks worldbuilding elsewhere. No occult concern: the 'madness and cures' material is period medicine/alchemy theorizing, not a rite enacted on the page. Leaned on density and protagonist-consistency rather than the travelogue plot, which is competently assembled but not more; risk that the historical-detail vehicle crowds out a real idea, per at least one reviewer's read.

Nearly a dozen first-person narrators with no unifying voice, and multiple independent reviewers report real disorientation specifically in the opening third - one calls the narrative choice itself an irritating distraction, another says they had no idea what the characters were doing, or why. That is shape one of the opening filter, several lines running before any is legible, which is what ended Guards! Guards! at 30. Moved down a band 2026-08-28. The old range rested on reviewers reporting that the pieces crystallize into a rewarding whole by the end, and that defence is worthless whatever the shape of the confusion: Caropisci 30 was abandoned in chapter one, so a payoff several hundred pages away is a payoff this reader never collects. What keeps it off the floor rather than at it is that the themes - love, obligation, death, redemption - sit close to what he responds to, and the magic is handled without incantation-and-spellcasting cliches so occult is clear; neither pays if he stops on page twenty.

Reception is genuinely split in a way that raises real doubt about axis:ideas: Kirkus calls it a dramatic, complex imagining of Stonehenge's origins, but the Washington Independent Review calls it 'wildly oversimplified' with a plot that could be jotted on a Post-it note, and multiple reader reviews call the leads 'one-dimensional' and the story 'simply plotted' with 'not enough there' for 700 pages. I can name the premise (a priestess's vision of a stone monument, opposed by drought and tribal mistrust) but not a worked-through idea beyond it, which is exactly the exit test. Stopping at C-low; occult status (Neolithic seasonal/religious ceremonies at the monument) is unexamined at this exit.

A single declared premise - reality itself runs on two-valued logic in Winter and three-valued logic in Summer - is carried through consequences on physics, law, psychology, religion, and even the book's narration, exactly the rule-following-its-own-rules axis Project Hail Mary 92 and Speaker for the Dead 90 both score on. The protagonist, a gambler blackmailed into government service, is given a real arc (he becomes a 'shaper' and declares himself a Mathematician of History), avoiding the passive-lead problem that cost Promena 58 and Oliver Twist 57. Two risks hold this back from a higher band: the political landscape is dense enough that one reader summary found it hard to keep track of who represented what, and a secondary faction is an ice-worshipping cult literally led by the real Rasputin - close enough to real-world occultism to fail the Source test if it is actually enacted on the page. I could not confirm a specific on-page ritual scene, and reviews describe it as a background power-struggle thread next to the main logic-of-reality plot, not the book's focus.

t: Loutkar z Krakova (The Dollmaker of Krakow)
