The premise - sin and desire made visible as black Smoke, with the aristocracy hiding theirs behind sweets while ruling the smoke-marked poor - is a real idea about hypocrisy and class, the kind of thing Divergent 58 was faulted for lacking. It is declared as mechanism, not invocation (no witchcraft, spellcasting or devotion on the page), so it clears axis:occult cleanly. But Vyleta explicitly does not explain where Smoke comes from within this book - reviewers confirm the origin is 'never fully defined' here and is instead the hook for the sequel Soot - and a sequel's answer does not count under the worldbuilding rule, so the book undertakes an explanation it does not itself deliver. Three child protagonists open the book together at one school, a mild multi-pov risk short of the confusing-opening filter.

The opening itself clears the reader's sharpest filter: a boy with no memory is raised into a walled Glade in a single third-person-limited thread, one concrete situation rather than several plot lines starting at once, closer to Hitchhiker's 83 than to the Gunslinger/Discworld openings that ended unfinished. But the book declares a capability - an organization built an enormous, mechanically elaborate maze specifically to map immune brains - and does not carry its own consequences: reviewers and fans alike single out the maze's actual purpose as under-explained to the point that one review states the explanation is worse than no explanation at all. This book withholds the fuller account to sequels, which the reader's own worldbuilding rule does not let count. That declared-but-uncarried premise is the same shape of failure that sank Divergent 58 and Mortal Engines 55, so axis:worldbuilding is what this number leans on rather than the opening, which is clean. Discovery (axis:discovery, 2026-10-24): a lead with no memory in a world he must understand to escape is the shape exactly, but the answer, as argued above, is withheld or worse than none, which forfeits the lift; the number holds.

A shipwrecked teenager survives 227 days on a lifeboat with a Bengal tiger, then at the end offers investigators a second, darker version of the same events substituting people for the animals - neither is provable, and the book asks which one the reader would rather believe. That is a real worked idea about faith versus reason, not plotless dressing, the sort of idea Animal Farm 78 also leaves behind. Pi's drive is survival plus an examined, three-faith spiritual practice, graded on axis:faith rather than axis:occult - organized worship (Hinduism, Christianity, Islam), not witchcraft, seance or invented ritual, so it is not a veto, the same distinction that let Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus score 91. Risk: the ordeal is sustained and often brutal (starvation, a parent's death, the darker retelling's implied cannibalism), the mild-but-real bleakness discount that cost 1984 and Promena, and Pi is 16 for most of the book, a small life-phase pushback like the one that marked down Ender's Game.

t: Lizni si a hrej (Play It as It Lays)
why: Maria Wyeth drifts through a collapsing marriage and Hollywood career between a mental-hospital stay and her friend BZ's suicide, told in eighty-seven fragmentary chapters built around the idea that nothing means anything. That is heavier and less resolved than 1984 (60, 'too depressing'), the log's own ceiling for sustained bleakness, and Maria is passive throughout in the same way Metamorphosis's Gregor (58) is - acted upon by despair rather than pursuing anything. Casual infidelity appears ('unengaged affairs') but is incidental color inside the numbness, not the source of the doubt here.

t: Mel jsem psa a kocku (I Had a Dog and a Cat)
why: A collection of Capek's newspaper feuilletons about his own dogs and cats - warm, humorous, occasional pieces rather than a worked argument or premise. About half the book is the well-known childrens story Dasenka. There is no idea here to point to the way Animal Farm 78 or Labyrint sveta 70 have one; this is charm and anecdote, which is exactly the occasional-piece profile the low band exists for.

Fourteen loosely thematic stories (boxing, bullfighting, war, aging) with no through-line premise - the same collection gap that keeps Red Cavalry in this band rather than with Animal Farm's 78 single worked idea. t: Muzeum prazvlastnich veci (The Museum of Extraordinary Things)
why: Coralie, exhibited by her father as a 'living wonder' from childhood, ultimately uses that same tank herself to save the man she loves rather than be used by it - a rootable protagonist working toward something she wants, the axis that separates Mockingjay 91 from Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65. t: Nikola Suhaj Loupeznik (Nikola Suhaj the Outlaw)

Nikola is a sympathetic, rootable lead who robs the rich for the poor and is killed by betrayal from his own men, the kind of heroism-and-friendship material that carries The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings to 84. The tragic, betrayed ending is a bleakness risk the way it was for The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65, though softened by the myth surviving him rather than ending on pure defeat.

Testimony of eleven months in the women's orchestra of Auschwitz and Bergen-Belsen, and it does deliver what this reader's log rewards in memoir - insight into how a specific group survived an extreme experience, the axis that put Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus at 91. But this is not a clean repeat of that case: a 2016 scholarly rebuttal drawing on 17 fellow orchestra survivors argues large parts are embellished, and a reader review independently describes the narrator as self-important and hard to warm to, particularly in her account of the conductor. That is a real dent in the examining-what-is-actually-true criterion that carried Qureshi to the top of the log, and it is a protagonist-likability concern on top of it, so I am setting this below the memoir ceiling rather than near it. The camp setting is sustained bleakness but survival-through-companionship (the orchestra itself), which the reader's log treats more gently than solitary bleakness.

t: Pariz ve 20. stoleti (Paris in the Twentieth Century)
why: The predictive dystopia -- cars, elevators, fax machines, a society that has abandoned art for commerce and profit -- is a genuinely nameable idea, so this does not exit at gate 4. But reviews are consistent that the execution around that idea is thin: a Publishers Weekly assessment (via AbeBooks) found little here in the way of either plot or character development, and a LibraryThing review calls the characters flat and one-dimensional in a story with little room left for actual plot, plus a maudlin, tragically pessimistic tone through to a sad, poignant ending. That is close to the failure mode books-read.md already recorded for Promena at 58 -- a real, nameable idea undercut by a thin protagonist and unrelieved bleakness, without the lighter touch that kept Animal Farm at 78 despite its own dystopia. Leaning on protagonist and bleakness rather than the idea itself, since the idea is what earns this book its reputation, not what a reader experiences page to page.

A hacker seizes eight self-driving cars and forces a government jury to vote on who lives, in a mandatory-autonomous-vehicle future. The idea (algorithmic ethics, mob justice broadcast as spectacle) is nameable, but the mechanics needed to sustain it - a jury duty summons that turns into a live-broadcast execution game the authorities cannot simply shut down for two and a half hours - read as convenience rather than a thought-through world, the same doubt that sank Mortal Engines (55, DNF on unaccounted-for logic) and capped Divergent (58, 'ideas borrowed from other books and assembled without cohering'). Below the line on that doubt alone, whatever the twist ending does.

t: Podivuhodny pribeh Benjamina Buttona (The Curious Case of Benjamin Button)
why: The catalogue's own annotation describes this specific edition as a simplified version for intermediate English-language students, not the full original text -- functionally an abridgement even though cz.edition is recorded as print, similar in effect to the adapt-edition case. The original story's reverse-aging premise is a real, nameable idea about time, vanity and appearance versus reality, but a graded-reader abridgement strips a literary novella down to vocabulary-level plot beats; treat it like an occasional piece under axis:short-idea-driven, at the lower band rather than the one the underlying story would otherwise earn.

t: Podzimni mouchy, aneb, Zena z davnych dob (Snow in Autumn)
why: A Chekhov-homage novella following the Karin family's nanny Tatiana as revolution destroys the household and drives them into Parisian exile. The idea of dislocation and lost home is real, but it is delivered as elegy and atmosphere rather than a premise worked through consequences, and Tatiana herself only witnesses and follows rather than wanting anything of her own - the same passivity that held Oliver Twist (57, 'acted upon rather than wanting anything') under the line despite a correctly identified idea.

Confirmed as middle-grade (ages 8-12, Lexile 650L) - younger and simpler than Ranger's Apprentice 74, closer to the register that cost Narnia 67. There is a workable premise in peaceful robots who eliminated humanity for the planet's own good meeting the one human girl left, but at this reading level it will be stated plainly rather than worked through, so the default competent-but-under-68 band applies rather than the harsher no-idea band.

Not an infidelity premise despite the medium-tier lexicon hit - the marriage is abusive and controlling, not unfaithful, and the plot is an identity-swap escape thriller: two women meet by chance at an airport and swap tickets, and one flight crashes. The premise has real, worked-through consequences (the survivor must live inside a stranger's dangerous life), but it leans on a large, convenient coincidence to get there, the kind of premise logic that undercut Mortal Engines 55 and Divergent 58 rather than the tightly held-together plotting of Red Rising 95.

The alien-invasion thread (the Grand Galactics deciding humanity is a threat) reads as bolted onto Ranjit's Fermat-proof plot rather than growing out of it - reviewers describe the novel as lacking a rounded arc and ending precipitously, a declared idea whose consequences are not actually carried through, the same failure mode (if unrelated content) that sank Mortal Engines 55. A genuine idea is named - a young mathematician's proof reshaping his life and drawing world attention - but the larger novel built around it does not cohere, so the doubt sits on axis:ideas.

Vancura's reputation rests on stylistic experiment (avant-garde, archaic rhythmic prose) rather than a worked-out idea, so this exits at the litfic-plus-collection line rather than being researched further.

An idea-driven satire on a dictatorship, and the ideas are the case for it - the story is the regime, not the marriages. Its four wives and one mistress are noted by reviewers as one-dimensional 'sexual concubines' rather than people, which is undifferentiated, crude treatment layered onto the satire. t: Prorok - Zahrada Prorokova (The Prophet / The Garden of the Prophet)
why: Twenty-six poetic-prose addresses by a sage, Almustafa, on love, marriage, work, joy and sorrow, freedom and death, delivered as parting wisdom before he sails home; the sequel gathers further such pieces. Short-idea-driven work has the character rules suspended here since there is no plot and no protagonist to root for, only a mouthpiece, but the suspension only removes penalties, it never adds points - and the axis:ideas test asks for one nameable idea, while this book offers wisdom on two dozen separate topics rather than a single premise worked through, closer to a diffuse anthology than to a book like Labyrint sveta 70, which lands one sustained idea. Faith runs through it as a thread (love, transcendence, the eternal) rather than being the whole subject, so axis:faith does not veto, the same distinction that let Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus score 91.

t: Proti padu noci (Against the Fall of Night)
why: Diaspar's stagnant immortality against Lys's embrace of growth and mortality is a clean, worked idea in the mold of what carries Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 - critics explicitly note ideas outweigh character work here, the axis:short-idea-driven trade this reader already accepts without penalty. The opening is one concrete situation, one city and one restless citizen (Alvin), the pattern Red Rising 95 and The Hunger Games 89 share and that Guards! Guards! 30 and The Gunslinger 30 both lacked. Characterization is real thin, though - critics say figures are 'identifiable mainly by their names' - closer to the risk profile of Silmarillion's 80 than to a character-forward book, so axis:protagonist is what could pull this down. Discovery (axis:discovery, 2026-10-24) is present but partial: the search for what lies beyond the city is the spine and the hidden history answers it, but the drive is curiosity rather than need, and with the lead the open doubt it prices at nothing; the number holds.

A novelization of the Nibelungenlied: Siegfried slays the dragon Fafnir, wins the Nibelung gold and an invulnerability that comes with it, then helps Gunther win Brunhild by trickery, setting up the betrayal and bloodshed that follow - myth-scale stakes in the vein of the dragon-and-treasure plots that worked in The Hobbit 84 and The Silmarillion 80. But reviewers describe it leaning on genre-fantasy and Hollywood beats rather than evoking the saga's own weight, calling it undemanding entertainment rather than a considered reworking - the opposite of what let The Silmarillion 80 hold up without a continuous protagonist. I would put axis:ideas in risks: nothing found suggests the retelling does more with the fate-and-greed material than restate it. The magic here is mythic-artifact fantasy (a cloak of invisibility, dragon blood, a cursed ring) with no rite performed as ritual and no source in real occultism, so it is not a filter concern.

t: Ross Poldark (Ross Poldark: A Novel of Cornwall 1783-1787)
why: Reviewers single out exactly what tops books-read.md: extensive internal dialogue revealing what characters think and want, the same quality behind Pride and Prejudice's 75 ('motives and what characters want are the entire book'). Ross returns from war to find his home neglected and his fiancee married to his cousin, then rebuilds a life and eventually a marriage with a servant girl he takes in -- a motive-driven, character-centered story in the same register as that comparison, with no hard-filter content in this opening volume. Held below the top of that band because reader reception is mixed on pacing (some stretches called slow or under-developed), and Graham writes Cornish dialect phonetically, which more than one review flagged as tricky to follow -- a density cost, not a character one.

A collection of standalone Kara ben Nemsi/Old Shatterhand adventure episodes across North Africa, the Middle East and the Boer War - episodic pulp adventure with no premise worked through, and May's 19th-century Orientalist framing of the region trades on the same kind of stated-as-fact ethnic stereotyping that cost Ranger's Apprentice 74 a few points, here without that book's redeeming easy momentum across a single throughline.

t: Sajlok, to jsem ja (Shylock Is My Name)
why: Reimagines The Merchant of Venice: a modern Jewish father, Strulovich, meets an undying Shylock and works through questions of justice, mercy and Jewish identity via a present-day pound-of-flesh plot (forced circumcision instead of a bond) - the idea is developed rather than just gestured at, in the vein of Animal Farm 78. Strulovich is driven by wanting to protect his daughter and defend his heritage rather than by what happens to him - the motives-over-action axis that tops the log at Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90. It opens on one concrete scene, a cemetery encounter, the same single-situation opening that worked for Hitchhiker's Guide 83. No occult: Shylock's 400-year persistence is an authorial fantastical device, not a system drawn from real occultism, and no rite is enacted on the page. Risk: reviews describe a dense, 'multidirectional' novel where several storylines develop after the opening, which could cost on the density/momentum axis the way Les Miserables' looser digressions did relative to Monte Cristo.

Naturalist essays adapted from 1950s BBC radio broadcasts about animal-collecting expeditions - entertaining anecdotes and a conservation message, but not an examination of what is actually true the way Seeking Allah Finding Jesus 91 or Son of Hamas 75 earn their scores; reviewers note it reads as perfunctory radio-script material rather than a worked idea. The memoir/testimony form earns nothing by itself, and there is no single idea to name here beyond animals being interesting and worth protecting.

A chronological cycle of Czech founding legends and later Prague legends - Cech's arrival, Libuse and her prophecy of Prague, the Maidens' War, then Charles-era and Wenceslas-IV-era city tales - carrying an explicit ideological throughline (religious tolerance, coexistence of peoples) that Jirasek wrote into the old material on purpose, a real nameable idea rather than a plain retelling. Like The Silmarillion 80, it has no continuous protagonist and no single plot, yet that structure did not cost Tolkien's mythic collection and need not cost this one on the same grounds. Libuse's founding prophecy is treated with reverence as national myth, not resemblance-for-its-own-sake, so axis:prophecy grades clean. Risk: one late tale, 'Zito the sorcerer,' is a court magician who performs actual transformations for an audience - closer to invented trickster folklore than to a source in real occultism, but the one point in the collection where something resembling a rite could be read as enacted on the page, so I am flagging rather than clearing it outright. Re-derived 2026-09-03 under the new collection axis: a multi-story book is read from the front and put down on its weakest early pieces, not averaged and not skipped past. Ja, robot 55 is the anchor - the reader stopped after three stories, on the first story's cast and the third story's implausible behaviour, and never reached the pieces the prediction was built on. Retold legends in sequence with no arc and no continuing cast, and the occult question on this volume is still open - the older strata of these tales run on soothsaying and on prophecy taken as literally efficacious. An open occult check plus an opening the reader meets cold is the configuration the new axis is most cautious about.

t: The cider house rules (The Cider House Rules)
why: Homer and Candy's affair starts while Wally is presumed dead at war and continues in secret for roughly fifteen years after his crippled return - a sustained subplot, not the premise, since the book is fundamentally Homer's bildungsroman around Dr. Larch, St. Cloud's orphanage, and the abortion debate, all of which stand on their own. The affair is handled with guilt and conflicted loyalty rather than celebration, so per the infidelity axis a subplot with neutral framing lands in the same middling penalty territory as Metamorphosis (58). The orphan's-search-for-a-home idea underneath is real and worked out, which keeps this from falling further, but the axis is what carries the number.

t: The famous stories (Slavne povidky / The Famous Stories)
why: This is a bilingual graded-reader adaptation for English learners (mirror Czech/English text, simplified language, vocabulary notes, MP3 narration by a listed adapter, Sabrina D. Harris) rather than Poe's original prose - exactly the 'slight collection, simplified' case the lower C-low band exists for. Even granting Poe's originals real ideas, a simplification aimed at intermediate language learners does not carry the same weight, so the doubt sits on axis:short-idea-driven rather than any individual story's merit.

Joanna Eberhart moves to a suburb where wives are quietly being replaced by docile robotic duplicates by their husbands' 'Men's Association.' The premise is declared once and then followed through with total consistency, including on Joanna herself, in a single clean POV with a concrete inciting situation - the opposite of a premise that collapses under thought, closer to what Project Hail Mary (92) rewards for working consequences through than to Divergent's (58) unexamined premise. But the ending offers no escape at all, nearer 1984's (60, 'too depressing') totalizing bleakness than Animal Farm's (78) fable distance, which is what keeps this well under the top of the band despite the idea holding up cleanly.

t: Tri legendy o krucifixu a jine baje o lasce (Three Legends of the Crucifix)
why: Three linked novella-legends, each turning on a figure who finds redemption through suffering (an artist's model, a persecutor of Christians, a scorned simpleton) - a real idea in the vein of what makes Animal Farm 78 and Labyrint sveta 70 work as short idea-driven pieces, so this clears the axis:ideas exit that a plain story collection would trigger. But the theology is not a thread here, it is the whole engine of all three plots - miracle, apotheosis, salvation are the point - which sits closer to the apologetics the faith axis penalises than to Seeking Allah Finding Jesus 91's honest examination of belief. Ornate 1890s neo-romantic prose is also a density risk, the kind of heavy description that costs elsewhere in the log.

t: Ustrickova smutna smrt a jine pribehy (The Melancholy Death of Oyster Boy & Other Stories)
why: Twenty-three brief illustrated rhyming poems about misfit children, each a self-contained mood piece rather than a worked idea - closer to Havran 40, the log's one verse entry, than to any prose the reader has liked. Verse itself carries a penalty independent of subject matter per that entry, and the illustrated, simple-rhyme, YA-marketed format sits close to the picture-book end of axis:childrens, which the log puts in the 30s-40s. There is no single idea beyond a repeated mood of macabre misfit melancholy to lean on the way Animal Farm's 78 allegory can.

This is the fifteenth Cotton Malone book, and this log already has one clean case of a long-running series thinning out - Hitchhiker's dropped from 83 to 70 across its sequels. Reviewers describe the relic hunt (the Arma Christi) here as largely a MacGuffin, meaning the book doesn't actually work out consequences of its own central conceit - the real content is a history lesson on Cold War Poland attached to a conspiracy-thriller chase, not a premise carried through.

t: Vecny Adam (The Eternal Adam and Other Stories)
why: The title story's twist -- a far-future archaeologist deciphering a survivor's journal from a forgotten cataclysm, only to realize his own 'advanced' civilization is just the latest turn of an endless collapse-and-rebirth cycle -- is a strong, nameable idea in the same vein as Animal Farm's 78: a compact premise whose consequences are worked through to a real twist. But this record is a multi-story anthology and most of its contents are far less known than the title piece; the Eternal Adam text itself is credited to Verne but was largely completed by his son from a draft after Verne's death, an authorship complication worth flagging. Leaning on axis:short-idea-driven rather than crediting the whole collection with the title story's idea, since an anthology is judged as a whole and the rest of its contents were not established.

Two unnamed men are stranded by rising water on a Danube island where the willows and unseen forces seem to hunt them; the story is deliberately unresolved about what the forces are or want. Motives here belong to the environment, not the two leads - there is little of what the men themselves want beyond survival, the axis Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 score highest on and that Unfinished Tales 69 was marked down for lacking (its pieces not logically connected to each other). I would put axis:ideas in risks too: the piece works as mood and dread rather than a premise worked through to consequences. Exiting at C-low per the gate order, so occult status is accordingly unexamined (axis:occult stays in deps for when it is checked).

Winston Graham's Poldark novels are consistently praised for exactly the trait that tops books-read.md: page time on inner motive over event, reviewers noting his frequent use of internal dialogue to reveal what characters think and want, the same axis behind Pride and Prejudice's 75 ('motives and what characters want are the entire book'). Against that baseline, this entry carries a specific cost: a pivotal scene has the married protagonist force a final encounter with his former fiancee on the eve of her second marriage, breaking his own marriage vow -- not incidental, but also not the premise of a book equally concerned with a banking collapse and a mining business, so it grades as a subplot rather than a reject. Framing is condemned rather than approving: the act devastates the protagonist's marriage, plunges him into guilt, and traps the other woman in an unhappy second marriage -- the 'subplot times condemned' cell of the infidelity grid, which costs a few points rather than the more severe cells. That pulls the estimate down from where the motive-driven writing alone would place it.

t: Z Divokeho zapadu (From the Wild West)
why: Ten self-contained Western short stories about lone gunslingers, praised by reviewers for humor, tension and raw atmosphere but not for any single premise carried through. Same doubt as the reader's other episodic-pulp cases: I cannot name a worked idea the collection is building toward, only a mood and a setting, so axis:ideas is what this number leans on. No content concerns turned up (no occult, no detective frame, no romance-as-premise) so nothing else is at risk of collapsing it further.

t: Zazrak v Andach (Miracle in the Andes)
why: A first-person account, written thirty years after a 1972 Andes plane crash, of the 72 days a Uruguayan rugby team spent stranded on a glacier - starvation, an avalanche that killed eight more survivors, and finally Parrado's own trek across the mountains to bring back rescue for those who stayed behind. What earns points on the memoir axis is examining what is actually true rather than just having lived through something, the same rigor that put Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus at 91 - reviewers single out the book's honesty about the survivors' hardest choice (eating the dead) and call it a meditation on love and camaraderie rather than a straight survival thriller. It is a companionship and self-sacrifice story, Parrado trekking to save the others rather than just himself, the same combination that put Project Hail Mary 92 above The Martian 82, the latter docked for sustained loneliness. Risk: the ordeal itself is severe and sustained, the mild-but-real bleakness discount the log applies elsewhere.

A retired teacher inherits a house on Ibiza and, investigating clues left by a friend whose diving death looks less than accidental, encounters unexplained paranormal forces and undergoes a personal transformation. The investigation is a real thread but reads as a device for a self-discovery story rather than the book's payoff, so this is a flag rather than the detective veto. What decides the exit is the idea itself: reviewers are split, with at least one describing the themes as delivered like a lecture rather than earned, and the paranormal elements are reportedly left deliberately unexplained rather than worked through - which is the doubt axis:ideas is meant to catch. The 72-year-old lead is a small, not disqualifying, life-phase distance from the reader.

Thirteen-year-old Rose Rivers resents being groomed for a decorative future while her twin brother is sent to boarding school - a real, stated want, the axis this log rewards most. But unlike Little Women (79, 'clears the propose line on characters alone'), reader reviews of this specific book note Rose has 'nothing to really root for' and little that sets her apart, closer to Narnia (67, 'not bad, but... lacks higher things to think about'). A subplot where Rose, thirteen, kisses the adult artist hired to paint her mother is treated as scandal - he is banished - rather than explored, which is a content concern worth flagging even though it is not the book's premise.

Retrospective critics single out the book's late pivot - Falkenberg abruptly marrying Glenda Ruth Horton with an implied kingship, after most of the book followed CoDominium politics through Senator Grant - as a cliched shift rather than a consequence the earlier chapters built toward, the same premise-not-carried-through problem that sank Mortal Engines 55. The political-military worldbuilding up to that point is reasonably well regarded (Poul Anderson called it thought-provoking), but the ending doesn't follow from what the book declared and set up earlier.

A journalist joins an eccentric scientist's expedition to a Brazilian plateau where dinosaurs and ape-men still survive, culminating in public vindication when the team brings back living proof. Reviewers consistently praise the imaginative concept and the plot's pace over more than a century of readers; this is companionship-driven expedition adventure rather than solo survival, closer to the profile the reader rewarded in Project Hail Mary 92 than to The Martian's docked isolation. It sits below the reader's SF ceiling because the leads are drawn with Victorian broad strokes - Challenger arrogant, Malone motivated as much by pride as courage - rather than the deep interiority that wins the top of the log, so axis:protagonist is the one risk that could pull this down; axis:worldbuilding is what actually carries the number, since the lost-world premise is realized vividly and consistently rather than merely asserted. Discovery (axis:discovery, 2026-10-24): an expedition into a world nobody believes in, but the drive is proof and wonder rather than need and the lead is the open risk, so it prices at nothing; the number holds.

t: Ruda jizda a jine prozy (Red Cavalry and Other Prose)
why: Thirty-five loosely linked war vignettes narrated by the same outsider - a litfic story collection with no single premise running through it, so axis:ideas has nothing to lean on the way it does in Animal Farm 78 or Labyrint sveta 70, both of which hang the whole book on one worked idea. Individual stories carry real ideas (an intellectual's attraction to Cossack violence) but nothing sustained across the whole book, so it exits here rather than being researched further.

The central thread is the narrator processing her widowed mother's murder over the following year, not an affair - remove the affair and the book about grief and family still exists, so this does not reach premise level and is not a reject. But a sustained subplot runs the length of the book: the unmarried narrator's year-long affair with a married man who may or may not leave his wife. Framing reads as neutral rather than condemned or celebrated - it is treated as part of her rebellious, black-sheep identity, not punished and not held up as brave. Subplot prominence with neutral framing is the middle cell of the reader's own infidelity matrix, which is what this number leans on. The low end is nudged three points under that cell's floor on purpose: reception is mixed to negative on the book's substance (Kirkus called the premise banal and the novel bloated), which argues for room below the matrix cell rather than a reason to push the range up.

A collection of James novellas headlined by 'In the Cage,' whose plot centers on a telegraphist who becomes obsessed with a married client's secret affair. Infidelity here is a dominant subplot the unmarried protagonist only observes rather than the premise of her own life, and the ending reveals the lovers as mercenary rather than romantic - closer to condemned than approving, well short of premise-level under the reject test. It is still a story collection with no book-wide idea, the same gap that keeps a collection off the pace of an idea-driven allegory like Animal Farm 78 or Labyrint sveta 70.

A Bierce war-story collection built around the title tale, in which a soldier's celebrated battlefield courage turns out to be driven by a woman's taunting letter rather than honor - real irony-driven ideas within the story, but assembled as a story collection with no single premise across the book, the same gap that keeps a litfic collection off the pace of an idea-driven allegory like Animal Farm 78 or Labyrint sveta 70.

An episodic collection of autobiographical fishing-and-family stories spanning prewar, wartime and postwar Czechoslovakia (the family, half-Jewish, was deported and returned) - warmly regarded and emotionally textured, but held together by chronology and voice rather than a single premise worked out. No nameable idea the way Labyrint sveta a raj srdce 70 has one - that book hit precisely because it is a short allegory with a premise you can name, the reasoning axis:ideas plus axis:short-idea-driven was built for; this collection has voice and warmth but no equivalent single idea. The short-idea-driven suspension removes the length penalty but does not add points on its own.

t: Amari a Nocni bratri (Amari and the Night Brothers)
why: A 13-year-old finds a briefcase left by her missing older brother nominating her for tryouts at a secret Bureau of Supernatural Affairs, and must navigate trials while hiding an illegal power to find out what happened to him. Reviews are consistently strong on the protagonist - brave, observant, caring - the trait the log rewards most directly (Mockingjay 91, The Hunger Games 89), enough to offset the modest cost the profile assigns to a middle-grade register, comparable to Ranger's Apprentice 74. The finding-her-brother thread is an investigation-shaped subplot, not the reader's core satisfaction (which is Amari's belonging/found-family arc), so it is a flag rather than the detective veto. The magic is framed as innate 'talents' (mutant-style ability) rather than invoked witchcraft, which would pass the occult mechanism test, but a 'League of Magicians' and references to spellbooks were not conclusively pinned down as ritual-free, so occult is a risk rather than a cleared question. Leaned on axis:protagonist and axis:childrens.

t: Amari a Velka hra (Amari and the Great Game)
why: Direct sequel: Amari, now a probationary agent, is offered leadership of the secretive League of Magicians and her refusal triggers a power struggle (the titular Great Game) inside magiciankind. The same protagonist strength that carries book one continues here, and the log rewards that trait most directly (Mockingjay 91, The Hunger Games 89); the modest middle-grade cost is unchanged from book one, comparable to Ranger's Apprentice 74. The League of Magicians and spellbook references were not conclusively confirmed as ritual-free on this volume either, so occult carries forward as the same unresolved risk as book one, per the shared author-level research. Leaned on axis:protagonist and axis:childrens.

A near-future second American civil war told through Sarat Chestnut, whose radicalization from refugee child into an instrument of Southern terrorism is the entire point of the book, not backdrop - reviews stress this is a character study of why ordinary people turn to violence rather than a war-action plot, the axis that tops the log (Mockingjay 91, Speaker for the Dead 90: motives over what happens). It opens on one concrete, legible situation - one family, one flooding farm, one refugee camp - the shape the log rewards (Hitchhiker's Guide, 83). Risk: Sarat ends the book as the war's chief instrument of mass destruction and the ending is openly cyclical and hopeless ('the whole ugly cycle starts again'), closer to 1984's 60 ('too depressing') than to a redemptive arc, with none of the companionship or self-sacrifice that lifted Project Hail Mary over The Martian. Unlike Coriolanus Snow (Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, 65), reviewers say the reader stays attached to Sarat because her descent is earned through victimhood rather than ambition, which should keep this above that floor.

t: Byla jednou jedna reka (Once Upon a River)
why: Set on the 1887 Thames, a drowned girl revives and three families claim her, against local folklore about Quietly, a ferryman who carries the dying across the river. Checked specifically for the occult filter: there is no witchcraft, divination or rite performed on the page - the supernatural is left deliberately ambiguous, filtered through unreliable village storytelling, and the author has said in interview she means it to stay that way. That is a self-consistency choice, not a cheat, and reviewers credit exactly this: a real, sustained tension between Nurse Rita's rational investigation and the folklore that is never resolved either way, the log's 'author must follow his own declared rules' test passed by deliberately committing to ambiguity rather than breaking it. Opens on one concrete situation - a beaten stranger arrives at an inn with a dead child - the shape the opening test rewards. Risk: several reviews independently call it a slow burn with subplots that were not strictly necessary, the density discount the log applies to Les Miserables (71) rather than a bar.

t: Chlapec na moste (The Boy on the Bridge)
why: The series' core idea - that the infected are not simply monsters but a next evolutionary stage worth moral consideration rather than extermination - carries over, and reviewers specifically praise the same ambiguity here ('some zombies are zombies and some are not'), which is the axis:ideas this reader wants a book to leave behind. Stephen's characterization as an anxious, precise thinker gives him real interiority rather than making him a mission-object. Risk: it is an ensemble piece split across a full military-and-science crew rather than one throughline, and it is a prequel rather than the original - this reader's log shows prequels and sequels landing below their originals often enough (Hitchhiker's sequels 70 vs 83, Ballad 65 vs Sunrise 87) that the range should not assume it matches its predecessor. Discovery (axis:discovery, 2026-10-24): the expedition exists to find out how the pathogen works, and what the boy finds changes what they are there for, the shape of Project Hail Mary 92; partial, so +2.

t: Dalajlamova kocka (The Dalai Lama's Cat and the Claw of Attraction)
why: Sixth book in a long-running series where the cat narrator's function is to deliver Buddhist teaching to visiting characters. One reviewer warns it is worthwhile 'only if you want to learn more about Buddhism' and flags its treatment of Buddhism as the sole path to enlightenment; another calls the plot 'deceptively simple... not complex'. Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus (91) works because it examines what is actually true from inside a real conversion; this instead reads as the theology being the whole of the book rather than a thread within a story, the exact case the reader profile marks as earning nothing on its own.

A 12th-century Cistercian monk's apocryphal journal of building the abbey of Thoronet, written by an architect (Fernand Pouillon) who actually built things for a living, while in prison. The idea it leaves behind is nameable and specific - the relationship between beauty and necessity, human effort and natural order, worked out through real construction problems (deaths on site, material failures) rather than asserted - the same kind of worked premise the log rewards in short idea-driven work (Labyrint sveta a raj srdce, 70). Faith runs through it as the monk-narrator's lens rather than as a standalone theological argument, so it reads as a thread rather than the whole subject. Risk: several readers explicitly recommend reading it in fragments rather than straight through, calling the pace closer to poetry than plot, the same density discount applied to Les Miserables (71); and the faith framing is close enough to the book's whole texture that it is worth tracking rather than dismissing.

Second half of the Flawed duology: a girl branded for moral failure by a judgmental society goes on the run. The branding-as-social-control premise is the same shape as Divergent's engineered-faction society (58), and reviews describe this sequel as leaning on 'preachy' speeches and familiar YA-dystopia beats rather than developing the premise further; none credit it with a worked-through idea beyond the branding conceit. That is the axis:ideas doubt this gate tests for.

t: Dopisy na konec sveta (Love Letters to the Dead)
why: An epistolary YA novel in which Laurel, grieving her sister's death, writes unsent letters to dead celebrities (Kurt Cobain, Amy Winehouse, and others) that gradually reveal a hidden trauma. The core idea - processing guilt and grief through addressing the untouchable dead - is real and nameable, but multiple reviewers call the structure repetitive (the same letter conceit worked over and over) and one flags the narrative voice as actively irritating, plus a direct, repeated comparison to Perks of Being a Wallflower as heavily derivative. That is the story-density problem the log treats as a penalty in its own right - a thin idea stretched thin across the page count - rather than a hard-filter issue, since the sexual content here is a disclosed backstory trauma rather than a plotline built around sexual behaviour.

YA gothic horror: siblings sent to live with secretive grandparents whose house hides old murders and apparitions. Reviews are mixed-positive on atmosphere but call the plot 'forced along' and say it was 'never really genuinely creepy'; one reviewer notes the book 'isn't really about the ghosts' despite the title. No idea beyond family-secrets atmosphere is nameable, closer to Chronicles of Narnia (67) than to a book that leaves something behind. Occult status is left unexamined by exiting here at C; nothing in the reviews describes a performed rite, only ambient hauntings.

t: Dum polamanych andelu (The House of Broken Angels)
why: A Mexican-American family gathers for a mother's funeral and a dying patriarch's last birthday over two frantic days - warm, semi-autobiographical, and consistently praised for heart and voice, but every review's substance is mood and family texture rather than a premise with consequences to trace; there is no single idea here worth writing down the way Animal Farm's or Labyrint's can be. Reviewers also flag a large, easily-confused cast of relatives ('wished for a family tree'), a real risk layered on top of the thin idea. Nothing here hits a hard filter.

t: Fotograf z Mauthausenu (The Photographer of Mauthausen)
why: This is the true story of Francisco Boix, the Mauthausen prisoner who smuggled out negatives an SS officer used to document camp deaths, evidence later used at Nuremberg - exactly the kind of memoir/testimony that earns points under the reader's rule (examining what actually happened, real insight into a group's lived experience), the pattern behind Seeking Allah Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75. A Goodreads reviewer specifically praises its restraint: 'no purposeful emotional scenes, no forced moral points, just the closest picture of that time'. Risk on axis:protagonist because the comic-panel format necessarily gives less interior monologue than prose memoir, and the reader's strongest preference is page time on what a character wants and why; risk on axis:bleakness for the concentration-camp setting itself. The library's 'detective' signal does not describe a whodunit - it flags Boix's own investigative documentation of Nazi crimes, not a mystery the reader is meant to solve.

t: Jeho kralovstvi (The Secret of the Kingdom)
why: This is not faith as a thread inside a larger story - the entire plot is Marcus's investigation into whether Jesus's claims and kingdom are true, which reviewers describe directly as a book 'if you want to explore your faith' and as dramatizing 'the dilemma of modern man... in gaining and retaining a faith.' That is theology and apologetics as the subject in its own right, which this reader's rules mark down regardless of craft - contrast Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91, which scores high as first-person testimony examining what one person actually believes and why, not as a novel built to walk its reader toward a doctrinal claim. The annotation's 'detective-like obsession' pursuing the meaning of Jesus's words is metaphorical, not a whodunit, so axis:detective is a flag here, not a veto.

Opens on one concrete situation - retired mercenary Clay Cooper's old bandmate shows up needing help to save his daughter - which is exactly the legible single-starting-point shape the reader rewards, unlike the several-plot-lines confusion that sank Guards! Guards! and The Gunslinger. Reviews consistently single out motive over spectacle as the book's strength: a story about aging, friendship and loyalty forcing old bandmates to confront past deeds, with humor used to carry rather than replace emotional weight - the same axis that tops Red Rising and the Collins trilogy in the log. Passes the occult test cleanly: multiple sources describe no defined magic system, with the wizard's tricks played for comedy rather than any invoked or ritual power, so there is no rite on the page to veto. Worldbuilding is a mild risk rather than a strength to lean on - the loose, undefined magic system is the opposite of the declared-and-consequential systems (Sanderson, Bennett) the reader credits. Content tags list infidelity and sexual content only as 'minor', which reads as backstory texture rather than a plot thread; not examined further given budget, so treat as an open flag rather than a graded finding.

A YA horror-thriller about an orphaned girl who discovers her aunt runs a body-snatching syndicate supplying cadavers to a men-only anatomy school in 1850s Philadelphia. Molly's driving want - to be admitted to a world of medical knowledge closed to women, alongside a real class critique of the wealthy's 'performative philanthropy' - gives it a nameable idea and an actively wanting protagonist, the combination the log rewards most (Red Rising, Mockingjay). The subject matter (grave-robbing, anatomy) is medical/scientific rather than occult, so that filter is a clean pass with no rite or real-world religious practice involved. A murder investigation runs through the book too - Booklist calls it 'part mystery, part thriller, part family discovery' - which keeps the whodunit thread as a genuine risk to watch rather than the book's sole engine, since strong reviews (a starred Booklist review, YALSA Best Fiction pick, blurbs from established YA authors) suggest the mystery does not crowd out the character and idea work. SCREENED 2026-09-02 on axis:sex-portrayal, verdict mild, was [70, 80]. Molly wants to be a surgeon in 1855 Philadelphia and the male cohort works collectively against her - the students bully her in class, Dr LaValle gatekeeps the all-male anatomy group, Edgar is a suspect and the Knifeman mutilates women - so the men are largely obstacles or predators while Molly is the clever one. Discounted only mildly because the exclusion has a real historical in-world reason, LaValle is genuinely learned, and aunt Ava is as compromised as any man. The dock is the profile's stated convention (mild -2, moderate -5), not a measured magnitude - the axis has no high-contrast anchor yet.

Elizabeth Zott is a determined, competent protagonist whose whole arc is about what she wants (to do real chemistry) and why 1950s-60s institutions won't let her, told in a voice reviewers describe as immediately captivating ('in love with it by the end of chapter one') - the same want-and-why axis that carries Pride and Prejudice to 75. The idea she leaves behind (using a cooking show as covert scientific and feminist re-education) is concrete and namable. Risk on axis:worldbuilding/self-consistency: more than one reviewer notes the plot resolves 'too conveniently' for a story whose own thesis is that science, like life, is messy and rarely goes to plan - exactly the kind of author-declared commitment the reader's rules hold a book to. SCREENED 2026-09-02 on axis:sex-portrayal, verdict moderate, was [71, 80]. A clear case: reviewers describe a male cast that is near-uniformly demeaning or abusive, with the obstacles supplied by hardheaded, domineering, lust-driven men of science and then men in every walk of life, while Elizabeth Zott is the brilliant one and even the sympathetic Walter Pine is described as inert and unable to stand up to anyone. Calvin Evans and Wakely keep it short of strong, and 1961 institutional sexism is a partly stated in-world reason, but the male authority figures are made incompetent as well as bigoted. The dock is the profile's stated convention (mild -2, moderate -5), not a measured magnitude - the axis has no high-contrast anchor yet.

A kidnapped 13-year-old chess player, the lonely boy who visits her captivity, and the detective racing to find her, told across shifting POVs and a scrambled week-by-week timeline. The perpetrator is known from early on rather than concealed, so this reads as a survival thriller rather than a whodunit and does not trigger the detective filter. But it is a pure suspense/thriller with no idea to name beyond the tension itself, and even positive reviews note the explanations are 'thin' and the ending 'messy' and 'abrupt' - the same kind of thin-premise signal the log treats as a ceiling (contrast Mortal Engines' unworked premise at 55). Child endangerment content is present throughout, but the reader's rules treat a child protagonist and violence as non-objections in themselves.

A classic German early-reader caper: two boys set a trap to recover their grandmother's stolen musical coffee grinder from a robber, then get entangled with a rival sorcerer who has to be outwitted. It is a slight, whimsical adventure aimed at very young children with no idea to name beyond bravery and friendship winning out - closer to the picture-book end of the spectrum than Little Prince 82, which earns its score on a real idea despite also being short and child-led. Ranger's Apprentice 74 and Narnia 67 at least carry some adventure plotting to think about; this is thinner than either. The sorcerer performs transformation magic on the page, which would need checking under axis:occult, but since the book lands well under 68 on ideas alone, that question is left unexamined rather than spent on.

The book earns points the way Project Hail Mary 92 does: it follows the disaster's second-order consequences instead of gesturing at them - an insulin shortage traded for thermite gas, a societal split between a technological meritocracy and an anti-tech faction, a debate over defending the last nuclear plant. That is the worldbuilding/ideas combination that tops this reader's log, applied here to a single anchoring event (the comet) that every character orbits, rather than several unrelated plotlines, so the large disaster-film ensemble is a multi-pov risk rather than the confusing-opening failure that sank Discworld and The Gunslinger to 30. The dated, at points overtly stereotyped treatment of its Black characters, flagged repeatedly by reviewers as a period problem, costs on the same axis:content line that marked down Ranger's Apprentice 74 for stereotypes stated as fact, trimming the range below where the pure ideas/worldbuilding case would otherwise sit.

t: Ma sestra je seriovy vrah (My Sister, the Serial Killer)
why: Korede, a nurse, keeps cleaning up after her beautiful younger sister Ayoola's killings - the killer is named on page one, so this is not a whodunit and does not trigger the detective filter. The book's actual engine is exactly the axis the log rewards most: why Korede keeps protecting a sister she knows is guilty, what family loyalty costs her, and how beauty buys Ayoola a pass from a world that would convict anyone else - page time on motive over event, the same quality that put Mockingjay and Golden Son at the top of the log. Korede is a genuinely rootable, conflicted lead rather than a passive one. Risk: several reviews call the ending abrupt, with the moral reckoning the setup promises left unresolved - a momentum/payoff concern rather than a premise failure. SCREENED 2026-09-02 on axis:sex-portrayal, verdict moderate, was [70, 80]. The two sisters hold all the agency - Korede the competent nurse, Ayoola the manipulator - while the men are uniformly beauty-blinded and thinly drawn: reviewers repeatedly call Tade thoughtless, shallow, easily swayed, one calling him flat next to the sisters, and everyone believes Ayoola's absurd stories because she is pretty. Only Muhtar, a comatose patient, escapes, and no in-world reason is offered, so the diminishment is doing the work of the joke. The dock is the profile's stated convention (mild -2, moderate -5), not a measured magnitude - the axis has no high-contrast anchor yet.

Reviewers keep landing on the same thing: a morally compromised character (Kite, who commits real, unforgivable violence) that the book still makes the reader care about without whitewashing him - the same needle Golden Son 92 threads with Fitchner, and that a flat villain lead (Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65) fails to thread. The time-loop mechanic is used to ask what a single choice across history is worth, a nameable idea rather than time travel as furniture. Risk: several reviewers, including ones who otherwise loved it, say the ending leaves the central mystery under-resolved with too many unanswered questions, the same self-consistency weakness that cost Mortal Engines its whole score. There is also a marriage-of-convenience subplot - Joe is wed, unhappily and through wartime circumstance, to a woman he does not love while his real bond is with Kite - but it reads as incidental to a war-and-time-travel premise rather than the engine of the book, so it is graded here, not vetoed, though it costs something.

A dying historian assembles her own life non-chronologically, centered on a wartime affair with a tank commander who is then killed - built around her own explicit thesis that history is kaleidoscopic, true from several angles at once, never one straight line. That is a real, nameable idea about how history and memory actually work, and Claudia herself - described across reviews as cynical, selfish, brilliant and magnetic - is the kind of interesting-and-flawed lead the log rewards over a merely likeable one (contrast Oliver Twist, 57, acted-upon rather than wanting). Booker Prize winner. The task line's 'occult' signal does not hold up on checking - nothing found ties this book to magic, ritual or the supernatural; it is straight historical/literary fiction. Risk: the central relationship ends in the lover's death and the loss of their unborn child, and the book is generally elegiac rather than hopeful, so bleakness (a mild but real discount in the log) could pull it down a few points; a secondary, ambiguously incestuous relationship with her brother is a content note rather than a filter.

The pivotal scandal (chapters 18-22 of the source, per SuperSummary) has 19-year-old Vivian and her friend Celia both sleep with Arthur Watson, who is married to Vivian's mentor Edna - a marriage-scoped infidelity that is a subplot rather than the premise (the novel spans Vivian's whole life, not just this incident), but Arthur 'gets away with his misdeeds' and stays married with no real consequence while the two women are professionally and socially ruined. Under the reader's rule an unpunished participant counts as approving framing, and subplot-plus-approving is a real deduction on its own, not just a footnote - it does not reach the reject threshold only because the book is not built around the affair itself. On top of that, reviewers (Book and Film Globe) independently flag that 'there's a lot of sex' across the book, which is a volume cost per the reader's rules regardless of how tastefully written. Vivian's voice and self-invention arc are genuinely engaging (the axis that could have carried a higher number), but two reviewers (Bibliofile, NPR) note the first half stays superficial and personal growth only lands 250+ pages in - a density problem that keeps this from clearing 65 rather than pushing it into A territory.

A blood-fever survivor with an illusion power and a disfiguring scar is hunted by an Inquisition that destroys people like her, and joins a secret society of fellow survivors bent on overthrowing the crown. The author has stated she set out to write a villain's origin, and reviews confirm Adelina is deliberately built as an anti-heroine whose fear and hatred progressively consume her - the same shape that cost Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 twenty-two points against Sunrise on the Reaping 87 for the identical reason, a villain lead the reader cannot root for. Reviewers also call the Renaissance-set world derivative of Sanderson's Mistborn/Allomancy but less thought through, an innate elemental-style power (not invocation or ritual) that passes the occult mechanism test but earns nothing extra on worldbuilding. Leaned on axis:protagonist, anchored on Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65; axis:worldbuilding is a risk given the 'inferior to Mistborn' comparison.

A dead abuser's ex-wife, estranged wife and current girlfriend team up for revenge; the women were involved with him in sequence, not concurrently, so axis:infidelity is a subplot at most, not the premise. Multiple reviews flag the central captivity scheme itself as needing heavy 'suspension of disbelief' and becoming 'more and more extreme' as it goes, the same premise-collapse problem that capped Mortal Engines at 55 and Divergent at 58. The idea does not survive its own escalation, which is the axis:ideas doubt this gate is built to catch.

Rural-romance novel touching grief, terminal illness and access to rural healthcare, treated with sensitivity per multiple reviews, but it is a genre romance execution of those themes rather than one that works an idea through to a conclusion. Nothing here clears the bar the reader sets for axis:ideas, which is the recurring reason this imprint's books settle just under 68.

The City is a declared, consistent system - people from across decades and nations are 'imported' for a stated but withheld Experiment, and the book follows through on what that means rather than treating it as scenery: the sun works like a stage light switched on and off, and the Mentors' unresolved mystery is part of the premise, not an authorial gap. That satisfies the same self-consistency test that rewards The Silmarillion 80 despite an unconventional structure. Reviewers call it the Strugatskys' magnum opus and compare it to Kafka for its serious philosophical satire rather than to lighter Strugatsky work like Roadside Picnic. Risk is pace and tone: it is long and career-spanning, and one reviewer who otherwise respected it still came away 'underwhelmed', so there is real room for it to land closer to 1984 60 if the satire outweighs the throughline. Discovery (axis:discovery, 2026-10-24): the Experiment is the book's unknown and the authors never answer it, by design, which forfeits the lift; the number holds.

t: Ordinace v divocine (No Job for a Girl)
why: Rural-romance novel about a safety officer proving herself in a male-dominated Outback mining camp; the workplace-sexism angle is drawn from the author's own family experience and reads as authentic rather than invented, but reviews frame it as a straightforward romance plot rather than one that works the idea through in any depth. No idea I would defend beyond 'competent romance with an authentic setting', so axis:ideas keeps this under the line.

Laura Bow builds a personal AI at 17, and the book spends five decades tracing what actually happens when that premise meets the world - corporate weaponization, privacy erosion, a rival AI (SCION) that harms people through information rather than a Terminator-style uprising. That is a premise worked out into real, non-generic consequences, the same test that made Project Hail Mary 92 and sank Mortal Engines at 55. Reviewers single out Laura as 'a real, fully rounded character' rather than a vehicle for the tech idea, the second half of what the log rewards. It opens on one concrete situation - a teenager building a chatbot in her bedroom - not several competing threads. Risk: a dissenting review calls some of Laura's personal backstory (absent father, self-harm) familiar-trope shorthand rather than earned motive, which could undercut the character work if it reads that way on the page. SCREENED 2026-09-02 on axis:sex-portrayal, verdict mild, was [70, 80]. Laura Bow's Organon is nurtured and humane while the male-run rival project SCION is raised on war games and causes the disaster amid its programmers' Skynet jokes, and reviewers note the two male narrators - bitter ex Charlie and journalist Cesar - are markedly less developed than Laura. Only mild because the book grounds the difference in how each AI was trained rather than in the sex of its makers, Laura's father is the original talent, and Cesar is a capable ally. The dock is the profile's stated convention (mild -2, moderate -5), not a measured magnitude - the axis has no high-contrast anchor yet.

Jaxie is exactly the kind of lead this reader rewards: damaged but clearly wanting something concrete (freedom from his father, reunion with Lee, safety), and the whole book is his voice working through that want - the same motives-over-action axis that tops Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90. Reviewers consistently call the voice, not plot mechanics, the driving force, and note he stays sympathetic despite ugly edges rather than becoming a villain lead like Coriolanus Snow 65. The risk is sustained bleakness - an abusive dead father, total isolation, a 'doomed journey' tone throughout - which this reader discounts mildly (The Martian 82, 1984 60) rather than treats as disqualifying, so it trims the top of the range rather than capping it low.

The idea is nameable in a sentence: time is one frozen lattice, a change to the past is paradox noise that settles into a single history that always was, and only a mind can travel, riding a living host who can argue back. That is axis:ideas earning, and the time mechanics meet the axis:worldbuilding obligation rather than spend it: Locus calls this one of the few time-travel stories where paradox does not cheat, and a reviewer finds the closing twist demonstrated earlier, the Golden Son 92 reveal earned rather than sprung. Two readers say the ending breaks its own rules; the one specific objection seems to assume the grandfather paradox the book's declared model replaces, but Ja, robot 55 shows what a broken declared system costs this reader, so the floor carries it. Valentina, a 71-year-old teacher of the last generation who must persuade her host rather than command her and finally puts herself in danger for others, is the rootable, self-sacrificing lead of Project Hail Mary 92, and thriller pacing supplies the drive Pocitani hvezd 85 lacked. Thin side characters, a sabotage strand told second-hand and an out-of-order structure whose switches the Czech typesetting leaves unmarked keep it under Valka stareho muze 87, the nearest scored mind in a borrowed body. Standalone; no sex, no occult, no detective plot.

A serious genre outlet (Strange Horizons) makes exactly the case this gate asks about: the premise promised something fresh - AI, war and social media combined - but the book 'squanders' it, anthropomorphizing the ship's AI into the same cliche it seemed to be critiquing, leaving the themes as 'window dressing for a fairly bland and antiquated tale.' A second, separate reviewer calls the four leads 'almost caricatures' of their archetypes. That is sourced axis:ideas and axis:protagonist doubt, not signal noise - other reviews are positive, but this is the kind of specific criticism the ladder is built to catch cheaply rather than confirm at six sources.

A near-future dystopia where an immigrant underclass ('Dregs') is forced to perform deadly circus acts for the entertainment of a racially 'Pure' ruling class. One reviewer calls it a blunt polemic with an unconvincing vision of the future that hits every dystopia cliche, and another found the central romance's insta-love unearned with two-dimensional leads - the same combination of an unexamined premise and a thin, hard-to-root-for cast that sank Divergent to 58 in this log. The allegory itself is nameable (xenophobia and dehumanization of outsiders), so it does not drop to the lower band, but nothing in the reviews suggests the premise is worked out carefully enough to clear 68. No occult content is indicated by the catalogue signals, so that question was not separately examined.

Historical fiction set during the final construction of the Vanderbilts' Biltmore estate, following a local woman whose family land is the last piece needed to complete it, with a murder investigation woven through the class-conflict plot. The class/inequality theme is a real idea, but one reviewer explicitly says the book cannot decide if it is a mystery or a social commentary, with mystery elements dropping out for long stretches, and another felt it needed more editing - the kind of unevenness between competing threads that the log treats as a density penalty rather than a fatal flaw. The murder investigation is a subplot rather than the book's main satisfaction, so it is flagged rather than treated as a detective-genre reject.

Dual-timeline family saga (present-day Fleur unravelling an aunt's diary from a 1930s Gulf Country cattle station). Multiple independent reviewers, including a longtime fan of the author, single out the same problem: feeling detached from Fleur despite an interesting plot - the protagonist axis does not land. No standalone idea beyond the familiar inheritance/family-secrets shape either, so this settles just under 68 like most of the queue's family sagas without a nameable idea.

t: Prvni herecka (The First Actress: A Novel of Sarah Bernhardt)
why: A fictional first-person biography of Sarah Bernhardt built around what she wants and why - the Historical Novel Society calls the prose 'immersive' and Gortner's fluid first person the strength of the book, and an independent reviewer was 'completely captivated from the very first page'. That is exactly the axis the reader rewards most, and the underdog shape (a rebellious daughter fighting free of a mother who tried to sell her into the same courtesan trade) makes her genuinely rootable, comparable to the motive-driven engagement that earned Pride and Prejudice 75. Risk on axis:sexual-content because her mother arranges her as a paid companion to an older man and she becomes an unmarried mother at sixteen - real content, though reviews describe it as handled as serious biographical fact rather than crude or explicit.

t: Rim jsem ja (Roma soy yo (I Am Rome))
why: Opens on one concrete, legible situation - a corrupt senator about to be tried, and a 23-year-old Julius Caesar unexpectedly stepping up as prosecutor - which is exactly the single-starting-point shape the reader's opening rule rewards, not the several-plot-lines confusion that sank Guards! Guards! and The Gunslinger. Caesar is an ambitious, motive-driven lead the reader can root for, and the book works through a real idea (how rhetoric and law function as levers of power against an entrenched elite) rather than just delivering costume-drama events. No occult content: religious material is limited to a legal charge of 'sacrilege' in the trial, not a depicted rite, and sources describe no explicit sexual content despite an intense Caesar-Cornelia romance. Posteguillo's Rome novels run long and some readers flag repetitiveness, which is the risk that could pull this down; not leaning on worldbuilding since historical-fiction plausibility is a different axis than the reader's self-consistency test.

t: Sam proti inkvizici (Against the Inquisition (La gesta del marrano))
why: A fictionalized biography of a real 17th-century doctor, raised Christian, who returns to Judaism and is imprisoned by the Inquisition for twelve years - resourceful and brilliant throughout (he out-argues visiting Inquisition theologians and manufactures ink and a pen from a chicken bone and a sharpened nail to keep writing in solitary confinement), the kind of active, competent, worth-rooting-for lead the log rewards over a passive one (contrast Oliver Twist, 57). The idea - what a person is willing to pay to defend a belief he could simply have hidden - is concrete and real, closer to Seeking Allah Finding Jesus's examined-conviction rigor (91) than to abstract theology. Risk: the history is a matter of record and ends in his execution, and twelve years of imprisonment and torture is sustained, not incidental, bleakness; and because the whole plot turns on his religious conviction, faith carries more narrative weight here than the 'thread, not the whole subject' rule prefers, closer to Quo Vadis (66, also historical persecution-for-faith) than to a book where faith is one thread among several.

t: Sberatel ztracenych veci (The Keeper of Lost Things)
why: A retired writer who lost his fiancee decades ago spends his life collecting lost objects and writing stories about them, then bequeaths the mission - and a ghost - to his assistant Laura. The ghost is a benign, whimsical presence rather than any rite or real-world occult system, so it does not trigger the occult filter. But even sympathetic reviewers call the plot device-driven ('ridiculous coincidences'), and one harsher review specifically names Laura a 'lackluster protagonist' in an 'underdeveloped' cast - directly on the axis the log weighs most (contrast a thin lead sinking Artemis to 69 despite good worldbuilding). There is no idea here beyond 'grief and lost things reconnect people', which is sentiment rather than a worked premise.

Narration rotates among the seven Shaw siblings and their father across a non-chronological span from 1911-1959, bound by their mother's ambiguous death (accident or suicide) and its long aftermath. Unlike a true anthology, reviewers (Kirkus, Booklist, Library Journal) consistently praise how the individually 'story-like' chapters compile into one coherent family portrait rather than reading as scattered - closer to the precedent set by Male zeny 79 (a domestic, premise-free story that still clears the line on character work alone) or Silmarillion 80 (no single protagonist, still coheres) than to the disjointed Unfinished Tales 69. Leaned on axis:character-differentiation because that cohesion-through-distinct-voices is exactly what the positive reviews single out. Risk on axis:multi-pov because eight rotating narrators structurally dilute the single, rootable protagonist the reader's rules weight above almost everything else.

Dual-timeline family saga: a model with a fragile mental state, mourning her adoptive father and a breakup, learns from a stranger's letter that she has living family. Reviewers describe the series formula as well-researched and entertaining but repeatedly note the contemporary strand is thin next to the historical one and the plots lean on melodrama and exposition rather than a worked idea. Unlike idea-driven successes such as Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82, there is no idea to name beyond 'trace your roots', which is the pattern the gate-4 default band exists for. Leaned on axis:ideas for the number; axis:protagonist is a risk given the recurring criticism of thin present-day leads across the series, the same failure mode that capped Promena 58 and Oliver Twist 57.

A sweeping historical romance (1930s London, Paris and the Spanish Civil War) built around a love triangle between Annabelle and two men. Reviews are consistently mixed on the same point across independent sources - readable and atmospheric, but predictable, with characters called 'basic' and lacking depth. There is no idea beyond the standard romance/war-backdrop shape, so axis:ideas is the risk that keeps this below 68 rather than something to score on.

t: Smrt a dalsi stastne konce (Death and Other Happy Endings)
why: Jennifer Cole learns she has three months to live and writes closure letters to the people who hurt her most. Multiple reviewers call the premise familiar and the three addressees (ex-husband, sister, ex-boyfriend) stock 'narcissist' archetypes, even while praising the book's warmth and humour. There is no idea here beyond a comfort-read closure arc, the same shape as other competent, well-liked but unremarkable commercial fiction that lands just under this reader's line.

The premise - an authoritarian leader manufacturing a monster myth to rule an isolated settlement through fear - is nameable but thin in execution: reception splits from enthusiastic to a flat 'not a book I would recommend', with one reviewer recommending a similar book instead as the stronger version of the same idea. That is the axis:ideas doubt this gate asks about. A teen lead forced toward marriage is worth a small life-phase deduction, not a bar - Narnia 67 and Male zeny 79 both clear similar terrain. One source establishes premise and the split reception; not enough to trust a tight number, so C-low at the default band.

t: Starec a reka (The Old Man and the Sand Eel)
why: A three-generation fishing memoir with a nameable idea - that chasing bigger catches and competitive achievement hollowed out the simple connection the author once had with his grandfather and the river, and that recognising this is what let him rebuild it. That is a genuine examined truth in the sense the reader's memoir rule rewards, unlike the insight-free Yorkshire vet travelogue in this same batch. Literary-press reviews (Spectator, Literary Review) are enthusiastic about the prose itself ('sharp and clever', 'loved all of it'), though one review found it lacking the 'poetic dimension' that would make it a classic, which caps the estimate below the Seeking Allah/Son of Hamas tier of memoir.

Five girls sold as children to a brothel and branded with magical marks escape after one of them kills a client in self-defense, and flee across a fantasy Wild West setting pursued by the law. Reviews consistently praise a plot-and-character-driven structure with a single concrete inciting incident (no confusing multi-thread opening) and a protagonist, Aster, driven by a clear want - protecting her sister-figure and the group - the same motive-clarity axis that tops the log via Mockingjay 91 and The Hunger Games 89. The central idea, girls reversing the power dynamics of their own exploitation, is a real, well-received idea rather than a borrowed one, unlike the C-band default case. The magical brands and 'shadowless' curse are an invented system with no real-world ritual described in any review found, passing the occult mechanism test. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:protagonist; axis:bleakness is a risk given the sustained trauma/PTSD content reviewers flag, though the log treats bleakness as only a mild discount (1984 60 vs. sustained-bleakness books scoring near it for other reasons).

t: Stesti si te najde (The Happiest Little Town)
why: Three-POV women's-fiction comfort read (a grieving teenager, a divorcee, an ageing actress) unified by a community-theatre plot in a small Queensland town. Reviewers consistently describe it in comfort-read terms - 'feel good', 'wraps you up in a hug' - rather than pointing to any idea worth carrying away. The split across three POVs is a mild structural risk but not what keeps the score down; the absence of a nameable idea is.

The closing volume of an alternate-history trilogy where a silver-barred wall separates early-20th-century Warsaw from an enclave of monsters, with a Polish alchemist and a Russian officer as leads. Polish reviewers praise it for an original blend of real history and the fantastic and for a vivid sense of place, which speaks well to axis:worldbuilding, but nothing in the available coverage establishes whether the two leads are drawn with real interiority or mainly carried by plot and setting - the doubt that decides this gate is whether the characters are worth rooting for, and I could not confirm it either way from Polish-language reviews alone. Given that uncertainty and that this is the third of three volumes read in isolation, the safer number is the default band rather than assuming the idea and cast both hold up.

Lakshmi is a self-made, sympathetic protagonist - fled an abusive marriage, built an independent business and reputation from nothing in 1950s Jaipur, worth rooting for in the way Little Women 79 rewards a domestic-but-purposeful lead. The book has a real thematic throughline (women's independence and class facade in newly-independent India), which the reader's ideas axis rewards. It carries a subplot affair between Lakshmi and a married patron, Samir, but the affair is one strand among family secrets and business survival, not the premise, and its fallout (a gossip campaign that nearly ruins her) reads as consequence rather than celebration, so it costs only a modest deduction rather than a reject. Leaning on protagonist and ideas rather than worldbuilding, since some reviewers found the supporting cast (particularly Radha) thin.

A dozen Native characters converge on an Oakland powwow that ends in a mass shooting, built around a real, awarded idea - what Native identity means when it survives displacement into a city rather than a reservation, the kind of 'something to think about' the log rewards over plot events (Animal Farm 78). It opens with one character's legible chapter (Tony Loneman) rather than several threads competing at once, so it does not fail the confusing-opening test that sank Guards! Guards! and The Gunslinger at 30. The real risk is the ensemble itself: with no single protagonist across a dozen POV chapters, at least one critical reading calls the climax 'surprisingly inert' precisely because no character is developed enough to carry it - the opposite of what worked for the log's one no-protagonist success, The Silmarillion (80), which leaned on dense mythic prose rather than contemporary trauma realism. The reader has separately marked a villain-descent lead down 22 points for being hard to root for (Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, 65); the risk here is thinness of any single lead rather than unlikability, but it points the same direction.

t: Tanci, jako by te nikdo nevidel (Dance Like No One's Watching)
why: Sequel to Sing Like No One's Listening: a London stage-school romance where the leads face a long-distance strain, alongside a subplot investigating the protagonist's late ballet-dancer mother's past. That mother-mystery is a subplot, not the book's main satisfaction, so axis:detective is examined and does not fire. No idea beyond a standard coming-of-age relationship arc is established in any coverage found (only trade/publisher copy and a Kirkus plot summary), which fits the default C-low band.
