A worked-out double premise: a mid-level bureaucrat destroyed by a single media-pileup over one careless remark, intercut with a kafkaesque afterlife bureaucracy that grants entry to Heaven based on data logged in a celestial computer - the two halves mirror each other as satire of surveillance, moralizing media and dehumanising bureaucracy, closer to the idea-driven allegory that earns Animal Farm 78 than to the passive-protagonist bleakness that sank Promena to 58. Reviews call it funny and corrosive rather than oppressive, so the bleakness discount stays mild. Leaned on axis:ideas because the satire is genuinely carried through both narrative strands, not just declared. Risk on axis:protagonist because Simon has real, if 'benign', hidden vices and is not unambiguously worth rooting for, and on axis:density because multiple reviewers flag overlong passages and a weaker final chapter.

A forensic-psychologist protagonist investigates a prisoner who can drive people to suicide by whispered suggestion. Reviews are split on execution, one titled 'Good Premise, Weak Implementation', and one reader singles out the lead as 'spineless and despicable... a pathetic whiner... an adulterer', saying that aversion made it hard to stay invested. His infidelity is characterisation/backstory, not the book's premise, so axis:infidelity is graded only. The unlikeable-lead problem matches what separated Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes (65) from Sunrise on the Reaping (87) in this log: a workable premise capped by a protagonist not worth rooting for.

Single-POV Tudor court novel narrated by Margaret Tudor, built almost entirely on sibling rivalry and political motive against her sister Mary and sister-in-law Katherine of Aragon - the axis that tops this log (Pride and Prejudice 75, Mockingjay 91). The opening is a single clear situation (12-year-old Margaret meeting the newly arrived Katherine), not a confusing multi-thread start. But two independent reviews confirm the same failure mode that held Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes to 65 against Sunrise on the Reaping's 87: Kirkus calls Margaret 'venal, petty, and jaundiced', and the Historical Novel Society calls her 'proud and stubborn, and one who does not seem to learn from experience', concluding 'without a likeable protagonist, this story may fall short of expectations'. That confirmed protagonist problem, not the well-realized political motive it is built on, is what carries this estimate down. One review also flags length and repetition ('could be shorter'), a secondary axis:density risk. No occult or infidelity elements are present.

The lead is built to withhold exactly what this reader scores highest on: the Vagrant never speaks and the book gives no internal monologue, so there is no page time on what he wants and why - the axis that four separate author comparisons in this reader's log agree matters most. Reviewers confirm the effect reads as disorienting rather than intriguing: one calls the opening chapters 'pretty confusing' before the setup resolves, echoing the delayed-legibility problem that sank The Gunslinger and both Discworld tries to 30. It is a well-regarded book on its own terms (a Morningstar Award winner), but the structural choice cuts directly against this reader's strongest preference rather than being merely a stylistic risk.

t: Udoli nadeje (In the Valley of Rainbow Mist)
why: 1925 Australian romance in which a young woman flees a family scandal to the countryside and becomes an accidental bestselling author. German-market reviews (the book's primary review base) are split, one calling it the author's weakest work - 'shallow', little suspense, tragedy arriving late and predictably. No idea worth naming beyond the standard scandal-and-redemption romance shape, which is what keeps this under 68 rather than any single fatal flaw.

t: Ve svetle toho, co vime (In the Light of What We Know)
why: A banker's disintegrating life is interrupted by the reappearance of Zafar, a mathematics prodigy from Bangladesh whose story of Oxford, Kabul and a broken engagement the narrator tries to reconstruct - the book is explicitly a meditation on the limits of what anyone can actually know about another person, themselves, or history, a real idea in the vein the log rewards (Animal Farm 78, Labyrint 70). It touches the infidelity axis: Emily's affair with the narrator happens while she is engaged to Zafar, not married, which the rule scopes in, but it is a subplot within a much larger book about knowledge and war, not the premise, and it is played as tragic and destructive - Zafar's discovery of it triggers the novel's darkest turn - rather than approved, so subplot-plus-condemned costs only a few points here, not a reject. The larger risk is the book's own reputation: reviewers repeatedly call the digressive, non-chronological structure 'plodding' and its erudition self-indulgent, the same kind of penalty the log applies to sprawling digression (Les Miserables, 71) rather than tight momentum (Monte Cristo, 75).

A contented bachelor falls for his new neighbour, and a decade into their marriage a serious accident forces him to decide whether to keep her on life support. Reviews call it a light, pleasant read with a heartfelt central dilemma but otherwise unremarkable - 'wasn't fantastic, just okay' - and the life-support choice functions as an emotional plot device rather than an idea examined in its consequences, closer to the log's C-band pattern than to an idea-driven read like Animal Farm 78. Leaned on axis:ideas for the number; no graded axis looks likely to push it below the range, so risks is empty.

t: Vsichni jsme utkani z hvezd (We Are All Made of Stars)
why: The task line's infidelity screen flagged premise:true on the word 'vdana' (married), but two separate searches confirm there is no affair: Stella's marital strain is her husband Vincent's war-injury trauma and emotional withdrawal, not adultery, so axis:infidelity does not actually apply here despite the screen hit. The real hook multiple reviewers single out is the hospice-letters device - Stella writes her dying patients' unsaid final words to those they love - which is a genuine, specific idea about what people leave unsaid, in the spirit of the motive-driven examination that made Speaker for the Dead score high in this reader's log. Risk on axis:bleakness for the hospice/death setting and the husband's war trauma, though reviewers stress the tone stays warm rather than oppressive.

Irish Famine saga: a family fights eviction and starvation while a daughter loves a poor tenant farmer opposed by her father and a cruel landlord. A starred trade review calls it powerful, but reader reviews describe it as dense, multi-character and unrelentingly 'doom and gloom', with famine suffering arriving throughout rather than building. Exodus 68 and Quo Vadis 66 show that solid historical fiction built on real atrocity still tends to sit right at or under the line in this log, and this book's mix of trade praise with reader complaints of grimness and density tracks the same pattern. Leaning on axis:bleakness rather than the famine setting itself, which is not in question.

t: Zachary Jing a Draci cisar (Zachary Ying and the Dragon Emperor)
why: A middle-grade adventure explicitly compared to Percy Jackson by reviewers, in which a 12-year-old hosts the spirit of China's first emperor to seal a portal to the Chinese underworld. There is a real idea here - the ambivalent legacy of Qin Shi Huang and Zack's disconnect from his heritage are handled with some nuance per reviews - but it does not clearly clear the bar: one reviewer calls the pacing meandering, and the format is fast-paced action in the Percy Jackson mold rather than the sustained motives-and-consequences focus the log rewards. That comparison is a warning sign in its own right: Percy Jackson landed at 57 in this log specifically because a real-world pantheon and underworld (not an invented system) is used on the page, and Zachary Ying's underworld portal and spirit-possession by real historical Chinese emperors sits in the same real-world-derived territory. Since the book already looks likely to land under 68 on the ideas/execution balance alone, that occult question is left unexamined rather than spent on.

Stile's abilities are total rather than earned, and reviewers across decades name the exact failure mode this axis describes: 'good at pretty much EVERYTHING... got to be ridiculous... a superman' despite pages spent on how he suffers for being short. That undercuts the underdog premise the book is trying to sell. A murder-mystery subplot (who killed Stile's double) and an Adept magic system with declared spell rules are both live questions this exit does not settle - axis:detective and axis:occult stay unexamined and undecided, not cleared, per this gate. One review pass is enough to see the unearned-competence pattern is structural across the trilogy rather than incidental to book one.

t: Zare davno pohasla (A Brightness Long Ago)
why: Kay's Renaissance-Italy analogue is a meditation on memory and fortune told in retrospect by Danio Cerra, a tailor's son whose life is upended by two rival mercenary captains and a duke's daughter he loves. It stays true to the reader's motives-over-action preference - reviewers describe it as a character-driven reflection on choices and fate rather than a plot-machine - and it is as historically self-consistent as Kay can make it, with only a ghost, a prophetic gift and two moons as fantastical touches, none of which involve any rite, invocation or real-world occult source: a clean pass on axis:occult, the same territory as Tolkien's background magic in Silmarillion 80 and LOTR 84. One reviewer flags Danio himself as a little flat and says watching him is not really the appeal of the book, which is a direct risk given the reader's rule that a thin lead outranks strong worldbuilding (Artemis 69). There is one mildly explicit consensual sex scene and off-page but discussed sexual sadism tied to a villain's characterization, which is bleak but condemned rather than eroticized, closer to a bleakness discount than a sexual-content deduction.

A married couple's true account of being deported together to Auschwitz, separated on the ramp, and finding each other again a year later. French reader reviews consistently describe it as stripped-down and unliterary in style - 'not literature, but the rawness of everyday life' - which is the same plain, honest first-person register that earned Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91: it is not reaching for effect. Unlike Diary of a Young Girl 40, which the log marks down partly for ending in death with nothing resolved, this account is built around survival and reunion, so the sustained bleakness of the camp material is balanced by an actual outcome rather than left open - the mild bleakness discount applies, but nothing like the collapse that sank Anne Frank. Coverage of this book is thin (reader reviews on French retail/community sites, no professional press review found), so the number is held to two sources rather than the normal four.

Burnt-out city woman swaps homes with her rainforest-dwelling godmother; a dual storyline of self-discovery and a buried secret coming back on the godmother. Reader reviews are warm ('engrossing', 'uplifting') but describe an uplit comfort read rather than a book with a thesis to argue - the axis:ideas shortfall this imprint's uplit line runs into: warmth in place of a thesis.

Reception is split, and the specific complaint that recurs is the one this reader has scored hardest on before: the protagonist Siren is described by more than one reviewer as an 'ideal, completely unfeeling superrobot' with no concrete goal, her dynamic with her companion Artem amounting to 'they just walk somewhere together' rather than characters revealing what they want - the opposite of the motives-over-action axis that tops this reader's whole log. The dense, well-researched post-apocalyptic society is a genuine strength (Strugatsky and Lem are cited approvingly as comparisons), but 1984 60 and Divergent 58 both show that grim setting and clever worldbuilding do not rescue a book when the lead doesn't carry it, and here the doubt is squarely on the lead.

t: Zverolekarem v Yorkshiru (My Yorkshire Great and Small)
why: A cosy travelogue-memoir of a TV vet's anecdotes about Yorkshire itself rather than his practice or his own life, praised by reader reviews mainly as a comforting armchair trip rather than for insight; one Goodreads reviewer even notes it does not read in the author's own voice, having been written with a journalist. The reader's rule is explicit that memoir/testimony earns nothing by itself - what earns is examining what is actually true or giving insight into another group's experience - and this book, unlike Seeking Allah Finding Jesus 91 or Son of Hamas 75, is not attempting that; it is light, pleasant local colour with no idea worth naming.

t: Divka v zrcadle (The Girl in the Mirror)
why: 'Mirror twins' Iris and Summer are set against each other by their father's inheritance scheme; when Iris is stranded alone on the family yacht and later lets Summer's husband mistake her for his wife, she steps into her twin's life and its secrets. It's a psychological/domestic thriller about deception rather than a whodunnit investigation, so it does not trip the detective filter. But multiple independent reviews call the twist ending logically holed - 'buries itself in tropes and gapes with logical holes,' 'a letdown' - which is exactly the self-consistency failure this reader has docked before (Divergent 58, Mortal Engines 55): a plot mechanism that does not survive scrutiny once revealed. That puts axis:worldbuilding under risk and there is no other idea strong enough to carry the book past it.

The core premise - a virus that snaps individual humans back into Homo erectus, millions of years of evolution undone in one infection - is exactly the kind of declared mechanism the reader's rules hold an author to, and reviewers report the book never earns it: its large cast of national stereotypes is 'fairly caricatured and predictable', and more than one reviewer felt something was missing for the read to be as gripping as the pitch promised. That is close to the Mortal Engines 55 pattern - a hook that does not survive being thought through - though Erectus is graded rather than abandoned since it does have a real, statable idea and a functioning thriller plot, unlike a DNF.

A short theatrical retelling in which Rousseau narrates his own life and thought (childhood injustice, abandoning his own children, the pleasure of music, his ideas on society and education) while staging his last opera. Unlike the companion Nietzsche volume in the same imprint, reception here is genuinely split: one reader found it a fair first contact with Rousseau's ideas, but another called it 'nothing but mockery, a demonstration meant to ridicule him,' faulting the self-focused framing and reductive shortcuts. That doubt about whether the ideas are handled with real substance rather than caricature is enough to put axis:ideas under risk rather than treat it as a clear Labyrint-svetа-style hit, so this sits at the gate-4 default band rather than going on to full research.

t: Male divadlo Hannah Arendtove (Hannah Arendt's Little Theater)
why: A short (64-page) allegorical fiction: an elderly Hannah Arendt is visited on a small stage by the child she once was, and together they re-enact her core ideas - that thinking is itself a form of acting, that faceless bureaucracy tries to remake the world 'out of paper,' and the banality of evil. That is a real, nameable idea, delivered through invented allegorical figures (a forest, a wolf, paper-men) rather than religious material, so it clears gate 4 the way Labyrint svetа a raj srdce (70, hit its predicted band on axis:ideas) and Animal Farm (78) did. It is published in a children's philosophy imprint and one critic felt the format forces damaging shortcuts, but another found real substance in it, and reviewers agree the allegory reads better for teens/adults than young children - so the childrens axis is a small pushback, not a wash, closer to Little Prince (82, ideas carry it despite a child-facing package) than to a picture book.

Told by two siblings, Jovan (a secretly trained poison-taster) and the physically disabled Kalina, after the Chancellor is poisoned and their city-state is besieged. It opens as a murder mystery ('I was seven years old the first time my uncle poisoned me'), but reviewers agree the investigation is only the hook - by the middle the siege, politics and the siblings' personal stakes take over and 'the mystery... gets lost a bit as other plot threads take over' - so this is a mystery-shaped subplot in an otherwise eligible epic fantasy, a flag rather than a detective veto. There is no magic system at all; poison is a trained craft and a political metaphor for corruption, so the occult filter never engages. What carries the estimate is character work this reader responds to: two clearly differentiated POV siblings with personal, non-interchangeable motives (Jovan's guilt and duty, Kalina's search for her own role despite her disability), the same kind of distinct-wants writing that lifted Golden Son over Divergent. It stays out of the 80s because reviewers flag real pacing sag in the middle once the mystery hook fades.

A rags-to-riches Victorian-London business saga: James Falconer rises through a shipping magnate's company while juggling a fire, a past liaison with an older woman, a new romance, and shifting feelings for the magnate's difficult daughter. This is a commercial multi-generational family/business saga in the Bradford mould - plot-forward melodrama (will James choose the company or his own path) rather than a single worked-out idea, so axis:ideas goes under risks the same way it would for a competent but unremarkable historical soap opera. No infidelity premise: James is unmarried and the romantic entanglements are ordinary courtship, not marital betrayal.

t: Navrat na panstvi Tyringham (Return to Tyringham Park)
why: An Irish country-house saga built on a swapped-at-birth secret and its fallout across two generations and two continents. Reviews call it 'densely plotted' but also 'repetitive'; Goodreads ratings sit at a modest 3.2-3.4/5, well under the reception of the log's successful sagas like The Count of Monte Cristo (75). It is also a sequel, and 'sequels are not safe bets in this log' (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70). No idea beyond the swapped-identity melodrama is established in any review found.

Continues the same motive-driven Caesar as he is exiled, captured by pirates, and returns to fight his way into the Senate against Cicero and Cato - the same rhetoric-and-power idea continues to be worked through rather than just staged as costume drama. This is a sequel, and sequels are not a safe bet in this log: they can hold nearly steady (Ender saga, a 9-point settle) or fall hard (Hitchhiker's, 13 points), and without direct reviews of this specific volume's character work the safer read is a modest step down rather than assuming it holds level. Same density risk as before - Posteguillo's Rome novels run long.

A sequel: the freed girls, now scattered, regroup to organize a wider resistance against the brothel system rather than just escaping it. The idea carrying the book - reversing the power dynamics of exploitation - and the protagonist axis (Aster's want to protect and free others) are the same pair that anchor the log's high scorers such as Mockingjay 91. As a sequel, the number sits a little lower per the reader's own recorded pattern that sequels are not safe bets in this log - Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70 even without any new defect appearing. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:protagonist; axis:bleakness remains a risk given the sustained trauma content of the series.

Half-brothers Shasa Courtney and Manfred de la Rey, raised on opposite sides of a family secret, become political and personal enemies against the backdrop of Depression-era South Africa and the runup to WWII. Reviews split hard: praised for historical grounding and an unflinching look at pre-apartheid racial politics, but also described as descending into 'plodding soap opera' after a strong opening, with a melodramatic middle. That split reception, plus a sprawling multi-generational family-saga structure rather than one worked-out premise, means I would list axis:ideas under risks - closer to Exodus 68 or Quo Vadis 66 (competent historical sagas without a single idea to carry them) than to Monte Cristo 75, whose revenge plot is a single unified engine. It is also the 5th book in the Courtney series, and this reader's sequels have not held up (Hitchhiker's -13, Ballad -22 vs. its pair).

A sequel: having fled after being betrayed by family and allies, Adelina builds her own army fueled explicitly by fear and hatred, continuing further into a villain arc. The reader's log already shows this exact shape costing heavily - Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 lost 22 points against Sunrise on the Reaping 87 purely on an unrootable, darkening lead - and here the descent reads as more entrenched still, so the number sits below that anchor. The elemental illusion-based power system remains an innate-ability mechanism rather than invoked ritual, so it does not trip the occult veto, but the derivative-worldbuilding complaints in reviews persist, earning it nothing extra. As a sequel, sequels are not safe bets in this log either (Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70). Leaned on axis:protagonist, anchored on Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65; axis:worldbuilding remains a risk.

A short (63-page) fictionalized retelling of Thus Spoke Zarathustra: Nietzsche comes down from his mountain to teach people to set down their burdens, confronts a dragon representing fear and resentment, and works through self-overcoming, a morality built on guilt, and joy versus resentment. Unlike the mixed-to-negative reception of the companion Rousseau volume in the same imprint (criticized by one reader as mockery), reviews of this one are consistently positive about its philosophical content, treating the ideas (self-overcoming, becoming what one is) with real seriousness rather than reducing them to a joke - so axis:ideas is a genuine strength, in the register of Labyrint sveta a raj srdce (70) rather than a thin gate-4 exit. It touches critique of religious/guilt-based morality but as philosophy-of-ideas, not as an apologetic or theological work, so axis:faith is not really in play. Published for a 9-99 children's philosophy imprint, so a small childrens-register pushback applies, similar in kind to Ranger's Apprentice (74).

A sequel within an apocalyptic-horror survival series: survivors trapped in a cabin by endless snow and haunted by apparitions. Reviewers repeatedly say the book 'doesn't really advance the story', call the series 'fine' but 'a bit unremarkable', with 'no desire to spend any money to finish the series'. No idea beyond the survival-horror premise is nameable in any review found, which is exactly the axis:ideas doubt this gate tests for. Occult status is left unexamined by exiting here; nothing in the reviews describes a ritual or invoked entity, only ambient apparitions.

t: Tichy strazce (The Secret Keeper of Jaipur)
why: A sequel within the Jaipur Trilogy, alternating three POVs (Lakshmi, Malik, Nimmi) around a real historical hook - corruption tied to the 1968 Gold Control Act and a fraud investigation into a collapsed theatre balcony. The fraud plot gives Malik real motive-driven agency (uncovering a cover-up as a former street child who "always knew to keep his own counsel") rather than being acted upon, which the reader rewards. The task line's infidelity flag (hit on 'vdana') is a false positive on inspection: Lakshmi is simply happily remarried, and the Malik/Nimmi romance involves no married party, so the axis does not fire here. The investigation into the cinema collapse is a mystery-shaped subplot, not the book's whole satisfaction, so it is a flag rather than a detective-gate reject. This is a sequel, and sequels are not a safe bet in this log - Hitchhiker's fell 13 points in its sequel, though Ender's settled only 9 - so the estimate is discounted a shade for the extra POV split and that sequel risk.

Sent to stay with relatives, Tom discovers a Victorian garden that only exists at midnight and befriends Hatty, a girl who ages a little with each visit - until the ending reveals the cranky old woman upstairs, Mrs Bartholomew, is Hatty grown old, and that Tom has been visiting her memory. The magic is a single unexplained time-slip device (an old clock), not a system, ritual or pantheon, so it does not touch the occult filter at all. What earns the score is a real, nameable idea worked out to its conclusion - that an old person is still the child they were, and that time is carried in memory rather than lost - the same kind of idea-carries-a-short-book case that lifted The Little Prince to 82 despite a child lead. It stays under the mid-70s rather than reaching that high because the frame is still a children's classic (Carnegie Medal winner) with a child protagonist throughout, closer in register to Narnia (67) than to the adult-facing allegory of The Little Prince.

t: Vanoce v Shelter Inn (Christmas at the Shelter Inn)
why: A small-town holiday romance about a woman returning home to help her pregnant sister and reconnecting with a local doctor. Reviewers are warm about the emotional beats (family, forgiveness, community) but explicitly call the plot predictable, and nothing in the coverage points to an idea beyond a comfort-read arc of healing old wounds - competent, pleasant genre fiction with nothing to set it above the C-low default band.

t: Volani srdce (Fliegende Aerzte - Aufbruch ins Outback)
why: The catalogue's orig title, 'A Moment in the Sun', does not match any Elizabeth Haran novel and instead belongs to an unrelated John Sayles book - a mismatched record. The translator field carries the real German title, 'Fliegende Aerzte - Aufbruch ins Outback', part of a Flying-Doctors-themed series, which matches the Czech annotation exactly (young English nurse, late 1930s, journey to the Australian outback). Reader reception calls it a pleasant feel-good read that is 'a bit cheesy and not too deep'. No idea to lean on beyond the standard rural-romance shape, consistent with the rest of this imprint's entries.

A dual-timeline novel: in 1950s Merham, evacuee Lottie and her friend Celia are drawn into a bohemian household with tragic consequences; fifty years later, single mother Daisy restores the same house and uncovers what happened. It won the Romantic Novel of the Year award and is well-liked for its bonding/coming-of-age throughline, but it is character- and mood-driven women's fiction rather than a book built around one worked-out idea - closer to the competent-but-unremarkable end of this reader's historical/litfic reads than to something like Animal Farm 78 or The Little Prince 82, which earn their scores on a specific idea. Axis:ideas goes under risk on that basis. No infidelity premise: the 'ambiguous relationships' in the bohemian household are backstory colour, not a marriage plot.

A gothic thriller about an apartment-sitter who uncovers a wealthy building's secret: the rich harvesting organs from the poor tenants they take in. The class-exploitation premise is a real, nameable idea, and reviewers praise the plotting as tightly constructed with a twist that pays off rather than a cheap fake-out. But the catalogue does not carry a detektivni tag for this record, and the genre framing (gothic horror-thriller, not police-procedural mystery) keeps it out of a hard reject - though reader reviews do call it 'a compulsive mystery' built around figuring out who is behind the disappearances, which is close enough to whodunit satisfaction to flag rather than ignore. Absent a deeper idea beyond the twist itself, this sits in the same territory as a well-made but not idea-driven thriller - competent, but nothing here suggests it clears 68.

A virus makes animal meat lethal, so human 'special meat' is legalized; single-POV protagonist Marcos works at a processing plant until a gifted specimen starts to feel like a person to him. The premise is genuinely worked through with no loose ends (an Orwell-adjacent, self-consistent dystopia, unlike Divergent 58 or Mortal Engines 55), so it clears gate 4 on axis:ideas alone. But two costs compound: reviewers are unanimous that the ending is 'one of the bleakest in fiction' with 'not so much as a glimmer of hope' - well past Animal Farm 78's detached, thought-provoking bleakness and closer to or beyond 1984's 60, which this reader marked down mainly for being 'too depressing.' On top of that, Marcos does not stay someone to root for: by the end reviewers describe him making 'increasingly disturbing choices' that go 'beyond what we assumed he was okay with,' the same rootability failure that separated The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes (65) from its prequel pair by 22 points. Both axes fire together here, unlike 1984 (bleakness only) or Ballad (protagonist only), which is why the estimate sits below both.

t: Daleko od hluciciho davu (Far from the Madding Crowd)
why: Bathsheba drives the book on what she wants - independence, then a costly infatuation, then hard-won self-knowledge - the same axis that carried Pride and Prejudice to 75, and she is both interesting (proud, capable, fallible) and eventually worth rooting for once she earns her ending with Gabriel rather than being rescued into it. Against that: Hardy's Wessex pastoral description runs heavier than Austen's drawing rooms, and the Fanny Robin thread (an abandoned pregnant woman who dies in a workhouse) plus Boldwood's murder of Troy add weight the courtship frame doesn't fully absorb. No marriage exists before Troy's secret wedding to Bathsheba, so nothing here rises to axis:infidelity - Troy's prior involvement with Fanny predates any marriage.

Overspent this gate (2 sources against C-low's budget of 1) before the pattern was clear enough to stop. Critics repeatedly describe the exact failure this reader has already docked LOTR 84 and Les Miserables 71 for: one review calls the plot 'episodic and disjointed' with description that is 'more style than substance,' and even sympathetic readers say the ornamentation turns 'tiresome' and the book 'lumbers forward.' The cosmology (a living city, a cloud wall, a flying horse) is mythic and invented rather than drawn from real occult tradition, so occult is not the doubt here - density is.

Dual-timeline novel: a woman inherits a debt-laden chateau and vineyard in Provence and uncovers her father's hidden WWII resistance past through a parallel wartime storyline. Reviews are largely positive on the researched WWII strand but repeatedly call the present-day heroine naive and the modern plot thread weaker and predictable, with one review noting a central relationship simply fizzles out rather than resolving. There is no idea beyond a family-secrets mystery, the same shape that lands the reader's C-band books like Exodus 68 and Quo Vadis 66 rather than the idea-driven successes. Leaned on axis:ideas; axis:protagonist is a risk given the specific 'naive' complaint about the contemporary lead.

t: Pristi rok v tento den (This Time Next Year)
why: A romantic comedy about two strangers born minutes apart whose fates seem swapped by a hospital mix-up. One reviewer (The Modest Reader) specifically criticises the lead as reading like 'a punching bag for the plot' rather than an agent in her own story, and the fated-birthday hook is a whimsical device rather than a premise the book actually works through - it is not chased to any real consequence the way the reader's rules reward. The praised mental-health subplot is real but a subplot, not the engine, so it does not lift this past a competent-but-unremarkable rom-com ceiling.

Contemporary billionaire/single-mother romance, one night in Paris leading to a will-they-won't-they arc. Pride and Prejudice (75) shows romance carrying the whole plot is not itself a problem in this log, and the marketing ('light and spicy') and reviews describe moderate content rather than a plot built mainly around sexual behaviour, so axis:sexual-content is graded, not vetoed. But nothing beyond the stock 'wounded billionaire meets single mom' tropes is named in any review found - no idea to point to, which is the axis:ideas doubt this gate asks about.

Same series structure: a sister searches for her biological family using a clue left after her adoptive father's death, paralleled by a historical storyline about a woman who built a pearl empire in Australia a century earlier. The task line's 'detective' signal is the genealogical search itself, not a whodunit - the reader's satisfaction is family discovery, not solving a crime, so gate 1 does not fire. Series-level reviews describe the formula as entertaining but exposition-heavy with a weaker present-day thread, and there is no idea beyond 'trace your roots', the pattern that lands the C-band default rather than an idea-driven score like Animal Farm 78. Leaned on axis:ideas; axis:protagonist is a risk given the series-wide complaint about thin present-day leads.

Same series formula as the rest of the Seven Sisters books: a withdrawn sister follows a clue left after her adoptive father's death into a parallel historical storyline a century earlier. Series-level reviews consistently describe the present-day frame as the weaker half and the plots as running on exposition and coincidence rather than an examined idea. No idea to name beyond 'discover your origins', the pattern the C-band default exists for, as against idea-driven reads like Animal Farm 78. Leaned on axis:ideas; axis:protagonist is a risk given the series-wide complaint about thin contemporary leads, the same failure that capped Promena 58.

t: Vzkaz v lahvi (Message in a Bottle)
why: A divorced journalist finds a love letter in a bottle and tracks down its widower author, falling for him even as his late wife's memory pulls at their new relationship, with the book ending on his death at sea rather than a conventional happy resolution. Reviews are split between finding it emotionally powerful and calling it predictable and simplistically written; the theme of grief and whether one can love again is present but functions as a sentimental plot engine rather than an idea worked through in its consequences, closer to the pattern behind the log's C-band books than to an idea-driven read like Animal Farm 78. Leaned on axis:ideas for the number; no graded axis here looks likely to push it below the range, so risks is empty.

Penultimate volume of the series: the six found sisters search together for the mythical seventh sister before their father's memorial cruise. Same formula as the rest of the series - series-level reviews describe it as entertaining but exposition-heavy, with the contemporary thread consistently the weaker half. No idea beyond the family-search premise, the pattern that lands the C-band default rather than the idea-driven reads in the log such as Animal Farm 78. Leaned on axis:ideas; axis:protagonist is a risk given the series-wide complaint about thin present-day leads, echoing what capped Promena 58.

t: Tajemstvi hrabenky Anny (The Shadow on the Bridge)
why: A dual-timeline novel: present-day Sarah, grieving a childhood loss, uncovers a book of poems tied to Anne Howard, a Tudor countess investigating her brother's death at the hands of her scheming father-in-law. There is a mystery-shaped thread in the Tudor strand (who killed Anne's brother), but it sits as one thread in a dual-timeline healing/discovery story, not the reader's whole satisfaction, so it is a flag rather than a detective veto. A reviewer calls the contemporary mystery 'pretty obvious and unnecessary,' and the book reads as a fairly standard atmospheric dual-timeline women's-fiction entry (comped to Philippa Gregory/Kate Morton) without a single idea to carry it, so axis:ideas goes under risk the same way it would for any competent-but-generic historical romance.

Self-published Czech YA fantasy, second in the 'Agnes' series: two years after escaping the Forbidden Mountain, Agnes must face Shadow creatures possessing her village. Enthusiastic fan reviews cite 'plenty to think about' around the theme of a community losing itself to possession, but no professional review was found to confirm depth beyond fan impressions, and the audience is explicitly children/YA (audiobook, 'publikace pro deti' heading). Placed with Ranger's Apprentice 74 and Narnia 67, where childrens-register books 'pay a little' rather than nothing.

Second in a New Adult contemporary romance trilogy (the 'BAM' friend group) about a charming, wounded man who hides childhood trauma behind humor until a woman insists on seeing past it - a familiar emotionally-guarded-love-interest arc with no idea beyond the relationship itself. It clears the filters (no occult, no marriage, in Czech) without making the positive case the reader's estimates require. The genre is known for repeated explicit content, an unexamined volume/explicitness risk since no source detailed this specific book's scenes.

A 24-page picture book for ages 3+ with a simple ecological-responsibility moral. Reader reviews confirm real reception (not just publisher copy) but describe it as 'super thin' - a slight, occasional piece whose message is straightforward rather than a worked idea with consequences. This is the picture-book case the C-low band's lower range exists for: a form that suspends the character and momentum rules entirely, with nothing beyond the surface moral to carry a higher number.

Self-published techno-thriller in the Dan Brown/Crichton mold: an Atlantis-derived genetic gift explains the human species' near-extinction 70,000 years ago. Reviewers repeatedly flag the two leads as thin ('don't have large personalities', 'similar to Dan Brown, not character-driven') and the plot as an overstuffed kitchen sink of tropes (Nazis, 9/11, Roswell, ancient aliens, a pandemic) that some call 'over-complicated' and 'too cliche'. This reader ranks protagonist depth and worked-out premises above plot density -- Golden Son 92 was marked down from Red Rising 95 for leaning toward action over interiority, and Divergent 58 sank specifically on ideas 'assembled without cohering'. A commercially huge, competently paced conspiracy thriller, but nothing in the reviews suggests it clears the bar this reader sets on either axis.

Middle book of the Atlas trilogy: the five surviving initiates, shaken by an initiation ritual and Libby's disappearance, splinter into new alliances as more of the Society's true plan is revealed. This is the volume reviewers single out for exactly what this reader values most - 'deeply philosophical,' interiority-driven, characters that are 'realistically messy' with clearly differentiated arcs (one reviewer names Libby's chapters specifically for having real movement and stakes). The initiation ritual itself is candidates taking turns psychically projecting trauma at each other inside a possibly-sentient archive - a psychic/mechanistic ordeal, not witchcraft, divination or prayer to any real deity, and nothing enacted resembles source-based occultism, so the filter does not apply. The magic system is deliberately left vague rather than declared-then-broken ('exquisite... unknowable without being unbelievable' per one reviewer), which under this reader's own rule ('vague, numinous magic owes little') is a small risk rather than a violation. As the middle volume of a trilogy it carries the usual sequel risk, and side plots (a one-sided rivalry that 'goes nowhere') are noted as pacing weaknesses.

A genuinely worked speculative premise - the reader loves consequences actually worked out, and this one follows its own rule (changing the future risks the baby she's seen). But multiple reviews say the payoff 'got very silly' and the anticipated twist 'didn't fully materialize,' a direct signal that the idea's execution doesn't hold up under its own premise the way this log requires - closer to Mortal Engines' premise-collapse (55) than to a Weir-style worked consequence. That doubt is exactly what axis:ideas is for at this gate.

t: Buffy, premozitelka upiru (Buffy the Vampire Slayer (2019 relaunch))
why: Boom! Studios' 2019 continuity reboot of Buffy, restarting the story at Buffy's new high school; reviews (NYT, CBR) are positive but describe it as a fresh start rather than a book carrying a stated idea - a teenager wants an ordinary life despite an imposed destiny, which is premise, not a worked-through idea. Comic format and teen-school setting put it in the same childrens-adjacent bracket as Narnia 67 and Ranger's Apprentice 74, which 'pay a little' rather than nothing. Occult content (the Buffyverse eventually includes witches) is left unexamined here since nothing under 68 changes on that answer.

Spent 3 sources against the gate-4 budget of 1, overspend noted. Task line's infidelity screen ('milenka', tier weak, premise false) was examined and is not premise-level - checked and cleared, not treated as a filter. Czech historical-fantasy romance (1480s Naples, revenge plot) rated a mixed ~75% on the fan database. One review specifically flags that a large portion of the text is devoted to characters' internal thought processes at the expense of pacing, and that the first two of three parts feel disorienting before the plot 'ties together' late - the log's own axis:density complaint ('heavy description with little story'), closer to how Les Miserables 71 is described than to a digression like the Silmarillion 80 that earns its length. No reviewer names a larger idea beyond the revenge/atmosphere plot.

Three royal siblings (a monk, a soldier-in-training, a scholar-politician) are scattered after their father's assassination and drawn separately toward the conspiracy behind it. The idea that carries this is the Csestriim: an ancient antagonist race whose evil is unexplainable specifically because it cannot feel human emotion - evil defined by the absence of motive rather than a bad one - the same 'understand the alien Other' shape of idea that scores well here in Speaker for the Dead 90 and Old Man's War 87. Magic (the 'leach'/'Well' system) is mechanism-based: each leach draws power from a personal object, declared rules, no invocation or priesthood, so it passes the occult mechanism escape the way Allomancy does. A single on-page 'trial by fire' scene reads like a real miracle from a goddess but is unmasked as a leach's mechanical trick, which reinforces rather than undermines that reading, so axis:occult clears without needing a deeper pass. Multiple reviewers confirm the three-POV opening (monastery, military island, capital) resolves clearly rather than confusingly - 'the narrative flipped between each of them smoothly ... I knew exactly who was whom' - so this does not trip the confusing-opening failure that killed Discworld, The Gunslinger and Foundryside for this reader. Held below Old Man's War by two things specific to this volume: reviewers flag weak, mostly-decorative female characterization here, touching the axis that separated Golden Son 92 from a thinner book by 22 points elsewhere in the log; and the assassination-conspiracy plotline is investigation-shaped enough to flag under axis:detective, even though the trilogy's satisfaction is epic-fantasy politics and war rather than a whodunit.

t: Co zbylo z moji sestry (My Sister's Bones)
why: Clears the cheap filters: not a whodunit (the tension is Kate's own unreliable memory and PTSD, not a detective inquiry), no marital infidelity, no sexual-behavior plot - the engine is a sister relationship and a war reporter's trauma. Reviews describe a slow first half built on atmosphere before a twist-heavy second half, which reads as competent unreliable-narrator genre mechanics rather than a clearly nameable idea. I cannot name what this book leaves you thinking about beyond 'trauma distorts memory,' which is closer to a device than a worked idea - I'd list axis:ideas under risks if pushed further, which is the C-low test.

Closes the Cicero trilogy through the eyes of his secretary Tiro, opening cleanly with Cicero's exile after the Catiline conspiracy and running chronologically - a single throughline, not several plot lines starting at once. Kirkus calls Cicero 'immensely likable... wise but not pedantic, moral but not sanctimonious,' the worth-rooting-for case the reader requires, and one retrospective names a genuine idea - how emergency powers become permanent and temporary measures calcify into precedent - close to what the reader means by a book that leaves something behind. Risk: several reviewers found the middle stretch slow, with 'dull family dramas' and politics happening at a remove from Cicero himself, a density complaint similar to what cost Les Miserables points, and it is the third of a trilogy some readers rate below the first two entries.

t: Divka na utesu (The Girl on the Cliff)
why: A dual-timeline family-secrets romance saga in a genre this reader has liked before (Pride and Prejudice 75 on motives, The Count of Monte Cristo 75 on momentum), but reviewers call the plot 'pretty typical' with an ending 'too neatly packaged' - nothing suggests a worked idea beyond the reveal-the-family-secret mechanic common to generational sagas. I cannot name what it leaves you thinking about, so axis:ideas would be a risk if researched further.

t: Dnesek neni naposled (All Our Wrong Todays)
why: A 1965 divergence (a clean-energy engine) is followed through to real consequences - flying cars, moon bases, moving sidewalks - the same kind of worked-out second-order thinking that lifts Project Hail Mary to 92 and that Mortal Engines 55 conspicuously lacks. Framed as a self-aware fictional memoir with a single narrating POV starting from one concrete situation (Tom's utopian world); Kirkus calls Tom 'an impressive feat of memory and consciousness' by the end, and his visible flaws (self-deprecation, recklessness) are the kind of interiority the reader rewards over action, the axis that tops Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90. Risk: reviewers flag pacing and intimacy loss in the back half and a screenplay-like, cliffhanger-heavy structure some found jarring - closer to what dragged down The Martian's 82 ending.

t: Einstein (Einstein: Die fantastische Reise einer Maus durch Raum und Zeit)
why: More substantial than the average children's picture book - a real premise (a homemade time machine, a specific overshoot consequence) that is actually followed through, plus a nonfiction appendix explaining Einstein's theories, closer to a genuinely worked idea than average juvenile fare. But it is still a picture-heavy children's mouse-adventure aimed at young readers, the same register this log caps at Ranger's Apprentice 74 and Narnia 67 even when the story itself is good - axis:childrens is the ceiling here regardless of how clever the premise is, so I'd flag it under risks if I researched further rather than assume it clears 68.

t: Epos, okridleny ohen (Epos the Flame Bird)
why: Beast Quest is a ghost-written (house name 'Adam Blade'), highly formulaic UK series for readers 7+: Tom fights one enchanted beast per short volume, sold on collectibility (beast cards) rather than depth - reviews describe it as built for 'reading stamina' and 'hooking reluctant readers,' not literary depth. No idea worth naming beyond 'boy defeats monster of the week', so axis:ideas is a clear risk and this exits at C. The default band applies rather than the picture-book band: it is a real short novel with chapters and dialogue, not a collection or picture book, even though in substance it reads slighter than the children's comps in the log (Narnia 67, Ranger's Apprentice 74). axis:occult left unexamined per the C-low rule - the evil wizard Malvel's curse on Epos reads as invented fantasy magic, not obviously real-world-mould, but nothing here would change the exit either way.

Hard-SF first-contact novel praised by multiple reviewers as idea-dense and ambitious (LA Review of Books calls it Brin's career high point), which is the strongest single predictor in the log - Project Hail Mary 92 and Old Man's War 87 both top the log on exactly this. But several independent reviews single out the opening POV character Gerald, and the wider ensemble cast, as thin and hard to care about, explicitly framing the book as idea-driven rather than character-driven, with one reviewer directly comparing it to Asimov using characters 'only as props to explore an idea'. That is the same failure mode the log already recorded once: Artemis was predicted 80 but scored 69 because the prediction 'leaned up on strong worldbuilding while the lead was visibly thin'. Pulling the estimate down from where the idea alone would place it, rather than repeating that mistake.

t: Ferno, ohnivy drak (Ferno the Fire Dragon)
why: Beast Quest is a ghost-written (house name 'Adam Blade'), highly formulaic UK series for readers 7+: Tom fights one enchanted beast per short volume, sold on collectibility (beast cards) rather than depth - reviews describe it as built for 'reading stamina' and 'hooking reluctant readers,' not literary depth. No idea worth naming beyond 'boy defeats monster of the week', so axis:ideas is a clear risk and this exits at C. The default band applies rather than the picture-book band: it is a real short novel with chapters and dialogue, not a collection or picture book, even though in substance it reads slighter than the children's comps in the log (Narnia 67, Ranger's Apprentice 74). axis:occult left unexamined per the C-low rule - Malvel's curse on the beasts reads as invented fantasy magic, not obviously real-world-mould, but nothing here would change the exit either way.

An orphaned girl secretly enters a men-only warrior trial so no one else suffers as she did - a nameable idea about who gets to protect others - but a Czech review of the same edition says the pacing is unnecessarily rushed and the resolution 'embarrassingly bland', i.e. the idea is stated but not worked through. That is the same category of doubt Divergent 58 earns for ideas that don't cohere, even though here the setup itself is clear rather than borrowed.

A real idea, clearly nameable: a critique of women's confinement under both Ottoman patriarchy and a West that 'wakes them to greater misfortune' rather than truly freeing them - the kind of premise-with-consequences this reader rewards (Pride and Prejudice 75 for motives as the whole book; Animal Farm 78 for an idea worth carrying). It opens with two parallel introductions (the novelist, then a girl facing an arranged marriage) rather than several unresolved plot lines, so the opening risk is low. The cost is heavy atmosphere - reader reviews single out the beauty of the setting and emotional tone over incident, the story-density axis this reader dislikes, and the ending is stated as tragic (flight or death), which taps mild bleakness. No infidelity: Djenane's yearning for the visiting novelist reads as unconsummated and she is not shown married or engaged to another man in what I found. No sexual content, no occult, no detective structure.

A rational, science-minded young teacher in 1899 Olomouc hides a family curse and has sworn off love, until a man who risks everything for others enters her life. Consistent reader praise across Goodreads and Databaze knih centers on Dany as a character worth rooting for and on the romance itself, the axis Pycha a predsudek 75 shows 'costs nothing' when what characters want carries the book, plus researched period detail (teacher celibacy rules, period press excerpts) that reads as self-consistent rather than decorative. Docked for the YA ctu (young-adult) imprint and for being a loose sequel, where the log discounts on the Hitchhiker's 83-to-70 pattern. The curse is presented as inherited folk superstition rather than a rite shown on the page, so it is not flagged for the occult filter, though this was not independently sourced.

Middle-grade Czech sci-fi (~112pp, Pikola imprint, Zlata stuha-nominated) about a starship crew searching for a habitable planet. No source establishes a worked-out idea beyond the survival premise itself - unlike Project Hail Mary 92, where astrophage's consequences are actually explored, nothing suggests the habitable-planet search gets developed beyond plot beats (hibernation, a lunar base contact, hostile raiders). Short-idea-driven suspends the character-focused rules but adds nothing on its own, so without a nameable idea this settles under the line like any other thin book. Genre and audience mirror Ranger's Apprentice 74 and Narnia 67, both of which paid a small childrens-axis cost.

WWII sabotage thriller: SOE agent Felicity 'Flick' Clairet assembles an all-woman team to destroy a German telephone exchange ahead of D-Day, based on real resistance operations. The premise gives real stakes and motive-driven characters (a positive, similar in kind to what the reader liked in Old Man's War), and the opening is a single clear mission objective rather than a confusing multi-thread start. But this grades down hard on axis:sexual-content: reviewers repeatedly flag 'too many' explicit sex scenes and, more seriously, sexualized torture written in explicitly eroticized terms ('they got erections as they inflicted wounds... experienced orgasms during their victims' death throes'), described as recurring across multiple scenes. Violence itself costs nothing under this reader's rules, but this is the sexual-content axis firing on crudeness and explicitness at real volume, which is why the estimate sits below the C-low band rather than in it.

t: Kralovna Tearlingu (The Queen of the Tearling)
why: Spent 3 sources against the gate-4 budget of 1, noted rather than hidden. Multiple reviews independently flag unexplained worldbuilding gaps - a post-collapse society where nobody reads books and there is no medical knowledge, neither ever accounted for - the same kind of unaddressed-consequence breach that cost Harry Potter and Mortal Engines, and one reviewer calls the setup 'very typical, almost Star Wars-like'. That reads as ideas assembled without cohering, the exact language the log already used for Divergent 58. The magic (a protective sapphire, a sorceress villain) is described by reviewers as vague and underdeveloped rather than a worked-out system, so there is no worldbuilding strength to lean on instead.

Reviews are near-uniformly positive on imagination, pace and invention, with no worldbuilding-inconsistency complaints of the kind that cost Tearling or Mortal Engines - the opposite pattern from those two. The opening is a single concrete situation (Twig, raised by trolls in the Deepwoods, sets out to learn his origins), matching the log's favored 'one concrete starting situation' over several plotlines at once. This is the same 'no penalties' shape the log used to explain the Hobbit's 84: friendship and adventure carried competently with nothing that costs points. Held below the Hobbit's ceiling because, unlike the Hobbit's heroism/friendship throughline, no reviewer names a real idea beyond episodic adventure - closer to a thin-ideas case landing in the high 60s/low 70s despite strong craft.

An interactive gamebook, not authored narrative fiction: the reader assembles a party and drives outcomes through skill checks, so there is no single protagonist whose motives the text develops - exactly the axis this reader weighs most heavily. It is genuinely well-regarded as a gamebook (4.55 on Goodreads, compared favorably to Fabled Lands), but reviewers praise it for open-ended replayability and party mechanics, not for character or idea, which is a different kind of achievement than the one being scored here. No fixed ending short of death, and no idea to name.

t: Leva ruka bozi (The Left Hand of God)
why: Cale, raised from age six or seven inside the brutal training of a fanatical religious order (the Redeemers, an inverted mirror of Christianity built around a 'Hanged Redeemer'), is revealed as the prophesied 'Left Hand of God' - the angel meant to end humanity for its unrepented sin. That is a real idea (guilt, free will and destiny inside an apocalyptic theology), but multiple reviewers finish the book with 'no clue as to what Paul Hoffman is trying to achieve,' and a trilogy retrospective calls it 'simultaneously brilliant and original, while also frustratingly lazy,' citing inconsistent world-building (Italian/British/invented names mixed with no apparent logic). I would flag axis:ideas as a real risk to the payoff holding up, which is what exits this at C on the default band. axis:occult is unusually clear here and established rather than deferred: multiple reviewers note the book has no magic at all despite fantasy trappings ('complete lack of magic,' reads 'like an alternate history') - not a concern. Protagonist rootability is a genuine open question: Cale and his fellow trainees are described as 'tough, sociopathic and accomplished liars,' the same shape of concern that cost the villain-adjacent lead in The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 twenty-two points against a rootable protagonist by the same author in Sunrise on the Reaping 87. Content is dark even by this log's tolerant standard - reviewers flag torture, child abuse and sexual abuse among the mature content - which touches axis:bleakness, the mildest objection in the log but a real one at this concentration.

A geopolitical hacking thriller (Britain weaponizes an autistic teenage hacker against Russia, North Korea and Iran) that reviewers praise for pace and plausible, well-researched topicality. But the central figure is the weak point on exactly the axis this reader weighs most: one critic calls Luke Jennings 'effectively a black box' dramatically, with his hacking feats presented as 'ghost in the machine stuff' that 'just happen' at convenient moments rather than being earned or explained - unearned competence with no consequence-carrying explanation, the opposite of what the reader rewards in Red Rising or Project Hail Mary. Without a protagonist whose motives get real page time, this settles under the line despite strong pacing and topicality.

Dr Rieux, who stays in plague-stricken Oran to work rather than join his sick wife, is exactly the rootable, motive-driven lead the reader rewards - reviewers describe him as persistent rather than heroic-postured, choosing 'a stubborn readiness to do one's work' over despair, the same quality that carries Old Man's War to 87. The idea is explicit and nameable: resistance to the absurd is not one heroic act but repeated ordinary labor, and multiple sources read the whole book as an allegory of occupation and moral choice under it - a real idea left behind, unlike Divergent 58's borrowed-and-unassembled ideas. Risk: sustained death and isolation is the book's whole atmosphere, which the reader discounts mildly (as with 1984 60) rather than penalizes heavily, since Rieux's active resistance, unlike Gregor Samsa's passivity in Metamorphosis 58, keeps the book from reading as merely bleak.

t: Muz, ktery pozoroval nebe (El hombre que miraba al cielo)
why: A minimalist 98-page literary novella built on mood and atmosphere - reviewers describe the prose as precise but note it reads 'as if there were no protagonist, everyone part of one entity,' which works against the protagonist-must-be-interesting-and-rootable rule this log weighs most heavily (the 22-point Snow/Sunrise gap). The mystery-of-the-old-man setup is a genuine hook, but nothing found names a worked idea beyond mood and atmosphere, so I cannot rule out axis:ideas collapsing the estimate - the short-idea-driven suspension only removes penalties, it never substitutes for a nameable idea.

Three Mouse Guard members investigate a missing grain merchant and uncover a conspiracy against their protected territories. Reviews praise the art and distinct character personalities, but reception on engagement splits - one reviewer explicitly 'didn't sense the characters' personalities' and 'didn't care what happened' - and no reviewer names a theme beyond a loyalty-and-duty animal adventure, the missing-idea gap the log docks in the 60s regardless of craft quality.

Second Kingsbridge novel, following four children - Merthin, Ralph, Gwenda, Caris - across four decades (1327-1351) around Kingsbridge cathedral and its two rival monasteries, through a plague epidemic. Plot momentum and density hold up the way they do in Follett's other doorstoppers (Count of Monte Cristo 75 shows length itself isn't a penalty here), and the multi-generational cast gets real page time on what they want. But reviews converge hard on the axis this reader weighs heaviest: sexual content that is frequent, graphic, and, worse, repeatedly treats rape and consensual sex in the same undifferentiated register - multiple reviewers flag 'rape victims... enjoying it' and describe the villain Ralph's rise to power as built substantially on rape used as spectacle rather than consequence. That is volume, explicitness and crudeness all firing together, in the same family as what sank Ready Player One 55 and The Witcher 53 but by most accounts worse on the crudeness dimension, so the estimate sits below the C-low band rather than in it.

t: Nanook, ledovy netvor (Nanook the Snow Monster)
why: Beast Quest is a ghost-written (house name 'Adam Blade'), highly formulaic UK series for readers 7+: Tom fights one enchanted beast per short volume, sold on collectibility (beast cards) rather than depth - reviews describe it as built for 'reading stamina' and 'hooking reluctant readers,' not literary depth. No idea worth naming beyond 'boy defeats monster of the week', so axis:ideas is a clear risk and this exits at C. The default band applies rather than the picture-book band: it is a real short novel with chapters and dialogue, not a collection or picture book, even though in substance it reads slighter than the children's comps in the log (Narnia 67, Ranger's Apprentice 74). axis:occult left unexamined per the C-low rule - Malvel's curse on the beasts reads as invented fantasy magic, not obviously real-world-mould, but nothing here would change the exit either way.

t: Nikdo neni ostrov (Niemand ist eine Insel)
why: Not a whodunit - Sylvia's guilt is stated from the outset via her own indictment, so this is a confession-driven melodrama about motive and the treatment of disability rather than a mystery to be solved, which clears the detective filter. But German reader reviews call it 'below average for Simmel' and say it 'drags in circles for too long,' exactly the kind of doubt that belongs under axis:ideas - a social-conscience premise (disability, isolation) is stated but reportedly not carried through tightly enough to trust at full research cost.

t: O cem reka vi (What the River Knows)
why: Dual first-person YA historical fantasy: a Buenos Aires socialite sails to 1880s Cairo to learn what happened to her missing archaeologist parents, sparring and falling for her guardian's associate along the way. The enemies/rivals-to-lovers dynamic carrying two POVs is the same what-characters-want-and-why axis that lifts Pycha a predsudek to 75. Multiple independent reviews (YA Books Central, A Literary Escape, another ARC review) flag a slow, description-heavy first half before the plot accelerates - a density risk rather than a thin-story one, since the source is heavy period detail, not a lack of plot. The touch-activated artifact magic is repeatedly called vague and underdeveloped by reviewers rather than shown as a rite on the page, so it does not trip the occult mechanism test but earns no worldbuilding credit either.

Czech dual-timeline thriller: a modern woman with 'Kafkaesque traits' is betrayed by a lover and crosses between the present and the year 1463, meeting real historical figures. No independent review of this specific book turned up beyond retailer copy repeating the annotation, so the premise doesn't yet resolve into a statable idea from what is findable - the same doubt Divergent 58 earns for 'ideas borrowed from other books and assembled without cohering'. A review of the same author's other novel found its storytelling grows 'increasingly chaotic', which is a genre-level flag on the author rather than evidence about this book, so it goes in flags, not the estimate itself.

Czech YA portal fantasy, openly Harry-Potter-inspired (the author does not deny the influence): three children from a children's home discover a hidden world of wizards, dragons, unicorns, harpies, sirens and genies living alongside ordinary people. Czech reader reviews are positive on execution ('velmi dobra kompozice a hloubka pribehu'), but the premise - orphaned children discover a hidden magic school/world - is the same generic template that sank Harry Potter 51 and Percy Jackson 57 for this reader, and I cannot name an idea beyond it, so axis:ideas is a real risk and this exits at C. axis:occult left unexamined per the C-low rule: harpies, sirens and genies are drawn from real-world mythology and folklore, the same category that cost Percy Jackson its occult points, so this is a live question for any future full pass, but it does not change today's exit.

Award-winning academic history (National Jewish Book Award, starred Kirkus) whose actual thesis is 'why Auschwitz', tracing the town across seven centuries with architectural plans and survivor testimony to explain how it became the camp, rather than retelling the Holocaust generally. The log's rule that memoir/testimony form earns nothing by itself but examining what is actually true does - the exact praise Seeking Allah Finding Jesus 91 got - applies directly here, and this is more rigorously sourced than a personal memoir. Held below that ceiling because it is 448 pages of dense archival and architectural detail rather than a single first-person voice, which risks the density penalty, and the subject matter is unrelieved Holocaust history with no companionship/self-sacrifice arc to offset the bleakness the way Project Hail Mary's does. Landed closer to Son of Hamas 75, a rigorous nonfiction examination without Qureshi's personal-narrative pull.

Opens the Psy-Changeling series: Sascha Duncan, a Psy who secretly feels emotion in a society that enforces total emotional 'Silence' on pain of a mind-wipe, is paired with changeling alpha Lucas Hunter to catch a serial killer targeting his pack. The Silence/PsyNet worldbuilding is followed through with real consequences (Sascha's mother disowns her at the end) rather than declared and dropped, and the emotional-repression theme is a genuine idea worked out in the plot, not just a backdrop for romance - both real credits against this reader's core axes. The book is graded down hard for sexual content, though: reviews consistently call it genuinely explicit ('quite explicit... hottest scenes'), and it is a recurring, structurally central genre element, not an incidental scene, so both volume and explicitness cost even though the treatment is called 'appropriate to the story' rather than crude. The serial-killer plot is an investigative subplot, not the book's core satisfaction, so it's a flag rather than a gate-1 filter.

t: Pan Cavendish, jestli se nemylim (Mr. Cavendish, I Presume)
why: Amelia Willoughby, engaged to a duke since infancy, falls for the man contesting his claim to the title - a companion novel that retells The Lost Duke of Wyndham's events from the other couple's viewpoint. Multiple reviewers call the gimmick the weak point: 'probably one of the weakest Quinn books,' 'over 300 pages of deja vu,' predictable because the events are already known from book one. Content is mild (a single, non-crude love scene, per multiple reviews), so sexual content is not the issue - the issue is that the parallel-retelling structure is not a worked idea in its own right, closer to Hitchhiker's sequels' 13-point series decline than to a book that earns its number independently.

t: Pet prani pana Murrayho McBridea (The Five Wishes of Mr. Murray McBride)
why: A 100-year-old widower finds a reason to live by helping a terminally ill 10-year-old boy complete a wish list. Commercially very popular (4.61 on Goodreads) but critical reviews repeatedly flag exactly the doubt this gate asks about: 'realism and plot be damned', 'thrown-together, soap opera ending', 'I just can't suspend belief this much... way beyond any belief'. That is a worked example of the sentimentality-over-plausibility pattern this reader has never rewarded highly; nothing in the reviews names an idea beyond the tearjerker premise itself. The child co-lead is graded on axis:childrens/life-phase rather than vetoed, but it costs a little given the reader's own calibration (Little Women 79 is the ceiling for domestic, character-only stories with no idea to work out, and this one carries a heavier plausibility complaint than that comparison does).

A heavily illustrated children's comic/picture book -- officially catalogued among the 'Best Books for Children 2015/2016' -- with a deliberately naive, simple, pun-driven plot for young readers (two robots exploring a post-human Earth). Reviewers praise it as exactly that: simple, cute, aimed at children who get a strong reading experience from it, with the artwork doing most of the work. This reader's own calibration puts a picture book in the 30s or 40s regardless of charm; there is no idea beyond the gentle premise itself.

Second Psy-Changeling book: F-Psy Faith NightStar, whose precognitive visions have started showing her both murder and desire, is drawn to changeling jaguar Vaughn while a Psy councilor tries to exploit her sight. The PsyNet/Silence worldbuilding keeps expanding with real consequences (the Council 'becoming monsters', the NetMind fracturing), which rewards this reader's worldbuilding axis, and the precognition is framed as an inborn psychic trait rather than any real-world occult practice - no ritual, divination or invocation on the page, so the occult filter does not apply. Same heavy sexual-content penalty as book 1 (same 'high heat' series-wide reputation), compounded here by a subplot where Faith's sister is murdered by the same serial-killer thread, adding a bleakness note; as a sequel it also carries the risk the reader's own log shows for series decline (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70).

Adare, having exposed her father's killer, flees the palace to gather allies against the coup, drawing followers who believe she has been touched by the goddess Intarra. The idea carrying this trilogy is the Csestriim: an antagonist race whose evil is legible only as an absence of human motive, the same 'understand the alien Other' shape of idea that scores well here in Speaker for the Dead 90 and Old Man's War 87. Magic (the 'leach'/'Well' system) is mechanism-based - personal objects, declared rules, no invocation or priesthood - so it passes the occult mechanism escape the way Allomancy does, and an on-page 'trial by fire' miracle earlier in the trilogy is unmasked as a leach's trick rather than real divine power, reinforcing that reading. A real risk worth naming on its own evidence rather than the book's: this is a sequel, and sequels are not automatically safe bets in this log - Hitchhiker's dropped from 83 to 70 across its series - so I am not predicting up purely on trilogy momentum.

t: Runy (Runes: The Creature of a Thousand Faces)
why: Spent 3 sources against the gate-4 budget of 1, overspend noted. This is a heavily illustrated children's comic from Flying Eye Books (the same UK publisher as Hilda), reviewed mainly for its art (pastel colors, Adventure Time/Ghibli comparisons) rather than for any adult-legible idea. The reader-profile scale is explicit that a picture-book-adjacent work 'lands in the 30s or 40s', and at 160 pages aimed at young children this sits closer to that end than to a YA graphic novel. The closest thing to a stated theme - deciphering ancient runes / understanding a friend who uses sign language - is a young-reader-level lesson, not a worked-through idea of the kind Labyrint 70 or Animal Farm 78 get credit for.

t: Sepron, morsky plaz (Sepron the Sea Serpent)
why: Beast Quest is a ghost-written (house name 'Adam Blade'), highly formulaic UK series for readers 7+: Tom fights one enchanted beast per short volume, sold on collectibility (beast cards) rather than depth - reviews describe it as built for 'reading stamina' and 'hooking reluctant readers,' not literary depth. No idea worth naming beyond 'boy defeats monster of the week', so axis:ideas is a clear risk and this exits at C. The default band applies rather than the picture-book band: it is a real short novel with chapters and dialogue, not a collection or picture book, even though in substance it reads slighter than the children's comps in the log (Narnia 67, Ranger's Apprentice 74). axis:occult left unexamined per the C-low rule - Malvel's curse on the beasts reads as invented fantasy magic, not obviously real-world-mould, but nothing here would change the exit either way.

t: Skandar a zlodej jednorozcu (Skandar and the Unicorn Thief)
why: Multiple reviews explicitly state this bestselling MG debut 'does not try to do much of anything new', is built from 'familiar tropes', and warn 'don't expect depth' - the reviewers' own words landing squarely on the log's axis:ideas test. That places it below Ranger's Apprentice 74, the log's ceiling for competent-but-unambitious YA/MG adventure fantasy, and closer to how Divergent 58 and Mortal Engines 55 read once a reviewer says a fantasy premise is assembled from familiar parts. Character relationships (with his sister and a rival-turned-ally) are praised as the book's strongest element, but not enough on their own to clear the line given the explicit lack-of-originality criticism.

t: Stezka v troskach (The Road Beyond Ruin)
why: A well-regarded (4.06/5, 15k+ ratings) WWII drama about strangers converging in postwar Germany, built on a real idea - that the war doesn't end for ordinary people when it ends for nations - close to what the reader rewards. But the author's own account confirms a back-and-forth timeline device that 'made my own head spin,' and at least one detailed review calls the present-day thread 'painfully slow' next to the past thread and the ending 'disorderly' and rushed - the drawn-out, jumbled-ending pattern that cost points elsewhere in the log (The Martian 82, Les Miserables 71). That doubt about whether the structure holds together keeps this under the line rather than predicting it up on a premise that may not survive its own device.

A real, worked idea - what freedom actually means for the newly emancipated amid persisting hatred - carried mainly through multiple close POVs on what each character wants (George's guilt and hope, Prentiss's wariness, Caleb's fear), the axis this log rewards most (Mockingjay 91, Speaker for the Dead 90). Booker-longlisted and repeatedly praised for probing beyond genre convention. The opening is a single legible situation - a grieving father meets two men on his land - not several unresolved threads, so this log's strongest predictor is clear. Risk: the book is genuinely bleak (a beating, a shooting, prejudice throughout) though reviewers note 'a tinge of hope,' closer to Old Man's War's mild bleakness discount than to 1984's flat penalty; juggling five-plus POVs also risks diluting the single-protagonist focus this reader prefers, though reviews suggest it is handled cleanly. Caleb's relationship with a fellow soldier is romantic but not depicted with volume or crudeness in anything found, so sexual-content is not a concern. No infidelity, no occult, no detective structure - the plot turns on hiding and revealing a relationship and a killing, not solving one.

Beast Quest is a ghost-written (house name 'Adam Blade'), highly formulaic UK series for readers 7+: Tom fights one enchanted beast per short volume, sold on collectibility (beast cards) rather than depth - reviews describe it as built for 'reading stamina' and 'hooking reluctant readers,' not literary depth. No idea worth naming beyond 'boy defeats monster of the week', so axis:ideas is a clear risk and this exits at C. The default band applies rather than the picture-book band: it is a real short novel with chapters and dialogue, not a collection or picture book, even though in substance it reads slighter than the children's comps in the log (Narnia 67, Ranger's Apprentice 74). axis:occult left unexamined per the C-low rule - Malvel's curse on the beasts reads as invented fantasy magic, not obviously real-world-mould, but nothing here would change the exit either way.

A near-future dystopia where infertility has made every birth state-monitored and every parenting slip grounds for a child's removal. Reviewers call the premise 'horrifyingly plausible' (Guardian) and 'entirely plausible' given its starting condition (GeekDad), unlike Divergent 58, which sank on a premise that 'collapses under thought'. Kit's arc is built entirely on what she wants and how far she will go to keep her family, the same axis Mockingjay 91 tops the log on. The consistent complaint is sustained heaviness -- 'The Road levels of parental anxiety', 'not the cheeriest' -- the same objection that was 1984's sole knock at 60, so it is carried as a risk rather than folded into the number; unlike 1984, Kit is actively fighting rather than passively crushed, which the rules treat as mitigating bleakness.

t: The house in the Cerulean Sea (The House in the Cerulean Sea)
why: Linus Baker, a rigid caseworker sent to assess six 'dangerous' magical children, is repeatedly the reason reviewers love this - his warming from bureaucratic fear to found-family devotion is the worth-rooting-for arc the reader rewards, in the spirit of the friendship-and-heroism case that carries The Hobbit to 84. Risk: several reviewers note thin plot tension ('no real huge plot moments,' a mid-book confrontation 'resolved in a snap') and at least one critique calls its allegory (echoing real residential-school history) 'shallow' - doubt about whether the idea is actually worked out rather than gestured at, closer to what stalls competent books in the 60s. The magical children (a gnome, a sprite, a wyvern, a boy prophesied as the Antichrist) are innate traits, not an invoked ritual or real-world occult system - no rite is enacted on the page, so this clears occult on mechanism/absence grounds.

A Texas oil-boom family saga (called 'Dickensian' by reviewers) about twins separated at birth and reunited as adults. The separation stems from their mother's affair while married to another man, but that is backstory the characters uncover, not a present-day marriage being unravelled on the page - exactly the 'betrayal in a backstory' case the rules mark as not-premise, costing a point or two rather than triggering a reject. No source names a worked-out idea beyond 'love, loss and betrayal amid an oil boom' - a family-secrets structure closer to the reviewer's own verdict ('a misnomer for these mostly decent people') than to the motive-driven case that lifts Pride and Prejudice to 75. Without a nameable idea this settles under the line.
