The investigation into the postcard's sender (private detective, graphologist) is a genuine mystery-shaped subplot inside an otherwise eligible family history, not the book's premise, so it is flagged under axis:detective rather than rejected. No occult, infidelity-as-premise or sexual-plot content surfaced in any review. Confidence is medium rather than high because only one search was run, even though it returned unusually detailed structural and reception information for a well-covered Goncourt-winning bestseller.

A 24-hour ticking-clock thriller - Ballista alone in Rome racing to stop an assassination before the emperor leaves the Colosseum - built explicitly in the lone-operative ticking-clock mode, which reads as pure momentum with little of the motive-driven interiority the log rewards most (Speaker for the Dead's 90, Mockingjay's 91). One reviewer flags the opening physical ordeal as implausible survival even by the author's own admission - a version of the ability-given-rather-than-earned problem that helped hold Divergent's Mary-Sue-style lead to 58. Reads as competent action-thriller filler rather than a book with a strong positive case beyond pace.

t: Posledni ukol Mabel Beaumontove (The Last List of Mabel Beaumont)
why: The task line flags detective, but on checking this is a reunion quest, not a whodunit: a newly widowed 86-year-old follows her late husband's note ("Find D") to track down a childhood best friend she lost touch with sixty years ago, meeting an intergenerational community of women along the way. Not the whodunit satisfaction the detective filter targets. Checked the love story too: Mabel's youthful love for Dot predates her marriage to Arthur and is the reason she chose a conventional marriage under 1950s social pressure - that is backstory, not an affair conducted during the marriage, so it does not touch the infidelity filter either. What is left is a pleasant, competently reviewed grief-and-friendship novel without a strong idea to hold onto - one review calls the central twist predictable and sums the book up as "perfectly pleasant but not memorable," which is exactly the doubt-the-idea-holds-up test this ladder uses to exit here. REVISED 2026-09-02 for the new axis:same-sex-romance (prominence light), was [58, 68]. Backstory only - mid-century condemnation of same-sex love as the reason for Mabel's marriage, not a present relationship. Light end of the graded range. Magnitude is not separable from the single data point: Caropisci 67 lost about thirteen points to this, the hierofant rite and the portrayal warning together, so this dock states a direction and a prominence tier, not a measured size.

A grain shortage and a conspiracy calling itself the Liberators threaten Emperor Claudius in a Rome where betrayal is everywhere - palace-intrigue plotting on the same recurring engine as the rest of the series, which reviewers describe as carried by the leads' friendship inside a formula rather than a single worked idea. That places it with Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68 in this reader's log rather than with anything idea-driven; I would put axis:ideas under risks. Well into a long series, where this reader's sequels tend to settle rather than climb (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70).

A Depression-era reporter stages a photograph of children 'for sale' for his career, and the staged lie's real consequences - a desperate mother actually selling her own children after a misdiagnosis - is a nameable idea about the cost of a media fabrication, the kind of premise-worked-into-consequences the reader responds to. But reviews describe the back half fanning out into an orphanage plot, a gangster, a family raid and a search for the family, with one reviewer unsure if it wanted to be historical fiction or mystery, and multiple subplots described as present but shallow. The search for the sold children is a subplot within a broader story, not the book's whole satisfaction, so it is a flag rather than a detective-filter veto.

The world's history has been shattered and reassembled into a patchwork of eras, and this closing entry follows the struggle between a 1900-era British Empire and a Roman Empire led by the returning heroine to control the new Europe that results. Czech reader reception is largely positive and the premise - fragments of history colliding rather than just one alternate timeline - is the kind of consequence-worked idea this reader responds to. It is a sequel, and sequels are not a safe bet in this log: Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70, and one detailed review here specifically felt the concept's potential was left unexploited, since the fractured-timeline map implied a wider world than the book actually uses, plus a slower, more political final act that some readers found dragged. That combination - a strong idea only partly cashed in, on a closing volume - keeps this under the line rather than at the level the opening premise alone would suggest.

This is a comic (graphic novel), a short-form work where the character/emotion rules are suspended rather than earned, so the number rests on whether there is an idea to name. Reception is split but the specific complaints line up: The Comics Journal argues the book never shows the regime's actual effects on ordinary people, reducing the plot and characters to 'empty signifiers'; a Goodreads reader found 'no plot point unexpected and no investment in the characters'; another review calls it 'a rather standard rebels versus evil empire storyline'. Praise centers almost entirely on the art rather than the story. Exiting at C rather than researching further: this is a doubt about whether an idea holds up, which is exactly the gate 4 test. Occult status is left unexamined per the ladder rule, despite reviewer mentions of 'ancient mysticism' and grotesque religious ritual imagery tied to the antagonist theocracy - that is why axis:occult stays in deps for a later look if this axis is ever revisited.

Part of an international children's educational comic series recreating prehistoric animal life from the fossil record; this volume follows a Pteranodon fishing and avoiding predators. It is a short, picture-book-style factual recreation for young children rather than a story with a premise to work out - the closest comparison in this log is a picture book, which the reader's own rules place in the 30s-40s. There is a survival narrative here rather than pure captioned facts, so I am not going as low as a bare picture book, but there is no idea beyond that survival framing to lean on.

Set on the eve of the 1956 Hungarian revolution: Csilla's parents were executed by the secret police as Zionist traitors, and she has to decide whether to flee or demand the injustice be acknowledged now that they've been posthumously exonerated. That is a real, worked idea - what it costs to be seen after your family has been erased - carried by a protagonist reviewers repeatedly call worth rooting for. Checked the occult question directly: the magic is a personified river and an angel-of-death character drawing loosely on Jewish folklore (a golem, Azriel), but the one described working scene is Csilla sinking a newspaper into the river and pulling out a flame that won't go out, with a murmured word and a whispered reply - closer to invented magic-realism using folkloric vocabulary as flavor than to an enacted rite of real-world occultism (no invocation, no priesthood, no prayer to a deity). Passing this narrowly, not confidently. Risk: several reviewers found the magic's mechanics genuinely unclear ("it whispers to her, it turns to stone, silver... I just don't understand"), and pacing is criticized as slow to start with too much crammed into the ending.

A charity-run children's book (catalogued under 'publikace pro deti') built around four young friends whose parents work in the rescue services, mixing prevention-education vignettes - bullying, a rafting accident, peer pressure to drink - with retold stories of lesser-known WWII resistance figures. There is no larger idea beyond the safety-education message itself, and no professional literary reception exists to argue otherwise; it reads closer to the picture-book end of the reader's own children's-book scale than to Ranger's Apprentice 74 or Narnia 67, both of which at least carry a continuous adventure plot.

Phoebe watches her friends' bodies corrode into an unexplained body-horror transformation in a dying 1980 Cleveland neighborhood - a real idea (girls' bodies as metaphor for a town and its expectations collapsing), the kind of nameable premise the reader wants. But it is never mechanically explained, and reviewers split hard on whether that pays off: some call the ambiguity the book's real strength, others call the transformation's own description 'vague and unsatisfying' and want the passive Phoebe to 'actually do something to move the plot' - the same passive-protagonist problem that held Oliver Twist to 57, acted upon rather than wanting anything. Two sources were spent settling this, one over the one-source C-low budget.

Macro leaves the legion to help his mother run an inn and manage a veteran's land grant - a quieter, more personal entry than most of the series, which is a point in favour of motive over pure action. Even so, it is still one installment of a series whose reviewers describe the draw as the leads' friendship inside a repeating formula rather than a single worked idea, so it sits with Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68 in this reader's log rather than climbing past the line; I would list axis:ideas under risks. Well into a long series, where this reader's sequels tend to settle rather than climb (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70).

Cato and Macro escort a client king back to his throne in Armenia, a mission that is really about great-power maneuvering between Rome and Parthia rather than about the two leads' own wants. Same shape as the other entries in this series: reviewers describe the appeal as the leads' friendship carrying a repeating political-intrigue formula, not a single explored idea, so this lands with Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68 rather than with anything idea-driven in this reader's log - I would put axis:ideas under risks. It is also deep into a long series, and this reader's sequels tend to settle rather than climb (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70).

A Czech YA original set in a world where magic is an ordinary part of daily life; four girls near their sixteenth birthdays investigate what really happens at the coming-of-age Rite that a mysterious Judge presides over. A reader review describes the book as dragging until the Rite itself finally plays out near the end, and another praises it mainly for playing genre cliches for laughs - between them, no source names an idea worth carrying beyond a coming-of-age mystery-box. This exits on that doubt at one source over budget (a second was needed to locate any review at all), so axis:occult is left unexamined per the C-low rule - the magic and the Rite read as an invented system from the synopses available, not confirmed drawn from real-world practice, and that status should be checked before this title is ever proposed to read.

A comic Czech family chronicle about a household of children and dogs living through renovation mishaps and small dramas, carried by voice and an ensemble of distinct characters rather than by any idea worked out - the same shape as Saturnin 78, which 'scores in the A band on voice and character rather than on any idea worked out, so the humour register carries no penalty here.' Reader reception is consistently warm (83% rating, repeat readers), but nothing in it suggests the sharper wit or lasting reputation Saturnin earned, so the estimate sits a notch under it.

t: Sadako Sasaki a tisic papirovych jerabu (The Complete Story of Sadako Sasaki and the Thousand Paper Cranes)
why: Written by Sadako's own older brother with a co-author, explicitly to correct the contradictory, incomplete versions that had circulated - the same thing that earns points for Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75 in this log: an insider genuinely examining what actually happened and giving real understanding of a group's experience (here, Japanese A-bomb survivors and the long tail of radiation sickness). Unlike the Diary of a Young Girl 40, this is not a raw child's own voice but an adult retrospective account, which is the structural feature that separates the memoirs that worked from the one that didn't in this log. Marketed and formatted as a middle-reader biography with a paper-crane craft tutorial at the back, which pulls toward the children's-book register this reader discounts mildly (Male zeny 79 shows that discount has a real ceiling, not a floor). Subject matter - a child dying of leukemia from wartime radiation exposure - is sustained bleakness, discounted the same mild way as elsewhere in the log.

Ten loosely linked stories, washed ashore as ten pipes, each following a different owner across Tsarist Russia, Siberia, pre-war Berlin and South Africa, with recurring figures (a Sand Woman, Amundsen, Rasputin) threading between them. That recurrence is a structural device, not a single premise whose consequences are worked out, so there is no axis:ideas to lean on the way a genuine idea-driven short work would need - the same gap that keeps most literary short-story collections under the line in this ladder. Czech reader reception is split ("provazanost postav mne uchvatila" against "zapletky povrchni, nekdy i hloupe"), which reads as competent craft without a governing idea rather than either a standout or a failure.

Reviews describe Sharpe as the reader's kind of lead: a working-class outsider who rises on competence, with a clear code (right and wrong times to kill, elastic honesty toward strangers only) rather than being merely likeable - the kind of want-driven characterization Golden Son 92 and Mockingjay 91 both score on. This entry adds a real deduction: Sharpe's wife Jane, still married to him, takes his fortune and falls for Lord Rossendale while hoping Sharpe dies abroad - a marriage betrayal, but one thread among the treasury-theft chase and Sharpe's own arc toward Lucille, not the engine of the book (remove it and the revenge plot against Ducos still stands), so it grades rather than vetoes: a subplot, condemned in its framing (Jane is shown as mercenary, not sympathetic), costing a few points per the axis. The theft-and-frame plot is investigation-shaped but the culprit (Ducos) is known to Sharpe almost immediately, so it reads as a revenge chase, not a whodunit. Landed near Quo Vadis 66 and under Count of Monte Cristo 75 - similar revenge-adventure momentum but without Monte Cristo's structural tightness, and reader reviews of this specific entry call it plot-wise the weakest of the series even while praising the character work.

Three childhood friends each want something different and act on it as fascism and the Nazi occupation close in on Rome - Elisabetta chasing authorship, Marco and Sandro rivals for her heart while their families are pulled toward collaboration or persecution. That is the motive-driven engine that tops the log in Pride and Prejudice's 75 and Mockingjay's 91. Reviews split hard on whether it pays off: some praise 'rich character development,' others call the trio two-dimensional and fault the author for moving characters to where the plot needs them without earning it - a real risk next to a book like Golden Son, where the trio's distinctiveness (Darrow, Sevro, Mustang each thinking and wanting differently) was singled out as a strength. Grounded in a real, well-researched historical event (the 1943 Rome roundup), which the reader responds to when a book actually examines what happened.

t: Sloup do nebe (Pillar to the Sky)
why: A scientist and engineer fight political and financial obstacles to build a working space elevator as a real solution to an energy and water crisis - the premise is worked through with actual engineering consequences, the same trait that carries Project Hail Mary 92 and Old Man's War 87. No occult (hard SF, no magic system at all) and no detective, infidelity or sex-plot in any source found. What holds it down from that band: reviewers repeatedly flag slow, repetitive pacing and a genuinely messy climax chapter, which reads as the axis:density penalty this reader applies to a thin story stretched long, not present in the higher comparators.

The Iceni queen is captured and several British tribes rise up together, giving Cato and Macro their hardest fight yet - a straightforward escalation of the series' recurring war-and-politics formula, which reviewers describe as carried by the leads' friendship rather than a single worked idea. That places it with Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68 in this reader's log, not with anything idea-driven; I would list axis:ideas under risks. Deep into a long series, where this reader's sequels tend to settle rather than climb (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70).

Ben, a bait-shop worker plagued by inexplicable trivia knowledge he can't explain, is kidnapped by an alien bounty hunter who reveals Ben is a 'Stringer' carrying fragments of other lives, and dragged into a hunt across alien factions. Reviewers repeatedly single out the friendship between Ben and his best friend Patton as the book's real emotional core - genuine warmth and stakes when the pair are captured together - which matches this reader's preference for motive-driven pages over pure action, in the comic-SF register that made Hitchhiker's Guide 83 work. The reincarnated-knowledge premise is followed through to an actual answer rather than left as a gimmick. Humor leans on gross-out and crude jokes throughout, which several reviewers call polarizing, but that is a register objection this reader does not penalize, distinct from sexual content, which does not feature here.

A schizophrenic teenager, Will, walks out of a psychiatric hospital into the New York subway, driven by a delusional conviction that he can stop global warming by losing his virginity to a girl he once hurt - almost entirely page time on what he wants and why, which is the axis this reader responds to most. Reviewers with clinical familiarity single out how thoroughly the psychosis itself is researched and internally consistent, not just colorfully written. A detective and Will's mother pursue him in parallel chapters, functioning as an investigation-shaped subplot rather than the book's core satisfaction - it is not a whodunit, and critics actually fault the mystery beat (Violet's secret) for being guessable long before the detective catches up, which argues against reading this as detective/mystery. Two real risks: Will has a violent past against the girl he's chasing, which could make him hard to root for despite the illness framing (the log's clearest parallel for an unrootable-but-sympathetically-drawn lead is Promena 58, where a passive rather than dangerous lead still cost points); and the claustrophobic subway setting and psychiatric subject matter are sustained bleakness, which this reader discounts mildly rather than rejects.

A licensed Marvel/Disney tie-in comic continuing established Star Wars film continuity right after Return of the Jedi, split into three short vignettes for Luke, Han and Leia. Reviews describe it as competently setting up franchise-familiar threats (mercenaries, an underworld mystery, a new political alliance) rather than introducing any standalone idea of its own - it exists to continue the canon, not to work out a premise. As a single comic issue this is also a short, suspended-test form. Han's thread is framed as an investigation ('investigates a deadly underworld mystery'), which is a mystery-shaped subplot inside one of three vignettes, not the book's whole structure, so it is a flag rather than a detective-filter veto.

A long-running Czech pulp SF series: humanity has fought aliens for decades from a ring of orbital cities, and agent John Francis Kovar investigates a weapon threatening the wider setting. Nothing in the available material names a distinguishing idea beyond that generic decades-long-war premise - reader reactions are split between calling it one of the weakest entries ('the aliens don't work, no action, no humor') and praising its internal consistency and tension, with no clear consensus on it standing out. That reads as a competent genre entry rather than one with a nameable idea, landing it at the default C-low band. It is also the twelfth book in a long series, which this log treats as a real but secondary risk on its own (Hitchhikers sequels fell from 83 to 70).

t: Sto roku Lenni a Margot (The One Hundred Years of Lenni and Margot)
why: A terminally ill 17-year-old and an 83-year-old on the same hospital ward decide their combined ages add up to one hundred years, and set out to paint one hundred pictures - one for each year - telling both their life stories. That is a concrete premise carried through to its structural conclusion, the exact shape of book this reader rewards (the same shape, differently applied, that Labyrint sveta 70 hit on). Reviewers consistently describe Lenni herself as the reason it works ("broke through my stony exterior"), and the book is built entirely around companionship rather than solitary suffering, which is the specific thing Project Hail Mary 92 shows this reader rewards on the bleakness axis - Margot is not a device, she is the friendship the book is about. Terminal illness and an approaching death are still sustained bleakness, discounted mildly rather than ignored, and Lenni's age is the standard small life-phase pushback.

t: Strasliva zavrat (When We Cease to Understand the World)
why: Five linked pieces about real 20th-century scientists (Heisenberg, Schrodinger, Grothendieck, Haber, Einstein), blending fact and invention with each successive piece more fictionalized than the last, built around one thesis - that scientific genius and destructive madness are inseparable. It is literary fiction structured as a short-story collection, the pattern this reader's log shows landing under 68 far more often than not even when the pieces are well reviewed (this one was Booker-shortlisted) - the short-idea-driven suspension removes the character-driven penalty but does not add points on its own, and a linked-story structure has no single protagonist to carry the number instead. No occult content - the subject is real historical physics and mathematics, not magic - so that question closes without needing the budget it would cost elsewhere.

Ten stories by ten different Czech authors, unified only by setting and period (the Sudetenland before the German expulsion), not by a single worked-out premise - by construction this is a themed anthology, not a book pursuing one idea to its consequences. Reviews are consistently positive on authenticity and regional texture (Novinky.cz praises how convincingly ordinary lives are rendered; several contributors grew up in the resettled regions themselves), but that is craft and voice, not the idea-driven case this reader's higher scores lean on.

A historical-fantasy reimagining of Vlad III Dracula as a vampire seeking vengeance against those who arranged his death, entangling the Ottoman and Hungarian courts in 1477. The author is praised for historical detail, but a recurring, specific complaint is exactly the kind of self-consistency break this reader's worldbuilding axis penalizes - a Goodreads reader flags modern metric units ('meters and kilometers in 1477?') inside a book that otherwise leans on painstaking period research, and Czech readers separately describe the pacing as dragging in places and the ending as rushed. Vampirism here is a supernatural-creature premise, not witchcraft, seance or prayer to a real deity, so the occult source test is not in play, though whether any specific rite is depicted was not separately confirmed and stays unexamined at this exit.

t: Tajemstvi modrych tresni (A Fistful of Cherries)
why: A post-apocalyptic England where every child collapses into chronic exhaustion on reaching adolescence, and a mismatched pair set out into a mutant-infested wasteland to find a rumoured cure. It had its first publication anywhere in this Czech edition. Reader reception is enthusiastic, but the one professional review found (iLiteratura) flags the book as pulled between inconsistent narrative levels and an ambiguous genre identity, symptoms of a premise not fully thought through rather than a stylistic quirk - the same shape of doubt that sends Mortal Engines 55 and Divergent 58 below the line in this log. Aimed explicitly at children from age 10, which caps how much weight the premise can be asked to carry.

A Czech blogger's first-person account of a stillbirth followed by a high-risk second pregnancy, written to break the social taboo around losing a child and, by reader accounts, more shaken by the medical system's coldness than by the loss itself. That is the axis that earns points in this reader's memoir rule - not the form itself but examining something actually true and giving insight into an experience most readers avoid thinking about, the same case that carried Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus to 91. Reviewers single out the voice - blunt, funny, unsentimental, each chapter opened with a fantasy-novel quote - as what keeps a heavy subject from becoming purely miserable, which caps the bleakness risk rather than letting it dominate. No occult, detective, infidelity or sexual-plot content in any account found - it is a short, real, continuous first-person narrative with no confusing opening. Only one search was run for a book this well-documented in Czech retailer and reader reviews (91% reader rating on Palmknihy), so confidence stays medium rather than high on source count alone.

Othello transposed onto a single day at a 1970s American schoolyard, with a clean one-to-one character mapping that keeps the play's psychological engine intact: a classmate's manipulation and the new boy Osei's descent into jealous rage are entirely about what each character wants and why, the axis that tops the log in Speaker for the Dead's 90 and Mockingjay's 91. Reviews single out Osei as 'a standout' with a real arc from openness to defiance, not a flat or unrootable lead. The children are eleven, but this is adult literary fiction examining racism through Shakespeare rather than a childish register, so the childrens axis costs little. The real cost is the tragic, ambiguous ending, covered by the mild bleakness discount rather than a bigger penalty given the otherwise strong reception.

A girl is pulled into an unfinished storybook world after its author dies mid-manuscript, and must help set the world's chaos right. It is a Czech children's fantasy (nominated for the Zlata stuha illustration/children's-book award) whose own summaries name only friendship, family bonds and a mother's love as its themes - no idea beyond the standard portal-adventure furniture surfaced in any source, and I would list axis:ideas as a doubt rather than a strength.

Sixteen-year-old Finn dies in the opening pages and narrates from between life and death, watching her family and friends survive the wreck of the accident - a device close to The Lovely Bones. That makes her almost entirely a watcher rather than an actor, the same passive-protagonist problem that held Oliver Twist to 57: acted upon rather than wanting anything. Reviewers also note the afterlife premise is never developed much beyond the device itself, so there is little idea to lean on either. A teen lead adds the small life-phase pushback on top.

Nero exiles his lover, a freed slave, to Sardinia to appease his political rivals, and Cato is ordered to escort her there while carrying a second, separate mission. The infidelity is Nero's, told as a court intrigue happening around Cato rather than to him or about his own marriage - it is incidental to the actual plot and stated neutrally as historical fact, so it costs at most a point or two and does not change the outcome. The book still runs on this series' recurring formula, which reviewers describe as camaraderie over a single worked idea, placing it with Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68 in this reader's log; I would list axis:ideas under risks. Well into a long series, where this reader's sequels tend to settle rather than climb (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70).

The catalogue's own annotation frames the book around the differences in the motivations of its key characters - Edith Pretty, digger Basil Brown, and archaeologist Peggy Piggott each want something different from the 1939 Sutton Hoo dig, the axis that tops the log in Speaker for the Dead's 90 and Mockingjay's 91. Reception is strong across major outlets, though some reviewers find the restrained prose keeps the three leads 'a bit too far below the surface to be extremely compelling' - a real but secondary risk next to Oliver Twist's 57, where the protagonist problem was severe enough to define the whole book. A minor, mostly implied unhappy-marriage subplot for Peggy appears in the novel itself, incidental rather than the engine of the book, so it costs a little rather than vetoing anything.

t: Vzkaz na zdi zachodku (Words on Bathroom Walls)
why: A teenager newly diagnosed with schizophrenia tries an experimental drug so he can pass as normal at a new school and be with the girl he likes, narrated with heavy interiority - what he wants (to be seen as Adam, not as a diagnosis) and why drives nearly every scene, which is this reader's top-weighted axis. Reception is warm on the lead specifically (YALSA: "hilarious and infinitely lovable"), but there is a real, repeated critique that the illness is softened into "almost a fun personality quirk" to make room for a fairly conventional YA romance - that is a self-consistency concern (declare a serious illness and the book should carry its actual weight) rather than a settled strength, so it is graded down slightly rather than credited fully. Teen lead is a small, standard life-phase pushback, not a real cost.

t: Zariva noc hvezd a ledu (A Brilliant Night of Stars and Ice)
why: Dual real-life POVs - Captain Rostron racing the Carpathia to the wreck, and third-class survivor Kate Connolly - built around a single night's rescue, praised repeatedly for pace. But reviewers explicitly flag it as an 'experience-driven' story with Kate in particular wanting 'a little bit more depth,' and a dropped subplot about a boy in the lifeboats left unresolved. No larger idea beyond the historical event itself to lean on, so the number rests on pacing and the real-event grounding, with thin protagonist depth as the risk that could pull it down.

t: Zil jsem mezi malomocnymi (In the Sanctuary of Outcasts)
why: A journalist serving time for bank fraud is imprisoned in a facility that shares grounds with America's last leprosy colony, and his growing friendship with patients like Ella Bounds, exiled from her own family as a girl for a disease rather than a crime, gives him - and the reader - real insight into a stigmatized group most people never think about, the axis that carried Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus to 91 and Son of Hamas to 75. Set below those because one reviewer's specific complaint is a rootability problem this reader weighs heavily: White reads as 'charmingly unsympathetic,' with self-justifying passages that sit oddly in a redemption memoir even though the same reviewer praises how vividly he renders the people around him. No occult, detective or sexual-plot content in a straightforward memoir with a linear structure.

t: Zlata sbirka pohadek (Peter Pan (Zlata sbirka pohadek))
why: This volume belongs to a Disney-branded weekly collectible fascicle series (87 issues, sold at newsstands from 2021) that retells classic fairy tales for young children in simplified, illustrated form. Per the reader's own scale a picture book lands in the 30s-40s, and this is exactly that register - no idea beyond the familiar Peter Pan story, well below Hobbit 84 or Little Prince 82, which pay nothing for their child audience only because real ideas carry them.

A dual-timeline reimagining of the real 18th-century thief Jack Sheppard as trans, framed as a manuscript being annotated by a present-day academic whose footnotes gradually take over the book. The premise (who gets to tell history, and what it costs to "liberate" a text or a body from the record) is genuinely worked through, not just gestured at - a positive case in the reader's own terms. But by the author's own description the book is "pretty dirty" and reviewers independently describe erotic content in nearly every chapter and most scenes, in an explicit register - that is volume and explicitness both landing high, which is the axis that sank Ready Player One 55 and The Witcher 53 in this log regardless of how well-regarded the surrounding book is. The footnote-within-manuscript structure and a late-book reveal about "radical librarians" tampering with the text add real structural complexity; one reviewer called it a book that "may push away the average reader" with its layering, so the opening is a genuine risk rather than a settled pass.

Military-political adventure: Cato is sent as an envoy to negotiate with the Parthian king while Corbulo stalls for time before a real campaign. Reviewers of the wider series frame its appeal around the Cato-Macro camaraderie and a repeating formula of new posting, new antagonist, political intrigue from above, rather than a single worked-out premise - closer to Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68 in this reader's log than to an idea-driven book, and I would list axis:ideas under risks if I pushed further. It sits deep in a long-running series, and this reader's log shows sequels settling lower than openers (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70), which does not raise the case for going on. Competent, grounded in real Roman politics, but nothing here argues past the line.

Thomas of Hookton has a clear want - complete an urgent task before he can rejoin the Black Prince's campaign, while a rival churchman hunts the same relic for his own ambition - the axis Golden Son 92 and Mockingjay 91 both score on. The central relic, La Malice (said to be the sword of Saint Peter), is deliberately kept ambiguous rather than shown working: reviewers and TV Tropes both note Cornwell never confirms real supernatural power, and the book ends with the sword indistinguishable from scrap metal on a smith's discard pile - the same restraint the series uses for the Grail itself, where the danger is what people believe about the relic, not magic it performs. That keeps the book clear of the occult filter: no rite is shown functioning on the page. Reviews single out the climactic Poitiers battle as an unusually strong set piece. Estimated close to Count of Monte Cristo 75's adventure-momentum baseline, docked slightly for being a sequel - sequels are not a safe bet in this log, per Hitchhiker's fall from 83 to 70.

That puts it in the territory of Rangers Apprentice 74 - easy, likeable, competent children's adventure with 'not much to think about' but no real penalty either - rather than lower; I am not leaning up on the idea itself since I have no independent confirmation the alien-artifact mystery is rigorously worked out, only that reviewers found it engaging. The one real risk is that this is a sequel, and this log treats sequels as unsafe bets on their own (Hitchhikers sequels fell from 83 to 70).

This is assembled entirely from deleted scenes, alternate drafts, and a production journal - fragments left over from a screenwriting process, not a narrative with a premise of its own. Reviewers themselves call it inessential outside fandom ('not a necessary addition... but kind of a must have' for fans specifically), which is a tell that there is no standalone idea here to weigh. The fragmentary, notes-plus-deleted-scenes shape is close to what cost Unfinished Tales 69 its footing in this reader's own log - 'the pieces aren't logically connected to each other' - only here there is no finished novel sitting alongside the fragments to anchor them, so it settles below even that.

OPENING, from the publisher's excerpt: two prologues of a few pages come first, a drowned golem watching sunken ships and an unnamed clacksman killed on a tower, and neither means anything yet. Then one lead and one situation for the whole first chapter: a confidence man is hanged, wakes in Vetinari's office, is offered the Post Office or a door with no floor, runs, and is carried back by a golem. That is not the Guards! Guards! 30 shape, and a few pages of mood are not the Čaropisci 67 one; a note that the prologues pay off covers them. CASE: Mort 83 shows the author and the comic register cost nothing, and this adds what Mort lacks. The clacks are declared, priced and owned, and the plot follows: a monopoly bought by financial trickery and run down for profit, an institution rebuilt against it, a race run on what a semaphore can and cannot carry, the Project Hail Mary 92 habit. The lead travels the way Caeden did in Stín věcí ztracených 93: a golem tells Moist he has killed 2.338 people without touching one, and he confesses to a victim of his own forgeries. COSTS: the money to rebuild comes from a faked miracle at four temples, religion played for laughs on the Já, robot 55 side; golems run on holy words put in by priests, as lore, never staged; and readers in both languages report a slack stretch after chapter one and a rushed end, the Počítání hvězd 85 complaint.

REVERSED 2026-09-03, and by a real score rather than by a re-reading. The idea is still nameable in one sentence - a god's power is exactly the number of people who actually believe in him, and a church, an inquisition and a holy war are all consequences of that arithmetic - and on ideas alone this would sit where it used to. What has changed is that the faith axis now has an anchor. Ja, robot 55 was abandoned partly because the third story's robots build a religion and it read as satire on the main religions and on blind faith, which the reader disliked in his own words. This book is that treatment at novel length and on purpose: the state religion is modelled on real monotheism down to the prophets, the holy book and the inquisition, and the comedy is aimed at institutional belief. The defence, and it is why this is a graded drop rather than a reject, is that the one believer left is treated sympathetically and the book's target is the church rather than the belief - but that is a distinction the reader did not draw when he made this objection. Leaned on faith rather than on the idea, because the idea is the best thing here and cannot outrun the treatment. OPENING VERDICT: one thread, one lead, a novice in a garden, entered through a short essayistic passage - legible and single-stranded, not the many-threads shape that scored 30 twice in this setting. WORLD VERDICT: the premise is followed through to the end, including the cost to the believer, so both forms hold.

LEANS ON THE LEAD, the axis that outranks worldbuilding. A girl cuts her hair and enlists in her country's army under a false name to find her brother; she is interesting and worth rooting for from the first chapter, which is the pairing that separates Speaker for the Dead 90 from Artemis 69, and her want is stated rather than implied. OPENING VERDICT: single thread, one recruit, one recruiting sergeant, no invented vocabulary to decode - the concrete starting situation the filter demands. This is also a standalone with its own print edition, so nothing has to be read first. WORLD VERDICT: the declared thing is a state religion that keeps adding to a list of Abominations, and the book prices it - the country is starving and at war with everyone because of what it has forbidden, which is the society-as-subject face the Divergent 58 factions failed. Real ideas on top: atrocity propaganda and what a nation tells itself, the register that earned Animal Farm 78. RISK is bleakness, the mildest recorded objection, and it is bleak-with-ideas rather than immersion in misery. SCREENED 2026-09-02 on axis:sex-portrayal, verdict mild, was [74, 83]. The premise runs on foolish male authority: Lieutenant Blouse is named after 'a big girl's blouse' and is book-smart but combat-incompetent, while the regiment's real competence is female. Heavily mitigated in-world, though - the genuinely competent Sergeant Jackrum and several senior officers who drove Borogravia into the war also turn out to be women, reviewers read Pratchett's point as women being just as good and just as bad as men, and Blouse is granted real grace. The dock is the profile's stated convention (mild -2, moderate -5), not a measured magnitude - the axis has no high-contrast anchor yet.

LEANS ON THE PREMISE plus a now-scored author. Declared premise, and the library's annotation states it outright: Death is dismissed from his post, so nothing on the disc dies properly and the unclaimed life force has to go somewhere. The consequences are then worked out rather than asserted, which is form one, and one of the two strands is a man who has never had a life discovering he now has a finite one - motives as content, the axis that puts Mockingjay 91 above Catching Fire 83. OPENING VERDICT and the reason for the risk: TWO plots start close together, the dismissed reaper taking work on a farm and Ankh-Morpork filling up with surplus vitality. Two staggered threads are explicitly fine on this profile - LOTR 84 and Golden Son 92 both anchor one before the next arrives - and roughly six at once is what scored 30 twice here, so two is the tolerated end of the axis and not the filtered end. If they open simultaneously rather than staggered, this is a 30 and not a 70; that is what the risk means. WORLD VERDICT: the rules of the declared mechanism are obeyed and the urban strand is where they are tested, though the second strand is closer to a running joke than to a worked-out system. Occult passes: a personified death is not a rite.

LEANS ON THE WORLD, and the guard against doing that applies and is cleared: the lead is not thin - he is a stated confidence trickster with a want and a nerve problem, so this is not the Artemis 69 configuration where a strong premise was carrying a flat protagonist. Declared premise, straight out of the library's annotation: he is handed a royal mint that loses money on every coin it strikes, and the plot is paper currency being introduced into a metal economy - a bank run, the question of what actually backs a promise, and a vault that no longer holds what everyone thinks it holds. That is form four of the heaviest axis, a resource declared and then made to behave that way, and it is the face the Divergent 58 premise failed at. OPENING VERDICT: one lead, one situation, he is summoned and given the job - legible from the first page and nothing like the many-threads start that scored 30 twice in this setting. RISKS: it continues a lead established in an earlier volume, and sequels are not safe bets on this profile - Stopaduv pruvodce fell thirteen points to its own sequels, the steepest series decline in the log - so read the earlier volume first; and the lead being carried over means his want is partly already spent. Occult passes: an undead accountant is a character, not a rite.

LEANS ON THE IDEA, and it is the strongest one in this author's Death strand: belief is load-bearing, you learn to believe the small untruths so that you can believe the large ones that a civilisation actually runs on. Declared premise, which the annotation gives obliquely - the fat man who brings the presents has been removed by going after the belief in him rather than the man, and the reaper takes over the round to keep the sun coming up. The consequences are followed through, which is form one. OPENING VERDICT, and it is the reason the range is not higher: FOUR strands start close together - the granddaughter, the reaper, the assassin and the auditors - and that is the failure shape that produced two abandoned reads at 30 in this setting, only at four rather than six. WORLD VERDICT: the belief mechanic is declared precisely and obeyed, and the book leans on it in every scene, so the obligation is high and it is met. A second risk is the lead: the granddaughter is competent and sardonic but the reaper takes the best scenes, and a divided centre is not the interesting-and-rootable pairing that earns the top of the log. Faith appears as a mechanism rather than as devotion, so it is a listed dep and not a live risk.

t: Uzasny Mauric (The Amazing Maurice and His Educated Rodents)
why: LEANS ON THE IDEA. Declared premise, from the annotation: a cat and a troop of rats have become self-aware, and the book is about what awareness costs them - they take names, argue about a story they have inherited, and have to decide whether they are still allowed to run a confidence trick on human beings. That is a nameable idea in a phrase, which the sharpened short-form rule demands, and the rats are differentiated the way Golden Son 92 differentiates its cast. OPENING VERDICT: one situation and a small legible cast, a talking cat and a boy with a pipe walking into a town to work the trick - concrete, and no invented vocabulary. WORLD VERDICT: the mechanism is a wizarding university's rubbish heap and the book does not undertake to explain it, so little binds; what it does declare - that these rats think - it then honours in every scene. RISK is the register, graded and never a filter: an audience-childrens book pays nothing when there is an adult layer for the deduction to grade, which is why Hobit 84 and The Little Prince 82 pay nothing and a nursery-register book lands in the 60s, and the layer here is real. Occult passes: no rite, no invocation.

LEANS ON THE IDEA: belief and mass, with pyramids declared as structures that dam up time and a kingdom that has spent seven thousand years paying for them. One lead, a boy sent away to be trained as an assassin and recalled to be a god-king, and the annotation frames it exactly that way - being a pharaoh in adolescence. OPENING VERDICT: an examination at a school of assassins is a single concrete situation with a clear goal, which clears the filter; the mild pushback is that the book then jumps to a second setting. WORLD VERDICT: the declared resource behaves as declared and the consequences arrive, so form four holds. RISK, and it is the one that could collapse this: OCCULT. The kingdom's priesthood, embalming and pantheon are modelled closely on documented ancient Egyptian religion rather than invented, and rites are performed on the page - the source test and the depiction test are both in play, and Percy Jackson 57 is what it costs when a real pantheon is prayed to and sacrificed to on the page. Anyone proposing this must run the depiction check first and lead with it, not with the idea. A second, small risk is the lead's age reading young from the inside, the Ender's Game 87 pushback.

LEANS ON THE IDEA and the lean is honestly weak, which is why the range sits in the B band. Declared premise: a kind of music arrives that is itself alive and possesses the people who play it, and a granddaughter inherits the reaper's round. The consequences are followed through in places, but a large share of the book is a sustained joke about rock and roll history rather than a premise worked out, and a running gag is voice rather than an idea you can name in a phrase - Saturnin 78 shows that voice and character alone still reach the A band, so this is not a failure, it is a ceiling. OPENING VERDICT and the live risk: two strands start close together, the possessed band and the inherited duty, which is the tolerated end of the multi-thread axis rather than the filtered end, but this book has less to compensate with if the entry does not hold. WORLD VERDICT: the mechanism is declared loosely, so little binds and little is breached; the deduction is that nothing much is built on it either. Occult passes.

STATED CONFIDENCE: MEDIUM-HIGH, and the reason is on the record - the library's annotation for this volume is pure publisher boilerplate with no premise in it, so everything below rests on outside knowledge of the book rather than on the catalogue. LEANS ON THE WORLD: a printing press arrives in a city that had no news, and the consequences are the plot - a trade guild's monopoly broken, a readership invented, a competitor selling invented stories that sell better than real ones. That is form one, and it is the same face that the good worldbuilding rows in the log are praised for. OPENING VERDICT: one lead, a gentleman's son who writes a newsletter, and one situation - the press literally runs him down in the street. Legible, single-thread, the opposite of the shape that scored 30 twice here. RISK, and it must be stated first when proposing: the SPINE of the plot is the lead investigating who framed Ankh-Morpork's ruler for attempted murder, and that is the hard-filtered genre as the book's structure and not as a subplot. The profile says an investigation-shaped strand inside an eligible book is a flag rather than a drop, but here the strand is the engine, so this is recorded and flagged rather than proposed clean.

LEANS ON THE WORLD, and this is the purest example of form one in the whole holding: a locomotive is declared, and the annotation itself describes the consequence rather than the machine - steam rising over a continent, a technology that reorganises trade, war and who can reach whom. Declared capability then society visibly different for it, which is the reader's own formulation of the axis. OPENING VERDICT: single situation, an engineer and an engine, legible from page one. RISKS are what hold this in the B band. First, story density: this is widely reported as thin on plot for its length, with long stretches of speech-making about progress rather than events, and a thin story spread over many pages is precisely the penalty term - Monte Cristo 75 and Les Miserables 71 were both docked for digression and they are far better plotted than this is reported to be. Second, it continues a lead established two volumes earlier and is late in a long run, and sequels are not safe bets here. Access note lives in the cache and not in this field. Occult passes.

LEANS ON THE WORLD and then is pulled back down by the lead, which is the Artemis 69 guard applying rather than being cleared. Declared premise: a place is found where the barrier between what is imagined and what is real has worn thin, and an entertainment industry grows on it - the consequences are worked out, an economy, a labour market and a hazard all following from the declaration, so form one holds. But the profile is explicit that a flat lead beats a strong world, and the two young protagonists here are vehicles for the joke rather than people who want things; the wizards and the supporting cast take the best material. OPENING VERDICT and the second risk: the cast fans out early across several locations with no single figure carrying the entry, which is the shape the filter names, and the two abandoned reads at 30 in this setting are what it costs. Recorded rather than proposed. Occult passes: the mechanism is a thinning of reality, not a rite.

BLOCKED 2026-08-31 by inheritance. The commander, his watch and his marriage are all established in the volume read and abandoned at 30, and the book assumes every one of them. Its own detective risk was already the second-heaviest thing against it. Was recorded at a low range. Prior assessment, kept for the audit trail: LEANS ON THE IDEA, which is real: how two cities talk themselves into a war over an uninhabited rock that has just surfaced, and what patriotism looks like from inside the machinery - the register that earned Animal Farm 78, though carried much more lightly. RISKS are two and they compound. First, the spine opens as an inquiry into the first casualty and the lead is a police commander running it, so the hard-filtered genre is the structure; the profile flags an investigation-shaped strand rather than dropping it, but here the strand is the frame. Second, the entry: the disputed island, the two governments, the commander's watch and a diplomatic party all start close together, which is the many-threads shape that produced two abandoned reads at 30 in this setting - and one of those two is this same lead's first volume, so the closest read comparator is a 30. WORLD VERDICT: nothing much is declared beyond a plausible pseudo-Mediterranean politics, so little binds and little breaches; there is no worldbuilding case to predict up on. Recorded, not proposed. Occult passes.

The library's own annotation is the diagnosis: it announces that the book introduces a fresh set of protagonists - a barbarian hairdresser and a reluctant destroyer - inside a save-the-world plot that is already under way, with the wizard carried over from the volume abandoned at 30. This is the sub-series whose FIRST volume the reader read and abandoned at 30 on an unclear, confusing start, and the objection is now correctly scoped: Mort 83 proved the author and the comic register are fine, so what is being priced here is this strand's structure and not Pratchett. The strand is picaresque - a cowardly wizard is carried through a sequence of set pieces with no single declared situation, and new protagonists are introduced into a plot already running. OPENING VERDICT: that is the filtered shape, arrived at from the read score on volume one rather than from a fresh reading of this volume's first chapter, so it is inference and is labelled as such. WORLD VERDICT: almost nothing is declared and the magic is deliberately unsystematised, so the obligation is low and nothing is breached - but by the same rule there is no worldbuilding case to predict up on either, and rules add obligation and never bonus. Occult passes: comic invented spellcasting with no rite in the historical mould. RECORDED, NOT PROPOSED - a low range so that the title stops resurfacing as an unscreened find, which is the whole point of writing it down. BLOCKED 2026-08-31 by inheritance, and doubly: a strict continuation of one hard-excluded volume, and half its cast is established in another. Was recorded at a low range. Prior assessment, kept for the audit trail: Two casts running in parallel, the carried-over wizard stranded on a far continent and a party of academics lost at a different point in time, with no single situation anchoring the entry. That doubles the structural objection rather than easing it. This is the sub-series whose FIRST volume the reader read and abandoned at 30 on an unclear, confusing start, and the objection is now correctly scoped: Mort 83 proved the author and the comic register are fine, so what is being priced here is this strand's structure and not Pratchett. The strand is picaresque - a cowardly wizard is carried through a sequence of set pieces with no single declared situation, and new protagonists are introduced into a plot already running. OPENING VERDICT: that is the filtered shape, arrived at from the read score on volume one rather than from a fresh reading of this volume's first chapter, so it is inference and is labelled as such. WORLD VERDICT: almost nothing is declared and the magic is deliberately unsystematised, so the obligation is low and nothing is breached - but by the same rule there is no worldbuilding case to predict up on either, and rules add obligation and never bonus. Occult passes: comic invented spellcasting with no rite in the historical mould. RECORDED, NOT PROPOSED - a low range so that the title stops resurfacing as an unscreened find, which is the whole point of writing it down.

A guardian angel falls for the boy she is assigned to protect and has to hide it from strict superiors. That is one clean situation rather than a confusing fan-out, which is the thing this reader most needs, but it is also the whole of the book: a forbidden-love complication, not a premise whose consequences get worked out, and I can name no thought it leaves behind. Doubt on that axis is what decides the exit and the band. The risk is the declared setup - once you assert a supervised angelic order with rules about contact, the rules bind, and Harry Potter 51 is in the log partly because a concretely declared system was never followed through into how the world would actually work. What reader comment exists is about repetitive phrasing and a quick read rather than about anything the book achieves. Occult status unexamined at this exit; the angelic apparatus is what would need checking there. One source, within budget.

Exited at the below-the-line gate. Form and genre are settled - a military-adventure SF novel opening a six-book run - and the idea is a conspiracy hook rather than a premise worked out: three unexplained zones on the map, an invading Shadow that destroyed Atlantis ten thousand years ago and is back. That is a machine for producing set pieces, and set-piece action with no character revelation is dead weight for this reader; it is what pulled Golden Son 92 below Red Rising 95 even where the writing was strong. I would list axis:ideas in risks, so the gate fires. The larger danger is the opening: reviewers describe the author's habitual method as two to four sets of characters introduced in parallel and followed across different eras, which is the shape that ended Guards! Guards! 30 and The Colour of Magic 30 unfinished. That risk is what could take it well under the range rather than what sets it. Occult status is unexamined, which the early exit accepts.

A standalone with its own lead and premise; the excluded books by this author are a different sequence set in Anglo-Saxon England and nothing here continues them, so no inheritance - decided on the book's own plot summary, not on the hint. It then exits at the below-the-line gate. The positive is a legible single-situation opening, one archer under sentence of the noose in 1414, which is exactly the concrete start this reader wants and the opposite of the failures at 30. But I would put axis:ideas in risks: the last quarter is the battle, the bulk before it is siege and campaign detail, and reviewers repeatedly describe the characters as two-dimensional and hard to build rapport with - a thin lead outranks strong research here, which is the whole lesson of Artemis 69. Set against Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68, the historical band in this log, that lands under the line. Two smaller deductions are already visible and neither changes the exit: the lead has an affair with a married woman, which is incidental rather than the premise and costs a point or two, and his patron saints speak to him on the page. That second thing is a live occult question which I deliberately did not examine, because the book is already below the line either way.

The hook is genuinely promising - the tyrant is dead and the hero of the book is the tyrant's son, hunted by the good queen's soldiers - and a lead who has to find out whether he is his father is a real want to follow. What sinks the estimate is self-consistency: the one substantive reader account describes valkyries, vampires, trolls and assorted magicians assembled into a world that does not cohere, characters who alternately fight like lions and inexplicably give up only to be rescued anyway, and convoluted explanations. That is the Divergent 58 failure exactly - ideas borrowed and assembled without cohering, with the plot saved when it suits the author - and it is the axis carrying the number down. Ideas are the risk rather than the lean: I cannot name a thought the book would leave behind beyond the premise's own irony, and doubt on that axis is what sends this out at the gate. Occult status unexamined at this exit. One source, within budget.

I examined the infidelity axis first, within its two-source budget, and decided not to reject. Removing the adultery does not remove the book: the engine is the Japanese invasion of Malaya, the flight south by yacht, the poisoning plot pursued by a servant girl carrying out her mother's curse, and the pirates - so this is a prominent subplot, not the premise, and where the doubt is real the rule says grade rather than reject. The doubt is real here and I am recording it: a married woman's attraction to another man is the emotional centre of the middle of the book even though it is not its plot. What the axis then costs is severe, and it is the framing that does it. The marriage is written as loveless with the husband at fault, and the publisher's own copy presents the new attachment as a discovery of freedom - approving framing, which the measured table puts at thirty to forty for a subplot and which the log says bites even when brief. There is a second, consummated adultery in the recent past as well, so this is not a single moment. Against that I can name no idea the book leaves behind: it is a wartime escape story with a romance inside it, and colonial complacency shattered is a setting rather than a premise worked out. That is the below-the-line exit, and between the two bands the lower one is the honest one, because the axis table would place it lower still. Note that I spent the gate-two budget of two sources before exiting, and nothing further. Occult status is unexamined at this exit by design.

Exits at the below-the-line gate. Form is a novel of about 592 pages, genre a procedural war thriller built on a real weapons programme. I would put axis:ideas in risks and that is the exit: the satisfaction on offer is whether the weapon is found in time, and reviewers converge on the same complaint, that the research swamps the story and the reader wanting deep psychological characterisation is in the wrong book. That is the log's heaviest objection stated plainly - page time on what characters want and why beats page time on what they do - and it is joined here by the density penalty, a plot embedded in a hundred pages of hardware detail, which is what cost The Lord of the Rings 84 its difference over The Hobbit and what the reader named against The Martian 82. Two things I checked and neither fires: the reader's satisfaction is a hunt for an object rather than finding out who did it, so this is not a detective novel, though the intelligence-gathering is investigation-shaped and worth flagging; and the opening is reported as strong rather than confusing, so the several-plot-lines-at-once filter that sank three books at 30 does not apply even though the narrative cuts between Washington, London, Baghdad and the desert. Occult status is unexamined at this exit by design.

t: Bud jako reka (Go as a River)
why: Form and genre settled at one source: a historical novel, autumn 1948, one point of view, opening on a single concrete situation - a seventeen-year-old carrying late peaches into town is stopped by a stranger asking directions. That is the opening shape The Hunger Games 89 rests on, and it is a genuine positive. Where I doubt it is what it leaves behind. The material is atmosphere and endurance: a chance meeting, a tragedy, then a long stretch alone in the mountains while the valley is flooded for a reservoir, and reviewers describe the pacing as meandering and several significant events as touched only lightly. Solo survival as the sustained theme is also the specific thing the reader marked The Martian 82 down for and that companionship beats. No premise is being worked out, so I stopped at the idea question rather than research the graded axes. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

The opening situation is concrete and legible, which is worth saying because that is the one thing that has ended books unfinished in this log: one boy, one night, one errand in a named landscape, and the trouble arrives to him. Past that I cannot name an idea the book leaves behind - it is marketed as a funny story full of romance and mystery, a Czech young-adult fantasy whose interest is the adventure rather than a premise whose consequences get traced. Reception supports the doubt rather than settling it: readers praise the readability and repeatedly call the writing beginnerish and the ending unclosed, and the log punishes exactly that shape, an open or unresolved close costing The Martian 82 and pieces that do not connect costing Unfinished Tales 69. Worldbuilding obligation is a further exposure, since a system named and used is binding and it is what took Harry Potter 51 down alongside its other objection. So I would put axis:ideas under risks, which is the below-the-line gate's own test, and I stopped there on one source. Occult status is unexamined and is a live question: the book turns on Walpurgis Night and three figures met in a wood, which is real-world folklore rather than an invented mechanism.

Form and genre settled at one source: a multi-generational family-saga novel with a dual timeline and several points of view, built on a dead mother's recorded account of a life her children never knew about. A domestic story with no premise to work out is not itself a problem here - Pride and Prejudice 75 and Little Women 79 both clear the line on motives and character alone. What I doubt is whether anything is left behind: migration, class, race and the inheritance of secrets are the book's subject matter rather than a premise whose consequences get worked out, and the engine is a sequence of revelations about the past. That is the reason a competent book most often stalls in the 60s, so I stopped there rather than research further. The non-linear structure across two timelines and several viewpoints also puts the opening under some load, the axis behind the log's four abandoned books. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

Infidelity was checked first, because the catalogue calls her his mistress and the screen bound the needle to the first sentence, and it does not fire at premise level. The relationship begins before he marries, is set aside because Roman law forbids a senator to marry a freedwoman, and resumes after his wife's death; the obstacle the book is constructed on is statute, not adultery. Doubt remains about how the novel handles the married middle years, so this is recorded as a subplot-or-less grading with that doubt stated rather than a clean sheet - a wrong reject is unrecoverable and a wrong grading is not. The detective hint attached to this author does not reach here either: this is a standalone with its own lead, written before and separate from her investigator novels, and nothing about their exclusions depends on or propagates to it. The positive case is genuine and sits on the reader's heaviest axis - two people over forty years, each wanting something specific, with imperial politics seen from close range, and Pride and Prejudice 75 shows romance as the central subject costs nothing when motives are the whole book. What stops it here is that a climb through four reigns is a chronicle, and this log puts well-textured historical novels with no worked-out idea at Exodus 68 and Quo Vadis 66. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist because Caenis is by every account the interesting part. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

There is a real claim on seriousness here. The author called this the most important thing he wrote and said it was written in his own blood, and the subject - an adolescent Czech Jew working out an identity between marxism and zionism while the century closes on him - is one the reader has rewarded highly when a book actually examines what is true rather than merely feeling it. The trouble is that everything sourceable about this book praises the writing and not a proposition: painful and beautiful in Orten's manner, comparable to Peroutka and Hostovsky, an almost ruralist-zionist motif of work on the land. Beautifully written is not an idea, and the reader's literary record punishes precisely that: 58 for a canonical short novel whose idea was real but whose lead was passive, and a DNF at 40 for first-person wartime witness that examined nothing. So axis:ideas is nameable in outline and not trusted to hold, which is the gate, and the file stops at one source. Leaned on it rather than axis:bleakness because the war is background here rather than the subject, and rather than axis:life-phase because a teenage lead is only ever a couple of points. Occult status is unexamined at this exit, and it is a live question: the publisher's own copy mentions a mysterious farm where both Germans and witches figure, and whether anything is enacted on the page is unchecked.

A runner steps sideways out of our world while fleeing danger, finds an Order of travellers, learns the knack and uncovers why her father vanished. The opening is one concrete situation, which is the thing that matters most here, but the book is a discovery plot - learn the power, meet the villain, solve the family secret - and I can name no thought it would leave behind. That doubt is the exit. Worldbuilding is the risk and the readers point at it themselves: an infinity of worlds is a capability declared broadly, one reviewer says things stay under-explained and the book should have been longer, and unexplained declared capability is what put Mortal Engines at 55 as a DNF. The lead is a teenager and the log prices that at a couple of points at most, so it is not doing any work in this number. Occult status unexamined at this exit. One source, within budget.

t: Chasidske povidky z doby holocaustu (Hasidic Tales of the Holocaust)
why: Eighty-nine short self-contained tales gathered from oral testimony and told in the traditional tale form, each a rebbe or a disciple and a reversal. Form and genre settled, and that is what decides it: the suspension for short idea-driven work removes the character and emotion penalties but adds nothing, and there is no single premise to work out across eighty-nine pieces. Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 are the short books that score, and both score because one nameable idea is carried the whole way; Unfinished Tales 69 is what the log gives to a book whose pieces are not logically connected to each other, and that is the shape here. The subject also puts the faith axis under load - the reader wants faith as a thread inside a story rather than as the whole of it, and here the religious response is the whole of it. I doubt what the collection leaves behind, so I stopped at that question. Occult status is unexamined at this exit: the tales include miracles and supernatural intervention, and whether any rite is performed on the page was not checked.

There is a real idea and the readers who liked it name the same one I would: a being that knows nothing of our world comes alive and has to work out what it is for, with a girl showing it the humanity in a stone heart. That is a premise, not just a setting. What holds the number down is the register - 120 illustrated pages published for children, one situation and one journey through Prague legends - which is graded and costs a little, the Ranger's Apprentice 74 and Narnia 67 position of easy reading with not much to think about rather than the picture-book end of the scale. Ideas are the risk and the reason for the gate exit rather than the lean: the idea is announced but one reader reports the ending turns sanctimonious, so whether it is carried through is exactly what I would doubt. Occult status is unexamined here and the ghosts and apparitions of old Prague are what would need checking. One source, within budget.

Exits at the below-the-line gate, and the axes carrying the number are axis:ideas and axis:multi-pov. Form is a novel, genre historical panorama - roughly 800 pages tracking Chinese, British and American families from the First Opium War to the present. The opening deals the reader several strands at once, a Chinese official's secretary and a British merchant among them, with no single starting situation to be invested in, and that is the log's most reliable predictor of a bad outcome: The Colour of Magic 30, Guards! Guards! 30 and The Gunslinger 30 all died on exactly that. Panoramic history is not automatically fatal - The Silmarillion 80 scored well with no single protagonist and no continuous plot - but that book had mythic ideas behind it, whereas here the thing the book leaves behind is historical information about how the West humiliated the Qing, which is education rather than a premise worked out, so axis:ideas belongs in risks and that is the exit condition. Reviewers also report organisational problems and a contrived recurring character. The reader's own historical-novel results cluster right at this line: Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68. The positive case is genuine, and it is the axis that earned Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 - the book gives the Chinese side its own viewpoint rather than the foreign one only. Length itself is not counted against it; the concern is thin story per page. Occult status unexamined at this exit, as the ladder permits.

A Norse-legend adventure a century after Siegfried: the gods are talked into bending time, the young prince and his betrothed wake in a black century under an immortal tyrant, and they have to unwind it. The lean is self-consistency, because time being rewound by divine favour is a capability declared loudly, and the log is unforgiving where a declared capability is not carried through - the one concrete complaint on record here is precisely that, a sword turning into Excalibur on a timeline that does not add up, which is the Divergent 58 shape. Ideas are the second doubt and the reason for the gate exit: readers describe an overcooked finale counted down page by page rather than anything left behind. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log - the Hitchhiker's fall from 83 to 70 is the steepest decline recorded. Occult status is unexamined at this exit, and the gods intervening directly is exactly what would need checking, given the Greek pantheon is what put Percy Jackson at 57. One source, within budget.

Checked the detective gate first because the catalogue flagged it, and it does not fire: reviewers describe the book as detective-shaped in manner only, and the satisfaction on offer is recovering what happened to a girl and her Jewish friend under the occupation, not identifying a culprit. That is a flag rather than a veto. The positive case is genuine - two time layers braided together, a lead reviewers call believable and dryly funny, and a subject worth having. But the number is carried by how juvenile the telling is and by how much of the idea is borrowed rather than made: a hundred and twelve illustrated pages that introduce the Holocaust to children, where the reader's objection to Narnia 67 was precisely children as leads plus nothing higher to think about, and where first-person testimony about the same period produced the log's joint-lowest score at 40. A reviewer's complaint that the girl uncovers every detail of the past quickly and easily is the unearned-competence cost on top. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source; occult status is unexamined.

The infidelity axis was examined despite no screen hit on the task line, and it does not veto: the lead marries the diplomat only after the man she loved is killed in a plane crash, so the marriage is one of convenience entered in grief, not an affair, and no adultery is the engine of the plot. The espionage plot that follows sends her back to Poland to find a traitor. I could not establish how the marriage resolves, and a novel with this title and a lost love kept alive in it can turn that way, so the axis sits in risks rather than in the number. On form and genre the exit is clear: a commercial wartime historical novel with one point of view opening on a single concrete situation, a survivor at liberation, which is a genuine positive - but I cannot name what it leaves behind beyond the setting, and that is the axis that stalls competent books in the 60s. Exodus 68 is the log's anchor for the historical novel that is carried by its subject rather than by an idea, and Quo Vadis 66 sits just under it. Leaned on the idea question, which is what the exit turned on.

The detective question was asked first and answered no: this is a dual-timeline family novel in which a wartime secret surfaces, not a novel whose satisfaction is identifying a culprit, so the filter does not fire and the buried-crime strand is a flag rather than a veto. It then exits at the below-the-line gate on axis:ideas, which is the axis carrying the number. Form is a novel, genre historical and contemporary women's fiction. I cannot name an idea the book leaves behind - the material is family secrets, a house to be restored and a wartime romance, and reviewers report a slow start with unattractive characters, a one-dimensional boyfriend subplot and a rushed, anticlimactic ending - so axis:ideas belongs in risks, which is the exit condition. That is the pattern the log records for competent books with nothing to think about: Ranger's Apprentice 74 with its stronger momentum, and lower here because the reader also flags drawn-out and unsatisfying endings, which cost The Martian 82 points it had earned. The positive case is a concrete opening situation - one woman, one letter, one house - which is the shape this reader wants, and Rebecca's practical restoration work gives her something she actively wants. Occult status is unexamined at this exit, as the ladder permits.

t: Holky z Detroitu (A Matter of Happiness)
why: Exited at the below-the-line gate. Form and genre are settled - a dual-timeline commercial historical novel, 2018 Kentucky against 1920s Detroit, joined by a journal found in an inherited car - and the question it puts is whether a woman must trade her freedom to marry. That is a theme the book restates in two eras rather than an idea it works out, and restating a contrast across timelines is what the genre does; I would list axis:ideas in risks, so the gate fires. Pride and Prejudice 75 shows that romance as the central subject costs nothing here when what characters want and why is the whole book, so the ceiling is not the subject matter - it is that the journal frame keeps the reader at one remove from the earlier woman's motives, and page time on what she does in speakeasies is not page time on what she wants. axis:multi-pov is the risk rather than the lean: two timelines opened together is the fanning-out shape this reader has abandoned books over, though a journal handoff is a legible way to do it. On the infidelity axis, examined because it is mandatory: the modern lead has a broken engagement behind her and the historical lead's question is whether to marry at all, so no marriage or engagement is betrayed. Occult status is unexamined, which the early exit accepts.

t: Hrichy rodu Borgiu (Sins of the House of Borgia (originally The Book of Love))
why: Both hard-filter questions were examined and neither fires, then the book exits at the below-the-line gate on axis:ideas and axis:sexual-content, which are the axes carrying the number. On infidelity: the central attachment is an unmarried lady-in-waiting's obsession with Cesare Borgia, so the reader's marriage-or-engagement scope is not clearly engaged - his own political marriage is offstage and unwritten - and the affairs of a fellow lady-in-waiting with two brothers of Lucrezia's husband are one thread of court colour rather than the plot; that is a subplot grading with the doubt stated, not a reject, because a wrong reject is unrecoverable.
