On sex as the plot: the book is a court chronicle of Ferrara and Lucrezia's household, so removing the romance leaves a book, and the veto does not fire. What is left is graded and costs. Reviewers report crude sex scenes, and crudeness is the one dimension the log anchors cleanly - Ready Player One 55 was sunk by the kind of sexual content rather than the amount, and Artemis 69 was docked for exactly this at small volume. Form is a novel, genre historical fiction; the idea I can name is a converted Jewish girl watching Christian power from inside it, but reviewers describe a slick soap opera that drags in the middle with a narrator they found frustrating and acted-upon, so axis:ideas goes in risks, which is the exit condition - the Oliver Twist 57 shape, a lead who is moved rather than wanting. Occult status is unexamined at this exit, as the ladder permits.

This is a bound-up run of ten short comics episodes first printed in a children's magazine, about a father-and-son climbing pair who meet weather, prehistoric creatures and family history in a few pages each. Craft is not the question - it took a Muriel for best children's comic - but there is no idea I can name, and there is no room for one: each episode restarts, so nothing accumulates and no premise gets its consequences worked out, which is the axis that carries Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 and is exactly what is absent here. The episodic comics form also suspends the character tests rather than passing them, and the suspension removes penalties without adding points. That combination - no nameable idea plus a form that cannot earn on character - is the lower of the two below-the-line bands. Register is squarely juvenile, which the log costs at Narnia 67 and more steeply as a book moves toward picture-book territory. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source; occult status is unexamined.

Exited at the below-the-line gate: literary fiction and a collection of short pieces at once, which is the mandated stop. The pieces are routines written for magazines over several years, not a book with one premise, so there is no single idea to name and the short form suspends the character rules without putting anything in their place - the suspension removes penalties, it never adds points, and Animal Farm 78 earns its place by having an idea, not by being short. Kirkus's verdict that the parts are better than the whole is the same finding. The heavier reason for the low band is the reader's most reliable negative predictor: he ended The Gunslinger, The Colour of Magic and Foundryside in their first pages at 30 apiece for openings where a lot happens and none of it is yet legible, and hallucinatory discontinuity is the declared method here rather than an accident of the first chapter. Occult status is unexamined, as the early exit permits.

There is a real subject here - four generations of Philippine history under the Spanish, the Americans and Filipinos themselves, and what the country's educated class is actually for - and the book does open on one concrete situation: a body pulled from the Hudson and a student setting out for Manila. That is why this is not scored at the floor. What sinks it is how the telling arrives. From the start the reader is tracking the narrator's story, his unfinished biography of the dead man, excerpts of that man's poems, novels, interviews and memoirs, a critic's blog, a running series of jokes, and meta-narrative commenting on the narrator, in both first and third person, with a fictional apparatus presented as real. Reviewers consistently report it as exasperating to enter and ask the reader to trust that the pieces will cohere. That is the reader's most reliable predictor and it has three separate 30s behind it - the diagnosis the reader himself settled on was 'lots happening, none of it meant anything yet', and an incident-rich opening is no defence against it. Unfinished Tales 69 is the mild end of the same complaint, pieces not logically connected to each other, and it is the lowest Tolkien by a clear margin. Leaned on the opening rather than on ideas because the ideas are only reached by a reader who gets past the structure, and this reader has twice not.

t: In the lives of puppets (In the Lives of Puppets)
why: The positive case is that this is a premise with a question in it and the ending actually answers it: the boy raised by machines saves his inventor father by wiping the memories of the machines who love him, doing to them what was done to humanity, so the title's question of who the puppet is gets turned back on the protagonist. That is an idea left behind rather than a theme announced, which is the axis Animal Farm 78 and Labyrint sveta 70 both score on. The telling is also motive-heavy: the page time goes on what Victor and Hap each want from the other and what they are willing to accept, and that is what tops the log at Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90. Two filters cleared on sources: the opening is one concrete situation in a single point of view, Victor twenty feet up a scrap heap on a home-made pulley salvaging a circuit board, which is the opposite of the confusion that sank three books at 30; and the powers are machines, with no rite and no invocation anywhere. Now the deductions. The nurse robot's running joke is bodily and sexual - explicit exchanges about genitalia, whether androids have them, and whether the protagonist is aroused - and that is the crudeness dimension at low volume and low explicitness, which is exactly the Artemis 69 docking and the kind rather than the amount that took Ready Player One to 55. The world is also the weaker half: reviewers read it as assembled from other robot books, and a post-human society whose Authority and history are asserted rather than worked out will not hold up under the scrutiny that Valka stareho muze 87 passed and Divergent 58 failed. I leaned on the idea and the motives rather than on the worldbuilding, because the log's clearest lesson is never to predict up on a world when the human material is what is carrying the book.

Roman military adventure done with confident period detail, and the opening situation is exactly the shape the reader wants: one man, one legible task, escort a deposed king to a town and put him back on his throne. Reviewers credit seamless co-writing, solid research and well-drawn military detail. Beyond that it is battles. The five-part serial origin shows in the pacing, the army-life material is reported as thinner than in the authors' main sequence, and the appeal reviewers name is the crescendo of action towards the end. Ranger's Apprentice 74 is the ceiling in this log for easy, well-made adventure with not much to think about, and that book had fourteen volumes of character to lean on where this has one campaign; so axis:ideas is the doubt that closes the file at one source. Leaned on it rather than axis:momentum because the pacing seam is a minor complaint and the missing idea is not. One live hazard sits above the range rather than inside it: a druidic sect drives the second half, druids are real historical pagan priests, and whether any rite is enacted on the page is unexamined at this exit - if it is, the number goes well below this band.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. There is a real premise - a boy on a colony ship learning to cook, meaning to gene-engineer, living creatures, and wanting to build a dragon - and one reviewer says the small details are planted and pay off, which is genuine credit on the axis that Golden Son 92 scores on. But it is a short illustrated adventure for children and the appeal reported by readers is excitement, friendship and pictures, not something to think about afterwards; that puts axis:ideas in the doubts and is what the below-the-line gate asks. Register sits below The Hobbit 84 and nearer Narnia 67, which the reader marked down precisely for lacking higher things to think about. Occult status is unexamined, as the early exit permits.

Exited at the below-the-line gate, on the lower band, and the form is what decides it. This is a forty-page illustrated picture book for preschool and first-year children, written as a practical aid for telling a child that someone has died and usable as a methodical handbook in kindergartens - the profile puts a picture book in the thirties or forties outright. There is no idea I can name in the sense that earns here: the animal allegory carries a purpose, not a thought, and the recorded complaint from readers is exactly that it states the fact of death without answering the child's why, where he went or what death is. The Little Prince 82 shows a short allegory can score high, but it scores on the thoughts it leaves behind, and that is what is missing; the suspension of the character rules that comes with this form removes penalties without adding anything. Bleakness is the risk that could take it lower - readers report stalling with children at the picture of the dead brother lying on the rock. Occult status is unexamined, which the early exit accepts.

t: Kdo odejde, uz se nevraci (All Who Go Do Not Return)
why: This is the closest thing in the log to Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91, and for the same reasons: honest first-person, a closed religious world made legible from inside, and above all a man testing what he was raised to believe against what he can actually credit - the rigour the reader singled out as the thing that earns high tiers. The idea is nameable in a phrase: what it costs to find out whether the thing you were forbidden to question is true. The opening is a single concrete situation with one point of view - a boy of thirteen taken to a village he did not want to visit - so the failure that ended four books in their first chapters is not in play. Held below Qureshi 91 because the movement here is out of belief rather than toward a settled position, so what the book arrives at is loss, exile and a custody fight rather than a resolved case, and because the reader wants faith as a thread inside a story rather than as its whole subject; that is the risk, not the lean. Son of Hamas 75 sets the floor for the same form with less self-examination in it. Leaned on the memoir form and the idea rather than the protagonist, since the narrator's interest is entirely in what he is working out.

Exits at the below-the-line gate on axis:ideas and axis:density, which are the axes carrying the number. Form is a novel of about 520 pages, genre historical romance set on Cyprus around the 1974 Turkish invasion, with a present-day frame in which a young woman wants the truth about her soldier father. The infidelity axis was examined because it is mandatory: the central relationship is between an unmarried sixteen-year-old emigre and a British soldier, so the marriage-or-engagement scope is not engaged by anything I can source, and the frame narrative's withheld paternity is not evidence of an affair inside a marriage - graded as not applicable rather than rejected, with the doubt stated. The reason for the exit is that the idea does not hold: a Czech reviewer reports substantial padding, repeated situations and weak dialogue, and complains of learning almost nothing about the period or the place while being given the heroine's entire wardrobe. That is the reader's density objection exactly - a thin story spread over many pages, which cost The Lord of the Rings 84 the ground its ideas had won - and it puts axis:ideas in risks, the exit condition. Positive case: the exchanged letters give page time to what the two want and why, which is the axis the log rates highest, and readers do credit the book with reflections on war, totalitarianism and freedom. Occult status unexamined at this exit, as the ladder permits.

Detective was the first question and it does not fire. This is reportage, not a whodunnit: the killing and the conviction of the ex-wife who ordered it are public record, the author covered the five-month trial from the courtroom, and readers report that the murder occupies roughly the opening and closing chapters while the body of the book is boardroom fights, family lawsuits and an investment bank's eighteen-month buyout. The satisfaction on offer is not finding out who did it. What is on offer is three generations wrecking what they built, with real access behind it - and that is events, not an idea. The reader's non-fiction record is unambiguous about which half earns: Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 scores because it examines what is actually true and shows how another group experiences the world, while The Diary of a Young Girl 40 shows the form itself earns nothing at all. Corporate history of a fashion dynasty offers neither, and there is nobody in it to root for. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:density because what the book is for, not its length, sets the number. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

Exits at the below-the-line gate on axis:faith and axis:ideas, which are the axes carrying the number. Form is a mosaic of autobiographical stories rather than a novel with one plot line, genre reflective testimony. Two things put it under the line. First, the reader's stated position is that faith works as a thread inside a story but not as the subject in its own right, and a Databaze knih reviewer reports the book is strongly organised around the author's newly found belief in God and is markedly esoteric and spiritual throughout - that is the whole subject, not a thread. Second, a collection assembled from whoever the author happened to meet has no single premise to work out, so there is nothing for axis:ideas to lean on; the short-idea-driven suspension removes penalties but never adds points, and the log's short books that scored - Animal Farm 78, The Little Prince 82, Labyrint sveta a raj srdce 70 - are all carried by one nameable idea, which this is not. So axis:ideas belongs in risks, which is the exit condition. Positive case is real: a warm Czech storytelling voice, and Saturnin 78 shows voice and character alone can reach the A band here. Occult status is unexamined at this exit, as the ladder permits, and the esoteric register is the specific thing to check if it is ever reopened.

t: Kniha ztracenych jmen (The Book of Lost Names)
why: First the inherited-exclusion question, because the task flagged an already-excluded book by this author. It does not carry: that book is a separate standalone with different characters, a different setting and no shared plot, this novel introduces its own lead and its own premise from scratch, and there is nothing here to depend on - the exclusion propagates only through dependency, never through an author or a shelf. On its own infidelity axis, examined independently, both people in the central relationship are unmarried and no marriage or engagement is betrayed, so nothing fires. That leaves the below-the-line gate. Form and genre are settled - a dual-timeline WWII novel - and the idea is more nearly present here than the genre usually manages: forged papers erase children's real names, so someone has to keep a record of who they were, and identity kept against erasure is a thing to think about rather than only a thing to feel. The lead is also active and worth rooting for, risking herself for others, which is the combination the profile puts above worldbuilding. What keeps it under the line is that the record is used as a plot object and a frame for a love story rather than pressed for what it means; Exodus 68 and Quo Vadis 66 mark where a solid historical novel settles when the thinking is not the point, so I would still list axis:ideas in risks and the gate fires. axis:multi-pov is the risk, not the lean: a present-day frame opened before the wartime story is a mild version of the fanning-out shape, mild because the frame hands over quickly. Occult status is unexamined, which the early exit accepts.

The premise is a real one - Alexander does not die in Babylon in 323 BC and turns his Indian war elephants on Carthage - and it is carried by an outsider, an elephant handler raised into the Macedonian command, watching power corrupt the man who raised him. That is a motive-shaped spine, the axis that tops the log in Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90. But I doubt the idea is actually worked out: the book is sold and reviewed as a fast battle adventure, the alternate history is a setting rather than a consequence traced, and the second lead is a captured general's daughter whose thread is romance rather than argument. Set-piece action without character revelation is dead weight for this reader - it is what docked Golden Son 92 below Red Rising 95 and what sank the second arena in Catching Fire 83. Historical fiction that entertains without leaving an idea behind sits at Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68, and that is the band I expect. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source; I would list axis:ideas under risks, which is the gate's own test, so I did not research the graded axes. Occult status is therefore unexamined here.

This book asks the reader to spend four occupied years inside a woman whose entire project is keeping her money, and who collaborates with the Reich and then spies for it to do so. The reader's clearest recorded verdict on that shape is 65 for a book by an author he otherwise tops the log with, on the single ground of a lead descending into evil with nobody to root for - and reviewers here say Ewen walks a fine line between humanising Chanel and empathising with her, while another credits her with not sugarcoating the actions or the personality. Interesting is not the problem; rootable is, and those are two separate failure modes in this log. Leaned on axis:protagonist rather than the period detail because the strongest single case in the log is that a lead the reader cannot back outranks everything well built around them. What the book leaves behind beyond a portrait is the further doubt, hence one source and a stop. Infidelity was examined and does not fire: the lead is unmarried and the engine is the fight for control of the perfume company plus the collaboration, not an affair. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

The opening is the reader's single most reliable predictor and here it is clean rather than a hazard: 1593, one viewpoint, an Edinburgh goldsmith with a pregnant wife summoned again and again to a teenage queen who loves jewels. One concrete situation, nothing fanning out, and an outsider lead who is both interesting and easy to back - reviewers specifically praise the choice to tell the union of the crowns through the money man instead of through the king, Shakespeare and Jonson. Against that, at just over 200 pages one reviewer reports it reading as a set of fictionalised episodes rather than a continuous novel, and what the book is for is atmosphere and court intrigue rather than a proposition worked out; the praise it draws is for economy, sensory detail and viewpoint. That is the doubt about axis:ideas the gate asks for, and Exodus 68 and Quo Vadis 66 mark where well-textured historical fiction without one settles in this log. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:opening precisely because the opening is a positive here and cannot be what holds the number down. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. A near-future surveillance dystopia with a walled rich quarter, drones, implants and a mafia underworld, and a parent who takes an untested offer to let a dying child continue in a virtual world. The premise is nameable, but the reader's bar is that a declared premise has its consequences worked out - that is what separates Project Hail Mary 92 and Old Man's War 87 from Divergent 58, where the engineered society did not cohere - and this is a debut from an author-services press with no critical reception at all to indicate the second-order questions get answered. So axis:ideas belongs in the doubts, which is the gate's own test. The dystopian setting itself costs nothing; the reader said as much about Divergent. Occult status is unexamined, as the early exit permits.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. Nine unconnected stories with no single premise, so there is no idea to name that the book as a whole leaves behind - and the short form suspends the character rules without adding anything, which is why Animal Farm 78 earns its score on its idea rather than on its length. Unfinished Tales 69 is the closest thing in the log to this shape and it is the reader's lowest Tolkien precisely because the pieces are not connected to each other. Genre readers rate this below the same author's better-regarded books and no critical reception exists. The murderous angels in the blurb are a comic conceit rather than an investigation, so the detective filter does not fire. Occult status is unexamined, as the early exit permits, and would be worth checking if the axis is ever bumped - vampires and angels appear in the descriptions.

t: Legenda o Brokenu (The Legend of Broken)
why: There is a real idea here and it is nameable - a fortress society dooms itself through the corruption of its merchant and priestly classes while a banished philosopher beats it with what amounts to science - and the worldbuilding is worked, thirty years of it, down to an invented language. That is the sort of thing that earns points, and it is why this got full research rather than an early exit. The number is nevertheless low, and it is density and the opening that carry it. The main text runs past 650 pages with 80 more of notes that several readers report are effectively mandatory in the early chapters to know who and what anything is, the prose is a deliberate pseudo-archaic translation, and the narrative alternates between two peoples from the start. This reader's most reliable failure is exactly that - not slowness, which is forgiven, but arriving in a world whose context is withheld while material piles up, the diagnosis that produced three separate scores of 30. Reviewers also report the pace stays slow past the opening and that the confrontation the whole book is built toward deflates into everyone sitting down and agreeing, which is the drawn-out ending that cost The Martian its position at 82. I leaned on those two rather than on the ideas because the log shows an idea cannot rescue a book that is not got through. Occult is a live risk not resolved: the sorcery is reported to have natural explanations, but both peoples have priesthoods and one character practises moon-worship and healing, and devotions to an invented deity performed on the page now cost a graded deduction rather than a veto. The plague investigation is an investigation-shaped thread, flagged rather than treated as the book's satisfaction.

No inheritance applies: the already-excluded book by this author is a separate standalone novel with its own cast, nothing here continues it, and the exclusion there was a detective heading rather than anything this book depends on - so I judged this volume on its own. Both content gates were examined and neither fires. The love the annotation names is between two unattached people meeting late in life; there is no marriage or engagement in evidence being betrayed, so the infidelity axis does not reach premise level, and I am recording that as a non-hit rather than an unrecoverable reject. Nor is the plot sexual: the erotic thread is one strand beside a camp past, a death, Jerusalem politics and a divination motif. The positive case is that the material is real and hard-won - a Czech-Israeli writer's late book on farewell, on the past dissolving into the present in one city. What I doubt is that it resolves into an idea worked out rather than a mosaic of motifs recapitulating a life, and the critical account of this author's prose supports the doubt: a sensitive, meditative narrator taking stock, not a premise whose consequences are traced. That is the shape the log settles in the high sixties - Labyrint sveta a raj srdce 70 earned its place on one nameable idea, while pieces that do not connect to each other cost Unfinished Tales 69. Add a mild bleakness discount for death and farewell as the register and a small life-phase pushback for leads far past the reader's age. Exited at the below-the-line gate; occult status is unexamined, and the publisher's own copy naming a divination secret makes that a live question rather than a formality.

The catalogue flagged this as possibly a detective book and it is not: reviewers state plainly that the identity of the hunted woman is known and the book is not built as a whodunnit, so the satisfaction is a pursuit and a reckoning, not an investigation. That clears the cheap gate but leaves the below-the-line one. Form and genre are settled - a post-war manhunt novel - and the strongest thing in it is one lead, a Siberian night bomber pilot with a wholly distinctive way of wanting things, which is the character-differentiation earner that Golden Son 92 was praised for. Against that, what the book leaves behind is a situation rather than an idea: that Nazi hunters were left to private individuals once the world's attention moved to communism is interesting history, not a thought the novel works out, so I would list axis:ideas in risks and the gate fires. The larger danger is structural. Three points of view are started at different moments in different countries and different years and reviewers note how long they take to converge; several plot lines beginning at once before any is legible is the most reliable predictor of failure in this log, the cause of Guards! Guards! 30. That is the risk that could take it under the range, not the thing setting it. Two sources were spent against a budget of one at this exit, because clearing the flagged detective question came first. Occult status is unexamined, which the early exit accepts.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. A short post-apocalyptic novella with one clear starting situation - Karel wakes in a fallout shelter under Prague and every person and animal is gone - so the opening is not the risk. The idea is the problem: readers report the philosophical passages read as duty rather than as consequence, and that the short form kept the premise from being developed or closed. That is the failure the reader punishes hardest, since Project Hail Mary 92 and Old Man's War 87 both score on consequences actually being worked out, and it puts axis:ideas squarely in the doubts. Sustained emptiness and solitude is also the objection that held The Martian to 82 against Project Hail Mary's 92. Occult status is unexamined, as the early exit permits.

A painted comic told by an old man looking back on being born in an alien zoo to a human mother and a godlike ball of light, then surviving a war across the galaxy. There is a theme - a search for enlightenment, and a religious authority who took power by owning the economy - but a theme is not the same as a premise whose consequences get worked out, and reviewers themselves say there is no antagonist to speak of and that the narrator is deliberately unreliable and romantic. That is the case where I would list axis:ideas under risks, and the rules say exit when I would. Sexual content is the leading risk on the number rather than the lean: the recurring companion is written as lecherous and readers list sex and debauchery among the registers the book runs through, and crudeness at small volume is what docked Artemis to 69 without any other objection needing to fire. Density is the second risk - an episodic picaresque with no single line to follow is the sparseness that cost Unfinished Tales its 69. Sex is plainly not what the plot is for, so no filter fires there. Occult status unexamined at this exit. One source, within budget.

The positive is concrete and better than the packaging suggests: a man comes home from the war on a wooden leg in 1864 wanting to build steel-framed apartment houses uptown, and the book follows that want through Tweed-era corruption, tenement money and Wall Street. Page time on what a character wants is the reader's heaviest axis and there is a real want at the centre here. What there is not is anything to think about afterwards. Trade reviews call it competent enough with flat dialogue and contrived scenes, note that the pace often lags across the sprawl, and the warmest of them sells it as a page-turning guilty pleasure plus a history lesson. Exodus 68 and Quo Vadis 66 are where historical novels with real texture and no worked-out idea land in this log, and that doubt about axis:ideas is what closes the file at one source. Leaned on it rather than axis:density because length has never been the objection on its own - what costs is a thin story spread wide, and the sprawl only compounds a book that was not going to leave an idea anyway. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

One idea is declared and carried the whole way: a story survives because each generation copies it out again. That is the axis Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 score on, and it is genuinely worked out here, not decoration. Against it sits the reader's most reliable negative predictor, and this book walks straight into it. The prologue opens inside a sealed vault on a generation ship in mission year 65 with a girl and an AI; then a fake ancient text arrives with its own dedication to an ailing niece; then chapter one alternates an octogenarian Greek translator rehearsing children in a library with a boy carrying a bomb into it. Six characters over five timelines in non-chronological order, with the connective context withheld by design. That is the Foundryside 30 failure exactly - plenty happening, none of it meaning anything yet - and the reader settled that diagnosis himself: an action opening is no defence against missing context. Leaned on axis:opening rather than axis:ideas because the log shows the opening decides whether the ideas are ever reached; four books scored 30 on it and none got far enough for their premises to matter. Density at over 600 pages and the bleakness of the bomber thread are further costs but neither is doing the work here. The range is wide because the outcome is bimodal: an abandonment near 40, or a book he finishes and rates on its idea.

The infidelity screen flagged the word for lovers in the title, but the axis is marriage or engagement only and the relationship here is between two unmarried students, which is ordinary relationship material and does not touch it; no marriage appears anywhere in what I found, so no filter fires and the axis grades at nothing. Exited instead at the below-the-line gate on one source. The premise is a political one - a Directive on religious correctness has made Islam part of Europe, and a Czech doctor falls for a devout Muslim student - and a premise of that kind is binding: the reader marks a book down when a society taken as its subject does not cohere, which is most of why Divergent sits at 58. There is no critical reception at all on a book by a retired regulator writing outside his usual line, so I would put axis:ideas in the doubts rather than bet the argument holds together. Faith as the subject rather than as a thread inside a story is the second discount. Occult status is unexamined, as the early exit permits.

An illustrated adventure written for eight-to-ten-year-olds and deliberately typeset to be easy for dyslexic readers: twins get a cat with a medallion and travel through fantasy landscapes. The register is what carries the number, and this axis is graded rather than a veto - but it is graded by how far toward a children's book the thing actually sits, and this one is squarely inside that audience rather than adjacent to it, which is the end of the scale where a picture book lands in the forties, not the end where The Hobbit pays 84 and Little Women 79 clear the line on characters. There is no idea I can name that would be left behind - the stated purpose is to awaken imagination and a love of reading - and the form suspends the character tests without adding anything in their place, which is what puts this in the lower of the two bands rather than the default. Occult status unexamined at this exit. One source, within budget.

There is a genuine idea here and it is why the number is not lower: descendants of an advanced human civilisation come back to a sixteenth century of slave-hunting and Catholic-Protestant hatred, and the book argues for human greatness reached without weapons. On ideas alone this could have sat with Animal Farm 78. What sinks it is the opening, and this is the most reliable predictor in the whole log. Readers independently describe the start as extremely sprawling and overcrowded, with many elements that do not mean anything yet, several time planes cut against each other, and so many protagonists that they are numbered - and they report losing track of them and abandoning the book. That is exactly the diagnosis the reader settled on for the three books he stopped in the first chapters at 30 apiece: lots happening, none of it meaning anything yet. I leaned on the opening rather than on the ideas because the ideas cannot be reached from behind it, which is the whole lesson of those failures. Two novels bound as one volume also invites the thin-story-over-many-pages penalty that cost The Lord of the Rings 84. Occult status is left unexamined at this range: the second novel's title refers to wizards, and at an estimate this far under the line the distinction would change no decision. STAMPED 2026-09-02 with the new axis:sex-portrayal: this is the only row on the shelf whose recorded reasoning already carries evidence for it. The range does not move - it is far under the line already on the opening, so the axis changes no decision here.

t: Na prvni pohled (You Had Me at Hello)
why: The infidelity axis was examined and it does not veto. The lead's own engagement ends early and of her own doing, and the man she reconnects with is married - but reviewers who specifically avoid books with married leads report that the thread never becomes an affair, so infidelity is the obstacle rather than the premise: remove the marriage and there is still a reunited-friends novel. It is not clean either. Much of the book is a woman waiting for a married man's marriage to fail, there are two further adultery threads, and nothing in what I found suggests the treatment condemns any of it - prominence I could establish, framing I could not, so this belongs in risks rather than in the number. On the exit itself: Pride and Prejudice 75 shows that romance as the central subject costs nothing when what characters want and why is the entire book, but there the wanting is examined and here I cannot name anything the book leaves behind. That is the axis that most often stalls a competent book in the 60s, so I stopped.

The memoir form earns nothing by itself in this log - the same shelf holds Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and The Diary of a Young Girl 40 - so the number rests on what this particular account delivers, and it delivers the thing the log rewards: insight into how a group nobody can interview experiences the world. A conscious mind sat inside a body treated as empty for years and heard what people say in front of someone they believe is not there; that is an idea, statable in a phrase, and it is why axis:memoir-form and axis:ideas carry the number rather than the prose, which several reviewers call ordinary and which is a real ceiling on the range. It also sits on the right side of the reader's companionship rule: the arc ends in being recognised, communicating, marrying and working, so it is not the sustained solitude that cost The Martian 82 its ground against Project Hail Mary 92. Deductions: the middle of the book is institutional confinement plus physical and sexual abuse by carers, and bleakness is a real if mild discount here - 1984 60 was disliked for being depressing - which is why bleakness and content sit in risks rather than in the lean. The subject is twelve to twenty-three across the confinement, so a child's inner life occupies a good part of it, which is the small life-phase pushback and part of what sank the one memoir in the log that failed. Anchored between Son of Hamas 75 and Seeking Allah 91: stronger material than the former, without the analytical rigour that earned the latter. Occult does not arise. Opening structure is not sourced, so this is medium, not high.

The premise is nameable - a miracle-worker turns up in the worst part of a city and the woman who shelters him has to work out what he is - and it opens on one concrete situation, a drug-dependent woman needing a fix and dodging the pimp she ran from, which is the single-situation start this reader needs. But the retailer material describes the payoff as a dark world of strange people, blood, madness and magic plus a powerful secret society taking an interest, which is a genre machine rather than a premise worked out, and there is not one review anywhere to say the idea is carried through. That doubt about axis:ideas is what sends it out here. Protagonist is a risk on the rooting half rather than the interest half: an addict who is chiefly pushed by need and pursued by others is the Oliver Twist 57 pattern of a lead acted upon. The messiah figure is the second risk, since the log prices this axis on reverence and a careless resonance costs. Sexual content was examined and is not the plot - her work is background to the boy's story. Occult status is unexamined at this exit and the miracles are what would need checking. One source, within budget.

The positive case is the lead. Addison is told in one first-person voice from one concrete starting situation - a man who cannot be looked at, living under the city - and he is both interesting and easy to root for, which is the axis that separates Sunrise on the Reaping 87 from The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 and that Oliver Twist 57 failed on. There is a nameable idea rather than only events: the monster is the innocent and ordinary people carry the corruption, an inversion the book actually commits to, which is what keeps Animal Farm 78 above the competent-but-empty band. Sexual content is close to absent - the central relationship is deliberately untouchable - so nothing of what cost Ready Player One 55 applies. Against that: reviewers describe the scenes as loosely connected and dreamlike over a long book, which is the thin-story-over-many-pages penalty that pulled The Lord of the Rings 84 down to the level of The Hobbit; and the resolution turns the novel into an apocalyptic religious statement, which is faith as the subject rather than as a thread inside a story. I leaned on the protagonist and the idea rather than on worldbuilding because the supernatural machinery is deliberately never explained, so it declares little and owes little - it cannot carry the number either way.

The premise is at least declared precisely: girls whose magic can only be given away, never used on themselves, sold by the night to paying clients of the great houses and married off when the season ends. That is a system with an obligation attached, and reviewers do credit the city and the elemental rules as the strongest thing here. But the idea the book actually leaves behind is a patriarchy critique delivered as theme rather than worked out as consequence - the reviews that praise it praise the atmosphere and the world, and the sharpest one says the storylines stay conventional under the feminist framing - so I would put axis:ideas under risks, which is the below-the-line gate's own test. Two further costs point the same way: three leads share the book, and several plot lines live at once is the most reliable negative predictor in this log, at 30 for three separate books; and reviewers report the pace as gentle for much of the length, which is the thin-story-over-many-pages penalty that cost The Lord of the Rings 84 its difference over The Hobbit. Exited on one source; occult status is unexamined and is a real question, since the church in the book hunts these girls as heretics and the transfer is enacted by a kiss.

Identified and the form settled at one source: a nineteenth-century adventure of conspiracy, escape and patient justice, and the Czech holding is a modern retelling for young readers rather than a translation of the text. The Count of Monte Cristo 75 is the direct anchor and it is instructive both ways - it earned its 75 because plot momentum held up across a very long book, and length was explicitly not the objection. A retelling keeps the plot skeleton and removes the pages that generated the momentum, and it lowers the register toward a children's book, which the log prices at a few points. Beyond justice pursued patiently over fifteen years I cannot name an idea it leaves behind, and Ranger's Apprentice 74 is what easy, well-paced adventure with little to think about earns; a condensation of one earns less. I stopped at that question.

The positive case is genuine and it is why this did not exit at the cheap gate: there is a nameable idea, a parable about whether social change is possible at all and what hope and belief are worth, and this reader does reward an idea-carrying allegory - Labyrint sveta a raj srdce 70 landed exactly there and Animal Farm 78 above it. What pulls it under those is the shape. It is a short quasi-historical parable hung on the factual record of a seventeenth-century messianic movement and a false prophet, so faith is not a thread inside a story here, it is the subject, and the profile is explicit that faith works as a thread and not as the whole. On top of that the telling is dream-to-surrealist motifs laid over realist narration with no continuous plot or single lead to hold, which is the story-density penalty rather than a length objection: The Silmarillion 80 shows that a plotless dense work can still work, but Unfinished Tales 69 shows what happens when the pieces do not connect, and this is closer to the second. I leaned on density and faith rather than on ideas because the ideas are really there - the problem is the delivery, a philosophical treatise more than a story. Occult was examined and nothing in the available material describes a rite enacted on the page; the material is heresy as historical subject matter, and I could find no critical source analysing that layer, so the range is set with that uncertainty acknowledged rather than resolved.

t: Od seminka v prach (Seed to Dust: A Gardener's Story)
why: Exits at the below-the-line gate on axis:ideas and axis:density, which are the axes carrying the number. Form is nonfiction, a year of small essays following the seasons in one Welsh country garden, with the author's homelessness, marriage and ageing woven through; genre is reflective nature writing. The reader's rule on this form is explicit - the memoir or testimony form earns nothing by itself, and what earns is examining what is actually true plus insight into how another group experiences the world, which is why Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and The Diary of a Young Girl 40 sit at opposite ends of the same shelf. Here I can name a theme, mortality read through a garden's cycle, but Publishers Weekly reports the effect spoiled by unrelenting man-of-the-earth posturing and another reviewer finds the apercus formulaic and some of them squishy, which is a theme rather than an argument, so axis:ideas belongs in risks and that is the exit condition. Compounding it, the book is almost entirely description with no story to carry it, and heavy description with little story is a named deduction - the same objection that cost The Lord of the Rings 84 its distance over The Hobbit. Positive case: a real occupation observed closely by someone who did it for two decades, and prose the Guardian and Booklist both singled out. Occult status unexamined at this exit, as the ladder permits.

A commercial Australian family saga: an inheritance, a hidden truth about a father, a stepmother who hates the heroine, and a fatal love arriving on cue. Form is a full-length novel and the genre is mainstream saga, so the character rules apply rather than being suspended - and there is no idea here I can name that the book would leave behind, which is exactly the axis that keeps competent books in the 60s. Nothing announced in the material suggests a premise being worked out, only a plot being turned. That doubt about axis:ideas is what decides the band and I stopped there; the protagonist is the risk, since an heiress who is chiefly acted upon by other people's schemes is the failure that put Oliver Twist at 57. Occult status was not examined - the gate exit precedes it. Exited at gate 4 on one source, within budget.

t: Panna ve zbroji (Personal Recollections of Joan of Arc)
why: The positive case is a lead who is both interesting and worth rooting for: a peasant girl who wants one thing with total clarity and is destroyed by an institution for wanting it, and a trial section built out of the actual transcripts that is the part every reader singles out. That is the axis Mockingjay 91 scores on - motives and what someone is trying to accomplish, over the fighting itself. The number is held down by the same axis from the other side: the narrator is her page, so she is observed and never inhabited, and Twain writes her as flawless, which is the thin-from-inside problem that put Artemis at 69 even with everything else in place. Density is the second half of the lean - the middle campaign chapters are uneven and slow, and this reader forgives length but not a story stretched thin, which is what cost Les Miserables its position against Monte Cristo 75. The opening is safe: one narrator, one village, one girl, in the Hitchhiker's 83 shape of a single concrete situation. Faith is the risk, because the treatment is openly reverent hagiography and the log wants faith as a thread inside a story rather than as the subject; the prophecy element is played entirely straight, which the rules price at nothing. Her voices are Christian vision, not a rite performed on the page, so this is the faith axis and not the occult one. Placed against Exodus 68 and Quo Vadis 66, which is where earnest historical novels have actually landed.

The best thing here is that the trouble is emotional rather than external: a friendship that is not what it was, a boy displaced by his friend's new friend and by the girl's interest in him, and a run from home that is a want rather than an event. Page time on what a character wants and why is the axis that tops this log at Mockingjay 91, and a children's adventure that spends its first act on it is doing the right thing. Against that I cannot name an idea the book leaves behind - it is a boys' treasure-and-old-letters adventure in an explicitly retro tradition, and the hundred-year-old letters are a plot engine rather than a subject - so axis:ideas belongs in risks and the below-the-line gate fires. The juvenile register costs on top, past the Narnia 67 position, and the book continues a cast and two earlier discoveries rather than restarting, which is the sequel exposure that took Hitchhiker's from 83 to 70. The hunt for the letters' story is investigation-shaped; I read that as a flag, not the detective filter, since the satisfaction is the boys' friendship and the find, not identifying a culprit. Exited on one source; occult status is unexamined.

This is a first-reader title in an edition built for six- and seven-year-olds learning to read: a blackbird chick narrates a run of small episodes from one spring in a garden, a magic rain, a jumping flowerpot, a friendship. There is no idea to name and no room to build one, since the episodes restart and nothing accumulates; the log is explicit that shortness earns nothing by itself and that a short book with thin ideas lands low like any other, the earning being done by a nameable idea as in The Little Prince 82. The beginning-reader form also suspends the character tests rather than passing them, so nothing can be recovered on motives, the axis that tops the log. Both conditions for the lower below-the-line band hold. On the children's axis, which is graded and never a veto, this sits at the far juvenile end, well past the Narnia 67 position. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source; occult status is unexamined, though the magic here reads as ordinary fairy-tale furniture.

This is a fourteen-page interactive board book that teaches preschoolers to count: a bungling wizard turns one dragon head into six and the child is asked to count them. There is no idea to name, because the fairy-tale frame exists to carry a counting exercise rather than to be about anything, and the log is clear that a short book with thin ideas lands low like any other thin book - what earns is the nameable idea in Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82, not the shortness. The picture-book form also suspends the character tests instead of passing them, so nothing can be earned back on the axis that tops the log, page time on what people want. Both conditions for the lower below-the-line band are met. The children's axis is graded rather than a veto, and it is graded by how far toward a children's book the thing sits; this sits at the far end, well past the Narnia 67 position. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source; occult status is unexamined, though the wizard is a fairy-tale device rather than a practice.

Examined the infidelity axis first and did not reject, with the doubt stated: the husband's serial adultery is the wound the book works on and his current mistress persists past the diagnosis and even follows the family abroad, so this is well above incidental - but the spine the plot actually moves along is the wife's ALS and the year she has left, and removing the adultery leaves a book about dying and reconciliation rather than no book at all. So it grades as a heavy subplot, framed as destructive (the husband is written guilt-ridden and the daughter is the collateral), which under the rule costs a few points rather than the range. The separate sexual-content axis was examined on its own and is not the plot. What then decides the number is that I can name no idea the book leaves behind: an illness is used to generate feeling, and reviewers call it none-too-subtle and a three-tissue finale, which is the pattern that keeps a competent novel just under the line. The excluded work by this author named on the task line is an unrelated standalone crime novel in no series with this one and nothing here continues it, so that exclusion does not carry. Overspend acknowledged: two sources at a gate-4 exit against a budget of one, because the infidelity question was the more expensive one and was settled first.

The excluded books by this author are a separate sequence set in Anglo-Saxon England with a different lead and no shared plot; this is Civil War fiction and does not depend on them, so the occult exclusion does not carry - decided on the series listing rather than on the hint. On its own merits it exits at the below-the-line gate. There is a genuine motive thread here, the feud with the brigade commander and a colonel whose faith is a frail weapon against his drinking, and faith as a thread inside a story is something this reader accepts. But I would put axis:ideas in risks: the book is organised around Cedar Mountain and Second Manassas rendered in campaign detail, and page time on what is done outweighs page time on what is wanted, which is the log's heaviest objection - Catching Fire 83 lost points for an arena existing for its own sake. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log (Hitchhiker's 83 down to 70). Historical novels here sit at Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68, so under the line whatever else I find. Occult status is unexamined at this exit by design.

t: Prezil jsem varsavske ghetto (Der Junge im Schrank: Eine Kindheit im Krieg)
why: Form and genre are settled: a short first-person Holocaust testimony, a boy of five to ten hidden with paid strangers and finally in a wardrobe, written down sixty-five years later. Readers describe its strength as its plainness - nothing dramatised, nothing embellished - which is an accurate description of a book that records what happened and does not set out to explain anything. That is where I doubt it: I cannot name an idea it leaves behind, and the log is explicit that the testimony form earns nothing by itself. Anne Frank 40 is the warning at one end, a child's inner life set down without an argument, and Son of Hamas 75 is what the form earns when it explains a world the reader could not otherwise see. This sits nearer the first, with the small further pushback that the narrating consciousness is a child's. Leaned on the idea question because that is what the exit turned on.

t: Pribeh Biafry (The Biafra Story: The Making of an African Legend)
why: Exits at the below-the-line gate. Form is non-fiction, an eyewitness account written by a reporter who covered the war and then went back freelance; genre is first-hand testimony shading into political history, about 286 pages. The reason to exit is the axis the log measures hardest on this form: the memoir and testimony form earns nothing by itself, and what earns is examining what is actually true plus insight into how another group experiences the world. Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 got both; Anne Frank 40 is the DNF that shows the form alone guarantees neither. This book is one man's outrage at Western duplicity, and its partisanship is the standard critique of it - readers describe it as a dry journalistic account and reviewers note that other authors read the same events as more complex. Advocacy about who was to blame is not the same as testing what is plausible and believable, which is precisely what the reader praised in the account that scored 91. So I would put axis:ideas in risks alongside the form doubt, and the non-fiction band here sits at Son of Hamas 75 for a personal account and lower for anything less personal. Occult status is unexamined at this exit by design.

A dual-timeline family-secret saga running from the Raj to the present: an Indian companion to a princess, an English estate, a lost child, a descendant retracing a manuscript. Kirkus calls it a solid but earthbound love story that derails near its conclusion, and Library Journal files it with ghost story, romance and family drama - which is a description of a plot engine, not of an idea. I can name no thought the book would leave behind, and that doubt about axis:ideas is the whole basis of the band; a saga of revealed secrets earns its keep on momentum, and the log puts that class of pleasant, thoughtless competence just under the line rather than above it. The opening is the risk rather than the lean, because two timelines and two casts starting together is the shape that ended books unfinished in their first chapters. Occult status is unexamined at this exit, and the heroine's second sight is the thing that would need checking. One source, within budget.

Exited at the below-the-line gate, and the axes carrying it are axis:ideas and axis:unearned-competence. Form is a novel, genre historical siege adventure. There is a nameable idea - a man raised Muslim as a child levy and now indifferent to both creeds, walking between the Turkish camp and the Knights, which is the same 'how another group experiences the world' vein that earned Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 - but reviewers describe a plot in which the invented hero personally supplies every winning stratagem while the real commanders execute them, which is ability granted rather than earned and is the failure the log punishes; and the trade praise is for thrill and gore rather than for what the book leaves behind, so axis:ideas goes in risks, which is the exit condition. Comparable historical epics sit right at this line for this reader: Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68. Two graded deductions on top: reviewers report gratuitous sex scenes, and the sexual axis costs on volume and explicitness independently, the way Ready Player One 55 and The Witcher 53 record; and PopMatters found the prose relentlessly, viscerally overwritten, which is density. Violence is not an objection at all here, so the siege brutality costs nothing. Occult status unexamined at this exit, as the ladder allows. The plot is a search for a lost child rather than an investigation, so the detective filter does not fire.

The excluded books by this author belong to a separate sequence set in Anglo-Saxon England; this is American Civil War fiction with its own lead, its own premise and no plot carried over, so the occult exclusion is not inherited - checked on the series listing, which shows the two sequences share nothing but an author. On its own merits it exits at the below-the-line gate. The premise has a real motive engine - an abolitionist preacher's son fighting for the South partly to spite his father - and that is the axis that tops the log (Mockingjay 91, Speaker for the Dead 90 both score on wanting and why). But I would put axis:ideas in risks: reviewers describe a long stage-setting middle and a payoff that is the Bull Run battle rendered in period detail, which is set-piece action rather than character revelation, and the same reviewers report difficulty rooting for Starbuck at all. That is the Oliver Twist 57 shape, where the lean on the protagonist was right and the number still came in under the line, and the historical-novel band in this log sits at Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68. So under 68 whatever else I find. Occult status is unexamined at this exit by design.

Two things carry the number. First there is an idea worth naming and it is not just a setting: a city that has traded away the ability to dream for safety and abundance, and a boy whose incurable illness is the only reason he can still dream. That is a premise with a consequence built into it, the shape that keeps Animal Farm 78 and Labyrint sveta 70 above the merely competent band. Second the opening is legible, which matters more here than anywhere else - a reviewer describes it as deliberately slower, unfolding Omnicloud, the drones and the Council of the Wise gradually and explaining the futuristic elements clearly before the story accelerates. That is the opposite of the fault that ended three books at 30 in the first chapters. The lead is an outsider who is easy to root for and is helped by his sister and an old ally rather than surviving alone, which is the Project Hail Mary 92 over The Martian 82 preference. Against that, three protagonists and three interleaved plot lines is more to track than the tight single narration that put The Hunger Games at 89; reviewers report the worldbuilding does not fully cohere - it is never clear what became of the rest of the world or why the City ignores it - and that is the reader's heaviest objection, the one behind Divergent 58; and the questions are sometimes put didactically, with tasks addressed to the reader, which is a children's-register cost of the kind that held Narnia to 67. I leaned on the idea and the opening rather than on the protagonist because the reports of him are second-hand and the interiority is what I could not check.

Exited at the below-the-line gate. Form and genre are settled - a debut juvenile SF adventure novel - and the idea I can name is only the stock one the annotation states, that a technology which promises everyone a carefree life turns out not to be idyllic. Nothing in the material suggests the consequences of that are worked out; the visible content is robot duels, programer clans and a robo-championship, which is page time on what characters do rather than on what they want, the axis Mockingjay 91 wins on and Catching Fire 83 lost points on. I would put axis:ideas in risks, so the gate fires. The juvenile register costs a little on top - Ranger's Apprentice 74 and Narnia 67 are the anchors for an easy read with not much to think about - but that is a graded deduction, not the reason for the number. Occult status is unexamined, which the early exit accepts.

There is a real subject under this - an old allotment colony that shelters animals and people, and a new mayor who wants it flattened - and a book about what a place is worth to the people in it could earn on the axis that tops the log. It is not that book. This is a hundred-and-forty-page illustrated story for readers of about ten, in which a magic cat delivers three girls to the next location and the conflict is resolved at that register, so there is no premise whose consequences get traced and no idea I can name that survives the last page. That is the below-the-line gate's own test and I would put axis:ideas under risks. The juvenile register costs as well: Narnia 67 was marked down for children as leads and nothing higher to think about, and this sits further toward the children's end than that. It is also a sequel with a cast and a device already established elsewhere, and sequels are not safe bets in this log - Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. Exited on one source; occult status is unexamined, and the magic cat is a live question there.

Exited at the below-the-line gate, and the axis that carries it is the lead. Form and genre are settled - a two-sister immigrant saga around the Titanic - and the strongest critical reading is that the sisters are passive, flip between likeable and unlikeable, and do little to move the plot, with half the book narrated by the less likeable of them. That is the single most reliable downgrade in this log: Oliver Twist 57 was marked down for a lead who is acted upon rather than wanting anything, and Artemis 69 sits twenty-three points below the same author's best because the lead was thin however solid everything else was. The premise itself - a stolen identity that has to be maintained - is a decent engine and there is a real question in it about who a person is allowed to become, but it is used for plot turns rather than pressed, so I would list axis:ideas in risks too and the gate fires either way. axis:multi-pov is the risk, not the lean: two alternating narrators from the first pages is the fanning-out shape this reader has abandoned books over. Occult status is unexamined, which the early exit accepts.

This is the profile the log rewards. One lead, one concrete starting situation, and the whole book is what she wanted and why: a girl from a privileged Pyongyang family, made an emigrant not quite by her own choice, who hands the reader her account and asks him to judge her life. Page time on motive rather than on event is the axis Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 both top, and the second earner is present too - real insight into how another group experiences the world, which is a named reason Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 scored where it did. There is a nameable idea, what a person can sell of herself to buy her own freedom, and it is pressed rather than decorated: both worlds read to her as equally false. Two deductions hold it under the A band. The account is delivered as eight separate records framed as courtroom testimony, and a fragmented structure has cost before - Unfinished Tales 69 is the log's warning about pieces that do not join. And the strongest critical reading is that both halves, the childhood and the resettlement centre, skim the surface, which limits how far the insight earner can carry. I leaned on motives and ideas rather than on the testimony form, because the form earns nothing by itself here - Son of Hamas 75 is roughly where a competently told first-person account lands without the examining rigour. Bleakness is the risk that could pull it lower: 1984 60 was marked down for being too depressing, and a totalitarian childhood is that material.

The setting is genuinely unfamiliar and the machinery is the kind of worked-out detail that can carry a book: vouchers issued to every citizen, a starved oil company, and two outsiders trying to buy a controlling stake before the mafia and the proto-oligarchs notice. What it does not have is anyone to want something for. Readers who finished it report not caring much about a single person in it, say it is debatable who the good guys even are, and the one who liked it most said that as fiction alone, stripped of its true-story briefing, it would rate two out of five. That is the Artemis 69 and Oliver Twist 57 pattern precisely - apparatus intact, lead thin - and the log puts the lead above every other axis, including everything built well around it. Leaned on axis:protagonist rather than axis:momentum because pace is not what readers complain about; they complain about caring. Whether it leaves anything behind beyond how the vouchers worked is the further doubt that closes the file at one source. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

t: Silena touha tancit (A Mad Desire to Dance)
why: Wiesel's standing is not the question; what the book leaves behind is. The provocation it opens on - can a man who knows he is mad be mad - is nameable, so the test is whether I would list axis:ideas as a doubt, and I would: readers who followed it to the end report the roots of the neurosis landing as less revelation than dull thud, and a major-paper review calls it among the most impenetrable books published by a serious author in recent memory. Named but not trusted to hold is exactly the gate, so the file stops at one source. Form gives nothing back either: a narrator raving in manic bursts, alternating with his analyst's case notes and addressing the reader as 'you', is the opposite of the one concrete starting situation the reader wants, and inherited Holocaust grief runs the whole length, where 1984 60 shows sustained gloom costs even when the idea is undoubted. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist because Doriel is at least interesting; it is whether his madness means anything that decides the number. Occult status is unexamined at this exit - Doriel believes a dybbuk possesses him, and whether any rite is enacted on the page rather than merely believed in is unchecked. Low end of the band is where I would actually expect it.

This does not exit early because the opening is exactly the shape the reader wants and there is something to think about: one girl on Murano in 1486, her father killed in a workshop accident, brothers not yet skilled enough, so she takes up beadmaking to keep the family fed - one concrete situation, one thing she wants, and the whole book is her wanting it against a trade that forbids it, which is the motives axis that tops the log and the ground on which Male zeny 79 and Pycha a predsudek 75 clear the line with no premise to work out at all. What holds the number down is axis:worldbuilding, and it is the axis I am leaning on. The book declares a rule - time on Murano runs slowly, so the same people live from 1486 to the Covid years while history passes outside - and the reader's standard is that whatever an author foregrounds becomes binding: declare a capability and the world must carry its consequences. Reviewers report the opposite, that the conceit does not hold, that the heroine grows less vivid with each jump until the character shatters, and that it reads as two incompatible books joined. That is the shape of the log's harshest structural verdicts: Mortal Engines 55 was abandoned on premise logic alone and Divergent 58 marked down for a premise that collapses under thought. Rules add obligation, not bonus. Two further costs keep it out of the B band's upper half: reviewers call the ending rushed and confusing, which is the objection that cost The Martian 82, and a lead who thins out across the timeline is the thin-protagonist failure that dropped Artemis to 69 despite consistent worldbuilding - so protagonist and density sit in risks. No occult: glassmaking is a craft, described as work. Opening is sourced; the occult question is inferred rather than sourced, so this is medium.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. This is an author-illustrated Christmas fairy tale for children of about ten, printed at 24 by 31.5 cm - the picture-book end of the axis, which the reader prices in the thirties and forties, well below The Hobbit 84 and The Little Prince 82, where the ideas do the work. I cannot name an idea it leaves behind; what is praised is the Prague legends and the pictures, and the endnotes explaining the landmarks. Readers also report it drawn out and wordy, with at least one abandoning it, which is the thin-story-over-many-pages penalty rather than a length objection. Both the juvenile form and the missing idea point the same way, so the low band rather than the default one. Occult status is unexamined, as the early exit permits.

The honest positive is that the natural history is accurate - readers note the squirrel facts are real - and that the book is built on children choosing to help something that cannot help itself, which is closer to the self-sacrifice the log rewards over solo survival than most books at this level get. But it is a hundred and twenty-six illustrated pages for readers of about seven, the arc is find the animal, call the rescue station, hope, and I cannot name an idea that outlives it; the log says shortness and gentleness earn nothing by themselves and that only a nameable idea does the earning, as in Animal Farm 78. So axis:ideas goes in risks, which is the below-the-line gate's test. The juvenile register costs further, past the Narnia 67 position, and there is no premise here to trade against it the way The Hobbit 84 traded on friendship and ideas. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source; occult status is unexamined and is a non-question in a realistic nature story.

It opens on one concrete situation with a want attached - a girl going to camp without her best friend and dreading it - which is the shape this reader asks for and the opposite of the confusion that ended three books at 30. Readers name tolerance, friendship and getting past fear as what it is about, so there is at least a stated theme. But a theme named in a blurb is not an idea worked out, and at a hundred and twenty-eight pages for readers of eight the book resolves both threads, the camp and the injured stork, at that register; I cannot name anything it leaves behind, which is the below-the-line gate's own test and puts axis:ideas in risks. The juvenile register costs beyond the Narnia 67 position, and a nine-or-ten-year-old lead adds the small life-phase pushback the log prices at a couple of points, never more. Nothing here reaches for the friendship-and-ideas trade that carried The Hobbit 84. Exited on one source; occult status is unexamined and is a non-question in a realistic camp story.

t: Strach ma velke oci (Masha and the Bear: Spooky Stories)
why: Exits at the below-the-line gate, on the lower band. Form is a collection of nine short stories in a large-format 128-page hardback with a glow-in-the-dark cover, recommended for age four and up; genre is gentle contemporary stories for the very young, built around a television character who closes each piece with advice on handling a fear. There is no idea I can name: each story states a childhood anxiety and then names the coping tip, which is instruction rather than something left behind, and the log is clear that short form removes penalties without adding points, so the canonical short books score for their ideas and this has none to score for. That is a collection with no single premise and therefore no axis:ideas to lean on. The form also suspends the character tests entirely, since nine four-page pieces cannot build a protagonist who is interesting and worth rooting for, so the two conditions for the lower band are both met. The log's measured floor for register is explicit that a picture book lands in the thirties or forties, and this sits at that end rather than at the Male zeny 79 or Narnia 67 end. Occult status is unexamined at this exit by design; the spooky framing in the catalogue annotation was not investigated.

Exits at the below-the-line gate, on the lower band. Form is a bedtime story collection credited to a collective of authors; genre is licensed fantasy, the pieces being short retellings of film properties - Mowgli against the tiger, the Hundred Acre Wood telling spooky tales, Peter Pan outwitting the pirate captain. There is no idea I can name and the marketing states the operative one for me, that good and courage always win, which is a reassurance rather than something the book leaves behind. Both conditions for the lower band hold: no nameable idea, and a form that suspends the character tests, since these are pre-existing characters re-narrated in a few pages each and nothing can be built about what any of them wants. The log's own measurement puts a picture book in the thirties or forties, and a licensed retelling for small children sits there rather than near Male zeny 79, which earned its place on characters this format cannot attempt. Note also that a retelling of other works is a different object from the works retold. Occult status is unexamined at this exit by design.

A generational melodrama: an Italian aristocrat orphaned by the war, raised by nuns in America, married into a hostile American dynasty, widowed, remarried disastrously, then the story passes to her daughter. The form is a full novel so the character rules apply undiminished, and the engine is reversal after reversal rather than a premise worked out - I can name no idea it would leave behind, which is the axis that decides the band and the one I stopped on. The risk is density in the log's sense: a thin story spread across decades and two generations is exactly the sparseness that cost Lord of the Rings its difference from The Hobbit, and here there is no mythic weight to offset it. Occult status is unexamined; the exit precedes that gate. One source, within budget.

Seven interviews with North Korean defectors, selected from several dozen by a Czech Koreanist who has been inside the country twice. The positive case is precisely what earns on this reader's non-fiction axis: real insight into how another group experiences the world, the thing that carried Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75. And there is a nameable finding rather than only material - that reverence for the leader survives the escape, which is a harder and more interesting result than the atrocity catalogue a reader would expect. Ordinary lives are the subject: a student, a driver, a trader, a professor, a pensioner, on whether there are nightclubs and what adolescence is like, which is where the understanding actually comes from. Deducted because the form gives nothing to follow - no narrator, no arc, seven voices that do not connect to each other, and Unfinished Tales 69 is the log's price for pieces that are not logically connected; the testimony form also earns nothing by itself, as Anne Frank 40 shows. Leaned on the memoir form rather than the protagonist because there is no protagonist to lean on, and the interview format leaves the seven speakers largely undifferentiated. Two sources' worth of research at a full exit, below the normal budget, because the form and the finding were both settled at once.

t: Svetlo po valce (The Light After the War)
why: Exited at the below-the-line gate. Form and genre are settled - a post-war romance following two survivors from Naples to Caracas - and I cannot name an idea it works out. Survival, friendship and one true love are the material, and the strongest critical readings call the central romance too easy with an inevitable whirlwind courtship, and the characters one-dimensional against weak historical content. That is the axis Artemis 69 was marked down on and Oliver Twist 57 lands under: a lead who is carried by events rather than wanting something the book makes us feel. I would list axis:ideas in risks, so the gate fires, and axis:protagonist is the risk that could take it lower rather than the thing setting it. The friendship at the centre is the one genuine positive - companionship over solo endurance is what put Project Hail Mary 92 above The Martian 82. On the infidelity axis, examined because it is mandatory: the romances found in the sources are between unmarried people and no marriage or engagement is betrayed in anything I could read, though the abrupt disappearance of the first love interest is unexplained in the sources, so this is a checked absence rather than a settled one. Occult status is unexamined, which the early exit accepts.

t: Tajemstvi hvezd (A Bend in the Stars)
why: The positive case is real and it is why this was researched out rather than dropped at a cheap gate: a declared premise with its consequences pursued - a Jewish physicist in 1914 Russia racing an eclipse to complete a theory of gravity, with the antisemitism and the stolen credit that follow from his position worked into the plot rather than decorating it. That is the axis Project Hail Mary 92 and Valka stareho muze 87 win on. The number is not set by that, and the reason is the infidelity axis, which is why it lands where it does. The heroine is engaged to her mentor at the opening - the catalogue's own summary calls him her fiance - and while searching for him she attaches to the soldier she rescued, ends the book carrying his child, and stays with him. Framing is the part that bites: sources describe the attraction as inescapable and the outcome as the satisfying one, so the affair is presented as the right choice rather than as damage, and nothing condemns it. Prominence I read as subplot rather than premise, with the doubt stated: the main plot survives if the triangle is removed, though the strongest critical reading holds that the book's most powerful emotional pull is exactly her being torn between the two men, so this is close to the line and I chose the grading rather than the reject because a wrong reject cannot be recovered. An approving subplot on this axis lands in the thirties, and the worked-out premise is the only thing lifting the top of the range. axis:opening is the risk, not the lean: the setup is described as unnecessarily convoluted and the premise over-reiterated before the journey starts, which is the shape that has ended books here unfinished. Occult was checked and there is none - the heroine is called a witch by superstitious patients, which is a remark about her, not a practice on the page.

Examined the detective question first and it does not fire as a filter: there is no investigator and no culprit to name, the engine is a family absorbing a returned mother, so the shape is domestic suspense and the mystery element is a flag rather than a veto. That leaves the below-the-line gate, and it fires. Form and genre are settled - a 271-page psychological suspense novel - and the idea is a situation rather than a thought worked out: what a family owes someone who comes back after eleven years. Czech readers report the ending is predictable and that it reads as family drama rather than thriller, so the plot engine does not carry it either, and I would list axis:ideas in risks. axis:multi-pov is the risk, not the lean: three narrators, the returned wife, the daughter and the second wife, all starting at once is the fanning-out opening that has ended books here unfinished. The one thing pulling upward is that the material is all motive - who wants what from whom inside one household - which is the axis Mockingjay 91 tops, and it is why the range is the default band and not lower.
