Occult status is unexamined, which the early exit accepts.

Exited at the below-the-line gate, and the axis carrying the number is self-consistency. Form and genre are settled - a WWII novel with one speculative device - and the device is the problem. A closet in a bookshop that carries whoever enters it into the future is a declared capability, and once declared, this reader holds the world to its consequences: reviewers report the mechanism is underdeveloped, leaves open questions and could have been cut, and that plot lines are dropped. That is precisely the breach that made Mortal Engines 55 a DNF in the first chapters on the worldbuilding alone, and that put Divergent 58 in the C band for a premise which collapses under thought. It also blunts what would otherwise be the earner - Project Hail Mary 92 is high in this log because a single invented fact gets its second-order consequences explored, and the contrast is unflattering. On the occult question, examined: a device that moves people through time with no invocation and no devotion is a mechanism, not a rite, so nothing fires there. axis:multi-pov is the risk, not the lean: two narrators in two different decades with a ten-year hole between them is the fanning-out opening that has ended books here. Occult status is otherwise unexamined beyond that, which the early exit accepts.

Form and genre settled at one source: a young-adult paranormal romance novel, seventeen-year-old lead, a rare inborn power her father concealed, both parents killed in chapter one, werewolves who want her and a destined protector who arrives. I cannot name an idea it leaves behind, and that is the axis that stalls competent books in the 60s even when nothing else is wrong - Ranger's Apprentice 74 is the log's benchmark for a readable series with 'not much to think about', and it has no given-power problem on top. Here the ability is handed over rather than earned, which is a named objection of its own, and the Mary Sue lead is what the reader listed first against Divergent 58. The [58, 68] band is the standard record for an exit at this question; on the evidence available the honest weight sits at its lower edge rather than its middle. Occult status is unexamined at this exit - the supernatural here is inherited identity rather than practice, but no rite question was checked.

A hundred and twenty pages for readers of about seven, built as a string of small domestic episodes around a nine-year-old, her extended household and three friends, with the main thread being the making of fizzy bath bombs as a present. There is no idea to name at all, and the episodic form suspends the character tests rather than passing them - the log is explicit that the suspension removes penalties without adding points, and that the short books which score are canonical for their ideas, not for being short, which is why The Little Prince 82 earns and a book like this cannot. Both conditions for the lower below-the-line band therefore hold. The children's axis is graded and it grades this near the picture-book end, well past the Narnia 67 position, with the small life-phase pushback for a nine-year-old lead on top. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source; occult status is unexamined and is a non-question in a realistic domestic story.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, and I would bet on the bottom of the band rather than the top. The question the blurb poses - whether humanity deserves to survive - is nameable but it is posed rather than worked out, and an insignificant soldier who turns out to decide the fate of the species is the unearned-competence shape that the reader called a Mary Sue when he put Divergent at 58. Readers praise it as quick and twist-filled and one says the idea was good but the execution was not; three separate retailer reviews independently complain about the proofreading, which is a real signal about a subsidy-press debut where the reader's standard is that an author follows the rules he lays down. That puts axis:ideas in the doubts, which is what this gate asks. Occult status is unexamined, as the early exit permits.

Exited at the below-the-line gate, and on the lower band. Form and genre are settled: a biographical novel assembled from the author's own pre-war and wartime diaries, published posthumously from his estate. The memoir form earns nothing by itself in this log - it produced both the highest non-fiction score and an outright DNF - and what earns is examining what is actually true, which is exactly what this book declines to do: the author states he gave up on the wider historical context in favour of a personal, subjectively coloured account. So there is no idea I can name, and the testimony form suspends the character tests without adding anything, which is the pair the lower band exists for. Readers repeatedly fault the composition - jumping about in time, bare clipped sentences, poor continuity - and that is the shape of Unfinished Tales 69, the lowest Tolkien, marked down precisely because the pieces are not logically connected; The Diary of a Young Girl 40 is the anchor for first-person testimony that did not work at all. axis:opening carries the risk that it lands lower still rather than the number itself. Occult status is unexamined, which the early exit accepts.

The infidelity axis was examined and does not veto. The husband is secretly queer and has a lover while married, and the wife's attachment to a wealthier man is at most emotional, but the book is about a family's financial and moral collapse with four withheld secrets, of which this is one - remove it and there is still a book, so it grades as a subplot rather than the premise, and the framing is destructive rather than approving, which the reader's table prices at a few points. That deduction, plus the possibility I have misjudged its prominence from reviews rather than the text, is why it sits in risks. What carries the number is axis:motives and axis:character-differentiation, and they carry it upward: the entire architecture is four people covering the same months and each revealing what they wanted and why the others could not see it, which is the axis that put Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 at the top of the log, and each Barnes wants something visibly different, the way Golden Son 92 was credited for Darrow, Sevro and Mustang thinking differently. Against that, three real costs keep it out of the A band. It is around 640 pages and reviewers report over-reliance on flashbacks and contrived coincidence, which is the thin-story-per-page objection that cost The Lord of the Rings 84. One long section is written without punctuation as a character effect, and reviewers who defend the choice still call it a beast to get through - legibility is this reader's single most decisive requirement. And it stops mid-action on an unresolved trigger-pull, where drawn-out or unearned endings have already cost The Martian 82. The opening itself is sourced and is favourable - part one is a single third-person section following one teenager with one concrete situation, not several strands at once - so the Guards! Guards! 30 failure is unlikely, but the strands do multiply afterwards, which keeps the axis in risks. Occult does not arise, so this is medium and not high. REVISED 2026-09-02 for the new axis:same-sex-romance (prominence middle), was [64, 74]. A main character's own same-sex affair, though the book is about a family's financial and moral collapse across four viewpoints. Middle of the graded range, and it compounds with the infidelity axis already examined here. Magnitude is not separable from the single data point: Caropisci 67 lost about thirteen points to this, the hierofant rite and the portrayal warning together, so this dock states a direction and a prominence tier, not a measured size.

t: Ve stinu sfingy (Jake Ransom and the Howling Sphinx)
why: Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. It is a middle-grade portal adventure for roughly ages eight to twelve: a chase, a captured princess, dinosaurs and an evil king with a superweapon. I can name the premise but not an idea it leaves behind, and axis:ideas belongs in the doubts, which is the strongest single predictor of landing under the line. That is the Ranger's Apprentice 74 shape - easy to read, not much to think about - but pitched younger and without the fourteen-book acquaintance with the lead that earned that score, and reviewers already report the characters reading thin and distant here. Being a sequel is a further discount on its own terms, the way the Hitchhiker's sequels fell to 70 from 83. Occult status is unexamined, as the early exit permits.

t: Velka laska malych rozmeru (A Great Love of Small Proportion)
why: Checked the infidelity gate first because the catalogue flagged the book on love: it does not fire. The triangle is between unmarried people - a painter, the daughter of a powerful house, and a knight who wants her - and the rival denounces the painter to the Inquisition before any marriage takes place, so there is no marriage or engagement being betrayed. Sex is not the plot either; the book is a love story set against the Inquisition and the fall of Granada, and romance as the central subject costs nothing here, Pride and Prejudice 75 being the proof. The positive case is that wanting is the whole engine: a deformed converso painter who prefers to be unloved, a woman who wants a life she is not allowed, a friend who wants what he cannot have. Against that, I doubt the idea holds up - this is commercial historical romance whose interest is the situation rather than anything worked out, and the lead is written as ugly, angry and self-isolating, which is the not-worth-rooting-for failure that put The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 twenty-two points below the same author's other prequel. A reviewer also reports the fates left unresolved after Granada, and a drawn-out or unsatisfying ending is a recorded cost, as in The Martian 82. Overspend to declare: I used two sources at a one-source gate, the second only to settle the infidelity question, because a wrong reject is unrecoverable. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. This is a gamebook aimed at nine- to twelve-year-olds - 313 riddles and ciphers, 999 numbered positions and 65 possible endings - so the reader chooses the branches and there is no continuous interiority to spend page time on what a character wants and why, the axis that tops the log with Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90. I cannot name an idea it leaves behind, which is the single strongest separator below the line, and the puzzle-book form suspends the character tests without adding anything in their place, so the low band applies rather than the default one. Register sits well below The Hobbit 84 and The Little Prince 82, which pay nothing for being child-facing because their ideas carry them; nearer a picture book on that axis. The search hit on investigation is a treasure hunt for a vanished ancestor, not a whodunnit, so the detective filter does not fire. Occult status is unexamined, as the early exit permits.

t: Vrazedna pole (Survival in the Killing Fields)
why: The positive case is an idea, not just events: a regime that classified knowledge itself as the crime, so a physician had to spend years pretending he was a taxi driver to stay alive, and the book works out how that logic ran differently in each zone the country was carved into. That is the axis Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75 both score on - insight into how another group experiences the world - and it opens on one concrete situation, a middle-class childhood in rural Cambodia, single first-person and chronological. Held under those two because the book testifies rather than examines: Qureshi's 91 came from genuinely weighing what is plausible against what he had been taught, and this narrator has no argument to test, only a record to give. Deducted for sustained bleakness, the objection that cost 1984 60 and that the reader named again on The Martian 82 when misery became the theme rather than the setting - here it runs for hundreds of pages of forced labour, starvation and three spells in prison. Leaned on the memoir form and the idea rather than on the protagonist, because Anne Frank 40 is the standing proof that first-person testimony earns nothing by the form alone; the voice is also mediated, shaped from the narrator's halting English by a journalist co-author.

t: Vyhled pres strechy (The View Across the Rooftops)
why: Exited at the below-the-line gate. Form and genre are settled - a commercial WWII occupation novel - and the real positive is the two-hander at its centre: a withdrawn widowed professor and the impulsive student he hides, opposite temperaments forced into one attic, which is page time on what two people want and why. That is the axis Mockingjay 91 tops and it is why this is not lower. What keeps it under the line is that I cannot name an idea the book works out beyond courage and community pulling together under occupation, which is the sentiment of the genre rather than a thought left behind; Exodus 68 and Quo Vadis 66 are where competent historical novels settle in this log. I would put axis:ideas in risks, so the gate fires. axis:density is the risk rather than the lean, since a single hiding-place setting over a long war is the thin-story-over-many-pages shape that cost The Lord of the Rings 84 its difference from The Hobbit. On the infidelity axis, examined because it is mandatory: the professor is a widower and the student's forbidden attachment is to an unmarried non-Jewish girl, so no marriage or engagement is in play - no deduction. Occult status is unexamined, which the early exit accepts.

Exits at the below-the-line gate, and the axes carrying the number are axis:ideas and axis:opening. Form is a slim book of associative autobiographical prose in three named parts with subchapters of unequal length, not a novel; genre literary fiction. That combination triggers the exit condition twice over. There is no idea I can name - the material is grief for a dead grandmother, a lost flat and a lost city, and the Respekt reviewer calls the text narratively formless to a degree while arguing that is not a fault, which is a description of a mood rather than of something worked out. And the time layers are deliberately non-linear, interleaving life stages by flashes of memory, which is precisely the condition the reader has ended books on: a reader tracking several strands at once with no concrete starting situation killed The Gunslinger 30, The Colour of Magic 30 and Caropisci 30. Placed in the lower band rather than the default one because both conditions hold - nothing nameable to think about, plus a fragmentary form that suspends the character tests instead of passing them; Unfinished Tales 69 is the log's warning that pieces which are not logically connected to each other cost even a beloved author his floor, and this has neither the ideas nor the affection behind it. Positive case, stated in its own words: the writing works by circling very small concrete things until they turn into something present, and reviewers who like it like it for that. Occult status unexamined at this exit, as the ladder permits.

Exits at the below-the-line gate. Form is a short illustrated novel of about 88 pages, genre contemporary Czech realism written for children, and it belongs to an issue-book line produced with a specialist publisher to help children handle difficult situations. There is an idea I can name - what a displaced child and her new classmates each fail to understand about the other - and that is the axis the log rewards most in non-fiction, since Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 earned its score on insight into how another group experiences the world. That is why the band is the upper one and not the lower. But I would still put axis:ideas in risks, and that is the exit: in a didactic 88-page book for ten-year-olds the idea arrives as a lesson to be taught rather than a premise whose consequences get worked out, which is what separates Animal Farm 78 from a book that merely has a theme. Against that sit the register deductions the log has measured - Male zeny 79 pays almost nothing for being children's-adjacent, Narnia 67 pays a little for children as the leads and for lacking higher things to think about, and this is written well below the level of either. Occult status is unexamined at this exit by design.

The detective filter was checked first and does not fire: a naval officer is sent to investigate settlers' violence, but the book's weight is the moral tragedy of an extinction rather than the identification of a culprit, so this is an investigation-shaped strand in an otherwise eligible book - a flag, not a veto. The idea is real and nameable, which is why the book does not exit early: how ordinary self-interest, misunderstanding and blind loyalty add up to the erasure of a people, with sympathies made to shift as each character's background comes out. That is the axis Animal Farm 78 scores on and the page time on motives is the axis at the top of the log. What pulls the number under the line is axis:opening, and it is the axis I am leaning on because it is the log's most reliable predictor. Reviewers consistently report that the narration is far from straightforward, that the timelines are fractured across four viewpoints and long reminiscences, and that the first half is hard going before it comes together - which is exactly the failure that ended The Gunslinger 30, The Colour of Magic 30 and Caropisci 30 in their first chapters, and the reader's stated requirement is one concrete starting situation he can be invested in immediately. Unfinished Tales 69 is the milder version of the same cost, docked for pieces that are not logically connected. Bleakness and density sit in risks rather than the lean: a book that ends with a people vanishing and a captive woman dead of tuberculosis is sustained gloom, which is a discount rather than a bar, and the poetic landscape writing that reviewers praise most is description doing work a story could be doing. Occult does not arise. Opening structure is sourced only through reviewers' accounts of the whole, not through a description of chapter one, so this is medium.

t: Znameni, ktere neprislo (Are You Proud of Me, Joanna?)
why: The detective hint was checked first and does not fire: the one critic who has read it says plainly that this is not a crime thriller but intellectual contemplation with a heavy political charge dressed in an adventure shape, and what the narrator uncovers is a political and moral truth about where the guilt actually lay, not a culprit's name. The investigation shape is a flag, not a veto. What remains is the thing this reader most wants a book to have. A diplomat who spent a career believing words are what work, against a daughter who believed only deeds are, and then her killing and his own share in it - that is a proposition rather than a plot, and page time on what people want and why is the axis Speaker for the Dead 90 and Mockingjay 91 both top the log on. It is close-focused too: one narrator, his guilt, and a scene in an isolated Virginia cabin where he confronts armed the man he holds responsible. Two things hold the number down rather than lift it. The book is bleak by construction, and 1984 60 shows sustained gloom costs even where the idea is undoubted, while Animal Farm 78 shows the reader forgives it only when a book gives him something to think about instead of immersing him in the misery. And I could not establish how it opens: the one substantial review does not describe the first chapter and says the narrative moves across nearly half the planet with interwoven timelines, so the axis that has ended books in their first chapters is unverified here - that is why the number is not higher and the confidence is not high.

t: Mezi truny lvu (To Lie with Lions)
why: A sequel set deep inside a long sequence, and in this reader's terms that is the whole difficulty. The book begins with a bank whose fortunes rest on manoeuvring already done, a small son just taken from an estranged wife whose grudge was earned earlier, a feud with a half-brother who refuses to acknowledge him, rival trading houses already in the field and an enemy who already holds his secrets - all assumed rather than established - and then it sails for Iceland. Sequels are not safe bets in this log even when what came before worked: Hitchhiker's Guide fell from 83 to 70 across its continuations. What decides the number is that the reader's one unrecoverable failure mode is an opening whose incident arrives ahead of its context, the diagnosis behind four separate scores of 30, and a book beginning on this much withheld ledger is that shape by construction. Leaned on axis:opening rather than axis:density because prose and trade detail are what admirers praise and length alone has never been an objection here. Whether it leaves an idea behind is the further doubt: the sharpest reader complaints are that the marital war has become tiresome and even stupid, which is a plot people got bored by, not a proposition. Infidelity was examined and is not the premise - the engine of this book is the banking and political campaign, with the marriage as one thread. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

Exits at the below-the-line gate, and on the lower band. Form is a 112-page illustrated children's adventure novel, one instalment of an ongoing series about six travelling teenagers; genre is disaster peril. I cannot name an idea it leaves behind at all - the takeaway readers actually report is practical advice on what to do in a tornado, which is information, not an idea, and the log is explicit that a short book with thin ideas lands low like any other thin book. There is one small positive worth recording, that the book sets the reality of Oklahoma against the romantic notions of Native Americans children get from adventure stories, which is the opposite of the lazy stereotype stated as fact that cost Hranicaruv ucen 74 several points. It is not enough to build a case on. With no nameable idea and a formulaic short franchise episode whose form suspends the character tests rather than earning on them, the lower band is the honest one; Hranicaruv ucen 74 is the ceiling for easy-reading children's series and this sits well under it on ambition. The series is shelved partly as detective and adventure stories, but this instalment is a survival story with no investigation, so gate one does not fire. Occult status is unexamined at this exit by design.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on axis:ideas, which is the axis carrying the number. Form is a novel and genre is Roman military historical adventure, part of a long-running campaign sequence whose selling points in the trade copy are nonstop action and clean intelligent fun. The nearest thing to an idea I can name is the Roman army as a career machine seen from the ranks, and that is a setting rather than a premise worked out - so axis:ideas belongs in risks, which is the exit condition. The log is consistent on this shape: Ranger's Apprentice 74 was marked down as easy to read but with not much to think about, and the reader's heaviest axis is page time on what characters want and why rather than on set-piece action, which is what a battle-and-siege novel spends its length on. A sequel besides, and sequels are not safe bets in this log - Hitchhiker's 83 to 70. Positive case is real but modest: two contrasted leads, a veteran and a bookish subordinate, whose friendship is the series' actual subject. Occult status is unexamined, as the ladder permits at this exit; the arms-smuggling strand is investigation-shaped but the satisfaction is the campaign, not the culprit, so the detective filter does not fire.

Commercial novel, and the genre is a woman's escape story alternating past and present. What the book offers is insight into how another group experiences the world - the closed lives of privileged women in a Gulf monarchy - and that is the trait that earns in this log, but the trade reviews are the problem: the resolution is called predictable, and the one reviewer who went in hoping the author's own background would lift it out of the standard abused-woman-escapes formula concluded it did not. So I can name a subject but not an idea the book works out, which puts axis:ideas in risks and exits at gate 4. Neither content filter fires on the evidence I have: the detective signal on the task line is a murder inside the story rather than an investigation, and the adultery in the book is a friend stoned for it in the protagonist's childhood plus a false accusation her husband constructs, so infidelity is neither the premise nor a relationship the reader is asked to spend the novel inside. Occult status is unexamined, per the ladder.

Czech original novel, described by its own author in a newspaper interview as a political thriller, and the structure is what decides it: three unconnected leads in three countries, each reaching a crisis at once - a Czech businesswoman whose firm and marriage are both failing, a Basque journalist leaving a terrorist past, a Moscow teacher working for a suspect patriotic organisation. Several plot lines starting simultaneously before any is legible is the single most reliable predictor in this log and the cause of both abandonments at 30, and nothing in what I could find suggests the strands converge early. On top of that I found no published critical review at all - only reader ratings around 70 to 76 per cent - so I cannot name an idea the book leaves behind, which is the gate 4 condition, and the author's own account of writing it (four dead ends, four returns to the beginning) is not reassuring about the plotting. I leaned on the opening rather than on the idea because the structural risk is concrete and sourced while the idea is merely absent from the record. The marriage crisis is one strand of three and there is no evidence of an affair as premise, so no filter fires; occult is unexamined.

A history-teaching adventure for twelve-year-olds: a magic atlas drops the same girl into a period, she meets a real historical figure, she learns what the period was like. The frame is a delivery device rather than a premise with consequences, and the period is the content, so there is no idea worked out that survives the last page - the standard reason a competent book settles in the 60s here. Ranger's Apprentice 74 is about the ceiling for this kind of easy educational adventure, and what it was docked for was stating lazy historical claims as fact, which is a live hazard for a book whose whole purpose is to teach history to children. Leaned on axis:ideas; axis:protagonist is not the argument, since a recurring twelve-year-old traveller is neither the strength nor the flaw here. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source: the atlas looks like a transport device rather than a rite, but the occult question was not examined.

t: Babka z domku na kuri nozce
why: This is a 64-page square-format illustrated storybook for readers of six and up, narrated by the cottage itself, and that form is what carries the number: the reader's own scale puts a picture book in the 30s or 40s, and short work has the character tests suspended without gaining anything in return - The Little Prince 82 and Animal Farm 78 are short books that score on ideas an adult can chew on, which is the thing I cannot find here. The nearest thing to an idea is that life does not end when you retire, which readers do praise as unusual in a children's book, but it is a sentiment rather than a premise with consequences, so axis:ideas is where the doubt sits. Lower band rather than the default because both conditions hold at once. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

A 64-page picture story recommended from age two and a half: a small boy who loves diggers starts a real one, falls into the hole and gets home through the underground with a toy digger that turns out to be magic. This is the register the reader profile puts in the thirties and forties, and the log supports it from above rather than below: Narnia 67 is already under the propose line on a juvenile cast and nothing higher to think about, and it is a full novel. There is no idea to name and no space for a lead who wants anything beyond the next scene, so axis:ideas carries the number down and axis:childrens sets the band. One source at the below-the-line gate, so occult status is unexamined - the magic toy is asserted, never operated to declared rules.

Identified as the closing volume of the Powerless trilogy (Czech order Bezmocna, Bezohledna, Bezradna), a 576-page YA romantasy about a caste of Elites and powerless Ordinaries. Gate 2 first, because the premise is a forced political betrothal to Kitt while Paedyn wants Kai: that engages the marriage-or-engagement scope, but a coerced dynastic match with a love triangle is not a book whose premise is an affair - remove the betrayal and the rebellion plot still stands - so I graded rather than rejected, and I state the doubt plainly. Gate 3 is clean: reviewers describe it as YA-clean, kisses and yearning, so volume and explicitness are both low, and low volume mitigates as it did for Old Man's War 87. That leaves gate 4, and it fires: the blurb's own stated stakes are which boy she chooses, the trilogy is reviewed as delivering on its romance and little else, and I cannot name an idea the caste conceit works out, so I would put axis:ideas in risks. Pride and Prejudice 75 shows romance as the central subject costs nothing when motives and wants are the whole book, but Divergent 58 shows what a borrowed caste-and-trials premise assembled without cohering is worth, and this reads far closer to the second. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist because Paedyn is at least active and wants something; it is the thinness of what the book is about that fixes the band. Occult unexamined at this exit. Honest overspend: two sources at a gate budgeted for one, because identifying which volume this Czech title is took a search of its own.

A 64-page illustrated children's book built as one chapter per grandchild, each pairing a small trouble with a herb - St John's wort, dead-nettle, cornflower, marjoram, chamomile. The episodic one-child-one-plant shape is what decides this: Male zeny 79 is the log's ceiling on a juvenile register and it is carried entirely by characters the reader gets to live with, which seven children at eight pages each cannot be; Narnia 67 is already below the propose line for a juvenile cast with nothing higher to think about. I can name a botanical topic and no idea, so axis:ideas carries the number and axis:childrens fixes the band. One source at the below-the-line gate, so occult status is unexamined, and it is a live question here - the grandmother is described as kouzelna and the book is about what plants can do.

A YA heist fantasy whose declared subject - a colonial trading power and what it does to the people it feeds on - is a real idea, and that is what keeps it out of the low bands. But the reviewers who liked it are the ones saying the theme got a few hundred pages when it needed more, and that the caper itself runs about twenty pages after a build-up that eats half the book. That is the pattern that stalls competent books in the 60s in this log: events, with the idea gestured at rather than carried through, the way Narnia 67 is not bad but lacks higher things to think about. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:worldbuilding because the log's clearest lesson is that a strong setting rescues nothing when the centre is thin - Artemis 69 against Project Hail Mary 92 by one author. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, so the opening structure is unexamined and so is the occult status of the vampires; a heist already in motion with a crew arriving unexplained is the shape of a recorded DNF, which is why axis:opening is a risk rather than a deduction.

The idea I can name is time as a governed resource - clocks as instruments, a second world drifting toward ours - and I doubt it holds up, which is what decides this. Czech reviewers who recommend the book still describe a naivety readers of fantasy have to get past, a heroine who reasons illogically, and adult characters whose motivation is still missing halfway through the cycle. Motive left unwritten is the reader's heaviest axis running the wrong way: it is what put Speaker for the Dead at 90 and what left Divergent at 58 reading as parts assembled without cohering. A girl discovering a hidden magical country and going away to learn its craft is also the exact shape of Harry Potter, which scored 51 here on the magic and on a world never reorganised around what it declares, so the worldbuilding obligation is high and the reviews suggest it is not met. Nothing in the annotation triggers a hard filter I could confirm at this cost. I leaned on ideas rather than on the protagonist because it is the whole premise I doubt, not only the girl carrying it.

The positive case is real: the subject is not the itinerary but two people under strain - a man looking for inner strength, a woman wanting security - and page time on what people want and why is the axis that tops this log, with Pycha a predsudek 75 showing a relationship as the central subject costs nothing. Against that I cannot name an idea the book leaves behind beyond 'eight months of Africa tests a couple', and the testimony form earns nothing by itself here: Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75 earn by examining what is actually true, while The Diary of a Young Girl 40 shows first-person witness alone can fail outright. An author-published travelogue novel with no critical notice found gives me nothing to set against that doubt, so axis:ideas carries the number rather than axis:motives, which I could not verify is actually worked out on the page. Exited at gate 4 on one source, so the occult question is unexamined.

The nameable idea is guilt that has outlived its statute of limitations, and that is a real subject - Animal Farm 78 shows that short idea-driven prose scores well when it leaves you something to think about. But the book is not built to work that idea out: the publisher describes a sarcastically pitched stream of recollection and reflection hung on a car journey, which means the suspension short work enjoys removes the character penalties without adding anything, exactly as the log records. Labyrint sveta a raj srdce 70 is the honest anchor - an allegory with a genuinely nameable idea that still landed in the B band - and this has less structure than that and no canonical standing behind it. So axis:ideas is what I am doubting and what carries the number, not the protagonist, who is barely a character in a text of this kind. Density sits in risks: digression is the recorded penalty term and it is what separated Les Miserables 71 from The Count of Monte Cristo 75. Occult was not examined at this exit.

There is a real idea here and I am not doubting it: a man who gives up a career and a family to become a man with qualities, and an account of post-Soviet lives that the Magnesia Litera jury read as an essay on a lost national soul. What sinks the number is the shape. The prize citation itself says the book can be read four different ways at once, and readers who liked it describe a bit of everything - diary, travelogue, ethnographic study, love story, reportage - with too much space given to description; that is exactly what Unfinished Tales 69 was docked for, the pieces not being logically connected to each other, and it is the lowest Tolkien in the log by a clear margin. A two-part work of this length with dozens of characters woven around the core also puts the heaviest recorded predictor at risk: The Colour of Magic 30 and The Gunslinger 30 both died on a start where much was happening and none of it meant anything yet, and a seemingly chaotic trajectory is advertised on the cover here. So the number is carried by density and legibility rather than by ideas, and the range sits under the line rather than in the F band because the writing is award-level and one continuous narrator holds it.

t: Chlapec, ktery letal s dracky (The Boy Who Flew with Dragons)
why: There is a genuine positive here and it is not the dragons: the whole book is a boy trying to keep a promise he no longer wants to keep, letting go of a friend because he said he would. That is page time on what a character wants and why, which is the axis Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 top the log on, and it is a real emotional idea rather than an errand. What holds it under the line is scale. It is written for roughly ages six to nine, illustrated throughout, and the conflict is settled in one register with no consequences that reach past the garden - Narnia 67 was docked for lacking higher things to think about with considerably more world behind it. The dragonfruit tree is also a declared capability whose consequences the book has no interest in following, and the reader audits exactly that: Harry Potter 51 was marked down because a concretely declared magic never reorganises the society around it. A sequel too, and sequels are not safe bets in this log - Hitchhiker's 83 falls to 70. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist because the boy is likeable and adequate; it is the ceiling on what the idea can reach, not the lead, that fixes the number. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

Form and genre are settled cheaply: a mass-market archaeological conspiracy thriller of about 300 pages, a found-manuscript leading to a secret cave and then to deaths arranged to look accidental. The idea I can name is the secret in the cave, and that is a plot device rather than something the book is about - the publisher's own copy has nothing to offer beyond the setup, and the machinery around it, a fourteenth-century manuscript plus Roger Bacon, John Dee and alchemy, is the standard furniture of the form. I would put axis:ideas under risks, so gate 4 exits here. Two consequences of stopping, both deliberate: the occult status is unexamined, and the alchemical material is exactly where it would need looking, and I did not settle whether the satisfaction is an investigation - there is no detective and the payoff appears to be the cave's secret rather than an identification, which is why this is not a gate 1 reject.

This is a collection of newspaper columns an actor wrote for a Friday supplement in the early 2000s, gathered without a subject: wordplay, quick observations, irony aimed at his surroundings and at himself. There is no premise to work out and no single idea to name, and a collection with no premise has no ideas axis to lean on, which is the strongest separator in the reader's data. The form also suspends the character and motive tests rather than passing them, and that suspension removes penalties without adding any points. Nor does the non-fiction route rescue it: what earns here is examining what is actually true or showing how another group experiences the world, which is why Seeking Allah Finding Jesus reached 91 and Son of Hamas 75, and occasional comic columns do neither. Czech comic voice alone can do better - Saturnin sits at 78 - but that is a novel with characters, and voice with nothing under it is what this is. I leaned on ideas because there is no other axis with anything to weigh.

t: Draci boure (Dragon Storm: Cara and Silverthief)
why: A short illustrated chapter series for ages seven to ten, one child and one summonable dragon per instalment, eight-plus instalments to a template. I can name no idea it leaves behind, and the premise is the opposite of one worked out: the child turns out to be one of a handful who can summon a dragon, which is ability conferred rather than earned - the reader's Divergent 58 note names a Mary Sue protagonist among its reasons, and Ranger's Apprentice 74 stayed in the B band only because a boy is trained over many books rather than simply selected. There is a thread worth a point or two, a street child who has never had friends learning who to trust, but at this length and audience it is stated more than shown, which is the reverse of the interiority that puts Red Rising 95 at the top. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist because Cara herself is a reasonable lead; it is the absence of anything to think about, in a form short and illustrated enough to suspend the character tests, that fixes the band. Occult status is unexamined at this exit; summoning is the word to check, since a called dragon with no mechanical account of the calling is the shape the reader vetoes.

A forty-page illustrated story for four- to six-year-olds: a boy in a barren valley carves a door into a dead tree, hoping it opens somewhere he will not be laughed at. There is a message - keep at your own dream - and Czech readers note an unusual melancholy and a lot left implied, which is more than most books this size attempt. But it is a picture book, and the axis is explicit that a picture book lands in the thirties or forties whatever else is true. What lifts The Little Prince 82 clear of its own brevity is a sustained argument about grown-ups, not a single closing sentiment, and the same readers who like this one say the illustrations are doing most of the work. The form also removes the character tests rather than passing them, which is what puts it in the lower band. Leaned on axis:childrens, since register and audience are the whole objection - the writing is not the problem. Exited at the below-the-line gate, so the occult question was not examined.

t: Earhart (Earhart: The Incredible Flight of a Field Mouse Around the World)
why: Graded on the children's axis, never vetoed, and the number is essentially that axis alone. This is an illustrated picture book carried by full-page paintings, with a mouse who should not be able to fly building a machine and doing it anyway, plus a few closing pages of real aviation history. The log's scale is clear about what that costs: The Hobbit 84 and The Little Prince 82 pay nothing because an adult reads them as books, Narnia 67 pays for child leads and no higher things, and a picture book sits below all of them - so the low band, and the reason is the form and register rather than any failure of the book at what it is doing. What it leaves behind is an encouraging sentiment about ingenuity rather than an idea worked out, so axis:ideas is the risk. Against that, a small mechanical hero who earns his flight is the opposite of the given competence the log penalises, and there is nothing on any filter here at all - which is not itself a case for reading it. Occult was not examined; talking mice building aeroplanes is not where that question lives.

The positive case is real: one boy, one place, one trade, opening on a concrete situation - a seaside guest house for consumptives and an apprenticeship to a drunk tattooist - and a Booker shortlisting for the prose. But the recurring critical verdict is the exact penalty this log charges: too much description and too little plot, one reviewer advising the reader to set plot quibbles aside and let the language carry him, another that it could have been cut. That is what docked The Lord of the Rings 84 despite far greater ideas, and it is the whole of the Les Miserables 71 objection. What the book leaves behind is skin as a canvas and a body signed over to another person, which is thinner than it sounds once the plot is conceded, so axis:ideas sits in risks rather than under the number, and density is what carries it. Content is the second risk: a cool trade review notes recurring visions of bodily secretions and an almost childlike fascination with ordure, which is not the sexual crudeness that cost Artemis 69 - a coarse register is not an objection here - but it is unappealing matter on the page in a book that has already conceded story. Not a gate-3 reject: the tattooist's relationship with the tattooed woman is one thread of a life story, not the plot.

It has a real positive: iLiteratura calls the telling assured and unlike anything else on the Czech market, mixing Prague legend, wordplay and offbeat humour, and a comic voice carrying a book is something this log rewards - Saturnin 78 scores in the A band on voice and character with no idea worked out at all. What it does not have is anything to think about beyond its stated moral, that courage is overcoming your own fear for the good of others, and 'not much to think about' is exactly what held Hranicaruv ucen 74 and The Chronicles of Narnia 67 down. So axis:ideas is where the doubt sits and it carries the number; the register pushes the same way, since the lead is a girl not yet at school. Occult status is unexamined at this exit, and the annotation's wizard and enchanted statues are the reason it is worth reopening if the number ever matters.

t: Fantasticka dobrodruzstvi Alfreda Kroppa (The Extraordinary Adventures of Alfred Kropp)
why: Arthurian action-adventure graded for ages eleven to fourteen, and the reviews that liked it liked it for pace and jokes: one calls it lighthearted, entertaining and occasionally half-witted, another says the easy language over three hundred pages makes it undemanding. I cannot name an idea it leaves behind, which is the gate 4 condition, so it exits here. The nearest thing in the log is Ranger's Apprentice 74 - easy to read, not much to think about - and I have deliberately set the band below that, for two reasons: this sits further toward a children's book than Flanagan does, and the lead's decisive quality is handed to him by ancestry rather than earned, since a self-described loser turns out to be the last descendant of Lancelot. That is the unearned-competence axis and it is one of the things that sank Divergent 58. Stopping here leaves the occult status unexamined, and it is a real question rather than a formality - Excalibur, Merlin's cave and a death-and-rebirth through the sword are all real-world legendary material rather than an invented system, which is the distinction that put Percy Jackson at 57.

A contemporary school story about a novice rider trying to belong, and its real strength is that reviewers name the lead as the reason it works - which counts for a lot here, because axis:protagonist outranks everything else in this log. But nothing is left behind: finding your forever herd is a situation, not an idea, and that is the most common reason a competent book stalls in the 60s. Ranger's Apprentice 74 is the shape of it - easy to read, not much to think about - and this sits below that, being slighter, illustrated, and footnoted with horse facts for a middle-grade audience. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist precisely because the lead is the part that is working, so it cannot be the axis carrying a number this low. An anonymous-note thread is investigation-shaped and is recorded in flags; the reader's satisfaction is fitting in rather than identifying the sender, so no filter fires. Exited at the below-the-line gate, so the occult question was not examined.

The positive case is one declared premise and its consequences: a trading system built to measure fear starts manufacturing fear, because that is what it was told to optimise. The best sequence in the book is a consequence check rather than a set piece - the lead cuts power in the server room and the machine keeps trading - which is the kind of follow-through that put Project Hail Mary at 92 and Old Man's War at 87. It also opens on one concrete situation, an intruder in the house at night, so the opening filter that ended The Colour of Magic at 30 does not fire. Docked because the lead is a paranoid billionaire quant unravelling across a single day: interesting but hard to root for, which is the exact split that separated Sunrise on the Reaping 87 from The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65, and the same thin-lead drag that revised Artemis down to 69. Docked again because reviewers report the third act abandoning the ambiguity for an action-movie chase, so the machine-consciousness account is asserted rather than mechanically earned - the self-consistency axis that sank Divergent to 58. I leaned on ideas rather than on worldbuilding precisely because the log forbids predicting up on a setting when the lead looks thin.

t: Jak postavit lod (How to Build a Boat)
why: It survives gate 4 because there is an idea and the book actually works it out: a boy wants a perpetual motion machine because he believes ceaseless movement is how he reaches the mother who died giving birth to him, and the answer the book gives him is a currach and the Irish idea of meitheal, communal effort - the impossible private machine replaced by a thing several people can only build together. That is a premise whose consequences are pursued, and the whole book is page time on what one boy wants and why, which is the axis that tops this log. Male zeny 79 is the anchor for how far characters alone can carry a book with no genre premise, and The Little Prince 82 shows a child lead costs almost nothing when the ideas carry. The deductions are structural rather than moral: three points of view with the adult sections reported as flat beside the boy's, speech set without quotation marks, secondary characters reduced to single traits, and reviewers calling the whole thing derivative of better-known books. Those are why the band sits at the propose line rather than above it. I leaned on motives and the idea rather than on prose or prize status - Booker longlisting earns nothing in this log - and axis:opening is under risks because I could not establish how many points of view are live in the first chapter, which is the log's most reliable predictor.

The honest positive is that the motives are the plot: three students enter a school beauty-and-talent contest for three different reasons - tuition, a following, respect - and page time on what people want and why is the axis that tops this log. What I doubt is that anything is left behind. Readers repeatedly call it over-combined, anorexia and steroids and vitiligo and bullying at once, and several report flat characters; a book that assembles issues without any of them cohering is the Divergent 58 failure, and 'not much to think about' is what held Hranicaruv ucen 74 down even where the reading was easy. So axis:ideas is where the doubt sits and it carries the number. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

An illustrated picture-story book for children from four years old, about a pre-school boy on a mountain farm who talks to llamas and ends up in the magic burrows of a mole queen. The reader profile puts a picture book in the 30s or 40s and the reason applies exactly: the form is too slight to carry any test of what characters want and why, the axis that tops the log with Mockingjay 91, so the suspension removes penalties without adding a thing. There is arguably something nameable here - Czech readers read the sheep who spread nonsense about the exotic llamas as a warning about judging what is foreign - but that is a moral drawn from two pages, not a premise whose consequences are worked out, so axis:ideas stays a risk rather than the lean. Even the log's most generous children's-adjacent result, Little Women 79, is a full novel carried by characters, and Narnia 67 already pays for children as leads with less to think about; a four-plus book sits well below both. I leaned on axis:childrens rather than axis:protagonist because the register and audience, not Jura himself, are what fix the band.

An omnibus of episodic animal tales written for children from age five, with the author's own illustrations carrying much of each page - Pytlik opens a painting school, walks a tightrope, eats breakfast three times. The reader's floor for this register is explicit: a picture book lands in the 30s or 40s, and this is closer to that than to Male zeny 79, which cleared the propose line on characters a domestic novel had room to build. Here the form is against it twice over. A collection with no single premise has no axis:ideas to lean on - the same double penalty the reader's own Unfinished Tales 69 note describes as pieces not logically connected to each other - and the short-work suspension removes penalties without adding points, so the beetle's comic incompetence is charm rather than something left behind. Saturnin 78 shows a Czech comic voice can carry a book on its own, but that is an adult novel with a sustained narrator, not preschool episodes. Leaned on axis:childrens because the audience and register are what fix this, not any single weakness. Occult status is unexamined at this exit; one episode has Pytlik chasing off ghosts, which is comic and would be the thing to check.

A 64-page illustrated first-reader for lower primary: two small girls, a herbalist grandmother, and a flying dog bed, with the herbs doubling as a lesson in what each plant is good for. Narnia 67 fell below the propose line on children as the main characters plus nothing higher to think about, and this has both in a far shorter and simpler telling; Hranicaruv ucen 74 shows even a long, competent juvenile series only reaches the low 70s once there is nothing to think about. The teaching-about-herbs frame is the honest reason I cannot name an idea rather than a lesson, so axis:ideas carries the number and axis:childrens fixes the band. One source at the below-the-line gate, so occult status is unexamined - relevant here, because the plot turns on folk herbalism and wishes granted.

A house-pseudonym early-chapter series written to a template - two girls cross into an enchanted valley, a wicked unicorn steals one magic object per book, they get it back - at around 120 illustrated pages an instalment. There is no idea to name, and that is the finding rather than an omission: the plot is a stolen medallion and a deadline, so nobody in it wants anything the book is interested in, which is precisely the axis Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 are highest in the log for. Two interchangeable best friends is also the failure Divergent 58 was marked down for in a much longer book - characters who do not think or want different things, against Golden Son 92 where they demonstrably do. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:childrens because the register alone would leave it nearer Narnia 67; it is the template plus the empty premise, over a form that suspends the character tests, that puts it in the 40s. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

t: Kralicek by mel uz spat (Bunny Should Be Sleeping)
why: A forty-page bedtime picture book: a small rabbit climbs out of his cot, loads a wagon with water, a blanket, a biscuit and a book, and goes to check on his sleeping father. The role reversal is charming and it is one gesture, not a premise with consequences, which is what the below-the-line gate asks. The profile puts a picture book in the thirties or forties on register, and the log's high short books earn their way out of that with ideas a grown reader keeps - Maly princ 82 and Animal Farm 78 - while Narnia 67 is already under the propose line on a juvenile cast plus nothing higher to think about, at novel length. So axis:ideas carries the number down and axis:childrens sets the band. One source at the below-the-line gate, so occult status is unexamined, though nothing in the record suggests any arises.

The idea is nameable and the book states it itself: the ring changes nobody, the girls' own effort does. That is a real thing to leave behind, and courage against one's own fear is the kind of material the reader rates - his Labyrint sveta 70 came in exactly where an allegory with one nameable idea was predicted, and the faith risk on it did not fire. But the same row is the ceiling here, because this is a didactic children's book from a religious publisher and the moral is announced rather than discovered, where Animal Farm 78 earns its score by giving you something to think about instead of telling you what to think. Four friends who are described as a foursome rather than differentiated is the weakness Divergent 58 was marked down for, and the reader's Ranger's Apprentice 74 note shows how quickly stated-as-fact material costs points. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:faith because the moral, not the publisher, is what sets the number; the annotation frames the lesson in terms of conscience and inner strength rather than doctrine, and theology as a subject in its own right is the thing the reader objects to. Occult status is unexamined at this exit; a ring that delivers messages would be the thing to check.

A formula early-chapter fantasy for ages 7-10, around 128 heavily illustrated pages per instalment, sold with a collectible charm, and I can name no idea it leaves behind: a girl must recover eight lost magic horseshoes before the Royal Games so a talking-pony island can be saved. That is a collect-the-objects errand, and it gives almost no page time to what anyone wants and why - the axis Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 both score on. The reader's children's-register anchors bracket this from above rather than support it: Narnia 67 was docked for exactly 'lacks higher things to think about', and Male zeny 79 shows the register costs little only when characters carry the book, which they do not here. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:childrens because register alone would not push it this far down; it is the total absence of anything to think about over a form that suspends the character tests. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

t: Kudy kam s kapackou (Trip mit Tropf)
why: The idea is nameable and the handling is what earns the points: a child's long illness, never named on the page, carried entirely by concrete detail - a drip stand dragged across a continent, hair loss, nosebleeds, IV bags freezing - so it stands for any chronic illness rather than being a lesson about one. And the shape is the one the reader has explicitly said he prefers: two unlike creatures who owe each other something, not solo endurance. His Martian 82 note says outright that the sustained loneliness was not a theme worth enjoying and that Project Hail Mary 92 beats it on having a companion instead of isolation; this book is on the companion side of that line, with a code of obligation as the reason they travel together. What keeps it below the line is form and register. It is 192 pages of full-colour comics with pop-culture gags and cinematic pastiche, so the page time on what either character actually wants is thin by prose standards, which is what the reader weighs heaviest. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:motives because the illness handled without naming it is the thing that would stay with him, and the friendship, while the engine, is worked in gags more than in interiority. Occult status is unexamined at this exit and nothing raises it.

t: Ledni medvidek (Little Polar Bear and the Husky Pup (Kleiner Eisbaer, lass mich nicht allein!))
why: A watercolour picture book of roughly 32 pages: a polar bear cub rescues a stranded sled-dog pup and walks him home. The reader's own scale for this axis puts a picture book in the 30s or 40s, and that is what this is - not a short chapter book but a read-aloud with a few sentences a page. Nothing here reaches for what Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 both have, an idea that survives the page count; kindness to an animal that could have been dangerous is a sentiment, not something to think about afterwards. Reviewers of the English editions note the series repeats one shape - Lars leaves home, gets lost, makes an animal friend, returns - which is the opposite of a premise whose consequences are worked out. Leaned on axis:childrens rather than axis:ideas because the form is what fixes the ceiling; a picture book cannot be argued up on ideas it has no room for. Occult status is unexamined at this exit and is not in doubt from the annotation.

Unusually for a gate-4 exit I can name the idea: a forest is an old organism with its own rules and breath, and looking after one means learning to listen to it rather than stripping it and then failing to stop the calamity - and it is decorated with real standing, winning Zlata stuha 2024 in both the literary and the art category. I am still writing the lower band rather than the default, and the reason is form, not the absence of an idea: this is a 72-page large-format author's picture book for readers of six and up, and the reader's own scale puts a picture book in the 30s or 40s, while the short books that score - The Little Prince 82, Animal Farm 78 - are ideas an adult reads for himself, not captions to illustrations. So axis:childrens carries the number. The poetic text may be set as verse, which would cost again after Havran 40; I could not settle that, hence the risk. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

The positive case is real: an all-ages quest fantasy with a warmly reviewed heroine and a friendship that critics single out as the thing the book is actually about, which is closer to the motive-over-action axis that tops the log than most of what fills this register. But the form is a graphic novel, so the interiority that separates Red Rising 95 from Golden Son 92 has almost no room on the page, and the premise - stop the mythic bird that stole the sun - is a quest errand rather than an idea worked out, so axis:ideas belongs in the doubt. The Unfinished Tales 69 comparison is the honest one: attractive material that does not add up to something to think about. A sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log - Hitchhiker's 83 falls to 70 for the continuations - and it resumes directly after a battle rather than re-establishing its situation, which is the reader's most reliable failure mode. Leaned on axis:ideas over axis:worldbuilding because Irpa is inventive but the reader does not pay for invention alone. Occult status is unexamined at this exit; the annotation's 'water spirit' and future-seeing Arsai would be the things to check.

t: Lucinka a kouzelny oslik (Lucy (Anne Booth's Christmas animal-rescue series) - exact original title unconfirmed)
why: There is no idea here I can name, and that is the finding rather than a gap in my research. The form is a short illustrated Christmas story for children just starting to read independently - simple language, very short chapters, craft and animal-care activity pages at the back - so the character and emotion tests are suspended, and the suspension removes penalties without adding anything. What is left is a wish granted by a magic object so a baby animal and a farm's finances both come right by Christmas Day, which is a want satisfied rather than a want examined, the reader's heaviest axis idle. The log puts a ceiling on this directly: The Little Prince reaches 82 because the ideas carry it despite a child lead, Narnia pays a little at 67, and the reader's own scale places a picture-level book in the thirties or forties. This sits nearer that end than Narnia's. I leaned on ideas and on how juvenile the telling is because at this register nothing else is doing any work.

t: Lucinka a ztracene stenatko (Lucy (Anne Booth's Christmas animal-rescue series) - exact original title unconfirmed)
why: No idea I can name, which is itself the finding, and the form is a short illustrated Christmas story for children just learning to read alone - simple language, very short chapters, activity pages at the back. That suspends the character and emotion tests, and the suspension only removes penalties; it never adds points. The plot is a lost puppy searched for and found, so nothing is worked out and nobody's motive is in question, which leaves the axis the reader weights heaviest completely idle. The log fixes the range: The Little Prince gets to 82 only because the ideas carry it, Narnia pays a little at 67 for lacking higher things to think about, and the reader's own scale puts a picture-level book in the thirties or forties. This belongs at that end. I leaned on ideas and on how juvenile the telling is because at this register nothing else is doing any work.

This is the volume named after the quarrel itself - lusy are the lots by which shares of the communal woods were allotted - so what the book is about is a village lawsuit, resolved by a count's intervention. I can name that, but I doubt it is a higher thing to think about, and no nameable idea is the strongest separator in the data. It is also a sequel that continues figures established earlier rather than restarting, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's Guide fell from 83 to 70, and Unfinished Tales sits 12 under The Silmarillion for pieces that do not stand on their own. Add the form - 1920s rural realism as regional chronicle, in Chod dialect - and a thin story across many pages is the reader's stated penalty term, the one that cost The Lord of the Rings its margin over The Hobbit. Against Exodus 68 and Quo Vadis 66, the reader's two historical settles, this lands at or below the line. No hard filter is inherited here: nothing anywhere in this trilogy carries an exclusion, so the dependency question does not arise as a taste matter, only as a reading-order fact. I leaned on ideas rather than on density because it is the substance rather than the pacing that I doubt most.

A picture book for ages nought to six: an orange panda cub is rejected by the black-and-white pandas, walks through the forest meeting ibises, monkeys and tigers, and comes home to his mother. The reader profile puts a picture book in the thirties or forties on register alone, and the log gives no route out of that here: Maly princ 82 and Hobit 84 are the proof that a short and simple book can score high, and both do it on an idea a grown reader takes away, whereas belonging is stated on the last page rather than worked out. Narnia 67 sits below the propose line for a juvenile cast with nothing higher to think about and is a novel. So axis:ideas carries the number down and axis:childrens sets where it lands. One source at the below-the-line gate, so occult status is unexamined, though nothing in the record suggests any arises.

The inherited exclusion does not apply. The excluded titles by this author are standalone adult novels with their own leads and their own mythologies; this is a separate YA science-fantasy line with a new lead, Joey Harker, and a premise introduced from scratch, so nothing here depends on the excluded material and the taste filter has nothing to travel along. Judged on its own, it exits at gate 4. The premise I can name - every alternate version of one boy conscripted into the same war - is a recruitment hook for an adventure plot rather than something the book works out, and the lead's decisive ability arrives as an innate gift, which is the axis Divergent 58 was marked down on. Against Ranger's Apprentice 74, easy to read with not much to think about, this is shorter, thinner and more juvenile, so I would list axis:ideas under risks and stop here. Consequence of the ladder: the occult question is left unexamined, and the HEX faction is described as gothically magical, which is exactly where it would need looking.

t: Mia a svetlovladci (Mia and the Lightcasters)
why: The strongest thing in it is the lead's own reversal: a girl who wanted to be an umbra tamer, then met one on the Nightmare Plains and was frightened out of it, has to go back to the thing she is afraid of to get her parents out. Reviewers make that arc the centre, and a protagonist who is both interesting and worth rooting for is the axis that separated Sunrise on the Reaping 87 from Ballad 65 by twenty-two points, so this is not nothing. What keeps it under the line is that the book beyond the arc is a rescue quest with a hooded overlord, and I cannot name what it leaves behind - the same place Narnia 67 stalls. The city thrown into permanent night and the creatures that bond one-to-one with a human are declared concretely enough to invite the self-consistency audit that cost Harry Potter 51, and I did not research whether the book carries it. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist because the lead is the part that works; it is the absence of a higher thing to think about that fixes the number. Occult status is unexamined at this exit and it is the live doubt - taming shadow creatures and a title built on 'casters' is the shape that still vetoes if it reads as spellcasting in the witchcraft mould, and costs a graded deduction if it is an invented rite enacted on the page, and Percy Jackson 57 shows what an actual pantheon costs.

An official game tie-in: three teenagers thrown together on community service find an old computer with a server full of riddles left by a hidden figure and follow them into the game world. By the accounts of readers who liked it, the best thing in the book is the offscreen material - three kids with nothing in common, each carrying real worries outside the group - and that is the axis this log rewards most. But it is licensed work built to send players back to the game, the puzzle chain is the plot, and there is no idea that outlives the last page, which is the standard reason a competent book settles just under the line. Ready Player One 55 is the caution about a book whose substance is references to a game; this is cleaner and gentler than that and carries none of the crudeness that sank it, but it is not carrying more either. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist, since the characters are the part that works. Three alternating viewpoints are a real opening risk and were not examined, and neither was the occult question, because this exited at the below-the-line gate.

A mass-market medical thriller, and the premise is declared very precisely, which in this log adds obligation rather than credit: a chemical damages the brain cells that suppress memories of past lives, so what looks like a personality disorder after surgery is a previous life speaking. Declaring a mechanism that specific means the book owes the consequences - if past lives are chemically recoverable then history, law and medicine all change - and a chase novel that ends up hunting an eyewitness to events of two thousand years ago is plainly not going to pay that. Divergent 58 and the Mortal Engines 55 abandonment are both premise-logic failures of exactly this shape. So the idea is the whole selling point and I would list it under risks, which exits at gate 4. Not a gate 1 reject: the doctor is chasing an antagonist he has already identified rather than establishing who did it. Occult is unexamined by design and stays a live risk, since recovered past lives are a real-world occult practice however pharmacological the account given for them.

The one genuinely new thought here is worth naming: a virus makes human blood lethal to vampires, so the whole society reorganises around an expensive synthetic substitute, and the class system that follows from who can afford it is the setting. That is a premise with consequences and it is why this is not lower. But the reviews that praise the book settle on frothy, angst-y fun as the verdict - the first half is relationship drama, the body does not turn up until past the midpoint, the rising action and climax are crammed into what is left, and the central relationship runs on miscommunication. So the idea is present without being worked out, which is the standard reason a book stalls just under the line. Divergent 58 is the warning about a society engineered around a premise that does not cohere; this is nowhere near that bad, but neither is it Old Man's War 87, where each consequence followed from the last. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:worldbuilding because the setting is the good part and the follow-through is the doubt. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, so the occult question is unexamined. REVISED 2026-09-02 for the new axis:same-sex-romance (prominence heavy), was [58, 68]. GRADED, NOT REJECTED, and deliberately so: both leads are girls and one is an out lesbian with the establishment's hostility to it a stated theme, but a conspiracy and a body drive the second half, so premise versus thread is genuinely unclear. The standing guard applies - grade it and say so, because a wrong reject is unrecoverable. Heavy end of the graded range. Magnitude is not separable from the single data point: Caropisci 67 lost about thirteen points to this, the hierofant rite and the portrayal warning together, so this dock states a direction and a prominence tier, not a measured size.

The positive case is that almost nothing here is action: four days of negotiation in which two men have to decide what they are willing to betray, and the book spends its pages on why rather than on what happens. That is the axis that put Speaker for the Dead at 90 and Mockingjay at 91 - motives and understanding over set pieces. And it leaves a real argument behind, that the agreement bought a year Britain needed, which is a nameable idea rather than a mood, the thing that lifted Animal Farm to 78 and Labyrint to 70. The opening is one concrete situation, an anniversary dinner interrupted by a summons, so the confusion filter that ended Guards! Guards! at 30 does not fire even though a second viewpoint follows. Docked for two things. Critics who liked the book still call the English lead two-dimensional and the German the more interesting of the two, and a flat lead is the drag that revised Artemis to 69 and separated the two Collins prequels by 22 points. And the outcome is known from the title down, so tension has to come from character rather than from plot, where the reader's historical reads settle - Exodus 68, Quo Vadis 66 - rather than climb. I leaned on ideas and motives rather than on worldbuilding, which has nothing to do here.

The form itself is one this reader has scored at both extremes, so it decides nothing: Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75 against The Diary of a Young Girl 40, and what separated them was whether the account genuinely examines what is true and shows how another group experiences the world. Reviewers here describe a raw, uncensored confession that opens the door into an anorexic's view of herself - the second half of that requirement - but they explicitly say it is not an examination and offers no method or reflection, and one reader reports the diary sections do not connect to each other, the same fault that made Unfinished Tales 69 the lowest Tolkien. That doubt about axis:ideas is the gate-4 test and it carries the number; I did not lean on axis:motives, which the book supplies in quantity but without perspective on them. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

The starting situation is single and concrete - a girl whose boyfriend has died of a heart condition, writing him letters she cannot send - and grief handled through what a character wants is the axis that tops this log, with Pycha a predsudek 75 confirming that a relationship as the central subject costs nothing. What stops it is the same thing readers name repeatedly: the serious opening turns into a light summer romance, the outcome is obvious two-thirds through, and the ending is unclear. That is a book that does not carry its own premise to a conclusion, so I would list axis:ideas under risks, which is the gate-4 test, and that doubt carries the number rather than axis:motives. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

t: Myska a medved a jejich cesta za poznanim
why: A set of linked fairy tales for the youngest readers, 80 large-format illustrated pages, each tale ending in a piece of wisdom about courage, kindness, honesty and fear. Both gate-4 conditions hold together: there is no single premise to work out, so there is no axis:ideas to lean on, and the form suspends the character tests without adding anything - the suspension only removes penalties, and the short books that score in this log, The Little Prince 82 and Animal Farm 78, are canonical for their ideas rather than for their length. The register pushes the same way, well past the point where The Chronicles of Narnia 67 paid for having children at the centre. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

I cannot name an idea this book leaves behind. It is 112 pages of walking sketches and the author's own landscape photographs, and the strongest claim made for it is that it captures silence, light and the smell of the forest vividly - the log is explicit that beautifully written is not an idea, and the one reader verdict I found is that the book is average, neither offends nor excites. The short form removes the character and emotion penalties but the log is equally explicit that the suspension never adds points, and the canonical short books that score well score for their ideas: Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 both have a premise, and this has a place. That is why the low band rather than the default one - no nameable idea, and a form of occasional pieces that leaves nothing for the character tests to grip. Density is the risk behind even this range: description with little story is the recorded penalty term, and here there is no story at all to spread. The occult screen word is a false positive; nature writing about silence and humility is not a practice on the page.

The premise is genuinely inventive - an SS unit arriving in the Middle Ages with modern armour is a real what-if - and the log rewards a premise whose consequences are worked out, which is what put Project Hail Mary 92 above The Martian 82. But the leads are a German tank ace and an Ahnenerbe officer of the SS order, and the book's own copy sells the spiritual change of a man who became an ardent adherent of an extreme ideology. That is the single most expensive thing this reader has recorded: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 lost 22 points to the identical author, world and form purely because the lead was a man descending into evil with nobody to root for, and that book was otherwise excellent. Here the same penalty lands on a short novel by an unknown whose reader reception is largely negative - one summary being an imaginative plot not well used - so there is no craft above it to absorb the loss, which is why I am writing the low band rather than the default one and why the protagonist axis alone carries the number. Worldbuilding sits in risks because a declared time gate and modern weapons in a medieval world is exactly the kind of promise Mortal Engines 55 was abandoned for not honouring. The occult question is deliberately unexamined at this exit, and it is a live one - an Ahnenerbe egyptologist in a secret order of the SS is where real-world occultism would sit if it is enacted at all - so axis:occult stays in deps for a later pass.

A richly illustrated book explicitly for beginning readers - Czech reviewers report an eight-year-old weak reader finishing it in two days - about a boy who discovers he has grandparents, that they live and work at a cemetery, and that a family of hungry vampires is hiding there. It has a good concrete opening, one situation and a strong hook, which is the shape the log wants and which The Gunslinger 30 and The Colour of Magic 30 lacked. But that is not enough to reach the line at this reading level.
