The form is a first-chapter book, so the test of what characters want and why cannot be run on it, there is no idea an adult reader carries away, and one Czech reader specifically calls the story abbreviated and mildly illogical towards the end, which is the self-consistency objection the log rates heaviest. The reader profile puts work this juvenile in the 30s or 40s and Narnia 67 is already discounted for child leads plus nothing higher to think about. Leaned on axis:childrens rather than axis:ideas because the audience and length are established facts while the reported plot logic comes from a single reader, so that stays a risk. Occult unexamined at this exit; garlic and vampires are folklore furniture here rather than a practice I established.

t: Nezbedny myval (Nove pribehy se stastnym koncem – Nezbedny myval)
why: A 136-page illustrated animal-rescue story for young readers, one of a numbered series the publisher sells as true stories from Czech nature: two children at their grandparents' track down what is stealing the eggs and find a raccoon on the roof. The positive is that it opens on one concrete domestic situation and stays there, which is the shape the log wants. Beyond that the form decides it. The series title guarantees the ending, so nothing is at stake; the reading level is such that no test of what characters want and why can be run; and what the book leaves behind is a fact about invasive species, which is instruction rather than an idea whose consequences are worked out - Animal Farm 78 is what a short book scores when the idea is the book. The reader profile puts work this juvenile in the 30s or 40s, and Little Women 79, the ceiling for axis:childrens, is a full novel about people. Leaned on axis:childrens rather than axis:ideas because there is a nameable point here, thin as it is, so the audience and register are the honest carrier of the number. Occult unexamined and not plausibly at issue in a realistic nature story.

A 56-page illustrated book of rhymes for small car-lovers, in which a little car and its girl driver go on outings, rescue a ski-lift operator and meet aliens, with tasks for parents and children at the back. Two things settle the band without further research. The form is verse, and verse is the one form the log penalises outright - Havran 40 ties the lowest completed score and the reader named the form itself as a cause - so this cannot be treated as short prose that merely fails to earn points. And the audience is pre-school: the reader profile puts a picture book in the 30s or 40s, and the traffic-safety lesson at the back is instruction, not an idea the book leaves behind. I leaned on axis:childrens rather than axis:verse because the audience is established from publisher copy while the verse form comes from retailer and reader description, so it is the less certain of the two and belongs in risks - if it is confirmed as verse throughout, the number should sit at the bottom of the range or below it.

This is not a book to be read so much as a reading exercise: three traditional tales, 70 pages, in which dozens of words are replaced by pictures so an adult reads aloud and a pre-literate child supplies the pictured word. Gate 4 is decided the moment the form is established. There is no idea to name - the content is Red Riding Hood and the gingerbread man retold at the simplest possible level - and the pictogram form removes any test of what characters want and why, the axis that carries the top of the log. The reader profile puts a picture book in the 30s or 40s and this sits at the extreme end of that: Little Women 79 is the ceiling that axis:childrens can reach and it is a full novel about people, while The Little Prince 82 is short but is carried by its thoughts. Neither defence is available here. I leaned on axis:childrens rather than axis:ideas because it is the form and audience, not a weak idea, that fix the number - the book is doing a different job from the one the score measures. Occult unexamined and not plausibly at issue in traditional Czech nursery tales.

t: O princezne naruby (Prinsessa joka lahti kalppimaan)
why: A forty-page illustrated fairy-tale subversion for readers from four: a princess refuses the marriage her parents arranged and walks through the classic tales telling their heroines they need not wait to be picked. The idea is nameable, the jokes are pitched at two audiences at once, and the illustrations hide extra ones - that is the best of it. It is still a picture book, and the axis puts a picture book in the thirties or forties on register and audience alone. A single reversal repeated across a set of borrowed tales is a joke structure rather than a premise whose consequences get worked out, so it does nothing like what Animal Farm 78 does in a book barely longer. Leaned on axis:childrens. The curse hanging over the kingdom is fairy-tale furniture played for comedy rather than reverence, which the prophecy axis grades cheaply. Exited at the below-the-line gate, so the occult question was not examined.

t: O vlkovi se sklerozou a jine pohadky
why: A collection of upside-down nonsense retellings of Czech and classic fairy tales - a wolf who forgets to eat Red Riding Hood, an earthworm that goes to school. Both of gate 4's triggers are present: the form is a short collection with no single premise, so axis:short-idea-driven suspends the character tests and adds nothing, and the nonsense register means there is no idea to name at all - the point is the joke each time. That is the lower band on its own terms, and it is where the reader profile places work this far toward a children's book: The Little Prince 82 is short and pays nothing because the thoughts carry it, whereas this offers inversion rather than thought. Unfinished Tales 69 already shows what disconnected pieces cost even from an author the reader likes at 84. I leaned on axis:ideas because it is the only axis a book of this form can be judged on; there is no protagonist across the collection to lean on instead. The only reception I found is a handful of reader ratings on Czech aggregators, and one academic thesis treats it under Czech nonsense writing - no professional review exists, so the number is thinly sourced by design at this exit. Occult unexamined.

t: Obycejny muz (An Ordinary Man: An Autobiography)
why: This is the shape of memoir that has worked twice in the log rather than the one that failed. Son of Hamas 75 is the direct anchor - a first-person account from inside a violent, ethnically split society by a man who acted against his own side - and Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 shows what lifts that form higher: genuine insight into how another group experiences the world. Both are on offer here, and the idea is nameable in a phrase: that the only weapon available was talk, favours and bribery, and that a hotel manager's professional habits were what turned out to matter. It also scores on the axis that separates Project Hail Mary 92 from The Martian 82 - saving other people rather than surviving alone - which is the reader's stated preference and pulls against the bleakness of the subject. Bleakness itself is only a mild discount in this log. I leaned on the subject as protagonist, interesting and clearly worth rooting for, rather than on the form, because the form earns nothing by itself and because the account's factual reliability is the one thing that could collapse the estimate: the promotional copy alone varies tenfold on how many people sheltered at the hotel, and the book's version of events has been contested. That is axis:memoir-form under risks, and if it fires it takes away exactly the rigour that earned the Qureshi score.

There is a nameable tension here and it is a decent one: a woman who carries the national-revival ideal set against villagers whose real quarrel is over shares of the communal forest, so the book asks what an idea is worth to people with material interests. What makes me stop is the form. This is 1920s rural realism written as a regional chronicle - interlocking village figures, Chod dialect, ethnographic detail - and a thin story spread across many pages is the penalty term the reader states outright, the same charge that cost The Lord of the Rings its difference from The Hobbit at 84 and dropped Les Miserables to 71 for digressions. A chronicle with many figures also puts the opening at risk, and confusion in the first chapters is the one failure that has actually ended books here at 30. Set against the reader's historical reads, Exodus 68 and Quo Vadis 66, this sits at or under that line rather than above it. I leaned on density rather than on ideas because the idea does exist - it is the delivery I doubt.

t: Paradni pejsci (Perfect Puppies: Alfie the Cheeky Puppy)
why: An early chapter book from age six in a franchise series: a girl new in town is matched with a puppy at a shelter where a magical lead decides which dog is yours, and the plot is the dog's mishaps plus saving the shelter from closure. The shape is the thing the log punishes twice over - a template that swaps in a different animal each time gives axis:character-differentiation nothing to work with, and there is no idea to name at all. Hranicaruv ucen 74 marks the top of what an easy juvenile series reaches when there is not much to think about, and that is fourteen books of genuine plotting; Narnia 67 is below the propose line for a juvenile cast plus no higher thing to think about. So axis:ideas carries the number down and axis:childrens sets the band. One source at the below-the-line gate, so occult status is unexamined - the magical lead is asserted rather than operated, but I did not test it.

The form is the finding here, and it is the one form this log records as costing rather than merely failing to earn: the book is a tale told in linked poems, and Havran 40 ties the lowest completed score with the reader naming verse itself as a cause, independent of what the poem was about. On top of that it is a didactic animal story for young readers - a one-eyed dog learns that what is different need not be frightening - which is a moral stated rather than an idea worked out, and both audience and register sit at the juvenile end. That combination is exactly the lower below-the-line band: a form that carries a penalty, a childrens register, and no idea to name. Leaned on axis:verse, because the same story in prose would sit higher; axis:childrens is a compounding deduction, not the thing carrying the number. Exited at the below-the-line gate, so the occult question was not examined.

t: Plasmyska (Plasmyska - Jak maly mysak hledal odvahu)
why: Fifty-six small-format pages, eight short chapters, each opening on a double-page illustration: a mouse everyone mocks for being frightened goes looking for courage and meets rats, hares and weasels. The premise is literal-minded in a way that is worth naming - the child is told courage is a thing you collect - and that is a lesson rather than an idea, which is the finding gate four asks for. Narnia 67 already sits under the propose line on a juvenile cast plus nothing higher to think about, and this is far shorter and simpler; Male zeny 79 is the ceiling on a juvenile register and it is bought entirely with characters, which eight illustrated chapters cannot buy. So axis:ideas carries the number and axis:childrens sets the band. One source at the below-the-line gate, so occult status is unexamined.

Ninety-six pages, eight comforting fairy tales for small children, each ending happily by design - a friendly witch, a kind old man, household objects that come alive to help. Two things compound. A collection has no single premise for axis:ideas to lean on, and the stated aim here is reassurance rather than anything to think about, which is the exact fault that put Narnia 67 below the propose line in a much more substantial book. Disconnectedness also costs directly in this log: Unfinished Tales 69 is the lowest Tolkien precisely because the pieces are not connected to each other. Male zeny 79 shows a juvenile register can be paid off by characters, but eight separate twelve-page casts cannot do that. So axis:ideas carries the number and axis:childrens sets the band. One source at the below-the-line gate, so occult status is unexamined - and the task line flags a witch, so that gate is genuinely open, not merely skipped.

A 128-page collection of humorous fairy tales for the youngest readers by an author known for children's theatre, framed by fates gathering at a small boy's cot. Both of gate 4's triggers hold. The form is a short collection with no single premise, so axis:short-idea-driven suspends the character tests and adds nothing - the log's own case against unconnected pieces is Unfinished Tales 69, and that was from an author scored 84 elsewhere. And there is no idea to name at all: the stated organising principle is humour for small children. That combination is the lower band by definition, and the reader profile puts work this far toward a children's book in the 30s or 40s, whereas The Little Prince 82 pays nothing only because the thoughts carry it. I leaned on axis:ideas because a collection has no continuous protagonist to lean on instead. Reception is a couple of reader comments on Czech aggregators, one of which found some tales fine and others odd; no professional review exists. Occult unexamined at this exit - the framing device is fate-spinners foretelling a life, which is worth a look if the axis is ever bumped.

The hook is genuinely good - an epidemic in 1908 Siberia in which tens of thousands die in a loving embrace, and a doctor of experimental medicine sent to stop it - and a premise whose consequences get worked out is what earns Project Hail Mary 92. The trouble is that the one professional review describes a book running six genres at once (Siberian horror, a crashed alien entity, viral thriller, crime story, a Frankenstein variation, harder SF) and concludes it does not hold together and would have been far better as one of them. Self-consistency is the axis the reader audits hardest, and incoherence assembled from borrowed pieces is what sank Divergent 58; that doubt, not the setting, carries this number, and it means I would put axis:ideas in risks too, which is the gate-4 exit. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

Identified with confidence: the CooBoo 2024 volume with Quinn and Matilda is Co bylo dosud ztraceno, and the task annotation matches its publisher copy line for line. It is YA hidden-world fantasy - a magical realm called Okraj with fairies, gargoyles, a sphinx and the ghosts of historical figures - and it runs on romance plus a chain of secrets, which is exactly where gate 4 bites: the blurb's own framing is that every revealed secret hides another riddle, and a book whose engine is the next reveal rather than a premise worked out has no axis:ideas to lean on. Narnia 67 is the anchor: liked, competent, and marked down for children as the main characters and for lacking higher things to think about, and this asks less of the reader than Narnia does. Two alternating narrators are declared, which the log treats as a real hazard - Guards! Guards! 30 and The Colour of Magic 30 both died on several lines starting at once - but here the two POVs are a stated device rather than an unreadable opening, so I did not lean on it. I leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:worldbuilding because the hidden world is charming and consistent enough on the evidence, and it is the absence of anything left behind that fixes the band. Occult is genuinely live here and deliberately unexamined at this exit: fairies and talking statues are invented furniture, but I did not establish whether any rite is performed on the page.

A portal-fantasy adventure for eight to ten year olds that closes its trilogy: two children go back through a music box into Rondo to face the Blue Queen, her dragon and a prophecy. The positive is real - one concrete situation, a declared antagonist, friendship and courage as the subject, and reviewers call the ending satisfying and cleverly assembled - and the log likes exactly that combination, since the Hobbit 84 note is friendship and easy reading with no downsides. But gate 4 fires. I cannot name an idea it leaves behind beyond bravery, which is the commonest reason a competent book stalls, and an adult reviewer specifically reports easy deus ex machina resolutions and a seer's prediction that is too obvious - that is the self-consistency objection the log rates heaviest, the same one that cost Divergent 58 and ended Mortal Engines 55. Narnia 67 is the direct anchor: children as leads and not much to think about, and this asks less. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:worldbuilding because the worldbuilding concern is reported second-hand from a single reader and would only push the number lower, so it belongs in risks. Prophecy is present and graded on reverence, not resemblance, so it is not a filter. Occult unexamined at this exit and it matters here: seven witches and wizards are named allies.

t: Pribeh Ellie (Ellie's Story: A Dog's Purpose Puppy Tale)
why: The one thing here that is genuinely worth knowing is procedural: how a search-and-rescue dog is actually trained from puppyhood, which the annotation makes the book's explicit second purpose. Real information counts for something - the reader's top non-fiction result, Seeking Allah Finding Jesus at 91, earned it by examining what is true - but a training manual folded into a dog's life story is information, not an idea, and I would put ideas in risks, so this exits here. The register costs too: an illustrated middle-grade chapter book told by the dog from birth aims below Narnia, which paid a little at 67 for lacking higher things to think about, and well below Ranger's Apprentice at 74. A dog narrator also cannot do the reader's heaviest axis, page time on what people want and why, because it does not understand the humans it reports on. I leaned on ideas and on how juvenile the telling is rather than on the protagonist, since Ellie is competent and sympathetic and is not what holds the number down.

t: Pribeh Lily (Lily's Story: A Puppy Tale)
why: The book has one clean device and I can state it: the smallest puppy in the litter and the smallest child in the family are the same story told twice, so being underestimated turns out to be the qualification. That is a neat structure but it is a lesson rather than an idea worked out, and I would put ideas in risks, which is what decides this exit. The register is the other cost - an illustrated chapter book for eight to twelve with a discussion and activity guide at the back - and the reader grades that: Ranger's Apprentice sits at 74 for being easy to read with not much to think about, Narnia at 67 for lacking higher things to think about, and this aims younger and lower than either while Little Women's 79 shows what the ceiling needs, characters strong enough to carry a book with no premise. A dog narrator also spends its page time on what is happening rather than on what anyone wants and why, which is the axis the reader weighs heaviest. I leaned on ideas and on how juvenile the telling is rather than on the protagonist, who is likeable enough that she is not the problem.

t: Pribeh ukryty v notach (The Story Orchestra: The Magic Flute)
why: This is a sound-button picture book for ages three and up: about ten illustrated spreads, each with a press-to-play ten-second orchestral clip, plus a short life of Mozart and a glossary of musical terms at the back. The reader's scale puts a picture book in the 30s or 40s and nothing here argues it up - the object is the music, so the text is a compressed retelling with no room to give any character a want, which is the axis Speaker for the Dead 90 and Mockingjay 91 both score on. It is also a retelling of somebody else's work rather than a book with a premise of its own, and the reader's Unfinished Tales 69 note shows how little credit fragmentary or derivative material earns even from an author he otherwise rates. Leaned on axis:childrens over axis:ideas because the form decides this outright; there is no page count in which an idea could be developed. Occult status is unexamined at this exit - the annotation names a sorcerer and 'magie', which in a Mozart retelling is stage business, but I did not verify it.

t: Priserne pribehy z Cerne lodi (Tales of Terror from the Black Ship)
why: A framed collection of maritime horror tales for younger readers: two sick children at a cliff-top inn are told grisly stories by a sailor through a storm, and a twist at dawn reverses the frame. The frame is a genuine positive - it opens on one concrete situation, which is the shape the log rewards (Hitchhiker's 83 was credited for the house and then the Earth rather than fanning out) - and reviewers agree the stories are linked more tightly than the author's earlier collection and that the payoff lands. But gate 4 fires on both of its triggers at once. The form is a story collection, so axis:short-idea-driven suspends the character tests without adding anything, and Unfinished Tales 69 is the log's own verdict on pieces that are not logically connected to each other. And I cannot name an idea it leaves behind: the tales are engineered so that one small treachery brings tragedy, which is a mechanism, not a thought - Animal Farm 78 is what a short book scores when it does give you something to think about. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:bleakness because grisly is not the same as sustained bleakness and the log rates that objection mildly anyway. Occult is unexamined at this exit and is a real risk: apparitions and supernatural revenants are the substance of the stories, and Havran 40 shows what questioning the dead costs.

The idea I can name is the engineer's complicity - a man who wanted spaceflight and got a terror weapon - and the counter-battery mathematics done with slide rules against a five-day clock, and I do doubt it holds up, which is why I stopped here. Reviewers who praise the pacing still call the book morally simple and the engineer's remorse too convenient, and a moral question conceded rather than worked out is what leaves a competent book in the 60s, the position of Exodus 68 and Quo Vadis 66. The second complaint is worse for this reader: the two strands are unequal, the English strand described as wooden and its late twist foreseeable, and uneven characters are what cost The Silmarillion nothing only because it never pretended to have leads. Well researched and fast is not a positive case on its own - Ranger's Apprentice 74 was easy to read with not much to think about and still only reached the B band. I leaned on ideas rather than on the protagonist because there are two leads and the argument is about what the book concludes, not about who carries it. Honest overspend: I read two sources against the one this exit allows.

An 84-page early reader in Albatros's Druhe cteni line, stated age seven and up: a second-grader in love with a Croatian classmate who is going home for the summer. The material is genuinely about what a child wants and why, which is the axis the log rewards most - Little Women 79 is a domestic story with no premise to work out that still clears the line on characters alone. But that ceiling was reached by a full novel, and eighty large-print pages for seven-year-olds cannot do the same work, so the form removes the test rather than passing it, and there is no idea an adult reader would carry away. The reader profile puts books this far toward a children's book in the 30s or 40s and Narnia 67 already pays for child leads plus nothing higher to think about; this is a much shorter and simpler book than Narnia. Leaned on axis:childrens rather than axis:protagonist because Oliver is a perfectly good small lead - it is the register and audience that fix the band. Occult unexamined at this exit: the blurb ends on the line that Marica is a witch, which on the evidence I have reads as a child's nickname or a light fancy rather than practice, but I did not establish it.

A 272-page middle-grade fantasy for ages 10-12, so the character tests are not suspended and there is something to grade: twin siblings who cannot understand each other, one training as a spring-guardian and one refusing to, have to combine forces against a revived sea serpent. Sibling friction that has to be resolved before the plot can move is at least motive-shaped, which is the axis Mockingjay 91 tops the log on, and the reader's own note on The Martian 82 says companionship beats solo survival. Against that, I cannot name an idea it leaves behind - it is a save-the-underwater-kingdom errand with a deadline - and axis:ideas in the doubt is what puts this under the line, the same place Narnia 67 sits for the same reason. It also alternates two viewpoints, and a divided opening is the reader's single most reliable failure mode. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:worldbuilding: an undersea city with declared ice magic invites the self-consistency audit that sank Mortal Engines 55, but I did not research it at this exit. Occult status is likewise unexamined, and it is the live question here - the annotation has gods reviving the serpent and a child practising ice magic, and Percy Jackson 57 shows an actual pantheon costs the reader real points.

It clears gate 4 on a nameable idea that the plot is actually built out of, not just themed around: the lie a lonely man tells his own child to spare her, and what it costs him to make the lie true. That is a want with a deadline attached - the daughter is coming - so the book is motives and consequences rather than events, which is the axis that tops this log. The lead is the strong part on both halves of the protagonist test: interesting, because the second timeline gives him a whole life arriving from Jamaica into a hostile London and nursing a wife through dementia, and easy to root for. Saturnin 78 and Male zeny 79 are the anchors for how high a warm character novel with no premise to work out can reach here, and both are above the propose line. Deductions keep it out of the S band: reviewers call the campaign plot far-fetched and the present-day half fable-like, the neighbour who triggers everything reads flat beside him, and the resolution is engineered. Bleakness is present but is the mildest recorded objection and the book is companionship rather than solitude, which is the direction this reader prefers. I leaned on the protagonist rather than on the idea because the idea is a good hook rather than a hard argument, and the number would not survive a thin lead.

The material is congenial: The Lord of the Rings 84 and The Silmarillion 80 are both in the A band, and a reviewer credits this author with real attention to the legendarium rather than parody, so the setting itself costs nothing. The number is carried by axis:protagonist, and it is carried downward: the one substantial Czech review of it calls the heroine the most unlikeable she has met, and a lead you cannot root for is the single most expensive fault in this log - it separated The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 from Sunrise on the Reaping 87 by 22 points on that alone, same author and same world. A retelling also has no premise of its own to work out, so there is no axis:ideas to lean on the other way, which is the gate-4 test. Exited there on one source, leaving the occult question unexamined.

t: Sen o lidske tvari (Sen o lidske tvari)
why: The premise is one concrete situation and a good one: a boy raised to accept the regime falls for the daughter of a family the regime dispossessed, and has to decide what he actually believes. Romance as the central subject costs nothing here - Pride and Prejudice 75 is entirely what characters want and why, which is the axis that tops the log - and the political education plot has somewhere real to go. What I cannot support is that the idea gets worked out rather than asserted: this is a 2024 novel from a very small press with no critical reception at all, and the only thing I could confirm beyond the library annotation is that the book and its publisher exist. Exodus 68 and Quo Vadis 66 are where competent historical novels land in this log even with reputations behind them, so the honest range is under the line and axis:ideas is what carries it. The protagonist sits in risks because a young man who is mainly acted on by his times is the Oliver Twist 57 failure, and nothing I found tells me which way this one goes.

t: Sipka a Koumes (Sipka a Koumes: Mise Egypt)
why: This is not a novel at all: 112 pages of attention and logic exercises for ages seven to eleven, written by a child neuropsychologist, in which the puzzles set the order the pages are read in and a medal is awarded at the end. The character rules are suspended because there is no continuous narrative to apply them to, and the profile is explicit that the suspension removes penalties without adding anything - so there is nothing left to earn a number with. Hranicaruv ucen 74 is the ceiling for easy juvenile reading with not much to think about, and that is real storytelling; an exercise book sits far under it. axis:ideas carries the number down and axis:childrens sets the band. One source at the below-the-line gate, so occult status is unexamined, though nothing in the record suggests any arises.

The positive case is the axis that tops this log: nearly all the page time goes to what these children want and why - a girl who wants to be educated by a father who does not think girls need it, a boy who wants not to be sent back to school, a cousin who wants to be worth something - and very little to what they do. It also leaves an idea behind rather than only events: what the war took from one generation, and what was refused to the clever girls of it. And the opening is the exact shape this reader needs, the opposite of the recorded DNFs - one concrete situation, a birth and a mother's death, a single legible thread from the first page. Against that, three real deductions. The story is thin for its span, roughly two decades in a short book of short episodic chapters, with reviewers calling the pacing awkward: that is the Lord of the Rings 84 complaint, where sparseness cancelled the reach. The register and audience are firmly childrens, which cost Narnia 67 a little - though unlike Narnia the higher things to think about are actually here. And the bleakness is real but distributed across the book rather than arriving at once, which is the mildest recorded objection. That lands it with Male zeny 79, a domestic story with no premise to work out that clears the line on characters alone. Leaned on axis:motives and axis:protagonist rather than axis:worldbuilding, which a realist family saga barely engages; axis:density is the axis that could pull it under. Infidelity was examined and is absent: the family's damage is a widowed father's indifference, not an affair. Sexual content is not the plot either - a young man's love for another man is one thread, treated as period hostility, and hostility and violence are not objections in this log.

t: Smrt je mym remeslem (Death Is My Trade (La mort est mon metier))
why: Everything that usually earns here is present. It is one concrete starting situation in one voice - a boy under an authoritarian, devout father who has decided he will be a priest - so the confusion filter that ended two books in the log does not fire. It is entirely motives: Merle's declared aim was to reconstruct how obedience replaced conscience, and he insisted the man was not a sadist, which is a harder and more interesting claim. The idea is nameable and lands hard - the section where the narrator solves the killing of the Jews as a technical problem, in units treated and output per hour. Against that sits the objection the log punishes most heavily after the hard filters. This is a first-person novel spent inside a man slowly becoming a mass murderer, with nobody to root for, and that is exactly what put The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 twenty-two points below the same author's other prequel on the protagonist alone. 1984 60 shows that sustained grimness costs on top of it. So the ideas are better than either of those books' and the lead is worse, and the two land it in the same region. I leaned on axis:protagonist rather than axis:ideas because the log is explicit that a repellent lead outranks a book's other strengths, and because leaning up on the strength while the lead is the visible problem is the documented way these predictions fail.

t: Space Wars (Space Wars: Gravity Squid (Beast Quest: Space Wars 2))
why: A 160-page illustrated adventure for early readers, a spin-off of a long monster-quest franchise and built to that franchise's formula: a creature arrives from deep space, the boy engineer defeats it, the next one arrives. There is no idea here to name at all, and the form removes the character tests rather than passing them, which is what the lower of the two below-the-line bands is for. Where this log rewards a childrens book it is for something the book adds - The Little Prince 82 for its thoughts, The Hobbit 84 for friendship and for having no downsides at all - and a franchise episode adds neither. A sequel too, and sequels are not safe bets here: Hitchhiker's 83 to 70. Leaned on axis:childrens because register and audience are the whole objection, not the plot. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, so the occult question was not examined.

t: Stroj na zuzu (Klub objevitelu: Stroj na zuzu)
why: A hundred-page illustrated adventure for readers from six - colour on every page, large type: a girl inventor gets stuck inside her own globe of amusements, is rescued by an airship captain who calls himself an explorer, and the two set out to find why the marshmallow machine has broken while pirate piranhas get in the way. There is no idea to name, and register and audience sit at the picture-book end of the axis, which together are the lower below-the-line band. This log does reward a childrens book that brings something of its own - The Little Prince 82 for its thoughts, The Hobbit 84 for friendship and for having no downsides - and a whimsical machine-fixing errand brings neither. Leaned on axis:childrens: the plot is not the objection, the audience is. Exited at the below-the-line gate, so the occult question was not examined.

Graded, not vetoed - the children's question always gets a number. The positive case is that it does not condescend about its subject: an eleven-year-old lands in Terezin and meets hunger, dirt, disease and fear, the real Petr Ginz appears, and the book closes with factual material, which is why teachers recommend it and why some readers think it too oppressive for the age it is sold at. But the register is the number here. The log prices this axis carefully: Little Women 79 and The Hobbit 84 pay nothing because they are books an adult reads as a book, Rangers Apprentice 74 pays a little for being easy with nothing to think about, Narnia 67 pays more for child leads and no higher things, and a book written for readers of nine with a magic object as its transport device sits well past Narnia on that scale. What it leaves behind is a history lesson delivered rather than an idea worked out, which is why axis:ideas is the risk and the juvenile register is the lean. The transporting atlas is a device with no rite, invocation or devotion attached, so it is not where the occult question would bite, but the axis stays in deps because the range is under the line and I did not examine it properly.

t: Toto kocici nindza a syrova loupez stoleti (Toto the Ninja Cat and the Incredible Cheese Heist)
why: Publisher-stated audience is 7-10, a heavily illustrated comic animal caper built on puns about stolen cheese, and I cannot name an idea it leaves behind - which is the separator that matters most here. axis:childrens is graded not vetoed, but this sits far further toward a children's book than Hobbit 84 or The Little Prince 82, both of which paid nothing because grown ideas carried them; Ranger's Apprentice 74 is easy reading that already lost points for having little to think about, and this has less. The juvenile early-reader form also suspends any test of what characters want and why, the axis that tops the log with Mockingjay 91 - so the suspension removes penalties without adding anything. I leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist because a ninja cat is a serviceable comic lead; it is the absence of anything to think about that fixes the band. Exited at gate 4 on one search, so the occult question is unexamined.

There is no single idea to name, and that is the finding rather than a gap in my research: the book's own description is a list of subjects - wisdom, ethics, morality, existence, society, reality, mind, soul, knowledge, logic, beauty - which is a table of contents, not a premise. The log is unambiguous that short idea-driven work only scores when the idea is nameable in a phrase, and that the suspension of the character rules removes penalties without adding anything; Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 each carry one idea worked out, and Labyrint sveta a raj srdce 70 shows where even a canonical Czech allegory with a nameable idea actually lands. A self-published collection of aphorisms with no editorial vetting, no reviews and three ratings has neither the idea nor the form to earn points, which is why the low band. The name invites a comparison with Wittgenstein that the book has nothing to do with. Occult was not examined at this exit; the record shelves it partly as spiritual literature, so that axis stays in deps.

The positive case is a single legible starting situation and a voice: one teacher in one border town, a Don Quixote frame stated openly, and readers who report both humour and questions worth thinking about. Saturnin 78 shows that a comic Czech register costs nothing at all and can carry a book into the A band on voice and character alone. What stops me going further is that the idea on offer is a complaint about the school system rather than a premise worked out, and the most consistent reader objection is political opinion inserted into the story - the same shape as the lazy claims stated as fact that took Rangers Apprentice 74 down, where a book that was easy to read simply had nothing under it. So axis:ideas is what I am doubting and what carries the number; the protagonist sits in risks because a self-pitying burnt-out narrator can fail the worth-rooting-for half the way Oliver Twist 57 failed the wanting-something half. The infidelity screen hit is a false positive - the annotation's svadi is svadi vnitrni boj, wages an inner battle, not seduction - and while there is a love thread with a young teaching assistant, no source shows a marriage or engagement for it to betray. Occult was not examined, the range being under the line already.

A real womans account written up by a travel writer, and the library framing places it in the established market of hardship stories about Muslim women rather than in a book with something of its own to say. The axis that earned Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75 is not the suffering itself but a first-person account that examines what is actually plausible and true; a second-hand novelisation by an author whose other titles are atlases and guidebooks is the form least likely to do that, which is why axis:ideas is what I am doubting and therefore what carries the number. Against it, the material is genuinely one concrete situation with forward momentum, so it is not a low band. Sustained bleakness sits behind the range as the risk, and it is the mildest recorded objection, not a bar - 1984 60 shows what an unrelieved book costs. The gate-2 check does not fire: the forced marriage and the later love in Bohemia are the escape, not an affair the book is built on, so nothing here is premise-level infidelity - the detective and romance screen words are both false positives on this annotation. Occult was deliberately not examined, since the range already sits under the line.

t: Utek z male pevnosti Terezin (Utek z male pevnosti Terezin)
why: The positive case is strong and specific: one concrete starting situation, three named men in a Gestapo prison who plan and carry out the escape, and the thing the log rewards most reliably after motives - companionship and self-sacrifice over solo survival, which is precisely why Project Hail Mary 92 beats The Martian 82. The author is one of the three, so the material is first-hand. What keeps it under the line is what readers report about the telling: the first third registers as nothing before it picks up and then runs fast, and the moralising and pathos grate even on a reader who grants that it was all genuinely lived. Slowness is not the reader's filter - confusion is - so that is a discount rather than a bar, but a dragging opening third plus sermonising is the shape that left The Martian 82 short of its ceiling and it is the opposite of the examination of what is actually true that took Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 to the top of the non-fiction. So momentum carries the number, with the ideas and the form as the risks. Occult is not in question here and was not researched. I spent two sources against a budget of one at this gate, and say so rather than leave it unrecorded.

t: Utek z planety Alcatraz (Escape from Planet Alcatraz)
why: A hi-lo illustrated adventure series from Capstone's Stone Arch imprint - short, heavily pictured instalments in which two boys cross one hazard per book on a prison planet: a bottomless pit, a swamp of fire-spitting snakes, a monster arena, a chamber of eight doors. The design goal is a reluctant reader turning pages, and that goal is the finding: I can name no idea it leaves behind, and each episode is a set piece with no character revelation, which the reader's log treats as dead weight - it is exactly why Catching Fire 83 sits under Mockingjay 91, arena for its own sake. Nor is there a premise being worked out; a penal planet is a backdrop for obstacles, where Project Hail Mary 92 earned its score on second-order consequences. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:childrens because the register is only part of it: Ranger's Apprentice 74 is easy reading with little to think about and still clears the B band on characters the reader followed for fourteen books, and there is no comparable investment available here. Occult status is unexamined at this exit and nothing in the annotation raises it.

There is a genuine idea and I am not doubting it - the narrator's own line that schizophrenia is not an illness but a way of life, held across 370 pages of diary entries, is real insight into how somebody else experiences the world, the axis that took Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 to the top of the non-fiction in this log. The problem is legibility, which is the most reliable negative predictor recorded. Readers repeatedly report losing track of what is reality and what is hallucination, and one concedes that this may be deliberate; deliberate or not, that is the Foundryside 30 and Gunslinger 30 failure, where plenty was happening and none of it meant anything yet, and the reader has ended books in their first chapters on it twice. Layered on that is a second recorded penalty: readers also say little happens, and a thin story spread over many pages is what docked The Lord of the Rings 84 despite its ideas. So the number is carried by legibility and density rather than by ideas, and it sits under the line for that reason rather than in the F band, because the prose is well regarded and the book was a Jiri Orten Prize finalist. Bleakness is the risk behind the range, mild by the log's standards - 1984 60 is the anchor. Reported vulgarity does not move the number by itself; a profane register is not an objection in this log, and whether any of it is sexually crude, which is what cost Ready Player One 55, I did not establish.

t: V pohode na vode (V pohode na vode)
why: A realistic illustrated children's story: two siblings expecting a week at the sea are taken on a canoe trip instead, and the book's business is showing what sleeping in a tent and singing round a fire are like. That is a holiday recreated for a child, not a premise with consequences, and the log is clear about what that costs even when done well at length - Hranicaruv ucen 74 is easy to read with not much to think about, and Narnia 67 falls below the propose line on a juvenile cast plus no higher thing to think about. Here there is no invented world or moral scheme to reach even that far. So axis:ideas carries the number down and axis:childrens sets the band. One source at the below-the-line gate, so occult status is unexamined, though nothing in the record suggests it arises.

t: Vcelka Meduska (Vcelka Meduska - Pohadky z rozkvetle louky)
why: An illustrated fairy-tale collection for readers from about four: 80 large-format pages of a nurse bee teaching newly hatched bees to tell flowers apart and find the hive again. Narnia 67 already sits below the propose line for exactly the two properties this book has more of - children as the whole cast, and nothing higher to think about - and Narnia is a full-length novel with an invented world behind it. Male zeny 79 shows a juvenile register can be paid off by characters worth following, but an episodic picture format at eight pages a scene has no room to build one. I can name a moral, courage before the first flight, and not an idea, and that is the finding: axis:ideas carries the number down and axis:childrens sets where it lands. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, so occult status is unexamined.

t: Velke cisteni zubu v ZOO (Der grosse Zahnputztag im Zoo)
why: A talking-animal picture book with an explicit hygiene lesson: the zoo animals stop brushing their teeth, the director sends a hedgehog round with toothpaste on his spines, and by the end everyone agrees brushing is worth it. A book whose whole purpose is to persuade a four-year-old to brush is the clearest possible answer to the below-the-line gate - there is no idea to name, only an instruction. The profile puts a picture book in the thirties or forties on register, and the log's short high scorers, Maly princ 82 and Animal Farm 78, get there on ideas a grown reader carries away. So axis:ideas carries the number down and axis:childrens sets the band. One source at the below-the-line gate, so occult status is unexamined, though nothing in the record suggests any arises.

t: Velky zly lisak (The Big Bad Fox (Le Grand Mechant Renard))
why: This one has an idea that can be stated in a phrase and it is not the joke: a predator who cannot be what he is told he is ends up raising the food he was supposed to eat, and the chicks, on learning he is a fox, decide they must be foxes too. Nature against what you are called - reviewers in BCCB and Kirkus both make identity and reversal the substance, not the gag. That earns something: the reader's own Animal Farm 78 is a short animal allegory that scores on leaving an idea behind, and Saturnin 78 shows a comic register carries no penalty by itself. What holds it under the line is form and audience. It is about 190 pages of panel-less watercolour comics pitched at grades three to six, so the interiority the reader rates above everything - the reason Red Rising 95 edges Golden Son 92 - has almost no room, and slapstick set pieces take much of the page count. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:childrens because the idea is what lifts this out of the 40s where the rest of the register sits; the juvenile audience is what stops it clearing the line. Occult status is unexamined at this exit and nothing in the material raises it.

The idea is nameable - revolutionary conviction curdling into the daily reality of socialist Cuba, watched by a young Czech technician sent there as fraternal aid - and idea-driven short prose is exactly the shape that got Animal Farm to 78 and Labyrint to 70. What makes me stop is that I doubt this one holds up. Two strands are braided from the start, a real historical figure's last preparations and a fictional young man's posting, and the publisher adds a third frame, a deliberate dialogue with Hemingway's novella. Three registers competing in a short book is a density problem, and several things starting at once before any is legible is the reader's most reliable negative predictor, the failure that ended books at 30. A famous revolutionary as one of the two leads also raises the rooting question the log treats as decisive, the split that put 22 points between two Collins prequels. There is no critical footprint at all to check any of this against - the book is from the author's own imprint and no substantive review exists - so the doubt cannot be resolved cheaply. No exclusion is inherited: the flagged excluded title by this author is a separate standalone work in a different genre, not a predecessor this book continues, and nothing here depends on it. I leaned on ideas because the idea is the only thing that could lift this above the line.

t: Vlci oko (L'Oeil du loup (Eye of the Wolf))
why: The positive case is the axis that tops this log outright. A 112-page fable spends almost all of it on what two beings have wanted and lost - a wolf who was caught saving his sister, a boy orphaned by a war and passed across a continent - and almost none on what anyone does, which is the Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 property stated plainly. The idea is nameable in a phrase: neither of them ever had a choice, and being truly looked at is what lets the wolf open his shut eye. The opening is one concrete situation, a wolf pacing a winter cage and a boy who will not look away, so the failure that produced The Colour of Magic 30 and Caropisci 30 does not apply; the two life stories are nested inside that frame in sequence rather than started at once, though the doubling is the reason axis:multi-pov sits in risks. Ceiling is set by Maly princ 82 - a short allegory whose ideas carry it past a child lead - and I go under it because this is pitched at confident young readers with large print and illustrations, and because the war and captivity material carries the mild bleakness discount that Animal Farm 78 also paid. No occult: the eye contact is a fabulist device with no rite, invocation or practice anywhere in it. Leaning on axis:ideas and axis:motives rather than on axis:protagonist, because two half-drawn lives is not the same as one lead to root for.

The nameable idea is decent and the author states it himself: a dissident is anyone, worker or intellectual, who refuses to stain his conscience by consenting, and a first-hand account of StB persecution is the kind of insight into how another group experiences the world that earned Son of Hamas 75. What holds the range under the line is that the log is explicit that the testimony form earns nothing on its own - what earns is examining what is actually plausible and true, which is the specific thing praised in Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 - and the little reception that exists points the other way, one reader calling it fairly primitive anti-communism and reporting that it closes on the claim that 1989 was steered from above and abroad. Assertion in place of examination is what I am doubting, so axis:ideas carries the number. Faith is the named risk rather than the lean: the author frames the whole book as a path of spiritual growth towards God, and this reader wants faith as a thread inside a story, not as the subject in its own right. The memoir form is the second risk, since the same form produced both the highest non-fiction score in the log and an outright DNF at The Diary of a Young Girl 40. Occult was not examined at this exit.

t: Warren XIII. a septajici les (Warren the 13th and the Whispering Woods)
why: A heavily designed illustrated middle-grade gothic caper, stated ages eight to twelve: a twelve-year-old innkeeper whose hotel walks is separated from it in a forest of witches, talking trees and riddles. There is a positive worth stating - Warren himself is dogged, kind and competent at a job he actually does, which is the interesting-and-rootable pair the log rates above worldbuilding - and Kirkus and the blogs agree the design and atmosphere are the draw. That last point is where gate 4 fires: the praise is almost entirely for the object and the mood, reviewers reach for Lemony Snicket and Gorey rather than for anything the book says, and I cannot name an idea it leaves behind. Narnia 67 is the anchor, marked down for child leads and lacking higher things to think about, and this is a lighter book than Narnia with the same shortfall. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist precisely because the lead is the book's strength, not its weakness. Occult is unexamined at this exit by design and is the risk most likely to matter: a witch queen, a witch-hunter and a shape-shifter are central, which is the historical-witchcraft mould that cost Harry Potter 51 rather than an invented mechanism.

t: Zajeci kamaradi Hup a Hop (Zajeci kamaradi Hup a Hop)
why: An illustrated animal story for small children: a timid hare mistakes a rolling ball of yarn for the sun come to grant his wish, and follows it out into the world to find a friend. The friendship theme is the one this reader does respond to - it is named in Hobit 84 and in Lord of the Rings 84 - but in both cases it is carried by characters and consequences over hundreds of pages, and a talking-animal picture story at this register has neither. Narnia 67 is already below the propose line for a juvenile cast with nothing higher to think about, and this sits much further toward a children's book than Narnia does. So axis:ideas carries the number down - the moral is be brave, which is a lesson, not an idea - and axis:childrens sets the band. One source at the below-the-line gate, so occult status is unexamined.

t: Zivot je slehane hruskove pyre (Zivot je slehane hruskove pyre)
why: A young-adult allegory with a genuinely legible opening - one girl on a cliff above her city, stopped by two strange beings who offer to walk her to the last judgement - and one nameable question, whether a life is in our own hands or fate's. That is the right shape for this reader: Labyrint sveta a raj srdce 70 is a guided allegorical walk through a city of the world and landed inside its predicted range on exactly the axis:ideas plus axis:short-idea-driven pairing. What holds the number under the line rather than above it is that I cannot establish the question is worked out rather than only posed. The publisher states it as a theme, the reception is a handful of reader comments and no criticism, and the described middle is bizarre encounters and a weave of unfamiliar streets and memories - which is a book that could as easily dissipate as build. Animal Farm 78 shows what a short allegory earns when the consequences actually land; nothing I found demonstrates that here. So axis:ideas carries the number, not axis:protagonist, whose lead I never got a real look at. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, so occult status is unexamined - the two guide-beings and the last judgement make that a genuinely open question, not a formality.

An Ice Age survival story built on real anthropology, paleobotany and climatology, and that research is the strongest thing in it - the publisher's own claim is that the material is evidence-based, and the readers who liked it liked the unsentimental competence of the hunting. The problem is the shape. Czech readers describe a description of adventures rather than a story, a set of independent episodes with the same cast, with the plot the title promises only starting at three quarters and then ending fast. That is the Unfinished Tales 69 objection stated exactly - pieces that are not logically connected to each other - and Unfinished Tales is the lowest Tolkien in the log by a clear margin. Period detail is information, not something to think about after the last page, so axis:ideas is what carries the number; leaned there rather than on axis:worldbuilding, which is the part this book actually gets right. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, so the occult status of the shamanic material was not examined.

About fifty pages in the second person: a letter in which a young woman explains and half apologises for betraying her twin. It assumes a full novel that it never re-establishes, so almost nothing in it stands on its own. No excluded predecessor was named on the task line and nothing in the reading log excludes this author, so no inherited exclusion applies here; the dependency itself is a fact and is recorded in flags, and it would be the thing to re-check if that predecessor is ever excluded on a taste filter. What the form does is sit the reader inside a narrator who did the wrong thing and wants to be understood for it, and that is the log's cleanest single-axis failure: Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 lost 22 points against the same author's other prequel purely because there was nobody to root for. Nor is there an idea to lean the other way on - reviewers call it a marketing piece and a side dish, and the one theme they name, how old tales treat women who want power, is a remark rather than a premise worked out. So the low band: no nameable idea, and a form short enough to suspend the character tests without earning anything back. Leaned on axis:protagonist. Infidelity was examined and falls outside the rule's scope - the betrayal is between unmarried partners, with no marriage or engagement in place when it happens. Exited at the below-the-line gate, so the occult question is unexamined, and the fae material is the obvious place it would bite.

The positive case is real and it is the log's heaviest axis: almost the whole book is page time on what two people want and why, and it leaves a nameable idea behind - that race is something you only discover you have by emigrating, which Ifemelu turns into her blog. Romance as the central subject costs nothing here; Pycha a predsudek 75 settles that. The opening is one legible situation, a train to a braiding salon in Trenton, with the second chapter handing over to Obinze, so the confusion filter does not fire. What decides the number is the infidelity axis. I judged this a subplot and not the premise, and therefore not a reject: strip the adultery out and the American section, the blog and the return to Lagos are all still there, and the affair only becomes actual in the last of seven parts, which the rule names explicitly as sub-premise. But the framing is approving - Obinze asks his wife for a divorce and arrives at Ifemelu's door having left her that day, and the book treats this as its resolution - and an approving subplot lands at 30-40. I have placed it above that band because the peak the deduction is subtracted from is unusually high, and I state the doubt: a reader who counted the frame rather than the page count could call this premise level, and my own reading of the framing as approving rather than neutral is contestable given how much of Kosi's humiliation and Ifemelu's disgust at being a mistress is shown. I did not lean on axis:ideas or axis:motives, strong as both are, because on this axis the deduction is the number.

t: Propustka na svobodu (A Place Called Freedom)
why: The positive case is momentum and a concrete grievance: a Scottish miner bound to the pit by a pledge he argues is illegal, then framed, transported and worked as a servant, which is the plot-engine virtue that carried Monte Cristo 75. The book opens on one situation in one place, so the confusion filter does not fire. What decides the number is the infidelity axis, and I judged subplot rather than premise, so not a reject: the freedom plot stands on its own if you remove the romance, and the title names it. But Lizzie is married to Jay when her relationship with Mack develops in Virginia, that is established across the publisher summary and the Kirkus review, and the framing is approving in the strongest sense the rule describes - the husband is the one punished, the adultery is never treated as a moral question, and the book closes with the wife riding off with the other man. An approving subplot lands at 30-40; I have set the band a little above it because the coerced debt-marriage to a villain is a genuine mitigation and because the plotting itself is competent. t: Frankenstein, aneb, Novodoby Prometheus (Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus)
why: One premise stated precisely and then followed to its end: a man makes a living person and refuses to answer for him. The book's centre is the creature arguing his own case - why he wants what he wants, and what he was owed - which is page time on motive rather than on incident, the axis that puts Speaker for the Dead 90 and Mockingjay 91 at the top of the log, and it leaves an idea behind in one phrase, that responsibility does not end at the act of creation. Two hard filters checked and both clear. The opening is one concrete situation, not several at once: letters from a man whose ship is stuck in the ice, who then finds Victor - the nesting is sequential, so nothing like the several-threads-at-once failure that ended three books at 30. And the occult tests both pass: the alchemists Victor reads at thirteen are named as a discredited enthusiasm he abandons for chemistry after the lightning-struck oak, and the creation itself is withheld - no incantation, no apparatus, no lightning, only the instruments of life - so no rite is enacted on the page. What keeps this out of the Animal Farm 78 band is the man telling it. Victor flees the creature twice within a page of making it, faints, spends months in a fever and worries most about his reputation, which is the passive, hard-to-root-for lead that took Promena 58 twelve points under its prediction and left Oliver Twist 57 near the bottom; the gloom is also unbroken, and 1984 60 was marked down as simply too depressing. Add the embedded De Lacey and Safie tales and the Alpine set pieces, which is thin story spread over pages, the LOTR 84 deduction. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:motives rather than axis:worldbuilding, which earns nothing here because the science is deliberately unexplained and so incurs almost no obligation. Four sources.

t: Harry Potter (Harry Potter (Warner Bros. film companion volume))

Calibration is available directly here and it is not encouraging: the source novels are books the reader has read and scored 51, on the witchcraft and on a declared magic the society is never reorganised around, and a picture-led companion supplies the same setting with none of the reading that scored what it scored. Occult status unexamined at this exit, as the ladder allows. One source, the C budget.

t: Musim te zradit (I Must Betray You)
why: One concrete starting situation and one voice: a seventeen-year-old is pulled out of class into the director's office and blackmailed into informing on the family, with his grandfather's leukaemia medicine as the price. That is what this reader wants an opening to be, and the secret-police reports set between chapters are documents rather than a second point of view, so nothing fans out. The idea is nameable and it is the book's entire subject - surveillance as something you end up carrying inside rather than something merely done to you, and what informing costs among people who trust you - and it is tested against what actually happened in Bucharest in December 1989, which is the rigour behind the log's highest non-fiction score of 91. Page time goes to what he wants, to write and to be believed, rather than to incident. Two real deductions: it immerses the reader in the deprivation instead of standing back from it, which is why the log's dystopian classic sits at 60 while a short allegory that hands over a thought sits at 78, and the telling is YA-plain with short chapters, so the story itself is simple even where the atmosphere is not. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:motives, not on axis:worldbuilding, which a novel bound by the historical record cannot earn points on.

Two gates checked and neither fires. Infidelity: a palace guard with a wife and a child on the way is taken over by the queen-to-be's mind control, which is coercion rather than an affair, it is shown as appalling rather than approved, and it is one thread of a rise to power - remove it and the book still exists, so this is subplot at most and stays graded. Sexual content is likewise not what the book is for. What decides the number is the lead. The whole point of the book is time spent inside the series' villain, and the log has a controlled measurement of exactly that: Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65, same author, same world, same prequel form as Sunrise on the Reaping 87 and 22 points below it because there was no one to root for. Here it is worse, because the vanity, the assassination of a three-year-old and the mind-controlled seductions leave nothing to root for at all, and reviewers who wanted to sympathise report they could not. I would also put axis:ideas in risks - a bridge book supplying backstory has no premise of its own to work out - and the short form removes penalties without adding points. That is the gate 4 exit, and I take the low band because both things that could have carried a short book are absent. Two sources, one spent on the infidelity and sexual-content checks. Occult unexamined at this exit.

That plus a nonsense-word register aimed at young children puts it at or under Narnia 67 rather than near The Hobbit. Leaning on axis:childrens plus axis:ideas together because either alone would understate it. Occult status unexamined at this exit, as the ladder allows. One source, the C budget.

Gate 3 does not fire. Half the book is a family collapsing after a soldier's death in Afghanistan - a twenty-year-old burying her father, a mother who falls apart, two younger siblings to hold together - and reviewers describe the romance as slow-burn, so the plot is grief and obligation with a love story running through it, not sexual behaviour. Remove the sex and the book stands. No marriage or engagement is betrayed, so the infidelity axis is untouched. The positive case is that the pages go on what people want and why, which is the axis that tops the log in Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90. But gate 4 still fires: I can name no idea the book leaves behind - a family gets through a bereavement - and that doubt is the exit. The downside risk is volume on axis:sexual-content, which the reviews put at moderate but constant, and volume alone took Ready Player One 55 down. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:bleakness, which the log treats as mild and which grief handled warmly does not trigger. One source, this gate's budget. Occult unexamined at this exit.

The positive case is real: reviewers consistently say the many viewpoint characters are distinct, each with its own voice and wants, and character differentiation is the axis the log rewards most - Golden Son 92 was praised for exactly that, three leads who think and want different things. It is also the one thing that protects it from the reader's worst failure mode, since the openings that ended books unfinished at 30 were confusing rather than merely crowded. But gate 4 fires on both of its own terms. There is no idea I can name that the book leaves behind: it is the resolution of a fairy-tale-retelling adventure, and its business is finishing the war rather than examining anything, so axis:ideas goes in risks. And 823 pages is where the log's density penalty bites - reviewers' commonest complaint is that it is too long, with characters repeatedly separating and reuniting, which is the same objection that cost LOTR 84 points for a thin story over many pages and left The Martian 82 with an ending that dragged. A sequel is not a safe bet here either; the log's steepest fall is Hitchhiker's 83 down to 70. One source, this gate's budget. Occult unexamined at this exit, though the sources describe the Lunar gift as a bioelectric manipulation rather than magic.

t: Za hranice lasky (Beyond What Is Given)
why: Gate 3 first, since this is a New Adult romance. The plot is not mainly sexual behaviour: it is two people with concealed pasts thrown together as flight-school roommates, with an instructor-and-student complication, so remove the sex and the book still stands - graded, not vetoed, and Pycha a predsudek 75 establishes that romance as the central subject costs nothing by itself when motives are what the pages are spent on. Neither lead is married or engaged elsewhere, so the infidelity axis is untouched. What holds the number under the line is gate 4: I can name no idea the book leaves behind, and that is the strongest single separator in the log, so axis:ideas goes in risks and I stop. The genuine downside risk is volume on axis:sexual-content - reviewers call this the steamiest of its series, with recurring open-door scenes, and volume is what sank Ready Player One 55; if it runs as they describe, the number sits at the bottom of the range or under it. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist because a competent NA romance normally gives its leads clear wants, which is the axis this reader rewards. One source, this gate's budget. Occult unexamined at this exit.

t: Zanechal jsi mi jen vzpominky (History Is All You Left Me)
why: REJECTED 2026-09-02 on filter 7, a same-sex romance as the premise of the book (new axis, ruled the same day off Caropisci 67). Built entirely on the narrator's relationship with his dead boyfriend, with the chapters alternating between that relationship and grieving it. Remove it and there is no book - premise level under filter 7. Framing never enters this test, exactly as it does not for infidelity. Prior assessment, kept for the audit trail: The positive case is genuine: a single voice speaking directly to the dead boy he loved, and compulsions written from the author's own experience rather than researched, so the interior life is specific. But what the two timelines mainly withhold is information - why one friend was resented, how the drowning actually happened - and readers report that solving those puzzles is what kept them turning pages, which is momentum borrowed from an investigation rather than a thought handed over. I can name no idea the book leaves behind beyond grief being survivable, and that doubt is the gate 4 exit. Sexual content is moderate but recurrent across several encounters, and volume alone is what sank a book to 55 in this log; the lead is also messy and hard to root for, the axis that separated two books by one author in one world by 22 points and outranks everything else graded here. Infidelity tags attached by readers concern unmarried teenagers, so gate 2 does not reach it. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:protagonist, not on axis:opening, which is concrete - a funeral on the first morning. Occult does not arise but is formally unexamined at this exit; two pages are cited where gate 4 budgets one.

REJECTED 2026-09-02 on filter 7, a same-sex romance as the premise of the book (new axis, ruled the same day off Caropisci 67). The romance IS the plot: a cross-country trip between two girls who slept together once and then stopped speaking, with withheld conversation as the whole engine. Remove it and there is no book, so this is premise level under filter 7. Framing never enters this test, exactly as it does not for infidelity. Prior assessment, kept for the audit trail: A cross-country trip in the mothers' ice-cream truck between two girls who slept together once and then stopped speaking. The engine is withheld conversation - reviewers who liked the voice still call the miscommunication the whole mechanism and land on merely OK - and what the book is for is repairing a friendship, not an idea; I can name none it leaves behind, which is the gate 4 exit. On the two gates that come earlier: the plot is a relationship rather than sexual behaviour, so gate 3 grades rather than vetoes, and the sex is a single flashback night, low volume that mitigates without clearing; no marriage or engagement is in scope for gate 2. The narration breaks the fourth wall and makes the lead knowingly unreliable, which cuts at the rooting-for half of the protagonist test - the axis that outranks every other graded one for this reader, and the one that dropped a strong-worldbuilding novel to 69. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:protagonist. Occult status unexamined at this exit, and two pages are cited where gate 4 budgets one.

One voice and one concrete starting situation: Matthias, the third and last son of his family to follow Alexander east, enlists after his father dies out there, and the whole book stays inside his head as an infantryman. That is the shape this reader wants from an opening - The Hunger Games 89 and Hitchhiker's 83 both start on a single legible situation - and the page time goes to what he decides and why rather than to what happens: he refuses to kill a prisoner, frees an enslaved woman, and the honour code he has walked into runs its logic all the way to her own kin killing her. A system the author declares and then holds himself to is what earns points here, Project Hail Mary 92 and Valka stareho muze 87 both on that axis, and the enemy who hides among civilians and sends women and boys to fight gives the book something to leave behind. Deductions: sustained grimness with an atrocity for an ending, which costs mildly since 1984 60 is the only case where bleakness did real damage; a lot of campaign action, the complaint that held Golden Son 92 under Red Rising 95; reviewers reporting that it does not grab from the first page, which is momentum rather than confusion and so is graded; and a young lead, a couple of points at most. Historical fiction has topped out lower in this log than SF - Monte Cristo 75, Exodus 68, Quo Vadis 66 - which is why the range straddles the line instead of sitting above it. Leaned on motive and idea rather than on worldbuilding, the setting being history rather than invention. Confidence is medium because the occult question was answered only from the publisher framing the Macedonians as secular and humanist, not from a scene-level source: an army that sacrifices before battle on the page would change the verdict.

A house-name animal fantasy for ages eight to twelve: panda triplets separated by a flood, raised apart, drawn together by a threatening tiger to fulfil a prophecy made before their birth, told in chapters that rotate between all three. Two things put it under the line and neither needs a second source. There is no idea I can name - the prophecy is the plot's engine rather than something the book has a view about, and reverence is the axis prophecy is judged on, not resemblance. And the telling rotates three separated leads from the start, which is the log's most reliable negative predictor: Guards! Guards! 30 was abandoned at page fifteen with several lines of plot open at once, so a structure built on three is a real risk rather than a stylistic note. I took the lower band rather than the default because the register is juvenile enough that the character tests are suspended without anything replacing them, and Narnia 67 - children as leads, nothing higher to think about - is the ceiling that shape reaches, not the floor. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, and the form is the answer: 40 pages, 125x200 mm, written and drawn by an illustrator for small children, addressing the reader directly and inviting him to imagine what the world would be missing if the wind stopped. That is a picture book, which the reader's own calibration places in the 30s and 40s, and the lower band applies because both of its conditions hold - the character and emotion tests are not merely failed but suspended, there being no character at all, and I cannot name an idea. The positive case, and it is a real one, is that the book has a genuine conceit rather than just pictures: subtract one ordinary thing from the world and enumerate the consequences, which is the move that makes short allegory work for this reader, The Little Prince 82 and Animal Farm 78 both scoring well on brevity plus a nameable thought. But the suspension removes penalties and never adds points, and a conceit played purely for whimsy at a preschool register does not become a thought - the reader's short high scorers are canonical for their ideas, which is selection, not a property of small books. Leaned on the children's register rather than on ideas because the register is established and settles the number on its own, and I did not spend a second source to refine it. axis:occult was not examined at this exit and nothing suggests it applies.

It has the two things the log rewards in historical fiction: one concrete starting situation told by a single first-person narrator - a younger brother scraping a living in Elizabethan London, resentful of the famous one - and a period world built precisely enough that the theatre business, and specifically the fact that a company owning a script owned the play, becomes the engine of the plot. That is the Monte Cristo 75 shape. What it lacks is anything to think about afterwards, and the momentum is weak by the author's own standards: reviewers agree the recovery of the stolen manuscript is the only action, it is brief and nobody dies, and the first stretch is slow. I would put axis:ideas in risks, so gate 4 fires: the ceiling here is the Exodus 68 / Quo Vadis 66 band for a competent historical novel that leaves nothing behind, and the slow start pulls the low end down. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:momentum rather than axis:protagonist, because a resentful, thieving narrator with a clear want is interesting enough to carry a book. Exited at C-low, so the occult question is unexamined; nothing in what I read suggests it arises.

It opens the way this reader wants a book to open - one concrete situation, four children and a dinghy on one lake, nothing to decode - which is the exact opposite of the failure that ended The Gunslinger 30 and The Colour of Magic 30 in their first chapters. Friendship is the theme and friendship is what the reader named as the good part of The Hobbit 84. But the whole of it is holiday play written straight: camping, sailing, a treaty with rival children, an argument with an uncle. There is no premise to work out and nothing left behind afterwards, which is the axis:ideas doubt, and the reader's own verdict on Narnia 67 was children as the main characters plus a lack of higher things to think about - that applies here without even the mythic layer Lewis had. Over twelve and a half hours of it the axis:density risk is live too, since the incident is small-scale by design. I lean on axis:ideas over axis:protagonist because the children are perfectly good company; what is missing is anything for an adult reader to carry away, and The Hobbit's ideas are precisely the difference between 84 and this band.

t: Bylinkova vila (Bylinkova vila - Pruvodce svetem lecivych rostlin pro deti)
why: This is a herbal guide for small children in fairy-tale dress: the fairy Kvetuska faces an examination in identifying medicinal and poisonous plants, each chapter pairs the episode with an instructional section, and the book closes with a quiz for the reader.
