The story exists to carry the teaching, so there is no premise whose consequences get worked out and no idea to name in the sense the log means - the payload is factual, and its value is whether a child learns to recognise plants. Gate 4 fires on axis:ideas, and this is the clearest case for the lower band: the form suspends the character tests entirely and adds nothing back, which is the picture-book end of the scale the reader placed in the 30s and 40s, well under where Narnia 67 sits with a real narrative. Leaned on axis:childrens and axis:ideas because the register decides everything here; there is no protagonist question to weigh in an educational frame this thin. Exited at C-low, so the occult status is unexamined - a herb fairy and a grandmother herbalist involve no rite in what I read.

Three short stories in which the author renders her own early childhood in the Terezin ghetto in a child's language and a child's images, illustrated by herself and pitched by reviewers at second or third grade. The subject is unimpeachable and the number is not about the subject. The log is unusually clear here: the memoir form earns nothing by itself, what earns is examining what is actually true and showing how another group experiences the world - Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 does that - and the counter-case is exactly this shape, The Diary of a Young Girl 40, first-person child testimony left unfinished, penalised again for being a child's inner life. Three brief picture-stories told in a small child's voice sit on the wrong side of that comparison, and I can name no idea being worked out, only remembered images. Leaned on axis:childrens and axis:memoir-form rather than axis:bleakness: the bleakness is mild by this reader's standards and is offset in the book itself by the Seder and other small victories. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

t: Chlapec z nocniho trhu (The Boy from the Night Market)
why: A picture book: terse, plain text carried at least equally by full-page illustration, in which a nameless boy narrates growing up at his mother's food stall in a Kaohsiung night market after his father dies in a crash. There is one genuinely interesting thing in it - the market's Vietnamese and migrant vendors cooking against homesickness - but that is an observation, not a premise with consequences to follow, and the boy is a vantage point rather than someone who wants something, so axis:ideas would go into risks and this exits at the below-the-line gate on one source. Leaned on axis:childrens with axis:ideas: at picture-book length the character tests are suspended and nothing takes their place, and the log's short high scorers - Male zeny 79, Animal Farm 78 - earn their numbers on characters or on a nameable idea respectively, neither of which is available here. Bleakness is present but mild and is not what sets the number. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

This is a genuine picture book and the object is the point: a village modelled out of bread crumb and scraps of textile, photographed, with the text typeset as a parish chronicle and comics panels between. A professional review credits it with an ethical message about home resting on relationships between people, so there is something rather than nothing - but that is a sentiment, not an idea whose consequences get worked out, and the same review's own summary plus a reader's note that the story has no real plot and merely floats poetically tells me axis:ideas belongs in doubt. Against real scores this cannot reach the register that earned The Little Prince 82, which is short but is a sustained argument about what matters, nor Little Women 79, which has no premise but does have characters over hundreds of pages. Fifty-odd illustrated pages of an invented hamlet with a chronicler as narrator suspends the character tests without earning anything in their place, and axis:childrens is at its most expensive here. I lean on axis:childrens over axis:density because length is not the objection - there is barely any text to be thin.

A 1964 conto by a major Portuguese poet, still set reading in Portuguese schools: a knight leaves Denmark on pilgrimage to Bethlehem, prays a night at the grotto, and works his way home through Venice and Florence, meeting Cimabue, Giotto and Dante, with tales told inside the tale. The frame is the problem, not the writing. The knight has exactly one want - to be home for Christmas - and everything else is inset episodes he passes through, which is the structure Unfinished Tales 69 was marked down for, pieces not logically connected to one another, and it is the lowest Tolkien in the log by twelve points. Asked what it leaves behind I get a tour of medieval Europe rather than an idea worked out, so axis:ideas belongs in risks and this exits at the below-the-line gate. Leaned on axis:protagonist rather than axis:faith: the pilgrimage is a frame and a thread, not theology as a subject, which is the arrangement the reader accepts. The devotion on the page is Christian prayer, not the pantheon that cost Percy Jackson 57. Occult status is otherwise unexamined at this exit.

t: Denik jedne patacky (Penny Draws a Best Friend)
why: An illustrated diary for eight-to-twelve-year-olds, and the Czech reader response places it by comparison with Denik poseroutky - a cartoon-diary format whose unit is the gag panel and the aside. The worries are age-real (a move, a creaking bedroom, a school play, a best friend changing) but there is no idea to name: nothing is asserted and then followed through, which is the axis:ideas doubt gate 4 turns on. The diary form does give interiority, so this is not a book with nothing inside it - but the interiority available to a ten-year-old narrator drawing cartoons is not what earned Mockingjay 91 or Speaker for the Dead 90, which is page time on what people want and why. Against real scores the constraint is register: Little Women 79 is the ceiling for a domestic story with no premise, and it clears the line on characters sustained over hundreds of adult-readable pages, which a heavily illustrated middle-grade diary cannot attempt. That puts axis:childrens at close to its full cost. I lean on axis:childrens rather than axis:protagonist because the girl is likeable and clearly drawn; the form is the limit.

The setup is one situation and two people with something real at stake: an orphaned sixteen-year-old moves in with the brother who walked out on the family twelve years earlier and never wrote. That is want-and-why material rather than incident, and Pycha a predsudek 75 shows relationships as the central subject cost this reader nothing. What holds it under the line is that it is a Czech divci roman from a prolific small-press writer of the same, a form whose business is emotional resolution rather than an idea worked out, and I can name no thought it leaves behind - the most common reason a competent book stalls in the 60s. Male zeny 79 is the ceiling for a domestic story with no premise, and that took Alcott's cast to reach. I leaned on axis:ideas because that is the doubt carrying the number, not on axis:protagonist, which the annotation actually argues for. The catalogue flagged 'vypatra' but that is a solicitor tracing an address, not an investigation, so axis:detective does not fire. Exited at gate 4, so occult is unexamined and a contemporary family story does not raise it.

t: Doktor Proktor a vana casu (Doktor Proktors tidsbadekar (Bubble in the Bathtub))
why: Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. Form and genre: a comic children's novel, slapstick time travel built around a bathtub and a bar of Time Soap, from a crime writer working in a deliberately silly register for eight-to-eleven-year-olds. The positive case is that the humour is well made and reviewers say it works for adults reading aloud too, and a juvenile or profane register is explicitly not an objection for this reader - Saturnin 78 and Hitchhiker's 83 both score in the A band on comic voice. But the time travel is a joke-delivery device, not a premise with consequences: the trip exists so the children can turn up at Waterloo, the Moulin Rouge, the guillotine and Joan of Arc's cell, and a device whose declared capability is never allowed to bind anything is the opposite of the worked-through worldbuilding that earned Valka stareho muze 87. I would put axis:ideas in risks, which is the exit condition, and I can name no idea at all. The lower band because that absence coincides with a form that suspends the character tests rather than passing them - farce for children, where nobody is required to want anything - and because the children's register here sits far below Ranger's Apprentice 74, near the end the reader places in the 30s and 40s. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe in this log, Hitchhiker's falling 83 to 70. Leaned on the children's register and the missing idea rather than on protagonist, since a farce is not trying to build one. axis:occult was not examined at this exit.

t: Dotyk smrti a jine povidky (Dotyk smrti a jine povidky)
why: The positive case is real: these are tightly built peril stories by a man who had actually been to the places he writes about, and momentum plus a concrete opening situation is what the reader rewards - Monte Cristo 75 held up on plot momentum alone. But the volume gathers roughly fifty five-to-ten-page pieces sorted by continent, so nothing accumulates: no character is on the page long enough to want anything, and there is no premise whose consequences get worked out. That is the Unfinished Tales 69 shape - the reader's stated objection there was that the pieces are not logically connected to each other - and it lands lower here because Tolkien's fragments at least carried ideas, while a reader comment on this author concedes the stories are not literary gems and do not aspire to be. I lean on axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist because the form removes the protagonist question entirely; the short-idea-driven suspension takes the character penalty away without adding anything back. Exited at gate 4 after one search; occult status is therefore unexamined, which is acceptable because nothing under 68 is proposed either way.

The positive case is craft: 296 pages for readers from ten up, a talking-animal cast with distinct temperaments - a boastful raccoon, a vain gecko, a tortoise - set in a Renaissance Florence that is actually used, Leonardo's workshop and the Medici bank included, and readers who single out the language and the sustained tension rather than just the plot. But it is a caper with a treasure at the end of it, and asked to name what it leaves behind I cannot, so axis:ideas goes in risks and this exits at the below-the-line gate: Hranicaruv ucen 74 is the log's ceiling for easy-to-read adventure with not much to think about, and a talking-animal book aimed several years younger sits below that. The theft and the false accusation make the shape investigation-adjacent, but the satisfaction on offer is the chase and clearing his own name, not the identity of a culprit, so I flag axis:detective rather than firing it. Leaned on axis:childrens because the register, not the plotting, is what caps this. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

t: Hvezdy nad Berlinem (A Berlin Love Song)
why: Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, and the exit was a near thing worth recording. Form and genre: a young-adult historical novel about the Nazi persecution of Roma and Sinti, dual-narrated, opening in the present day with an old man sitting down to write his memories - one concrete situation, legible from the first page, nothing like the several-threads-at-once failure that ended Guards! Guards! 30. The positive case is that the subject is real and under-known, up to half a million Romani dead, and the author built the book out of research rather than out of a plot; the reader's log rewards exactly that kind of examination, Seeking Allah Finding Jesus 91 scoring on insight into how another group experiences the world. Why I still exit: I would put axis:ideas under risks, because the vehicle is a star-crossed teenage romance and a forbidden love story tends to leave the reader with the lovers rather than with the history - and the log's own historical novels sit right at the line, Exodus 68 and Quo Vadis 66, which is where a book with a serious subject and a conventional shape lands for this reader. Sustained bleakness through the Auschwitz Zigeunerlager and a Panzer division at Caen costs a little more, the mild discount that took 1984 to 60. Leaned on ideas rather than protagonist because both leads look sympathetic and clearly motivated; the doubt is what the book leaves behind, not who carries it. axis:occult was not examined at this exit and nothing suggests it applies.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, and it was a close call worth stating. Form and genre: an original Czech dystopian SF novel for readers of about eleven and up, illustrated. The positive case is substantial - the premise is one concrete situation stated precisely, boys vanish on the day they turn eight and only the ones with damaged nervous systems remain, so the lead's supposed defect is the reason he survives and the reason he can see the thieves. A premise that turns its own cost into its mechanism is the shape that earns, and it comes with real recognition, a readers' award at Magnesia Litera 2021. What sends it to C anyway is that I would put axis:ideas in risks: reviewers who liked the debut describe this one as rushed and underdeveloped, with description that generalises, an abrupt ending and so much fighting that interest fell away - and page time on what characters do rather than on what they want is the reader's heaviest single objection, the axis on which Golden Son 92 was docked below Red Rising 95. A legendary saviour named Finis is played straight, which the reverence rule treats as fine, so prophecy is not the deduction. Bleakness is present and mild by the reader's own weighting, 1984 60 being the anchor for too depressing. Leaned on ideas rather than worldbuilding because the premise itself is good; the doubt is whether the book follows it through or spends itself on set-pieces. axis:occult was not examined at this exit.

t: Jak zlomit draci srdce (How to Break a Dragon's Heart)
why: The positive case is momentum and voice: a memoir frame in which an old man remembers being a boy who found it hard to be a hero, one concrete predicament per book, and prose playful enough that reluctant readers finish it in a day - the easy-to-read virtue that carried Hranicaruv ucen 74. Reviewers say this instalment is where the series darkens, delves into the tribe's history and turns on what we owe those who love us, so it is not empty. But the register is a heavily illustrated slapstick series for eight to twelve year olds, several steps more juvenile than Narnia 67, which the reader marked down for child leads and for lacking higher things to think about; that scale puts this in the 50s at best. It is also a sequel that continues an arc established before it - a prophecy, a hidden throne and a returning enemy - and sequels are not safe bets in this log, where Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. Gate 4 fires: axis:ideas is a risk, since the theme reviewers name is delivered through comic Viking business rather than worked out. Leaned on axis:childrens and axis:sequels rather than axis:opening, which the series form makes a non-issue. Exited at C-low, so occult status is unexamined; the dragons are creatures of the world, not a practice, in what I read.

t: Je to pravda, Tygriku? (Tiger-Tiger, Is It True? Four Questions to Make You Smile Again)
why: A picture book, and that is the whole of the form: a small tiger believes his parents do not love him and his friends have left him, a wise turtle asks four questions, and he sees that the suffering came from his thoughts about the events rather than the events. There is something nameable here - the self-inquiry maxim - so this is not a book with nothing in it, but it is a single therapeutic technique delivered as instruction, not a premise whose consequences are worked out, and it is the author's adult method adapted downward rather than a story that arrived at anything. That is precisely the distinction the log draws: The Little Prince 82 is short and for children and scores high because the thoughts are its own and go further than the frame, and this does not reach that. Gate 4 fires on axis:ideas, and the illustrated picture-book form is the reader's own 30s-to-40s register, so the lower band. Leaned on axis:childrens and axis:ideas; axis:faith is in scope because the content is a New Age self-help practice presented as wisdom, which is the it-is-the-whole-of-the-book case the reader dislikes, but I did not need it to reach the number. Exited at C-low, so occult status is unexamined; the method is psychological inquiry with no rite.

t: Kdo se boji, nesmi do skoly! (Kdo se boji, nesmi do skoly)
why: A 64-page illustrated first-reader for children from six, five short chapters, built on the pun that the grandfather lives in a town called Hrob - grave - among the cemetery's inhabitants, with garlic, vampires and a wrestling craze doing the comic work. The opening is legible and concrete, which the log rewards, and there is a real hook in the empty letter that the adults read as illness and the boy reads as a coded message. But nothing is worked out past the joke, there is no idea to name, and a fifth of the book is reportedly a recipe; readers who liked it liked it as first reading material and the sharper ones call this instalment thinner in plot than its predecessors and a set-up for the next. Gate 4 fires on axis:ideas, and the early-reader form is the register the reader places in the 30s and 40s: the character tests are suspended and nothing is added back, which is why this sits well under Narnia 67. Leaned on axis:childrens and axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist, which an early reader of this length cannot fairly be judged on. Exited at C-low, so occult status is unexamined - comic vampires and garlic, with no rite in what I read.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. Form and genre settle it: 160 illustrated pages of episodic comic school stories about two boys, published with a recommended age of six and upward. The positive case is genuine but small - the humour is well liked, one reader noting that the moral is hidden well enough that a child absorbs it without noticing, and comic register carries no penalty for this reader at all, Saturnin 78 scoring in the A band on voice and character alone. What it cannot do is earn: there is no idea here I can name in a phrase, only a friendship tested by both boys liking the same classmate, so axis:ideas belongs in risks and that is the exit condition. The lower band rather than the default because both of its conditions hold - no nameable idea, and a form that suspends the character tests rather than passing them, since episodic slapstick written for six-year-olds is not doing the work that separated Sunrise on the Reaping 87 from Ballad 65. The children's axis is what carries the number: this sits far below the Narnia 67 position, well past Ranger's Apprentice 74, near the picture-book end the reader puts in the 30s and 40s. Occult was not examined at this exit; the signal that fired traces to a stage-magician word in the publisher's recap of earlier adventures, not to anything in this story.

Eighty illustrated pages of summer-holiday episodes - three friends found a club, get a clubhouse, run trips, earn money, hold a camp - sold for ages six to fourteen and estimated at one to two hours of reading. Nothing is at stake and nothing is worked out; there is no idea I can name at all, which is the finding rather than a gap, so axis:ideas decides this at the below-the-line gate on one source. Leaned on axis:ideas over axis:character-differentiation because at this length and register the character tests are suspended anyway, and the suspension removes penalties without adding points: Male zeny 79 shows a domestic story with no premise can still clear the propose line on characters alone, and that is exactly what eighty pages of holiday sketches cannot supply. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

A light illustrated chapter book for young girls: three friends are left in charge of an old man's peculiar animals, discover they can cast spells, and turn their annoying brothers into dung beetles. There is no idea to name at all, and the register suspends the character tests rather than earning anything by them - Czech reader reviews describe easy reading that blends friendship and magic and warn against expecting anything more of it. That combination is what the low band at this exit is for. Against the log, a children's register is free when the thinking carries it, The Little Prince 82, and costs when it does not, Narnia 67; this sits well below Narnia because the revenge comedy is the entire content rather than an adventure with themes attached, and Male zeny 79 shows the ceiling belongs to a domestic story of real characters at adult length. Leaned on how juvenile the telling is and on the absence of any idea, not on the protagonist, who is fine for the audience. Occult status is deliberately unexamined at this exit.

t: Krajina paseraku (The Wettest County in the World)
why: The material has a real shape - three brothers running whisky in Prohibition Virginia against a corrupt local power, drawn from the author's own family - and the atmosphere is widely praised. What decides the number is the telling. The narrative braids two timelines about five years apart, a number of chapters carry no date, and reviewers repeatedly report losing track of which year and which brother they are in, one calling the device confusing and unnecessary and another switching format because of it. Confusion is the most reliable negative in this log and the only cause that has actually ended books unread: The Gunslinger 30 was abandoned for reading a long stretch without grasping what the story was, and Caropisci 30 died on missing context rather than missing incident, which is exactly the complaint here. Nothing offsets that risk, because there is no idea to name - the moral weight is atmosphere, and the publisher's own guide points at a short-story-cycle model of loosely linked panels rather than a worked-out premise. Leaned on the opening structure and the absence of ideas rather than on protagonist, since Jack is a serviceable lead. Occult status is deliberately unexamined at this exit.

t: Kralovny a poutnici (Kralovny a poutnici: Pribehy prvniho tisicileti)
why: This is real content, not a colouring book: 272 illustrated pages on the first millennium in the Czech lands, written and drawn by an author with a shelf of historical titles behind her, and with a stated intent - forget Vysehrad, forget Bivoj - to replace the Jirasek legend with what the archaeology supports. Against that, the form is a survey for readers from nine up, with no protagonist and no continuous plot; The Silmarillion 80 is the one book in the log that survives those two absences and it does so on the weight of its ideas, which a school-age overview of tribal names and daily life is unlikely to match. So I doubt the idea holds up - axis:ideas goes in risks - and the below-the-line gate settles it at one source. Leaned on axis:density and axis:childrens rather than axis:ideas because what will actually decide the reading is 272 pages of illustrated survey aimed low, the same thin-story-over-many-pages complaint that cost The Lord of the Rings 84 its distance from the top. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

t: Kumewawa, syn dzungle (Kumeuaua, la filo de la gangalo)
why: The idea is nameable and it is the good kind: castaways who cannot feed themselves are kept alive by a twelve-year-old who wants nothing in return, and the moral weight lands when they try to pay him. Self-sacrifice and companionship over solo survival is the axis on which Project Hail Mary 92 beat The Martian 82 in this log, and the lead is both competent and easy to root for. What holds it under the line is the register: the publisher's own word for it is simple and instructive, the recommendation that exists pitches it at nine to fourteen, and the lesson is delivered rather than tested - the travellers' arrogance dissolves because the book needs it to. That is Narnia 67 territory, children at the centre and not much higher to think about, and Ranger's Apprentice 74 is the ceiling only because it had length and momentum to spend. I lean on axis:childrens with axis:ideas rather than on axis:protagonist, because the boy is the strongest thing here and would push the number up, not down; what caps it is how much of the telling is aimed at a young reader. Occult status is unexamined on this exit - Amazonian custom and a stated relationship to Mother Nature is the sort of thing worth a look if the book is ever bumped above the line.

t: Legenda o Prazskem orloji (Legenda o Prazskem orloji)
why: Twenty-four pages, a legend retold for children with comics-style three-colour illustration doing much of the work - the councillors blind Master Hanus so that no other city can have his clock. As material that is not nothing: a maker destroyed by the people who commissioned him is a hard, memorable image. But twenty-four illustrated pages cannot work a premise out, Hanus is a figure in a story rather than someone whose motives get page time, and the axis that tops this log is precisely page time on what characters want and why. So axis:ideas would go into risks and the below-the-line gate decides it at one source. Leaned on axis:childrens with axis:ideas because the form is the whole constraint here; the cruelty of the ending is not an objection, the reader does not count violence against a book at all. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

It is honest about something real - a great-grandfather's dementia seen by the small boy who has to live with it - and the treatment is warm rather than grim, so axis:bleakness barely applies. But the form governs the number: 81 pages in a first-reading edition for six-year-olds, short paragraphs, colour illustrations, a child narrator at the far end of axis:life-phase. That is the register the log puts in the 30s and 40s, well under Narnia 67, which was already docked for child leads and for lacking higher things to think about, and far under Male zeny 79, which clears the line on adult-sized characters a first-reader cannot carry. The topic is nameable but it is a topic, not an idea worked out: the book explains an illness to a child rather than leaving a thought behind, which is exactly the way Animal Farm 78 earned its score and this cannot. I leaned on axis:childrens over axis:ideas because even a stronger idea could not lift a text pitched this young. Exited at gate 4, so occult is unexamined; nothing in the annotation raises it.

t: Macjusevi prygody (King Matt the First (Krol Macius Pierwszy))
why: One premise stated precisely and then followed to its end: a boy inherits absolute power and tries to use it well. He makes his ministers teach him, goes to the front in disguise to see what war actually is, decrees chocolate for every child, jails ministers who tell him a thing is impossible, and convenes a children's parliament - and the reforms then run out of his control until he loses the kingdom. That is consequences worked out rather than events, which is the axis that separates Project Hail Mary 92 from Divergent 58, and it is written by a man who ran some of these reforms in a real orphanage, so the idea is not decorative. Labyrint sveta a raj srdce 70 is the closest calibration - an allegory with a nameable idea landed exactly in its predicted band - and Animal Farm 78 shows a bleak political allegory scores when it leaves something behind rather than immersing you in misery. Leaned on axis:ideas together with axis:protagonist: Matt wants things, is wrong in interesting ways and is worth rooting for, which is the pairing that beats worldbuilding whenever they compete. The deductions: the telling is a fairy tale for children, the register Narnia 67 and Hranicaruv ucen 74 both paid for, an episodic 330 pages that can read as one incident after another, and a downfall rather than a resolution. Not leaned on axis:bleakness - the loss is mild by this log's standards - nor on axis:life-phase, which is a couple of points at most. The opening is one concrete situation: the old king dies and the boy is on the throne, single thread, no competing plot lines, the shape The Hunger Games 89 and Hitchhiker's 83 are praised for and the opposite of the confusion that ended three books at 30.

It opens on one concrete situation - a girl walks into the lost-and-found in a hotel cellar and asks the boy who runs it to find her parents - and the two leads are differentiated in the way the log rewards: he is honest to a fault and that is why he has the job, she works out the clues. The seaside town is the real attraction, and reviewers are unanimous on its atmosphere and its inventions, the book dispensary with the mechanical mermonkey above all. What is missing is anything left behind: the payload is a monster legend and a town of eccentric names, and reviewers note the central question of the parents is not even resolved. Gate 4 fires on axis:ideas. The register is a children's illustrated adventure for ten and up, more juvenile than Narnia 67 and with less to think about, which is the lower band on the reader's own children's scale. The satisfaction is also substantially an investigation - clues, a pursuer, a secret behind a disappearance - and while that is a flag rather than the filter, since the resolution is a creature and an adventure rather than a culprit named, it sits close to the reader's least favourite shape. Leaned on axis:childrens and axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist, which is a strength here. Exited at C-low, so occult status is unexamined; what I read describes a legendary creature and a wish-granting egg, not a practice.

There is a clear central conflict - a surgeon who lost a hand to a British cannonball against a trader trying to talk blockaded New York into seceding in 1812 - and the period is vividly done, which is the kind of momentum that carried Monte Cristo 75 over its whole length. Three things hold the range under the line. Reviewers describe a large ensemble whose threads jump rapidly before they weave together, and several live plot lines before any is legible is the most reliable negative in this log, the one that ended two Discworld attempts at 30 apiece unread. The Washington Post notes there is far more desire than war here and ranks the war below pirates, prostitutes, kidnappings and buried treasure, which puts the sexual-content axis in play on volume, the dimension that sank Ready Player One 55. And nothing is left behind afterwards: it is a swashbuckling entertainment rather than a premise worked out. It is also a sequel, and continuations are not safe bets here - Hitchhiker's 83 falls to 70. Those deductions argue for the bottom of the range rather than the top. Leaned on the absence of ideas and on the opening structure rather than on protagonist, who is a serviceable adventure lead. Occult status is deliberately unexamined at this exit.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. Form and genre are settled and cheap: an original Czech middle-grade adventure novel, recommended from about fourth grade, with a light SF object at its centre. The positive case is real - the meteorite is not a free wish-machine but a trade, luck bought with physical strength and with suspicion of everyone around you, and a premise that charges a price for its gift is the shape the reader rewards when it is followed through, as in the astrophage consequences of Project Hail Mary 92. But I would list axis:ideas under risks, and that is the gate's own exit condition: readers describe it as a simple story without digressions and a plot that thins in the second half, so the cost is likely stated and then dropped rather than worked out, which leaves events instead of an idea - the reason competent books stall in the 60s. The children's register costs a little on top, the Ranger's Apprentice 74 position rather than the Hobbit 84 one, since the telling is aimed squarely at readers a long way from 28. Leaned on ideas rather than worldbuilding because the object's rules are barely declared, so there is little for a consistency check to bind to. axis:occult was deliberately not examined at this exit.

t: Muj tata pise knihu (Mano tetis raso knyga)
why: A 54-page illustrated picture book for pre-schoolers and early readers, and reader response confirms where its weight sits - the comments that exist praise the pictures as the reason to own it and describe the story as something to talk about with small children. The nearest thing to an idea is that inspiration hides everywhere and adults should sometimes listen to the smallest, which is a charming closing sentiment rather than a premise whose consequences are followed; that is exactly the axis:ideas doubt gate 4 asks about. The reader pays nothing for a children's audience when the ideas carry the book - The Little Prince 82 proves that - but this is a different register entirely: a picture book has no room to be interesting about what anyone wants, so axis:childrens costs at its maximum and the short-form suspension removes penalties without adding anything. I lean on axis:childrens rather than axis:protagonist because the boy is likeable and the book is simply too short for a protagonist test to mean anything. The detective signal on the task line is a false positive - it comes from a toy police helicopter in the boy's room, not from an investigation.

t: Muz z hodin, aneb, Proc se na podzim meni cas (Muz z hodin aneb Proc se na podzim meni cas)
why: The conceit is charming and concrete - the autumn clock change is explained by a stolen hour hand and a clockmaker who shut himself inside a station clock to stand in for it - and the opening is one situation with one child and one adult following one missing object, which is the legible start the log demands. But it is 80 illustrated pages of pure fairy-tale polarity of good and evil, the subtitle gives the point away before the story starts, and the reviewer who liked the Art Nouveau setting found the telling carried by colour and props rather than by any dramatic stake or layered story. So there is no idea to name: the whimsical explanation is the whole payload, not something the book leaves behind, which is exactly where The Little Prince 82 earns its score and this cannot. Gate 4 fires with axis:ideas in doubt, and the register puts it in the lower band - a short illustrated children's tale suspends the character tests without adding anything, and readers report the text is heavy going for its own audience. Leaned on axis:childrens and axis:ideas rather than axis:opening, which is clean here. Exited at C-low, so the occult question is unexamined; the magic on show is a living clockmaker inside a clock, with no rite involved in what I read.

This is an illustrated early reader of about 112 pages pitched at seven-year-olds: five girls whose initials run A to E take turns hosting birthday sleepovers, and the narrator dreads her friends meeting her severely disabled older sister while one of the group needles her about it. There is a real subject there, and the publisher and reviewers credit the handling of bullying and disability, but a subject is not an idea worked out, and at this register the character and emotion tests are suspended rather than passed - the suspension removes penalties and adds nothing. That is what the low band at this exit is for. Against the log: a children's register is free when the thinking carries it, The Little Prince 82, and costs when it does not, Narnia 67, while Male zeny 79 marks the ceiling for a domestic children's-adjacent story - but that is an adult-length novel of characters and this is a school reader at a fraction of the length. Leaned on how juvenile the telling is and on the absence of an idea, not on the protagonist, who works for her audience. Occult status is deliberately unexamined and nothing suggests it is live.

t: Novy domov Tracy a Jess (We Are the Beaker Girls)
why: A junior domestic story narrated by a ten-year-old: her mother takes over a seaside antique shop, she goes looking for a better partner for her mother, and she befriends a boy stealing ice creams on the beach who turns out to have run away from foster care. Professional reviewers credit the handling of neglect, poverty and life in care, and fostering as a central subject rather than a background detail is genuinely unusual in children's fiction - but a subject is not an idea worked out, and the telling is pitched at young children with cartoon illustrations throughout, so the character and emotion tests are suspended rather than passed. That combination is what the low band at this exit is for. Narnia 67 already pays for child leads and for lacking higher things to think about while being far more ambitious than this, and Male zeny 79 clears the line on characters at adult length; a junior chapter book sits below both. It is also a direct continuation that assumes its narrator's situation from elsewhere, and continuations are not safe bets in this log - Hitchhiker's 83 falls to 70. Leaned on how juvenile the register is and on the absence of an idea rather than on the protagonist, who is likeable. Occult status is deliberately unexamined and nothing suggests it is live.

There is a real subject here and it is stated sharply: thinness as the currency a closed school runs on, and starvation spreading between girls the way a rumour does. Critics back the voice and the satire. The reason I still expect this under the line is that the idea is reported as being undercut by the book's own plotting - a professional review calls the headmaster strand incongruous and hurried and says it explains the darkness away too easily, and another finds much of the prose rambling and the first half weaker than the second. So axis:ideas is exactly what I would list in risks, which is the gate 4 exit. The deductions then compound in directions the log measures: 1984 60 shows what sustained grimness costs even with a first-rate idea behind it, and here anorexia, drowning, self-harm and sexual abuse arrive as the texture rather than as a gradual turn - the same at-once bleakness that helped sink Promena 58. A fifteen-year-old lead is only the small axis:life-phase pushback and is not doing the work. The mystery strand is a flag rather than the veto: the satisfaction on offer is the satire and the girls' psyches, not finding out who did it. Sexual abuse appears as content, not as what the plot is for, so filter 6 does not fire either.

The strength is voice and a cast of four boys who are written as distinct from each other, and Saturnin 78 settles that a comic register carries no penalty with this reader when character and voice do the work. The plot is also concrete from the first page - they want a clubhouse and someone else wants it too - so nothing here risks the confusion that ended The Colour of Magic 30. What caps it is that the book is a school year of pranks: episodes strung together for the laugh, with nothing to think about afterwards, which is the exact note that held Rangers Apprentice 74 down, and this is pitched several years younger than that. It is also a continuation of a long-running series and sequels do not hold their level in this log - Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. I leaned on axis:ideas because that is the doubt that fixes the number; axis:character-differentiation is the one thing arguing upward and it cannot carry a book with no destination. Exited at gate 4, so occult is unexamined - the title is a joke about a teacher, not a subject.

The subject is exactly what this reader says he wants a book to leave behind. Two young doctors take opposite positions on what madness is - a life story or an organ - and the novel argues both of them out at length, including the theory that men once literally heard the voices of gods and that religion is the residue of a faculty that disappeared. Genuinely examining what is plausible and what is not is the rigour that put Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 at the top of the non-fiction here and Speaker for the Dead 90 near the top of the fiction, and it opens on one legible situation per thread, two sixteen-year-olds in 1876, one in Brittany and one in England, rather than several plot lines at once. Against that stands the heaviest form of the density penalty in the log: 576 pages in which reviewers agree there is a great deal of research and little story, with both men's argumentative lectures transcribed whole and digressions described as tests of patience. LOTR 84 was docked precisely for a thin story over many pages, Les Miserables 71 for its digressions, and Unfinished Tales 69 is the floor for material that does not cohere; two leads and a mixed apparatus of letters, journals and speeches add to that. Leaned on ideas against density, the two axes that actually fight here, rather than on protagonist. The occult axis is a real risk rather than a settled question: late in the book a grieving character consults a medium who stages a summoning of the dead, which is a rite on the page even though it is presented as fraud and the novel's own thesis is neurological.

t: Popel a duse (Schwingen aus Rauch und Gold)
why: Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. Form and genre are cheap and decided: a 320-page young-adult urban fantasy translated from German and set in Prague. The positive case is one good concrete image - a girl for whom the doomed lose their colour, so her gift is a visible fact rather than an announcement, and the city read as grey is that gift made into a mood. Beyond it I would put axis:ideas in risks, which is this gate's exit condition: the frame is a twelve-year imbalance between light and shadow policed by immortals called the Eternal, a good-versus-evil scaffolding declared rather than worked out, and the reader's objection to Divergent 58 was exactly a premise assembled from parts that never cohere. Nothing in what I can establish suggests the balance mechanic carries consequences the way astrophage does in Project Hail Mary 92. A teen lead costs only a little on its own, the small pushback rather than a tier. Leaned on ideas rather than protagonist because the lead is at least given a specific problem to want out of; it is the world's reasoning I doubt. Note the axis:occult status is unexamined at this exit - foreseeing death and a heaven-and-hell cosmology are both places a rite could be enacted on the page, and I did not check.

t: Pravidla se maji porusovat (Rules Were Meant to Be Broken)
why: It opens on one concrete situation and one want, which is what this reader asks for: a girl who has written herself rules against getting attached because her mother keeps moving them in with a new man. Motive-led YA is not a handicap - Pride and Prejudice 75 shows a relationship as the central subject costs nothing when wants and why are the whole book. What holds it down is that the reviews describe the cast as flat, each character carrying a single hobby, and thin distinctness is the failure that sank Divergent 58 and cost Artemis 69 its band; against Golden Son 92, where three leads each think and want differently, this has no case to make. Nor is there an idea beyond the rule-list device. I leaned on axis:character-differentiation rather than axis:ideas because the doubt about the cast is sourced rather than inferred. Infidelity was examined and does not apply - the mother's serial partners are unmarried, outside the marriage-or-engagement scope. Exited at gate 4, so occult is unexamined, and it is not a question a contemporary YA blurb raises.

The positive case is real and small: a six-year-old's princess fantasy is taken literally, the family actually goes, and the book spends its length on what a traditional Pacific village is like once the fantasy meets it - a declared premise whose consequences are at least followed, which is the shape that earned Labyrint sveta 70. But the idea stops at culture shock; the register is a modern fairy tale for young children with a helper figure and 328 illustrated pages of fauna, flora and travel description, and story density is the reader's penalty term (LOTR 84 lost its margin to thin story over many pages). A six-year-old lead is the far end of axis:life-phase, where Ender's Game lost points for reading as a child from the inside even at 87. I leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:worldbuilding because there is nothing declared here to hold up or fail; the number turns on whether anything is left behind, and I doubt it is. Exited at gate 4 on that doubt, so the occult question is unexamined - Polynesian belief could be enacted on the page and I did not check.

t: Priste bude vsechno dobry (Neste gang blir alt riktig)
why: Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. Form and genre are the whole of the cheap work here: a 104-page colour graphic novel of literary Nordic family fiction for adults, translated from Norwegian, with a single protagonist and a single thread - a librarian, an estranged mother, a father's death - so the opening carries none of the risk that ended Foundryside 30. The positive case is squarely on the reader's heaviest axis: this is a book made almost entirely of what one woman wants from her mother and cannot get, page time on motive rather than incident, and reviewers single out empathetic, credible characterisation and the alternation of large existential questions with ordinary days. That is the axis that puts Pycha a predsudek 75 in the A band with no premise to work out. Against it I would still list axis:ideas under risks, and that is this gate's exit condition: iLiteratura itself calls it another variation on a favourite Nordic subject, not-very-idyllic family relations, and a well-executed variation on a familiar theme leaves a mood rather than something to think about, which is where competent books stall in the 60s. The comics form compounds it a little, since 104 drawn pages give less room for interiority than prose does. Leaned on ideas rather than protagonist because the protagonist looks like the book's strength, not its risk. axis:occult was not examined at this exit and nothing suggests it applies.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. Form and genre come cheap and settle most of it: an urban fantasy novel translated from Swedish, published for readers of about ten and up and illustrated in the Czech edition. On gate 1 the disappearances make the plot investigation-shaped, but the satisfaction on offer is a girl holding a city together against beings stronger than she is, not finding out who did it, so that is a flag and not the detective filter. The positive case is a clean single situation stated in the first line - she names herself and her job - with an inherited duty and the grandmother who held it now gone, which gives her something concrete to want and to fail at. Against it I would put axis:ideas in risks, this gate's exit condition: a hidden supernatural community policed by a teenage guardian is a well-worn frame, and the reader's complaint about Harry Potter 51 was precisely that a magical society declared in detail was never reorganised around what it declared - a hidden Stockholm with elves living inside it invites exactly that audit and there is nothing here suggesting the book undertakes it. Children's register and a fifteen-year-old lead each cost a little, the Narnia 67 position rather than a tier. Leaned on ideas rather than worldbuilding because the world may well be pleasant and consistent and still leave nothing behind. axis:occult was deliberately not examined at this exit, and with supernatural beings being managed rather than invoked it is the axis most likely to move this number.

This one has an idea I can name, which is why it goes above the picture-book register rather than into it: children whom nobody notices, and adults who do notice and are limited in what they are allowed to do about it - a boy left alone so long that the food runs out and the power is cut, who then builds a night broadcast for other children in the same position. That is a premise with consequences worked out rather than a situation described, and the opening is one concrete image, a boy alone in a flat, with warm socks and food coming through the letterbox. Against it: the register is a children's novel for readers from eight or nine, told in a fairy-tale voice with a device - people who can sense a forgotten child through a wall - that is asserted rather than explained, and the reader's log puts even the best children's-adjacent work at Male zeny 79 and marks Narnia 67 down for child leads and thin thematic weight. Gate 4 exits at the default band on that basis: competent, warm, likely just under the line. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:childrens rather than axis:protagonist, whose risk is only that a lonely nine-year-old is far from the reader's life phase. One reviewer reports errors in the Czech text. Exited at C-low, so occult status is unexamined; nothing in what I read involves a rite.

Four linked stories about four twelve-to-fourteen-year-olds, children of emergency-service parents, who meet at camp and then keep meeting crises - a flood, a road accident, a fire - and who are written so that a reader learns what to do in each. The purpose is instruction, and it shows: readers report the stories are not complex and become repetitive, which is the shape the below-the-line gate is for. There is no idea I can name here, only a syllabus, so axis:ideas carries the exit at one source. Leaned on axis:ideas with axis:childrens rather than on the darker content: the self-harm and addiction material is real but the reader treats bleakness as the mildest objection in the log and does not object to violence at all, so it costs a little and decides nothing. Short didactic fiction gets the character rules suspended, and the suspension removes penalties without adding points, which is why this sits under the band where Animal Farm 78 sits on a nameable idea. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

t: Rikej tomu, jak chces (Call It What You Want)
why: The positive case is genuine and it is the axis that tops this log: both leads are defined by what they want and why - a boy rationing pocket money while nursing the father who ruined his classmates' families, a girl living down having invalidated a whole room's exam scores - and the book asks outright whether it is acceptable to do something wrong for the right reasons. That is a nameable question, and the reader gave Pride and Prejudice 75 precisely because motives and wants were the whole book. What stops me predicting above the line is that the question is posed rather than worked out: reviewers land on 'nothing is clear-cut and maybe that's okay' and on people being misjudged, which is a discussion prompt, not a premise whose consequences bind the plot, and the resolution is carried by the romance. That is the Ranger's Apprentice 74 failure mode of easy reading with not much to think about, minus the adventure momentum. Two live viewpoints from chapter one is a mild concern on axis:multi-pov, but both are concretely situated, so this is nothing like the six-threads-at-once opening that produced Guards! Guards! 30. Neither hard filter fires: the father's embezzlement is a crime in the backstory rather than an investigation the reader solves, and the sexual axis is not what the plot is for. I lean on axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist because the leads are the strong part.

This opens on exactly one legible situation - two women in a Siberian labour camp in 1933, one of them dying, the other deciding to break out and cross thousands of miles to find the man who might save her - and the motive is self-sacrifice for a friend rather than solo survival, which the reader states outright as a preference: Project Hail Mary 92 beat The Martian 82 on companionship and self-sacrifice specifically. The camp bleakness costs only mildly, since 1984 60 is the one case where bleakness did real damage. What keeps the number under the line is that there is no idea to name: Booklist calls it a somewhat unrealistic though riveting story, and the escape-and-romance machinery is the point, so the book leaves events behind rather than thinking. Leaned on ideas rather than on protagonist, since the two women are the strongest thing here. Occult status is deliberately unexamined at this exit.

The positive case is real: one concrete starting situation (a Chinese communist saves the girl's life in the opening pages) and a lead who wants something specific and urgent, since she steals to keep her mother fed in a Russian exile slum in 1928 China. Page time on what a character wants and why is the axis that tops this log, Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90. What holds the number under the line is that nothing is left behind afterwards: trade reviews describe an improbable star-crossed romance with too many characters and unnecessary plot points blurring the focus, so the book is a sweeping entertainment rather than a premise worked out, and that is the shape that has stalled competent historical novels in the 60s here - Exodus 68, Quo Vadis 66. The marriage-affair axis is clean, the mother being a widow and the lead unmarried, and the plot is flight and romance rather than sexual behaviour. Leaned on ideas rather than protagonist because the lead is vivid enough; it is the thinking that is missing. Occult status is deliberately unexamined at this exit.

The engine is clear and the opening is one concrete situation: a seventeen-year-old Russian aristocrat fleeing the Bolsheviks watches his mother murdered and his twin sister carried off when their Trans-Siberian train is attacked, and spends the book in Shanghai hunting the commissar who did it. Revenge sustained over a long book is a form this reader has enjoyed - Monte Cristo 75 held up on plot momentum alone. Two things keep the range under the line. Nothing is left behind afterwards; Publishers Weekly calls it an unflinchingly gory yarn that evokes a decadent era, which is atmosphere rather than an idea. And the same review calls it frankly erotic and lists the hero bedding a relative's mistress and rescuing the city's most famous madam among the first things he does ashore, so the sexual axis is in play on volume and on the crudeness of the treatment - volume is what sank Ready Player One 55, and Artemis 69 was docked for crude treatment even at small volume. That argues for the bottom of this range. The filter itself does not fire, because the plot is revenge rather than a sexual relationship. Leaned on the absence of ideas together with the content axis rather than on worldbuilding, the setting being history. Occult status is deliberately unexamined at this exit.

It starts from one concrete situation - a school empties for a dance competition, the boy left behind as punishment wakes the octopus - and a legible single thread is the thing this reader most needs, the absence of which ended The Colour of Magic 30. That is the whole of the positive case. It is 112 pages of tie-in prose written after a 70-minute television comedy for children, a school of water sprites and nymphs played for gags, with no idea behind it and no interiority to spend pages on; the log puts that register in the 30s and 40s, well below Narnia 67, which at least had a moral scheme to disagree with. The magic is also undeclared and decorative - living water simply works - so axis:worldbuilding neither earns nor loses much, unlike the collapse that ended Mortal Engines 55. I leaned on axis:childrens because the register decides this regardless of execution. Exited at gate 4, so the occult question is unexamined and it is a live one here: Czech folk water spirits and a reviving 'living water' could well be enacted on the page, which is what Percy Jackson 57 was docked for.

A full-colour nine-chapter fairy tale told at read-aloud level: a meadow gnome leaves home lonely, is advised by a frog and an owl, helped by a squirrel and a butterfly, and gains a friend by helping one. That is a moral, not a premise whose consequences get worked out, and there is no idea I can name behind it, so axis:ideas belongs in risks and the below-the-line gate decides this at one source. Leaned on axis:childrens rather than axis:protagonist: the gnome is not badly drawn, he is drawn for six-year-olds, and at that register the character rules are suspended without anything replacing them - the suspension removes penalties, it never adds points. Placed under the band that costs Narnia 67 only a little, because that book at least had higher things to reach for; occult status is unexamined at this exit.

The positive case is that it leaves an idea behind and it is not the obvious one: not 'be yourself' but what it costs the ordinary boy to stand next to someone who is, and how quietly he sells her out to get his place back. Leo narrates alone, in the first person, fifteen years later, and the book opens on one concrete situation - a boy, a porcupine tie from an anonymous sender, a new school - so nothing here risks the confusion that ended Guards! Guards! 30 and The Gunslinger 30, and the single close POV is what the reader named as why The Hunger Games 89 works. Two things pull the number down. First, the title character's interior life is deliberately withheld - the reader never learns what Stargirl wants or why, and page time on motive is the axis Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 top the log on, so the book declines the one thing he values most. Second, it is a high-school novel about popularity, pitched at twelve and up, and axis:childrens costs a little at that register just as it did for Narnia 67; Male zeny 79 marks the ceiling a book of this kind reaches, and it got there on a much larger cast. Content is clean - a kiss or two, no occult, no investigation, no marriage in it - so nothing else deducts. I leaned on axis:ideas and axis:motives rather than axis:worldbuilding, which does not exist here, and kept axis:protagonist as the risk: Leo chooses the crowd, and a lead who cannot be rooted for is what cost The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 twenty-two points against the same author's own best work. If Leo's regret reads as cowardice rather than as honesty, this lands below the range.

The opening is exactly the concrete hook the reader asks for - a boy finds a numbered key on the way to school - and momentum is clearly not the problem. But the form governs: 152 illustrated pages sold as an interactive puzzle book, with ciphers and riddles printed in the text for the child to solve, aimed at readers of about ten. The satisfaction on offer is working the puzzles, not what anyone wants or why, and page time on motive over incident is the axis that tops this log with Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90. There is no idea to name behind the rescue-and-secret plot, and an activity book suspends the character tests without earning anything back. I leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:detective because the latter does not fire: the payoff is a hidden secret and a kidnapped teacher freed, not the identity of a culprit deduced, so this is adventure with puzzles rather than a whodunnit - a flag, not the filter. Exited at gate 4, so occult is unexamined; the castle secret reads as historical rather than supernatural but I did not confirm it.

One declared goal drives the whole thing: a seventeen-year-old walks into Stalin's Russia in 1930 to get her father out of a labour camp, and wanting something that badly is what this reader pays for, Mockingjay 91 being the log's clearest case of motive over spectacle. Two deductions hold it under the line. It is a sequel that assumes its lead and her situation from elsewhere rather than establishing them, and sequels are not safe bets in this log - Hitchhiker's 83 falls to 70 for its continuations. And there is no idea to name: reviewers treat the appeal as the historical sweep and the romance, so what is left afterwards is events. Leaned on ideas and on the sequel axis rather than on protagonist, since the lead is the asset here. Occult status is deliberately unexamined at this exit.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. On gate 1 first, since the annotation trips the detective signal: the leads are a licensed anti-ghoul squad sent to solve a case around an old ghoul family, so the plot is investigation-shaped, but the satisfaction of this material is body-horror action and the hero's divided identity between hunter and monster, not the naming of a culprit - a flag, not the filter. Form then decides the number: this is one instalment of a long-running comics serial, and it opens with the story already well in progress - promotions already awarded, a returning acquaintance from the protagonist's past assumed rather than introduced. That is the confusion failure by construction, and the reader has ended three books on it, Foundryside 30 for exactly this - lots happening, none of it meaning anything yet. There is no idea I can name that belongs to this instalment rather than to the whole serial, which puts axis:ideas in risks and gives the gate its exit; and the comics form suspends the prose character work that separated Sunrise on the Reaping 87 from Ballad 65 rather than passing it, so both conditions for the lower band hold. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log, Hitchhiker's falling 83 to 70. Leaned on the sequel dependence and the missing standalone idea rather than on content, since violence and gore are not objections for this reader at all. axis:occult was not examined at this exit.

The one thing it has to offer is the turn the annotation puts at its centre: the disliked English neighbour becomes the rescuer, which is a want-and-why beat rather than an incident, and the friendship material is the sort of thing that carried The Hobbit 84. Against that, it is a 290-page children's adventure whose payoff is an accident on the rocks and a rescue - events, not an idea - and Rangers Apprentice 74 marks the ceiling for exactly that (easy to read, not much to think about) with a far more practised author behind it. Three child leads of different nationalities also split the page time the reader wants spent inside one head; the tight single POV is what he named as the reason The Hunger Games 89 works. I leaned on axis:ideas because that is the doubt carrying the number - I can name no thought this leaves behind - rather than on axis:character-differentiation, which I could not judge from what is available. Exited at gate 4 on that doubt, so the occult status is unexamined; the 'mystical warning' in the annotation reads as village superstition but I did not verify it.

t: Utopia Avenue, aneb, Cesta do Tramtarie (Utopia Avenue)
why: The positive case is real but narrow: the chapters are built as songs, each from the POV of whoever wrote it, so a lot of page time goes on what these people want out of making music rather than on events - the axis that tops the log in Speaker for the Dead 90 and Mockingjay 91. Against that, the form is a chronicle with no premise to work out: a band forms, records, tours and meets famous people, which is the thin-story-over-many-pages penalty that cost LOTR 84 its difference from The Hobbit and that reviewers here name as the main complaint. I would list axis:ideas under risks - I cannot name an idea the book leaves behind beyond the ache of making art - so gate 4 fires and I stop. Leaning on axis:ideas and axis:density rather than axis:protagonist, because the leads are drawn with care; what is missing is a thing to think about afterwards. Sexual content and drug use are present in the rock-novel register and would dock further, on the volume dimension that sank Ready Player One 55, but I did not establish how much. Exited at C-low, so the occult status of the supernatural strand around the guitarist is unexamined, and the opening structure is inferred rather than sourced.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, and the form answers the question by itself: 34 pages, 190x190 mm, richly illustrated, publisher's recommended age three and upward, written partly as a conversation-opener for a family expecting another child. That is a picture book, which the reader's own calibration puts in the 30s and 40s. The positive case is that it has a subject rather than just a scene - what a child feels before being born, tracked as the child grows - and short work has the character and emotion rules suspended, the position that let The Little Prince 82 score high on a child lead. But the suspension removes penalties and never adds points, and it earned nothing here: the reader's short high scorers are canonical for their ideas, and I cannot name an idea in this one beyond the tender fact of gestation, so axis:ideas is a risk and both conditions for the lower band hold. Leaned on the children's register rather than on ideas because the register is established and the idea is simply absent; nothing about the telling asks a 28-year-old reader to think. Occult was not examined at this exit.

Four framed episodes told round a campfire, each a self-contained gag adventure for small children, running about eighty minutes in total. There is no premise to work out and no thought left behind, and short form suspends the character tests without adding anything in their place - the reason The Little Prince 82 scored was its thinking, not its length. The cast is drawn from a fifty-year comic strip where the four friends are fixed types rather than people who want different things, which is the opposite of what the reader praised in Golden Son 92, and the register sits below Narnia 67 by a long way. I leaned on axis:ideas because that is the doubt that fixes the number; axis:character-differentiation is not even contested here. The catalogue flagged 'patrani' but this is not an investigation the reader has to follow, so axis:detective does not fire. Exited at gate 4, so the occult status is unexamined - one episode visits devils and another a werewolf, both in the Czech comic-fairy-tale idiom, and I did not check what is enacted.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. Form and genre are settled and unambiguous: 160 illustrated pages of original Czech children's fiction, publisher's recommended age nine and up, a boy-and-animal story with one concrete starting situation and a single thread, so nothing in the opening resembles the confusion that ended Colour of Magic 30. The positive case is that it is about wanting: the boy wants to keep the cub, his father knows what the cub will become, and that is a conflict of motives rather than incident, which is the axis that tops the reader's log. There is even a nameable thought - that loving an animal can mean giving it up - and the reader gives credit for that kind of plain moral, Male zeny 79 clearing the propose line on characters alone with no premise to work out. Against it: I would still put axis:ideas in risks, because the summary resolves the whole arc before the book begins and what remains is one sentiment rather than something to think about. The children's register costs a little more than the Narnia 67 position, since the telling and the stakes are pitched at nine-year-olds. Leaned on the children's register and the thin idea rather than on protagonist, because the boy does want something clearly - it is the size of the book's thought, not the lead, that holds the number down. axis:occult was not examined at this exit and nothing in the material suggests it applies.

t: Vlk a lev (Le loup et le lion: le roman du film)
why: The story does have a clean want and a cost - a girl hides two cubs to keep them from people, and loses both when the secret breaks - and companionship over solitude is the axis on which Project Hail Mary 92 beat The Martian 82, so the material is not the problem. The problem is what the book is: 112 pages of tie-in prose written for seven-year-olds from someone else's screenplay, so the interiority the reader values is not there to have, and the shape of the plot is fixed by a film rather than worked out. That is the picture-book and early-reader end of axis:childrens, below Narnia 67 by a wide margin. Nor is there an idea past 'people should leave animals alone', which is asserted rather than examined - the opposite of what earned Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 its score. I leaned on axis:childrens because the register and the derived text fix the number whatever the plot does. Exited at gate 4, so occult is unexamined; a realist animal story does not raise it.

Both gate-4 conditions fire together here, which is as clear as this decision gets: it is literary in intent and it is a collection with no single premise. Forty-eight pages of small observations - pumpkins, the attic, hide-and-seek, the seasons - seen by children of five and seven, in an art book whose illustrations are embroidered. There is nothing to work out, no want driving anything, and no idea I can name; the suspension of the character rules for short work removes penalties but adds nothing, and what the reader liked in The Little Prince 82 was the thoughts, not the brevity. Even Male zeny 79, the highest children's-adjacent result in the log, earned it on characters over a whole novel, which this form has no room for. I leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:childrens because a gentler register would not matter if there were something here to think about. Exited at gate 4, so occult is unexamined and the subject matter does not raise it.

t: Zadni draci nejsou (There's No Such Thing as a Dragon)
why: This is the rare short book where the idea can be named in a phrase - a problem denied grows until it fills the house, and shrinks the moment it is admitted - and that is genuinely the Animal Farm 78 move, one figure carrying one thought. But axis:short-idea-driven only removes the character rules, it never adds points, and here the form is a 32-page picture book: a few sentences a page, pictures doing the work, one gag repeated to its conclusion. The Little Prince 82 is the proof that a short allegory can score, and the difference is decisive - that book has pages of thinking to spend, this one has a joke and a moral. A reader for whom Narnia 67 already lacked higher things to think about gets about four minutes here. I leaned on axis:childrens rather than axis:ideas because the idea is not the weak part; the amount of book is. Exited at gate 4, so occult is unexamined, and a friendly cartoon dragon does not raise it.

The positive case is stronger than the shelf it sits on suggests. There is a real subject - children sheltering underground while a city is bombed, tied to the actual Bethnal Green stairway disaster of March 1943 - and a professional review credits the author with writing war and the children in it plainly, factually and without cliche, which is the honesty the reader rewarded in Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75. The lead is a small boy the older boys will not have, with one much younger friend, so there is somebody to root for. What keeps it under the line is the size and the register: ninety-six illustrated pages recommended from age seven, and a time-slip that carries a small boy from the past into the present, which is a device for making the parallel legible to a child rather than a premise whose consequences get worked out. That is the axis:ideas doubt - the theme is delivered rather than tested - and axis:childrens costs here in the way it cost Narnia 67. I lean on those two rather than axis:bleakness, because the reader's objection to bleakness is the mildest in the log and a book written for seven-year-olds will not deliver it at 1984 60 strength.

Four separate lives are carried in parallel - a writer with an unresolved problem in her marriage in Paris, a model in New York, an art teacher in Australia, a divorced photographer in America - and the book's business is their reconciliation with what life dealt them. That is the structure the log punishes hardest: four storylines opening at once is the shape that ended three books unfinished at 30, and four leads split the character work that Pride and Prejudice 75 and Mockingjay 91 earn their scores on, so no one of them gets the page time that makes a protagonist interesting. I cannot name an idea the book leaves behind - accepting that a step back is not resignation is a sentiment, not a premise worked out - so axis:ideas belongs in risks and gate 4 fires. Effectively four novella-length character sketches rather than one book, which is why I put it in the lower band rather than the default: the form spreads the character tests thin without a premise to carry it. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:character-differentiation rather than on the marriage material, which I could not size from the publisher's synopsis. Exited at C-low, so the occult status is unexamined and nothing suggests it arises. Overspend note: none, one source, and no independent review of the book appears to exist.

A wish-granting children's fantasy for readers from nine: a girl wishes to be big, a cat warrior takes her to a reborn island, the king of the giants hears the wish and her fate turns out written otherwise. The one thing in its favour on the log's terms is that the wish is not simply granted - the twist is that it cannot be - but the whole apparatus is ability handed over rather than earned, which is the axis the reader marks down, and there is no idea to name beyond be careful what you wish for. Gate 4 fires on axis:ideas. The lower band rather than the default because the register is a short illustrated series adventure that suspends the character tests without adding anything: Male zeny 79 shows children's-adjacent work clearing the line on characters alone, and there is nothing of that order here. Leaned on axis:childrens and axis:ideas rather than axis:opening, which I could not source but which a fourth wish in a running series makes unlikely to be the problem. It also assumes a wish-arc frame established before this one, which cuts against reading it cold. Exited at C-low, so the occult status is unexamined; the magic on show is talking cats and wishes granted by a giant king, with no rite in what I read.

t: Tajemne zmizeni Nikoly Tesly (Tajemne zmizeni Nikoly Tesly)
why: A short illustrated children's time-travel adventure: Alex and Qiang, already established as time travellers, jump to 1893 after Tesla vanishes, and the trail runs to Tunguska. The historical hooks are the appeal and they are decoration - a famous inventor and a famous explosion used as destinations - and time travel here is a way to reach set pieces rather than a premise with rules whose consequences get followed, which is exactly the demand the log makes: Project Hail Mary 92 earned its score by working second-order consequences out, and Divergent 58 lost its on a premise that collapses under thought. I can name no idea, so axis:ideas carries the below-the-line exit at one source. Leaned on axis:ideas with axis:childrens because the register and the missing premise both point the same way; axis:sequels sits in risks because the book opens on facts a reader is assumed to already hold from what came before, and series decline is real in this log - Hitchhiker's 83 to 70. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

The device is genuine allegory rather than decoration: the ADHD is a person, an invisible companion only the girl can see, and the school day is told as what he does to her and what the teacher who cannot see him makes of it. That does leave a thought behind - being judged for something nobody else can perceive - and short allegory with a nameable idea is the shape The Little Prince 82 and Labyrint sveta 70 both scored on. It still cannot be put much above the floor. It is a picture book, the register this reader's grading puts in the 30s and 40s, and it is written in verse, the one form he has named as a cause of a low score in its own right: Havran 40 ties the lowest completed score in the log and the form was the first reason given. Those two compound, and at picture-book length there is no room for the idea to be pressed any further than stating it. Leaned on axis:verse and axis:childrens rather than axis:ideas, because the idea is present and it is the form that decides the number here. One source, the C-low budget.

A 304-page YA debut with one concrete starting situation and a single close POV - Julie, seventeen, whose boyfriend has died, calls his phone to hear the voicemail and he answers - which is exactly the shape of opening the reader wants and the opposite of the confusions that ended books at 30 in his log. The premise is also declared precisely: the connection is temporary, Sam cannot tell her anything useful, and every call makes letting go harder. What stops it short is that the book spends that premise on feeling rather than on working it out; reviewers describe an emotional grief narrative that makes readers cry, and their common complaint is a rushed ending and hurried summary between the big scenes, which is momentum failing where the consequences should have been drawn. So the answer to whether the idea holds up is no, I would put axis:ideas in risks - the reader's high scores go to books that examine what is plausible and true (Seeking Allah Finding Jesus 91) or whose premise is followed to its second-order effects (Project Hail Mary 92), and a grief story that uses its device as a way to say goodbye lands where competent, moving, unexamined books land. A teenage lead is only a small pushback (Ender's Game 87 with a child lead). Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist, who by all accounts is sympathetic and active. A C-low exit leaves axis:occult unexamined, and it is a real question here: speech with the dead is what the reader called divination in Havran 40, though nothing described is a rite and no system is invoked. One source, within the gate budget.

t: Aru Sah a konec casu (Aru Shah and the End of Time)
why: The opening is legible and it has a lead with a want: a twelve-year-old who embroiders the truth to be liked lights a museum lamp on a dare and frees what was behind it, then has to undo it. Nothing there is confusing and nothing trips a filter on the blurb. What is absent is anything to think about afterwards - it is a comic middle-grade quest told in jokes, pyjamas and a talking-pigeon guide, and the mythic apparatus is inherited from an epic rather than built, so there is no premise being worked out in the sense that earns points here. The nearest thing the reader has actually read to this shape is Percy Jackson 57, which he put in the C band and whose reason he named as the pantheon, so the range belongs below the line rather than at the Hobbit 84 end of writing for children. Leaned on axis:childrens and axis:ideas. axis:occult is deliberately not examined at this exit, and because the gods here are a living tradition's own it could later make this a reject rather than merely lower it. One source, the C-low budget.
