t: Baba Bedla (Baba Bedla a divka na hrebeni)
why: This one has something to name, which is why it sits a band above the picture books this pool is full of: a girl alone through six winters on a mountain ridge, eaten by the wish for revenge, is walked through other people's stories from other times until she can forgive. Revenge giving way to forgiveness by way of hearing what happened to other people is a real idea, and the log rewards exactly that - Animal Farm 78 and Labyrint sveta a raj srdce 70 both score on an idea a reader can state in a phrase rather than on plot. It is also a mycelium-and-lichen conceit about everything being connected, which is a thought rather than an event. What holds it down is register and delivery. This is an art-house illustrated children's book, painted in sprays and watercolour, and reader reception in this series includes the complaint that the story is sketchy and unfinished with the praise going to the pictures - which is the failure that put Unfinished Tales at 69 even in Tolkien's hands, pieces that do not connect. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe in this log: Hitchhiker's 83 falls to 70 for its continuations. Leaned on axis:childrens because the format and audience are established and they cap it under the line, with the idea kept as the risk because a lyrical children's book can carry a theme without ever working it out. One source, the gate budget; occult status unexamined, as a C exit allows, and the magical mushroom woman makes that a live question.

t: Bambi, aneb, Pribeh z lesu (Bambi, une vie dans les bois)
why: What is held here is not the 1923 novel but a forty-page illustrated retelling of it for five-year-olds: a fawn grows through the seasons from first steps to independence. The source has real substance, and a retelling this short keeps the life-course and drops whatever the original was arguing - the shape that made Unfinished Tales 69 the lowest Tolkien, pieces of a larger work that do not connect into anything. No idea survives in nameable form, the register is read-aloud, and both conditions for the lower band therefore hold. The Little Prince 82 proves a short illustrated book is no bar in itself and equally proves what has to be present for it to score. Leaned on axis:childrens and axis:ideas rather than axis:density, because the fault is not a thin story spread over many pages - there are few pages - but that nothing is worked out in them. Occult unexamined at this exit. One search, inside budget.

There is a real question at the centre and it is the kind this reader answers well to: why does one settlement on a colonised planet live in want while the one across the forest has every comfort, and who profits from that. It is worked out as a chain of things the children find out rather than as set-piece action, which is the axis Speaker for the Dead 90 tops, and the arrival of the island and the robot is one concrete event to start from rather than several threads at once. The doubt is whether the premise pays off. It is written for ten-year-olds, and the one substantive reader account of it says the last quarter loses pace and forces the story off the colony and back to Earth - a premise that stops being followed through is what the log punishes hardest, Divergent 58 having collapsed exactly there. Some of its satire also assumes a Czech reader who remembers the regime it is aimed at. Leaned on axis:ideas because the colonial-inequality question is the only thing here that could earn a good number; axis:childrens is a real but smaller pushback at a 10+ reading age. One source, the C-low budget.

A short illustrated Czech children's story: a girl on a school visit to the cemetery at All Souls' loses the group, sets a candle on a forgotten grave and crosses into a land of the dead. The subject is real - a grandfather who died before there was a goodbye - but a subject is not an idea worked out, and at this length and register nothing is followed through, so axis:ideas belongs in risks. A read-aloud pitch and an illustrated short form leave the character tests nothing to test, which meets the second condition for the lower band. The Little Prince 82 is the counter-case for children's illustrated books and it earns its score on the thinking its text carries. Leaned on axis:childrens and axis:ideas rather than axis:bleakness, because a child's bereavement handled gently is not the sustained gloom that cost 1984 60. A lit candle and contact with the dead put the occult question live and it is unexamined at this exit; Percy Jackson 57 shows what that can cost. One search, inside budget.

t: Byl jednou jeden zazrak (Veilles et merveilles creoles (Creole Folktales))
why: This is the gate-4 case the rule was written for - serious literary material in the form of a collection - and it exits there, but with the default band rather than the low one, because there is an idea and it can be named in a phrase: how a colonised people teaches itself to survive by cunning, that the brutal strong man's brutality is the start of his own defeat. That is the same kind of moral machinery that earns Animal Farm 78 and Labyrint sveta 70, and the reader's short-allegory suspension applies, so a child's register costs little here - The Little Prince scores 82 with a child at its centre. What holds it under the line is that the suspension removes penalties without adding points: a set of separate folktales has no single premise whose consequences can be worked out and no continuous character to want anything, so there is nothing for the axis that tops the log to attach to, and the collected form was the reader's stated complaint about Unfinished Tales at 69, his lowest Tolkien, where the pieces were not connected to each other. Leaned on axis:short-idea-driven and axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist, which a folktale collection does not have. One source, on budget; folktale supernatural is therefore unexamined against the occult filter.

t: Catwoman (Under the Moon: A Catwoman Tale)
why: This is a young-adult comic, not a prose novel: a fifteen-year-old runs from her mother's violent boyfriend, sleeps rough and starts stealing, told in vignettes with the art carrying most of the load. Two things put it under the line and neither is the subject matter, which this reader does not object to - violence is not an objection at all. First, the arc is a slide toward the criminal the character will become, and the critical split is precisely there: the sympathetic reviews praise how believable she is, the negative one records that by the end there is nothing to praise her for having accomplished. That is the Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 failure exactly - 22 points under Sunrise on the Reaping 87 on the protagonist alone, because a lead descending into what she becomes is not one to root for. Second, the comics form gives away the thing this reader values most, page time inside what a character wants and why, which is what makes Red Rising 95 the top of the log; pictures do not do interiority. I can name no idea it leaves behind beyond the case that neglect makes the criminal. Leaned on axis:protagonist because the rooting problem is established by the reviews and it is what caps the number, not the darkness, which costs only mildly. One source, the gate budget; occult unexamined, as a C exit allows.

There is a real hook here - Mariana's dread of fire, seeded by a nightmare on the first night and paid off when the dry hills above the trail catch - and six friends with assigned roles, so the telling is competent rather than slack. What it does not have is anything to think about afterwards: the nearest thing to a takeaway is the appended set of forest-fire survival rules, which is instruction, not an idea, and that is exactly the axis that keeps a competent book in the 60s (Narnia 67, marked down because it 'lacks higher things to think about'). An ensemble of six also leaves little page time for what any one of them wants and why, the axis that puts Mockingjay 91 at the top of the log. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:childrens because a juvenile register on its own costs almost nothing - The Hobbit 84 pays no penalty at all for it - while a thin idea is what actually holds the number under the line. Exited at gate 4 on one source, inside budget; occult status is therefore unexamined by design.

The honest positive is that it does put a want at the centre - Tonca does not want to share her father's attention, and the book stays with that rather than with events - which is the axis the log rates highest. But it is a short, heavily illustrated book issued in a series built to walk young children through a difficult family situation, with downloadable worksheets attached, and its lesson is the lesson itself: a nine-year-old comes round to a new sibling. That is a moral, not an idea to leave behind, and the log's floor for children's-adjacent work with real characters and no premise to work out is Little Women 79, which this is far too slight to approach - the telling suspends the character tests rather than passing them, and the suspension removes penalties without adding points. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:life-phase because a child lead is only a couple of points (Ender's Game still 87), whereas there is nothing here for the idea axis to hold. One source, gate 4, inside budget; occult unexamined by design.

A 32-page picture book for three- to five-year-olds: one summer night in a tent, meteors and the Moon, and a grandfather telling a boy that what you cannot see may still be there. There is a thought in that, and it is the one the reader responds to - The Little Prince 82 shows that a short book aimed at children pays nothing for the register when the thoughts are the substance. The difference is that the suspension of the character rules for short work removes penalties and never adds points, and here the thought is delivered as a single line of consolation rather than followed anywhere: the book is aimed at preschoolers and the publisher's own pitch is the bond between generations and processing loss, not a premise with consequences. So axis:ideas goes into risks, which is the C exit, and 32 illustrated pages put it in the lower band rather than the 60s. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:childrens because a juvenile audience is not itself the deduction - what fixes the number is that one line is all there is to carry. A C-low exit leaves axis:occult unexamined; nothing in the annotation points at it. One source, within the gate budget.

t: Den, kdy voskovky rekly dost (The Day the Crayons Quit)
why: This is a forty-page picture book for ages three to seven: a run of comic letters in which crayons complain about how they have been used, and one boy fixes it on the last spread. The joke is good and the gag has a point - other people's grievances look different from inside - but that is a gag, not an idea a reader carries away, and the short-form suspension in this log removes penalties without ever adding points. The Little Prince 82 is the exact control: short, illustrated, ostensibly for children, and it scores high because the thoughts in it are real and are the whole substance. Nothing of that kind is here, and there is no protagonist to root for either, so the estimate rests where the register puts it - the picture-book floor, well under the Narnia 67 mark that a full children's novel with child leads and little to think about already sets. Leaned on axis:childrens because form and audience are the established facts and everything else about the book follows from them. One source, the gate budget; occult unexamined, which a C exit allows.

t: Desive historky 3 (Michael Dahl's Really Scary Stories)
why: Twenty-five scares of a few pages each for nine-year-olds, with the author explaining afterwards where he got each one. Short work has the character and emotion rules suspended in this log, but the suspension only removes penalties and never adds points - and there is nothing here to add, because no premise is developed far enough to leave a thought behind. That is the position Unfinished Tales 69 was docked to for pieces that do not connect to each other, and this sits far below it on register: illustrated horror written to be read aloud to children. Bleakness is in it too (a Czech reviewer of it warns the endings are harsher than the 9+ rating suggests), but that is the mildest objection in the log and is not what carries the number. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:childrens. A vengeful ghost and a pair of enchanted boots are in the annotation, so the occult status is unexamined at this exit. One source, the C-low budget.

t: Dite, ktere zilo ve zdi (L'enfant qui vivait dans un mur)
why: A 32-page picture book built on one metaphor: a boy whom noise and touch frighten lives inside a wall, and his parents try every way they can to reach him. The subject carries real weight, and insight into how another group experiences the world is half of why Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 scored where it did - but that book earned on sustained first-person examination of what is actually true, and thirty illustrated pages state a metaphor rather than work anything out. The Diary of a Young Girl 40 is the log's warning that a sensitive testimony form earns nothing by itself. So axis:ideas goes into risks, the form leaves the character tests nothing to test, and both conditions for the lower band are met. Leaned on axis:childrens and axis:ideas rather than axis:memoir-form, because this is fiction with a purpose attached rather than testimony. Occult unexamined at this exit. One search, inside budget.

t: Divka v medvedi kuzi (The Girl Who Speaks Bear)
why: This is a real novel with a rootable lead and a clean starting situation - a foundling who wakes with bear legs and goes to find out where she came from - and the reader has no objection to a child lead in itself, so the character side is not what limits it. What limits it is that the payload is a theme rather than a premise: belonging, wildness and who names you, delivered through interleaved folk tales that turn out to be true, with the cause of everything a grandfather's excessive wishes. That is precisely the shape of Narnia 67, marked down as not bad but lacking higher things to think about, and of Ranger's Apprentice 74, easy but with little to think about - so I would list axis:ideas under risks, which is the exit condition, and the middle-grade register keeps the top of the band under the line. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist, because Yanka is the strongest thing here and would not be the reason for a mediocre score; occult status is unexamined at this exit, and it is a live question, since witches and a cursed transformation are on the page.

t: Dobrodruzstvi bajecnych kamaradu (Rowley Jefferson's Awesome Friendly Adventure)
why: A cartoon-and-text book for readers of seven and up, framed as a boy writing a formulaic quest fantasy while his friend keeps pushing in ideas that would sell merchandise: a barbarian sidekick, a sword pulled from a stone, a mother kidnapped by a white warlock. The joke is the framing, and it is a joke rather than an idea - the satire of franchise storytelling is a running gag on the page, not something the book pursues to a conclusion - so there is nothing to take away. axis:ideas and axis:childrens carry the number: the illustrated diary format suspends the character rules and, as the log says of that suspension, removing the penalties adds nothing, while the register is squarely juvenile. It is also a spin-off leaning on a cast established elsewhere, and the log's one measured series decline runs 83 to 70. Not leaned on axis:protagonist for the same suspension reason. The warlock and the enchanted sword mean the occult question would need answering before this could ever be proposed, and it is unexamined at this exit. One source.

t: Doktorka pro priserky (The Monster Doctor: Foul Play)
why: A gag comedy for early readers: monsters with comic ailments, a sports final, a referee eaten by the ball. The cast are joke types rather than people who want anything, so the axis that carries the top of the log - page time on motives, as in Mockingjay 91 - has nothing to work with, and nothing is left behind to think about, so axis:ideas is a risk and the C exit follows. Saturnin 78 settles that a comic register costs nothing in itself, so the deduction here is the juvenile pitch and the absent idea, not the humour. Ranger's Apprentice 74 is the log's floor for easy reading with little to think about, and this sits well below it in register, at the illustrated early-reader end where the reader's own scale puts the 30s and 40s. A sequel as well, and sequels are not safe bets here - Hitchhiker's 83 fell to 70 for the continuations. Leaned on axis:childrens and axis:ideas. Occult unexamined at this exit. One search, inside budget.

There is a frame with a small joke in it - a girl and a sprite who both love fairy tales go through the door into one and find none of the princesses and dragons they were promised - and then a run of loosely linked short pieces behind it. That joke is a premise for one story, not an idea a book leaves behind, and the linked-tale form suspends the character tests rather than passing them; Unfinished Tales 69 is where this log puts assembled pieces that do not connect to one another, and this sits far under that because it is written for schoolchildren of about nine, in colour-illustrated spreads, and self-published through a crowdfunding imprint with no critical reception at all. Nothing in it goes near a filter. Leaned on axis:childrens; axis:ideas is absent rather than doubtful, which is why the range sits at the low band instead of just under the line. Occult status unexamined at this exit. One source, the C-low budget.

Positive case: a real period delivered as adventure, and the log has no objection to historical fiction - Exodus 68 and Quo Vadis 66 both sit in the B band on it. The closest anchor is Ranger's Apprentice 74, easy reading with little to think about and marked down for history asserted carelessly, and this is pitched several years younger with the history simplified for a school-age reader. No idea is worked out; the story exists to deliver a setting, so axis:ideas goes into risks and the C exit follows. Full novel form, so the character tests are not suspended and the lower band does not apply. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:childrens rather than axis:worldbuilding, because a real period declares nothing the author must then carry the consequences of. A decoded message and an uncovered conspiracy make an investigation-shaped thread - a flag, not the detective filter, since the satisfaction is the period and the escape rather than whodunnit. Egyptian deities address the lead in a dream, which puts the occult question live; it is unexamined at this exit, and Percy Jackson 57 shows a real pantheon can cost. One search, inside budget.

A pirate chase written for eight-year-olds and built out of a puppet-theatre script, and that origin decides what it is for: a plucky orphan, a cook and a pet sail off to find a missing captain. I can name no idea it leaves behind, and the review describes the cast as tipping into caricature, so both of the things that carry high scores in this log are absent - the page time on what characters want and why that puts Mockingjay at 91, and an idea worked out, which is what lets a book as short as The Little Prince reach 82. The register is the number here. Hobbit 84 and The Little Prince 82 pay nothing at all for being read by children because neither is written down to them; Narnia 67 pays a little for child leads and thin thinking; this sits far below that, at the illustrated beginning-reader end where the character and emotion tests are suspended and nothing arrives to replace them. Leaned on axis:childrens rather than axis:protagonist because the register is established and the lead is not - a boy with one hand wanting to go to sea is a genuine want, but 160 illustrated pages for that audience will not develop it. One source, which is the gate budget. Occult status is unexamined, as a C exit allows.

t: Gita sotto l oceano (Field Trip to the Ocean Deep)
why: A wordless picture book: every page is image, so there is no prose in which motives could get page time, and page time on what characters want and why is the axis that puts Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 at the top of the log. The invention is real - a school submarine, a child stranded on the sea floor with a creature the book treats as not-quite-extinct - but that is a situation, not a premise whose consequences are worked out, so axis:ideas belongs in risks and that is the C exit. The Little Prince 82 shows a short illustrated book can score, but it scores for the thinking its text carries; where there is no text at all the short-form suspension only removes penalties and adds nothing, which puts this at the picture-book level the reader's own scale puts in the 30s and 40s. Leaned on axis:childrens and axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist, because with no words there is no interiority to judge. Occult status is unexamined at this exit. One search, inside the one-source budget.

A 40-page picture book for ages four to eight, in rhythmic captions under cartoon eggs: a model citizen who fixes everyone else's problems cracks under it, is told by a doctor to look after himself, and the crack closes. The moral is nameable - nobody is perfect and self-care is not selfishness - but naming a moral is not the test; the reader wants a premise whose consequences are worked out and a book that leaves an idea behind, and this states its lesson in the last spread and stops. That is axis:ideas in doubt, which is the C exit, and a 40-page picture book is the form the profile puts in the low band, where the character tests are suspended and nothing replaces them. The reader's ceiling for the juvenile register is set by books that earn it elsewhere - The Little Prince 82 on its thoughts, Male zeny 79 on characters alone - and neither route is open in forty illustrated pages of one running gag. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:childrens because it is the thinness of what is worked out, not the audience, that fixes the number. A C-low exit leaves axis:occult unexamined; nothing here suggests it. One source, within the gate budget.

A licensed Minecraft adventure for readers over ten - the publisher's own pitch is a blocky story on the pages of a book - in which four young characters brought together by a well-meant theft leave a walled farm and find the world of hostile mobs is nothing like the parents described. The one axis that could have earned something here is worldbuilding, and it is exactly the axis the licence forecloses: the rules are a video game's, so nothing is declared by the author and nothing can be followed through, and the reader's log is unforgiving where a setting is asserted and not thought about (Harry Potter 51 and Mortal Engines 55, the latter abandoned in its first chapters on that alone). Against that there is no idea I can name beyond the world being bigger than a sheltered boy was told, so the C exit is right and the low band follows: the register is aimed at children well below the level of a children's adventure the reader already scored at 67 for having nothing higher to think about, and no reviews exist to argue otherwise - every retailer page found had zero ratings. Leaned on axis:worldbuilding rather than axis:protagonist because a shy boy discovering the world outside the wall is a workable lead; it is the borrowed, unexaminable setting that fixes the number. A C-low exit leaves axis:occult unexamined; the game's mechanics are crafting and mobs, not rites. One source, within the gate budget.

An Albatros Druhe cteni early-reader title: a second-grader sets off on holiday with his parents, his father breaks an arm on the way, his mother takes the wheel and the boy is put in charge of navigating. It has the one thing the reader insists on - a single concrete situation to be invested in from the first page, the absence of which ended three books at 30 - and a librarian reviewer notes the simple family-trip plot carries a light geographical lesson. That lesson is the whole payload; there is no premise whose consequences are worked out and no idea I can name, so axis:ideas is the flag and the gate-4 exit. The low band rather than the default because a beginning-reader book of roughly seventy pages is the picture-book end of axis:childrens, where the reader's grading puts the register itself: The Hobbit pays nothing at 84 because it has ideas and friendship to trade, and there is no room for either at this length. Leaned on axis:childrens and axis:ideas over axis:protagonist, since a book this short cannot fail or pass the interesting-and-rootable test. One source, on budget.

A 120-page collection for readers of about eleven: four short ghost stories plus a dozen micro-horrors, held together only by a frame about a book found in a wardrobe. A collection with no single premise has no idea to lean on, and the short-form suspension in this log takes the character and emotion tests off the table without paying anything back - which is why the canonical short books that score well, The Little Prince 82 and Animal Farm 78, score for the thought in them rather than for being short. There is no thought of that kind on offer here; the reader reception describes the stories as simple and the whole as bland, and at four stories plus fragments there is not room to build anyone to want anything, which is the axis that tops this log at Mockingjay 91. Unfinished Tales 69 is the log's own warning about pieces that do not connect to each other, and that was Tolkien. Leaned on axis:short-idea-driven because form is the established fact and it is what caps the number. One source, the gate budget. Witches and werewolves are named among the contents, so axis:occult is live and deliberately unexamined at this exit.

This is an interactive children's book rather than a story: the reader is addressed directly and asked to help two explorers find the missing parts of a time machine so they can get home from the age of prehistoric giants. A book whose text is a set of tasks for a child has no protagonist to be interesting or rootable, no motives to spend page time on and no argument to leave behind, so axis:ideas and axis:childrens carry the number and there is nothing on the other side of the ledger; the scale puts a picture-and-activity book in the 30s and 40s and I see no reason to go above that. The publisher's list is translated popular-science with about a third of it for children, which fits the annotation exactly. Not leaned on axis:opening or axis:protagonist, neither of which this form puts in play. Occult unexamined at this exit. Overspend to declare: three sources against a budget of one, all spent failing to identify the title and none of them changing the decision the annotation had already settled - the first search should have been the last.

A children's comic: a hapless captain chasing a bravery award, a ship shaped like a cat, and a run of slapstick missions that go wrong. The satisfaction is the gag, and the panel form gives motives almost no page time, which is the axis that separates the top of the log from the rest - Mockingjay 91 scores precisely for showing what people want. Nothing is worked out and nothing is left behind, so axis:ideas is a risk and the C exit follows; a reading age of seven to nine sits well below Narnia 67, which already paid for its register. The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy 83 shows comic SF can land well, but it landed on one concrete situation and a real comic intelligence rather than on running gags, so its score does not transfer here. Leaned on axis:childrens and axis:ideas rather than axis:worldbuilding, because the setting is deliberately absurd and declares nothing it must then honour. Occult unexamined at this exit. One search, inside budget.

t: Jak prezit draci bouri (How to Ride a Dragon's Storm)
why: It starts from one concrete situation with a clock on it - a deadline, a swimming race, a father to get back - so there is momentum and no confusion, and none of what this reader dislikes is here: violence, silliness and a child lead are not objections to him at all. What is missing is the thing that separates the 70s from the 50s in his log. Ranger's Apprentice 74 was 'easy to read, but not much to think about', and that was pitched at older readers than this, which is written for roughly seven to eleven and told in gags, capitals and hand-drawn asides. I can name no idea it leaves behind. It is also a sequel that assumes a running cast and an ongoing plot, and sequels are not safe bets in this log - Hitchhiker's 83 fell to 70. Leaned on axis:childrens rather than axis:sequels because the juvenile register sets the ceiling whatever the reading order does. Occult status unexamined at this exit. One source, the C-low budget.

t: Jak se kral Zeme vil naucil nenavidet pribehy (How the King of Elfhame Learned to Hate Stories)
why: A companion piece rather than a book with its own engine: three tellings of one tale about a boy with a heart of stone and a cursed bride, wrapped around scenes from a life the trilogy has already covered, with much of its two hundred pages given to illustration. There is a nameable structural idea - the same story told three times to three different morals - and that keeps it in the default band rather than the lower one. Against it, the shape is what made Unfinished Tales 69 the lowest Tolkien: pieces that do not connect into one thing. And the lead is written as a cruel, unloved child growing into a cruel king, which is the log's sharpest single deduction - The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 sits 22 points under Sunrise on the Reaping 87, same author, same world, on rootability alone. So axis:ideas goes into risks and the C exit follows. Leaned on axis:protagonist and axis:sequels rather than axis:worldbuilding, because the world is inherited here rather than built, and a sequel is no safe bet in this log - Hitchhiker's 83 fell to 70. Faerie bargains and glamour put the occult question live and it is unexamined at this exit. One search, inside budget.

A picture book for readers from about two, with text so sparse that reviewers say the adult has to fill it in: forest spirits find that a night storm has hurt the tree one of them counts as a friend, and set about putting it right. The care-for-the-forest sentiment is clear, but nothing is worked out and no idea is left behind, and at this text length motives - the axis that tops the log in Mockingjay 91 - cannot get page time at all. Both lower-band conditions hold: no nameable idea, and a form in which the character tests have nothing to test. The Little Prince 82 shows the register costs nothing when the text carries real thinking; there is no comparable freight here, and the short-form suspension removes penalties without adding points. Leaned on axis:childrens and axis:ideas rather than axis:worldbuilding, because the invented forest declares nothing it must then honour. Occult unexamined at this exit. One search, inside budget.

t: Jak vznika duha (Jak vznika duha - Pohadky o zazracich prirody)
why: Nature fairy tales with a comprehension quiz after each one: where rain comes from, why leaves fall, which animals sleep through winter, why waste is sorted. The quizzes settle what the book is for - a teaching aid in story clothing - and a collection with no single premise has no axis:ideas to lean on, which is exactly the compounding the C exit exists to catch. A cheerful cloud and a busy bee are devices rather than people who want something, so the axis that carries Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 never engages. Both lower-band conditions hold: no nameable idea, and a slight collection for five-year-olds in which the character tests have nothing to test. Leaned on axis:childrens and axis:ideas rather than axis:density, because 64 pages are not a thin story spread thin - what is absent is substance, not compression. Occult unexamined at this exit. One search, inside budget.

t: Jednooky (Jednooky: Mala knizka o velkem Zizkovi)
why: This is a 128-page pocket-format schools book issued for the six-hundredth anniversary of Zizka's death, with comic-style illustrations, photographs with captions and factual info boxes spaced through the story. The fiction - three teenagers playing a city game across Zizkov - is the delivery vehicle for the history, and the reviewer's own summary is that it is packed with information for its size and doubles as a guide to the district. That decides the axis: an educational aim is not an idea the book leaves behind, and Rangers Apprentice 74 shows what this reader does with easy adventure that has little to think about, while also showing he actively resents history asserted at him when it is wrong. Nothing here is built to make three players want different things, which is the axis Mockingjay 91 tops, and the info boxes are the story-density objection in its purest form - narrative interrupted to deliver material. Leaned on axis:childrens because the format, the length and the schools-project origin are the established facts and they set the ceiling. One source, the gate budget; occult unexamined, as a C exit allows.

An episodic Czech children's book following a painted pebble from a treetop to a train, a suitcase, a mountain, an airport and finally America, built on the real hobby of leaving painted stones for strangers to find. The object is the through-line, so the people it passes are sketches, and the heaviest axis in this log - page time on what characters want and why - has nothing to work with. No idea is worked out across the episodes, and a reader complaint that too many themes are pushed in at once points the same way, so axis:ideas belongs in risks and both lower-band conditions hold. Little Women 79 marks the ceiling this register can reach when characters carry a book that has no premise to solve, and there is no cast of that kind here. Leaned on axis:childrens and axis:ideas rather than axis:character-differentiation, because the cast is too thin for differentiation to be the question. Occult unexamined at this exit. One search, inside budget.

A 56-page illustrated book, translated into fourteen languages and on the IBBY Honour List, that tells two Jewish children in a 1943 ghetto through images - a violin, a kite on a roof, black birds, then soldiers in black uniforms - and hands the child reader a pebble as the sign for memory and for the dead. The restraint is genuinely skilful and Czech Television called it a model of how to tell children about the Holocaust. But what the reader rewards is a premise whose consequences are worked out and a book that leaves an idea behind, and this is a symbol offered rather than an idea pursued: at picture-book length the Holocaust can be evoked and not examined, which is where axis:ideas goes into doubt, and the same length suspends the character tests without adding points. Compare the reader's one non-fiction high, Seeking Allah Finding Jesus 91, earned specifically for examining what is plausible and true, against The Diary of a Young Girl 40, a DNF where a child's inner life under the same history did not work; an illustrated 56-page telling has less room to earn than either. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:bleakness, which is the reader's mildest recorded objection and would move this by a point or two at most. A C-low exit leaves axis:occult unexamined; nothing suggests it. One source, within the gate budget.

t: Kdy se vraci papirovi draci (Kdy se vraci papirovi draci)
why: A 72-page illustrated first-reading book: the wind is personified as a mischievous teacher of leaves, a boy builds a kite with his father and the wind carries it off. It is a seasonal mood piece for small children, and the personification is decoration rather than a premise with consequences, so nothing is left behind to think about. axis:ideas and axis:childrens carry the number together: the log gives a childrens register no automatic penalty, but at this length and this age band there is no idea and no worked-out premise to earn anything either, which is the position the scale puts in the 30s and 40s. Not leaned on axis:protagonist - a first-reading book of this size suspends the character tests rather than failing them - and not on axis:momentum, which is not the issue at 72 illustrated pages. Occult unexamined at this exit. One source, the gate budget.

A large-format photograph book - 104 pages at 21 by 30 centimetres, with a press photographer credited as co-author - narrated by one of eight golden retriever puppies as the litter grows up, with the mother's bedtime tales about how to be a proper dog. The pictures are the work and the text serves them, which is the register this log prices at the floor: Hobbit 84 and The Little Prince 82 pay nothing for a young readership because neither is written down to its reader, and this is a picture book for a small child being read to. No idea is nameable, there is nothing to hold up under thought, and the puppy narrator is a device rather than a character who wants anything - and wanting is the axis that carries Mockingjay 91. The short-form suspension takes the character tests away without paying anything for them. Leaned on axis:childrens because format and audience are the established facts and they fix the number by themselves. One source, the gate budget; occult unexamined, as a C exit allows.

An illustrated animal tale for the youngest readers: a white kitten owns a book that changes fates, a wicked fox carries her off to a cave of fear and tasks, the captive animals find courage and a plan, and the king of the universe helps them. Library copy describes it as illustrated stories about overcoming fear and believing in good, which is a moral rather than an idea worked out - a book with a fate-changing book in it declares a capability and then does not have to carry any consequence at that length, so axis:ideas is where the doubt sits and axis:worldbuilding has nothing to hold. The reader's calibration is explicit that a juvenile register is free only when the ideas do the work (The Little Prince 82) and costs when there is nothing higher to think about (Narnia 67, docked on that alone); a picture-book fable for preschoolers is under that, in the lower band, where the short form removes the character tests without adding anything. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist because a kitten heroine in a fable is not the problem - Male zeny 79 shows characters alone can carry a children's-adjacent book, and there is not enough here to try. A C-low exit leaves axis:occult unexamined and it is a live question: a magic book that alters destinies plus a 'king of the universe' figure is the sort of thing that would need the rite-on-the-page test if the score ever mattered. One source, within the gate budget.

t: Kral medvedu (The Grizzly King: A Romance of the Wild)
why: There is a real idea here and it can be named: a hunter who has come to kill the largest grizzly in the range is made to see the hunt from the animal's side and concludes there is more to it than the killing - and the author, an avid hunter himself, wrote the book to change his readers' minds, so the argument is the point of the thing rather than decoration. It opens on one concrete situation, the bear on his own ground catching an unfamiliar scent, which is the structure the reader wants and whose absence ended three books at 30. Two things keep it under the line. The book runs its 234 pages through three viewpoints, two of them animals, and animal interiority cannot deliver what the reader weights heaviest - page time on what a character wants and why, the axis behind Speaker for the Dead at 90 - so the human lead is doing that work in perhaps a third of the book. And a 1916 wilderness romance is exactly where axis:density bites: the reader's stated objection to LOTR at 84 was a thin story spread over many pages, and this is a pursuit and a change of heart at that length. So axis:ideas is the axis I would flag as possibly too slight to carry it - the gate-4 exit. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:density rather than axis:worldbuilding, which is simply the real Canadian Rockies and declares nothing. One source, on budget; the occult status is unexamined, though a naturalist hunting novel gives no reason to expect it.

The one thing it has is a want with a reason behind it - a rabbit who knows he takes offence too easily and is trying, with help, to stop - and page time on why a character behaves as he does is the axis that tops this log. What it does not have is any consequence: it is a set of short animal episodes each ending in a stated lesson, addressed by the publisher's own blurb to children who sulk, so the idea is the moral itself and there is nothing to hold up under thought. That is the axis:ideas doubt the gate asks for, compounded by an episodic form which, per the short-idea-driven rule, drops the character requirements without earning anything back. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:character-differentiation, because the squirrel and the hedgehog being interchangeable is a symptom of the episode format and not what fixes the number; occult status is unexamined at this exit.

The premise has one nice turn - the pet is not the hamster the boy asked for but something that can imitate one - and a boy hiding it from a hunting cat is a concrete situation to start from. It is nonetheless a 72-page first-reader in chapters of two or three pages, described by its reviewers as pleasant bedtime reading without any real turns, and Czech readers complain the ending is simply cut off; that is a book with no idea I can name and a form that suspends the character tests, which is the exit condition. Little Women 79 shows a story with no premise to work out can still clear the line on characters alone, but that is a full novel with several differentiated leads, and this has one boy and a gag. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:childrens rather than axis:momentum, since the chapters do move - there is just nothing at the end of them; occult status is unexamined at this exit.

t: Krtkuv cernobily svet (Mole in a Black and White Hole)
why: There is a genuine parable in here and it is better than most of its register: a creature who has only ever known the dark is told colour exists, is too timid to go, and only moves once the lamp he was relying on is taken away - loss as the thing that makes courage necessary. But it is a 32-page picture book for readers of three and up, carried mainly by its graphic design, which was what got it nominated; the idea is a single figure rather than a premise with consequences, and that is the axis:ideas doubt this gate exists to catch. The Little Prince 82 is the ceiling this shape can reach and it reaches it by sustaining a chain of such figures, not one. Leaned on axis:ideas over axis:bleakness, because the dark opening resolves toward light rather than the sudden bleakness that helped sink Promena 58; occult status is unexamined at this exit, though nothing in the material suggests anything beyond a lamp and a mole.

t: Kterak zajic lakomy zjistil, jak byl pitomy (The Hare Who Wouldn't Share)
why: A well-made fable with a genuine turn in it: the hare who guards his turnips and refuses the neighbours' soup is the one who chooses to warn them when the boar arrives, so the change of heart is shown as an action under pressure rather than announced, and the animator's eye behind it earned starred trade reviews. That is the honest positive. It is still forty pages of picture book, where the reader's ruling puts the ceiling in the 30s or 40s, and the moral - sharing and good neighbours - is stated once and has no consequences to follow, so there is nothing to think about after it closes; The Little Prince 82 is what a short allegory looks like when the idea does carry, and this is a long way short of that. The character dialogue is set in verse while the narration is not, which adds a partial dose of the form the reader disliked outright at Havran 40. Leaned on axis:childrens because the format sets the ceiling here; the idea is present but too small to move the number. One source, gate 4, inside budget; occult unexamined by design.

t: Kuba a Verunka na ostrove pokladu (Kuba a Verunka na ostrove pokladu)
why: The one thing it has going for it is a clean starting situation - a girl who is tired of hearing about voyages stows away on one - which is exactly the concrete opening this reader asks for and the absence of which ended three books at 30. That is a filter cleared, though, not a reason to score, and there is nothing behind it: fifty-five unnumbered pages of illustrated episodes in which a treasure island supplies a cheeky monkey, a tiger, a scorpion and a river of crocodiles in turn. No idea can be named, and at this length and register the character and emotion tests are suspended rather than met, which removes penalties without earning anything. Little Women 79 is the log's ceiling for children's-adjacent work carried by characters alone, and this has neither the room nor the intent for that. Leaned on axis:ideas because naming the idea is where it fails outright, not on axis:childrens, which by itself costs little - The Little Prince 82 pays nothing for being for children. One source, gate 4, inside budget; occult unexamined by design.

It has one concrete engine and an active lead: a girl carrying a heartbreak she will not name, a brother who has stopped speaking to her, and a guidebook for the heartbroken that pushes them both across Ireland to real places. Romance as the central subject costs this reader nothing at all - Pride and Prejudice 75 is entirely what people want and why - and both sex-related filters were checked and are clear: reviewers report dating and a breakup discussed with nothing sexual shown, and the wedding in it is an aunt's, with no betrayal anywhere in the plot. What keeps it under the line is that the thing the book is about is withheld as a drip-fed secret almost to the end, and the reviewers who get there report the payoff is small; the nearest idea, living up to other people's expectations, is a theme rather than a premise worked out. A competent book with nothing to think about is what stalls just under the line here - Ranger's Apprentice 74 cleared it only on how easily it read. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist, because the lead is the part reviewers defend. One source, the C-low budget.

An 80-page large-format illustrated book by an author who draws her own work: a small newt who feels he fits in nowhere sets out, meets creatures, and learns that everyone has a place. The best thing found about it is not the story but the apparatus - reviewers single out inserts showing the Czech newt and frog species and their eggs so a child can match them up, and the developmental difference between newts and frogs. That is a nature primer wrapped in a fable, and 'everyone has their place' is a reassurance rather than an idea whose consequences get worked out, so axis:ideas is where the doubt sits and that is the C exit. The lower band follows from the form: at 80 illustrated pages for young children the character rules are suspended, and the reader's own note on Narnia 67 is that children's adventure with nothing higher to think about costs points even when it is far more substantial than this. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:childrens, since a juvenile register is free when the thinking is there (The Little Prince 82) and this book's strength is instead its pictures. A C-low exit leaves axis:occult unexamined; nothing in the annotation points at it. One source, within the gate budget.

A debut nature fairy tale for preschoolers with tasks to fill in and recognition games: a forest fairy walks a lost butterfly home and explains on the way why leaves change colour, how trees defend themselves and how moss heals. The teaching is the point and the story is its delivery vehicle, so no premise has consequences to work out and no character's motives get page time - the axis that tops the log in Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90. Both conditions for the lower band hold: nothing nameable as an idea, and a read-aloud activity form in which the character tests have nothing to test. The Little Prince 82 shows the illustrated children's register is no bar in itself, but it earns on the thinking its text carries and there is no equivalent here. Leaned on axis:childrens and axis:ideas. Occult unexamined at this exit. One search, inside budget.

It starts from one concrete loss - a father killed by a sea creature to get his two children clear - so there is no confusion about what is happening, and the drowned world is the part its readers praise: how people live on the water and what they built to do it. That is not enough on its own here. The same readers call the characters banal, and this log is explicit that worldbuilding never rescues a thin lead: Artemis 69 sits 23 points below the same author's best on exactly that. It is also a comic rather than prose, so the interiority that puts Red Rising 95 at the top of the log is not available to it, and the satisfaction on offer is dread and monsters rather than a thought to carry away. On top of that comes a recurring reader complaint that a fourteen-year-old character is drawn sexually during action scenes, and treatment is the dimension that cost Ready Player One 55 more than volume ever did. The plot is not about sex, so no filter fires; it is a deduction. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:sexual-treatment. One source, the C-low budget.

The invented premise is the strong part and it is genuinely elaborated rather than just stated - a hidden species that eats one sock of every pair, with its own kinds, laws and society - and internal consistency of that sort is what the log rewards, Old Man's War 87 scoring on a world that follows from itself. It is also a hunt for lost parents rather than a set-piece plot, so there are motives on the page. What holds it under the line is that the elaboration is whimsy: I cannot name the thought it leaves behind, and that is the axis on which competent books stall in the 60s. It is a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets here - the Hitchhiker's fall from 83 to 70 is the log's steepest - with readers saying repeatedly that the charm of the beginning is thinner this time. So axis:ideas and axis:sequels carry the number. The recorded risks are the ones that could take it well below: the book starts two separate strands that only later braid together and assumes a cast and a world introduced elsewhere, which is the failure that ended two books at 30 and one at 30 in the first chapter, and there is magic plus a secret Black Sock in the plot, unexamined here because this exit does not pay for that check.

An illustrated chapter book for readers of eight and up, opening on one concrete situation - a girl who can talk to animals, loved by every animal and afraid her classmates will think she is mad - which is the structure this reader wants and is worth saying, since a confusing multi-thread opening is the log's most reliable killer. The lead also has a want and a secret, so the character tests are in play rather than suspended. What stops it is that the series is an animal-rescue formula, one endangered creature per volume, and I cannot name a thought it leaves behind; the log's own case is Ranger's Apprentice 74, marked down as easy to read with not much to think about, and this is thinner than that and pitched several years younger. So axis:ideas and axis:childrens carry the number. Not leaned on axis:worldbuilding: the talking-to-animals gift is asserted and never systematised, so the book takes on little obligation and breaks little. The gift's occult status is unexamined at this exit. One source, the gate budget.

The idea is nameable and is genuinely worked out for a picture book: a manufacturer takes the last of a resource, the consequences arrive in order - the animals leave, the air fouls, the business collapses - and the ending withholds the fix and hands it to the reader. That is the Animal Farm 78 shape, an allegory that leaves something behind rather than only events. Two things hold it down hard. It is written in verse, and verse is the log's most recent and most explicit form penalty: Havran 40 ties the lowest completed score and the reader named the form itself, not the subject, as a cause - so this is not the short-idea-driven suspension, which merely fails to earn points, but a cost. And the register is a picture book of about sixty pages carried by its illustrations, which the reader's own ruling places in the 30s or 40s. Leaned on axis:verse rather than axis:ideas because the idea is the one thing here that argues upward; the form is what caps it. One source, gate 4, inside budget; occult unexamined by design.

t: Lovci strasidel na ledove stope (Ghosthunters: On Icy Trails (Gespensterjager auf eisiger Spur))
why: A 129-page illustrated early-chapter book with the author's own drawings, and its opening is clean - a ghost in the cellar, a frightened boy, a professional ghost-hunter who offers to help - which is the structure this reader asks for. The rest is a comic romp with a taxonomy of ghost types played for jokes, and I cannot name anything it leaves behind; the log's own scale for that combination of very young register and no idea sits in the 30s and 40s, and even the friendliest comparison, Ranger's Apprentice 74, is a far longer and more substantial read that was still marked down for having little to think about. So axis:ideas and axis:childrens carry the number. axis:occult is recorded as a live risk rather than settled: professional ghost-hunting with prescribed procedures against the dead is precisely the sort of thing that would need the source-and-depiction test, and a below-the-line exit does not pay for it. Not leaned on axis:protagonist, which a book of this length suspends. One source, the gate budget.

t: Lumpicek a Rostanda zachranuji les (Lumpicek a Rostanda zachranuji les)
why: It opens on one legible situation with a stated stake - thieves in the wood, helpers who must stop them - so the opening filter that ended two books at 30 is not in play, and the two leads have been given a want. But it is published in an explicit beginner-reading edition of about eighty large-type pages, the conflict resolves into a moral, and the only thing it leaves behind is 'look after the forest', which is not an idea worked out. Ranger's Apprentice 74 is already marked down for having little to think about while being a full novel for older children; a first-reader falls much further down the same axis, into the band the reader's picture-book rule fixes in the 30s and 40s. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:childrens rather than axis:worldbuilding, because nothing is declared here that the book could then break; occult status is unexamined at this exit.

Thirteen short pieces for readers of six and up, 96 pages at 23x23 cm by an author-illustrator, each taking one stock parental warning literally: a melon grows in a belly, a nose becomes a trunk, potatoes sprout in unwashed ears. The joke is real and the drawing is award-nominated, but it is one gag repeated thirteen times with a fresh child each time, so there is no protagonist to follow and no premise whose consequences are pursued past the punchline - a Czech reader even notes the moral inverts itself, because the threat comes true and then turns out nice. That is axis:ideas in risks, which is the C exit, and the picture-book format puts it in the lower band rather than the 60s. Calibration: the reader gives a juvenile register a free pass only when ideas carry it (The Little Prince 82) and docks a book that leaves nothing to think about (Narnia 67); a large-format gag collection for six-year-olds is further down again. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:character-differentiation because with thirteen one-page children there is nothing to differentiate. The 'sex' signal is a spurious lexicon match - the annotation is about parental warnings to small children and nothing on axis:sexual-content is in play. A C-low exit leaves axis:occult unexamined, though nothing here suggests it. One source, within the gate budget.

t: Mami, tati, jak vypada Jezisek? (Mami, tati, jak vypada Jezisek?)
why: This is an explainer, not a story: a white cat frames a walk-through of the nativity - manger, star, the three kings - and then of who Jesus grew up to be, in a series that does the same job for Mikulas, Halloween and Valentine's Day, written by an author whose other work is Czech-as-a-foreign-language teaching material. That form is the problem twice over. The reader's rule on faith is that it works as a thread inside a story and not as a subject in its own right, and here it is the subject and there is no story around it. And the memoir-and-explainer form earns nothing by itself in this log - Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and The Diary of a Young Girl 40 are the same form at opposite ends, and what separated them was examining what is actually plausible, which a nativity primer for small children does not attempt. Leaned on axis:faith rather than axis:childrens because the juvenile register alone is cheap while devotional exposition as the whole content is the thing that caps it. One source, gate 4, inside budget; occult unexamined by design.

A bedtime fairy-tale book for preschoolers from a long-running series about forest sprites: a small sprite finds a fallen swallow chick, raises it, and it flies to Africa and comes back in spring. Retailers place it in the preschool and fairy-tale category and it is illustrated throughout, so this is the register the log prices lowest - Hobbit 84 and The Little Prince 82 pay nothing for being read by children because neither is written down to its reader, whereas this is written for a listener who cannot read yet. There is no idea to name; the substance is gentleness and the seasons, and the episodic shape means nobody in it needs to want anything, which is the axis that carries Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90. The short-form suspension removes the character penalties without adding a point, exactly as it does for any thin short book. Leaned on axis:childrens because the audience and the format are the established facts and they set the whole number. One source, the gate budget; occult unexamined, as a C exit allows.

A 54-page illustrated book for preschoolers, built from full-page colour pictures with short blocks of text under them, by two graphic designers who crowdfunded it. The metafictional hook - a toy bear pulled bodily into the book he is reading, then chased through further books by a pirate collecting the parts of a broken book-making machine - is a device, not a premise whose consequences get worked out, and nothing survives the last page. That is what the number rests on: axis:ideas and axis:childrens together. The log pays nothing for a childrens register on its own, but it only pays well for a short book when the idea is the reason the book is short, as with The Little Prince 82 and Animal Farm 78; here I cannot name an idea at all, and the telling is as juvenile as the register gets. Not leaned on axis:protagonist, because a picture book of this length suspends the character tests rather than failing them. Occult status is unexamined - a below-the-line exit does not pay for that check. One source, which is the budget for this gate.

It is a thirty-six-page illustrated picture book recommended for children of two to three, in which one sister helps the other reach a wish and the message is that doing something differently from everyone else is not the same as doing it wrongly. That message is real and kindly meant, but it is a single sentence, and a single sentence is not the kind of idea that carries a short book: the log's short books that score - The Little Prince 82, Animal Farm 78 - are carried by an idea whose consequences are actually worked out, and the suspension of the character rules for short work removes penalties without adding any points. Leaned on axis:childrens rather than axis:ideas here because the register is the whole determinant: at this age band there is no room for a protagonist to want anything at length, and that is the axis that tops the log. The 30s-to-40s placement for a genuine picture book is the reader's own ruling; the upper end allows for the sisterly relationship being the actual subject, which is at least the right subject.

t: Miluju te naporad (I Love You Just the Same)
why: A written-and-illustrated gift picture book for ages three to seven, on the arrival of a younger sibling: a girl's world is upended and she travels through dream landscapes following notes from her mother back home. The subject is a feeling to be soothed rather than a proposition to be examined, and the reassurance is the whole payload, so there is nothing for the reader to carry away and argue with - the axis on which even competent books stall, and this is far shorter and softer than competent adult work. axis:ideas and axis:childrens carry the number together; a genuine picture book sits at the bottom of that axis, where the log's own scale puts it in the 30s and 40s, and I see no offsetting idea of the kind that lifted The Little Prince 82. Not leaned on axis:sexual-content or axis:infidelity, neither of which is in play. The annotation tripped an occult signal, which on inspection is the dreamlike enchanted-forest imagery of the journey; no rite is described anywhere I found, but the occult question is formally unexamined at this exit. One source.

A children's historical adventure with a real spine: a twelve-year-old hidden in the Moravian woods after his father's murder is forced onto the road, and the route runs by sea, mountain and the Silk Road to Tibet, China and the Mongol empire. Momentum across a long journey is something this reader tolerates well - The Count of Monte Cristo 75 held up on plot movement alone - and the historical genre carries no penalty in the log. But I cannot name what the book leaves behind: readers describe it as taking its shape from better-known journey books while keeping a Moravian colour, and one says outright that it never pulled him in, so axis:ideas is where the number rests. Two things could take it lower and are the recorded risks: the hero is handed thought-reading, plant-speech and healing hands rather than earning anything, which is the axis Divergent 58 was punished on, and a travelogue that states legend and foreign custom as fact is exactly what cost Ranger's Apprentice 74 its points. An ancient prophecy is present and that is graded, never a filter. The gifts and the herbalist raise an occult question that this exit does not pay to answer. One source, the gate budget.

Thirty-two pages, recommended from age three, one page per guinea pig, ten animals standing for ten character traits, meant for reading at bedtime. This is the picture-book floor of the register axis, and the register is the entire estimate: Hobbit 84 and The Little Prince 82 pay nothing for young readers because neither writes down to its reader, while this is a naming exercise for a listener who cannot read yet. There is no idea in the sense this log means - The Little Prince earns 82 for thoughts that go somewhere, not for being short and illustrated, and the short-form suspension only removes penalties, it never awards a point. Ten one-page sketches also cannot differentiate anyone: what makes Golden Son 92 work is that Darrow, Sevro and Mustang each want different things over a whole book, and a trait per page is the opposite procedure. Leaned on axis:childrens because extent, age band and one-page structure are established facts and nothing else is needed. One source, the gate budget; occult unexamined, as a C exit allows.

REJECTED 2026-09-02 on filter 7, a same-sex romance as the premise of the book (new axis, ruled the same day off Caropisci 67). Marketed and reviewed as a boys-love romance; the relationship is the book's subject rather than a thread in it. Premise level under filter 7. Framing never enters this test, exactly as it does not for infidelity. Prior assessment, kept for the audit trail: A contemporary Czech YA novel with a legible single situation to start from - a boy transfers to a boarding gymnasium in Olomouc for a clean slate and gets a roommate he cannot stand - and the substance is bullying in Czech schools and an unspoken trauma, with the concrete local setting and the grandmother singled out by readers as the best-drawn things in it. Rooting for the leads is not in question and the page time is on what they are hiding and why, which is the axis that tops the reader's log (Mockingjay 91). The stop is that reviewers who liked it say it stays at the surface for a YA and they wanted it to go deeper, and I cannot name an idea it leaves behind beyond 'bullying and trauma hurt': that is axis:ideas in risks, and the reader's most common reason a competent book stalls in the 60s is exactly having no higher thing to think about (Narnia 67). Checked the sexual-plot filter rather than assumed it: this is marketed as boys-love YA, but the plot is a school, a transfer and a trauma, and the reader's log is explicit that romance as the central subject costs nothing when motives are the book (Pride and Prejudice 75), so it grades rather than vetoes; volume and explicitness were not established and stay in deps. Leaned on axis:ideas, not axis:protagonist, which looks like the book's strength. A C-low exit leaves axis:occult unexamined; nothing suggests it. One source, within the gate budget.

Short allegory is the one form that has scored well here without a plot - The Little Prince 82 and Animal Farm 78 - and the publisher does claim more than a colour primer: courage to open what looks closed, a door or a person. The problem is that sixteen pages of a girl mixing up a yellow, a red and a blue world can state that theme but cannot work it out, and both of those anchors earn their scores by turning their idea over for a whole short book rather than gesturing at it once. So what I can name is a one-line moral, which is the axis:ideas doubt the gate asks about, and the register is a genuine picture book for the youngest readers - the end of the children's scale the reader's own rule fixes in the 30s and 40s. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:childrens alone, because a picture book with a real idea worked through would beat this range; occult status is unexamined at this exit.

This is the most promising shape in the low band, because it is an allegory with a subject that could carry one: an old bear left in an attic, used to talk to children about time passing and how little of what happens is kept. The log rewards exactly that when it is worked out - Animal Farm 78 is a short idea-driven allegory and The Little Prince 82 is a children's one - but the working out is the whole difference, and here the text is described as so spare that the story could be given in a single sentence, with the pictures carrying the rest. A theme gestured at in sixty-eight pages of graphic art is not a premise whose consequences are followed, and the short-work suspension removes penalties without adding points. A mild further discount for the settled sadness of the thing, which readers describe as dark rather than gentle - bleakness is the log's least severe objection but it is not nothing. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:childrens because the register would have been forgivable if the idea had been developed; it is the development that is missing. One source, gate 4, inside budget; occult unexamined by design.

A 128-page square-format illustrated book for young readers: a nearly ten-year-old boy falls asleep and wakes each night in a dream country that smells of candy floss, where a scatty sprite sets him tasks involving a red suitcase and giant flying forks. The dream frame is the problem this reader has named twice over. A dream land where everything is deliberately the wrong way round declares nothing and therefore holds up to nothing, and self-consistency is the axis that produced the log's two worst outcomes - Divergent 58 on a premise that collapses under thought and Mortal Engines 55 abandoned outright on it. Against that there is no idea to name and no want driving the boy beyond getting through the next task. The register is what fixes the number: Hobbit 84 and The Little Prince 82 cost nothing for a young readership because they are not written down to their readers, while this is illustrated on nearly every spread for a seven-to-nine-year-old, well under the Narnia 67 mark for a full children's novel with little to think about. Leaned on axis:childrens because format and audience are established facts and the worldbuilding doubt only widens the band. One source, the gate budget; occult unexamined, as a C exit allows.

t: O medvidkovi, co neumel plavat, ale naucil se cist (O medvidkovi, co neumel plavat, ale naucil se cist)
why: A richly illustrated picture book with an explicit purpose - a bear cub cannot swim, is mocked for it, and the book is there to tell a child that not being able to do something yet is fine and that a friend can help. The one thing genuinely in its favour on this reader's axes is that the difficulty is felt from inside the character rather than reported, and it is a want the story stays with. But that is one lesson stated once; there is no premise to work out and nothing left to think about afterwards, which is the axis on which competent books stall, and the picture-book register puts the ceiling where the reader's ruling puts it, in the 30s or 40s. Little Women 79 marks how high children's-adjacent work can go on characters alone, and a lesson book of this length has neither the length nor the intent to reach for that. Leaned on axis:ideas because that is where it plainly fails; axis:childrens on its own is cheap - The Hobbit 84 pays nothing for it. One source, gate 4, inside budget; occult unexamined by design.

t: O pande, ktera mela vsi (Le panda qui avait des poux)
why: Twenty-four pages of a counting escalation - each animal that starts counting another's lice catches them - inside a grandmother-hen frame. It is a device rather than a story: no premise to work out, no character with a want, and the only thing it leaves behind is that lice are survivable, which is a practical use and not an idea I can name in the sense the rule means. Czech reviewers add that the rhymed text is clumsy and half-rhymed, and verse is the one form this reader has named as a cause of a low score on its own, Havran 40. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:childrens rather than axis:verse, because the Czech verse quality is a translation complaint I have one source for while the picture-book register is certain from the format; occult status is unexamined at this exit.

t: O ropuse, ktera nechtela vstavat (O ropuse, ktera nechtela vstavat)
why: A twenty-four page bedtime gag: the fairy-tale toad who ought to turn into a prince simply will not wake up, and the other animals try kisses in turn. The joke is inverted fairy-tale machinery, which is a legitimate register - Saturnin 78 shows comedy carries no penalty here - but that entry earns its band on voice and character across a whole novel, and this has one repeated beat and a moral about the goodnight kiss, so there is no idea to name and nothing that could hold up or fail under thought. Czech reviewers additionally find the rhymed text awkward to read aloud, and it sits at the bottom of its own series on the Czech book database. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:childrens rather than axis:verse, since the verse complaint attaches to the translation and I have a single source for it; occult status is unexamined at this exit, and the transformation spell is fairy-tale furniture rather than a practice.

A 136-page children's animal story, filed by the publisher under dog stories: an assistance dog trained to sense an oncoming attack goes home with a boy whose illness can fell him at any moment, and the turn is that when something happens on a seaside trip the adults stop trusting the dog and the dog cannot speak to explain. That situation is concrete, which is the thing the reader most needs from an opening, and the assistance-dog premise gives it one honest subject. What it does not have is an idea pursued past the lesson - courage and loyalty are named as the themes by the publisher and by the only reader review found - so axis:ideas is where the doubt goes, and that is the C exit. The band follows from register and length together: this is written for readers of roughly eight to twelve, and the reader's own note on Narnia 67 is that children's adventure with nothing higher to think about is docked even at far greater substance, while a mute animal lead leaves little room for the page time on wants and motives that tops his log (Mockingjay 91, Speaker for the Dead 90). Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist, since a loyal dog is likeable enough and it is the thinness of what is worked out that fixes the number. A C-low exit leaves axis:occult unexamined; nothing suggests it. One source, within the gate budget.

t: Paddington v dzungli (Paddington in Peru: Picture Book)
why: It is a thirty-two-page picture-book retelling of a film, adapted from the screenplay rather than written as a book, and that is what fixes the number. The story it retells does have the one thing this reader asks for at the start - a concrete situation, an aunt gone missing from the home for retired bears - but a picture-book condensation of a screenplay has no room to work anything out, and there is no idea to name past the affection the character has always traded on. The reader's own ruling puts a genuine picture book in the 30s or 40s, and a licensed film tie-in of that length has less to offer than an original one. Leaned on axis:childrens because the format is the whole of the case; axis:ideas would say the same thing but the form is why there is nothing there to grade. One source, gate 4, inside budget; occult unexamined by design.

It opens on one concrete situation and a boy who wants something: sent to his grandmother for the summer, mocked by a cousin for his stutter, he keeps to himself until he finds tiny footprints and a lost shoe by the flowerbeds. Being laughed at for how you speak is carried as his own experience rather than delivered as a lesson, and page time on what a character wants and why is the axis that tops this reader's log. But the register puts a low ceiling on it: a short illustrated story for readers of about seven to ten, with a reassurance where an idea would be, and no reception at all yet to correct that reading - no review and no ratings were found. The log's high mark for a children's-adjacent book carried by character alone is Little Women 79, and that is a full novel of people; this is a summer episode with sprites in it. Leaned on axis:childrens; axis:ideas is thin rather than wholly absent, which is why the range is not at the very floor. Occult status unexamined at this exit. One source, the C-low budget.

It has a clean quest premise - a puffin whose own name is a puzzle, so he goes north to find out what it means - and the journey doubles as a route through Iceland and Greenland, the aurora, whale lifespans and retreating glaciers. That is more ambition than a picture book usually carries. But the two halves work against each other rather than compounding: the facts are delivered as encounters along the way, which is the thin-story-over-many-pages problem the log penalises as density rather than length, and the self-discovery half resolves into the small consolation that finding out who you are is the point of going. That is a sentiment rather than a premise with consequences, and 132 large-format pages illustrated on every side put the register squarely in the picture-book band the reader prices in the 30s or 40s. Leaned on axis:ideas because the naming of the idea is where it comes up short; axis:childrens alone would cost little, since The Little Prince 82 shows a children's allegory pays nothing when the idea is real. One source, gate 4, inside budget; occult unexamined by design.

A 112-page illustrated collection of episodes about a young boy and his classmates at an international school in Portugal - a school trip to the Azores, dolphins and orcas from a boat, a stray dog and an injured kestrel rescued - written by a Czech author from her own son's experiences, for readers of roughly six to ten. The positive case is warmth and a real place described from life rather than invented. But there is no premise whose consequences get worked out and no idea I can name to carry it, which is the gate-4 exit condition, and the episodic form means the axis the reader weights heaviest - page time on what characters want and why, the axis that puts Mockingjay at 91 - has almost nothing to work with in a five-page chapter. The low band rather than the default because the form suspends the character tests without substituting anything: this is closer to the picture-book end of axis:childrens than to Narnia at 67, which is at least a continuous novel with a plot. Leaned on axis:childrens and axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist because the register, not the lead, is what fixes the ceiling here. One source, on budget.

Seventeen free-verse pieces on grass, clouds, a spring, a rock and a woodpecker, framed as an ant nurse singing to a child, and reviewers reach for haiku to describe them - which is an accurate compliment and also the whole problem. Verse is the one form the reader has named as a cause of a score by itself: Havran 40 ties the lowest completed entry in the log and the form was cited, not just the subject, and nothing here offsets that the way an idea might. There is no premise, no protagonist and nothing to hold up under thought, so the character rules are suspended and, as the rule says, the suspension only removes penalties - it cannot pay for the one this form incurs. Leaned on axis:verse rather than axis:childrens, because the register is delicate rather than juvenile and would not on its own put a book this low; occult status is unexamined at this exit.

A collection of short fairy tales in which steam engines in a roundhouse talk to each other and meet a fairy and a water sprite - why an engine was afraid to whistle, a lost stationmaster's cap, a nest in a chimney - set in large print with short paragraphs for beginning readers, and with cut-out sheets in the back for building a paper station. Everything about that is the register axis at its floor: Hobbit 84 and The Little Prince 82 pay nothing for a young readership because neither is written down to its reader, and this is written for a six-year-old learning to read. There is no idea to carry away - the affection is for railways, not for a thought - and one-incident tales about talking machines have no room to make anyone want anything, which is the axis that carries Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90. The short-form suspension removes the character penalties and adds nothing, as it always does.
