Leaned on axis:childrens because the print size, the age band and the paper-model insert are established facts and they settle the number. One source, the gate budget; occult unexamined, as a C exit allows.

t: Pohadka o trech prasatkach (Pohadka o trech prasatkach)
why: This is a 20-page hardback retelling of a traditional folk tale in which every sentence is doubled by pictograms, published by a press that specialises in accessible formats; the stated purpose is teaching sentence structure and pre-reading skills to the youngest children and to readers with autism, developmental dysphasia or Czech as a second language. The moral is the folk tale's own - work properly and your house stands - and it is inherited rather than made, so there is no idea here that belongs to this book. axis:ideas and axis:childrens carry the number jointly: the log's short high scorers, The Little Prince 82 and Animal Farm 78, earn their place on an argument the book itself constructs, and a therapeutic reading aid constructs none. Not leaned on axis:protagonist or axis:momentum, which a 20-page pictogram primer does not put in play. Occult unexamined at this exit. One source, the gate budget.

t: Pohadky a pribehy (Fairy Tales and Stories (complete tales))
why: The texts here are Andersen's own, all 170 of them, translated straight from Danish instead of through the abridged retellings a Czech reader normally meets - so the individual pieces are the real article, and the best of them do exactly what this log pays for: one idea, declared in a few pages and carried through to its consequence, which is why The Little Prince 82 and Animal Farm 78 sit where they do. The problem is the object rather than the prose. It is a three-volume complete corpus with no single premise, and the reader's one recorded experience of a canonical author's assembled shorter pieces is Unfinished Tales 69, docked precisely because the parts do not connect to one another. A large share of the 170 are written for small children, and much of the rest ends grimly and abruptly - the bleakness arriving all at once that put Promena 58 twelve points under its prediction. Leaned on axis:short-idea-driven and axis:ideas: the ideas are genuinely there piece by piece, but the form gives them nothing to add up to, and that is what keeps the range under the line rather than at the allegory scores. One source, the C-low budget.

t: Pohadky na dobrou noc (A Bedtime Full of Stories)
why: Fifty tales retold from around the world, recommended from age four, in a large-format illustrated book of 128 pages - so each piece is a few hundred words and the object is a book to read aloud to a small child, which is the register this reader's grading puts at the picture-book floor. The short work that scores well for him scores for its own idea pressed all the way through, the way Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 do; a bedtime anthology of abridged classics and folk tales has no premise of its own to work out, and the abridgement takes away even what the originals had. There is no confusing opening and no filter near it, but clearing the filters is not a reason to score. Leaned on axis:childrens, with axis:ideas absent rather than doubtful. Occult status unexamined at this exit, though magic lamps and enchantments are in the contents. One source, the C-low budget.

t: Polevka pana Leprona (La zuppa di Lepron (Mr Lepron's soup))
why: This one does have an idea that can be said in a phrase: a good thing made once a year for your own household is destroyed by being made for the world in tins. That is the shape the log rewards in short work - Animal Farm 78 is an allegory whose whole construction is its argument, and The Little Prince 82 shows that a child register costs nothing when the thoughts are what carry the book. The reason this still sits under the line is that the argument is delivered as a closing moral over 48 large-format picture-book pages for three-to-nine-year-olds, with the consequences of the tinned soup asserted rather than traced; a fable that states its lesson leaves less behind than one that earns it. So the number is carried by axis:childrens - the register and the length - and axis:ideas is the risk that could take it lower, because a moral is not a premise worked out. Not leaned on axis:protagonist: a hare cooking soup is a fable figure, and the character tests are suspended rather than failed here. Occult unexamined at this exit. One source.

The premise is the strongest thing about it and it is a genuine one: a society that certifies its girls as pure by a blood rite, and a girl whose blood comes out the wrong colour and is conscripted instead of killed - a declared social machine whose consequences a book could work out, and the reader is unbothered by the violence such a setting brings. The reason I stop here is that the reviews converge on good ideas with middling execution: the setting is largely left unbuilt behind the lead's anxious inner monologue, the first half arrives as fragments joined by two-weeks-passed jumps, the arc settles into a chosen one sent away to train, and the twists are called predictable. That is the same failure Divergent 58 was scored for - a premise assembled from other books that does not cohere - and the reader's rule is explicit that strong worldbuilding never rescues what execution loses, so I would put axis:ideas in risks and the exit condition is met. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:worldbuilding rather than axis:protagonist, since Deka is sympathetic and reviewers' complaints about her are about how little of the world reaches the reader through her; occult status is unexamined at this exit, and with a priesthood, an imperial deity and a blood rite on the first pages it is a real open question.

t: Prasatko Peppa a jeji dobrodruzstvi (Peppa Pig Bind Up)
why: Four episodes of a licensed preschool television property bound into one 104-page volume for readers of three and up: a camping trip, a first day at nursery, a fair, a school sports day. Each is an incident that resolves in a few pages, written to a house style rather than by an author with a premise, so there is nothing on axis:ideas to name at all and no protagonist who wants anything beyond the day in front of her. That is the C exit with the lower band, since the form removes the character tests without adding anything in their place. The reader's own line on juvenile books is that they cost nothing when the ideas carry them (The Little Prince 82) and cost when a book has no higher things to think about (Narnia 67, docked for exactly that on a far more substantial work); tie-in episodes for three-year-olds sit well under Narnia. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:childrens because even a very juvenile register can score (Male zeny 79 on characters alone) and it is the absence of anything worked out that fixes this number. A C-low exit leaves axis:occult unexamined; nothing in the annotation points at it. One source, within the gate budget.

t: Putovani skritka Vltavinka po Vltave (Putovani skritka Vltavinka po Vltave)
why: The positive case is real but small: one concrete starting situation and a single companion, the plain shape that costs The Hobbit 84 nothing. Past that the book is an itinerary - a sprite is walked downstream so the child picks up the geography of the Vltava and the water idioms on the way - and there is no idea to name in a phrase, which is exactly the finding the short-idea-driven rule asks for; the suspension removes character penalties and adds nothing. On the reader's own children's scale, where Hobbit 84 and The Little Prince 82 pay nothing and Ranger's Apprentice 74 pays a little, a 112-page illustrated primer sits well past all of them at the end the rule puts in the 30s and 40s. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist because the sprite is a tour guide with no wants to fail at; occult status is unexamined at this exit.

There is a clear situation to start from and a motive-first engine: out of the prison and into the palace, sworn to a rebellion that wants destroyed the family she is coming to love, and lying to both sides. Divided loyalty is the axis Mockingjay 91 tops, and the book is credited with letting the monarchy be neither wholly good nor wholly bad rather than a cardboard target. The lead is the problem. The consistent complaint is that a woman who trusted nobody for ten years now trusts at once, and that is the log's declared-trait breach - state a trait and it has to be shown - against a reader whose heaviest axis is a protagonist who is interesting as well as worth rooting for; Artemis 69 is the case that a thin lead outranks every other strength a book has. Reviewers also report the world explained in monologue lore dumps and the twists telegraphed, so the plot is being handed over rather than earned. It is a sequel besides, and sequels are not safe bets in this log - Hitchhiker's 83 fell to 70. Leaned on axis:protagonist rather than axis:worldbuilding, because the world is the part reviewers praise and is not what would decide this. Elemental magic is central and its occult status is unexamined at this exit. One source, the C-low budget.

t: Rostaci v akci a tajemstvi kouzelne jeskyne (Rostaci v akci a tajemstvi kouzelne jeskyne)
why: A holiday adventure with a clean hook - a village where local legend says devils are sealed in a rock by a scroll, and the scroll goes missing - so the opening is legible and there is one question driving it. Against that it is an 82-page illustrated children's adventure whose payload is the legend turning out to be worth checking, which is not an idea in the sense that earns points here; the one substantive Czech reader review calls it overly descriptive and slow, and thin story spread over pages is the reader's actual density complaint, the one that cost The Lord of the Rings 84 its distance over The Hobbit. So axis:ideas belongs in risks and the exit is here. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:childrens rather than axis:detective, because the children are chasing a legend rather than a culprit; occult status is unexamined at this exit, and imprisoned devils plus a magic scroll make it a real question rather than a formality.

t: Ruce pryc od Kolobehu zivota (Hands off the Cycle of Life)
why: The best thing here is that the premise is actually pushed: a frog sets out to stop dying altogether, and the book then shows what a world without death would cost, down to the queue for the toilet. Following a declared premise into its second-order consequences is exactly what the log pays for - Project Hail Mary 92 is scored on precisely that - and short allegory with a nameable thought scores well for this reader, The Little Prince 82 and Animal Farm 78 both above the line. What keeps it under the line is the register: a hospice publisher's consolation picture book for ages four and up, where the argument is one joke long and the ending is a reassurance rather than a conclusion, and one reviewer found it did not deliver past its premise. So axis:childrens carries the number and axis:ideas is the risk that could take it lower. Bleakness is not the objection - the log's dislike of it is mild and this is a warm treatment of death, not an immersion in misery. Occult unexamined at this exit. One source.

The detective gate was examined first and deliberately not fired, and the doubt is worth recording: the plot is an investigation - three girls, pushed by a neighbour's cat, work out what happened to an old woman's lost love, a Jewish boy who survived the war and then vanished in 1948 - but the publisher's own account is that what they mostly find out is about themselves, and one reviewer records suspense built at length and then resolved quickly, which is a friendship story with a puzzle for a frame rather than a whodunnit. A wrong reject is not recoverable and a low number is, so this is graded with axis:detective left as a live risk. Graded, it lands well under the line anyway. It is 120 pages with large print, sold as being mainly for younger children and beginning readers, and that register is the number: Hobbit 84 and The Little Prince 82 pay nothing for a young readership because they are not written down to their readers, whereas this is, and Narnia 67 already shows what child leads plus little to think about cost in a full-length children's novel. No idea is nameable beyond the history the girls stumble on, and a cat that steers them to the answer is competence handed over rather than earned - the objection that helped put Divergent 58 where it is. Leaned on axis:childrens because the audience and the print size are established facts. One source, the gate budget; occult unexamined, as a C exit allows.

t: Simpsonovi (The Simpsons: Treehouse of Horror (Czech comics collection))
why: A licensed Halloween comics anthology of about 128 pages: unconnected horror and science-fiction parodies dropping a television cast into set-pieces outside their own continuity, drawn by a rotating team of artists. This is the gate-4 exit with nothing to argue against it - a joke anthology has no premise to work out, no idea I can name, and by construction no continuity, since each story resets characters who cannot change. The reader's stated objection to Unfinished Tales at 69, his lowest Tolkien, was pieces not logically connected to each other, and that is the format's design rather than a flaw in it. The comic register is not the problem: Saturnin scores 78 and Hitchhiker's Guide 83, so humour is free in this log - what is missing is anything for the axes that earn points to attach to. The low band because a parody anthology in panels is the slightest form on offer and suspends the character tests entirely. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:short-idea-driven rather than the register or the licensed origin. One source, on budget; the horror-parody supernatural is therefore unexamined against the occult filter, though a spoof idiom is not the practised-on-the-page case the filter targets.

t: Skrip, skrab, pip a zblunk (Scritch scratch dip clapote !)
why: A picture book with a sentence or two a page: a young frog is frightened by night noises after his parents say goodnight, until his father takes him outside to find where the sounds come from, and the joke at the end turns on the father. It does one thing cleanly, but a bedtime-fear story for the youngest readers works nothing out and leaves no idea behind, so axis:ideas goes into risks and both lower-band conditions hold - no nameable idea, and a form in which the character tests have nothing to test. The Little Prince 82 is proof the illustrated short form is no bar in itself, and equally proof that what scores there is the thinking the text carries. Leaned on axis:childrens and axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist, because there is not enough text for interiority to exist on the page. Occult unexamined at this exit. One search, inside budget.

An 88-page richly illustrated collection of short episodes for reading aloud to small children: sprites whose whole job is to bring cheer, who arrive whenever someone in the human world is sad - one pair introduces a lonely woman to a writer, another cheers an antique-shop assistant, another reconciles two friends over a Christmas present. That is the gate-4 exit at its clearest: there is no premise to work out, no idea I can name, and no jeopardy, since the sprites' success is the format rather than an outcome. Named sprites in interchangeable pairs also fail differentiation, the axis the reader praises Golden Son at 92 for. The low band rather than the default is not a judgement on the writing but on the form - this is the picture-book end of axis:childrens, where the log puts the register itself, against The Little Prince at 82 paying nothing because the ideas carry it. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:childrens rather than axis:protagonist, which a rotating cast of helper sprites does not have. One source, on budget - so although the title's carovani names magic, the occult status is deliberately unexamined.

t: Sovicka a jednorozec (Willow Tree Wood: The Owl and the Unicorn)
why: A short illustrated early reader in a translated four-part series: two siblings visit their grandmother next to a magical wood and, each time, help an animal in trouble - here an abandoned owlet and a unicorn who does not believe in himself. The positive case is a clean repeated structure and a kindness theme a five-to-eight-year-old can follow. Beyond that there is nothing to weigh: no premise worked out, no idea I can name, and a self-belief moral stated rather than earned, so axis:ideas is what I would flag and that is the gate-4 exit. The low band rather than the default because the form is the picture-book end of axis:childrens and suspends the character tests without replacing them - the reader's own ceiling for a childrens-adjacent book, Little Women at 79, is earned entirely on characters, and there is no room for that at this length. Leaned on axis:childrens and axis:ideas over axis:worldbuilding, because a magical wood at this register declares nothing precise enough to owe anything. I overspent slightly: a first search on the Czech title alone returned nothing usable and a second was needed to resolve it under the series name, so two queries produced the one source cited.

The strongest thing here is that the premise is a real one and it is carried out: a small boy abandoned in mid-1990s Moscow after the safety net collapses, kept alive through two winters by a pack of street dogs, then taken back into human care and finding that harder than the street - and reviewers single out that reintegration as the most painful part, which means the book does follow its own premise where it leads instead of stopping at the rescue. Starred Booklist, positive Kirkus and School Library Journal, graded 5-9. It also sits on the right side of the reader's loneliness objection: The Martian lost points at 82 for sustained solitude, and this is companionship and mutual dependence rather than solo survival. What keeps it under the line is that the idea stays at the level of a strong situation - what makes a person human, asked but not worked out - so axis:ideas is what I would flag, which is the gate-4 exit condition; plus a five-to-ten-year-old lead read from the inside, the distance that pulled Ender's Game down to 87 and helped end Anne Frank at 40, and sustained grimness, which the log docks mildly. Leaned on axis:ideas over axis:protagonist because the boy is genuinely active and rootable - it is the thinking the book leaves behind that is thin, not the lead. One source, on budget, so the occult status is unexamined.

t: Srdce z kameni (Minecraft: Srdce z kameni)
why: A licensed game tie-in comic of 88 colour pages in a children's line, built on one joke: a farmer who cannot stand his neighbours builds a tower into the sky to get away from everyone and discovers the neighbours up there are worse. The starting situation is concrete and the joke does resolve into a point - the people below were friends and he did not see it - but a point that small in a tie-in is not an idea a book leaves behind, and at this length in this form there is no interiority at all, which is the axis Red Rising 95 tops the log on. The world is a game's world rather than one thought through, so there is nothing to earn on worldbuilding either. Nothing here trips a filter. Leaned on axis:childrens and axis:ideas. One source, the C-low budget.

t: Star Wars - Thrawn Ascendence (Thrawn Ascendancy: Chaos Rising)
why: The positive case is genuine and sits on two axes the log rates well. First, a lead whose interest is how he reasons - reading an unseen enemy from the shape of the evidence - which is the strategy-and-psychology axis behind Ender's Game 87. Second, an alien society whose rules actually bind the plot: the Ascendancy's doctrine of never striking first is asserted and then made to carry its own consequences when the attacker leaves no trace, which is the self-consistency that earned Old Man's War 87 its highest praise. Against that, two deductions. The lead is admired rather than developed - reviewers note he is static while a secondary officer is the one who grows - and Artemis 69 is the log's proof that a thin lead outranks strong worldbuilding rather than being rescued by it. And the idea, once named, is only that doctrine question; there is no larger thing left behind, which is the Ranger's Apprentice 74 shape of easy competence with little to think about. Leaned on axis:worldbuilding and axis:protagonist rather than axis:ideas because the world is what is actually built here and the lead is what actually limits it. The range is conditional on axis:opening not firing, and that risk is unusually live: the book fronts a dramatis personae and a Chiss naming system in which one character answers to three names, then interleaves a second timeline of Memories chapters that all predate the prologue, and reviewers report losing track of who is who. Three books ended at 30 in this log on exactly that - several strands running before any is legible - so if it fires the number is not in this range at all.

This is the most promising thing in the group of registers it belongs to - a lead defined by wanting to know how a machine works, which is the curiosity that makes Project Hail Mary 92 and The Martian 82 work - and the reader has no objection to a child lead in itself. It does not survive the form: sixty pages aimed at preschoolers and new readers, whose actual payload is teaching the clock face, and a Czech reader review finds the promised machine is mostly just the clock and the treatment too fairy-tale to hold the engineering. So the idea I can name is a teaching objective rather than a premise whose consequences get worked out, which is the case for putting axis:ideas under risks and exiting here. Leaned on axis:ideas over axis:protagonist because Stepan is likeable and consistent - the book simply gives him nothing to solve; occult status is unexamined at this exit.

The opening is one concrete situation, which matters more in this log than anything else: a mother wins a competition, leaves for two weeks, and the promised live-in nanny turns out to be a hairy swamp-smelling monster the children cannot talk to. The premise is also declared quite precisely - the creature is presented as part of an official experiment in new childcare - and declaring a thing precisely is what puts an author on the hook. That is where the doubt sits: reviewers say the book leans on an in-story monster book to explain itself and leaves its own oddities unanswered, and a world that asserts a mechanism and then never makes society behave accordingly is what sank Harry Potter 51 and, on premise logic alone, Mortal Engines 55. Add that I cannot name what a reader takes away beyond the gag, and axis:ideas and axis:worldbuilding together carry the number under the line. The register is middle-grade for seven-to-eleven, which the log does not penalise by itself - The Hobbit 84 pays nothing for it. Occult unexamined at this exit. One source, the gate budget.

A 144-page illustrated collection of spooky Sumava tales for readers from ten up - forest sprites, the Black Lake, enchanted springs - written by a playwright with a genuine voice, and catalogued as legends and children's horror. The positive is atmosphere and the regional material, which is real and specific. But the form is a set of unconnected shivers with no premise to work out, no continuous lead to want anything, and no idea I can name behind the frightening: axis:ideas is what I would flag, and that is the gate-4 exit condition. The reader's own complaint about Unfinished Tales at 69, his lowest Tolkien, was that the pieces were not logically connected to each other, and that is this form by design. The low band rather than the default because a short illustrated shiver collection for children is the slight form that suspends the character tests and puts nothing in their place. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:short-idea-driven rather than the register itself, since Saturnin at 78 shows Czech comic-literary voice costs nothing on its own. One source, on budget - so although folk sprites and enchanted wells are the kind of material that raises the occult question, that status is deliberately unexamined here.

The setup is decent for its age group and it does the one thing the reader most wants from an opening: a single concrete situation with a stake - two children at a new school, one of them blamed for damage he did not do. But it is written for roughly five to ten year olds, with large type, illustrations on every spread and very little text, and the resolution is that a ghost in the classroom stove did it, so what the book leaves behind is a friendly ghost rather than an idea; that is the axis:ideas doubt this gate turns on. Little Women 79 marks the ceiling for a children's-adjacent book with no premise to work out, and it reaches that on several fully drawn characters over a full novel, which this length cannot attempt. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:childrens rather than axis:detective, because the who-did-it question is a schoolroom frame and not the source of the satisfaction; occult status is unexamined at this exit, and a resident ghost is a live question for it.

The positive case is structural. It opens on one concrete situation and one point of view - a disagreeable child left alone in an Indian bungalow after cholera has killed her parents and the servants - which is precisely the shape this reader asks for, and the opposite of the several-plot-lines-at-once opening that produced three scores of 30. The narrator calls Mary a selfish little pig in the first paragraph and then earns her change, so she is interesting before she is likeable, which is the harder half of the protagonist test and the half Oliver Twist 57 failed by being acted upon instead of wanting anything. And there is an idea, stated in a phrase and then worked out twice, on Mary and again on Colin: children are made sour by neglect and revived by having something to care for. That, with friendship as the engine, is the Little Women 79 and Hobbit 84 position - a book carried by characters and a plain want rather than by a premise. Three deductions keep it near the line. The register and the child leads cost roughly what they cost Narnia 67, and a little less because there is more to think about here. The book undertakes to explain Colin's recovery and the explanation does not hold - thought as medicine is asserted, not made to work - and an explanation the author volunteers and then cannot carry is the breach that sank Divergent 58. The moor and garden description over a slow middle is the thin-story-over-pages penalty that docked The Lord of the Rings 84, and the last third moves the camera off the interesting lead onto the recovering boy, thinning what the score rests on. Leaned on axis:protagonist and axis:ideas and deliberately not on the setting: Artemis 69 is this log's warning against predicting up on a well-built world when the lead is what actually carries a book, and here the lead is the strength while the declared explanation is the weakness. The daily circle where the children sit and chant at the garden, and the boy's line that God and Magic may be the same thing, was examined and is not treated as a hard filter - there is no spell, no divination, no deity other than the one in the hymn that is sung, so it is nothing like the Greek pantheon that put Percy Jackson at 57 - but a rite of a kind is performed on the page more than once, so axis:occult stays a named risk rather than a settled pass.

t: Tajemstvi Wilhelma Storitze (The Secret of Wilhelm Storitz)
why: One premise, declared plainly and then let loose: a man inherits from his father a liquid that makes him permanently invisible, and uses it to destroy a wedding he was refused. A stated capability whose consequences are then played out - a city that cannot see its enemy and panics - is the shape this reader rewards, and it opens on one concrete arrival rather than several threads at once. Two filters were checked and neither bites: the culprit is named early and the satisfaction is not finding out who did it, and the marriage axis does not apply because the woman refused the suitor rather than betraying anyone. What holds it under the line is that the consequences are not carried as far as this reader audits them. It is a late, posthumously edited work with a narrator who observes rather than wants - Oliver Twist 57 is what a passive lead costs here - and the standing objection to the book is that nobody in the town does the obvious thing an invisible intruder would provoke, which is the same self-consistency breach that made Mortal Engines 55 a DNF and cost Harry Potter 51. Leaned on axis:ideas because the invisibility premise is the only thing here that could earn a high number, and I doubt it survives the audit. One source, the C-low budget.

An occasional piece rather than a book: roughly a hundred pages on a single Christmas Day, rotating between three siblings' viewpoints, written to fill in a gap between the author's other work and padded out with illustrations and an extract from her novel. Two things decide it and neither needs deep research. First, there is no premise: a brother is home from a psychiatric hospital, the relatives ask intrusive questions at dinner, and the day is got through - Kirkus's praise is for a hopeful and honest outlook on recovery, which is a tone and not an idea worked out, so axis:ideas carries the number. Second, the form is the one the profile says removes the character tests without adding points, and three narrators in a hundred pages spends its length on switching rather than on any one person's wants, where the reader's top scores come from long stretches inside one head (The Hunger Games 89 on tight single-POV narration). It also assumes the reader already knows these people from elsewhere, and the log shows continuations are not safe bets on their own (Hitchhiker's 83 falling to 70 in its sequels). No hard filter presents itself and none is inherited: the family and the eating disorder come from other books but nothing excluded stands behind them. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:multi-pov because even a single-POV version of this would still have nothing to leave behind. A C-low exit leaves axis:occult unexamined; nothing suggests it. One source, within the gate budget.

A licensed tie-in to a preschool television cartoon: rescue puppies run a swimming-pool safety day, help stage a competition and teach teamwork, with the moral named in the publisher's own copy. The characters arrive fully formed from the screen and the episode structure means nothing is at stake and nothing is decided, so both of the log's heaviest axes are simply absent - no motives to spend page time on and no premise to work out. axis:ideas and axis:childrens carry the number: this is the far end of the childrens register, well below Little Women 79, which is the log's ceiling for childrens-adjacent work and got there on characters alone. Not leaned on axis:worldbuilding, since a broadcast franchise setting makes no declarations of its own to be held to. Occult unexamined at this exit. One source, the gate budget.

t: Tota lita (Tota lita: vyprava do Totality, zeme krale Totace)
why: An allegory with an idea that can be named in a phrase - how a totalitarian regime actually works, seen from inside it by a child who did not grow up under one - and it is worked out concretely rather than gestured at: bans and commands, dissidents, a ruling figure to be overthrown, and a grandfather to check the terms against afterwards. The reader's log rewards precisely this shape: a short allegory with a nameable idea landed on 70 and inside its predicted range, and a bleak idea-driven allegory that gives you something to think about took 78. What holds it under the line is that the delivery is didactic and aimed low - the author wrote it to explain the word to her small son, it ships with downloadable school worksheets, and the sharpest reader complaint is that the age window is narrow, since a ten-year-old found it too fairy-tale to tell what was real while smaller children miss the point. So the idea is real but the working-out is a lesson plan, which is why axis:ideas is the doubt that carries the number rather than the thing that lifts it; the register cost is the one Narnia 67 pays. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:childrens because a juvenile register is free when the thinking carries the book (The Little Prince 82), and here the thinking is the part that is simplified. A C-low exit leaves axis:occult unexamined; nothing suggests it. One source, within the gate budget.

One continuous story rather than a string of episodes, and it opens on a single concrete situation - a companion who does not come home, so the others go after him - which is the legible start this reader wants and nothing in it goes near a filter. Against that, it is written for preschool listeners: six garden gnomes named after their tools, a rescue trip, a wedding to finish on. I can name no idea it leaves behind, and the character tests are suspended by the register rather than passed, so nothing earns the points back. Narnia 67 already pays for putting children at its centre while still having something behind it; this sits well below that on register alone, near the picture-book floor. Leaned on axis:childrens rather than axis:ideas because the register is the established fact and the idea is simply absent. Occult status unexamined at this exit. One source, the C-low budget.

A walk through Hradcany and Mala Strana as a street-theatre piece, and the author's own account of how it was made is the finding: he wrote the text as a space for the illustrator's visual ideas and reworked it as the drawings arrived, and a reader note says outright that the book has no plot. That is the form that suspends the character tests while adding nothing - no protagonist who wants something, no premise whose consequences get worked out - so axis:ideas is where the doubt sits and I cannot name the idea it leaves behind. The reader pays nothing for a juvenile register when ideas carry the book (The Little Prince 82) and pays for the absence of higher things to think about (Narnia 67, marked down on exactly that); a catalogue of ghosts and legends with no story to hold it sits below Narnia, in the illustrated-book band. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:childrens because the missing story, not the audience, fixes the number. A C-low exit leaves axis:occult unexamined - the content is Prague apparitions and old legends. One source, within the gate budget.

An early chapter book of about 128 pages for readers aged six to nine, illustrated throughout, in which a girl is transported from a party to an Indian rain forest and rescues a tiger cub from a monsoon flood. The positive case is real but small: one concrete starting situation, a single clear want, and a rescue carried out by the child herself rather than handed to her. There is no idea I can name behind it - the animal is in danger, the animal is saved - so this is a gate-4 exit with axis:ideas as the thing I would flag, and the register puts it well below the level where axis:childrens costs only a little: Narnia at 67 and Ranger's Apprentice at 74 are full-length novels for older readers, and the reader's own ceiling case for a childrens-adjacent book, Little Women at 79, earns it on characters that a six-to-nine reader has no room for. The low band rather than the default one because the form itself suspends the character tests without putting anything in their place. Exited at one source, on budget; the magic that moves her between worlds is therefore unexamined against the occult filter.

A thirty-two-page illustrated Christmas story for age five and up, with one likeable want at its centre - a boy trying to save his family's failing bookshop by building the best window display he can - and a nice small touch in measuring his height in books. But the want is granted rather than worked out: the paper doe comes alive and the wishes come true, so the premise never has to hold up under thought, which is the axis on which the log docks hardest. No idea can be named beyond the sentiment that words and hope help, and at this length and register the character tests are suspended rather than passed, which removes penalties without earning points. Leaned on axis:childrens because the register decides the ceiling; the reader's own ruling puts a genuine picture book in the 30s or 40s, and the upper end here allows for the story having a real motive rather than only a mood. One source, gate 4, inside budget - so the occult question raised by the annotation's talk of magic was deliberately left unexamined, as a book that lands here is off the list either way; on the face of it this is a Christmas wish coming true, not a rite.

A 208-page illustrated Christmas chapter book for young readers: a rescued puppy reaches a shelter, two children talk their mother into a trial adoption, and the puppy causes one mishap after another. The positive case is that it does have one concrete starting situation and a single want, which is the structure the reader asks for and the thing whose absence ended three books at 30. That is all it has. There is no idea I can name - the mishaps are the content and the outcome is never in doubt - so axis:ideas is what I would flag, and that is the gate-4 exit. The low band rather than the default because the telling is pitched at a reader learning to read a chapter at a time, well below the register where axis:childrens costs only a little: The Hobbit pays nothing at 84 on ideas and friendship, Narnia pays a little at 67 as a real novel with a plot, and a comic-mishap animal story for seven-year-olds has neither to trade on. Leaned on axis:childrens and axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist, since a puppy protagonist is not a lead the reader's interesting-and-rootable test even applies to. One source, on budget.

t: Vombat Jirka je statecny (Vombat Jirka je statecny)
why: An illustrated picture book for roughly three-year-olds and first readers, with rhythmic near-verse text: the wombat plays hide-and-seek, smells a fox and stands his ground. Courage is the label on the episode rather than something the book examines, and there is no premise here at all, so axis:ideas and axis:childrens carry the number jointly - this is the youngest end of the register, where the scale puts a picture book in the 30s and 40s, and nothing offsets it in the way the thoughts offset the child register in The Little Prince 82. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log - the Hitchhiker's fall from 83 to 70 is the steepest in it - though at this length the point barely bites either way. Not leaned on axis:protagonist: a talking wombat toddler suspends the character tests rather than failing them. Occult unexamined at this exit. One source, the gate budget.

An illustrated collection of short explanations written down to a school child - parents divorcing, a friend who lets you down, a homeless man on the metro - so there is no continuous story, no protagonist and nothing whose consequences are followed through. The log's non-fiction anchors are Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75, and what earned there was a first-person account testing what is actually true plus insight into how another group experiences the world; advice pitched at eight-year-olds offers neither, and the form earns nothing on its own - The Diary of a Young Girl 40 is the log's warning on that. axis:ideas would go straight into risks, both conditions for the lower band hold, and the C exit follows. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:childrens rather than axis:protagonist, because the form has no protagonist to test. Occult unexamined at this exit. One search, inside budget.

A 112-page bedtime collection for four-year-olds: a postman on a magic bicycle, a snowflake afraid of heights, a wooden bridge with a secret wish, each piece carrying a gentle moral, with two guide figures walking the child through. A collection with no single premise gives axis:ideas nothing to hold, and pieces this short leave motives - the axis that tops the log - no page time at all; that combination is what the C exit is for. Saturnin 78 shows a Czech comic voice can carry a book on voice alone, but that is an adult voice doing adult work, and read-aloud morals for preschoolers are a different instrument. Both lower-band conditions hold: nothing nameable as an idea, and a slight collection in which the character tests have nothing to test. Leaned on axis:childrens and axis:ideas. Occult unexamined at this exit. One search, inside budget.

The gate to hell in the blurb turns out to be a local legend dressed on a treasure hunt: 128 richly illustrated pages of underground passages, mysterious statues, crooks, policemen and a hoard hidden during the Hussite wars, sold by the publisher as an adventure in the Foglar tradition. That places it exactly where this log prices easy adventure with nothing behind it - Rangers Apprentice 74 is the ceiling for that kind of book and it is a fourteen-volume series for older children, whereas this is a short illustrated one for a younger reader, and one reader's summary is that it reads well but is no literary achievement. No idea is nameable. The lead is the class troublemaker and there is a real want there in the friction with his teacher, but a treasure chase of this length will not develop it, and wanting developed on the page is the axis that carries Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90. Leaned on axis:childrens because extent, illustration and audience are established facts and they cap it well under the line. One source, the gate budget; occult unexamined, as a C exit allows, though the hell-mouth is presented as folklore rather than practice.

A 112-page girls' series novel about a twelve-year-old in love with a classmate, who falls in with a group of graffiti boys, paints a goat from her herd on a shed wall and is then asked to help make a film. First love as the central subject costs nothing by itself - Pride and Prejudice scores 75 precisely because motives and what characters want are the whole book - so the objection is not the romance. It is that at this length and register there is no premise whose consequences get worked out and no idea I can name: the plot is a sequence of small incidents and the emotional question is a crush resolving. That is the gate-4 exit condition, axis:ideas. The low band rather than the default because a short illustrated series volume for pre-teen girls suspends the character tests without substituting anything, and it sits below the level where axis:childrens costs only a little: Narnia pays a little at 67 as a full novel with something at stake, and the log's best childrens-adjacent result, Little Women at 79, earns it on a whole household of differentiated characters that 112 pages cannot hold. A twelve-year-old inner life also draws the small life-phase pushback the reader applies. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:childrens rather than axis:protagonist, who is at least active and likeable. One source, on budget.

A 224-page middle-grade novel for readers of eight to twelve, and it does the two structural things the reader asks for: one concrete starting situation - the class is staging a school play and the lead is told she may not audition for the girl's part - and a single legible want driving every chapter, which is the opposite of the confusion that ended three books at 30. Reviewers single out the narration, which uses female pronouns from the first page so the reader is inside the lead's own self-understanding rather than watching from outside; that is page time on what a character wants and why, the axis that tops this log. What holds it under the line is register and reach. It is written for a fourth-grade audience, and axis:childrens at that pitch has a ceiling: Narnia lands at 67 with children as leads and, in the reader's words, nothing higher to think about, and even the log's best childrens-adjacent result, Little Women at 79, has a whole family of differentiated adults to work with. The idea here is an identity affirmed rather than a premise whose consequences are worked out, so axis:ideas is what I would flag - the gate-4 exit condition - and the eight-to-twelve inner life also draws the small life-phase pushback that marked Ender's Game down to 87. Leaned on axis:childrens and axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist, which is the book's strength, not its problem. One source, on budget, so the occult question is unexamined - though nothing in a contemporary school story suggests it arises.

Twenty-seven self-contained comic episodes about four Prague schoolboys and an explosives-mad uncle, 192 pages, published from age nine, in the Czech comic-schoolboy tradition. The honest positive is the register: Saturnin scores 78 on voice and character alone, so Czech comic prose carries no penalty in this log by itself. What sinks it below the line is that the humour is situational and episodic - a catastrophe per chapter, reset at the end - so there is no premise whose consequences get worked out and no idea I can name, which is the gate-4 exit condition, and a sketch of a few pages cannot do the thing the reader values most, page time on what a character wants and why, the axis that puts Mockingjay at 91. Reader comments on the Czech book databases report the episodes feeling stretched and the attempt to update the setting falling flat, which is a hint about axis:sequels rather than evidence. The low band rather than the default because a collection of comic sketches for nine-year-olds is exactly the slight form that suspends the character tests and puts nothing in their place. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:childrens over the comic register, which is not an objection at all here. One source, on budget.

One declared premise and the book actually pursues its consequences: a flu that turned into a cancer killed almost every man, so a surviving twelve-year-old boy becomes state property, black-market stock and a cult's answer to prayer, and his mother has to move him through all three. Following a declared change through to its second-order effects is what put Project Hail Mary 92 above The Martian 82, and the same comparison rewards what carries this book - two people protecting each other rather than one person enduring alone, with the mother's reasons on the page rather than her tactics. The opening is one concrete situation, a mother and a disguised boy already running. Against it: the narrative shuffles three viewpoints including the antagonist's, Library Journal found some characterisation thin, and the long stretch among the cultists is widely reported to drag - a thin story spread over pages is the reader's own penalty term and it is what held LOTR to 84. Publishers Weekly rates the worldbuilding below the genre's best, so I leaned on axis:ideas and axis:motives rather than axis:worldbuilding: predicting up on worldbuilding while the character work looked thin is the error that missed Artemis by 11.

The positive case is a premise with one hard constraint that generates everything else: an artificial body passes Earth once every eight years, so a sentence is eight years long and there is no exit until the orbit comes back round. That is the kind of declared rule the reader rewards when the world is then organised around it, the axis that carried Valka stareho muze 87. And the lead is the right shape - one man, sentenced for defying the powerful, who fights the order he lands in rather than being carried by it, which is the difference between Sunrise on the Reaping 87 and Oliver Twist 57, where the lean on the protagonist was right and the protagonist wanted nothing. A reviewer confirms a single sympathetic viewpoint and a start on Earth before the prison, so the opening is one concrete situation and not the several-at-once failure. The deductions are specific and documented: stilted patches and typos, and above all that things are flagged as to be explained later and then are not, with the book stopping mid-thought on a large question mark. That is the self-consistency breach that ended Mortal Engines 55 and the non-connection that made Unfinished Tales 69 the lowest Tolkien, and it is why the range tops out where it does rather than in the 70s. I leaned on the protagonist and the one declared rule rather than on the idea, because what a man will do to survive is a situation more than a thought to take away.

t: Bezecky klub na konci sveta (The End of the World Running Club)
why: There is a real positive: one first-person voice and one concrete want that runs the whole book - an overweight, disengaged father cut off from his wife and children by five hundred miles of wrecked Britain, trying to get to them on foot. Motive-driven narration by a single narrator is the shape of The Hunger Games 89, and there is companionship on the road rather than solo survival, the complaint that held The Martian 82 down. Against that, the lead is what reviewers divide over, and it is the reader's sharpest recorded objection: a self-described slob who did the bare minimum for his family, with one reviewer unable to connect to the book for that reason alone. Twenty-two points separated two books by one author in one world on rootability, and the arc here is a bad father earning back the right to be one, so the whole estimate hangs on whether that arc lands. Nothing else is being worked out - the asteroid strike is scenery, the title's running club only appears halfway, and readers describe the book as dark and disturbing rather than enjoyable, with plausibility objections and an unreliable narrator speaking from the far end of the journey. I would list the idea as a risk, which is the honest answer, so this stops at one source and leaves the occult question unexamined.

t: Bitva o ceske zeme (Bitva o ceske zeme)
why: The title states the content and the content is the problem: a fleet battle for the homeland, in a world whose reviewed weakness is that it carries no argument. The substantive criticism of this alternate history is that the author abandoned any attempt at a clever story with reach beyond itself, with flat, undeveloped characters, a predictable plot and real twentieth-century engagements re-flagged rather than reinvented - and carrier aviation deciding the war is the most straightforwardly borrowed of those. Under the gate's own test I cannot name the idea, which puts axis:ideas in the risks and ends the research. It is a sequel too, and sequels are not safe bets in this log, where Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70 because a comic premise did not survive repetition. The positive side is real but small: readable prose and momentum are consistently praised, and readability with nothing to think about is the Ranger's Apprentice 74 shape - except that book had a lead the reader stayed with for fourteen volumes, and flat characters are the standing complaint here. One source, within budget; occult unexamined by design.

The premise is nameable and the front half of it is well made: electricity stops working everywhere at once, the hierarchy of values inverts, and the people who can organise groups and impose order come to the front, all followed through one Prague family. The author is a power engineer by training and readers say the technical collapse convinces. What decides the number is the other half. Readers report that the ending turns on telepaths whose cells communicate around the world, and say that this is the point at which a believable story stops being believable - one wrote that the finale outright poisoned the book and that leaving it as a post-collapse story about one family would have been fine. That is the self-consistency breach this log punishes hardest: Mortal Engines 55 was abandoned on nothing but that, where moving cities as such were acceptable and the logic around them was not. The family thread also spreads from rulers' palaces to South Bohemian cottages to America, which is thin story over pages rather than density earned. I stopped at one source with the doubt carried by axis:worldbuilding, so occult is unexamined.

The situation is a good one for this reader on the axis he weights heaviest: elite soldiers who answered only to the emperor are ordered home to be dissolved and have their record wiped, and the lead refuses the order. Loyalty repaid with erasure, and a decision to disobey, is a conflict made entirely of what someone wants and why - Mockingjay 91 is the log's favourite Collins book for showing the most of motives and the least of the arena. The lead is reported as sympathetic and well written, so the interesting-and-rootable pair is likely satisfied. What holds the range down. It is a sequel that continues a betrayal set up before it, and sequels are not safe bets in this log - Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70, the Ender saga settled from 90 to 81 - and a going-rogue plot with a commando unit is the kind that tends to resolve in action, which is what cost Golden Son 92 its points against Red Rising 95. The premise's genuine idea, enhancement paid for in lifespan, was declared and worked out already, so this book inherits it rather than posing a new one, and that is why axis:ideas sits in the risks. I lean on the protagonist rather than on the worldbuilding, per the Artemis 69 lesson that a consistent world rescues nothing when the lead has to carry the book. No occult: genetic modification treated as illegal medical technology, no rite anywhere.

t: Cesta vecnou noci (Through the Ever Night)
why: The positive is real and it sits on the axis this log rewards most: reviewers consistently single out the leader's dilemma - a young man who has to keep winning the loyalty of a tribe that will not accept the girl he loves - and page time on what people want and why is what put Mockingjay 91 above the rest of its trilogy. Alternating viewpoints keep it moving. Why it still lands under the line: the world is atmosphere rather than mechanism. Ether storms and enhanced senses are decorative, the plot is a journey and a romance rather than a premise being worked out, and reviewers say a lot of the length is set-up. A competent book that leaves events rather than ideas behind is the commonest way this reader stalls in the 60s - Rangers Apprentice 74 was easy to read with not much to think about, and that is the shape here with a thinner setting. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: the Hitchhiker sequels fell from 83 to 70. I lean on the idea, not on the protagonists, because the character work is the part I would defend. YA romance means some sexual content, small in volume on the reports I have. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, so the occult question is unexamined.

The setup is the best thing about it and it is a single concrete situation: the empire has lost the decisive battle, and the man responsible for putting it back together is locked aboard a crippled communications ship with nothing but the thing he is actually good at - he is an analyst, not a warrior, and he knows restoring order will be work rather than a battle won. That is a protagonist stripped to his motives, which is the axis Mockingjay 91 tops the Collins trilogy on by showing the least of the arena and the most of what people are trying to accomplish. A reviewer of another Kotouc title calls this one an excellent space opera about the emperor in exile, so the praise here is specific rather than inherited series reputation, and the heavy front-loaded exposition critics complained of is already discharged by the time this one starts. Against it: a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log - Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70 and the Ender saga settled from 90 to 81 - and the political-plus-fleet structure widens the cast, where the log's highest scores are narrow. Bleakness is a mild discount at most, and the imprisoned-emperor frame supplies the companionship the reader prefers to solo endurance. I lean on the lead rather than the worldbuilding because Artemis 69 settles that contest whenever they compete. No occult: genetic castes and starship engineering, no rite. The infidelity screen never fired on this record and nothing in the premise touches a marriage.

One narrator, one concrete starting situation - a robot nanny finds in the attic the box he was delivered in and understands he is a disposable object - and the rest of the book is the question that discovery sets him: obey the directive he was built for, or preserve himself. That is page time on what a character wants and why, the axis that puts Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 at the top of the log, and the lead is both interesting and worth rooting for, which is the 22-point difference between Sunrise on the Reaping 87 and Ballad 65. The idea is nameable and followed through: whether a machine built to love can be said to own that love once its owner is gone. Held out of the S band because reviewers agree the telling is simple, close to a young-adult register, with a firefight every few pages - action with no character revelation is dead weight for this reader, the charge that cost Golden Son 92 ground against Red Rising 95. It also belongs to a series, and series entries are not safe bets in this log (Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70). Leaned on the lead rather than on worldbuilding, because the robot society is sketched, not worked out the way Project Hail Mary 92 works its premise out, and Artemis 69 is the standing proof that worldbuilding does not carry a book on its own.

Four unconnected weird tales framed as the recollections of four old men between 1934 and 1937 - an archaeologist, a gendarme, an engineer and a works driver - which means there is no single premise for the book to carry through and nothing it leaves behind as a whole. Unfinished Tales 69 is the log's one direct reading of that shape and it is the lowest Tolkien by a clear margin, marked down precisely because the pieces are not logically connected to each other. Readers who like this author call this his weaker book against the earlier ones and single out one of the four as needlessly overcomplicated. Short fiction suspends the character tests, but the suspension only removes penalties and never adds points, so there is no way for this to climb: the atmosphere is the whole offer. Gate 4 answered yes on axis:ideas at one source. Occult is therefore unexamined, and it is worth a note that readers describe the register as mysterious rather than horror, with an asylum graveyard and multiple overlapping realities among the settings.

t: Dlouha cesta na malou, rozzlobenou planetu (The Long Way to a Small, Angry Planet)
why: Nearly all of this book is page time on what people want and why rather than on what they do, which is the heaviest axis in this log - it is the stated reason Mockingjay 91 is the favourite of its trilogy, for showing the most of motives and the least of the arena. The crew are also genuinely differentiated, with species whose biology and customs are worked through and each member thinking and wanting something different, which is what earned Golden Son 92 its praise. It opens on one legible situation, a clerk taking an administrative post aboard a tunnelling ship, so the confusion that ended three books at 30 does not apply, and the navigator's condition is biological rather than anything occult. The cost is the other face of the same virtue: reviewers agree there is no driving central plot and that conflicts resolve through good communication, so a long book carries a thin story - the penalty that held LOTR to 84 despite ideas the reader admired - and the many viewpoints cost depth, with arcs resolving a chapter or two after their climax. Three romances run through it, non-explicit and not crude by every account I found, worth a few points in the way a chapter of it cost Old Man's War 87 a few and no band; the captain's relationship breaks his partner's own species law rather than a marriage, so the infidelity axis was examined and does not apply. Leaned on axis:motives and axis:character-differentiation rather than axis:worldbuilding, since leaning up on worldbuilding is the error that missed Artemis by 11.

Gate one first, because the annotation reads like an investigation: the best agents are liquidated and a carousel of conspiracies, murders and double-crosses follows. It is not a whodunnit - the satisfaction on offer is a running battle, parallel worlds bleeding into each other and helicopters being shot down in a war under Switzerland, so the detective filter is not engaged and no reject is set. What decides it is the below-the-line gate. This is an instalment of a long-running dime-novel series written to a shared formula by a rotating stable of authors on the Perry Rhodan model, and the franchise premise - an agency that intervenes across parallel worlds to keep them from collapsing - is inherited scaffolding rather than an idea this book poses and answers. Asked to name what it would leave behind, I cannot, so axis:ideas belongs in the risks and the ladder exits. The stated opening compounds it: an assassination campaign, conspiracies, interpenetrating worlds and a subterranean war all announced at once is the shape that produced three scores of 30 in this log, where several plot lines start before any is legible. One source, within budget; occult status unexamined, which changes nothing below the propose line.

t: Do poklidne modri (Into the Still Blue)
why: The case for it is that reviewers call the ending earned rather than tidy - friendship, forgiveness and sacrifice given as much room as the romance, and nothing made perfect - and self-sacrifice for other people over solo survival is explicitly what this reader prefers, the reason Project Hail Mary 92 beats The Martian 82. Against that, this is a closing book of a chase: reviewers describe it as so fast paced it becomes a blur, and predictable, which is action displacing the motive-and-want page time that carries the top of the log. The world stays atmosphere - ether storms, a hidden safe valley - rather than a premise whose consequences are followed, so there is little idea to leave behind. It also cannot be entered here: it continues two leads and a plot established earlier, and a sequel is not a safe bet in this log, the Hitchhiker sequels falling from 83 to 70. I lean on the idea rather than on the protagonists because the leads and their wants are the strongest thing present. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, so the occult question is unexamined.

A post-apocalyptic debut whose method is withheld information: a man and his small daughter remember almost nothing of their past and slowly find further pieces of a puzzle, moving between our past and a distant future. Readers who liked it liked the atmosphere and say openly that it suits people who enjoy riddles and do not mind open endings; readers who did not call it confused, full of questions with no answers, with a very strange ending, and one says the author bit off too much and set several disjoint story lines running. That last complaint is the reader's single most reliable killer - not slowness but strands running before any of them is legible, which ended The Colour of Magic 30, The Gunslinger 30 and Foundryside 30 in their first chapters, and it is what carries this range. The second cost is that there is no idea I can name that the book follows through: a reviewer notes the pills the title refers to have no rational basis and are simply a supernatural substance, so there is no mechanism to work out either, and mysteries deliberately left open leave nothing behind. One source, so the occult question stays unexamined, which that supernatural substance makes worth revisiting if the axis is ever bumped. Discovery (axis:discovery, 2026-10-24): two people who remember almost nothing piece their past together, the shape exactly, but the ending is reported open and the questions unanswered, which forfeits the lift; the number holds.

The positive case is real but narrow: one named lead, a duke of stated principle, in a concrete political situation, and page time on what a man wants and what it costs him is the axis that tops this log (Mockingjay 91, Speaker for the Dead 90). Against that, this is franchise continuation written by hands other than the original author's, and the recorded complaint about that body of work is precisely the thing the reader wants most - that it settles for sensationalism instead of insight and does not reach the level of the books it extends. So I would list axis:ideas under risks: I can name what happens here but not what it leaves behind, and a competent book with nothing to think about stalls in the 60s the way Exodus 68 and Quo Vadis 66 did. Continuations are not safe bets in this log either - Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. I leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist because the lead is the one asset I would expect to survive; the idea is what I doubt. Exited at gate 4 on one source, so the occult question and the opening structure are both unexamined here.

Twenty separate stories sharing a year rather than a premise. The short idea-driven form suspends the character and emotion rules, but the suspension only removes penalties - it never adds points - so a collection has to earn its number on ideas alone, and here they are twenty provocations (rule by artificial intelligence, a colonised Moon, immortality, a new totalitarianism, a return to the stone age) rather than one commitment whose consequences get followed out. Animal Farm 78 is what a single declared idea earns when the book carries it all the way; Unfinished Tales 69 is the log's anchor for a set of pieces that are not connected to each other, and it is the lowest Tolkien by twelve points, which is the shape of this book. The one substantial review is on the blog of the shop that also publishes it, and it says plainly that the collection is even in quality but did not hit any literary heaven. Reader comments split the stories into the funny ones and the harsh ones, which is a range, not a thesis. That doubt about the idea is what carries the range, so I stopped at one source; the occult question is unexamined, and so is the sexual-content axis, which the publisher's own copy raises by advertising a story about how sex will be conducted.

The hook is genuinely good: four cosplayers are dropped inside the dystopia they love, kill its heroine within minutes by accident, and can only get home by letting the plot run to its end - which means one of them has to stand in for a protagonist who dies. But reviewers agree it never converts. School Library Journal calls the invented world underdeveloped and bland and the character motivations not always believable, and a blogger reports characters reduced to a single repeated tag. Those are the two axes that decide scores here: Divergent 58 was sunk by a premise that will not survive being thought about and by factions never written as what they claim to be, and Artemis 69 by a lead who simply was not interesting. A book that mocks the genre it is simultaneously reproducing leaves no idea behind either, which is what stalls competent books in the 60s. Gate 4 answers yes on axis:ideas at one source, so occult is unexamined. The sexual-assault scenes reviewers flag are incidents in a book about something else, not the plot, so filter six does not fire.

The positive is a concrete predicament with an engineering answer: a fleet of survivors adrift with no usable drives, a commander assembling a team to find the material that would let them move, and an engineer who has to be better than he believes he is. Practical problem-solving with a companion beside you is the axis that carried The Martian 82 and Project Hail Mary 92. The number is lower because this is a sequel and continuation earns nothing in this log - the Hitchhiker's sequels landed at 70 against 83 - and because the specific reported shift is away from a conflict of ideas toward family abuse and rebellion, with one reviewer calling the psychodrama exhausting and himself entertained but not gripped. Sustained grimness is only a mild recorded objection, so it discounts rather than sinks, and the platonic core relationship still means the sexual axis is not doing work here. I lean on the leads rather than the setting, since the edge-of-the-universe physics is the part most exposed to the reader's consistency audit. How this book opens is not sourced, hence medium.

t: Hlidka na konci vesmiru (The Last Watch)
why: Two leads carry this and both are the kind the log rewards: a commander with nothing to command with who keeps deciding to try anyway, and a disowned aristocrat who blew up his grandfather's genetics lab and is now the only engineer on board - reviewers repeatedly note the relationship between them stays deliberately platonic and is where the book does its emotional work. Companionship and people choosing to spend themselves for others is exactly what the reader ranked Project Hail Mary 92 above The Martian 82 for, and a misfit military crew whose world follows from its own rules is the Old Man's War 87 profile. It opens on one concrete situation, the new recruit's arrival and processing aboard the ship, so the opening filter is not in play, and the screen's detective hint is wrong: this is a penal frontier posting, not an investigation. No reviewer reports explicit content. Held short of the high 80s by two things - one reviewer calls it entirely plot-driven and better suited to film, and the shrinking-universe conceit is the sort of declared physics this reader audits, which is why axis:worldbuilding is the risk and not the lean; Artemis 69 is the standing warning against leaning up on a setting.

The positive case is the lead and what the book spends him on. Daniel Hankerson's defining ability is reading people - it is what he uses at the intelligence desk and at the card table, and it is how he works out that the routine mission he has been handed is not routine. A book whose engine is a man calculating what other people want is the axis that tops this log: Speaker for the Dead 90 and Ender's Game 87 both score on psychology and motive rather than on the set piece, and readers of this one report characters with depth and an empire held together by compromises whose internal enemies are worse than its external ones - a stated subject that has to cohere, in the way Old Man's War 87 earned its score by having its world follow from its own premises. Deductions are real and they are all structural. Reviews agree the first third is a slow, florid exposition dump before the events start rolling, and one describes the book as several chess games running in parallel at different levels - grand strategy alongside Daniel's ship - which is exactly the dilution of the tight single-POV momentum that anchors The Hunger Games 89, and one reader calls the world fairly black-and-white. I lean on the protagonist rather than on the worldbuilding deliberately: Artemis 69 is the log's proof that a strong world rescues nothing when the lead is thin, so the number has to ride on the lead, and here the lead is the reported strength. Occult does not arise - genetic enhancement and fleet technology, no rite of any kind. The infidelity screen's hit was the Czech verb for waging war, not an affair.

The conceit is the good part and it is genuinely arresting: interstellar transport is carried in the guts of enormous hyperspatial creatures, herded by cowboys, so whoever controls the cattle controls the galaxy. That is an economics-shaped premise with a stated consequence, the kind of thing Project Hail Mary 92 was rewarded for following through. The reviewed record says it is not followed through. The strongest reader objections are exactly the two that decide this reader's scores: the world does not hold together, and the characters do not make you feel anything, with one reviewer adding that there is essentially no plot and another calling the material the most cliched Wild-West-in-space imaginable. Mortal Engines 55 was abandoned on the worldbuilding alone and Artemis 69 shows a thin lead outranks a consistent world, so a book faulted on both has nothing left to lean on - the space-western jokes and the sheer scale are the defence its admirers offer, and voice can carry a book here, as Saturnin 78 shows, but a monopolist villain with cyborg armies and killer lizards is broad comedy rather than a voice. So the doubt sits on the worldbuilding and the lead, which is what carries this number; a book below the line either way, exited at that gate on one source, within budget. Occult not examined - the hyperspatial creatures are presented as biology, not as anything invoked.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. Form is a collection of five novellas, genre Czech SF. I would put ideas in risks, which is the exit condition, and here the reason is sharper than for an ordinary anthology: the commission was that each author write a new story inside his or her own established series, so every one of the five drops a reader into a continuity - a lunar cycle, a post-apocalyptic soldier's world, a space-opera cycle, an interstellar mineral saga - that the piece assumes rather than builds. There is no premise belonging to the book, and the parts have nothing to do with each other, which is the complaint that made Unfinished Tales the lowest Tolkien at 69 on good material. Reader reception is explicitly uneven across the five, with no agreement on which works. The short form suspends the character rules without adding anything, so nothing carries the number upward, and side-stories in ongoing series are the weakest form of the sequel case, which in this log fell 13 points from 83 to 70. Occult status is unexamined; one of the five is set in an author's world that mixes post-apocalyptic SF with fantasy, which is where to look if this ever moves up.

The system is declared precisely and the book then obeys its own rules, which is the axis this reader weighs heaviest: a state that watches everyone in order to assign each citizen the role in which he is most useful, machines doing all the labour, and a civil servant who administers that machinery until one wrong recommendation turns it on him. Reviewers consistently credit a thought-through world model and a surprising ending, and the sharpest idea in it is nameable - disputed facts are no longer verified but 'wikified'. Old Man's War 87 is what self-consistency earns; Divergent 58 and Harry Potter 51 are what its absence costs, and nothing here reads like that failure. Held to the B band by three costs. The genre skeleton is admittedly familiar - the true believer who trips and is ground down - so there is less left over than a first-rank dystopia gives. The first third is heavy with world description and at least one open info-dump, which is thin story over pages, the Les Miserables 71 penalty. And a surveillance state closing on a compliant man is the shape that made 1984 60 too depressing to enjoy. Leaned on the world and the idea rather than the lead, because a convinced functionary being crushed is not obviously someone to root for, and that is exactly why the range does not reach higher.

One premise stated cleanly and then followed to its end. A small-town doctor's patients start arriving to insist that a relative is not the person they claim to be; the town explains it away as contagious delusion and he accepts that explanation himself; and the book is the working out of what is replacing people and what exactly is lost when a copy has every memory and scar but nothing it feels. It leaves an idea behind - the same footing that carries Animal Farm 78 at similar length - and it is short, single first-person, one town, one concrete situation from the first pages, which is the shape this reader asks for and the opposite of the openings that ended books at 30. Momentum is high and there is no confusion to fight through. One deduction keeps it out of the S band. The explanation is undertaken and then wobbles: Damon Knight's objection that interstellar spores and three-foot pods cannot be the same thing is a declared-then-broken commitment of the kind that ended Mortal Engines 55, though here it arrives late and is not the engine of the plot. Miles is a competent, likeable everyman, and since 2026-10-24 that costs nothing: ordinary is not flat, which Valka stareho muze 87 proved by scoring eleven above a range built on that worry. The lean stays on the idea and the opening, and the lead is a risk only if he reads flat on the page; the range rose with that deduction gone. The novel ends markedly less bleakly than the films do, so that discount is small.

It has more going for it than a children's label suggests: one first-person girl narrator with a stated lack in her own life, a colony dystopia a reviewer calls a believable premise, and enough hard edges that the same reviewer says it is decidedly not a bedtime story. Interiority in a single narrating voice is what carries The Hunger Games 89, and a child lead costs only a couple of points on its own - The Little Prince 82 and Male zeny 79 set the ceiling on what a juvenile register can still reach. But what this particular book delivers is the reveal of a hidden passenger and then a finale full of action and aggression, and the log is explicit that set-piece action with no character revelation is dead weight: Golden Son 92 was docked below Red Rising 95 for exactly that shift, and Catching Fire 83 for an arena existing for its own sake. So the answer to gate 4 is that I can name the situation and not the idea it leaves behind, which puts axis:ideas in risks. Against Narnia 67, which lost points for children as leads and for lacking higher things to think about, just under the line is where this sits. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:childrens because the register alone would not sink it. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. Form is a short illustrated novel, genre middle-grade dystopian SF. The opening is a strength - a thirteen-year-old caring for his sick younger brother in a controlled city, hiding that they live alone, one concrete situation and something immediately at stake - and there is an idea I can name: a computer game nobody can finish is a covert selection test. But I would put ideas in risks, which is the exit condition. The reported problem is that the book is only a beginning: it sets the stage, introduces the mystery and stops on a cliffhanger, with reviewers noting relatively little worldbuilding, so the premise is announced rather than worked out anywhere inside these covers. That is the difference between a book with a premise and a book with a hook, and this reader's high scores go to premises whose second-order consequences get explored. Two graded costs on top: register and audience are pitched at eight-to-twelve with cartoon illustrations, which is the axis that cost Ranger's Apprentice a little at 74 and Narnia more at 67, and a child lead is a further small pushback. The brothers' relationship is singled out as the best thing in it, and companionship is the axis this reader rewards, which is why the number sits at the top of the band rather than lower.
