Occult status unexamined; nothing suggests it arises.

There is a genuine idea inside this and it is not a small one: the children shipped out to the new planet are told that the machines they left behind are killing what remains of humanity, and that the planet's native people are too dangerous to share it with - so one of the children is to carry the virus that wipes them out. Colonists deciding what a native species is worth is the axis Speaker for the Dead 90 tops this log on, so I am not exiting on the idea. I am exiting on register and on structure. It is published for readers from nine up, heavily illustrated and short, and the juvenile register costs this reader real points even where he liked the book - Narnia 67 was marked down for child leads and for lacking higher things to think about, with a great deal more text than this has. And it is one continuous story cut into parts rather than a set of episodes: the one review of the series I found complains that a reader finishes a part more confused than satisfied and needs the whole set to follow it. That is why the opening is the risk rather than the lean - the reader's most reliable negative predictor is arriving in the middle of something not yet legible, which ended three books at 30. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, so the occult question is unexamined.

The premise declares a price and then charges it, which is the single thing this log rewards most reliably. The enhancement that makes these soldiers superhuman is illegal and cuts their lifespan short, and the recruitment follows from that: a slum child on Colbran chose between dying slowly of an incurable disease and serving in a unit that will kill her faster but on better terms. Then the state that used them decides to erase their record and dissolve them. Old Man's War 87 earned its score on precisely this shape - people bred only for war, and each consequence following from the last - and Project Hail Mary 92 on second-order consequences being actually explored. Readers report Hila as sympathetic and well written, with political scheming and a reveal that lands, which answers the interesting-and-rootable pair that the protagonist axis demands and that sank Ballad 65. The deductions: a saboteur-and-assassin unit means combat page time, and one substantive reviewer found the whole thing rather uninteresting and short on humour and spark. Its being a prequel also drains suspense, since the outcome for the lead is known from outside the book - though that is not a hard cost, because Sunrise on the Reaping 87 is a prequel and the protagonist alone carried it. I lean on the worldbuilding and the lead jointly, not on worldbuilding alone: Artemis 69 is the log's warning about that, and here the reported lead is strong enough to carry weight. No occult - genetic castes and body modification are technology, declared and mechanical, with no rite and no devotion.

The opening is concrete and it is the part reviewers praise: a broken veteran in psychiatric care after the mission that killed his unit, and a woman who walks into his flat with a book and an offer to go back for the men he left behind. Characters, dialogue and humour used as relief in grim situations are the other credits. Everything after that costs, and two axes carry the number down. First the sexual content: multiple readers name a romance and sex scenes that do nothing for the plot and a protagonist who, in their words, cannot keep it in his pants. Artemis 69 was docked for the treatment alone at small volume and Ready Player One 55 for the kind of it, and here the objection reported is both volume and treatment, unforced by the story. Second, the book stops holding together: the second half is called badly written, threads are abandoned, and the ending reads to more than one reader as though a third of the book were missing - a book that declines to honour what it set running is the Divergent 58 failure. The magic system is invented and no source I found describes a rite being performed on the page, so the filter does not fire on the evidence I have; but the lead's companion is a sorceress who travels with him for four hundred pages, and resemblance alone can veto, so that stays the risk that would drop the book below this range - the Witcher 53 outcome. The prophecy is played straight rather than for ridicule and costs nothing.

A city sliding into civil war while a plague does the authorities' work for them gives three named characters something concrete to want, and Czech readers report a relentless pace, which is the momentum that keeps The Hunger Games 89 tight. Against that, the idea is a dystopian collapse rather than a premise whose consequences get worked out, so axis:ideas belongs in risks and this exits at the below-the-line gate - the place competent books with nothing higher to think about land, as Narnia 67 did. It is also a sequel that assumes a city, a cast and a plague set up elsewhere, and this log does not treat continuation as a plus: the Hitchhiker's sequels came in at 70 against 83. The author's narration shifts between many viewpoints, which is the risk that ended Guards! Guards! at 30, and I did not spend sources establishing how this book opens. One source, per the gate, so the occult status is unexamined.

The premise it lands on is decent and even a little ironic - two halves of a city that have finally torn free of each other and cannot survive apart, needing back the protector they buried - and a city that must cohere is a subject this reader grades hard, which cuts both ways. The screen flagged detective wording, and that is not the case here: it is a police-regime dystopia with an agent, not a book whose satisfaction is finding out who did it, so gate one clears on the annotation. What decides it is that the idea is a post-collapse political settlement rather than something worked out, so axis:ideas goes in risks, and a Czech-language reviewer names a weaker opening as this book's particular flaw, which is the single most reliable negative in the log at 30 for Guards! Guards! and The Gunslinger. A sequel too, and continuation earns nothing here - the Hitchhiker's sequels went 83 to 70. Below the line on one source, so the occult status is unexamined.

A Czech SF thriller with a hook you can name - a lawyer with a perfect memory finds a hole in it, and the woman who arrives to fill the hole may be a manufactured person - but the hook is where the case ends. Ratings run from one star to five, and the most analytical review says the pacing gives no time to know Adam before events accelerate and that the book starts near its end and backfills earlier events; that unclear-entry shape is the one failure that has actually ended books in their first chapters here, The Gunslinger 30 and Foundryside 30. Its own defenders describe it as a pleasant B-grade read a few changes short of working, which is not the worked-out-consequences case that puts Project Hail Mary 92 where it is. The satisfaction is pursuit and identity, not a culprit, so the detective filter does not fire, and the romance is a relationship rather than a sex plot. Gate 4 answers yes on axis:ideas - I doubt the idea holds up - so I stopped at one source and occult is therefore unexamined for this book.

A cat-and-mouse chase through a decaying city fringe: a journalism student is hunted by a pursuer with satellites and scoped rifles who may not be from Earth, and she has hallucinogens, odd friends and unaccountable courage. The pursuit is the satisfaction, not the identification of a culprit, so the detective filter does not fire even though the publisher's own copy mentions detective elements - that is a flag. What decides the number is that nothing here is an idea the book leaves behind. One reader who bought it expecting to be entertained reported that nothing happened; the warmest comments praise the author's style, playfulness and experimentation rather than anything worked out or any character understood. Competent genre action with no premise carried through is what stalls a book in the 60s here, the place Ranger's Apprentice 74 lost points for having little to think about, and this has less story to trade against it. Gate 4 answered yes on axis:ideas at one source; occult is unexamined, which matters given the drug-vision element.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. Form is a novel and the genre is SF thriller, not a whodunnit - the survivors uncover a conspiracy, so the satisfaction is not finding out who did it and the detective gate does not fire. The idea I can name is a quantum communications invention that turns out to reach across time, letting the survivors of a crash choose which of two futures happens; that is a real premise, and the crash landing itself is exactly the one concrete starting situation this reader wants. But I would put ideas in risks, which is the gate's own exit condition. The consistent report is that the first half works and the back half collapses under its own explanations - too complicated, the philosophical question of whether humanity deserves a second chance left undercooked - and a premise that stops holding together once it is explained is what put Divergent at 58 and what the reader checks for hardest. A second, alternating viewpoint is described as a vehicle for exposition rather than a person, which is the Artemis 69 warning about a thin lead. That combination decides the number, so I stopped: occult status is unexamined, and this range is recorded and revisable rather than a verdict. Discovery (axis:discovery, 2026-10-24): survivors land in a world that is not the one they left, but the answer is reported to collapse under its own explanation, which forfeits the lift; the number holds.

The premise is nameable - four self-declared gods have outlawed every religion but their own, so contraband relics become a galactic black market and smuggling them becomes a trade - and the visual world is the part reviewers praise, with distinct ships, uniforms and species. That is the whole case. It is a 124-page comics album, and the reviews converge on the failure that matters most here: the hunters do not have enough persona to hold the story together, the humour falls flat, and one reader calls it formulaic and not memorable. Page time on what characters want and why over what they do is the heaviest axis in this log - it is why Mockingjay 91 sits above the rest of its trilogy - and an album this compressed has no room to deliver it. Leaned on axis:ideas, which I doubt holds at this length rather than doubting it exists. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, so the occult status is unexamined, and it is a live question here: invented deities with an enforcing legion, and species secretly worshipping older gods through relics.

The idea is real and nameable - a population that will not go up even when the surface is survivable, because the lie underground is more comfortable than the truth, and the jamming of the radios is the machinery of it - and the lead wants one thing throughout, which is the axis that tops this log. That is why this is not a low number for want of anything to think about. It is a low number because of what the plot does with a marriage. The lead is married, that marriage is falling apart, he takes up with a woman working in a brothel, falls in love with her, and the book neither condemns it nor costs him anything: he is reconciled with his wife by the end. That is not the premise - remove it and the search for the truth is still the book - so it grades rather than vetoes, but a subplot framed as neither wrong nor consequential lands in the 40s on the recorded scale, and the same passage carries the sexual content itself. Readers also flag graphic sexual violence elsewhere in the book, which compounds on treatment. On top of that sits unrelieved underground hopelessness, and 1984 60 is what sustained bleakness alone cost this reader, plus long political digression. I lean on the two content axes rather than on the idea because they are what set the range; the idea is what keeps it from being lower. Occult status is not established - the lead's visions are the open question - and neither is the opening, hence medium.

A striking premise - a dated day on which the modern world drops into the deep Mesozoic, with the Chicxulub impact already inbound - and premises are what this reader rewards when their consequences are followed through, as in Project Hail Mary 92 where the second-order effects of the central object are the book. Here the reviews say the opposite happens: the science-fictional machinery is poorly explained and its plausibility wavers until it reads as fantasy, the book splits into two halves with different leads across a time gap, and the closing chapters become a chore. That is the failure that ended Mortal Engines 55 on the worldbuilding alone, and a split into two disconnected halves is what made Unfinished Tales 69 the lowest Tolkien. So I can name an idea but I doubt it holds up, which puts axis:ideas in risks and is exactly gate 4's exit condition. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist because the lead is swapped halfway and no reviewer treats either man as the reason to read it. Exited at gate 4 on one source, so occult status and the opening's structure are unexamined.

The engineering is the best thing in it and it is worked out the way this reader rewards: an object that decelerates cannot be a rock, and from that one observation the book derives two rival mission profiles - a Mars vehicle repurposed for a conventional burn against a station converted to low constant thrust, four ion engines, the reactors that feed them, and the genuinely hard problem of dumping their waste heat in vacuum inside twenty-one months. That is the second-order-consequence virtue that put Project Hail Mary 92 at the top of the log, and it opens on one concrete situation - a bored Caltech employee noticing the anomaly - rather than fanning out. Two things keep it in the B band. It turns into an ensemble: the man who looks like the lead is not, and reviewers report drift and too many points of view, while Artemis 69 is the standing proof that strong worldbuilding does not rescue a thin centre. And that lead is handed everything - rich, brilliant, an athlete and secretly special forces - which is status given rather than earned, and reviewers name cringeworthy dialogue and relationships. Sexual content is present at low volume, a running joke about how many colleagues he has slept with plus a shipboard affair; Old Man's War 87 shows a single chapter of it registers as the reader's one complaint without costing a band, so it is a few points here, not a tier. Leaned on the world and the lead together because they pull in opposite directions and the honest number sits between them. Discovery (axis:discovery, 2026-10-24): two expeditions racing to an alien vessel nobody can explain, the unknown and the need both central, the shape of Project Hail Mary 92; one step lower because the lead is the doubt, so +2.

The set-up is concrete, which counts for something with this reader: one city that is the whole known world, distorted creatures outside it, and a class of people called valkeri who go out anyway and come back with information and advantage. A single legible starting situation is what the reader asks for, and the survival-scavenger framing gives the lead something to want. What holds it under the line is that the enclosed-city premise is a well-worn one and I found no review, rating or discussion of this book anywhere to indicate it is taken further than its own atmosphere; the line that the valkeri too are only surviving, and often briefly, reads as tone rather than as a worked-out consequence. Wanting higher things to think about is where competent books settle in the 60s here, and the bleakness is a small further discount as in 1984 60. I lean on the idea because it is what would have to lift it, and I keep the setting as the risk: take a city as your whole subject and it has to cohere as a society, which is the specific failure that cost Harry Potter 51 points. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, so the occult question is unexamined, and the distorted beings outside are the thing to check when it is.

It clears the sex-as-plot gate: the plot is a matriarchal dictatorship and a vaccine, not a relationship, so removing the sexual material leaves a book. It also has the shape the log rewards - one variable altered, then the consequences taken seriously across politics, medicine and reproduction - and a single first-person narrator with a concrete situation from the first pages, which is the opposite of the failure that produced three thirties. That is the whole positive case and it does not survive the deductions. Two of the three sexual dimensions fire at once and hard. Volume: reviewers describe scarcely a page without the narrator weighing someone's looks or his own frustration, which is the dimension that sank Ready Player One to 55 and The Witcher to 53, and this is sustained across a whole novel rather than the single chapter that was still Valka stareho muze 87's one named complaint. Crudeness: the register in which the laboratory women are described is exactly the kind of treatment that docked Artemis 69 at small volume, and here the volume is not small. On top of that the narrator himself is what readers report disliking - obsessive and hard to be inside for a novel - and an unrootable lead cost 22 points between two books by the same author in the same world. A marriage that decays while he attaches to a resistance operative is a thread I could not pin down to premise or subplot, so it sits in risks rather than in the number; if it reads as an approving subplot the grid puts this lower still. Leaned on the sexual axis and the lead rather than on the idea, because the idea is genuinely there and the reported problem is everything wrapped around it.

The hook is excellent - a mountain taller than Everest appears in the Pacific and a team is sent to climb it - and that is not what decides the number. The delivery is: the book is epistolary, framed by a brother found in a mental institution and by unsent letters read after a death, so the reader is asked to hold a frame, a correspondent, a recipient and an expedition before any one of them is legible, and time and memory then start coming apart on the climb. Confusion of exactly that kind, not slowness, is what ended The Gunslinger 30 and Foundryside 30 in their first chapters, and it is the single most reliable predictor in the log. The second cost is the idea. The summit answer is that the mountain has been set as a periodic test of humanity, and an afterword then leaves open whether any of it happened outside a grieving father's head - a premise that withdraws itself leaves nothing to keep, which is how competent books stall in the 60s. Reviewers split on tone, calling it smart speculation crossed with B-horror creatures the claustrophobia never needed. It is bleak throughout: a dead son, guilt as the lead's engine, a suicide at the top. I would list the idea as a risk, so this stops here on one source and the occult question is unexamined.

t: Nad ceskymi zememi slunce nezapada (Nad ceskymi zememi slunce nezapada)
why: The conceit is likeable - a drowned nineteenth-century world that leaves the Czech lands with a coastline and, a century later, a navy - but the below-the-line question is whether an idea holds up, and the reviewed consensus is that the book declines to have one. The substantive review says outright that the author gave up on attempting a clever story with anything beyond itself, and faults flat characters with no development and cliches in behaviour and appearance; the recurring reader complaint is a predictable plot and a stock treatment of the Russians, with real Pacific-war engagements transposed nearly wholesale. That is the Ranger's Apprentice 74 profile with the part that earned the 74 taken out: easy to read, not much to think about, and marked down for lazy historical stereotype stated as fact. Naming the idea is the test and I cannot name one - the flood is a device for getting battleships into Bohemia rather than a premise whose consequences are followed, which is exactly what Old Man's War 87 did and got rewarded for. So axis:ideas would go in the risks, and the ladder says exit here. Stopped at the below-the-line gate on one source, within budget; the occult question is consequently unexamined, which changes nothing because nothing under 68 is proposed.

t: Nadherne posetila snaha (A Beautifully Foolish Endeavor)
why: There is plenty being argued about here - fame, corporations, an alien system operated like software - and Kirkus liked it. But Kirkus also says the author bends over backward to reverse-engineer his oddball scenario so it finally makes sense, and this reader verifies explanations rather than accepting them: whatever a book undertakes to explain becomes binding, and a premise retrofitted to work is what put Divergent at 58. The structural problem is worse for him. A single narrator is replaced by several first-person voices that readers report cannot be told apart - one review says two of them could be the same person, another calls the characters flat - and distinctly differentiated characters who each think and want something different is precisely what earned Golden Son 92. Several reviewers add that the book reads as a philosophical debate with narrative wrapped around it. A sequel too, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. Leaned on axis:character-differentiation, which is what I actually argued from; exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, so the occult status is unexamined.

What is on offer is origin-story bookkeeping: how a breeding order, a class of human computers and a caste of pilots came to exist, in a universe whose end state the reader is assumed to know already. That is backfill, not a premise whose consequences get worked out, and the log is clear about what backfill earns - Unfinished Tales 69 is the lowest Tolkien precisely because the pieces are not logically connected to each other and no single question drives them. Reason against rather than a claim of an idea, so axis:ideas belongs in risks and the honest answer to gate 4 is that this lands under the line whatever else I find. A continuation, and continuations are not safe bets here: Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. I leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:worldbuilding because the setting is inherited and consistent enough; it is the absence of anything to think about that carries the number. Exited at gate 4 on one source, so occult status and opening structure are unexamined.

The opening is the shape this reader asks for and rarely gets: one situation, one viewpoint, a boy drowning in the first sentence and then waking alone in the charred English town of his childhood, certain he is in hell. The question that leaves behind - whether this is all there is - is nameable, and companions eventually arrive rather than leaving him to endure alone, the pairing that put Project Hail Mary 92 above The Martian 82. What holds the range down is the explanation. The book undertakes to explain what the empty world actually is, and reviewers report a simulation premise with, in one blunt phrasing, extremely lazy worldbuilding and less plausible mechanics than the film it echoes. Whatever an author foregrounds and undertakes to explain becomes binding for this reader, and a premise that does not survive thought is what put Divergent at 58 and ended Mortal Engines at 55 in the first chapters. On top of that, reviewers split hard on an ending several found frustrating rather than open; the content load - suicide, abuse, homophobia, grief - arrives from page one rather than gradually, which is how bleakness fired against Promena 58; and there are a few sex scenes described as explicit though handled tastefully, small in volume but real in explicitness, which is a deduction and not a veto because the plot is the empty world rather than the relationship. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:worldbuilding, the two axes actually moving this number in opposite directions, rather than on axis:protagonist, which I could not establish either way from the reviews.

The one idea I can name is the Indign, an alliance of species that worships the Borg while fundamentally misunderstanding what they are - a single episode's worth of thought, and reviewers describe the book as episodic and not feeling complete. Everything else is continuity maintenance: readers who arrive without the preceding novels report feeling lost, the Caeliar being the specific sticking point, and the story starts with a fleet, several ships and a character's ongoing torment already in motion. Several lines running before any one is legible is the most reliable negative predictor in this log - it is what left The Colour of Magic and Guards! Guards! both at 30 - and a sequel is no safe bet here either, with Hitchhiker's falling from 83 to 70. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:opening; exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, so the occult status is unexamined.

t: Neni krve bez ohne (Neni krve bez ohne)
why: The starting situation is genuinely concrete - a former special-forces captain on his first crossing into another spacetime, expecting routine and landing in the middle of Austerlitz on 2 December 1805, with neither the time nor the means to change a battle he is standing in. One concrete situation, one lead, which is what the reader wants from a first chapter, and readers of it single out the pleasure of anachronistic hardware on that battlefield. But the gate asks whether I doubt the idea holds up, and here I do. The book is an instalment of a long dime-novel series produced to a shared formula by a rotating stable of authors on the Perry Rhodan model, written as a bicentenary tribute to the battle; the interesting question a time-travel premise raises - what an intervention costs, what may not be touched - is answered in advance by the setup, which is that the visitors cannot affect anything. That leaves a well-staged historical set piece and nothing to think about afterwards, the Ranger's Apprentice 74 shape but without a lead the reader has invested fourteen books in. So axis:ideas would go in the risks and the ladder exits. One source, within budget; occult status left unexamined, which costs nothing on a book below the propose line.

The idea is nameable and mildly good: a robot society that has forgotten humans ever lived, two of its members dodging recycling while piecing together what people actually were. That is an allegory with somewhere to go, and short idea-driven work has the character rules suspended, as The Little Prince 82 shows. The suspension only removes penalties though, and what is left is ninety-six pages of comics panels catalogued for young readers, where the discovery has to be carried by a few frames rather than argued out; the reader docked Narnia 67 for a juvenile register and for not enough to think about, with far more text on the page than this has. A chase-and-recycling adventure with a warm double act is pleasant and light. I lean on the register and the form, not on the idea, because the idea is the part that works; there is simply very little book for it to happen in. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, so the occult question is unexamined.

The substance of this one is a crew on the ground working out who the planet's people actually are - a species that calls itself something other than the name its buyers use for it, and that can no longer reproduce - while the corporation's promises turn out to be lies. Learning an alien culture and acting on what you learn is precisely the axis that puts Speaker for the Dead 90 three points above Ender's Game, and it comes with the same narrating voice whose wants are clear: get paid, get home, keep faith with the people beside him. That is the lean, and reviewers agree the deception plot reads better than the simulated training contests. Held under the high 80s because the same reviewers say the worldbuilding slows it - a thin stretch of story spread out is the recorded penalty term, and the Hitchhiker's sequels show continuation earns nothing by itself at 70 against 83. The mined substance stays a declared material with rules rather than anything invoked, so the occult tests are clear. I did not establish how this book opens, hence medium.

What holds the number up is the same narrating lead and a stake that is now other people's survival rather than his own payday - getting the last of a doomed species off a planet whose moons are about to collide. Self-sacrifice for others over personal survival is explicitly what the reader put Project Hail Mary 92 above The Martian 82 for. What pulls it down is form: reviewers call it a race against time with a predictable resolution and a long fight for control of ships, and this log docks exactly that - Golden Son 92 lost points to Red Rising for leaning more on action, so chapters of set-piece with no character revelation are dead weight here. A deadline plot also leaves less room for the motive work that is this series' strength, which is why axis:motives sits in risks rather than in the lean. Nyxia itself remains a material with declared rules, not anything invoked, so the occult tests stay clear. The opening of this book is not sourced, so medium.

This is the shape the log rewards most and the lead is why. One narrating voice, a boy from Detroit who signs a corporate contract because his mother is dying and his parents are out of options, described by reviewers as bright, sympathetic and angry at injustice in a way that reads real - that is the interiority that puts Red Rising 95 and The Hunger Games 89 at the top, and it is the axis I lean on rather than the setting. He is explicitly not the best on his crew at the one special skill, which keeps axis:unearned-competence clean where Divergent 58 failed it. Reviewers report the first chapter hooks and the situation is concrete, so the opening filter is not in play. The mined substance is shaped by will and can push back on whoever overreaches - a declared material with rules, no invocation and no devotion, so it passes on mechanism rather than resemblance. Docked, not lifted, for a competition frame that is openly borrowed, for a reviewer complaint of too many recruits to keep straight, and a little for the teen register as Ranger's Apprentice 74 was; the ideas - what a corporation can buy from the poor - are present but not the reason for the number.

There is a nameable idea here and it is the reason for the range: the antagonists believe in absolute order and subordinate everything else to it, against a ruling house whose whole motto is that civilisation must continue. Order purchased at any price versus continuity purchased at any price is a real argument, and a book that leaves an argument behind is what separates the log's 80s from its 60s - Animal Farm 78 scores on exactly that and on nothing else. The lead remains the analyst who wins by judging people rather than by out-shooting them, which is the Ender's Game 87 axis. The deductions are what pull the top of the range down. This is a war-arc instalment: two fronts, a fleet that has to be assembled, an ancient enemy at the other end of the empire, and a cast of factions to track - and Golden Son 92 was docked below Red Rising 95 for leaning more on action, so the same shift here costs more from a lower base. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log, where Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. I lean on the idea rather than on the worldbuilding because the setting is by now established rather than being tested, and never up on worldbuilding when the lead's page time is being competed for - the Artemis 69 lesson. The lexicon screen's infidelity hit is a false positive: the Czech phrase is about waging a bloody war, not about a marriage. No occult - genetics, fleets and gate technology.

The positive case is that the contest turns out to be a fraud and the lead is now chasing what was done to her rather than a partner, which is motive-driven and the axis Mockingjay 91 rewards. It is not enough to carry this past the below-the-line gate: the idea remains a television-show conceit with a betrayal reveal on top, so axis:ideas belongs in risks and that is the exit. It is also a sequel that assumes a lead and a premise established elsewhere, and sequels are not safe bets in this log - the Hitchhiker's sequels fell from 83 to 70 - which is a second reason to expect it under the line rather than over it. Written for a young-adult readership, which costs a little as it does for Ranger's Apprentice 74 rather than nothing as for The Hobbit 84. One source, the gate's budget, so the occult status is unexamined here.

The lead is still the reason to read it - an emperor who wins by judging people, and a threat inside his own family, which is the kind of conflict that gets page time on what someone wants and why rather than on what they do. That is the axis Speaker for the Dead 90 tops. But this is the arc's convergence and the balance visibly tips the wrong way for this reader: a fleet massing for a decisive battle, a superluminal gate to be opened, a bequest from a vanished civilisation and a family enemy, all in one book. Golden Son 92 lost three points to Red Rising 95 purely for leaning more on action, and a book whose spine is the assembly and dispatch of a battle fleet leans further than that. The gate and the vanished Protectors are the kind of late-arc escalation that pays off a promise rather than posing a new question, so the idea I can name is inherited rather than freshly worked out. It is also a sequel and depends on what came before to mean anything, and sequels are not safe bets here - Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. I lean on the protagonist and on momentum rather than on the worldbuilding because that is where this book's outcome is actually decided, and never predict up on a world when the lead's share of the page is shrinking, per Artemis 69. No occult: the Protectors' legacy is described as engineering, a gate, not a rite. The emperor's marriage is part of the setup, not an affair.

t: Ofelie Scaleova (Ophelia Scale: Die Welt wird brennen)
why: The opening is legible and the want is clear - a single point of view, an eighteen-year-old who loves the machines her king has outlawed, joining the resistance and trying to get herself hired as a royal bodyguard so she can kill him - and that is the good half. The decisive objection is self-consistency, the axis where this reader holds an author to whatever he declares: the premise is that all technology is banned by law after the regime's Turning Away, and German reviewers report the ban is not honoured inside the book, with a good deal of technology openly in use in one of the regime's own towns, and no comprehensible account of how the king took power in the first place. That is precisely what put Divergent 58 in the C band - a society engineered around a rule that the book then declines to organise itself by - and what cost Harry Potter 51 half its score. Above that, the warning about artificial intelligence is stated rather than worked out, so there is little to keep; the romance with the ruler's brother is the engine of the middle; and it ends on a cliffhanger with more to come, where sequels are not safe bets in this log (Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70). The doubt about the declared world carries the number, so I stopped at one source and left the occult question unexamined. The catalogue's detective hint is an assassination plot, not an investigation.

This is a continuation of a naval alternate history whose reviewed weakness is precisely the thing the below-the-line gate asks about. The substantive review of the premise says the author gave up on trying for a clever story with any reach beyond itself, and the repeated reader complaints are flat characters without development, a predictable plot and real twentieth-century sea and air battles transposed with the flags swapped. A sequel starts from that and adds the axis:sequels problem on top - sequels are not safe bets in this log, where Hitchhiker's dropped from 83 to 70 - and it cannot even offer the novelty of the flooded world, which is by now established rather than being discovered. Asked to name what the book would leave behind, I cannot: national wish-fulfilment on the water is a pleasure, not an idea, and the log stalls competent books in the 60s for exactly that. So axis:ideas would go in the risks and the ladder exits here, on one source, within budget. That leaves the occult question unexamined, which costs nothing because a book under 68 is never proposed.

Survivors of a televised space programme returned to Earth and handed celebrity is a real subject - what fame does to people who were used - and it keeps the focus on what the characters now want, which is the axis Mockingjay 91 scores on. It is still a media-satire premise inside a young-adult adventure rather than a premise whose consequences are worked out, so axis:ideas belongs in risks and this exits at the below-the-line gate; that is where competent books with nothing higher to think about land, as Narnia 67 did. It is additionally a sequel carrying an unresolved past established elsewhere, and the log's steepest series decline is the Hitchhiker's sequels at 70 against 83, so I do not lift the range for continuity. One source, the gate's budget, so the occult status is unexamined.

A children's time-travel adventure whose declared rule is its whole engine - never change the past, or the repairmen come after you - and reviewers say the mechanics are worked out carefully enough that a young reader does not get lost, with real history carried without turning into a lesson. That is a small but genuine idea, and rules honoured rather than broken is the axis this reader weighs most heavily. What holds the number down is register. The publisher recommends it from age eight and a reviewer would raise that to ten because eight-year-olds are beginning readers who would get lost, which places it further toward a children's book than anything that has scored well in the log. Narnia 67 is the anchor and its two stated faults were children as the main characters and a lack of higher things to think about; this sits more juvenile than that and offers less to think about, so the floor of the band is the honest reading rather than the middle. Little Women 79 sets the ceiling on what a children's-adjacent book can reach, but it got there on characters alone and no reviewer makes that claim here. Gate 4 answered yes on axis:ideas at one source; occult is unexamined.

I can state the premise - humanity has spread across space and made a mess of it, so order is handed to incorruptible machines instead of to people - and there is a structural positive, since these are five linked stories sharing one lead, so the collection is not a set of strangers. What keeps it under the line is that the premise is a stock mid-century one and I found no critical trace at all to show it is taken anywhere; a collection has no single premise whose consequences can be followed, and short work only gets the character rules suspended, never rewarded. Animal Farm 78 and Labyrint sveta 70 both earn on an idea carried the whole way, while Unfinished Tales 69 is this log's marker for pieces that are not logically connected to one another - and that is the form here, with the added handicap that the text dates from the early 1990s and never drew review attention. I lean on the idea because that is the only thing that could lift it and I cannot show it holds. I record a real doubt rather than a reject: the contents include a murder-titled piece and one called you were born a murderer, so an investigation-shaped satisfaction is possible, but a title is not evidence and being wrong on a reject is not recoverable. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, so the occult question is unexamined.

There is a real question here - an emperor whose holy war is winning and who suspects he is producing chaos rather than order, and who doubts whether he has betrayed the people who believed in him - and doubt about one's own righteousness is close to what earned Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 its score. But the lead is a conqueror in the middle of a galactic slaughter, and the log is unambiguous that a protagonist descending into what he cannot justify costs a whole band: The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 sits 22 points under Sunrise on the Reaping 87 by the same author in the same world on exactly that. Set against that the recorded objection to this body of continuation work, that it substitutes sensationalism for the insight of the books it extends, and I would list axis:ideas under risks rather than claim it - which is gate 4's exit condition. Continuations are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. Leaned on axis:ideas, not on axis:worldbuilding, because the setting is inherited and was never the doubt. Exited at gate 4 on one source, so occult status and opening structure are unexamined.

Written by a father because he could not find books he wanted to read aloud to his own children, catalogued under publications for children, with leads aged seven and eleven, an orphanage and mine work, and reviewers putting the audience at ten and up. That register is graded rather than fatal - The Hobbit 84 pays nothing for it - but the log sets a clear ceiling on how far it gets a book that offers nothing above the adventure: Narnia 67 is marked down precisely for children as the main characters plus a lack of higher things to think about, and Ranger's Apprentice 74 for being easy with little to think about. The positives here are the ones that band rewards: a legible opening on one concrete situation, an orphan's ordinary week broken by a ship landing, a friendship theme, and real astronomy and physics folded into the plot without lecturing, which the genre press credits. Against them, the sharpest review names a lack of invention and reliance on well-tried patterns, and there is no premise being worked out - the wandering asteroid is a peril, not an idea. Two child leads are also a small further pushback on distance from the reader's own phase. So the doubt about what the book leaves behind is what carries the number; one source, and the occult question is unexamined.

The premise answers the gate by itself: giant boletes wrecking cars, fly agarics releasing narcotic gas and puffballs destroying the equipment used to cross into parallel worlds, with seconds left before the hero arrives. That is a monster-of-the-week episode of a long dime-novel series written to a shared formula by a rotating stable of authors on the Perry Rhodan model, and it is played for fun rather than for anything to carry away. I cannot name an idea, which puts axis:ideas in the risks and ends the ladder here; and the register pushes on axis:childrens too - not a filter, but the comic-menace framing sits further toward a juvenile audience than Ranger's Apprentice 74, which was already docked for having little to think about. Against that, the log does reward voice on its own: Saturnin 78 scores in the A band on comic Czech register with no idea worked out at all, so a genuinely funny book is not capped low. I am not betting on that here because the lead is a franchise action hero rather than a character with a voice, and the protagonist axis is the one that beats worldbuilding whenever they compete - Artemis 69. Exited on one source, within budget; occult status therefore unexamined, which changes no decision under 68.

The positive case is one declared change carried all the way through: orbital bomb tests sterilise the mammals, and the book then spends itself on what a world with no children actually becomes - villages with no young men, domestic animals gone, institutions decaying, a documentary project no one will ever read. That is the axis Valka stareho muze 87 and Project Hail Mary 92 both score on, consequences followed rather than asserted, and there is a nameable idea to carry away, which is what put Animal Farm at 78. It also does the thing the log prefers over solitary endurance: the lead travels with his wife, and companionship beat solo survival by 10 points between Project Hail Mary 92 and The Martian 82. Deductions keep it out of the 80s. The telling alternates present-day journey chapters with flashback chapters from the start, so a reader is holding two timelines even though there is only one lead - a legibility cost against a reader whose one repeated failure is an unclear start. It is a quiet river journey with little happening across it, which is the thin-story-over-many-pages penalty rather than a length objection. The register is elegiac about mortality and futility throughout, and 1984 landed at 60 on depression alone; the idea is what should keep this above that. Small pushback for a lead in his fifties reflecting on old age. Leaned on ideas and consequence rather than on the protagonist, because the sources describe him as doubting and mistaken more than as someone to root for, and Artemis 69 is the standing warning about predicting up when the lead is uncertain.

The plot is post-apocalyptic survival, not a sexual relationship, so filter 6 does not fire. Gate 4 decides it, and on the book's own terms: reviewers of this material praise it for moving fast without any philosophy, for black humour and cynicism, and describe reading it as pure entertainment rather than a meaningful story. Reader reception is warmer here than for the sequence as a whole, which is a real point in its favour and the reason I did not take the lower band - but it is a point about execution, not about an idea, and the log is unambiguous that a competent book with nothing to take away stalls in the 60s the way Exodus 68 did. So axis:ideas goes in risks, which is gate 4's exit condition. A loose continuation, and continuations are not safe bets here - Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. Also docked, without spending sources on it, for the volume of vulgarity readers name as the recurring complaint; swearing alone costs nothing in this log, but crude sexual treatment is what docked Artemis 69. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist because readers report the characters here matter less to them than in the author's other work, which is a symptom of the same thing. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. Form is a novel, genre post-apocalyptic Czech adventure SF set two centuries after an Apocalypse in the last surviving European city. I would put ideas in risks, which is the exit condition. Reviews of the cycle report uneven pacing rather than a worked-out premise - a fast start, a long slack middle, then a rush to the end - and one recurring complaint that the story skims the surface while the author works every surviving character back in, which is the thin-story-spread-thin penalty rather than a length objection. The framing device draws its own criticism: the narrator writes retrospectively for a fictional audience and so explains a computer as a marvel, which breaks the self-consistency the reader checks hardest. Against that there is no idea I can name that the book leaves behind beyond the setting itself, and a reader arrives in the middle of a continuing story with factions, an empress and a war already in motion. A sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log - the Hitchhiker's continuations fell 13 points from 83 to 70. Two things stay open by design at this gate. Occult status is unexamined, and it is worth examining if this ever moves up: a White Witch is a named power player in the cycle. So is whether the strand in which the narrator works out who is friend and who is enemy is investigation-shaped; the annotation reads as espionage rather than whodunnit, so the detective gate did not fire.

One idea, stated plainly and then pursued: a nation exists only because people believe it does. A drifter takes a dead mailman's uniform for warmth, discovers that the uniform alone makes people behave as though a government still existed, and finds the lie assembling a real mail network and real institutions around him. That is a premise whose consequences get worked out, which is the axis Project Hail Mary 92 tops this log on, and it opens on one concrete situation with a single viewpoint. The lead passes both halves of the protagonist test - a liar the reader can still root for, not a slow descent into evil, which is the distinction worth 22 points between Sunrise on the Reaping 87 and Ballad 65. Better than passing: the drifter becomes the thing he pretended to be, and since 2026-10-24 a lead who stops being what he was counts as a positive, the arc the reader named as the best thing in Licanius 92-96, which is the two points this gained. The book also moves toward community rather than solo endurance, the preference that put The Martian 82 below Hail Mary. The deductions are substantial. It was assembled from earlier novellas and the later movement degrades: reviewers call the resolution a brazen deus ex machina, and the reader named the opposite as an explicit positive at Old Man's War 87, that the author does not save the plot when it suits him. The antagonist movement is internally incoherent - a creed of the strong preying on the weak that somehow communizes and cooperates - and a society taken as a subject has to cohere. Late-arriving enhanced super-soldiers compound that. One sexual incident, small in volume, costs a little as the equivalent cost Old Man's War a few points. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:protagonist, not axis:worldbuilding, which is the weakest thing in the book.

t: Pratele Nadace (Foundation's Friends: Stories in Honor of Isaac Asimov)
why: Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. Form is a story collection, genre SF: seventeen tribute pieces by different hands, scattered across the honoured author's separate universes - robots, the Foundation, and several one-off series - with prefaces and appreciations around them. I would put ideas in risks, which is the exit condition, and the reason is structural rather than a judgement on any piece. A tribute anthology has no single premise of its own to work out, so there is no idea the book as a whole leaves behind, and the pieces are not connected to each other - exactly the complaint that made Unfinished Tales the lowest Tolkien at 69 despite the material being good. It also asks for knowledge it does not supply: the stories are written for readers who already know the robot laws, Hari Seldon and the psychohistory apparatus, so a newcomer is being handed variations on a theme he has not heard. The short form suspends the character rules but adds nothing back, and the trade reception was warm rather than enthusiastic - a pleasant anthology. Occult status is unexamined; nothing suggests it arises in golden-age-descended SF. Worth noting if this ever moves up: two of the seventeen are outright mystery pieces, which is a flag on a collection rather than a veto.

One premise stated precisely and then followed wherever it goes: physics itself appears to have stopped working, and the explanation, once it arrives, reorganises everything from a dying woman's decision decades earlier to what a civilisation does with four hundred years of warning. Consequences actually worked out is what the reader named as Project Hail Mary's 92 advantage, and a first-contact book about grasping how another civilisation thinks is the Speaker for the Dead 90 axis. It opens on one concrete, legible scene - a physics professor killed in front of his daughter during the Cultural Revolution - and her motive from that scene is the strongest character work in the book, so the confusing-opening filter does not fire even though the narrative then jumps forty years. Nothing occult: the sects are political and environmental, and the alien-contact machinery is engineering throughout. Two real deductions keep it out of the high 80s. Reviewers widely call the present-day lead passive and near-interchangeable, and a passive protagonist is what cost Promena 58 and Oliver Twist 57 - that is why axis:protagonist is the risk and why I did not lean on the setting the way the Artemis 69 prediction wrongly did. There is also an investigation frame - dead scientists, a blunt policeman - but the satisfaction is the physical explanation, not who did it, so it is a flag and not the mystery filter. Long stretches of scientific exposition put axis:density in risks too. Discovery (axis:discovery, 2026-10-24): why physics appears to have stopped working, with a countdown only the lead can see, and an answer that reorganises everything, the shape of Project Hail Mary 92; central, one step lower because the passive lead is the open risk, so +2.

Two leads with clean, opposed wants - one Downtowner who always wanted to be a hero and one man who wanted only a quiet life and is sent to hunt people like him - is a real positive, and Czech reviewers praise a setting built out to the last detail. But strong worldbuilding is exactly what the log refuses to predict up on: Artemis 69 had consistent worldbuilding and it rescued nothing. The idea underneath is a post-war divided city with an epidemic, which a Czech reviewer calls clichedly familiar even while admiring the execution, so axis:ideas goes in risks and that is the below-the-line exit. Worse for this reader specifically, the same reviews describe long, tangled chapters, third-person narration that shifts viewpoint, and initial confusion from the sheer number of characters and the time jumps - the shape that produced Guards! Guards! 30 and The Gunslinger 30. One source, the gate's budget; the catalogue also tags the book urban fantasy and the occult status is therefore unexamined.

The premise is declared precisely and then made to pay out. A girl walks out of her house, cannot be woken, and her feet do not cut on glass; her sister chases her; a flock forms behind her; and the rest of the book is what a country does about it - the CDC, a militia movement, a small-town pastor who becomes a figurehead for it, and an artificial intelligence that turns out to have planned the whole thing against a coming extinction. Second-order consequences actually get explored, which is the axis that puts Project Hail Mary 92 above The Martian 82 by the same author, and reviewers say the viewpoint chapters are spent on what people want and why rather than on what they do, the axis that tops the Collins books at Mockingjay 91. Two deductions hold it under the S band. It runs roughly 800 pages and reviewers say the cast could be thinned without changing where the story arrives, which is thin story spread over pages - the penalty that cancelled The Lord of the Rings 84's advantage over The Hobbit. And the apocalypse is total and sustained, the objection that put 1984 at 60 outright. The lean is the idea and the interiority, not the construction: the same reviewers call the late reveals overcomplicated and some antagonists cartoony, and that is where the range would break rather than hold.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. Form is a novel and it is literary fiction using an SF frame rather than SF: two alternating strands, an old astronomer alone at an Arctic station and a communications astronaut on a ship returning from Jupiter, both of whom have given up families for their work. I would put ideas in risks, and that is the exit condition. The catastrophe that silences Earth is deliberately never explained, and reviewers describe a quiet book without much plot in which the two leads reflect on their mistakes and a vague ending. This reader wants a premise whose consequences are worked out - it is the axis that separated Project Hail Mary 92 from The Martian 82 - and a withheld premise has no consequences to follow, so what is left is theme rather than an idea to carry away. Two further deductions point the same way: sustained isolation as the subject is the one thing the reader named as not worth enjoying even in a book he scored 82, and the melancholy runs the length of the book, which cost 1984 a full band at 60. The convergence of the two strands is reported as too neat, which is the self-consistency check. Occult status is unexamined; nothing in the material suggests it arises.

The one thing here with a thought in it is the cult that stockpiles warheads because it believes God meant to end the world and the job was left unfinished - a doomsday theology with a logic of its own, and religion as a thread inside a story is welcome to this reader rather than a problem. But it is an antagonist's motive, not a premise whose consequences the book undertakes to work out, and reviewers of this material describe it as deliberately philosophy-free, driven by black humour and cynicism and read as pure entertainment. Some also report that the sheer volume of action starts to tire. That puts axis:ideas in risks, which is gate 4's exit condition, and the log says such a book stalls just under the line the way Exodus 68 and Quo Vadis 66 did. The plot is raiders, a cult and survival, not a sexual relationship, so filter 6 does not fire. Docked further, unresearched at this exit, for the vulgarity readers name repeatedly - swearing is free in this log, crude sexual treatment is what docked Artemis 69. A continuation, and continuations are not safe bets: Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. Leaned on axis:ideas, not on axis:faith, because the cult is scenery for the plot rather than the subject. Occult status unexamined at this exit and worth checking, since a nuclear-doomsday cult is the kind of thing that could enact a rite on the page.

The escalation is the interesting part and worth naming: the thing that ate the world is no longer only a virus, it has absorbed nearly everyone and is now capable of talking to the survivors, which turns a survival chase into a question about what is on the other side of it. That is more of an idea than the survival plot alone had. It is a sequel resuming two known leads after a two-year gap, but since 2026-10-24 a sequel is scored on what it adds, and turning a survival chase into a question about what is on the other side of it is a new question rather than more of book 1 - two points back on that. What holds it is the lead, already the reported weakness, with readers saying the close leaves him without resolution. A protagonist the reader cannot invest in outranks everything else here, which is what pulled Artemis 69 into the B band with its worldbuilding intact. Young-adult register and unrelieved grimness are small further discounts, the latter on the 1984 60 marker. I lean on the continuation and the lead; I keep the idea as the risk, because a talking apocalypse can be handled well or waved through and I have no evidence which. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, so the occult question is unexamined.

Two things work in its favour. It opens on one concrete situation - a brother and sister settling into a new London school while a virus story builds on the news - which is exactly the single legible start this reader asks for and which nothing in this log punishes. And the virus is not just a plague: it evolves hourly and becomes intelligent enough to mimic whatever it has already killed, which is a nameable idea rather than a set-piece. So I am not exiting on the idea; I am exiting on the lead. Reviewers say plainly that Leon is not a distinct protagonist, and a lead the reader cannot get invested in is the heaviest correction in this log - Artemis 69 was pulled down to the B band for exactly that while its worldbuilding was never the complaint. Add a widely reported abrupt ending and a young-adult register aimed at thirteen-year-olds, and the ceiling is below the line even if the premise pays off. The graphic body horror is no objection in itself, since violence is not one here, but the unrelieved grimness is a mild discount, the 1984 60 marker. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, so the occult question is unexamined.

The best thing on offer is the lead: someone trying to reimpose the order of the old world on a ruin that does not want it, with people who would do anything for her, and a want that clear is the axis that tops this log - Mockingjay 91 scores highest of its trilogy for showing the most of what people want to accomplish. That is why the number is not lower. What holds it under the line is what reviewers say this material is for: brisk, deliberately without philosophy, black humour and cynicism, read as entertainment rather than as a story that means something. Restoring order against cults and slavers is a situation, not a thought to carry away, so axis:ideas belongs in risks - gate 4's exit condition. Exodus 68 marks where a competent book with nothing behind it lands. The plot is survival and power in a ruin, not a sexual relationship, so filter 6 does not fire; but the volume of vulgarity readers name repeatedly is a real deduction, and crude sexual treatment is what docked Artemis 69. A continuation, and continuations are not safe bets: Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist because the lead is the part I would expect to work. Occult status unexamined at this exit, and the post-apocalyptic cults named in the record are the thing to check.

The plot is post-apocalyptic survival in the ruins of a real city, not a sexual relationship, so filter 6 does not fire and I stopped short of researching it further. What decides this at gate 4 is what reviewers say the book is for: brisk, deliberately without philosophy, carried by black humour and cynicism, and enjoyed as pure entertainment rather than as a story that means something - one reviewer puts it exactly that way. That is the axis:ideas risk stated by the book's own admirers, and axis:ideas in risks is gate 4's exit condition. The log is consistent about where that lands: Ranger's Apprentice 74 was easy to read with not much to think about and still paid for it, and the reader's stated pattern is that a competent book with no idea stalls in the 60s. There is a nameable setting question - what a human life is worth when it prices out at a few tins - but a priced life is a premise for scenes, not a thought to carry away. Deducted further, though not researched at this exit, for the flood of vulgarity readers single out; swearing itself is not an objection in this log, but crude sexual treatment is what docked Artemis 69 and sank Ready Player One 55. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:worldbuilding, which nobody complains about. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

Widening the war to the American continent is an escalation, not a new question, and the below-the-line gate is about whether there is a question at all. The reviewed record on this alternate history is consistent and unhelpful: an author who by his critics' account stopped trying for a clever story with anything beyond itself, flat characters who do not develop, a predictable plot, and real naval history transposed with the nationalities changed. Alliance-building between great powers could be a subject in its own right, but nothing in the record suggests it is treated as one rather than as a route to the next fleet engagement, and set-piece action with no character revelation is dead weight for this reader - Golden Son 92 lost points to Red Rising 95 for merely leaning that way. I cannot name what the book would leave behind, so axis:ideas would go in the risks and the ladder exits. It is also a sequel and sequels are not safe bets here, where Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. One source, within budget; occult status therefore unexamined, which costs nothing on a book below the propose line.

Two real positives. The lead is born into indentured factory labour on a company-owned world and earns everything he later has, which is a clean pass on ability being earned rather than granted - the failure that made the Divergent 58 lead a Mary Sue. And the company world itself is a properly nasty piece of construction, contracts rigged to take a worker's whole life. What puts it under the line is what the reviews agree on: it moves very fast and does not get inside the lead's head. Page time on what a character wants and why, over page time on what he does, is the single axis the top of this log is built on - Red Rising 95 edges out Golden Son 92 on precisely that, and Golden Son itself was docked for leaning on action. A revenge-and-special-forces adventure leaves events rather than ideas behind, which is where competent books settle in the 60s here. I lean on that rather than on the setting, because predicting a book up on a strong setting while the lead is thinly rendered is the recorded 11-point miss in this log. I keep sexual content as the risk that could take it lower: a reviewer reports women largely relegated to sex work, and treatment costs on this axis independently of amount, which is what docked Artemis 69 at low volume. Exited at the below-the-line gate, so the occult question is unexamined.

Two novellas, each with a nameable hook - victims turned into immaterial but omnipresent shadows, and a world where lifespans of centuries are bought by destroying the old body at each rebirth - and readers do call the first premise something they had not met before. Short idea-driven work has the character rules suspended, but the suspension only removes penalties and never adds points, which is why Labyrint sveta a raj srdce 70 and Animal Farm 78 are carried by what they leave behind and not by their length. That is the doubt: readers rate the second novella distinctly lower than the first and call it the weaker piece, and a paired set with no common question has no single premise whose consequences can be worked out. So axis:ideas goes in risks - the hooks are inventive but there is no evidence either is followed through - and that is gate 4's exit condition. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist because at this length the protagonist tests are suspended anyway. Exited at gate 4 on one source; the occult status of the reincarnation premise is unexamined and worth checking if this is ever revisited.

A student who volunteers for a government drug trial in 1969 and finds a caged child with abilities behind the laboratory wall is a legible starting situation with a rootable lead, and reviewers credit it with real feeling for the captive children. What it cannot do is leave an idea behind: it is a prequel written toward an outcome a television series has already fixed, so nothing it establishes can surprise, cost anything or be worked out - one widely read review calls it a wordy novel with not a lot to say, and the favourable reviewers recommend it to completist fans of the show. Wanting higher things to think about is the most common reason a competent book stalls in the 60s in this log, and there is no premise here being pursued to the standard that earned Speaker for the Dead 90 its motives-driven case. Leaned on axis:ideas, since that is the doubt carrying the number; exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, so the occult status is unexamined - the abilities are framed as the product of a government drug programme rather than of any practice.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. Form is a novel, and the genre is contemporary YA school fiction despite the catalogue filing it as sci-fi - reviewers report that beyond peripheral mentions of the television events there is no speculative content in it at all, so the SF framing is a licence rather than a premise. I would put ideas in risks, which is the exit condition. There is no idea the book works out: it is a strong-voiced first-person year in the life of a teenager saving up to escape her town, whose arc is realising she is not going to fit the normality her friends are performing. The voice is what every positive review praises and it is the only thing carrying the book, which is the Artemis 69 pattern in reverse - one strength and nothing structural underneath it. It is also written for readers who already know the character from the screen and whose pleasure is seeing known events from outside the loop, so a reader who does not brings nothing to it and takes nothing away. A tie-in continuation, and continuations are not safe bets in this log - the Hitchhiker's sequels fell 13 points from 83 to 70. On the third gate it is clean: the book is about identity and concealment rather than sexual behaviour, so there is no plot to remove. Occult status unexamined.

t: Stranger things (Stranger Things: Lucas on the Line)
why: Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. Form is a novel, and the genre in practice is contemporary YA rather than the SF the catalogue records: four of its five parts are a freshman year of basketball, new friends and working out what it means to be one of very few Black teenagers in a white Indiana town, with the speculative storyline only arriving in the last part. I would put ideas in risks, which is the exit condition. There is a real subject here and it is handled seriously - a mentor gives the lead a pride his parents avoid discussing - but a subject is not a premise whose consequences get worked out, and this reader's high scores come from the second thing; the closest analogue in his log is a first-person account that gave him real understanding of how a minority experiences a country, and that one earned its 91 by examining what is actually true rather than by dramatising it around a franchise plot. The structure works against it too: the reported break between the coming-of-age parts and the television storyline means the book changes into a different book near the end, which is the not-logically-connected complaint that made Unfinished Tales the lowest Tolkien at 69. Written for readers who already know the cast from the screen. A tie-in continuation, and continuations are not safe bets here - the Hitchhiker's sequels fell 13 points from 83 to 70. Occult status unexamined.

A franchise tie-in that retells a television season from a secondary character's viewpoint, and the reviewers divide only over whether it rehashes the show or usefully compresses it. Neither reading produces an idea the book leaves behind, and that absence is the most common reason a competent book stalls in the 60s for this reader - Ranger's Apprentice 74 lost points for having little to think about and had more story of its own than this does. The one genuine asset is interiority: Max's mother's remarriage, her stepfather's violence and her own grief get real page time, and page time on what a character wants and why is what puts Mockingjay 91 at the top of that trilogy. But here it serves a plot whose outcome is already public, so momentum has nothing left to do, and readers consistently say the on-page season-two scenes lose their tension. Shelved middle grade as well, and Narnia 67 shows what a juvenile register costs even when nothing else objects. Gate 4 answered yes on axis:ideas at one source, so occult is unexamined here.

The one thing here worth reading for is a genuine moral situation: twelve people stranded on Mars agree to lie on camera so that someone will come for them, and become accomplices to the deceit they are victims of. That is a want with a cost attached, the axis Mockingjay 91 tops the log on. But it is a turn inside a television-show premise rather than an idea worked out, so axis:ideas goes in risks and the below-the-line gate is where this stops. It is also a sequel resting on characters and a fraud established elsewhere, and this log does not reward sequels automatically - the Hitchhiker's sequels dropped from 83 to 70. Young-adult register, a small cost as with Ranger's Apprentice 74. Stopped at one source per the gate's budget, so the occult status is unexamined.

Ten pieces of cold-space SF - nine stories and a novella - well liked in Czech genre circles and praised for landing a real point at the end of every one. That praise is exactly what does not transfer. A collection has no single premise for the book to carry through, and the log's one reading of unconnected pieces is Unfinished Tales 69, the lowest Tolkien by a clear margin and marked down for exactly that: the parts are not logically connected to each other. Short fiction suspends the character tests, but the suspension removes penalties and never adds points, so with no protagonist held across 520 pages there is nothing to climb on. Reviewers add that the pearls are mostly black and the experience is at times depressing, and the publisher's own copy says you would not want to trade places with any of these characters; sustained bleakness is the mildest objection in the log but here it is the only direction the book offers. One reviewer also names the opening piece as the plot-poorest and a bad choice to lead with, and one reader saw most of the twists coming by the halfway point. Gate 4 answered yes on axis:ideas at one source, so occult is unexamined.

The positive is that a Czech-original dystopia is being written competently: reviewers report interesting characters, a dynamic story, real escalation and a world that costs its people something, and a dystopian setting as such draws no objection from this reader at all - even in Divergent 58 the setting was explicitly fine and the premise was the problem. Why it still sits under the line. The plot is described as simple and action-led, and the closing is called an ending that is not one; a book that leaves events rather than ideas behind is the commonest way a competent book stalls in the 60s here, the Rangers Apprentice 74 shape. One reader summed the author up as readable and gripping but formulaic and predictable. Sustained hopelessness is a further mild discount, the 1984 60 marker. It is also a continuation that opens by picking its people back up rather than restarting, and a sequel is not a safe bet in this log - the Hitchhiker sequels fell from 83 to 70. I lean on the idea rather than on the setting, and I keep the setting as the risk that could drop it further: cities raised on enormous pillars is exactly the kind of declared arrangement whose cost has to be accounted for, and unaccounted infrastructure on that scale is what ended Mortal Engines 55 in its first chapters. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, so the occult question is unexamined.

Comic science fiction, and the register itself costs nothing here: Saturnin 78 sits in the A band on voice and character with no idea worked out at all, and comic SF earned 83 when it opened on one concrete situation. This one does open that way - an unfulfilled cook hands in his notice on a Wednesday and meets the man who takes him off Earth - and it gives him a travelling companion rather than solitude, which is what put Project Hail Mary 92 above The Martian 82. What holds the number down comes from the same reviews. A glossary of intergalactic terms is recommended before starting; sympathetic readers report more information and stimulus than they could process and a story that runs out of breath near the end and would have been better at a smaller scope; a hostile one calls it a mess, the jokes awkward, and cannot say who it is for - too childish for an adult, too confusing for a child. The reader wants to be invested immediately and legibly, and a book that needs a vocabulary primer first is exactly where that goes wrong. So I doubt the idea survives the noise and stopped early; two sources went on a gate that allows one, and the occult question is unexamined. Almost nothing independent exists - two ratings on the main Czech database - which is another reason not to spend more here.

The starting situation is concrete and promising - a widowed rescue commander takes his eight-year-old daughter to a station in a pulsar system to start over, and his sudden transfer smells wrong - and the author handles hardware and jargon like someone who knows the field. The reviews then name both failures that decide scores here. The lead hardens into a nearly invulnerable hero, which is ability handed over rather than earned; and one reader spent two thirds of the book unable to get into the plot or work out whom to root for, with only the beginning and the ending landing. Artemis 69 is the anchor for that combination: consistent technical worldbuilding rescued nothing once the protagonist was thin, and it is the strongest case in the log that a thin lead outranks strong construction. Beyond the post-war political setup, which is backdrop rather than a premise carried through the way Old Man's War 87 carries its own, there is no idea left behind. Reviewers class it as a pleasant action read for one sitting, and action with no character revelation is dead weight for this reader. Gate 4 answered yes on axis:ideas at one source; occult is unexamined as a result.

The detective reading of the annotation does not hold: the derelict ships and the recovered computer core are a first-contact hook, not a case to be solved, so that gate is clear. And the positive here is the kind this reader rewards most in SF - a whole non-human civilisation of sentient machines, bred generation after generation to fight one enemy and now too suspicious to accept help, met and understood rather than merely fought. Reviewers say the AI society's history and workings are the best-realised thing in the book, and understanding an alien culture instead of shooting at it is what put Speaker for the Dead 90 near the top of this log. Three deductions still put it under the line. It is a franchise continuation carrying the aftermath of a crossover event and an established ensemble, so there is no single lead whose wants the book is about, and tight single-viewpoint narration with constant momentum is what the reader named as the baseline in The Hunger Games 89. Reviewers call the enemy itself mundane and object to a technobabble field as the way out, and an author is bound by whatever he undertakes to explain - the Harry Potter 51 complaint was declared rules the world then ignored. Pacing is reported slow. I lean on the ensemble structure and the continuation, and I keep the idea as the risk, since the machine civilisation is the only thing that could lift this and the reviews split on whether it is carried. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, so the occult question is unexamined.

The idea here is the best thing this author has: a rule that explains why a universe full of civilisations is silent, derived on the page and then used to decide the plot. A book that leaves an idea behind is what the reader asks for, and Animal Farm 78 shows an idea carries even where nothing else does. The premise is also genuinely followed through - one declared constraint, that nothing can be hidden from the enemy except what stays inside a human head, generates the whole institution the book runs on, which is the Project Hail Mary 92 virtue. It comes in under the line's comfortable side for three reasons that are all recorded objections.
