Reviewers consistently describe the first half as meandering philosophical drift before hibernation jumps the cast forward, and a thin stretch of story spread over many pages is the log's actual density penalty, not length. The chosen lead is called flat and unlikeable by several reviewers and has no plan for most of the book, which is the passive-protagonist cost of Promena 58, so that stays a risk and I lean on the idea instead. And it is a sequel, which earns nothing here - the Hitchhiker's sequels dropped from 83 to 70. Nothing occult; the science is mechanism throughout. On sexual content there is no sex plot - the frequent complaint is the objectifying treatment of a woman the lead has procured for himself, which is not one of the reader's filters but does not help either. How this book opens is not established, hence medium.

t: Tezka planeta (Where Do We Go From Here?)
why: Unusually for a collection this one has a stated purpose rather than just a table of contents: every piece is built on a specific scientific problem, and the compiler appends a commentary explaining which real physics or biology the story turns on and where it cheats. So something to think about afterwards is the organising principle here rather than a by-product. Dropped 2026-09-03 on two counts that arrived together. The compiler is the author of Ja, robot 55, the reader's first and only real score for him, and it is a DNF three stories in. And the new collection axis prices what that DNF showed: a multi-story book is read from the front and put down on its weakest early pieces, so the top of a range can no longer be set by the canonical ideas somewhere in the middle of the contents. Different hands, different casts, one problem each and nobody to follow between them.

t: Typhonsky pakt (Star Trek: Typhon Pact: Zero Sum Game)
why: The one thing here that could have been an idea - why a masked species wears the masks - is a repair to old franchise continuity rather than a premise with consequences, and reviewers who liked the reveal still found the society behind it interchangeable with another the franchise already had. The rest is an infiltration plot that reviewers describe as explosions and shootouts of the James Bond variety rather than tradecraft, with improbable conveniences and an ending one called unbelievable. Set-piece action with no character revelation is dead weight for this reader, and a plot that does not hold together logically is what he named against Divergent 58 and praised in Golden Son 92. A sequel-shaped continuation as well, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. Leaned on axis:ideas; exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, so the occult status is unexamined.

The lead is the asset carried over - a man who came out of a prison changed and has to start again knowing something almost nobody else does - and a protagonist who acts on what he wants is the axis that separates Sunrise on the Reaping 87 from Oliver Twist 57. But the documented character of this material is that it keeps posing questions and does not answer them: readers report the story does not resolve, that it merely hands the reader onward, and that the questions raised are still open when the sequence ends. That is why axis:ideas belongs in risks rather than in the case for reading it, and axis:ideas in risks is gate 4's exit condition. Continuations are not safe bets in this log either - Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70 - and the same reader reports quality slipping across this sequence. Weighed against Unfinished Tales 69, the log's marker for pieces that are not logically connected to each other, just under the line is the honest place for it. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist because the lead is the part I would expect to hold; the resolution is what I doubt. Exited at gate 4 on one source; occult status and opening structure unexamined.

A post-collapse republic that hunts its orphaned teenagers for sport is a premise I can name, and that is as far as the positive case goes. School Library Journal called the book a largely derivative work that borrows plot points from several popular dystopian novels, and readers report the camps, the government and the experiments left underexplained with a cop-out resolution. That is the exact objection that put Divergent at 58: ideas borrowed from other books and assembled without cohering, in a dystopian setting that was itself fine. Nothing in the reception suggests page time on what these characters want and why, which is the axis Mockingjay 91 wins on. Leaned on axis:ideas because the premise is the only thing carrying the number and I doubt it holds up; exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, so the occult status here is unexamined.

The idea is nameable in a phrase and it is the entire book: a commonwealth organised on reason with no private property, argued into place by a first half that says hanging thieves cannot repair a society that manufactures them. Short, idea-driven work with something genuinely left behind is a profile this reader rewards - Labyrint sveta a raj srdce landed at 70 on exactly that and Animal Farm at 78 for being bleak but giving you something to think about rather than immersing you in misery. The frame is legible too: one named traveller, one conversation, no competing lines starting at once. The deductions are structural and certain rather than speculative. The second half is a one-sided monologue cataloguing institutions, so nobody wants anything and nothing follows from anyone's choices - page time on motives is the heaviest axis in this log and here it is simply absent - and heavy description with little story is the reader's own named penalty. A long section on the island's religion also pushes toward faith as a subject in its own right, which he wants as a thread rather than as the topic. Leaned on axis:ideas and on the suspension that short idea-driven work earns, not on axis:protagonist, because there is no protagonist here to lean on.

t: Uvezneni v Robloxu (Perdus dans le Glitchox-verse)
why: Three primary-school children who like a video game are pulled into it by a trap and have to win the mini-games to get out. I cannot name an idea it leaves behind, and that failure is the finding rather than a gap in my research: the book is an unofficial game-fan novel, illustrated, pitched by its French retailers from age eight or nine, and its purpose is to put familiar game mechanics on the page. That register is what takes the number below the usual band. The reader's own scale for how juvenile a book is runs from Hobbit 84 and The Little Prince 82 at no cost through Ranger's Apprentice 74 at a small one, and Ranger's Apprentice was already marked down for being easy to read with not much to think about - this has the same objection with none of the compensating adventure or invention. Leaned on axis:ideas, since there is none to name; exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, so the occult status is unexamined.

t: V tajne sluzbe Koruny ceske (V tajne sluzbe Koruny ceske)
why: The shift from fleet actions to spies and saboteurs in a shipyard city, with ethnic friction between Czechs, Germans and Russian settlers, is the most promising material this alternate history has offered - a society under strain is a subject that could cohere into something. But the gate asks whether I doubt the idea holds up, and the reviewed record for this world says the author gave up on a story with any reach beyond itself, with flat characters, no development and a stock treatment of the Russians as the standing complaints. National friction handled by a writer who has already been faulted for stereotyping one of the nations in it is not an idea I would bet the number on; Ranger's Apprentice 74 was docked for lazy stereotype stated as fact, and that was a series with a lead the reader followed happily. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log - Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. Sabotage and espionage make an investigation-shaped plot possible, but the satisfaction here is a war being fought, not a culprit identified, so the detective filter is not engaged. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, within budget; the occult question is left unexamined, which changes no decision below the propose line.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. Form is a novel, genre post-apocalyptic Czech SF, a debut from a small publisher. The opening is the strongest thing about it and it is the shape this reader wants: one man in a hole he dug himself, certain that whoever is hunting him will kill him if they find him, with readers reporting it grips from the first lines rather than starting slowly. But I would put ideas in risks, which is the exit condition. What the author names as his own question - what happens if electricity stops working - is a survival scenario rather than a premise with consequences to follow, and the machines that killed most of the population are left unexplained by design, so there is nothing for the reader to check or think through afterwards. Reviewers describe the message as an environmental one about how everyday human activity damages the planet, which is a moral rather than an idea worked out, and the same reviewers describe the prose as overwrought and inexperienced, improving as it goes. Sustained survival bleakness is a further mild cost, the objection that cost 1984 a band at 60. Structurally the present-tense pursuit is interleaved with memories of the honeymoon that was interrupted, so a reader is holding two timelines, though only one lead. Occult status unexamined; nothing suggests it arises.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, and in the lower of the two bands rather than the default one. Form is a 112-page illustrated first-reader novel in twelve chapters broken into shorter sub-sections, with large type, quizzes for children and pop-culture asides for the parent reading aloud; reviewers place it at seven and up and recommend it as a bedtime book or for beginning readers. That is a form which suspends the character tests outright - there is no interiority to judge and none intended - and the suspension removes penalties without adding anything. I cannot name an idea the book leaves behind: a parcel courier who cuts corners by going against the flow of time is a comic gimmick, and the scientific terms that get dropped in are flagged by reviewers as things a parent will have to explain rather than things the book works out. The reader's own scale settles this: Ranger's Apprentice cost a little at 74 and Narnia more at 67, both full-length novels for older children, while a picture book belongs in the thirties or forties, and a large-type first-reader with a chocolate-obsessed animal sidekick sits much nearer the second. The Little Prince at 82 is the counter-case and shows exactly what would be needed to escape this band - ideas carrying a short children's book - and that is what is missing here. Occult status unexamined; nothing suggests it arises.

One concrete situation on the first page - a Manhattan bass player wakes with 108 specific predictions in his head - and then the book is its consequences rather than its gimmick: predictions that come true no matter what anyone does to prevent them, a man selling access to them anonymously, and corporations, governments and a church closing in on him. Kirkus reads it as a satire on behaviour and causality, which is an idea you can state in a phrase, and that is what earns the range; naming the idea is what carries Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 past everything they do not attempt. Two deductions. Reviewers repeatedly say the antagonist and a supporting wife are more interesting than Will himself, and a thin lead beats good construction every time in this log - Artemis 69 against Project Hail Mary 92 by one author. And the comic-book rhythm of cliffhanger into reveal wears thin, a momentum complaint rather than a density one. I leaned on the idea, deliberately not on the protagonist: if Will reads flat the number sits at the floor. The prophecy is treated as a commercial and political problem rather than reverently, so that axis costs little.

The detective signal on the catalogue record does not survive contact with the annotation: the satisfaction on offer is a succession struggle after an emperor's death, not finding out who did anything, so gate 1 does not fire and I did not spend sources on it. What is left is a book that begins on a funeral and hands the regency to a mentally ill and brutal ruler, with the mother returning to bury her son. Bleakness is only a mild discount in this log - Animal Farm 78 is bleak and scores well because it gives you something to think about - but 1984 60 shows what bleakness costs once there is nothing to take away from it, and that is my doubt here. I can name the situation and not the idea, so axis:ideas goes in risks, which is gate 4's exit condition. Also a continuation, and continuations are not safe bets here: Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist because there are several claimants to the lead and I have not established which the book actually follows. Exited at gate 4 on one source; occult status and opening structure are unexamined.

There is a decent engine here - a demagogue who takes half a sealed prison object by force and by lying to it, against a lead who has finally cracked the code to its core - and the question of how a crowd is won by a liar is a real one. Against it stands the one thing readers say most consistently about this material: the answers do not arrive. The sequence is reported to close with a row of questions still open, which is the Unfinished Tales 69 objection - pieces that do not connect - applied to the point in the story where connection was the whole promise. So I can name a situation and not an idea I trust will land, and axis:ideas in risks is gate 4's exit condition. A continuation as well, and continuations are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70, and readers here report quality easing off across the sequence. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:protagonist because the lead is inherited and was not the doubt. Exited at gate 4 on one source, so occult status and opening structure are unexamined.

The strengths are real and the reviews agree on them: a twenty-three-year-old first-person lead who reads as genuinely human, grief for her dead father worked through in flashback and holding the book together, a concrete Yukon setting and a gripping start. But every review that praises it says the same thing about the plot itself - the post-nuclear apocalypse is standard and what saves the book is voice and atmosphere. That is the profile of a book that stalls in the 60s here: nothing left behind to think about, which is the most common reason a competent book stops short. Kirkus adds that around the midpoint it loses the edge and sense of risk that had distinguished it, and that the science-fiction element feels forced when it arrives - a declared-late, unsupported turn of the kind that ended Mortal Engines 55 - and reviewers note Katniss-grade bow skills justified only in passing, which is competence handed over rather than earned. Sustained solitary survival in cold is also the one thing named as not worth enjoying in The Martian 82. Gate 4 answered yes on axis:ideas at one source and I stopped; occult is unexamined.

The premise is declared precisely - a planet loses its magnetosphere and becomes lethal - and a precise declaration is exactly what this reader holds an author to. The reviews say the book does not carry it. The most substantive critical reader objects to unoriginal pontificating put in the mouth of a twenty-year-old idealist, to dialogue in which characters state the obvious so that the reader can be informed, and to nothing feeling real; a mixed review that enjoyed the first half calls the saboteur twist absurd and the ending carelessly wrapped up, as though the author had lost interest; and readers do not even agree on which planet the story happens on. Mortal Engines 55 is the log's precedent and it is decisive here: the setting as such was fine, the logic around it was not, and the book ended in the first chapters. A declared scarcity that behaves inconsistently plus a resolution the reader calls absurd is that failure, and it is what carries this range rather than any objection to the concept. Stopped at one source, so the occult question is unexamined. The sabotage thread - suspicion falling on everyone - is investigation-shaped but there is no detective and no crime to solve as the point of the book, so that filter does not fire; it is a flag only.

There is a concrete starting situation and a lead with a stated want, and that is the positive case: an orphan who signs up for glory and a one-way ticket, which is the motive-first axis Mockingjay 91 scores on. But the idea behind it is a television gimmick - twelve teenagers paired off on camera to found a colony - and I would put axis:ideas in risks, so this exits at the below-the-line gate. A book that is competent and has nothing higher to think about stalls where Narnia 67 sits, and the register is written for thirteen-plus, which costs a little on axis:childrens the way Ranger's Apprentice 74 does. The reviewed structure narrates from the travellers, the audience on Earth and the people running the programme, so a reader is tracking several strands early - the log's most reliable negative, Guards! Guards! 30 - and that is a risk rather than the lean. Romance at that register is not what carries the number and the plot-is-sex test is not met. One source, per the gate, so the occult status here is unexamined.

The lead is the best thing here and it is a real positive: a fifty-year-old Quebecoise veteran whose rebuilt body is coming apart, hiding from the state that made her, which is the kind of interiority that puts Red Rising 95 at the top of this log. I am stopping under the line anyway, and on structure rather than on the idea. Reviewers describe short time-stamped chapters cutting between a street gang, a military scientist and a net war, with the recurring complaint that lots is going on but little of it relates - one calls it too obtuse for its own good, and it does not resolve on its own. That is precisely the shape that ended three books unfinished at 30, The Gunslinger, The Colour of Magic and Foundryside, and the reader wants one concrete starting situation to be invested in immediately. I lean on the opening and the split viewpoints rather than on the nanotech-and-space-race setting, which is the part critics praise, because predicting a book up on a strong setting while the way in is doubtful is the recorded 11-point miss in this log, Artemis 69. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, so the occult question here is unexamined.

The premise is declared and then its consequences are actually followed out, which is the reader's heaviest positive axis: not just an empty world but what happens to water, power, cattle, ants and roads once nobody tends them, and above all what happens to knowledge - the survivors are ordinary people, the school fails, and the lead ends up teaching bows because reading will not transmit. That is the second-order-consequence virtue that put Project Hail Mary 92 above The Martian 82, and the idea it leaves behind is nameable in a phrase: civilisation is a habit, not an achievement. It opens on one concrete situation, a man alone in the mountains with a snakebite who drives home to an empty highway, and companionship arrives rather than solitude persisting, which was the named complaint against The Martian 82. Two deductions keep it under the S band. The first and last movements meander - the middle decades pass fast, the ends are long meditations, and thin story over many pages is the reader's actual length penalty, the Les Miserables 71 problem. And the lead is a vehicle for the thought experiment more than a man with wants, which is why the number rests on the ideas and not on him; The Silmarillion 80 shows how far ideas alone can carry a book with a weak centre.

This is the one reviewers rate highest in the run - described as an outstanding follow-up by one Czech site and as the author growing with each book by another, with the further note that it can be read on its own, so the way in is not obstructed. The set-up has a genuine hook: people who fled upward returning to a surface that is not theirs any more, with the line that man was always man's worst enemy. Against that, everything the reviews praise is adventure and escalation rather than an idea being worked out, and the same author draws the charge of being formulaic and predictable; wanting higher things to think about is where competent books here settle in the 60s, and Rangers Apprentice 74 is the marker for easy to read with not much to think about. The bleakness is a mild extra discount, as with 1984 60. I lean on the idea rather than on the setting, and I keep the setting as the risk that could take it lower: cities carried on huge pillars is a declared arrangement that has to be paid for in the text, and it was unaccounted infrastructure of exactly that kind that ended Mortal Engines 55 in its first chapters. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, so the occult question is unexamined.

Roughly 550 pages on two threads that start together and alternate: a journalist in the first person chasing the keys her dead father left her as a game, and a third-person account of eight volunteers in a reality show who have agreed to leave the world for good. Two things decide the number at one source. The reader wants one concrete starting situation and to be invested at once - several strands running before any is legible is the log's most reliable killer, and it ended three books at 30 - and this book withholds on purpose, so that risk is live from page one. Second, what it is for is a message about media manipulation, the audience's appetite for other people's pain, and the climate, delivered rather than worked out; reviewers report the middle goes monotonous and the plot is predictable, and one of the harshest concedes the originality while rejecting the execution. Animal Farm 78 is what a short, declared idea earns when it is followed through; a long novel whose thesis the reader already agrees with is the standard way a competent book stalls in the 60s. That doubt about the idea is what carries this range, so I stopped at one source; the occult question is therefore unexamined. The puzzle-hunt frame is investigation-shaped but there is no crime and no detective, so that filter does not fire.

The premise is a genuine one and worth stating: the Earth has about a century of habitability left, and a fifty-year-old woman whose body was rebuilt for war is the only person the new starship can be flown by. A premise whose consequences get followed through is what earns Project Hail Mary 92, and an ageing, damaged, deliberate lead is far from the thin protagonist that cost Artemis 69. What holds the number under the line is delivery, not ambition. Readers describe the same jagged, short, time-stamped chapters as before, running four or five threads at once - scientists, teenagers, gangsters, a Chinese pilot, an AI - with motivations in constant flux, and confusion of exactly that kind is the most reliable negative predictor in this log, three books abandoned at 30. It is also a direct continuation rather than a restart, and a continuation is not a safe bet here: the Hitchhiker sequels fell from 83 to 70. Reviewers also report the ship going nowhere while conditions on Earth get catastrophically worse, which is the mild but real discount that 1984 60 marks. Leaning on the viewpoint structure rather than on the idea, because the idea is the part I would bet on. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, so the occult question is unexamined.

t: Zkouska ohnem (Star Trek: Crucible: Kirk - The Star to Every Wandering)
why: A dying man revisiting the one choice that cost him his happiness is a real emotional question, and this is the rare tie-in that puts a character's regret rather than a mission at the centre. But it is written to a fortieth-anniversary brief and pinned to the plot of an existing film, and reviewers report scenes recurring twice with variations, complain of the lightness and brevity of the piece, and one calls it a corporate product rather than a labour of love. Thin story spread over pages is the reader's own penalty term - it is what held LOTR to 84 - and there is no premise being worked out here to earn anything back, which is the most common reason a competent book stalls in the 60s. A sequel too, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. Leaned on axis:ideas; exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, so the occult status is unexamined.

A game tie-in whose documented, publicly apologised-for defect is precisely the axis that carries most weight in this log: the author does not follow the rules the world had already laid down. Fans catalogued roughly eighty lore and timeline breaches; an established character previously written as high-functioning autistic was reissued without any social difficulty; an isolationist slaver species that keeps outsiders off its worlds suddenly holds an embassy and admits humans. Harry Potter 51 and Mortal Engines 55 are both scored on exactly that failure and neither came with the publisher promising corrections. Against that there is nothing the book leaves behind - it carries forward a revenge plot begun before it and an assassin's rise that the games then declined to reference. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets here, with Hitchhiker's falling from 83 to 70. Gate 4 answered yes on axis:ideas at one source, so occult is unexamined. The floor of this band is the honest reading rather than the middle.

There is a nameable idea and it is a decent one: robots with no notion that humans ever existed go looking for a creator and end up finding out what they are to each other, and here they are separated for the first time and forced to look for themselves instead. Short idea-driven work has the character and emotion rules suspended, which is how The Little Prince 82 clears the propose line on a handful of thoughts. But the suspension removes penalties and never adds points, and this is a ninety-six page comics album catalogued for children, so the idea arrives in gestures and a couple of panels rather than being worked out - the reader's complaint about Narnia 67 was children as the leads plus not enough higher things to think about, and that was with a whole novel of text. An avalanche rescue and a buddy separation is a warm, slight story that will not leave much behind. I lean on the register and the form rather than on the idea, because the idea is nameable; it is the space given to it that is thin. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source, so the occult question is unexamined.

t: 2001: Vesmirna odysea. Rajske fontany (2001: A Space Odyssey / The Fountains of Paradise)
why: Two novels bound together, both idea-first and both with a payload you can state in a phrase: that our intelligence was installed in us by a machine and is meant to be outgrown, and that a two-thousand-year-old wish to build a stair to heaven finally gets paid for in engineering rather than in worship. That is the axis Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 score on, ideas left behind rather than events, and the second novel also does what this reader liked most in Project Hail Mary 92 - takes one declared capability and follows its consequences out into politics, weather and money. The opening is a single concrete situation, a starving man-ape watching for predators, and nothing about it needs looking up. On the occult bar the transformations matter and they clear it: the monolith is a machine, the ascension to the star-child is done to a man by that machine with no invocation, devotion or priesthood anywhere in how the power is conferred, and the monks who own the mountain in the second novel are an obstacle to an engineering project rather than a source of power - so the 2026-09-02 question about how power is conferred is answered mechanically at the origin as well as in use. The cost is the axis weighed heaviest here: Clarke's people are functions of the problem, reviewers of the second novel call the characterisation very thin and the plot thinner, and there is none of the interiority that put Red Rising 95 and Mockingjay 91 on top. Long stretches are description and specification rather than story, the Silmarillion-style density that this reader tolerates rather than enjoys. Leaned on axis:ideas and explicitly not on axis:worldbuilding: Artemis 69 is the standing warning against predicting a book up on a well-built world when the lead is visibly thin.

Exited at the below-the-line gate. Form and genre are settled cheaply: a comic adult fantasy thriller, the last dragon hiding in the Louisiana bayou with vodka and Netflix while a corrupt constable leans on the teenage boy who becomes his errand-runner. There is a real positive - reviewers agree the camaraderie between the two is what the book is for, and friendship is what earned The Hobbit 84 its band with nothing else to recommend it. But I cannot name an idea the book leaves behind, and reviewers describe it as part thriller, part action movie and wholly irreverent, which is page time on what characters do rather than on what they want; that is exactly the ceiling Ranger's Apprentice 74 hit with 'easy to read, but not much to think about', and this has a single volume's worth of goodwill rather than fourteen. Small further pushbacks: the human lead is fifteen, the small life-phase discount Narnia 67 and Ender's Game 87 both took, and the antagonist's predatory designs on the boy's mother are a threat thread rather than a sexual plot. The crude and profane register is not an objection at all by the profile. Occult status is unexamined, as the ladder permits at this gate. Leaned on ideas because that is the axis I actually argued from; the protagonist question is unresolved rather than negative.

The positive case is the two things The Hunger Games 89 was praised for and this book does the same way: one tight single POV and constant momentum. It opens on a concrete, immediately legible situation - a blackballed man in his flat watching the state television channel while his eighteen-month-old daughter coughs - and then runs 101 short numbered chapters as a countdown, so there is no confusion filter to survive and no drift. Motives are stated and stay stated: he goes on the show for medicine money, and the ending is a self-sacrifice that takes the broadcaster down with him, which is the shape the reader preferred in Project Hail Mary 92 over The Martian 82. There is an idea it actually works out rather than just asserting - the televised hunt as a mechanism for consent, and the pollution the poor breathe while the rich filter it. Deductions: the wife's prostitution is desperation shown as destructive rather than an affair, so it costs a point or two and no more, and there is a stretch of solo evasion where the loneliness is the content, the objection that docked The Martian 82. The number is held down and the range kept wide by bleakness: the family are dead before the climax, the lead dies, and 1984 60 is the log's evidence that sustained misery costs more than the profile's mild wording suggests, where Animal Farm 78 shows what a bleak book scores when it hands you an idea instead of immersion. Leaned on momentum and protagonist rather than worldbuilding, because the dystopia is sketched rather than engineered and the log's one recorded over-prediction came from leaning up on setting.

t: Cesta na okraj (The Road to the Rim)
why: Hornblower in space, and openly so: a newly commissioned officer takes passage to his first posting, meets combat on the way and is seasoned by it, in 117 pages of naval adventure transposed onto a starship by an author who really was a ship's master. It moves and it is competent, but the below-the-line gate asks whether the idea holds up and there is no idea here to hold up - readers who enjoy it call it classic space opera, readers who do not call it minor, dated and short on wonder, and both descriptions are about texture rather than a premise being worked out. Nothing is declared and followed through, nothing is left behind, and the officer's advancement is the whole payload; that is the pattern that stalls a competent book in the 60s in this log, where even Male zeny 79 had characters doing the work instead. Exited on axis:ideas, which is the doubt carrying the number, rather than on axis:protagonist - the lead is likeable enough and I did not establish him as thin. Occult status is unexamined at this exit by design.

Exited at the below-the-line gate. This is eleven commissioned short stories, one per screen incarnation of a television character, published by a children's imprint for a broadcast anniversary. The form removes everything the reader actually scores on: no protagonist to be interesting or worth rooting for over a book's length, no motives developed across chapters, no premise whose consequences get worked out, and the lead is a figure whose character each contributor must reproduce from the programme rather than build. I cannot name an idea the collection leaves behind, and the short-idea-driven suspension only removes penalties - Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 both earn their scores on one nameable idea, which an anniversary commission by eleven hands does not have. That combination, no idea plus an occasional piece in a form that suspends the character tests, is the low band rather than the default one. It also assumes familiarity with the programme it celebrates. Occult status is unexamined, as the ladder permits at this gate. Leaned on ideas because the absence of one is decisive and the register question only adds to it.

Exited at the below-the-line gate. Form and genre are settled: an SF novel that continues an established sequence, set a generation on from where that sequence had reached, with a clone dictator, an escape plan built around a dead scientist's brain used as a ship's core, a starving colony in revolt and a sentient kelp organism acquiring technology through contact with people. There are ideas in that list, but they are the sequence's ideas and this book inherits rather than establishes them - the world, the institutions and the surviving cast all arrive assumed, and reviewers and the plot summary alike treat prior reading as necessary rather than optional. A sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70, the steepest series decline recorded, and the Ender books settled nine points below their peak. What I doubt is that the reader comes away with one thing to think about instead of several strands of an ongoing story resolving, and that is the axis that keeps competent books in the 60s. Several viewpoint threads also split the page time that the log rewards spending on motives. A woman many believe to be a divine child sits at the centre of the plot and a pacifist religion runs the food supply, so this book's occult and faith status genuinely needs examining - it is unexamined here, as the ladder permits at this gate, and the title itself points at an ascension. Leaned on ideas because inheritance rather than invention is what I actually argued.

Exits at gate 4. Form and genre settle at once - eleven alternate-history adventure stories by ten hands, set between 1848 and 1950 in a shared invented world, 426 pages. The positive case is the conceit, which is nameable and does get consequences drawn from it: a mid-nineteenth-century catastrophe redraws the map, and the Czech-Slovak kingdom that results is a naval power with colonies a century later, with one story turning back to what the catastrophe actually was. That is why this takes the default band rather than the low one, and reader scores are high. The reason I stop here is that I would put axis:ideas in risks, because the collection's purpose is to expand a universe rather than to work out a premise - and the reviews say so, noting that a reader who is not already a follower of the series will not be reached by all of it, that some stories are markedly weaker, and that the volume declines a chance to resolve a character carried over from the main sequence. A setting is not an idea left behind, and the short form suspends the character rules rather than earning on them, so the axis that carries Speaker for the Dead 90 cannot be reached across eleven separate casts. Unfinished Tales 69 is the anchor for what an unconnected set of pieces costs even from an author this reader otherwise scores in the 80s. One flag rather than a deduction: crime and spy stories are among the eleven, so investigation-shaped material is present, but the volume is not a whodunnit and filter 4 does not fire. Occult is unexamined by design at this gate.

This one goes past gate 4 because the idea is real and nameable in a phrase: a pit dug as the foundation of a house for all the proletarians becomes, by the last page, a grave for one child - the utopia consumes the people it was for. That is the short idea-driven allegory shape that earned Animal Farm 78 and Labyrint sveta a raj srdce 70, and the opening is clean too, one concrete legible situation: Voschev is dismissed from his factory for thinking amid the general tempo of labour, and walks out. So neither the opening filter nor the occult filter applies, the latter established rather than assumed - the fantastical element is a blacksmith's bear, presented as a wonder and not as anything conferred by rite. What holds the number down to the low end of the ok band is what the reader has already priced twice. Animal Farm scored 78 explicitly because it gives you something to think about rather than immersing you in the misery; this book does the opposite, and the reader who found 1984 too depressing put it at 60. And the lead is contemplative rather than driving - Voschev wants the meaning of existence and is condemned for wanting it - which is the Promena 58 combination exactly, a passive figure hard to root for plus bleakness that arrives all at once. Prediction failures in this log came from leaning on the wrong axis, so I am naming both: the idea sets the ceiling, the bleakness sets the floor. Not leaned on density, though the deliberately deformed language the Czech edition documents at length is real - it goes in risks with the passive lead and the several viewpoints, because those are what could take this below the range rather than what sets it. Recorded low deliberately: this is a major novel that will probably not be an enjoyable one for this reader.

One idea declared and genuinely worked out: the fabric that makes a whole planet rich is a by-product of that planet's sun being about to go nova, so the economy and the doom are the same fact, and the colonial arrangement built on it collapses when the physics is stated. That is the premise-with-consequences pleasure of Project Hail Mary 92, in the plain declarative prose named as a virtue in Ender's Game 87. Against it, the lead is a man whose memory has been erased and who is carried, hidden and fetched by other people for most of the book, wanting nothing he can name - the Oliver Twist 57 failure of a lead who is acted upon. Dropped 2026-09-03 on this author's first real score: Ja, robot 55 was abandoned on a cast nobody could root for, and that is precisely the deduction this line was already leaning on.

t: Lod na milion let (The Boat of a Million Years)
why: This goes past gate 4 because the premise is genuine and its consequences are the book: a handful of people simply stop ageing, and the novel spends five thousand years on what that actually does to a person - hiding from neighbours who notice, being accused of witchcraft, outliving every family you make, searching for anyone else like you and mostly failing, and finally reaching a future where longevity is universal and nothing about it is what they expected. That is a premise declared and worked out, the Project Hail Mary 92 virtue, and the final turn is a real idea left behind. Occult clears cleanly and this was checked rather than assumed: the agelessness is presented as physiology, the witchcraft in the book is an accusation levelled at the immortals and not a practice any of them performs, and no rite confers or elevates anything. So why the number sits at the propose line rather than above it. The book is episodic by design - reviewers agree it is closer to a set of novelettes tied together by their subjects than a novel, and readers report spending most of it wondering whether there was a guiding point. Unfinished Tales 69 is the anchor and it is the exact diagnosis: the pieces are not logically connected to each other, and it cost this reader twelve points off an author he otherwise scores in the 80s. The Silmarillion 80 shows a mythic span with no single protagonist can survive that, which is why the range reaches to 70 rather than stopping lower. Against it: the late-twentieth-century section is the one every reviewer calls the weakest, where the nearest thing to a lead flattens into a mouthpiece and his opponent into a cartoon - a declared character not being shown, which this reader treats as a self-consistency breach. And the theme is the loneliness of outliving everyone, which is the specific complaint that held The Martian to 82 in a book he otherwise liked. Leaned on the idea for the ceiling and on the thin-story-over-many-pages penalty for the floor, not on protagonist - that one is in risks, because if the nearest thing to a lead never lands the whole range drops. Sexual content is present and small: one long-lived character works as a prostitute across centuries and there is a brief encounter, so volume is low and this is the Valka stareho muze 87 position of a few points, not a band.

t: Moznost ostrova (The Possibility of an Island)
why: There is a real idea here and it is worked out rather than gestured at: a sect promises immortality by cloning, actually delivers it, and the book alternates the original narrator's account with annotations by his own clones two thousand years later, who were designed without his sex drive and without his appetite for violence - so the future becomes an argument about what is left of a person once the weaknesses are engineered out, and the frame answers: nothing worth having. That is the Animal Farm 78 shape, an idea you carry away. Everything else costs, and it costs on the axis with the most measured weight. The narrator is a coarse professional provocateur whose life is his sexual appetite, and reviewers describe copious graphic depictions of every form of sexual activity across his two affairs: this is high on all three dimensions at once, where volume alone sank Ready Player One 55 and The Witcher 53, and where the kind of it alone was the reader's stated reason for the first of those. He is also not somebody to root for, the Ballad of Songbirds 65 objection, and the nihilism is unbroken from the first page, which is the 1984 60 complaint - three separate deductions off one good idea. No marriage or engagement is in play, so the infidelity bar does not fire, and the sect's immortality is delivered by laboratory cloning rather than by any rite, so the occult bar does not either. I judged sexual content a theme rather than the plot, since the plot is the sect and the clones, and I state the doubt plainly: the case for calling it the sixth filter is that the neohuman design is defined by subtracting exactly what the narrator is made of. Leaned on axis:sexual-content because it sets the ceiling here regardless of what the idea is worth.

t: Na komete (Off on a Comet (Hector Servadac))
why: The premise is the problem, and it arrives in the first chapter rather than accumulating. A comet clips the Earth, carries off a slice of the Mediterranean together with its air and three dozen people, and departs without the Earth noticing - and Verne, whose entire standing rests on making the mechanism his subject, simply asks the reader to accept it. What follows is honest work: the survivors deduce their new world from their own weight, from a six-hour day and from water boiling at 66 degrees. But this reader abandoned a book at 55 on nothing more than unaccounted energy for moving cities, said moving cities as such were fine and the logic around them was not, and ranks premises by plausibility explicitly - so a breach this size, in a book that undertakes to explain, is the live risk rather than a quibble. Exited at the below-the-line gate on axis:ideas as the doubt: past the arithmetic the payload is a cheerful survival adventure that brings everyone home, with the sort of national and ethnic caricature that cost Ranger's Apprentice 74 already priced in. Occult status is unexamined at this exit by design.

The book takes its own central claim and attacks it twice. First the last competent general is set against a prediction that says individuals cannot bend history, and he loses to his own emperor's fear rather than to the heroes - deliberately anticlimactic, and the point is that the theory held. Then a mutant who can rewrite what people feel walks through the same theory untouched, because a statistical science of masses has no term for one unrepeatable person. An author stress-testing his declared premise instead of protecting it is what the reader praised in Golden Son 92 and Old Man's War 87. Dropped 2026-09-03 on this author's first real score: Ja, robot 55 ended three stories in on a cast nobody could root for, and this is again two halves with different casts, so the idea has to carry a book whose people will not.

Exits at gate 4, at the floor of the band rather than anywhere near its top. Form and genre are settled: a short comic first-person novel, absurdist register, 250 pages in Czech. The positive case is that the device gets used rather than admired - the man is broke, unemployed and mid-divorce before anything happens, so the invisibility lands on a concrete situation with stakes already running, and readers credit the author with putting it to work rather than parading it. But I would put axis:ideas in risks without hesitation: it is a farce whose own reviewers describe it as absurd situations, sex and identity-swapping, one of them adding that it is barely distinguishable in register from the author's best-known book, and I cannot name anything it leaves behind. That decides the exit. The graded deduction is what pins the number to the bottom of the range and could plausibly put it under. Sexual content is described by a reader as a large component of the book rather than an occasional scene, and the register is crude by design - which is both dimensions that cost independently and compound, volume being what sank Ready Player One 55 and the kind of sex being what that log entry names as the actual cause. A lead who uses invisibility to spy on his estranged wife also puts the crudeness dimension squarely in play. Not leaned on protagonist: a shambling loser is not itself an objection here - Saturnin 78 shows the comic register carries no penalty - and it is the missing idea that sets the number. Infidelity was examined and does not fire: the marriage is already separating and no source describes an affair as the premise, so this axis is not the objection, but that rests on absence of evidence rather than on a source saying so. Occult is unexamined by design at this gate; a spoken formula that confers the power is a real question the higher band would have to answer. Declared overspend: two sources at a gate budgeted for one, spent establishing that the sexual content is volume rather than a scene.

t: Otcove prstenu (Tales Before Tolkien: The Roots of Modern Fantasy)
why: Exited at the below-the-line gate. Form and genre are decisive: an anthology of fantasy short fiction written before 1937, assembled by a Tolkien scholar to show what the genre grew out of. Its organising principle is historical influence rather than a premise, so there is nothing for the reader's main axes to grip - no protagonist across the book, no motives developed at length, no world whose declared rules must hold. What it does have is a documentary interest that a reader who scored The Silmarillion 80 and The Lord of the Rings 84 would actually feel, which is why the default band rather than the low one, but Unfinished Tales 69 is the log's warning about exactly this shape: a set of pieces marked down because they are not connected to each other, and there the pieces at least shared a world. Late-Victorian and Edwardian prose adds a density pushback the reader has already paid for once, in the famous digressions that put Les Miserables 71 below The Count of Monte Cristo 75. I doubt one idea survives the reading, which is what puts it under the line. Occult status is unexamined, as the ladder permits at this gate. Leaned on ideas because the collection form removing the character tests is what carries the number.

t: Posledni pan Prstenu (The Last Ringbearer (Poslednij kolcenosec))
why: The positive case is an idea I can state in a phrase and the book is built entirely out of it: the war was written by its winners, and the side called evil was the one civilisation that bet on rational knowledge. That is the kind of premise whose consequences get worked out rather than asserted, which is the axis Project Hail Mary 92 and Speaker for the Dead 90 both score on, and the reader already values this world at LOTR 84 and The Silmarillion 80, so the material is not a cold start for him. Against it, three deductions. A reviewer reports the early chapters switch confusedly between past and present tense and that political and military history arrives in info-dumps - the reader's heaviest filter is confusion in the opening, and while what is reported is prose-level rather than either of his two named shapes, and his LOTR reading supplies the terms and geography that shape two withholds, it is the reason the range starts where it does. The digressive history is the objection that put Les Miserables 71 nine points under The Count of Monte Cristo 75. And the plot is a sabotage-and-forgery operation carried by several viewpoints, so page time goes to machination rather than to what people want, the trade that docked Golden Son 92 below Red Rising 95 for leaning on action. Magic is used on the page, but in this author's hands it is the Tolkien system and cast as the thing to be got rid of, and Tolkien's magic drew no complaint at 84 or at 80, so it costs little here; the plot's target being a scrying mirror is the one part of that I would want checked against the text. Leaned on ideas rather than protagonist, because the argument is what would carry a reading and the two soldiers at the centre are functionaries of it.

Exited at the below-the-line gate. This is ten invented fairy tales in about 160 pages, illustrated, framed as folklore annotated by a fictional scholar - a companion piece to a novel sequence rather than a book with a premise of its own. I cannot name an idea it works out, and the form removes the tests the reader actually rewards: there is no protagonist to be interesting or worth rooting for, no motives worked over page after page, no worldbuilding commitment to hold up. That is the low band, not the default one, because the short-idea-driven suspension only removes penalties and never adds points - the log's short winners, Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82, both carry one nameable idea, and a cautionary-tale register in the fairy-tale mould is not that. Childrens register also pushes down: Narnia 67 paid a little for children's framing while being a full novel, and this sits further toward the picture-book end. Occult status is unexamined, as the ladder permits at this gate. Leaned on ideas rather than childrens because the absence of a premise is the decisive fact, not the audience.

Exits at gate 4. Form and genre are settled - a Czech monster-hunter novel in the self-described dirty-fantasy register, first person, present tense, with an emancipated lead who is explicitly not a model of decency. The positive case is narrow but real: the guild politics and the cost of her choice of partner give the plot a want driving it rather than a monster of the week, and reviewers credit distinct, gritty characters. What I cannot do is name an idea the book leaves behind - every source describes texture (raw world, coarse vocabulary, no illusions) and none describes a premise being worked out, so axis:ideas belongs in doubt and that is what carries the number. Two graded deductions push it to the floor of the band rather than its top. Sexual content is a declared feature of the register, not an occasional scene, and volume alone is what sank The Witcher 53; even the one chapter of it in Valka stareho muze 87 was that reader's single named complaint. And it is a sequel, which is not a safe bet in this log - Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70 - with reviewers reporting the continuous plot suits the material less well than the shorter form that preceded it. Not leaned on protagonist: a rough, willful lead is not itself an objection here, Pycha a predsudek 75 shows relationship-centred material costs nothing on its own, and it is the missing idea rather than the lead that holds this down. Infidelity was examined and does not apply - the lover is a partner, not a spouse or fiance, and this axis is marriage or engagement only. Occult is left unexamined by design at this gate: a hexer-and-vampire world with Dark Ones and fae plainly needs the conferral test run, and it would only lower the number.

t: Rej stinu (Shadow Show: All-New Stories in Celebration of Ray Bradbury)
why: Exits at gate 4. Form and genre are settled - twenty-six new stories by different hands, plus an introduction by Bradbury and a personal tribute appended to each story. The quality is not in doubt: a starred trade review, a Shirley Jackson nomination, contributors of the rank of Atwood, Gaiman, Ellison and Link, and reviewers agreeing the pieces sound like their own authors rather than pastiche. That is a competent book, and competence is exactly what the default C band describes. What decides the exit is that I would put axis:ideas in risks, and the reason is structural rather than a complaint about any story: the organising principle here is homage to a dead writer, not a premise whose consequences get worked out, and the recurring themes reviewers name - loss, marriage, death, loneliness - are moods rather than something the book leaves behind. Unfinished Tales 69 is the anchor and the diagnosis transfers exactly: the pieces are not logically connected to each other, and that cost this reader twelve points off an author he otherwise scores in the 80s. The short form then suspends the character and emotion rules, which removes penalties but adds nothing, so the axis that tops this log cannot be earned across twenty-six separate casts. Two smaller notes in the same direction: the paratext reviewers single out as the best part is tribute essays about Bradbury, which is of no use to a reader who has not read him, and the register runs to loss and death, the mild bleakness discount that put 1984 at 60. Not leaned on character-differentiation - with a new cast every story there is nothing for it to measure. Occult is unexamined by design at this gate, and with horror writers among the contributors it plainly needs running before any higher number could stand.

t: Sin slavy mistru fantasy (The Fantasy Hall of Fame)
why: Exited at the below-the-line gate. Form and genre are settled and they decide it: an anthology of classic fantasy short fiction, the contents chosen by a ballot of professional American writers, split across two Czech volumes. The stories are individually canonical, which is a real point in its favour and the reason this is not the low band - what the log's short winners have in common is one nameable idea each, and pieces selected by their own field for having lasted are more likely than not to carry one. But the book has no premise of its own to work out, no protagonist to be interesting or worth rooting for, and nothing to hold self-consistent, so the axes the reader actually scores on are unavailable to it and the short-form suspension removes penalties without adding anything. The nearest measurement in the log is Unfinished Tales 69, the lowest Tolkien, marked down because the pieces are not connected to each other - and that was one author's material rather than twenty writers'. So this lands just under the line, which is what the default band records. Occult status is unexamined, as the ladder permits at this gate, and is worth noting as genuinely open for a survey of the classical fantasy canon. Leaned on ideas because the absence of a single one is the whole argument.

Exited at the below-the-line gate. Form and genre are a young-adult portal fantasy novel: a London teenager under treatment for cancer falls asleep holding a notebook and wakes in a sixteenth-century Venice analogue, where he is drawn into an assassination plot against the city's ruler. There is one real thing in the premise - a boy whose waking life is illness and whose other life is health, which gives his wanting something a genuine engine - but I cannot name an idea the book leaves behind beyond the wish-fulfilment of the crossing itself, and the political intrigue is a plot rather than a question worked out. That is what keeps competent books in the 60s, and one more pushback sits on top of it: the register and audience are frankly juvenile, the cost Narnia 67 paid for children as the main characters and it lacking higher things to think about. The lead being destined to save the city is a chosen-one framing, and since 2026-10-24 that costs nothing for how central it is, only for careless or mocking handling, which nothing here suggests - so it no longer counts, and the range rose two points. The lead's age is the small life-phase discount only. The talisman-and-sleep crossing looks like a declared mechanism rather than a rite, but the order of Stravaganti and how their power is conferred is exactly where a rite hides late in a book, and that is unexamined here, as the ladder permits at this gate. Leaned on ideas because the absence of one is what carries the number.

t: Svata valka, kterou vedl Saddaj s Diabolem o hlavni mesto sveta, aneb, Ztrata a znovuziskani mesta Duse (The Holy War Made by Shaddai upon Diabolus)
why: The positive case is real and it is the same one that carried Labyrint sveta a raj srdce 70: a single conceit declared precisely and then worked out, the soul as a walled town whose gates are the eye and the ear and whose officers can be bought. Animal Farm 78 shows a book-length allegory with a nameable idea costs nothing for being allegory. Two deductions push it under the line anyway. First, the reader wants faith as a thread inside a story and not theology as a subject in its own right, and here the doctrine of grace is not a thread but the content, which is why axis:ideas sits in risks: what the book leaves behind may be catechesis rather than a thought. Second, and this is what carries the number, the cast is a list of labels - Understanding, Conscience, Willbewill - so nobody can want a different thing from anybody else, which is the exact axis Golden Son 92 scores on and the one Bunyan's form forbids. Leaned on axis:faith and axis:character-differentiation rather than axis:density, because length is not the objection; a 250-page siege conceit is thin story per page but the reader corrected that penalty to density, not length. Exited at C on one source, so the occult question is unexamined - petitions to Shaddai and Emmanuel sit inside a Christian allegory's own frame, the register of the 91 memoir and of Labyrint 70 rather than the Greek pantheon that put Percy Jackson at 57, but that was reasoned, not sourced.

t: Svet na konci casu (The World at the End of Time)
why: Exited at the below-the-line gate, and I overspent it by one source - two rather than the budgeted one - because the first told me the premise and not whether it holds. Form and genre are a standalone hard-SF novel. The idea is nameable and large: a colony's star is hijacked and accelerated by a plasma-based intelligence, and a man frozen and thawed across millennia watches his settlement drift toward the heat death of the universe. That is the shape the reader rewards when it is followed through - astrophage's second-order consequences are exactly why Project Hail Mary 92 beat The Martian 82. But the doubt is about whether it is followed through, and it is sourced rather than guessed: the contemporary review calls the book often irritating and never very satisfying, lots of tantalising bits and pieces but no shapely whole, the alien antagonist a disappointingly banal super-being, and the ending abrupt with half the author's attention on a sequel. An inventive premise that does not cohere into one thing is the reason Unfinished Tales 69 is the lowest Tolkien in the log, and a payoff that does not arrive is the opposite of the earned reveal that held Golden Son 92 together. Two strands alternating between the colonists and the plasma being also splits page time away from anyone's motives. So the doubt sits on ideas, which is why I stopped here rather than researching the graded axes; occult status is unexamined, as the ladder permits at this gate.

Exited at the below-the-line gate. Form and genre settle it cheaply: a retrospective collection of one Czech author's SF short stories, drawn from two earlier collections plus magazine pieces, the publisher's own framing being a return to the nineteen-eighties and a sceptical optimism about spaceflight and shared human ideals. Written in Czech originally, so nothing is lost in translation, and the log shows the reader is at ease with Czech voices - Saturnin 78 scores in the A band on voice and character with no idea worked out at all. But that is the ceiling case for a Czech book with charm and no premise, and it was a novel with one narrator; a collection has neither a protagonist to be interesting nor a premise whose consequences accumulate, and the short-form suspension only removes penalties. A stance is not an idea: I can name the mood the stories share but not one thing the book leaves behind, and Czech reader ratings for it sit in the middling band. That is the default band, just under the line. Occult status is unexamined, as the ladder permits at this gate. Leaned on ideas because it is the absence of a nameable one across a collection that carries the number.

Exits at gate 4. Form and genre are settled from the annotation and confirmed: a themed anthology of Czech biological science fiction, nine or ten contributors, one editorial brief. It has more of a case than most collections, and the case is the theme itself - what it means to be human and how long we stay that way, pushed to the boundary and across it - so I can name an idea, which is why this takes the default band rather than the low one. But I would put axis:ideas in risks and that is what decides the exit. A collection has no single premise whose consequences get worked out over a book, and reviewers of this one report exactly the failure that follows: quality fairly uneven, interesting ideas killed by confused or unfinished execution, endings and inconsistencies that needed more editorial care. The strongest read anchor is Unfinished Tales 69, the log's lowest Tolkien by twelve points, and the stated reason there was precisely that the pieces are not logically connected to one another. On top of that the short form suspends the character and emotion rules, which removes penalties but adds nothing, so the axis that tops this log - page time on what characters want and why, as in Speaker for the Dead 90 - cannot be earned across nine separate casts. One further note in the same direction: a reviewer faults one story for head-hopping between characters inside a single paragraph, which is the legibility problem that produced this log's three scores of 30. Not leaned on character-differentiation: with a new cast every story that axis has nothing to measure. Occult is unexamined by design at this gate.

Exits at gate 4 on the lower band, and the deciding fact is one the annotation conceals: this is thirty-two hardback pages with an illustrator credited alongside the author, written to introduce readers unfamiliar with Middle-earth to it. So it is a picture-book primer, not the encyclopedia the author's name suggests - he is separately known for genuine Elvish-language reference work, which is a different set of books. Both conditions of the low band are met. There is no idea of its own to name: it summarises another writer's invented world, notes that he built more than ten languages, and walks through a few figures - how Smeagol became Gollum, the dragon, the skin-changer - which is orientation for a newcomer rather than something left behind, and secondary literature earns nothing by its form, the point the log makes twice over with Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 against The Diary of a Young Girl 40. And the form suspends the character and emotion tests entirely: no protagonist, no plot, nothing for the axis that tops this log to measure. The profile's own scale for how juvenile a book is puts a picture book in the thirties or forties, and that is the register here - well below where Ranger's Apprentice 74 and Narnia 67 paid only a little. There is one real pull the other way, and it is why the band reaches to 55 rather than lower: this reader has read the whole Tolkien shelf and scores The Silmarillion 80, so the subject is genuinely his. But a thirty-two page introduction to a world he already knows better than the book explains it has nothing to tell him. Not leaned on childrens, though it applies: what carries the number is that no idea can be named at all. Occult is unexamined by design at this gate and there is no reason to expect it here.

t: Tri okamziky exploze (Three Moments of an Explosion: Stories)
why: Exits at gate 4, and on both of the conditions rather than one. Form and genre: twenty-eight literary weird-fiction stories, several of them formal experiments - film-trailer pieces, numbered-viewpoint fragments - which is the literary-fiction-plus-collection combination that sits below the line four times out of five. The conceits are undeniably strong and I can name them, which is what keeps this in the default band: icebergs adrift over London, drowned oil rigs walking ashore, carved patterns inside a cadaver's bones. But an image is not an idea worked out, and axis:ideas belongs in risks here on the reviewers' own account: the very short experimental pieces read as the author displaying a conceit rather than developing it, the title piece is faulted for having no room to develop, and the most-praised story is faulted for an ending that dodges. That is the Unfinished Tales 69 diagnosis - pieces not logically connected to each other, twelve points off an author otherwise scored in the 80s - with the twist that here the disconnection is deliberate. The short form then suspends the character and emotion rules, so nothing can be earned on the axis that carries Speaker for the Dead 90 across twenty-eight separate casts. One more thing points the same way and it is this reader's most reliable failure: the method reviewers describe as the collection's signature is starting mundane and then withholding what the world's rules actually are, and unresolved fragments of that kind are the shape that produced 30 for The Colour of Magic and The Gunslinger - though a story dropped is not a book abandoned, so it lowers the number rather than firing the filter. Not leaned on worldbuilding: nothing here is sustained long enough for self-consistency to be tested. Occult is unexamined by design at this gate; the register a starred review compared to Lovecraft makes that check necessary before any higher number.

Exits at gate 4. Form and genre settle at once - a young-adult vampire novel, five hundred pages, first person, running two parallel storylines. There is a positive case and it is on the axis this reader weights heaviest: the engine is a want and a vow rather than a set piece, a girl leaving her duty and her friend behind to find and kill the man she loves because she promised him she would, which is motive doing the work. That is why this takes the default band rather than the low one. What decides the exit is that I would put axis:ideas in risks and there is nothing to argue with there: it is a revenge-and-grief arc inside an established world, reviewers call the plotting simplistic and predictable, and I cannot name anything the book leaves behind. Three deductions in the same direction. It is a sequel and not an independent one - the vow, the turned lover, the psychic bond with the princess and the pact behind all of it are established elsewhere and assumed here, and sequels are not safe bets in this log, Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. Reviewers report the middle drags, the flashbacks do not propel anything, and the parallel storyline's timing is confusing where the lead sees through another character's eyes - which is the multi-viewpoint legibility problem this reader is least tolerant of. And it ends on a cliffhanger, which the log's one measurement of unresolved structure, Unfinished Tales 69, gives no credit for. Not leaned on childrens or life-phase: a teenage lead is not an objection in itself here, Sunrise on the Reaping 87 settles that, and the number is set by the absent idea. Occult is unexamined by design at this gate, and a world of elemental and spirit magic with a shadow-bond and the undead plainly needs the conferral test run before any higher number could stand.

t: Veda na Zemeplose (The Science of Discworld IV: Judgement Day)
why: Exited at the below-the-line gate on form. This is not a novel: it is a popular-science book whose chapters alternate with a short Discworld story, the science sections functioning, in the publisher's own phrase, as very big footnotes that interrupt the fiction. The log has one measurement of that shape and it is the worst Tolkien result - Unfinished Tales 69, marked down precisely because the pieces are not logically connected to each other - and here the disconnection is the design rather than an accident of assembly. The science half is reported to be less hard science than the psychology of religious belief, which is the one subject the profile rules out on its own account: faith is wanted as a thread inside a story, not as the subject, and a courtroom argument about whether the wizards' creation of our world mocks a religion is the subject. The fiction half is reviewed as not among this author's better stories, so the thing that would have to carry the book is the weaker half; that the author himself is not the obstacle is settled by Mort 83 against The Colour of Magic 30. I doubt it leaves one idea behind rather than a tour of several, which is what puts it under the line. Also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log - Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. Occult status is unexamined, as the ladder permits at this gate. Leaned on ideas because the doubt about what survives the reading is what carries the number; density and faith are the named deductions behind it.

Eighteen stories of colonial marines against xenomorphs, licensed, declared non-canon and written to one brief: a squad, a hive, kill or be killed. The below-the-line gate asks for one idea and there is none to name - reviewers say plainly that the appeal is more time inside a film's atmosphere, rate it story by story, and report the best material front-loaded and the back half thin. A collection has no single premise whose consequences can be worked out, so axis:ideas has nothing to lean on, and the short form suspends the character rules without adding anything back: eighteen casts introduced and dropped leaves nobody to understand or root for, which is the axis that separates Mockingjay 91 from Ballad 65 by the same author in the same world. Both conditions the lower band requires are met - no nameable idea and a form that suspends the character tests - so the number goes there rather than to the default. Exited on axis:ideas. Occult status is unexamined at this exit by design.

Exits at gate 4, and on the lower of the two bands. Form and genre are settled and both count against it: a collection of loosely chained stories in a pseudo-medieval hexer setting, whose organising principle is a biography - conception forward - rather than a premise. That is the shape where the character and emotion rules are suspended, so the collection cannot earn on the axis that tops this log; and having no single premise it has no idea to lean on either. I looked for one and cannot name it: sources describe a raw world, coarse vocabulary and a disillusioned view of things, which is a register, not something the book leaves behind, and 'it is short so the risk is low' is not a case for reading it. Both conditions of the low band are therefore met, which is why this sits below the default C range rather than in it. Two further deductions in the same direction. Sexual content is a declared feature of this register and reviewers single this volume out as the more erotically charged of the two, so it takes volume as well as treatment - the pairing that sank The Witcher 53. And a reviewer of these stories specifically reports getting lost in the texts and finding them disjointed, which is the log's most reliable predictor and the reason The Colour of Magic and Guards! Guards! both landed at 30 - though here it is one reviewer's reading experience rather than an established opening shape, so it lowers the band rather than firing a filter. Not leaned on protagonist: the lead is reported as vivid and distinct, so she is not the weak point. Occult is unexamined by design at this gate, and a hexer world with vampires and Dark Ones needs the conferral test run before any higher number could stand.

Exited at the below-the-line gate. This is an anthology of new Czech SF short stories commissioned for the bicentenary of Mendel's birth - an occasional piece in the literal sense, its unifying element a subject heading rather than a premise. Genetics is a topic, not an idea worked out: nothing accumulates across the pieces, there is no protagonist to be interesting or worth rooting for, no motives developed at length, and no declared world whose rules have to hold, so every axis the reader scores on is unavailable and the short-form suspension removes penalties without adding points. Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82 are the log's short winners and each carries one nameable idea to the end; an anniversary commission by many hands to a brief does not, and the log's one measurement of unconnected pieces is its lowest Tolkien, Unfinished Tales 69, where the fragments at least shared a world. No idea I can name plus a form that suspends the character tests is the low band by definition rather than the default one. Occult status is unexamined, as the ladder permits at this gate. Leaned on ideas because the absence of one is the entire finding.

t: Zkazky z planety Zeme (Tales from Planet Earth)
why: Fourteen stories written across four decades and gathered on nothing tighter than being set on this planet - undersea ranching, a wall of darkness, a man who ploughs the sea. Each has a conceit, so this is not a book with no idea in it, but there is no single premise whose consequences get worked out over a whole book, and that is what earns the high scores in this log; Unfinished Tales 69 is the standing measurement of what a set of pieces not aligned with each other costs even from an author the reader admires, and it is the lowest score that author has. Short fiction also suspends the character rules without adding anything back, so fourteen casts introduced and dropped cannot supply the interiority that puts Red Rising 95 and Mockingjay 91 on top, and readers rate this selection story by story with several duds among the good ones. Exited at the below-the-line gate with axis:ideas as the doubt: I can name the individual conceits but not one thing the volume leaves behind. Occult status unexamined at this exit by design.

t: Protovy svety (K-PAX III: The Worlds of Prot)
why: Exited at the below-the-line gate. Form and genre are an SF novel written as a psychiatrist's case record of sessions with a patient who says he is an alien sent to report on Earth, the reader never being told which he is. The premise is genuinely the reader's kind of thing - an outsider asking what about us is actually plausible and defensible is the rigour that earned Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 - and the ambiguity is a real idea. The doubt is that this book is where the idea gets worked out. It is a sequel, a further pass over a device already delivered, and the annotation itself leans on what came before to tell you who these people are; sequels are not safe bets in this log, where Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70 and the Ender sequence settled nine points off its peak. The session-transcript form is also episodic by construction - a run of interviews rather than a plot with momentum, which is the opposite of the tight single line and constant drive that put The Hunger Games 89 at the top of the log, and it puts the visitor's verdicts on humanity in place of anyone's motives developing. So my doubt lands on whether a sequel here leaves one new thing behind, and that is where I stopped; occult status is unexamined, as the ladder permits at this gate. Leaned on ideas rather than protagonist, because the patient is the interesting figure and the objection is repetition, not thinness.

Exits at gate 4. Form and genre settle quickly - a post-collapse survival novel, single small-town setting, two antagonist threads. The positive case is genuine and it is worldbuilding of the kind this reader rewards: a declared premise (all electronics dead) whose second-order consequences are actually followed through, right down to ether for surgery, canning taught at the college and a hydroelectric plant built for morale as much as for power. That is the Project Hail Mary 92 virtue in miniature. The reason I exit here anyway is that I would put axis:ideas in risks, and reviewers say why in plain terms: it adds no new concept to the collapse premise it inherits, and its own material - a warlord meant to be the hero's dark mirror, a truce whose aftermath is dropped, a raft of loose ends left for a further volume - is reported as not paying off. So the idea that would carry a higher number belongs to what came before, restaged politically here. Against that, two graded deductions. It is a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log - Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70 - and it cannot be read without its predecessor, whose plot and cast it assumes. And the register is sustained bleakness, mass death behind and coercion ahead, which is the mild but real objection that put 1984 at 60.
