Not leaned on protagonist: the lead is decent, competent and easy to root for, closer to the Exodus 68 historical-novel position than to the Oliver Twist 57 failure, and the number is set by the missing idea rather than by him. Occult is unexamined by design at this gate and there is no reason to expect it in this material.

t: Ze Zeme na Mesic (From the Earth to the Moon)
why: The founding text of the engineered-spaceflight story, and its virtue is one this log rewards: a premise declared to the decimal and then argued in public - the launch latitude, the recoil, the barrel, the metal of the shell, the wager that it will miss - which is the Project Hail Mary 92 pleasure at a nineteenth-century tech level, and the opening is one clear concrete situation, a club of artillerymen with nothing left to shoot at. Two things hold it down. Obligation scales with how precisely a thing is declared, and Verne declares everything, then glosses the single consequence that breaks it: the acceleration inside that barrel kills the passengers, and the leather padding and springs he offers acknowledge the problem instead of answering it - so the author does not follow the rules he lays down, at the one point he undertook to explain. And nobody in it wants anything a reader can sit inside: the stated motive for the whole enterprise is filling the hole the war left, the cast are functions with a running joke for characterisation, and the comedy is national caricature stated as fact, which is what marked down Ranger's Apprentice 74. It also stops rather than ends, with the shell off course and still in flight. Leaned on axis:motives rather than axis:ideas: the idea is real and it is the whole book, but committee minutes and ballistics with no interior life is what separates the 60s from the 80s in this log, as Pycha a predsudek 75 shows from the opposite direction - wants and why were the entire book there.

t: 100 chyb pri peci o lidi s demenci
why: The structure is a hundred numbered entries, each quoting an assumption carers make, then correcting it, grouped by attitude, environment, communication, difficult behaviour, use of the patient's biography, and feeding and hygiene. The underlying line -- that behaviour with dementia has a motive worth understanding and the person's own perspective governs the care -- is decent, and it is the same instinct as the axis that tops this log, page time on what someone wants and why. But it arrives as a hundred corrections rather than as an argument, and this reader's non-fiction hits, Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75, earned their scores by examining what is actually true in a life, not by listing practice tips. A list with no single premise has no axis:ideas to lean on, and the manual form suspends the character tests while adding nothing, so both low-band conditions hold. axis:ideas carries the number. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

t: 101 tipu jak vychovat poslusneho a spokojeneho psa (Dog Training 101)
why: A practical training manual of about 175 pages: step-by-step exercises for obedience and household manners with a dog. There is no idea to name because it is instructions, and the handbook form removes every axis that carries the top of this log - no motive, no protagonist, no story - without putting anything in their place. Male zeny 79 marks the ceiling for a book with no premise to work out, and it still has characters to carry it; a manual has neither. The reader's stated penalty for description with little story applies in its strongest form here, since there is no story at all. Leaned on axis:ideas. Gate-4 exit on one source; occult status unexamined below the line.

Czech original SF comics with a real following -- 86 percent from 91 raters -- and the theme the database states is good against evil with science set against faith, which is at least an idea rather than a set of events. What I cannot do is name what it actually leaves behind: the description available is the publisher's own, and it is entirely about form, scenes cut like a blockbuster and a world with no boundary between imagination and reality. That last phrase is the exact shape that failed this reader hardest: The Gunslinger 30 and The Colour of Magic 30 were both abandoned for reading along without a graspable situation, and a comic that opens mid-spectacle cannot supply the context in prose. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log -- Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. I would list axis:ideas under risks, so gate 4 says exit at C. Occult status is unexamined at this exit, and the science-against-faith theme is where it would need looking.

t: 150 terapeutickych her pro dospivajici (Therapy Games for Teens: 150 Activities to Improve Self-Esteem, Communication, and Coping Skills)
why: This is a numbered activity catalogue for a professional running groups: 150 recreation-therapy games needing nothing but paper, pencils, a whiteboard and tape, each with tips, talking points and open questions, described by its own endorser as a recipe format. There is no argument, no narrative and no idea to name -- the finding is that there is nothing to name, which the profile says to state plainly rather than manufacture. It is also the shape gate 4 flags hardest: a collection with no single premise has no axis:ideas to lean on, and the form suspends the character rules while adding nothing, which is both conditions for the low band. The author's nearly twenty years of recreation therapy, nine with at-risk teens, make it credible as a tool and do not make it a book to read. axis:ideas carries the number. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

Exited at the below-the-line gate. Form and genre are settled - a Czech science-fiction novel, shelved by at least one retailer under science fiction for younger readers - and the honest answer on the idea is that axis:ideas goes in risks. There are two halves to the blurb and they do not join: a setting premise, that technological progress wrecked the planet and the wealthy left for lunar colonies while those who stayed must repair the damage and build something better, and then a plot that is a salvage crew at sea overtaken by a chemical attack and a protagonist swept somewhere unexpected. The first half is the interesting one and nothing indicates it gets worked out; the second is incident. That split is what the log prices: a stated capability or division has to have its consequences carried, and where a book asserts a society as its subject it must cohere - the objection that keeps Divergent at 58. There is no reception at all, professional or reader, to argue the other way. That leaves a competent-looking book with events rather than something left behind, which the log names as the most common reason such a book stalls in the 60s, alongside Exodus 68 and Narnia 67. Leaned on the idea because it is the whole argument; the protagonist and the young-reader register were not examined, since neither could lift a book past this doubt. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

A Russian-language novel translated into Czech in 2024, and everything discoverable about it is the publisher's own copy: an artificial intelligence implanted in the human brain, combined with what it calls the archetypal basis of human being, producing extreme situations created by superhuman forces inside a person. That is not an idea I can name - it is a promise that one exists - and there is no rating, review or reader comment anywhere to test it, so axis:ideas goes in risks and the exit follows. The log is unambiguous that a premise which has not been thought through is what sinks a book rather than what saves it: Divergent 58 collapsed under exactly this kind of grand assembled setup, while the books that scored on a declared capability - Project Hail Mary 92, Valka stareho muze 87 - earned it by following consequences. Nothing establishable here says which of those this is. Occult status is unexamined at this exit and is worth naming as an open question rather than an absence: apotheosis language about superhuman forces and archetypes is precisely where the elevation-mechanic rite hides, and that check was not paid for.

The premise is concrete and the local setting is a real asset: an unexplained radiation kills everyone unprotected, under five percent survive, and a city has to reinvent light, water, food and a reason to be a nation from nothing. But the reports converge on the failure this log is least forgiving of - readers call it naive, without pace or plot, closer to a civil-defence handbook than a novel, with emotionless secondary characters, and the aggregate reader rating is near the bottom of its scale. Page time on what people want and why is the axis that tops this log, Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90, and a survival manual has none of it; a dystopian setting itself is fine, as Divergent 58 shows, but the premise has to hold when thought about. So the doubt sits on whether the idea is worked out as fiction at all, and that doubt carries the number. Gate 4 answered honestly at one source; the low end is soft. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

The conceit is declared cleanly - Newton watches a bubble rise instead of an apple fall, so from the 1600s ships sail a breathable interplanetary medium - and a premise whose consequences are actually worked out is exactly what earns the top of this log: Project Hail Mary 92 for following astrophage into space travel and the energy problem, Old Man's War 87 for a world where each stage follows from the last. That is not what reviewers report being done with it. The conceit stays a backdrop for a Napoleonic sailing voyage transposed into space, with a long slack middle, flat secondary characters and a male lead who gets an exposition dump late; the automaton navigator is the one part that is genuinely mechanism with consequences. So I would list axis:ideas as the doubt, which is the gate-4 exit condition, and the nearest anchor is Ranger's Apprentice 74 - easy to read, not much to think about - with a small further pushback for a seventeen-year-old lead. Overspend declared: two sources against a C budget of one. Occult was not examined at this exit; the alternate physics and clockwork automata are presented as mechanism.

t: Arthur a minimojove (Arthur et les Minimoys)
why: Exited at the below-the-line gate on both of its conditions. Form and genre are settled without research - a short fantasy adventure for young children by a film director, written as the front end of a screen franchise, with a ten-year-old lead who must win a miniature people's trust and a princess's favour to stop a swindler evicting his grandmother. Asked honestly whether the idea holds up: I cannot name an idea at all. There is a quest and a rescue and nothing left behind afterwards, so axis:ideas goes in risks and that decides it. The register is the other half. The log puts a ceiling on what juvenile telling can reach and it is reached by books with substance underneath - Hobbit 84 and The Little Prince 82 pay nothing because the ideas carry them, Ranger's Apprentice 74 and Narnia 67 pay a little, and Narnia's stated fault is precisely children as the main characters plus lacking higher things to think about. This sits well below Narnia on the second of those, with a simpler telling and a younger audience, which is why the lower of the two mandated bands is the honest one rather than the default. Leaned on the missing idea and the juvenile register together because those are the two things I actually argued; the protagonist was not examined, since nothing it could show would lift a book with no idea in it above the line. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

The question it asks is more specific than most post-apocalyptic setups and the author is a lawyer by profession, which shows: not what machines do to us but what happens to law when the state stops existing, with corporations selling protection under contracts that read as partnership and are asymmetric in practice, and a real geography carrying a centre-to-periphery meaning of its own. That is a positive case. Against it, the recorded reader objections are the two things this log actually pays for: the world's potential was left unused, and the characters were not developed enough. Golden Son 92 was praised because three characters each want different things, and Artemis 69 is the log's clearest case that a consistent world rescues nothing when the lead is thin - so my doubt is whether the premise is worked out on the page rather than in the author's interviews. That is gate 4 answered yes, and the doubt about the idea carries the number at one source. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

A journalist's column collected into a tour of more than a hundred curious places - a decommissioned nuclear store, an acid lake, a rude-service tavern. It is genuinely entertaining material, but it is a hundred separate two-page items: no premise to work out, nobody whose motives get page time, and nothing carried from one entry to the next. That is the shape the log punishes even in fiction - Unfinished Tales 69 is the lowest Tolkien precisely because the pieces are not connected to each other - and here the assembled form also suspends the character tests without putting an idea in their place, which is the low band rather than the just-under-the-line one. Exited at gate 4 on axis:ideas, one source, so the occult question was not examined.

The opening is exactly the shape this reader wants: one POV, one concrete situation on page one - a man surfaces from a submersible to find the world drowned, and God speaks to him. The idea is real and nameable, whether intelligent life can hold a moral civilisation together or whether the flaw is inside it, and the lead is active and inventive rather than acted upon, which is the difference between the top of this log and Oliver Twist 57. Everything after that deducts. Faith is not a thread inside a story here, it is the whole subject, argued directly with God, and this log wants theology inside a story and not as one. The bleakness is total and arrives as a sequence of atrocities ending in the lead's death and the loss of everything he taught, where 1984 scored 60 on being depressing alone and Promena 58 came in twelve under prediction because bleakness and a lead hard to root for both fired at once. The man-and-chimpanzee mating is handled clinically rather than graphically, so volume and explicitness are low, but it is crude in kind, and crudeness at small volume is precisely what held Artemis to 69 and what the reader named as the cause in Ready Player One 55. The close stages a ritual throat-cutting modelled on Abraham and Isaac, with a mourning prayer over the body - a rite enacted on the page, not lore about one. I did not reject on it, because the source is scripture and direct prayer to the real God rather than occultism, and the log's fourth-highest score is a book of prayer, but if that rite does count the range is void, which is why it is the first risk. I leaned on the bleakness and on faith-as-subject rather than on the idea, because the idea is the best thing here and still cannot lift the book over those deductions.

The author's own selection of his SF short stories, described as playing with serious and light-hearted themes about the universe, humanity and the individual. That is a heading, not a premise, and a collection with no single premise has no idea to lean on - so axis:ideas is the risk and the exit follows at the cheap gate. The band is the default rather than the lower one because this is a practised writer with real craft behind him and the genre database rates it his best book, so a competent read just under the propose line is the honest expectation: Exodus 68 and Unfinished Tales 69 mark that place, and the second of those is the closer parallel - the lowest Tolkien specifically because the pieces are not logically connected to each other, which is what a career selection is by construction. Short-form work suspends the character requirements without earning anything back, and the log's short winners - Animal Farm 78, The Little Prince 82 - each carry one idea a reader can restate. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

A fairy-tale picture book for small children about a hive: bees are born, a young bee is taught by an older one, the queen visits, the kind beekeeper appears, and the named characters carry jokey diminutives with instructive captions beside cheerful drawings. There is no premise to work out and no idea I can name beyond the natural history of bees told gently, which is the finding rather than a gap in my research. The log's ceiling for this shape is set from above and below: Male zeny 79 and The Little Prince 82 clear the line because characters or ideas carry them, and the profile puts a picture book in the 30s or 40s outright. The form also suspends the character tests rather than passing them, so nothing is left to earn points. axis:childrens carries the number here, not axis:ideas, because the register and audience are the whole objection. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

Military SF: two and a half centuries of peace have left the navy a dumping ground for unwanted officers, and one aging destroyer under a jaded captain meets the first thing that shoots back. There is one real positive to name - reviewers say the author, who has an aeronautics background, worked out the physics of his universe and grounded it in current theory, which is the self-consistency axis Valka stareho muze 87 is praised for. It is not enough, because the recurring criticisms hit the axis this reader weighs higher: familiar tropes, a plot guessable from the cover, characters that one reviewer says needed more flesh, and a slow, expository start before the action arrives. Artemis 69 is the log's decisive case that consistent worldbuilding rescues nothing when the lead is thin, and the reader's own warning is never to predict a book up on worldbuilding against a thin protagonist. Beyond the setup I cannot name an idea it leaves behind, and the setup itself - decayed peacetime fleet, hostile first contact - is furniture rather than a thought. Exited at gate 4 on one source, so the occult status is unexamined.

t: Chlapec a jeho robot (A Boy and His Bot)
why: A middle-reader written for ages nine to twelve: a sixth-grader falls through an Oklahoma mound into a machine world, acquires a tiny robot and a ten-foot slaughterbot, and must fetch a database to stop a tyrant. Kirkus calls it a loose-jointed picaresque and every review reaches for the same comparison, a journey-to-Oz tale, which is the finding rather than a compliment: the book's business is the sequence of odd robot places, and I cannot name an idea it leaves behind. That puts both of the graded axes against it at once. Narnia 67 is the anchor and it is docked for exactly this pair - child leads plus a lack of higher things to think about - and this sits further toward the children's end than Narnia does, while Ranger's Apprentice 74 is what an easy adventure with little to think about earns at best. The Little Prince 82 is the counter-case that shows a juvenile register costs nothing when an idea does the work, and that is what is missing. Exited at gate 4 on one source, so the occult status is unexamined; the fetch-object is a database, not a grimoire, despite its name.

t: Co te nezabije (What Doesn't Kill Us)
why: There is a nameable idea here - comfort has been engineered so completely that an adaptive capacity has gone unused, and brown fat plus cold exposure is the proposed mechanism - and first-person nonfiction that really tests what is plausible is the log's best non-fiction result, Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91, against The Diary of a Young Girl 40 where the form earned nothing on its own. The doubt is whether this book is on the first side of that line. Its evidence is the author's own conversion from debunker to practitioner, one subject who is plainly an outlier, and an epilogue that asserts autoimmune and weight-loss benefits the reported science does not carry; the book itself notes the subject's twin has the same brown fat without doing any of the method, which undercuts the causal claim it is built on. This reader marked Ranger's Apprentice 74 down specifically for confident claims that are not true, so I would put axis:ideas in risks, which is the gate-4 exit. One source; the occult question is unexamined.

YA dystopia: oxygen is sold by the corporation that owns the domes, a rich boy and a poor girl walk out and meet tree-planting rebels. The idea is nameable in principle - air as a purchased commodity and the class system that follows - but the reviews say it is not worked out: one reader argues the oxygen concept stays a side aspect with scientifically weak justification, and Publishers Weekly warns that the book leans on well-worn government-corruption and class-warfare themes. That is the Divergent 58 failure precisely, a premise assembled from other books' parts that does not hold up under thought, and Mortal Engines 55 shows this reader abandons a book on that alone. Kirkus credits a well-realised ruined world but calls the villains stereotypical, and several reviewers report never connecting with the characters - so neither of the two axes that could rescue it, worked-out premise or a lead worth rooting for, is on offer. Hunger Games 89 is what this reader wants from a dystopia and the gap is the premise and the characters, not the genre. Three alternating first-person teen narrators is a structural flag rather than a bar, since reviewers say it is easy to follow. Exited at gate 4 on one source, so the occult status is unexamined.

This one does have a thesis a reader can carry away - the unification read as Piedmont's ascendancy, which deepened rather than closed the north-south split that still defines the country - and one Czech reader calls the narration vivid and populous rather than dry. Against that: nearly five hundred pages covering the tenth century to the twentieth, which is the density penalty in its purest form, since what this reader dislikes is thin story spread over many pages and digression without momentum - the exact gap between The Count of Monte Cristo 75 and Les Miserables 71, and a survey history is digression with no plot underneath it. Another reader reports it does not read easily and that the author's sympathies are openly one-sided. So the doubt is axis:ideas at book level rather than chapter level, which is the gate-4 exit; one source, and the occult question is unexamined.

t: Diagnostika syndromu tyraneho, zneuzivaneho a zanedbavaneho ditete
why: A multidisciplinary professional monograph, 168 pages, written by a paediatrician, a social-work professor and a special educator so that clinicians can spot the first signs of child abuse syndrome; its most distinctive chapter publishes the editor's own unpublished research on diagnosis from children's drawings. That is a real contribution and it is aimed at a practitioner, not a reader. The log's non-fiction earns its scores by examining what is actually true in a life and giving insight into how other people experience the world -- Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75 -- and the profile is explicit that the form itself earns nothing. A diagnostic-technique handbook has no idea to leave behind and no protagonist, and the form suspends the character rules while adding nothing, so both halves of the low band apply. axis:ideas carries the number. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

t: Dinotopie (Dinotopia: A Land Apart from Time)
why: There is an idea and I can name it - a society in which two intelligent species are obligately dependent on each other, whose founding rule is 'survival of all or none' - which is why this does not fall to the lower band. What decides the exit is the form: 159 pages of paintings with a found-journal text between them, presented as a naturalist's travel diary. The book is a tour of a place, not a premise followed through, and heavy description with little story is a standing deduction for this reader. The log measures it twice on much stronger material - LOTR 84 was held down because the story is very thin for the number of pages despite ideas far greater than the Hobbit's, and The Silmarillion 80 is the one book that survives having no continuous plot, on mythic weight this does not have. Its lead is a father-and-son pair who are shown things rather than wanting anything, which is the Oliver Twist 57 shape, and the register is a crossover aimed as much at children as adults, the mild cost Narnia 67 records. Leaned on density and the idea rather than on worldbuilding, because the world here is genuinely well made and the log is explicit that worldbuilding must not carry a number when the lead is thin - Artemis 69. No occult system: the setting has a code and a culture, not a magic.

t: Dite a prirodni zakony (Les lois naturelles de l'enfant)
why: There is a nameable thesis - that children learn along their own developmental laws and that a classroom built to respect them outperforms one that is not - and it is argued from a specific classroom experiment rather than merely asserted, which is more than a survey manages and more than the reader's stated bar for non-fiction usually gets. But this is a practical handbook: no protagonist, no motives, no premise whose consequences are worked out in narrative, so every axis that carries the top of this log is simply absent. What non-fiction is rewarded for here it is rewarded for twice over - examining what is actually true and showing how another group experiences the world, which is what Seeking Allah Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75 have in common - and a method manual aimed at someone who is teaching does the first only partly and the second not at all. The testimony and memoir form earns nothing by itself, as the DNF at 40 in the same form shows. So the doubt is whether the idea is something to think about rather than something to apply, and that carries the number at one source. Occult is not in play.

t: Divky od svate Magdaleny (The Magdalen Girls)
why: A 304-page historical novel set in a Dublin Magdalen laundry in 1962: a sixteen-year-old is committed by her family after a young priest confesses to wanting her, is stripped of her name and contact with the outside, and endures forced labour and punishment under a Mother Superior with secrets of her own. The subject is real and worth knowing about, and several reviewers say the book sent them to read the actual history - but that is the subject doing the work, not the book, and gate 4 asks whether the idea holds up rather than whether the topic matters. What the novel offers is immersion in institutional cruelty, and this reader draws that distinction himself: Animal Farm 78 scored because it is bleak and still gives you something to think about 'rather than immersing you in the misery', while 1984 60 was simply 'too depressing'. Chapters alternate between two girls and the nun, which spreads the page time the reader wants spent inside one person, and trade-blog reception is middling rather than strong. The teen lead is only a small pushback on its own - Ender's Game 87 settles that age is not the objection. Nothing here triggers the content filters: the priest's confession and the girls' supposed offences are the premise of their punishment, not a sexual plot, and no marriage is involved. Leaned on axis:ideas because that is the doubt carrying the number. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

A 376-page splatterpunk action novel set in 2028: a government assassin is sent into a lawless zone that serves as a prison for the worst recidivists to extract someone. That is a mission, not an idea - readers who like it say so for the pacing and the one-liners and describe the SF as a flavour over an action thriller - so axis:ideas is the risk and this exits early. The second half of the number is the lead: the recurring criticism is that he is invincible and that his psychology is inconsistent from scene to scene, which is ability granted rather than earned, and the log's own positive on that axis is explicit - Valka stareho muze 87 was praised because the characters are not rescued by luck and the author does not save the plot when it suits him. Set-piece action with no character revelation is dead weight for this reader, and Golden Son 92 was docked a notch for merely leaning that way. Violence and crudeness of language are not objections at all here, so the publisher's warnings about brutality and cannibals cost nothing. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

There is no idea here to name. It is an unofficial, self-published tie-in to a video game, released weekly in short episodes of about eighty pages, in which ten-year-old twins use their father's virtual-reality rig to enter the game world and chase its folklore villain; the invented content is the game's own blocks, creepers and dragons rather than anything the book has thought of. The form takes the character and motive tests with it - there is no premise whose consequences could be worked out, and an episode that begins in the middle of a chase and ends before it resolves has nothing to leave behind. The reader's own gradient sets the number: Hranicaruv ucen 74 for easy reading with not much to think about, Narnia 67 for children as leads and no higher things, and a picture book in the thirties or forties. A short juvenile licensed episode sits at the bottom of that gradient, not the middle, which is why the lower band applies rather than the default. axis:ideas and axis:childrens carry it together; nothing else was researched because nothing else could move it.

The conceit is clean and the opening is the shape this reader wants: one girl, one concrete situation, the Match Banquet where the state names her husband, single POV throughout - the structure that makes The Hunger Games 89 the baseline favourite. That is where the positive case ends. The premise is a courtship dressed as a dystopia: the Society is described as controlling but comfortable, the resistance is left unspecified, and the political machinery yields the page to a love triangle - which is exactly the failure that put Divergent 58 in the C band, a dystopian setting that is fine in itself around a premise that will not bear thinking about. Nothing higher is left behind, and Narnia 67 is what the log pays a competent book with no higher things to think about. Leaning on axis:ideas, not axis:protagonist: Cassia wants something and acts on it, so the lead is not the problem - the premise is, and it cannot be argued above the line. Occult status is unexamined, which an exit at this depth allows.

The catalogue signal for detective does not survive contact with the book: Cassia is looking for a particular boy in the outer provinces, which is a pursuit, not an investigation, and there is no whodunnit for the reader's satisfaction to rest on - so nothing is rejected here. What is left is thin. The dystopia's machinery stays off the page while two narrators walk through canyons, and a sequel is not a safe bet in this log anyway: Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70, the steepest series decline recorded. Alternating narrators also spend the page time on where the characters are going rather than on what they want, which is the axis that separates Mockingjay 91 from Catching Fire 83 - an arena for its own sake was the complaint there and a landscape for its own sake is the same complaint. No idea is worked out that was not already stated by the setup, so axis:ideas is what carries the number; axis:protagonist is not the lean because Cassia is active and rootable throughout. Occult status unexamined at this depth.

This is the volume that finally puts the state's machinery on the page - a plague, a rebellion and a race for a vaccine - and that is a real premise to work out, so it is not dismissible. But three narrators now share the book, and the log is consistent that page time on what a character wants beats page time on what happens: Mockingjay 91 is the favourite of its trilogy for showing the most motive and the least spectacle, and splitting the narration three ways is the opposite move. The rebellion was under-specified when it was set up and the resolution has to invent its terms late, which is the self-consistency breach the reader named in Divergent 58 - ideas assembled rather than cohering. A sequel is also not a safe bet here: Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. axis:ideas carries the number because the plague plot is the book's one claim to substance and it arrives too late to be built on; axis:protagonist is not the lean, since all three narrators are decent people trying to do something. Occult status unexamined at this depth.

Exited at the below-the-line gate. Form and genre are settled - a Czech post-collapse novel - and the idea does not hold, so axis:ideas goes in risks. The premise is a moral rather than a mechanism: humanity has been spoiled by modern comfort and made life too easy, then one day the light does not come on, unease turns into a fight for bare survival within days, and the city becomes unliveable once technological convenience is gone. Nothing about the cause is offered and the framing states the conclusion in advance, which is the opposite of what the log rewards. The books that score in this territory earn it by making a collapse follow step by step from a declared cause - Old Man's War 87 for each stage of its world following from the last, Project Hail Mary 92 for chasing the second-order consequences of its premise - while a collapse asserted as a lesson about soft modern people gives events plus a message and leaves nothing worked out. Reader reception around 68 percent on a small sample is consistent with that and gives nothing to argue against it. So just under the line is the honest record. Leaned on the idea because it is the argument; the protagonist was not examined, and nothing in the material names one to lean on. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

t: Dospele deti emocne nezralych rodicu (Adult Children of Emotionally Immature Parents)
why: The idea is nameable and it is the whole value on offer: a parent can damage a child without abuse or neglect simply by being unable to give consistent empathy, and the internalizer / externalizer split gives a reader a way to recognise it. Against that, this is self-help written to be applied rather than an argument that has to hold - reviewers criticise the typology as too binary, the label as quasi-diagnostic, and the grounding in attachment and trauma research as thin. This reader's strong non-fiction result, Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91, came from an author examining what is true at his own expense, and Son of Hamas 75 from the same first-person exposure; a framework applied to other people is a weaker thing than either. That doubt about axis:ideas is what ends the ladder at gate 4, on one source; occult status unexamined below the line.

The premise is a 1947 cautionary tale in the Verne mould written under the immediate impression of the first atomic bomb: a scientist uncritically absorbed in his own invention, and the misuse that follows. That is nameable, but the warning is also the entire idea, and readers report two styles fighting inside the book - one genuinely interested in the period's physics, one straightforwardly naive action - with prose and plot reading as 1930s rather than as the 1968 revision. What this log rewards is page time on what people want and why, Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90, and a premise whose second-order consequences actually get explored, which is what Project Hail Mary 92 was scored for; a single-warning plot with period-naive action offers neither. The Czech volume also prints two separate novels together, and Unfinished Tales 69 is the log's anchor for pieces that are not connected to each other. Gate 4's question answers yes on the idea, so I stopped there. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

The dilemma is stated plainly and it is a dilemma about wanting: a young woman with a career starting well is called home by family trouble, and has to decide between the work and the people. That is the kind of question the log rewards, and romance as the central subject is not itself a cost, Pycha a predsudek 75. What stops it under the line is that the deciding is done by prayer rather than by the character - the annotation says outright that she puts the choice to God - so the resolution is supplied by the form instead of earned inside the story, and faith is the subject rather than a thread in it, the distinction the reader draws. Several suitors and the question of which is the right one is a shape with no consequences to work out; nothing is left behind that the book has not already told you. Male zeny 79 is the ceiling a characters-only domestic novel can reach and this is a much quieter book than that. axis:ideas plus axis:faith carry the number, not axis:protagonist - Christine is active and rootable.

The opening is the good part and it is the shape this reader rewards: one concrete situation, one point of view, a man in a police station an hour after his wife drowned, who is sure he saw himself on the riverbank. The Hitchhiker's Guide 83 note names that exact virtue - opens on one concrete situation rather than fanning out - so momentum and legibility are not the problem here. The idea is nameable too: every choice spawns another world, and the worst version of you is killing the women the other versions love. What I doubt is whether it holds, and that is the honest gate-four answer. Crossing between worlds is a hallucinogen cocktail injected by a psychiatrist, which is an assertion where a mechanism is needed, and this log punishes that harder than anything except the occult: Divergent 58 for a premise that collapses under thought and Mortal Engines 55 abandoned in the first chapters on nothing but that. Reviewers report the multiverse turn reads as arbitrary once it arrives. axis:ideas is the axis I would have listed as the risk, so by the gate rule I stopped and it carries the number instead. The detective bar was examined and does not apply - the killer's identity is given, the satisfaction is the chase. Occult status unexamined at this exit; the drug-guided crossings are what would need checking.

An illustrated pirate romp for primary-school readers - dragon pearls in the Sargasso Sea, wind gods, sirens, cannibals sharpening their forks, and a subplot about getting a friend's mother to stop being cross. The number is set by register, not by quality: on axis:childrens the log pays nothing for Hobbit 84 and The Little Prince 82 because the ideas carry them, a little for Ranger's Apprentice 74 and Narnia 67, and this is written several years younger than either, with jokes rather than anything to think about. I cannot name an idea it leaves behind, which is the finding rather than a gap. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log - Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70 - though the episodic adventure form means nothing is inherited that would block it. Exited at the below-the-line gate, so occult status is unexamined: wind gods and sirens are the thing that would need checking.

This is a set of short reflections, not a narrative, so the character and motive tests are suspended - and the log is explicit that the suspension removes penalties without adding any, so what is left has to be the thinking. There is a nameable thesis: that every age divides into those whose position lets them decide how others live and everyone else, and that the pattern repeats across history. A historian arguing that from the sources is not nothing, and one Czech reader credits it with leaving the conclusions to the reader rather than imposing them. But the reader's non-fiction bar is specific and high - Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 earns its place by genuinely examining what is plausible and what is not, and Son of Hamas 75 by insight into how another group experiences the world - and opinion columns on the present day, whose critics charge exactly a mixture of fact and speculation presented as folk wisdom, are the opposite operation. Nor is a subject argued in its own right what this reader wants; he takes ideas inside a story and declines them as a standing topic. Fragmented pieces also draw the objection that cost Unfinished Tales 69 its place at the bottom of that author's row, that the parts are not connected to each other. axis:ideas carries the number: the thesis is real but asserted rather than tested.

t: Evropske panovnicke rody (Eine feine Gesellschaft: Europas Koenigs- und Kaiserhaeuser im Spiegel ihrer Skandale)
why: Popular history of nineteenth-century courts told through their scandals: dynastic marriage markets, mistresses and secret partners, neglected children, playboy heirs, and the new mass press that sold all of it. Gate 2 was examined first and does not fire - affairs are recurring subject matter in a survey of court society, not the premise of a narrative the reader is asked to live inside, and the treatment is archival rather than approving - so I grade it and state the doubt instead of rejecting, because a wrong reject cannot be undone. What ends the ladder is gate 4: a chapter-per-scandal collection with no premise followed through, and the one thesis available, mass media turning dynastic misbehaviour into public scandal, is asserted rather than worked out. The short works that score here, Animal Farm 78 and The Little Prince 82, are there for one idea each; an anecdote survey has none. Leaned on axis:ideas. One source; occult status unexamined below the line.

A corporate-finance textbook: ratios, statement analysis and worked examples for students and practitioners. Judged as reading rather than as a course text there is nothing the log rewards - no premise whose consequences unfold, no character at all, nothing to think about once the method is learned - and the textbook form removes the character tests while adding no idea, which is the low band. This is a competence to acquire, not a book that leaves something behind, and even the shortest books that score here do so on one idea, Animal Farm 78. Exited at gate 4 on axis:ideas, one source, so the occult question was not examined.

Novel, 275 pages, adult satirical SF - the author's own subtitle calls it an escapade in the manner of science fiction, and library annotations decline to file it as genre SF at all, calling it an intellectual game played with the form. The idea I can name is a caricature of human political history run through an alien species - a theocratic state, a proletarian revolution, a dictatorship, then democracy - but I would put axis:ideas in risks and that is the exit: readers report the pace is placid, that it is description of the alien society and comparison with ours rather than anything happening, and that the author dropped the point he had set up before the end and moralised instead. That is the combination that stalled Unfinished Tales 69 and LOTR 84 - real material, no story pulling through it - and here there is no interiority to offset it, since the lead is a talking dog the author admits is a self-caricature. Occult status is unexamined at this exit; the theocratic phase of the alien society is exactly where a rite could sit, and it was not checked because a book at this range is off the reading list either way.

An illustrated Czech junior adventure: fifth-graders with a shrinking device that works for sixty minutes, a gothic underground railway beneath Prague, a comic villain professor, a noir pastiche register and a mini-airship. Reviewers place it at roughly nine to thirteen for independent reading and recommend parent-and-child reading, and the illustrations carry a share of the telling. On axis:childrens that sits well below anything the log has forgiven: Narnia 67 was already docked for children as the leads and for lacking higher things to think about, and Ranger's Apprentice 74 for being easy with little to think about - this is further from the reader's register than either, and there is no premise here whose consequences get worked out, only a gadget and a chase. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log - Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. No idea to name plus a form that suspends the character tests puts it in the lower of the two C bands. Occult status is unexamined at this exit. One source, within budget.

An illustrated Czech junior adventure aimed at roughly eleven to fifteen: three friends hunt a baroque alchemist's invention hidden in a secret chamber, then use it to fly to a doughnut-shaped counter-Earth, with a talking frog and a comic villain professor along the way. The catalogue signal for detective does not fire filter 4 - the satisfaction is a treasure hunt and a gadget, not finding out who did it - but nothing replaces it: there is no premise whose consequences are worked out, only a chain of inventions. On axis:childrens the register sits below Narnia 67, which was already marked down for children as the leads and for having nothing higher to think about, and below Ranger's Apprentice 74. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log - Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. No idea to name plus a form that suspends the character tests puts it in the lower C band. Occult status is unexamined at this exit, though the alchemist here reads as a source of gadgets rather than of rites. One source, the shared author-level source, within budget.

The positive case is the one the log rewards hardest twice over. First, page time goes to what people want and why: the whole book is Willem's conciliatory vision for a rebuilt society against Domingo's creed that men are animals, with the boy pulled between them and reading his father's openness as weakness - the axis that puts Speaker for the Dead on 90 and Mockingjay on 91. Second, the premise is worked out in order rather than asserted: food and warmth in year one, then raiding gangs, then committee factions and a pastor challenging the founder's authority, each following from the last, which is exactly the consequence-chaining credited to Old Man's War at 87 and to Project Hail Mary at 92. The lead also has a real fault to overcome and is not a villain descent, and the survival is shared rather than solitary, avoiding the one thing the log names against The Martian at 82. Deductions keep it under the 87 band: the narration is layered with Amanzi History Project recordings from many residents and handles time non-linearly, and reviewers say that disorients - the log's most severe structural objection, and the reason Unfinished Tales sits at 69 for pieces that are not connected to each other. The resolution is also widely called rushed and conveniently wrapped, and a drawn-out or unsatisfying ending already cost The Martian points. Sustained post-collapse bleakness costs mildly, and a thirteen-year-old lead a couple of points, both softened by the adult retrospective frame. Leaned on motives and worked-out consequences rather than on the protagonist, because the log's clearest warning is against predicting up on worldbuilding when the lead may be thin, and the boy's interest here is asserted by reviewers rather than something I could verify.

The premise is real and the book actually spends itself on it: two consciousnesses share one body and argue, so almost every page is what one of them wants and why the other resists, which is the axis the log tops out on at Red Rising 95 and Speaker for the Dead 90, and the invader coming to love what her host loves is a nameable idea. The opening is the shape the reader asks for - one concrete situation, one point of view, an alien waking up implanted in a captured woman - so filter 2 does not touch it, and there is no invented power system at all. Three costs pull it down to the line. It runs past six hundred pages on a story that reviewers agree sags for a long middle stretch, which is the thin-story-over-many-pages term that held LOTR 84 below its ideas and dragged out the ending of The Martian 82. The lead is handed almost no fault to work against - the recurring complaint is that the author likes her characters too much to put them under real stress - and a lead with nothing to overcome is the failure that separated The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 from Sunrise on the Reaping 87. And the parasite biology has gaps readers raise unprompted, the declared-capability-without-consequences breach that put Divergent 58 and Harry Potter 51 in the C band. Leaned on density and the lead rather than on ideas, because the premise is the one thing even hostile reviewers praise; worldbuilding is the risk that could take it under. Sexual content is low on all three dimensions.

Czech near-future SF, 188 pages: an energy conglomerate risen from the wreck of the state utility launches its own space television while its ships terraform planets, and an apparition recurs in a nuclear control room. That is a premise, and I could not find an idea it carries. The one substantive genre-press review is severely negative on exactly the axis this reader cares about - it reports that the book provokes bafflement and dissatisfaction and that even a reader used to demanding work is left unsure what the intended message is, and reader ratings put it well below the author's non-SF novels. Labyrint sveta a raj srdce 70 shows what carries an idea-led Czech book into the B band: an idea nameable in a phrase. Nothing here supplies one, and Saturnin 78 is the alternative route - voice and character - which the same review does not credit either. So axis:ideas carries the number and the number sits under the line. Exited at gate 4 on one source, so the occult status is unexamined despite the apparition and the Vatican device material.

t: Hvezdny hrad (Le Chateau des etoiles / Castle in the Stars)
why: The premise is clean and nameable -- the discovery of aether moves the space race to 1869, so Bavaria's dreamer king builds a spacecraft of copper and wood while Prussia hunts the research -- and a boy searching for the mother who vanished in a balloon at the edge of space is a concrete, legible starting situation, which is exactly what this reader wants after the confusing-opening failures. But it is comics, and every review that praises it praises the watercolour: the consensus phrase is Jules Verne meets Miyazaki, the plot is called a competent and occasionally silly Verne pastiche, and even sympathetic reviewers report the storytelling stalling once the spectacle is established. The book that carries that shape in the log is Hranicaruv ucen 74, 'easy to read, but not much to think about', and this has far less text to work with -- the medium does the wondering for you. Reviewers put the sweet spot at nine to thirteen, so axis:childrens costs about what it cost Narnia 67 rather than what it cost Hobbit 84. I would list axis:ideas under risks, so gate 4 says exit at C. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

t: Jak draha je nepoctivost (The (Honest) Truth About Dishonesty)
why: The idea is easy to name and it is a good one: almost everyone cheats a little, rationalises it, and is moved by conditions rather than by the size of the prize - the fudge factor - and the book is built on experiments meant to test it. The trouble is the axis this reader weighs most heavily in non-fiction. The 2012 PNAS study on signing an honesty declaration at the top of a form, one of the popular results this argument carries, was retracted in 2021 after analysts concluded the dataset was fabricated, and the insurer that supplied the data confirmed it had been altered; a further allegation about another of the author's datasets was published in September 2026. Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 scores where it does because it tests what is actually plausible, so a book about honesty whose evidence base has partly collapsed fails that test at its own subject. That doubt about axis:ideas is the gate-4 exit, on one source; occult status unexamined below the line.

t: Jak se uspesne ucit s ADHD (Erfolgreich lernen mit ADHS: Der praktische Ratgeber fuer Eltern)
why: A parents' handbook from two learning-coaching psychologists: strategies for homework battles, concentration, forgetfulness and chaos, protecting a child's self-worth after failure, and working with the school, developed in practice with hundreds of families. It is advice to apply rather than a case to follow - no premise whose consequences are worked out, no idea of its own to carry away - and the guide form removes the motive and protagonist axes that carry the top of this log without adding anything. The non-fiction that scored for this reader, Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75, both earn on first-person examination of something true and costly; a competent practical manual has no equivalent to offer. Leaned on axis:ideas. Gate-4 exit on one source; occult status unexamined below the line.

A 139-page film tie-in: a boy who can teleport to places he has been watches men murder his parents at nine and grows up with two goals, survive and kill them. Teleportation is a declared mechanism with no rite attached, and the opening is one concrete situation, so nothing disqualifies it - but that is only a failure to disqualify. What is missing is the idea: the book's business is survival and revenge, reviewers report a repetitive and predictable plot, and one argues it carries the usual tie-in weaknesses of rushed plot and thin cohesion. Ranger's Apprentice 74 is the ceiling for easy-reading adventure with little to think about, and that book at least had fourteen volumes of company rather than a commissioned 139 pages. It is also a series entry written to a screen adaptation, and continuations are not safe bets in this log - Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. A hunted teenage lead costs only a little, Ender's Game 87 settles that, so life-phase is not the objection. Exited at gate 4 on one source, so the occult status is unexamined.

One premise stated precisely and the whole book is its consequences, out to the largest one: if human observation is what collapses possibility into a single outcome, then a species that does that is destroying every other civilisation's futures - which is why something sealed the solar system off. Each step follows from the last rather than being asserted, the axis Project Hail Mary 92 and Valka stareho muze 87 are explicitly praised for, and it leaves an idea behind, which is the thing that lifts books out of the 60s in this log. The commercial neural mods are declared as engineering, with suppliers and prices, so the world carries the consequences of its own declared capability. Opening bar cleared: one concrete situation, a single first-person investigator taking a missing-person case, no second thread to track. Deductions, and they are why the range is not higher: the lead spends the book with his grief chemically suppressed and then has his loyalties overwritten by an implanted mod, so what he wants is not his own - the rooting failure that put Promena 58 twelve points under prediction and Oliver Twist 57 near the floor - and the close kills millions and leaves him in a refugee camp, the bleakness 1984 60 was docked for. Leaned on the idea and the self-consistency rather than on the protagonist, because the premise is the book and the man is its instrument; that is also exactly what could pull it below the range.

t: Kazdy je na neco chytry (You're Smarter Than You Think: A Kid's Guide to Multiple Intelligences)
why: The claim is nameable -- being clever is more than marks, arithmetic speed or memory, and Gardner's eight intelligences give a child eight ways to be good at something. The decisive fact is who it is written for: the publisher's own annotation puts it at children of roughly eight to twelve, and the book's mechanism is a child working out which of the eight kinds of smart he is, in phrasing pitched at that age. That is the heavy end of axis:childrens, where the profile puts a book whose register and audience are juvenile well below what Narnia 67 paid, and it is a self-discovery guide rather than a book that examines whether the multiple-intelligences theory is actually true -- the rigour that earned Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91. Non-fiction with no narrative, so the character rules are suspended and add nothing. axis:childrens carries the number rather than axis:ideas, because there is an idea here and it is the audience that sinks it for a 28-year-old reader. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

t: Klid pred bouri (Beyond the Gathering Storm)
why: There is a real internal conflict on offer - a foundling raised by another family choosing his adoptive father's vocation partly to outrun his own past, then finding the Mounted Police and a widow with a small son pulling in opposite directions. Motive over action is the axis that tops this log, and a book about which of two lives a man will pick is at least aimed at it; the widow is unattached, so there is no infidelity question to answer here at all. But the frontier-police setting is scenery rather than a premise with consequences, and the resolution of the pull is a moral lesson the inspirational form supplies in advance rather than something the book works out. Faith is the subject rather than a thread inside a story, which the reader separates deliberately. Against Male zeny 79, which shows a plotless domestic story clearing the line on characters alone, this is the gentler and much lower-stakes version, and Narnia 67 is what a competent book with nothing higher to think about is worth. axis:ideas and axis:faith carry the number rather than axis:protagonist, since Henry is likeable and wants something definite.

t: Kognitivni trenink pro treti vek (Kognitivni trenink pro treti vek)
why: A practical handbook of memory and cognition exercises for older adults and for people working with dementia - material to be worked through rather than read. Exit at gate 4 on axis:ideas: there is no idea to name at all, only a set of tasks, and the form removes everything the reader scores on - no premise, no consequences followed through, nobody whose wants get page time, which is the axis Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 win on. The non-fiction that landed in this log examined what is actually true from inside a life (Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91); an exercise book asserts nothing to examine. Lower band because both of the low-band conditions hold: no nameable idea and a form with no character tests to pass. A small further pushback on axis:life-phase, since the intended user is decades from the reader. Occult status is unexamined, as the ladder allows here. Overspend declared: two retrievals against a budget of one, because the record had to be located before it could be read.

t: Komu se da verit? (Who Can You Trust? How Technology Brought Us Together and Why It Might Drive Us Apart)
why: One argument, and it is nameable: trust has moved from local to institutional to what the author calls distributed trust, and the mechanism is the trust leap - we will not buy from a stranger but we will through a platform. That is the shape this reader rewards when the consequences are followed through; Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 sits where it does because it tests what is actually plausible. Here the follow-through is the weak part: the book concedes that distributed trust breaks down when things go wrong and does not resolve it, and the case material - platforms, the darknet, Chinese social credit - illustrates rather than argues, dated to 2017 reporting. That doubt about axis:ideas is what ends the ladder at gate 4, so the number is the band under the line rather than a refined figure. Leaned on axis:ideas and not axis:memoir-form, since none of this is testimony. One source; occult status unexamined below the line.

Two village children meet Czech saints in turn, each encounter a self-contained lesson in a named virtue -- courage, mercy, humility. That is catechesis in story form, and the profile is explicit that faith works as a thread inside a story and not as the subject in its own right, which is what this is: the structure is one saint, one value, repeat, with no premise running through it. It is also episodic rather than a single narrative, so the character and motive tests that top this log -- the page time Mockingjay 91 spends on what people want -- have nothing to attach to, and the form suspends those rules without adding anything in their place. Register and audience are small children, which is the heavier end of axis:childrens, well past what Narnia 67 paid. axis:childrens carries the number rather than axis:ideas, since the didactic frame is deliberate and doing its job for its own audience. Occult status is unexamined at this exit; the devotional material is Christian, which is the faith axis rather than that one.

t: Laska prichazi po spickach (Love Comes Softly)
why: The setup is genuinely character-shaped and the opening is one concrete situation with no ambiguity: a pregnant widow on the frontier accepts a formal marriage in exchange for shelter and the care of a motherless child. Motive is the whole engine - what each of them wants and will not say - and the log is clear that romance as the central subject costs nothing when that is what fills the pages, Pycha a predsudek 75. Male zeny 79 also puts a real ceiling in reach: a domestic story with no premise to work out can clear the propose line on characters alone. So why under it. The book's payload is a devotional lesson rather than an idea examined - this is the founding title of the inspirational category and faith is the subject, not a thread inside a story, which is the distinction the reader draws explicitly. What is left to think about afterwards is the lesson the book already stated. axis:ideas plus axis:faith carry the number; axis:protagonist is not the lean, because Marty is a woman who wants things and decides, not an Oliver Twist 57 being acted upon. Occult status unexamined at this depth.

An unseen power gives humanity thirty days to reach Antarctica, and the survivors' scientists then breed a cold-adapted subspecies intended as servants. Kirkus, the only professional review I read, praises the opening set piece and then says the novel loses its heart and narrative sweep to stiffly written scenes and didactic commentary and finds little character development - and this reader puts the protagonist above every other graded axis, Artemis 69 against Project Hail Mary 92 by one author being the log's cleanest demonstration. Readers also object that the ultimatum makes no sense when the invaders could simply have killed everyone or granted somewhere habitable, and that is the premise-logic complaint that stopped Mortal Engines 55 in its first chapters, the least plausible setting in the log. Sustained cold and mass death add the mild bleakness discount 1984 60 took. There is an idea in here - what a species owes the successors it engineers to survive it - so this is not a no-idea book, but delivered didactically and with the invaders deliberately left unexamined it is a risk rather than a support, which is why it sits in risks and the lead carries the number. Exited at gate 4 on one source, so the occult status is unexamined, though nothing in the material suggests a rite.

Twelve separate scholarly studies of how literature meets politics, worked through Franzos, Roth, Werfel and Broch and then through Russian, Chinese and American novels, with the indivisibility of freedom under collapsing empires and totalitarian regimes as the connecting claim. That claim is nameable, which is why this is not the bottom band. What holds it under the line is the form: twelve models means twelve arguments and no single one carried through, and the clearest anchor in the log for that shape is Unfinished Tales 69, the lowest Tolkien exactly because the pieces are not logically connected to each other. Academic comparative-literature apparatus also brings the density penalty, and criticism about literature is not the same experience as the literature it is about. Exited at gate 4 on axis:ideas as a book-level doubt; one source, so the occult question was not examined.

A pocket city guide built out of ranked lists of sights, restaurants and nightspots. Both of the things that carry this log's high scores are absent by construction: there is no one whose motives get page time, which is what puts Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 at the top, and there is no single idea left behind, which is how a very short book still reaches Animal Farm 78 or The Little Prince 82. A guide leaves an itinerary, and the reference form suspends the character tests without adding anything in their place, so the low band is the honest one rather than the competent-but-under-the-line band. Exited at gate 4 on axis:ideas, one source, so the occult question was not examined here.

There is a premise and it is the book's one praised element: a Prague of ten million in 2050 where any criminal with money can buy genetic and cybernetic enhancement, so the state has to field a federal unit against enhanced terrorists. That much is a nameable idea. What the reviews describe, though, is the premise used as backdrop for a shooting gallery -- a veteran hard-man inspector, one-liners, a predictable and clearly telegraphed plot, an ending several reviewers call underbaked, and one verdict of 'an action flick and nothing more'. Motives over action is the heaviest axis in this log, the one that put Golden Son 92 below Red Rising 95 for leaning on action, and this leans much further. I would list axis:ideas under risks, so gate 4 says exit at C. Kotleta's register is also crude and the reviews single out a busty sidekick, which is a live sexual-content deduction on top rather than instead. The hunt for a criminal is not a whodunnit, so gate 1 is clean. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

The one thing here that is worked out rather than decorated is the second world: a kitchen boy is taken through the rift as a slave into a rigid honour-bound empire, spends years in it, and comes back changed and outranking the people who lost him. That is a real cultural-contrast idea and it is why this is not a bottom-band number. But it is an adventure whose satisfaction is what happens next, not what it leaves behind, and the log prices that precisely: Hranicaruv ucen 74 was 'easy to read, but not much to think about', and Divergent 58 shows what happens when a fantasy premise is assembled rather than thought through. I would list axis:ideas under risks, so gate 4 says exit. A sequel too, and sequels are not safe bets in this log -- Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. Occult status is deliberately unexamined at this exit and it is the live question, because power here is wizardry with named paths, temple priesthoods and a death goddess; Harry Potter 51 and The Witcher 53 are where that lands when it fires. Overspend declared: two author searches against a one-source budget at this gate.

There is an idea and I can name it: child development runs a natural sequence that modern birth practice, schooling and anxiety interrupt, and the book is the case for that sequence. It exits early because the case is where the doubt is. Published 1977 and built on Piaget, it hangs rising autism, hyperkinesis and adolescent suicide on child-rearing errors, argues against teaching reading before eleven, and includes a chapter on child telepathy; the author concedes in his own preface that he stands at odds with the field. This reader's best non-fiction result, Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91, was earned specifically by rigour about what is plausible, so a book whose central claims fail that test belongs in the 60s rather than above them. Leaned on axis:ideas, not axis:memoir-form, because the objection is the argument and not the telling. One source, and note that the telepathy material leaves axis:occult genuinely open - the ladder stops before that gate below the line.

One catastrophe is declared and the rest of the book is its consequences worked out at the level the reader rewarded in Project Hail Mary 92 and Valka stareho muze 87: seed grain, the last two mares, who owns the guns, who is allowed to be priest, and what a village of twenty owes a fortress of ten. It is argued rather than staged - the bulk of the page time is men and women stating what they want and why, which is the axis that tops the log at Red Rising 95 and Speaker for the Dead 90 - and it runs through a single first-person narrator whose account is footnoted and contradicted by another survivor, so the lead has a visible flaw the book itself keeps pressing on. That is a stronger footing than Artemis 69, where a consistent world could not rescue a thin lead. Three deductions. The community-of-women arrangement is a sustained thread, and treating the one fertile woman as collective property is the treatment dimension that docked Artemis 69 at small volume, here at larger volume. The retrospective first stretch is slow going by every reader account, which is the thin-story cost that held LOTR 84 down and dragged out The Martian 82. Post-nuclear bleakness is the mild discount that 1984 60 measures. Leaned on motives and worldbuilding rather than on ideas because what stays with a reader here is the mechanics of a society reassembling, not a proposition. The improvised Christian priesthood is faith as a thread inside a story, which the log accepts at Quo Vadis 66, not the occult bar - no invented system, no rite of that kind.

Forty-eight short biographical portraits of women painters from the Renaissance onward, 224 pages, with the author's own drawings and - the recurring reader complaint - no reproductions of the work being discussed. That is the whole shape of the book: a survey with no single premise to work out and no continuous subject, so the character and motive tests that top this log have nothing to attach to and the short-form suspension removes penalties without adding anything. The non-fiction that earns here earns by examining what is actually true and by opening up how another group experiences the world - Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 - and forty-eight two-page lives cannot do either at that depth; Son of Hamas 75 marks the plain-account ceiling and this sits under it. axis:ideas carries the number by absence: I cannot name the thought it leaves behind beyond the framing claim itself. axis:sex-portrayal was examined and is not engaged - a history of who was excluded from the profession is not a competence contrast inside a cast. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

t: Matematika nas bavi! (Fabulous Figures and Cool Calculations)
why: An eighty-page juvenile mathematics book of facts, puzzles and experiments, catalogued as juvenile literature: no premise, no protagonist and no argument running front to back, so none of the axes that carry the top of this log has anything to grip. The children's register is graded rather than a bar and the log caps what it costs - Hobbit 84 and Little Prince 82 pay nothing for it - but that cap only rescues a book whose ideas carry it, and a set of exercises has no single idea to name. That is the low band's test exactly: nothing nameable, plus a form that suspends the character rules without adding anything in exchange. What non-fiction earns here is examining what is actually true and insight into how someone else experiences the world, the reason Seeking Allah Finding Jesus 91 sits where it does; an activity book attempts neither. Gate 4 at one source. Occult is not in play.

An illustrated comics story for children written and drawn by one hand, whose declared purpose is to make readers treat nature carefully. There is no idea here in the sense the reader wants one - a warning is a message, not a premise whose consequences are worked out - so axis:ideas goes in risks, and the form suspends the character tests rather than passing them: the leads are two mechanical fish on a journey, so nothing is wanted, nothing overcome, and the suspension removes penalties without adding anything, exactly as the log's short works show. That combination is the lower band. The ceiling on the children's axis is set by the log itself: Male zeny 79 and The Little Prince 82 show a juvenile register costs nothing when the writing carries characters or thoughts, and Narnia 67 shows it costs a little when it does not - a didactic comic sits well below both of those. Nothing establishable about it is negative in any other way; it is simply not addressed to this reader. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

Czech science fiction that opens in a Pilsen home for discarded secret agents, follows an escape and an assassin to the ruins of Tiwanaku, and then relocates the story to the planet Pu-ma, where mind and metal decide a millennia-old war; the declared influences are Frank Herbert's desert-planet saga and the ancient-astronaut theory. Readers who rate the ideas highly call the execution chaotic - unmemorable names, footnotes that explain either the notorious or the unknown by way of the unknown - and the split into two volumes reportedly left the later half with more battle and less worldbuilding. That is the pair the log punishes: Divergent 58 for ideas borrowed and assembled without cohering, and Golden Son 92 docked, at the top of the log, purely for leaning on action, since set-piece action without character revelation is dead weight. Ancient astronauts presented as the world's real history also invites the Ranger's Apprentice 74 objection to claims stated as fact. Naming the idea is possible but I would put axis:ideas in risks, which is the stated C exit, so the default band applies. Occult status is unexamined at this exit and it is a live question - the closing volume is framed by a creed thanking a Creator for immortal bodies - so this estimate should be revisited if the axis is bumped. One source, within budget.

The real asset is the half of the non-fiction axis this reader does reward: three months in two settlements reachable only by winter plane or two summer supply boats, written by someone who got inside the community and lets people say only what they choose to say. Insight into how another group experiences the world is what earned Son of Hamas 75 and half of Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91. But exit at gate 4, because I would list axis:ideas under risks: what the book carries is observed detail and a subject - assimilation, a hunting culture eroding, and what follows - rather than a proposition it undertakes to establish, and the reader's own note is that the memoir form earns nothing by itself. Two further drags at this end of the range: reviewers say the second half turns from literary reportage into a static travel diary, which is axis:density, the thin-material-over-pages penalty that also cost The Martian 82; and the eroded-culture consequences are alcohol, children not provided for and the world's highest suicide rate, so sustained bleakness applies, mildly, as at 1984 60. Default band rather than the low one because the material is genuinely first-hand and specific.

A Czech-written samurai novel told as the swordsman's own late-life notes, and the frame is a real positive: the narrator is looking back and asking what his path was for, which is page time on motive rather than on the duel, the axis that tops this log with Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90. Against that, the two historical novels actually read sit at the line - Exodus 68 and Quo Vadis 66 - and nothing here argues past them. axis:ideas is the axis I would have listed as the risk, which is the gate's own exit condition, so it carries the number here instead: the existential question is stated rather than worked out, the plot around it is a cursed Muramasa blade, mysterious attackers and a conspiracy that could destroy Japan, and the reception describes an admiring, earthier retelling of a life already famous, not a premise whose consequences get followed. That is the gate-four answer, honestly given. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets here - Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

t: Moje ADHD ma uzkosti (The Adult ADHD and Anxiety Workbook: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy Skills to Manage Stress, Find Focus, and Reclaim Your Life)
why: The clinical claim is defensible and narrowly useful -- treating ADHD and anxiety one at a time misses their overlap, so the programme addresses both together -- and the publisher's own description of the structure settles what kind of book it is: every chapter is guided exercises, reflection prompts and skill-building activities, with downloadable worksheets. That is a course to work through, not a book that leaves an idea behind, and this reader's two non-fiction hits, Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75, both earned their scores by examining what is actually true in a life; the profile states outright that the form earns nothing by itself. There is no protagonist, no premise and no narrative, so the character tests are suspended with nothing to replace them, and the low band's two conditions both hold. The Czech title's first-person framing does not change this -- it is a workbook, not a testimony. axis:ideas carries the number. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

The idea is real and nameable, which is why this is not a one-source exit: a stratospheric project to deflect sunlight is humanity's hope after decades of drought, a boy is born in Prague with the first rain, and seventy years later his brother is preaching the martyred boy's message to the survivors of the largest exodus in history - with the book's own point being that engineering the climate risks a cure worse than the disease. Readers who liked it liked the unsettling plausibility of the dystopia. The deductions land on the axes that outrank it. Reviewers report spare, documentary prose, weak dialogue and too little character depth to invest in emotionally, and the narrator is the brother who lives in the messiah's shadow and carries a legacy - a custodian rather than someone who wants something, which is the Oliver Twist 57 failure of a lead who is acted upon, and the log is explicit that the protagonist beats worldbuilding when they compete. The post-collapse world is separately called underdeveloped, and thin worldbuilding is this reader's least forgiving axis, having produced the Mortal Engines abandonment at 55. The tone is bleak throughout, which cost 1984 its 60. Faith here is the subject rather than a thread inside a story, which the profile marks down, though the treatment is serious and multi-confessional and refuses easy answers, so axis:prophecy costs almost nothing - reverence, not resemblance, is what that axis measures. Leaned on axis:protagonist rather than axis:ideas because the idea is genuinely present and it is the interiority that reviewers say is missing.

The subject is real and it is the strong part: a young border guard posted to stop people crossing to the West in 1948 who ends up walking them over instead, in the months when the frontier was sealed in law but not yet in fact. That is a life with a genuine moral turn in it, and the log's historical entries sit near the line -- Exodus 68, Quo Vadis 66. Two things hold the number down rather than lifting it.
