It is a comics retelling of somebody else's prose book, so the interiority that this reader rewards above everything -- the page time Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 spend on what people want and why -- is exactly what a 60-page comic panel-count cannot afford. And it does not tell the whole life -- the arc does not close here. Gate 2 was examined and is clean: the man is described as a great lover of women, but the book is about the crossings, not about an affair inside a marriage, so it is not premise level. I would list axis:ideas under risks on the adaptation grounds, so gate 4 says exit at C. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

t: Navrat na ostrov kamelii (Heimkehr auf die Kamelien-Insel)
why: Romance as the central subject costs nothing in this log - Pride and Prejudice 75 does well precisely because motives and what people want are the entire book - but that is also the standard this has to meet, and a comfort saga marketed on a Breton nursery garden is built on place and incident instead. The recurring reader objection is too much drama: a mother's dementia, a devastating storm flood and a dangerous accident stacked into one volume, which is event rather than revelation, and the log's own case against that is Catching Fire 83 marked down for an arena staged for its own sake. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets here - the Hitchhiker's fall from 83 to 70 is the steepest series decline in the log - and the lead, her claim on the island and her marriage are all established earlier and assumed rather than re-established. The infidelity signal does not bind: the earlier attachment named in the annotation is a past relationship of the husband's, not an affair inside the marriage, so that axis grades at nothing. What is left is the doubt that there is an idea here at all, and that carries the number at one source. Occult is not in play.

A children's SF novel that ran first as a magazine serial and was condensed for book publication, so the prose came second to the plot in its own production. The engine is a fetch-quest - a 25th-century expedition travels to 1984 to find a schoolboy's exercise books containing a principle for moving continents - and that is a device rather than an idea whose consequences get worked out, so axis:ideas is the risk and the exit follows. The log prices the rest: an easy-reading juvenile adventure with little to think about is Ranger's Apprentice 74 at its best and Narnia 67 when children carry the story and there are no higher things behind it, and this is written for a younger audience than either. It also arrives with several scientists in disguise as a group rather than one lead to follow, where the log's high scores run the other way on tight single narration - The Hunger Games 89. What can be said for it is that reader accounts split on book against television series, with the pro-book side saying it gives more of what the characters are thinking - the axis that matters most here - which is why the estimate sits at the top of the band rather than the bottom. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

The catalogue signal flagged detective and it does not bind: a vet on night duty is forced at gunpoint to operate on a wounded criminal, and what follows is coercion, an abducted daughter and entanglement with a trafficking ring run out of her own clinic. There is no investigator and the satisfaction on offer is escape and consequence rather than working out who did it, so the filter does not fire - the strand where she pieces together that the night visit was no accident is a flag, not the book's engine. Gate 4 then decides it. The form is a commercial thriller of 177 very short chapters, built for momentum, and I cannot name an idea it leaves behind; momentum alone is worth something in this log - The Hunger Games 89 and Monte Cristo 75 both bank it - but in both cases it came with a lead the reader wanted to follow and something to think about, and neither is in evidence here. What is left is competent peril, which is the shape that stalls a book just under the line. Leaned on axis:ideas as the doubt carrying the number. Occult status unexamined at this exit, as the ladder allows.

A coaching-and-therapy self-help book on the fear that comes with any change, arguing that the fear can be turned into an ally rather than treated as an obstacle. Exit at gate 4: I would put axis:ideas under risks, because that thesis is nameable but generic to the genre and there is nothing to work out - no premise with consequences, no characters whose wants get page time, which is the axis Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 win on and the one this form cannot reach at all. The reader's own non-fiction record is that the form earns nothing by itself (Anne Frank 40 against Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91) and what earns is examining what is actually true; advice literature asserts rather than examines. Default band because a thesis can at least be stated, not the lower one. Occult status is unexamined at this exit, and there is a specific reason to examine it if this ever gets promoted - see flags.

This is not a story at all: 128 pages of art instruction - materials, composition and light, then thirty step-by-step undead portraits with sketches and detail studies, aimed at fantasy illustrators and game artists. There is no premise, no protagonist and no argument, so every axis that produces a high score in this log has nothing to attach to, and there is no idea to name; the short-form suspension removes penalties without adding a point. The reader's non-fiction that worked, Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75, worked by examining what is true and by showing how someone else experiences the world, and a technique manual is a different object from either. Recorded low so it stops resurfacing rather than rejected, since no named hard filter applies - the undead here are a drawing subject, with no rite anywhere in the described contents.

This is an anthology of eight short stories by then-unpublished young Czech authors, put together by an editor whose name the catalogue records as the author, issued in 1980 by the state children's and youth publisher. Both halves of the cheap exit fire together. There is no single premise to name - the only thing common to the eight is a programme, extrapolating how people behave once technology has reshaped their circumstances, which is a heading and not an idea - and the story form suspends the character tests rather than passing them, so nothing can be earned back on the axis that tops the log. The log's short works that score well score for one idea each: Animal Farm 78, The Little Prince 82. The one that does not is instructive - Unfinished Tales 69 is the lowest Tolkien precisely because the pieces are not connected to each other, and a first-wave anthology by nine unknown hands is that failure by construction. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

The opening is a single legible situation and a Czech original with no translation between the reader and the prose, which is worth something on its own. The conceit is also concrete and rules-based: the biochip is the only property anyone owns, a conformity status decides where you work, live, eat and may go, and the young woman narrating has known nothing else until she meets a man with no chip who therefore does not exist to the system. Declared that precisely, the world has to carry the consequences, and this is where it stops. Czech readers who dislike it converge on two charges - that it is Orwell with the serial numbers filed off, and that the construction is not thought through and cut short, with dialogue at young-adult level. That is the Divergent 58 failure by name, ideas borrowed and assembled without cohering, and the reader's own 1984 60 shows even the original of the model only reaches the low C band for him. A thesis stated in advance and illustrated is not an idea left behind. axis:ideas carries the number and not axis:protagonist, because a narrator raised inside the system who starts to see out of it is a good vantage point that the book fails to spend. Erotic scenes are named in Czech reader complaints, so axis:sexual-content stays a risk although the plot is plainly not about them; occult status unexamined at this depth.

Romance at the centre of a book costs nothing with this reader - Pride and Prejudice 75 is exactly that, and it scores because what the characters want and why is the whole text - so gate 3 does not fire either: a romantic relationship as the plot is not a plot that is mainly sexual behaviour, and readers describe this as a warm romance with humour and a withheld secret. The case against it is the ordinary one. It is a contemporary workplace-and-flatmate romance with a man hiding his past, and nothing in the reported material is left behind after the couple resolves; the reader's stated complaint about competent easy reading with nothing to think about cost Ranger's Apprentice 74 real points, and this has neither a premise nor a canonical character study to offset it. Exited at gate 4 on axis:ideas, one source, so occult and the content axes were not examined.

t: Nikdy nedelej kompromis, aneb, Vyjednavej tak, jako by ti slo o zivot (Never Split the Difference: Negotiating As If Your Life Depended On It)
why: The positive case is that this is a book about what people want and why, which is the single axis that tops this log - Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 both win on page time spent inside motives rather than on action, and tactical empathy is that same move stated as a method: recognise the counterpart's perspective and say it out loud. It also does the thing the reader rewarded in Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91, which is testing whether a received account is actually true: it takes the Harvard problem-solving-and-compromise model, says the FBI abandoned it after Ruby Ridge and Waco because people are not rational, and argues the replacement from real kidnap and hostage cases. The idea is nameable in a phrase - concede nothing, get inside the other side's fears - and the case material is concrete rather than abstract, which is the opposite of the Unfinished Tales 69 fault of unconnected pieces. Deductions: the form earns nothing by itself, and a business book of techniques and anecdotes has no protagonist to be interested in or to root for, which is what keeps this out of the 80s that Son of Hamas 75 could not reach either. The range is held down mainly by axis:density, the reader's actual penalty term (The Martian 82 docked for an ending that dragged): the method is short and the book repeats it through case after case. A second, smaller drag is that reviewers find an adversarial vocabulary under the empathy - opponents to be disarmed, and borrowing a counterpart's religious vocabulary as an in-group signal - which is the kind of instrumental treatment of people that a reader who scores books on honest motive-reading may well dislike. Leaned on axis:ideas plus axis:motives rather than on axis:memoir-form, because the form is explicitly worth nothing here and the log's DNF at Anne Frank 40 shows first-person alone carries nothing.

t: Nota bene (Nolens volens, czyli, Chcac nie chcac)
why: This is an illustrated children's reference to Latin tags - where each saying comes from and what it means - not a work with a premise, so there is nothing to work out and nobody to root for, which is what the whole top of this log is made of. The children's register is graded rather than a bar, and the log caps what it can cost: Hobbit 84 and Little Prince 82 pay nothing for it because their ideas carry them, while Narnia 67 pays a little for lacking higher things to think about. That cap only helps a book that has an idea, and a list of separate entries has none to name; the form also suspends the character tests without adding anything in exchange, which is what puts it in the low band rather than the default one. What non-fiction earns here it earns by examining what is actually true and by insight into how someone else sees the world, which is why Seeking Allah Finding Jesus 91 sits where it does; a glossary does not attempt either. Gate 4 at one source. Occult is not in play in this form.

This is a gamebook - second person, branching numbered passages, character sheet and dice combat, about 264 pages - and that decides it before any content question. The axis that tops the whole log is page time on what a character wants and why: Red Rising 95 won on interiority and Mockingjay 91 on motives shown rather than action. A protagonist who is 'you' has no interiority to spend page time on and nothing to be interesting or rootable about, so the log's two heaviest axes are structurally unavailable. Reviews of the series report an interesting setting and promising premise let down by poor literary execution, awkward sentence construction, uncompromising difficulty, an unresolvable branch loop and fights settled on the first die roll, with a publisher-maintained errata page. The Mars conspiracy plot is an adventure hook, not a premise whose consequences get worked out. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log - Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. No idea to name plus a form that suspends the character tests gives the lower C band. Occult status is unexamined at this exit. One source, within budget.

A secondary-school revision compendium: literary periods, authors and set works compressed into tables, summaries and exam questions. It is a study aid about books rather than a book, so none of the axes that lift this log can engage - no premise, no protagonist, no single idea carried through - and the compressed reference form suspends the character tests while adding nothing, which is the low band. Its register is also pitched at pupils preparing for an exam, a further small pushback of the kind that cost Narnia 67 a little. Exited at gate 4 on axis:ideas, one source, so the occult question was not examined.

A 184-page adventure SF novel worked up from a comics serial the author ran in a children's magazine, and the catalogue files it under publications for children. The premise I can name is a heist - a mafia hires a former space pilot to steal the last nuclear bomb before the government fires it into the Sun - and that is a plot rather than an idea, so axis:ideas goes in risks and this exits here. Reader accounts back it up: the ones who love it say so out of childhood loyalty to the original comics and warn in the same breath that read with adult expectations the language is archaic and the plot full of gaps, and one reviewer of the book itself calls the author exhausted. Gappy plotting is the self-consistency cost, and a juvenile register is the mild deduction Narnia 67 and Ranger's Apprentice 74 measure, where Ranger's Apprentice also shows that easy reading with little to think about lands in the low 70s at best. Leaned on the missing idea rather than on the protagonist, whom nothing establishable makes either interesting or flat. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

A biographical novel about Tesla has a real subject and a good lead available - an inventor whose interior life is all wanting and reasoning, which is the axis the log rewards above all others, and gas-lit Prague and the Edison and Westinghouse rivalry are concrete ground to open on. What keeps it under the line is what the book proposes to do with it. The premise it declares is a friendship with Marconi turned into the dangerous rivalry that decides Tesla's life, which is an invented antagonism laid over documented people, and the reader has already docked a book for lazy historical claims stated as fact - Hranicaruv ucen 74, marked down for many of them. The publisher's own label is a historical science-fiction novel, so a speculative layer is being added to a life whose facts are checkable, and that is a self-consistency obligation the author is choosing to take on rather than one imposed on her. There is no idea beyond the biography that could be named from anything findable, and the book has no traceable reception at all to test it against. axis:ideas carries the number; axis:protagonist is not the lean, because Tesla as a subject is inherently interesting and it is the handling that is unknown.

t: Pan Tompkins stale v risi divu (The New World of Mr Tompkins)
why: This is a book whose entire reason to exist is leaving ideas behind, and they are nameable ones: length contraction and time dilation felt from inside, quantum indeterminacy, the birth and death of the universe, black holes and quarks, each delivered as a dream in which a bank clerk lives inside a physics regime instead of being told about it. That is the register the reader gave his highest non-fiction score to - Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 was praised precisely for examining what is actually plausible - and the short idea-driven suspension that carried Animal Farm 78 and Labyrint sveta a raj srdce 70 lifts the character requirements rather than failing them. But the suspension removes penalties and never adds points, and this book has less than those two to put in their place. Tompkins is a device, not a person: he wants nothing and overcomes nothing, so the axis that separates Sunrise on the Reaping 87 from The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 simply does not run. The dream-vignette structure means nothing accumulates, which is the thin-story cost, and the register is pitched at a young popular-science reader in the manner of the reviser's own children's physics books - the mild cost that Narnia 67 and Ranger's Apprentice 74 record. Leaned on ideas rather than on the memoir/testimony axis, because nothing here is a first-hand account of anything; the physics is the whole of the case. No filter is in play - no occult, no investigation, no sexual content.

The premise has one good turn in it - a planet used as a dumping ground for the empire's unwanted is also a graveyard where a dead alien species is not dead but stored as consciousness in liquid, and colonists who enter it come out shared. That is a declared capability with consequences available, the thing Project Hail Mary 92 is rewarded for pursuing. Two things put it under the line anyway. The book is built as a wide political space opera that changes character and plotline every chapter, and the log's severest structural objection is several threads starting at once with none of them legible - Guards! Guards! 30 was abandoned around page fifteen for exactly that, and the log's top SF is the opposite shape, the single tight narration of The Hunger Games 89 and Old Man's War 87. And the alien thread escalates to a mental evolution that would set off another Big Bang, which is a declared stake far too large for the story to keep honest, the self-consistency breach that sank Mortal Engines 55 on its own. Cliffhanger structure over three volumes adds nothing to think about at the close of this one. axis:ideas carries the number rather than axis:worldbuilding, because the setting is inventive and it is the reasoning around it that will not hold. On the occult bar I looked far enough to be comfortable it is not a filter here rather than to settle it: the alien powers are psychic and sect-organised but the merging is immersion in a physical medium with no invocation or devotion, so it grades at most.

t: Piseme pribeh (How to Write a Story, Grades 1-3)
why: A teaching resource: about 96 pages of reproducible worksheets and lesson material for getting six- to nine-year-olds to write a story. There is nothing here that the axes in this log measure - no premise, no characters, no idea worked out - and the register is aimed at a primary classroom, which is the far end of axis:childrens, where the reader's own scale puts a picture book in the 30s or 40s while Hobbit 84 and The Little Prince 82 pay nothing for being simple but complete. Both named axes carry the number: no idea, and an audience three decades away from this reader. Gate-4 exit on one source; occult status unexamined below the line.

t: Pisen, kterou se objasnuje svet (Song for the Unraveling of the World)
why: Twenty-two horror stories, literary in origin and speculative in furniture, and this is exactly the combination the below-the-line gate exists to catch: literary fiction plus a story collection, where the character rules are suspended without anything arriving in their place. There is a theme - the unreliability of perception, a world of paralysing delusion - but a theme is not a premise whose consequences get worked out, which is what Project Hail Mary 92 was scored for, and the canonical short books that do well in this log do well for one idea carried straight through, as Animal Farm 78 does. The method also cuts against this reader specifically: the stories are calibrated exercises in withheld information, and the three lowest scores in the log are all books that would not say plainly what was happening. Unfinished Tales 69, the lowest Tolkien by a clear margin, was marked down precisely because the pieces are not connected to each other. So the doubt is about there being an idea to lean on, and it carries the number at one source. Occult status is unexamined at this exit, and in horror it is where checking would be needed.

One thesis, projected forward and stated openly: a civilisation that discards its own foundations ends up governed by someone else's, and that rule then rots from exhausting the resources it did not build. Nameable, and the setting is concrete rather than invented. Against it, the recorded reader objections are the ones this log punishes hardest: the thesis delivered too explicitly, 'full of cliches', a book for confirming opinions rather than opening one, and doubt about the factual footing - and untrue things stated as fact are exactly what docked Rangers Apprentice 74, while the log's highest non-fiction score, Seeking Allah Finding Jesus 91, earned it for testing what is plausible and what is not. Several refugee strands also start in parallel across different countries, the shape behind the log's three 30s. Gate 4's question answers yes here, so the doubt about the idea is what carries the number and I stopped at one source rather than pay for the rest. Occult status is unexamined at this exit; mystical elements are reported but not checked.

t: Podivne nebe nad vychodnim Berlinem (Strange Skies Over East Berlin)
why: The hook is concrete and single-threaded, which is what this reader wants from an opening: one narrator, one situation, a craft coming down on the wrong side of the wall. The satisfaction is also not whodunnit - the plot is shaped like an infiltration rather than an investigation, so the detective bar does not fire, though it is worth flagging. What is thin is what the book leaves behind. Reviewers describe the narration as vague musings on truth and lies, call the writing flat and heavy-handed in places, and one dismisses the whole thing as forgettable; the alien is there mainly to force the agent to admit he is no innocent. A book should leave an idea behind - Animal Farm 78 scores on that alone - and 'who is the real monster' across four issues is not an idea worked out. The form compounds it: the top of this log runs on interiority, Red Rising 95 explicitly for more time inside the characters than on what they do, and a comics volume has little room for it. Gate 4 answers yes, so the doubt about the idea carries the number at one source. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

t: Podraz (The Betrayal: The True Story of My Brush with Death in the World of Narcos and Launderers)
why: Gate 1 first, because the catalogue files this as an American thriller and the annotation ends on finding a traitor: it is not a whodunnit and not fiction at all, but a former federal agent's first-person account of his own undercover operation inside cartel money laundering, so the detective filter does not fire - the traitor thread is investigation-shaped and flagged, not a veto. What the book leaves is procedure rather than an idea: how dirty money moves through banks, and what living under a false identity costs. Reviewers describe intricate deception rather than momentum, with a reader stalling halfway. The log's nearest real anchors are Son of Hamas 75, a first-person account of a double life sitting barely above the line, and Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91, which earns its distance by examining what is true about the author himself - not attempted here. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: the Hitchhiker's follow-ups fell from 83 to 70. That doubt about axis:ideas is the gate-4 exit, on one source; occult status unexamined below the line.

A comics album, not prose, and a continuation: the annotation opens on the aftermath of a fight that has already destroyed Bratislava Castle and Charles Bridge, so the reader is expected to arrive with the previous album read. It is a sequel, and continuations are not safe bets in this log - Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70 - and the opening as described is exactly the shape that scored 30 three times, several named characters and threads resumed mid-action with no context supplied. The content is a robot-run 2044 that bans books and teaches children that dumping plastic helps nature, opposed by fictionalised versions of real YouTubers, with a fourteen-year-old lead: a fandom product aimed young, and I can name no idea it leaves behind beyond the satire's single joke. Narnia 67 is docked for child leads plus a lack of higher things to think about and it is a far more substantial book than this. The low band applies because the comics form gives none of the interior page time that Red Rising 95 was scored for, so the character tests are suspended without anything replacing them - and the suspension removes penalties, it never adds points. Exited at gate 4 on one source, so the occult status is unexamined. Dep corrected 2026-09-03: this line carried the author id of the American SF writer of the same surname through a surname collision - the credited creators here are a Czech duo, and the estimate never argued from that author. Nothing else about the line changes.

Satire itself is no obstacle in this log: Saturnin 78 lands in the A band on voice and character alone, and Animal Farm 78 on one idea carried straight through in short form. But both are single works holding one register to the end, and this is a set of separate pieces attacking the same target from different angles, some of them shaped as political thrillers. That is the form the below-the-line gate catches - a collection has no single premise whose consequences can be worked out, so there is no idea to lean on, and the character rules are suspended without adding anything. Unfinished Tales 69 is the direct anchor: the lowest Tolkien in the log, marked down because the pieces are not logically connected to each other. Readers also report a real quality gap against the same author's novels, and the satirical target is a specific decade of a specific government rather than something general, which is where this kind of book ages out. The doubt about the idea carries the number at one source. Occult status is unexamined at this exit, though readers report the eerie and the supernatural staying close.

No idea can be named, and the one thing the annotation does promise makes it worse: the children start discovering superhero powers. Ability handed rather than earned is a graded objection in its own right, and it lands on top of a short unofficial game tie-in of about eighty pages, released weekly as an episode, whose invented material is the game's blocks and dragons rather than anything the book thought of. That form takes the character and motive tests away with it - there is no premise to work out and nothing is left behind. The reader's gradient places it: Hranicaruv ucen 74 for easy reading with little to think about, Narnia 67 for child leads and no higher things, a picture book in the thirties or forties. A juvenile licensed episode with powers issued to the cast belongs near the bottom of that, which is why the lower band applies rather than the default. axis:ideas and axis:childrens carry the number; nothing further was researched because nothing further could move it.

t: Pravidla, kterymi se vase matka neridila (Not Your Mother's Rules: The New Secrets for Dating)
why: A prescriptive dating manual: thirty-one numbered rules about texting, social media and waiting to reply, with anecdotes and no evidence behind them. There is no premise, no protagonist and nothing to think about afterwards, and the advice form suspends the character tests without supplying an idea, which is the low band. One thing worth recording rather than scoring heavily: the whole method rests on men being predictable creatures to be managed while women supply the strategy, which points the way axis:sex-portrayal points - the only measured case sits at the light end and the profile forbids quoting a magnitude, so this is a mild note, not the reason for the number. Exited at gate 4 on axis:ideas, one source, so the occult question was not examined.

Military historical adventure in the Marlborough campaigns, and the one genuinely good thing in the description is the point of view: Ramillies seen from a grenadier captain sinking into swampy ground under contradictory orders, unable to make out the grand strategy at all. That is a real perspective. But the book it belongs to is a Napoleonic-rifleman adventure sold as one, and what follows is a battle, a siege, a traitor-hunt and a renegade pirate - page time on what characters do, which is the log's heaviest deduction and why Golden Son 92 was docked below Red Rising 95 for leaning on action. The historical novels actually read land at the line, Exodus 68 and Quo Vadis 66, and The Count of Monte Cristo 75 shows what it takes to beat them: momentum plus a want driving every page. axis:ideas is the axis I would have listed as the risk - I cannot name what this leaves behind beyond the campaign itself - which is the gate's exit condition, so it carries the number. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

t: Prekonavani traumatu (Transforming the Living Legacy of Trauma: A Workbook for Survivors and Therapists)
why: A clinical workbook with two introductions, one for survivors and one for therapists, then diagrams and worksheets. The claim behind it - that re-telling the trauma story often reactivates it, and that symptoms read better as normal responses to abnormal events - is stated at the front and then practised rather than argued, and the body is exercises, modular and skippable by design. So nothing is developed for a reader to take away, and the form removes the motive, protagonist and story axes that carry the top of this log without substituting anything. Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 shows what non-fiction has to do to score here, which is examine something true at length and at the author's own cost; an instrument to be worked through is a different object. Leaned on axis:ideas. Gate-4 exit on one source; occult status unexamined below the line.

A dystopia whose declared rules are the point - a forearm monitor, retirement at ten percent, bodies renewed and memories wiped - and the reveal makes those rules follow from something rather than merely being decreed: the wealth gap between the islands was engineered so that the population would eventually want out of the arrangement. Consequences following from a stated setup is the axis Project Hail Mary 92 and Mockingjay 91 score on, and a hidden-truth dystopia read from inside one man's head is Hunger Games 89 territory. Opening bar cleared and cheaply: one concrete situation, a ferryman assigned to take his own father to the boat, the father breaking down on the pier - single lead, legible from the first page. Proctor is both curious and worth rooting for, which is the pair of tests the log weighs above worldbuilding. Occult passes both tests: the rebirth and the Designer are machine-side, there is no invocation, devotion or priesthood, and the elevation mechanic - replacing the mind that hosts the dream - is an erasure in a system, not a rite the story stages. Deductions: several reviewers say the last third is a lot of explaining and call the execution silly after a strong setup, which is the drawn-out-ending cost The Martian 82 paid; and a thread has the married lead father a child by another woman, an incidental-to-subplot infidelity whose framing I could not establish from the sources, so it sits in risks rather than in the number. Leaned on the worked-out premise and the lead rather than on worldbuilding, since worldbuilding is precisely what the critics split over. Discovery (axis:discovery, 2026-10-24): the lead's dreams are his way into what the archipelago really is, his own falling monitor makes finding out urgent, and the answer arrives and makes the rules follow from something, the shape the reader named in Project Hail Mary 92; central, so +4. How well the explaining third is told stays the deduction above.

t: Pribehy velkych mest (The Great Cities in History)
why: Sixty-eight cities, one short essay each, a different writer on every chapter and some 290 illustrations. The contributors are serious and the material is good, but reviewers agree the format caps each city at a few pages and never reaches why any of them became great - so there is no premise whose consequences are followed, and no idea of its own to name. The collection form suspends the motive and protagonist tests without adding anything: the short books that score in this log, The Little Prince 82 and Animal Farm 78, are canonical for one idea each, which is what an anthology of surveys has none of. Description with little story is a stated penalty and this is a survey of description. Leaned on axis:ideas, with axis:density secondary - length is not the objection, nothing accumulating is. Gate-4 exit on one source; occult status unexamined below the line.

A short Czech SF book assembled as diary entries from several aliens living among us, interleaved with the interrogation record of one of them. There is something nameable in it - a technology that lets them escape death at a cruel price - but nothing in the available coverage shows that consequence worked out rather than used as colour for the format, and short form removes penalties without adding points, so a thin idea lands in the 60s like any other thin book. Against that sits the structure: the only substantive review describes several narrators alternating rapidly in short sections plus a redacted name the reviewer found irritating, and this log's harshest verdicts are exactly that shape - Unfinished Tales 69 is the mildest outcome for pieces that are not logically connected to each other, and roughly six threads opening at once is the named cause of Guards! Guards! 30. The one positive note, that it is well thought out, comes from a reviewer who does not read SF and was approached by the author, so it does not carry weight. Exited at gate 4 on one source, which leaves the occult status unexamined.

t: Promente uzkost v nadeji pomoci KBT (The Positivity Effect: Simple CBT Skills to Transform Anxiety and Negativity into Optimism and Hope)
why: The framing sentence is genuinely a thought -- not being anxious is not the same thing as thriving -- and the author is credentialed, at Columbia's Teachers College with a positive-psychology background. But what the book is, by its own publisher's account and its own endorsers', is a set of exercises: the mechanism of change is the worksheets, and 'learned hopefulness' is a technique to practise rather than an idea to carry away. That is the distinction that matters for this reader, whose two non-fiction successes, Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75, earn their scores by examining what is actually true in a life, and whose profile says the form earns nothing by itself. So there is no idea I can name in the sense the log uses, and the workbook form suspends the character tests without replacing them -- both halves of the low band. The one substantive criticism found, that it does not address toxic positivity or that positivity is a privilege, points the same way. axis:ideas carries the number. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

Twelve stories by twelve different writers, tied only by Prague and a Kafka centenary, ranging from the historical to the science-fictional. That is the gate-four case exactly: a collection with no single premise has no idea to lean on, and the short-form suspension takes the character and motive tests off the table without adding anything back - so the two things that produce high scores in this log both go missing at once. The log already measures what unaligned pieces cost on material the reader otherwise loves: Unfinished Tales 69 is the lowest Tolkien by twelve points, and the stated reason is that the pieces are not logically connected to each other. Twelve authors is that objection at maximum. Reception describes a predominantly gloomy atmosphere, which adds the mild bleakness discount. I cannot name one idea the whole book leaves behind, which is the finding. Occult status is unexamined at this exit, and Prague fantastika is where it would need checking.

An illustrated first-aid reference: injuries and emergencies with the procedure for each. It is not a book that is read so much as consulted, so there is no premise, no one whose motives get page time and nothing left behind afterwards - the reference form strips out the character tests and puts no idea in their place, which is the low band rather than the just-under-the-line one. Nothing here engages a hard filter; it simply has none of the things that lift this log, where even the shortest high scorers earn it on one idea, The Little Prince 82 and Animal Farm 78. Exited at gate 4 on axis:ideas, one source, so the occult question was not examined.

The one thing here that reaches a scoring axis: a psychiatrist of thirty years' practice explains diagnoses to lay readers through concrete patient stories, written for people who have a mentally ill person among their close relations. That is a real go at how another group experiences the world, which is half of what earned Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75 - but only half, because the other half is a first-person life examining what is actually true of itself, and this is a clinician's explainer organised by diagnosis. Exit at gate 4: I would list axis:ideas under risks, since a glossary of conditions leaves understanding rather than an idea, and the form earns nothing by itself. Default band rather than the low one, because the case material and the lay-reader address do give it something a bare textbook has not. Occult status is unexamined, as the ladder allows at this exit.

t: Psychologie Atkinsonove a Hilgarda (Atkinson & Hilgard's Introduction to Psychology)
why: A university survey textbook - around 880 pages in eight parts, from method and neurobiology through cognition, emotion, personality, development and social behaviour to psychopathology, with boxed summaries, critical-thinking questions and a companion volume of test items. It is a reference instrument rather than a book with a premise: no idea of its own to name, and the form removes every axis that carries the top of this log, since there is no protagonist, no motive and no story. That is the gate-4 answer on axis:ideas and the exit. Leaned on axis:ideas with axis:density secondary - the length is not the objection, as this reader has said plainly that long is not a fault; nothing accumulating is. One source; occult status unexamined below the line.

A standing university textbook on advertising psychology, repeatedly re-issued and taught from: motivation theory, emotion and perception applied to advertising, with analyses of actual campaigns. Exit at gate 4 on axis:ideas - it transmits a field to marketing students rather than advancing a claim and following it through, and the reader's standard is a premise whose consequences get worked out (Project Hail Mary 92 for second-order effects, Divergent 58 when the premise will not hold). There is no motive-driven page time, nobody to be interested in, and nothing to carry away, and the log's non-fiction that landed did so by examining what is actually true from inside an experience (Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91). Lower band because both conditions hold: no nameable idea and a textbook form with no character tests to pass. Occult status is unexamined, as the ladder allows here. Overspend declared: two retrievals against a budget of one, because the record had to be located before it could be read.

A multi-author professional handbook for teachers and the helping professions, arranged to follow the human developmental line: partner choice, delayed motherhood, women's employment, trauma, abuse, post-divorce custody arrangements and substitute family care. Exit at gate 4 on axis:ideas - the organising device is a topic list, not a claim the book undertakes to establish and then follows through, which is the thing the reader rewards; a chapter-per-issue reference work has nothing for the motives-and-wants axis that tops the log (Mockingjay 91, Speaker for the Dead 90) and nothing left behind at the end. The non-fiction that scored here examined truth-claims from inside a life (Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91); this reports the field to practitioners. Lower band because no idea can be named and the reference form suspends the character tests without adding anything. On gate 2, partner relationships and divorce are among the clinical topics but the book is not about an affair, so the axis is graded at nothing rather than triggered. Occult status is unexamined, as the ladder allows at this exit.

A discipline textbook for students of special pedagogy: current research on intellectual-development disorders and autistic-spectrum conditions, the special pedagogue's role, inclusive schooling and diagnosis-then-intervention. Exit at gate 4 on axis:ideas - the subject is nameable but no proposition is advanced and worked out, and a survey of a field is not the thing that earns points in this log. Non-fiction here scores when it examines what is actually true from inside a life and shows how another group experiences the world (Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91, Son of Hamas 75); a professional handbook reports findings to practitioners instead, and its readers are pedagogues rather than the people described, so even the second half of that axis is not really engaged. Lower band because both conditions hold: no idea to name and a reference form that suspends the character tests without replacing them. Occult status is unexamined, as the ladder allows at this exit.

Exited at the below-the-line gate. Form and genre are settled - a 344-page Czech debut novel marketed as science fiction with horror elements - and the honest answer on the idea is that I would list axis:ideas in risks. What the publisher offers is a chain of hooks rather than a premise: a ruined far-future Earth, daily survival, a girl who has lost her memory hunting her own past, a lethal infection, and a deadlier enemy revealed behind it. Amnesia plus a concealed antagonist is a structure for withholding information, not a question the book is built to answer, and the only substantive reader report available praises exactly that - smoothly flowing, keeps its pace, full of twists - which is momentum rather than something left behind. That is the pattern the log parks in the 60s: a competent book that gives you events and no ideas, which is stated as the most common reason a competent book stalls there. Sustained post-apocalyptic bleakness is a further mild discount, and Narnia at 67 shows how little it takes to sit just under the line. Leaned on the absent idea because that is what I argued and what carries the number. The protagonist was not examined, and since 2026-10-24 that matters more: a lead hunting her own lost past is the shape the reader liked best in Licanius 92-96, so the top of the range opens two points on the chance the book does it well. Occult status is unexamined at this exit. Since 2026-10-24 the lead hunting her own past, credited above, is priced as axis:discovery, once; the number holds.

A forty-thousand-year-old body in Antarctic ice wearing modern clothing and carrying better-than-modern technology, then a chase from the Nazca lines to Area 51 to the Large Hadron Collider. SFX's review is the decisive evidence: it says the book contains essentially the entire catalogue of alien-conspiracy lore and spoon-feeds it, and a sympathetic reader concedes the plot is shopworn and goofy enough to strain disbelief. That is a premise assembled from other books' parts rather than thought through, which is what put Divergent 58 in the C band. A friendly reviewer states outright that the novel is driven by plot rather than character development, and a blogger finds the male lead almost superhuman - ability granted rather than earned, which this reader docks. The Count of Monte Cristo 75 shows momentum alone can carry a long adventure, but that book's lead wanted something for the whole of it. No idea is left behind, and that is the axis carrying the number. Exited at gate 4 on one source, so the occult status is unexamined, though the material points to conspiracy lore rather than to practised occultism.

There is a real idea here and it is declared precisely, then followed through: an algorithmic society where a shop's prediction engine ships what you will want before you order it, matchmaking is automated, a personal rating decides your standing, repair is illegal under consumption-protection law, and the presidential race is between an android running on universal basic income and a demagogue. The plot is one man deciding to return a product the algorithm insists he wants, which forces the system to admit it can be wrong - a premise whose consequences are the book, which is what earns Animal Farm 78 and what the log credits in Project Hail Mary 92. Comic register costs nothing on its own: Saturnin sits at 78 and Hitchhiker's at 83. What holds it down is a cluster the log prices specifically. Reviewers consistently report the lead as unlikeable and passive - compared to Kafka's Josef K, which is the objection that took Promena to 58 and Oliver Twist to 57 for a protagonist acted upon rather than wanting anything. The joke-per-paragraph density has critics calling it a collection of clever jokes rather than a novel and a stand-up routine in book form, and thin story spread across pages is the log's density penalty. A running gag about a malfunctioning sex droid plus frequent sex jokes and a flagged male gaze is low on explicitness but not on kind or volume, and kind is precisely what took Ready Player One to 55 and docked Artemis to 69. Leaned on the idea rather than on the worldbuilding, because the log forbids predicting a book up on worldbuilding when the lead looks thin, and here that is the specific complaint.

t: Rec emoci (The Language of Emotions: What Your Feelings Are Trying to Tell You)
why: This one does have a thesis I can state in a phrase -- every emotion, including the ones people try to get rid of, carries specific information and is worth reading rather than suppressing -- and it is worked through emotion by emotion in the second half, which is more than a technique list. That is why it sits in the upper band rather than the lower. What stops it going further is that the thesis is asserted from the author's own experience as a self-described lifelong hyper-empath and delivered in vocabulary inherited from energy healing: grounding, boundary-defining, burning contracts, releasing emotion on an energetic level. Examining what is actually true is the exact thing this reader singled out in Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91, and a taxonomy argued from felt experience rather than tested is the opposite move; the profile also says the memoir and testimony form earns nothing on its own, as The Diary of a Young Girl 40 shows. I would list axis:ideas under risks, so gate 4 says exit at C. Occult status is unexamined at this exit and it is a real question here, because the practices are prescribed for the reader to perform rather than merely described.

Exited at the below-the-line gate. Form and genre are settled - a 208-page Czech novel, shelved as science fiction but described by every reader who has written about it as a reincarnation story told through historical episodes: a man surfacing in intensive care with a head injury who recovers fragments of two earlier lives, one running to the Balkan front of the First World War and a grave on the African coast, the other under late Czechoslovak socialism. Asked honestly whether the idea holds up, I would put axis:ideas in risks. The distinctive twist readers name is that this is not a soul reborn into a new body but a dead person's soul taking over another - a mechanism, but one nobody reports being followed through - and the recurring verdict is that the historical texture is what works: one reader says the reincarnation strand did not take and the late-1980s socialism was the interesting part, another missed dialogue in both strands and calls it at times a pleasant travelogue. Period colour with a frame around it is precisely the shape that stalls in the 60s in this log; the nearest read comparisons are the historical novels Exodus 68 and Quo Vadis 66, both recorded there. Sixteen ratings and no professional review is not evidence to argue past that. Leaned on the idea because the doubt about what the reincarnation premise actually delivers is the whole argument; the protagonist was not examined, and a paralysed narrator listening from a hospital bed is not where I would go looking for a rescue. This book carries an unexamined occult status at this exit, and it is worth flagging that the premise is soul transmigration - a real-world esoteric belief - rather than an invented system, so the axis needs a real look before this is ever proposed.

Exited at the below-the-line gate. Form and genre are settled - a Czech first-contact novel marketed as suspenseful science fiction - and the premise does have a question in it: an alien civilisation asks to meet an unremarkable Prague taxi driver at his cottage in south Bohemia, and the hook is why him. But answering gate 4 honestly, I would put axis:ideas in risks. The setup reads as a comic-ironic conceit rather than a worked-out one, there is no evidence anywhere of the consequences being followed through, and the author is a journalist known for celebrity interviews rather than a genre writer with a track record of holding a premise together. That matters here specifically, because first contact is the log's highest-scoring territory only when the mechanism is thought all the way down - Project Hail Mary earns 92 for exploring the second-order consequences of its central substance, and Old Man's War 87 for each stage of its world following from the last. A conceit with a punchline instead lands where competent books with nothing left behind land, just under the line, which is where the log puts Exodus at 68 and Narnia at 67. Leaned on the idea because that is the argument; nothing else was examined, since no other axis could carry a book past this doubt. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

t: Rikal jsem mu Kravata (Ich nannte ihn Krawatte)
why: The positive case is the axis that tops this log outright. Roughly 140 pages in 114 very short chapters, one first-person narrator, and almost the whole of it is what two people want and why: a twenty-year-old who has not left his room in two years, edging back into the world from a park bench, and the middle-aged salaryman opposite who has lost his job and cannot tell his wife, whose own life story is then nested inside the young man's telling. That is the same weighting that puts Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 above their own series. The opening is one concrete situation with the context to read it - a bench, a watched stranger, a first-person voice - so the filter that produced the three scores of 30 does not apply, and reviews describe the early chapters as watching rather than exposition. The idea is nameable in a phrase: what withdrawal costs in a society that prices a person by his function, and that two failures can restore each other. Deductions: the sadness is sustained and a friend's suicide sits behind the narrator's retreat, and Promena 58 is the standing warning here - a literary novella with a real idea that lost twelve points off its prediction when a passive lead and unrelieved bleakness both fired. Two things separate this one: Hiro is trying to get back in rather than being acted upon, and the ending is companionship rather than solitude, which is the exact difference the reader named between Project Hail Mary 92 and The Martian 82. Not leaned on axis:ideas, because a quiet meditation can leave less behind than it promises; the interiority is what is certain, so axis:motives carries the number and the bleakness and protagonist doubts are stated as risks instead of widening the band further. No sexual content of note, no infidelity premise (the hidden job loss is a lie to a wife, not an affair), realist contemporary setting with nothing occult in it.

A university study text in the sociology of the family, issued in an academic teaching series. Exit at gate 4: I would put axis:ideas under risks, and here for two reasons at once. First the form - a study text is written to teach a field to students, and a survey of a discipline has no premise whose consequences get worked out, which is the reader's stated standard (Project Hail Mary 92 for second-order effects) and the axis on which competent books stall in the 60s. Second, and stated as doubt rather than finding: I could source the bibliographic record but no annotation or table of contents, so I cannot name the argument, and by the profile's own rule not being able to name the idea is itself the finding. Default band rather than the lower one precisely because of that gap - this author is a serious Czech sociologist and the possibility that the text carries a real thesis is open, so the low band would claim more than I established. No motive-driven narrative and no protagonist, so the axis that tops the log is not in play at all. Occult status is unexamined, as the ladder allows here. Overspend declared: two retrievals against a budget of one, and they still did not yield a content description.

A professional handbook for teachers and school psychologists on measuring and developing pupils' emotional intelligence, with programmes and exercises. Its value is instrumental - you use it if you run such a programme - and for a reader outside that job there is no premise, no one to follow and nothing left behind; the manual form removes the character tests but adds nothing, which is the low band. The log's nonfiction that worked did so by examining what is actually true and showing how another group experiences the world, Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91, and a set of school intervention protocols offers neither. Exited at gate 4 on axis:ideas, one source, so the occult question was not examined.

A young-adult horror novel that runs on atmosphere and reveal: three teenagers who cannot shake what happened to them return to the campus where it happened, chase a vintage carnival out of anonymous photographs, and dig into the town's buried past. The pleasure on offer is dread and a late disclosure about the lead's inherited connection to the institution's warden, and I cannot name an idea it leaves behind - which is exactly the answer that ends the ladder at gate 4. It is also a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70, the steepest series decline recorded. The register is young-adult, which is graded and not fatal - Narnia 67 and Ranger's Apprentice 74 show that costs a little rather than a tier - but there is no offsetting positive of the kind that put Speaker for the Dead at 90. The plot has an investigation shape (photographs, an abandoned town, a hidden history) and I judged it a flag rather than the detective filter, because the satisfaction is horror rather than working out who did it. Leaned on axis:ideas since that is the doubt carrying the number. Occult status is unexamined at this exit, as the ladder allows for a book already below the line.

t: Sejdeme se na piazzete (See You in the Piazza: New Places to Discover in Italy)
why: A travel diary through thirteen Italian regions, and what it offers is description: towns, hotels, meals, recipes, in no particular order, which reviewers say makes it unusable as an itinerary and slow to read straight through. I cannot name an idea it leaves behind, and the first-person form earns nothing by itself in this log - the same form produced Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91, which earns on examining what is actually true, and The Diary of a Young Girl 40, which did not work at all. Heavy description with little story is a stated penalty and it is most of the book, while the sketch-collection form suspends the motive and protagonist tests that carry the top of this log without substituting anything. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:memoir-form, because the telling is competent and the absence of anything to think about is the objection. Gate-4 exit on one source; occult status is unexamined below the line.

Exited at the below-the-line gate. Form and genre are settled - a Czech post-catastrophe novel shelved as both thriller and science fiction - and the idea does not survive gate 4. What is offered is a situation and no mechanism: a global catastrophe of unprecedented scale that two people happen by an odd coincidence to sit out in a Rocky Mountains shelter, who come out after two months to a landscape burned beyond recognition. The cause is not named, the survival is explicitly luck, and there is nothing indicating the consequences are followed through. Two things in the log bite there. First, luck as the rescue mechanism is the one thing Old Man's War at 87 was praised for never doing - the characters are not saved by chance and the author does not save the plot when it suits him - so this starts by conceding what that book earned. Second, a devastated world whose devastation is unexplained is a competent premise that gives events rather than something left behind, which the log names as the standard reason such a book stalls in the 60s. Reader reception sits around the mid-70s on a small sample, which is consistent with readable-but-unremarkable rather than with an argument to look further. So axis:ideas belongs in risks and the exit is right. Leaned on the idea because it is what I argued; the protagonists were not examined, and a two-person survival story would in any case face the log's stated preference for companionship and self-sacrifice over solo endurance without a premise underneath it. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

t: Snis o druhe Zemi? (Do You Dream of Terra-Two?)
why: Six teenagers trained since childhood launch on a twenty-three-year one-way voyage to a habitable planet - and the book closes about a year in, with the journey and the mission unresolved and much left open. That is the finding: the premise is set up rather than worked out, and working a premise out is what this reader's top scores actually reward - Valka stareho muze 87 was praised because each stage of its world followed from the last, and Project Hail Mary 92 for second-order consequences being explored. A voyage novel that stops before the consequences arrive has no idea to leave behind. The structure compounds it: six live narrators with flashbacks, alternate viewpoints and time jumps is the log's most reliable negative signal, roughly six threads at once being the named cause of Guards! Guards! 30, and reviewers split on the characters with one preferring the speculative scenarios to them outright. Teen leads are only a small pushback, Ender's Game 87 settles that, so life-phase is not the objection here. Exited at gate 4 on one source, so the occult status is unexamined.

t: Souziti s partnerem po mrtvici (When Your Spouse Has a Stroke)
why: A practical guide for the partner of a stroke survivor: what the damage does, how home care and rehabilitation work, how the relationship and the caring role change. It is written to be useful to people in that situation rather than read through, so there is no premise being worked out and nobody to follow, and the advice form suspends the character tests without adding an idea - the low band. The log's one clear rule about nonfiction is that the form earns nothing by itself and what earns is examining what is true plus insight into how another group lives, Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 against The Diary of a Young Girl 40; a caregiving manual delivers procedure instead. Exited at gate 4 on axis:ideas, one source, so the occult question was not examined.

It does have a thesis, and a slightly contrarian one: no sport is healthy in itself, injury risk is intrinsic to each, and the answer is understanding your own body, constitution and age rather than following a generic programme. A physiotherapist writing from his own caseload is also the closest this book comes to the axis that earned Son of Hamas 75 - practice examined from inside. But exit at gate 4, because I would put axis:ideas under risks: what it leaves behind is instruction and exercises, not an idea, and the reader's complaint about a book that teaches without thinking is already on record at Ranger's Apprentice 74. axis:density is against it too - 368 pages that a reviewer says would work at 150, padded with repeated reminders of which celebrities the author has treated, which is the thin-story-over-many-pages penalty (The Martian 82 lost points for an ending that dragged). Default band, not the low one, since the thesis is real and the writing is reported as readable.

t: Strategicky management lidskych zdroju (Strategicky management lidskych zdroju: moderni trendy v HR)
why: A research-based HR monograph: how to set up human-resource management, age management, corporate social responsibility, employer branding and sustainability as competitive advantage, carried by survey data with correlation coefficients and significance levels and Czech Statistical Office and Eurostat figures. Exit at gate 4 on axis:ideas - the premise is that people are an organisation's most valuable asset, which is a professional starting assumption rather than a proposition whose consequences the book works out, and the reader's standard is exactly consequences followed through (Project Hail Mary 92 scores for second-order effects, Divergent 58 falls for a premise that collapses). Nothing here engages motives, character or an idea worth carrying away, and statistical tables put axis:density against it as well. Lower band because both conditions hold: no idea to name and a reference form with no character tests to pass. Occult status is unexamined, as the ladder allows at this exit.

A 350-page standalone Czech novel with a genuinely likeable setup: alien portals open worldwide and their radiation is killing everyone, a divorced warehouseman from Most survives one at point-blank range, wakes with alien hardware inside him and the ability to close them, and is then escorted by the army while chrome constructs hunt him. The ordinary-man-as-hero angle is the one thing reviewers agree on and it is the right instinct for this reader. But the same reviews describe a book balanced on the edge between light entertainment and an idea with reach, packed with action from the first page to the last, with reader reservations about the premise itself, and a composition made of fragments from the viewpoints of more and less important characters that one reviewer says can produce confusion. That is the wrong shape twice over: Golden Son 92 was docked at the top of the log purely for leaning on action, Mockingjay 91 won by showing motives and the least of the arena, and the log's three 30s are all books whose openings were unreadable. The ability is also handed over by an implant rather than earned. Naming an idea is possible but I would put axis:ideas in risks, which is the stated C exit, so the default band applies. Occult status is unexamined at this exit. One source, within budget.

Exited at the below-the-line gate, and the form does most of the deciding. This is an edited anthology of science-fiction and horror short stories by classic authors of the genre, so there is no single premise, no protagonist and no continuity, and the log is explicit that the suspension of the character and emotion rules for short idea-driven work removes penalties but never adds points. With no one premise there is no axis:ideas to lean on and it therefore belongs in risks - individual stories may each leave something behind, but the book as an object cannot be argued to. The directly relevant measurement is Unfinished Tales at 69, the reader's lowest Tolkien by twelve points, and the stated reason is exactly this: fragmented, and the pieces are not logically connected to each other. An assembled multi-author anthology is that objection by construction, and being classics does not repair it, since canonical short books score well for their ideas and that is selection on the individual work, not a property the container inherits. The horror half is a further mild bleakness discount. So a shade under the line is the honest record. Leaned on the form and the absent single idea because those are the two things I argued from; no character axis was examined, since the form suspends them. Occult status is unexamined at this exit and is worth a real look before this is ever proposed, given that half the contents are horror.

The annotation's talk of hunting the supernatural is a misdescription of an SF book, so the occult bar is not what decides this: the blue Parasites are creatures a few damaged people can physically see, blasted with corporate hardware, with no rite, invocation or devotion anywhere in the setup. And there is a real idea - the crusade turns out to have been killing something that was not the enemy, which is the reader's own favourite move, the plausibility of a premise actually tested. But the idea arrives as a late reveal rather than as a premise whose consequences fill the book, and the reader's high scores go to books where the consequences are worked out from the start, Project Hail Mary 92 for following astrophage's second-order effects through. Before the twist it is an orphan-gang chase with corporate villains and Bond gadgets. The telling is juvenile in register with a fourteen-year-old lead and a kid ensemble, and the log pays that: Narnia 67 for children as the main characters with nothing higher to think about, Hranicaruv ucen 74 for easy to read with not much to think about. axis:ideas carries the number because the one substantial thought is deferred to the end; axis:protagonist is not the lean, since Cosmo has a want and a fault to work against.

England 1811: a widowed viscountess left bankrupt sends her prettier daughter to a London season to catch a rich husband, and the elder daughter goes along disguised as a widowed cousin. Romance as the central subject costs nothing in this log - Pycha a predsudek 75 is built entirely out of what people want and why - so the case for reading this would have to be that its motives are worked with that seriousness, and nothing indicates it: the engine is the disguise and the husband hunt, with no premise whose consequences get followed. Gates 2 and 3 were examined and neither fires - the plan is a marriage hunt, not an affair, and a reader review notes the book works 'ohne viel Sexy Time'. My gate-4 answer on axis:ideas is a yes, so it exits at C on one source, and axis:ideas is what carries the number rather than axis:protagonist, which I did not establish. Occult status unexamined below the line.

There is a real positive here: a girl married at fourteen into a household that mistreats her, with no power except a legal claim, who forces the head of the family to honour it. That is want and motive driving every page, the axis that tops this log with Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90, and Pride and Prejudice 75 shows a domestic subject costs nothing by itself. What holds the number down is the frame rather than the story: faith is not a thread inside this book, it is what the book is for - it ships with an in-depth Bible study for personal or group use, and the reader wants faith inside a story, not devotional material as a subject in its own right. Labyrint sveta a raj srdce 70 is the ceiling that frame reached even with a nameable idea behind it, and this is a shorter, more instructional object; the short-form suspension removes penalties without adding points. Two content axes were examined and neither engages: the infidelity axis requires a marriage or engagement breached and the relationship here is between a widowed daughter-in-law and her father-in-law, not an affair within a marriage; the sexual axis turns on one pivotal act rather than on the plot. Occult status unexamined at this exit, though the first husband is described as an idol-worshipper.

Near-future Czech SF, a novella of about 200 pages, and the idea is nameable - who owns a superhuman intelligence and what the people it displaces do about it. But I would put axis:ideas in risks and that decides it: the reports that praise it praise the perspectives on AI while saying the book is too short to develop them, and the reports against it name lifeless dialogue, characters whose reasoning does not follow, none of them memorable, and an over-complicated ending arrived at in a rush. Reasoning that does not follow is the breach that put Divergent 58 in the C band, and a cast nobody remembers is the failure that separates Golden Son 92, where three leads visibly want different things, from books that stall in the 60s. It is also told through several rotating characters with no clear lead, and the log's high scores run the other way - The Hunger Games 89 on tight single-POV narration. Leaned on the idea and the cast rather than on worldbuilding, which nobody who read it raised either way. Occult status carries no examination at this exit.

t: Tri socialni svety (Tri socialni svety: socialni struktura postindustrialni spolecnosti)
why: This one goes past the below-the-line gate because it has exactly what the reader says he wants from a book and what the 60s usually lack: one proposition, declared, then followed through. The claim is that society has moved from inequality to incommensurability - the elite, the middle strata and the declassed now living in conditions that cannot be measured against each other - and it is argued with data, traced to the processes causing it, and pushed to a consequence, that incommensurability threatens democracy and an open society. It also does the harder second thing, turning on its own discipline: the argument is that sociology's own fashionable vocabulary, social capital and social exclusion and new social risks, obscures the shift it is meant to describe. That self-auditing is the quality that put Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 at the top of the non-fiction here - examining what is actually plausible rather than restating it - and Animal Farm 78 and Labyrint sveta 70 both show an idea-carried work with no protagonist clearing the line comfortably. What holds the range down, and why the low end sits below 68: it is a scholarly monograph in an academic series, written for sociologists, and axis:density is the reader's real penalty term - stratification theory joined to urban sociology and the sociology of organisations over 211 pages is a lot of apparatus for one thesis, and Unfinished Tales 69 and Les Miserables 71 both lost ground to material that did not move. There is no protagonist and no motive-driven page time at all, which is the axis that tops the log, so the ceiling is the Silmarillion 80 shape at best. Leaned on axis:ideas and not on axis:memoir-form, because nothing here is testimony and the form earns nothing by itself.

The subject is the one thing non-fiction is rewarded for here: insight into how another group actually experiences the world, which is what Son of Hamas 75 scored on and a large part of why Seeking Allah Finding Jesus 91 sits near the top. But the form works against it. The testimony form earns nothing by itself in this log - the same form produced both its highest non-fiction score and an outright DNF at 40 - and what earns is a sustained first-person account that tests what is plausible and what is not, where this is a set of separate essays with no single argument to follow front to back. Unfinished Tales 69 is the anchor for pieces that are not connected to each other. So the doubt is whether there is one idea here to carry the book rather than a survey of many, and that doubt carries the number at one source. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

A 368-page Czech novel written to a brief - the name and site of an invented capital of a united Europe, taken from an architectural project - in which an antiquarian bookseller becomes the city's librarian, fails to settle, and comes to believe the city has a hidden life and a secret plan he has a part in. The concept is the strongest thing present, and that is the finding: a professional review judges the book a fragment of a larger mosaic that fails as a standalone work and reads the whole late-period pattern as grafting the author's trademark motifs onto new genres, while readers call the parallel-worlds story thin and predictable and say the city concept on its own would have sufficed. Premise as decor rather than premise worked out is what stalls competent books in the 60s here, and the log's harshest verdicts - Divergent 58, Mortal Engines abandoned at 55 - come from exactly this axis. Filter 4 does not fire: the plot is investigation-shaped, since he is uncovering what the city is for, but the satisfaction is not finding out who did it, so that is a flag rather than a bar. I would put axis:ideas in risks, which is the stated C exit, and the default band applies because the writing itself is well regarded. Occult status is unexamined at this exit and would be worth checking if the axis is bumped, given the author's mystical-Prague material elsewhere. One source, within budget.

Ten humorous short stories by nine hands in a small-format paperback, on what modern technology could take over in our lives if we let it. Both conditions for the cheap exit hold at once. That subject is a programme rather than an idea - there is no single premise whose consequences get worked out, which is what the reader actually rewards - and the story form suspends the character rules without adding anything, so nothing is recoverable on the axis the log tops out on. Comic register itself is free here: Saturnin 78 shows humour carries no penalty when voice and character do the work, and The Hitchhiker's Guide 83 that comic SF works when it opens on one concrete situation rather than fanning out. A mosaic of ten light pieces is the opposite arrangement, and it is also a sequel of sorts - sequels are not safe bets in this log, where Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

Exited at the below-the-line gate. Form and genre are settled - a 280-page first-person Czech SF novel, a 21-year-old author's debut on a self-publishing imprint - and the idea does not survive the one question that matters. The nameable premise is only the situation itself, a man waking alone from cryosleep on a ship of frozen dead with an AI for company, and the strongest review found says the craftsmanship is not there, the vocabulary is noticeably small, and too little is thought through, which for genre readers is fatal because everything has to be rock-solid; another reader who knows the obvious models says the author brought nothing new, original or surprising. So axis:ideas belongs in risks and that is the exit condition. Two things genuinely point up and are why this is not lower: single close POV on one concrete opening situation, and an AI companion rather than isolation - the log states plainly that a companion beats solitude, which is the first of the three counts that put Project Hail Mary 92 above The Martian 82. Against a book he actually read, the derivative-and-underthought verdict is the axis that put Divergent at 58 for ideas borrowed and assembled without cohering, and that is where the low end sits. Stopped at one source per the gate budget, so this book carries an unexamined occult status. Discovery (axis:discovery, 2026-10-24): a man waking alone with no memory on a ship of the dead is the shape exactly, but the review evidence says too little is thought through for the answer to hold, which forfeits the lift; the number holds.

The catalogue record carries a three-word annotation - it says only that this is an SF novel - and the book is absent from the Czech book databases entirely, so there is no plot, no premise, no page count and no reader verdict to work from. I cannot name an idea, which is the strongest single separator in the data, so axis:ideas is the risk and this exits at the cheap gate rather than absorbing research the record cannot support. The band is the default rather than the lower one because it is a novel and the character tests therefore still apply - they simply cannot be answered - and because a micro-press SF novel is not the slight form that band is for. What the log does say is that a competent unremarkable book lands just under the propose line: Exodus 68 and Quo Vadis 66 are the shape of a solid novel with nothing the reader singled out. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

Short - about 180 pages told in one unbroken linear run - with a concrete starting situation and two travellers: a district doctor and his simple-minded driver forcing horses through a snowstorm to carry vaccine to a village where the dead are reportedly rising, in a nineteenth-century Russia fitted with living felt, holographic radios and engineered creatures. Both content gates were examined and neither reaches premise level. The doctor's night with the miller's wife, whose lilliputian husband sleeps in her bosom, is one grotesque episode on the journey rather than the engine of the book, so filter 5 does not fire; I read the prominence as incidental and the framing as farce rather than approval, which grades at a few points, and I state the doubt because a novel this allegorical could be argued either way. Filter 6 likewise does not fire, but the axis grades rather than clears: the encounter is enacted on the page and the grotesque bodies around it are crude, and Artemis 69 is the log's anchor for crudeness costing at small volume. What sends this to a C exit is axis:ideas. Reviewers report a rich premise let down by uneven prose and a journey whose significance stays elusive, with the feeling that something is left buried in the snow - and non-connection is exactly what made Unfinished Tales 69 the lowest Tolkien, twelve under The Silmarillion 80, in a reader who otherwise tolerates dense mythic prose without a continuous plot. Default band, with the graded content deductions sitting on its low end.
