Occult status is unexamined at this exit; worth noting for whoever revisits it that the risen dead are given an epidemic account rather than a rite. Overspend declared: two sources at a gate budgeted for one.

A children's science encyclopedia by five contributors, built as reference entries across physics, chemistry, biology and space over about two hundred illustrated pages. There is no premise, no protagonist and no argument that runs from front to back, so the axes that carry the top of this log - page time on what people want and why, a premise whose consequences get worked out - have nothing to act on. The children's register itself is graded and cheap when ideas carry the book, as Hobbit 84 and Little Prince 82 show, but reference entries have no single idea to name and the encyclopedia form suspends the character tests without adding anything back, which is the low band rather than the default. Non-fiction earns its place here by examining what is actually true and by showing how another group sees the world, which is what Seeking Allah Finding Jesus 91 did; a survey encyclopedia asserts rather than examines. Gate 4 at one source. Occult is not in play.

t: Vepsano krvi vlastniho srdce (Written in My Own Heart's Blood)
why: Gate 2 was examined and does not fire: Claire's second marriage is contracted on a report of her husband's death, and when he returns the tangle is a legal and moral problem the book stages, not an affair the book exists to tell - remove it and the Philadelphia withdrawal, the disputed paternity and the twentieth-century thread are all still there, so this is subplot territory and a wrong reject here would be unrecoverable. Gate 3 likewise: the plot is a war and a family, not sexual behaviour. What sends it under the line is gate 4. There is no premise being worked out - it is a continuation whose leads, grievances and time-travel rules are all assumed rather than established, four or five live threads running at once - so axis:ideas is a risk and that is the exit condition. A sequel as well, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's fell from 83 to 70 and the Ender books settled from 90 to 81. One source, so occult and the content axes carry unexamined status.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on both conditions, and the form settles it cheaply: the catalogue files this under publications for children and science-fiction stories, and the publisher's own inventory of the book is two Earth children, a kitchen robot with a broken speech unit, an ex-marine pilot, a smart rocket and a gang of galactic poachers, sold as exciting and humorous. That is a comic juvenile adventure and there is no idea I can name in it - poaching is bad is a moral, not a premise with consequences - so axis:ideas goes in risks and the exit follows. The register carries the rest of the number. The log's juvenile ceiling is only reached by books with real substance underneath, Hobbit 84 and The Little Prince 82, while Narnia lands at 67 explicitly for children as the main characters plus lacking higher things to think about; this is a much simpler telling aimed much younger, with a malfunctioning-robot gag as its comic engine, so it sits below that and the lower mandated band is the honest one. Leaned on the missing idea and the juvenile register because those are what I argued; the characters were not examined, since a broken-robot sidekick and two child leads cannot lift a book with no idea in it over the line. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

Exited at the below-the-line gate, and this was the closest call of the ones I stopped on. Form and genre are settled - a 240-page Czech novel that begins as satire about a disillusioned young teacher and turns science-fictional after he meets a mysterious being. Two things point up: the publisher states the book is about where everything and humankind came from, whether the ancient philosophers, the religious dogmatists or the evolutionary scientists came nearest the truth or all of them are wrong, which is a nameable question rather than a set of hooks; and the one substantive reader account says you come to love the protagonist and root for him, which is the reader's single heaviest positive axis. Against that, gate 4 asks whether I would list axis:ideas in risks, and I would. A question posed is not a premise worked out, and this one is posed at a scale that in practice resolves as a revelation delivered by the mysterious being rather than as consequences the book carries - the same reader says the ending is a shock, which is a twist, not an argument. There is a second, specific hazard: the log allows faith as a thread inside a story but not theology as a subject in its own right, and adjudicating origins is exactly that subject. The nearest real comparison is Labyrint sveta a raj srdce at 70, an allegory with a nameable idea where the faith risk did not fire - and 70 is the ceiling that comparison sets, not a floor. So just under the line is the honest record. Leaned on the idea because that is the doubt carrying the number, not on the protagonist, which rests on a single reader review out of fifteen ratings. Occult status is unexamined at this exit, and the mysterious being is the reason to say so out loud.

Comic Czech SF for first-stage primary readers: a ten-year-old leaves a botched copy of Earth, applies for an intergalactic guardian post and picks up a magical animal companion. I cannot name an idea it leaves behind, and the register is the deciding term. On axis:childrens the log has a measured gradient - Hobbit 84 and The Little Prince 82 pay nothing because the ideas carry them, Ranger's Apprentice 74 and Narnia 67 pay a little for children as leads with nothing higher to think about, and a book written for six-to-eleven-year-olds sits well below the Narnia position rather than beside it. Male zeny 79 caps how far character work alone can rescue a juvenile register, and there is no comparable character claim here - the retailer framing is short, funny and brisk. Life-phase adds a small pushback on top, never a tier. Exited at the below-the-line gate, so occult status is unexamined; a magic animal companion is what would need checking.

Exited at the below-the-line gate, and here the doubt is about the premise holding rather than about there being none. Form and genre are settled - a Czech science-fiction novel about a mid-century artificial intelligence beyond its creators' control - and the declared chain is: the AI is squeezing humans out of power, wants to avoid a war over remaining resources, therefore decides to cut the human population drastically, but lacks the key to human survival on another planet, and that key is hidden somewhere deep in the past, so it mounts a secret mission back there. Every link there is asserted rather than derived, and the last two are the kind of thing the log punishes hardest. Mortal Engines was abandoned at 55 on the worldbuilding alone, for a declared capability whose costs the book never accounts for, and Divergent sits at 58 for a premise that collapses under thought and reads as borrowed ideas assembled without cohering. An AI that can plan a genocide and reach into the past but cannot solve off-world survival forward in time is exactly that shape of unexplained asymmetry, and the log is explicit that whatever an author foregrounds becomes binding. There is no critical coverage and no reader reception at all to argue against that reading, so I would list both axis:worldbuilding and axis:ideas in risks and the exit is honest. Leaned on the premise logic rather than the missing idea because premise collapse is the specific thing I argued from the blurb. Occult status is unexamined at this exit.

The log is unusually clear about what first-person testimony has to do to work: Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 earned its score by examining what is actually plausible and by showing how another group experiences the world, while The Diary of a Young Girl 40 is a DNF, so the form itself earns nothing. This is a blog assembled into a book - relapse, detox, abstinence - and the reviews that like it and the reviews that do not agree on the same structural fact, that the same emotions recur page after page and some passages read like status updates. That is no worked-out idea plus a compiled form that suspends the character tests, which is the low band, and the sustained misery is a further mild pushback of the 1984 60 kind. Exited at gate 4 on axis:ideas, one source, so the occult question was not examined.

t: Zena, ktera zacala zit (The Woman Who Came Back to Life)
why: Pearl has spent years hidden in a French woodland cottage when her estranged, dying father calls her back to England and leaves her a diary written in a code only she can read. The pull is a family secret rather than an idea - the publisher's own framing is life, loss and second chances - and I cannot name a premise whose consequences the book follows, which is the gate-4 answer that ends the ladder. The other thing worth recording is structure: two viewpoints, one of them initially unidentified, plus diary extracts jumping between 1981 and 2018 out of order. That is this reader's most reliable failure mode - Guards! Guards! 30 and The Colour of Magic 30 were both abandoned on several strands opening at once - so it sits in risks. Gate 2 was examined: the secret concerns a father who cut contact, and nothing found makes an affair within a marriage the premise; I record that as doubt rather than a finding, since a wrong reject cannot be undone. One source; occult status unexamined below the line.

A Slovak YA post-apocalyptic road novel in three movements - the journey, the city, the return - built on a map that promises the last refuge on Earth and a city that turns out not to be what it promised. The reveal is the whole payload and I cannot name an idea underneath it. Slovak reviewers reach for Divergent and The Hunger Games as the reference set, and that comparison cuts against the book here: Divergent 58 is what this reader gave a dystopia whose premise collapses under thought and whose lead is a Mary Sue, while The Hunger Games 89 earned its score on a tight single POV and on what the characters want - which a hidden-city twist does not supply by itself. Reader reviews name Zoya's indecisiveness as irritating and one complains of confusing, superfluous internal monologue and a shaky survival element, so the protagonist is not the rescue either, and this reader ranks the lead above worldbuilding, Artemis 69 being the case. The teen lead is only a small pushback, Ender's Game 87 settles that. Exited at gate 4 on one source, so the occult status is unexamined.

This is a secondary-school revision textbook: period-by-period survey with historical-social context, short excerpts and a chapter of literary theory, written to be examined on rather than read. Exit at gate 4 on axis:ideas - there is no idea to name at all, only a syllabus, and the form removes every axis the reader actually scores on: no premise whose consequences are worked out, nobody whose motives get page time, nothing left behind afterwards. The log's non-fiction that landed did so by examining what is true from inside an experience (Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91, Son of Hamas 75); a reference survey offers neither, and the suspension of the character rules removes penalties without adding anything (the Little Prince 82 route needs an idea to carry it, and there is none here). Lower band rather than the screening default because the reference form and the absent idea both apply. Occult status is unexamined, as the ladder allows at this exit.

t: Poselstvi megalitu (Die Botschaft der Megalithen: Wer erbaute die steinernen Wunder?)
why: This is pre-astronautics rather than archaeology: the author is catalogued as a parascientific writer whose field is the ancient-astronaut thesis, his best-known previous work claims extraterrestrial traces in East Asia, and retailers shelve this one under extraterrestrial beings. The central argument is an argument from incredulity - that we could not rebuild these monuments today for want of the technology - and that is simply not true; experimental archaeology has repeatedly moved and raised multi-ton blocks by period-plausible means. That is fatal on the axis this reader states most explicitly. The highest non-fiction score in the log, Seeking Allah Finding Jesus 91, earned it above all for genuinely examining what is plausible and what is not, and Rangers Apprentice 74 was docked specifically for lazy claims stated as fact when they are false - here the false claims are the book. So there is no idea that survives contact with its own subject, only a thesis, and the reference form leaves no characters or motives to fall back on, which puts it in the low band rather than the default one. Gate 4 answered as soon as the author was identified, at one source. Occult status is unexamined at this exit and would be worth checking if the book is ever revisited.

t: Stoparuv pruvodce Galaxii (Douglase Adamse) (And Another Thing...)
why: The comic register itself is not an objection - The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy 83 and Saturnin 78 both show that humour carries no penalty here, and Arthur, Ford, Zaphod and Marvin are characters the reader already got on with. Two things put it under the line. It is a sequel, and sequels are the least safe bet in this log: Hitchhiker's sequels 70, a thirteen-point fall from Hitchhiker's Guide 83 and the steepest series decline recorded, and this one is written by a different hand imitating a voice rather than by the author whose voice it was. And it has no premise of its own to work out - reviewers describe it as pastiche padded with Guide entries and a story that drags, which is the thin-story-over-many-pages penalty that cost The Lord of the Rings 84 its distance over The Hobbit 84. There is no idea it leaves behind that Hitchhiker's Guide 83 had not already left. Leaning on axis:ideas and axis:sequels rather than axis:protagonist, because the cast is inherited and was never the problem. Occult status unexamined, which an exit at this depth allows.

One question declared precisely and answered in the only form the book will allow, which is the shape this log rewards in short work. A superintelligence built to define the meaning of human existence declines to compute an answer and tells a story instead: the ferryman Ursanabi, who on this reading stole the flower of immortality himself, carried across history to Aristotle, Hypatia, the conquistadors and Wells's Doctor Moreau, arriving at storytelling as the characteristically human act, the old hunger for immortality, and responsibility toward living nature. Animal Farm 78 and Labyrint sveta 70 both scored on precisely that - a nameable idea in a short book - and The Little Prince 82 shows short allegory carrying ideas without paying the life-phase penalty. The occult question clears on evidence rather than assumption, which matters here because Percy Jackson 57 established that a real pantheon counts: the near-eastern and Old Testament material is retold inside the machine's monologue, not enacted, which is the mentioned-as-having-happened case, and no rite is staged and no power is conferred by one. Deductions keep it out of the A band. The reviewer describes long monologues rather than dramatised scenes and three narrative planes running at once inside a single day's frame, so density costs and the immortal is a vehicle for the argument more than a person with wants - and the suspension of the character rules removes penalties, it never adds points, so nothing here reaches the 80s. Readers also find the ending inevitable rather than earned. Leaned on axis:ideas rather than axis:worldbuilding because there is no declared system here to hold up; the obligation the book takes on is philosophical, and it meets it.

The opening is one concrete situation -- a sister goes missing, the boy is sent to an eccentric uncle, and an old machine in a cathedral extracts his seven deadly sins as literal monster companions -- which is exactly the followable, invested-immediately shape this reader wants, and reviewers confirm the wacky plot 'retains its own sense of logic.' The extraction device is engineering, not ritual: declared, mechanical, no invocation, so it clears the occult test the way Sanderson's Allomancy does. The idea -- your own vices made into argued-with, useful companions -- earns a little credit the way Little Prince 82's allegory does, but it is a broad children's comedy first, and one review flags a kitchen-sink pace that thins out key plot points, so it sits below Rangers Apprentice 74 rather than above it.

Reviewers call this the strongest opening of the series so far - a concrete scene about mercy and forgiveness (an enemy's stone is smashed, and he is invited along anyway) rather than a confusing in-media-res drop, and single out trust and forgiveness as real emotional content, not just incident. Emily is established across the series as having a clear want (protect her family, master the Amulet's power) with real doubt about the cost of using it, which reads as the protagonist axis holding up. As a children's graphic novel (ages 9-13) the childrens axis applies and costs a little, closer to Ranger's Apprentice and Narnia territory than to Hobbit's cost-free result.

A Czech splatter-pulp vampire-vs-alien series. Reviewers across the trilogy repeatedly flag heavy, gratuitous sex alongside the violence - one entry is called 'a porn version of Twilight,' another notes the sequel 'doesn't skimp on bullets or sex' - the volume-plus-crudeness combination that has already sunk Witcher 53 and Ready Player One 55 here, on a series otherwise praised mainly for fast pacing rather than for any idea of its own ('the plot barely gets stuck anywhere, it runs like a chainsaw').

t: Cestovni kancelar Jinosvety (The Strangeworlds Travel Agency: The Edge of the Ocean)
why: A children's portal-fantasy sequel: Flick and Jonathan step through a suitcase into a sinking pirate world to save a mermaid queen before her flat world collapses. The hook is a fun, concrete situation - closer to Hitchhiker's Guide's 'one concrete situation' opening (83) than to a confusing one - but the substance is episodic problem-solving ('how do you fit a whale-sized queen in a suitcase') rather than an idea worked out, and it sits in the MG register that costs Ranger's Apprentice (74) and Narnia (67) a little. It is also a sequel, and this log's sequels settle down rather than up (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70).

A Czech-original comic anthology presented as a fake 'translation' of an American pulp writer, following the villain Vosak through gag-driven episodes with mock scholarly footnotes. It is the short-idea-driven suspension with nothing to lean on - no single premise worked out, just a run of parody vignettes (a hero-killing dragon-lair prank, a vomiting punchline) - the same fragmentation gap that leaves Unfinished Tales (69) unaligned, but without Tolkien's underlying material to fall back on, so the lower of the two C bands fits.

A Persian-myth-inspired curse-breaking quest with a real idea at its core - 'not all curses need to be cured', Soraya's poison recast as strength rather than monstrousness, the kind of premise-worked-out payoff this log rewards. The central romance is the protagonist's own and lands as same-sex (she ultimately chooses the demon Parvaneh over the human suitor who turns out to be the true monster) - a main-character thread rather than the whole premise, the Caropisci (67) shape, so it grades rather than vetoes but still costs real points. The demon Soraya bargains with is drawn from real Persian/Shahnameh lore rather than invented, but the bargain itself is a magical trade for a cure, not a staged rite of sacrifice or divination, so it stays a mild occult concern rather than the heavy one that demoted Caropisci. Held down by a protagonist multiple reviewers call 'too naive' to fully invest in, and by generally mixed reception.

An MG magic-theatre school story: Harper is recruited into the Spectaculars, a troupe of star-powered performers persecuted as a 'Grade Six Dangerous Species'. The magic itself is mechanism, not occultism - starlight-powered stagecraft with declared effects (costumes that shift, arias that levitate), clearing the occult bar the way Allomancy does. The persecution angle gestures at a real idea, but the mechanics (a flying-canoe recruitment, a boarding-school apprenticeship, a save-the-school prophecy) read as standard MG furniture rather than a worked-through idea, and the 'Dangerous Species' status is asserted rather than shown functioning in a society. Sits with Ranger's Apprentice (74) and Narnia (67) - a little cost for the children's register, nothing worse.

t: Filix Wood (Filix Wood: The Night of the Greedy Dogs)
why: MG Swedish fantasy: a boy drawn into a hidden tree-village whose people sacrifice themselves to hold back an underworld evil, weighing a 'only the strongest survives' ethos against the courage to admit weakness. That is a real, statable idea (subverting the strength narrative, in the author's own words), which is what keeps this out of the lower band, but it is delivered in a straightforward children's-adventure register, and it is a sequel with no read anchor for how well the idea actually lands on the page. Sits with Ranger's Apprentice (74) and Narnia (67) rather than higher.

A prophecy of two queens born a thousand years apart is not a marriage-plot or a whodunit, and it is played straight rather than for cynicism, which the log treats as free. But reviewers describe repeated, graphic sexual content -- including a masturbation scene and encounters some readers flag as ambiguously consensual -- which is closer to the volume-plus-explicitness combination that sank Ready Player One 55 and The Witcher 53 than to Red Rising 95's low-on-all-three profile. Same-sex attraction here is Eliana sleeping with women alongside men and Rielle's ambiguous flirtations -- incidental to the plot, not a thread the story follows, so it costs little on its own axis. One reviewer titled their piece 'great premise, bad execution, bland characters,' which is the same failure mode that dropped Artemis from a predicted 80 to 69, so the range leans down rather than up on the prophecy's ambition.

A dark apocalyptic romance consistently reviewed as maximum-heat ('5-pepper') romantasy, with reader-compiled content warnings naming rape, torture and hostage dynamics alongside the sex; that goes past Ready Player One 55 and The Witcher 53, both sunk mainly by volume, and Famine's captor/captive dub-con framing adds the crudeness that docked Artemis 69 at far smaller volume. The apocalyptic-redemption idea (a being of destruction weighing whether humanity is worth saving) is real and Famine is a deliberate contrast to his brothers - he refuses to change - but that survives as an idea rather than lifting the score, because the sexual-content axis is what actually caps it. Opening is one concrete situation (Ana and Famine's earlier history, then their reunion), not multi-thread confusion. No real-world occult sourcing or on-page rite found; reviewers describe the series' treatment of religion as deliberately neutral, with no ceremony or invocation shown. leanedOn axis:sexual-content rather than axis:ideas because that is what a reader with this profile would react to first, matching the RPO/Witcher pattern in the log.

t: Hodina dynove kralovny (Hour of the Pumpkin Queen)
why: Sally falling through a portal into a Time Town where someone tampered with the clock is an investigation-shaped subplot, not the book's whole satisfaction (the point is Sally reclaiming agency as queen), so it is a flag rather than the detective veto. One reader review of this exact book calls it 'kinda more of the same but with new characters ... just a little repetitive,' echoing the same doubt that caps its predecessor: a licensed-tie-in plot rather than a worked idea of its own.

t: Jak zradit draciho hrdinu (How to Betray a Dragon's Hero)
why: The penultimate volume centers on Hiccup being tortured for information while trying to protect the human rebels, and on Snotlout's arc turning on a personal betrayal that costs him his whole family - the want-and-why focus the reader ranks above action (Mockingjay 91, Golden Son 92). Set against that, reviewers note the series is 'getting darker' with named character deaths, a mild bleakness cost per this reader's stated weighting. Excellinor is characterized across the series as a witch skilled in fortune-telling as well as poison-lore, a real-world-occult-coded archetype, but no source found within budget confirms an on-page divination or spellcasting rite in this specific volume - her page-time here is torture and manipulation rather than ritual - so this stays an open, unresolved risk rather than a veto.

t: Jane Doe (Jane Doe and the Cradle of All Worlds)
why: A girl crossing a portal to find her missing father is a quest structure, not a whodunit, so the detective signal does not bind. Kirkus called the worldbuilding utterly incoherent -- a mismatch of tech levels, idioms and foods that make no sense together, plus casual ethnic and disability tropes. That is the same kind of self-consistency failure that sank Mortal Engines 55, and it is sourced more sharply than the mild register cost that Rangers Apprentice 74 and Narnia 67 pay for being for children. No idea beyond the rescue-quest premise is nameable, so axis:ideas would sit in risks if this went further; it does not need to.

The opening is one concrete inciting scene -- a man's shadow vanishes at a market -- and losing a shadow costs you your memories, which then lets you unmake reality around what you have forgotten. That is a real premise worked into consequence, the axis Project Hail Mary 92 and Old Man's War 87 both score on, and Ory's search for his wife is motive-driven rather than event-driven, the axis that tops the log. It is not occult -- no invocation or source in real practice, just an unexplained fantastical plague. The risk is real: reviewers document the rules breaking their own logic (forgetting a marketplace erases it, but forgetting you need to breathe kills you instead of rewriting that need away), and the back half is called convoluted and bloated with a literal magic battle grafted onto a dystopia. That is the same self-consistency failure Kafka's bleakness-and-protagonist risks embodied for Promena, so the range is capped rather than pushed toward the memory-and-devotion premise's full potential.

French bit-lit (angels, demons, vampires) opening a trilogy about a body-possessing heroine hunting the vampires who destroyed her convent. A critic's own summary calls it 'a well-oiled mechanism that respects the codes of the genre' - competent commercial paranormal romance rather than a book with a case of its own, the same territory that left Witcher 53 and Ready Player One 55 without enough to lean on. Given the C-low exit, the angel/demon mythology's occult status was not examined and is carried unexamined in deps.

Neither the annotation nor the reviews found name a single point-of-view lead: the book centers on a growing goblin city and a hidden figure amassing power underground to seize it, which is worldbuilding and political intrigue rather than a want-and-why protagonist to root for, and reviewers themselves ask for more plot gradation and more magic. Without a lead to anchor on, this does not clear the doubt Gate 4 asks about the way the reader's actual high scorers (Mockingjay, Golden Son) do. C-low exit precedes the occult gate, so axis:occult is unexamined here (kept in deps).

t: Marcy a hadanka od sfingy (Marcy and the Riddle of the Sphinx)
why: This is a 56-page illustrated picture book for ages 5-9, described by one reviewer as 'a graphic novel in every sense because the graphics are the novel' -- the text is a prompt for the art, not a developed narrative. The theme (a fearful girl finds courage to rescue her father) is stated plainly rather than worked through, well short of the idea Little Prince 82 carries despite similar brevity. Encounters with Thoth, Isis and Ra are mythological-adventure trappings rather than a rite depicted on the page, but that is not confirmed beyond the blurb, so axis:occult is left unexamined at this exit.

t: Maruska Pulnocni a velka hmyzi olympiada (Marnie Midnight and the Great Critter Contest)
why: Early-reader insect-school chapter book (Minibeast Academy) built around winning an inter-species olympiad at all costs; no idea beyond the competition-and-friendship plot, so gate 4 exits on axis:ideas. Marketed explicitly as a bridge from picture books for beginning readers (younger than Narnia's audience, which still scored 67), so axis:childrens costs more here than in any already-read comp, putting it in the lower C-low band rather than the default one. Occult unexamined at this exit - gate 4 stops research before gate 5.

A thief talks his way into a palace guard post and is disappointed to be assigned to a library instead of glory -- a standard reluctant-hero fantasy setup with no idea beyond the setting itself. Reviews split between praising the atmosphere and finding it boring or leaving too many open questions by the end, which matches a book that has not worked out a premise so much as decorated one; no claim here rises to the level Silmarillion 80 or Little Prince 82 earn from an idea actually carried through.

A historical fantasy about a mermaid, Amelia, who leaves the sea for a fisherman and later becomes P.T. Barnum's live 'Feejee Mermaid.' Reviewers repeatedly single out Amelia as intelligent, determined and outspoken against both the era's treatment of women and slavery she witnesses on tour - the wants-and-why interiority this reader rewards in Pride and Prejudice 75 and Little Women 79, both character-carried books with no big plot engine. But multiple reviews also flag the book as nearly plotless, dragging past the midpoint with a rushed final act - the kind of thin-story-over-many-pages this reader penalizes as density, not length itself.

A Great War splits the world; the sklenari mining caste pays a heavy price for a rare gift, and 13-year-old Ilan hides as a boy to avoid conscription into it - an oppressed-underclass premise that echoes the axis topping Mockingjay 91 and Hunger Games 89. But multiple independent reader reviews of this specific book converge on the opposite of a worked-out idea: a bland, unmemorable heroine, a plot reviewers call empty of real events, and padded explaining that never answers the important questions, with one review calling it an 'ecological rip-off' of Frank Herbert's desert-planet saga that fizzles out - closer to Divergent's 58 (ideas borrowed and assembled without cohering) than to the reader's actual high scorers. C-low exit precedes the occult gate, so axis:occult is unexamined here (kept in deps).

t: Nejchladnejsi divka ve meste chladu (The Coldest Girl in Coldtown)
why: Opens on one concrete situation - Tana waking in a bathtub to find everyone else at the party dead - the single-POV, immediate-stakes shape this log rewards in Hitchhiker's Guide and The Hunger Games. The vampirism-as-epidemic logic (an infection window, a countdown before the craving turns fatal) is carried through rather than just declared, the axis Old Man's War and Project Hail Mary score high on. Tana is repeatedly praised across reviews as practical and goal-driven rather than swooning or waiting to be saved, which is the protagonist axis this reader weights above worldbuilding. Sexual content is real but reviewers call it infrequent though sensual (biting, blood-kissing) rather than crude or high-volume, closer to Old Man's War's single-chapter cost than to what sank Witcher or Ready Player One.

Thompson's want-and-why is stated plainly - survive, protect his family, avenge those who wronged him - the axis that tops Mockingjay 91 and Golden Son 92. But reader reception is split on whether he is rootable: one reviewer calls him rotten, preaching water and drinking wine, feeling wronged while wronging others, which is closer to the un-rootable villain-lead problem that cost The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 22 points against Sunrise on the Reaping than to a flaw a lead earns past. The book is also structured as linked short stories that reviewers say only work as a whole, closer to Unfinished Tales 69's fragmentation than a driven single arc, with no idea beyond a standard borderland revenge-and-survival premise to point to. C-low exit precedes the occult gate, so axis:occult is unexamined here (kept in deps).

t: Nejtemnejsi cast lesa (The Darkest Part of the Forest)
why: Fairfold's premise - siblings who grew up idolizing a sleeping horned fae boy now have to deal with him waking - has a real idea in it (outgrowing a childhood rescue fantasy, what the town's economy costs the people it exploits), but reader reviews describe the plot as crammed into the last third with an underdeveloped conflict and a villain played for laughs, which is exactly the premise-does-not-hold-up doubt this ladder exits on. Not rejected on anything hard; occult status from the fae content is unexamined at this exit per the ladder.

A deaf mountain village that loses even its remaining sense (sight) piece by piece until Fei's sudden, unexplained gift of hearing forces her down the mountain to save her people - a real, nameable idea (silence, sacrifice, the courage to act alone) in the vein of what the short-idea-driven allegories in the log reward. Held down by Kirkus's specific criticism that the Chinese setting and mythology are decorative rather than load-bearing - swap the names for medieval England and nothing changes - the same undertake-to-explain failure that costs points elsewhere in the log. The village's founding myth (guardian pixiu creatures whose slumber caused the deafness) is referenced as backstory rather than enacted as a rite on the page, so it is carried as a risk rather than vetoed outright.

An all-female-crew revenge story after a warlord's army kills Caledonia's family - a motives-driven premise (revenge, found family) similar in shape to what the log rewards (Mockingjay 91, Red Rising 95), and romance is confirmed secondary and thin rather than the plot's engine, so no filter applies despite the task line's detective signal (there is no investigation; the signal reads as a false positive on this book). Reviewer reception on the protagonist is split, though - some find her compelling, others call her 'stubborn and over-the-top for no reason' - close to the thin-lead problem that cost Artemis 23 points against Project Hail Mary. The warlord's control mechanism (an addictive drug plus brainwashing) is stated but not shown being worked through with the consequence-chasing the log rewards in Old Man's War or Project Hail Mary, so worldbuilding is a risk rather than a strength. No occult (drug/brainwashing control, not magic), no infidelity. leanedOn axis:protagonist because that split reception is what would move the number.

A grieving teen's town flips upside-down into an alternate world that is explicitly his depression given form - a genuine idea literalized and followed through, not just event after event, the same logic that rewards Animal Farm (78): bleak material that gives you something to think about instead of just immersing you in the misery. The whole book is Theo's want (to hold onto his friend, to be seen, to reconnect) rather than what he does, the axis that tops this log. Reviewers agree the ending is earned rather than a fairytale fix - it does not wallow, and trade reviews single out that it 'transcends the...adventure story' for something more profound. Docked for the content itself: on-page self-harm and suicidal ideation are heavier than this log's mildest-objection bleakness, and Theo is a teenager, a small pushback on its own.

The premise - a town founded on a buried magical secret it is forbidden to investigate - is a real idea (what actually happened, why history itself is dangerous here) rather than just incident, the kind of thing this log rewards in Animal Farm and Labyrint sveta. Reviewers call the payoff strong once the layered mystery unspools, though several flag the prose as dense and the riddles as overly clever, which costs on the heavy-description-with-little-story axis this reader dislikes. The 'Old History' interludes show magical-scientific experimentation with declared costs and mechanisms rather than invocation or worship, which looks like the mechanism escape from the occult filter, though this was not confirmed against a specific on-page ritual scene.

Sylvia Viktorina, a duke's youngest daughter dropped into hostile marsh territory who must build alliances among adventurers, orcs and monsters to survive, draws real reader praise for being distinguished from a generic love-interest type - the interesting-and-rootable combination the reader ranks above pure worldbuilding (Artemis 69 vs Golden Son 92). Against that, the wider series is repeatedly flagged for name-overload confusion and thin narrative momentum ('moc se toho nedeje'), which caps the range below the reader's A-band comparables. The fading antagonist Alarich Touraine is called a 'Dark Mage' with in-world religion discussed in interstitial worldbuilding chapters, but no source found describes an on-page rite; the question is not resolved from primary text, so axis:occult stays an open risk rather than a clean pass.

t: Pan ledove zahrady (Pan Lodowego Ogrodu (Lord of the Ice Garden))
why: Award-winning Polish science fantasy: an Earth agent, forbidden from interfering, must understand what happened to a scientific expedition on an alien world after some of its members seized planetary power and declared themselves gods. That non-interference, understand-the-culture engine is close to the axis that topped Speaker for the Dead 90 and drove Old Man's War 87's payoff. Set against it, reviewers single out the 'gods' concept itself as underdeveloped and note uneven treatment of side threads - a worldbuilding-consistency risk this reader has punished before (Artemis 69 over-predicted on worldbuilding while the lead was thin). The 'gods' are former human scientists who seized a planetary power, not real deities, and the ritual-sounding opening line reads as a stylistic epigraph rather than a rite a character performs on the page, so it is expected to clear the occult filter, though that was not confirmed with full certainty. Discovery (axis:discovery, 2026-10-24): sent alone to find out what became of a lost expedition on a world he does not understand, the unknown and the need are central, but reviewers' doubts about the gods concept leave the answer in question, so partial, +2.

Award-winning Czech fantasy (Cena Trifid 2005) about a Doorkeeper who opens and closes the gates of a magical House. One reader calls the prose genuinely poetic, but another finds the mostly-flashback structure and secondary cast (other doorkeepers, executioners) 'confusing,' and a third calls the whole book 'trochu zmatene' over the usual causality tangles of a time-travel plot - the same shape-one risk this reader has scored 30 three times (Gunslinger, Colour of Magic, Guards! Guards!).

t: Po schodech nahoru dolu (Poika ullakolla, poika kellarissa)
why: A well-liked Finnish children's novel (Finlandia Junior finalist) about two ten-year-olds who discover they live in the same house in parallel realities, whose friendship risks merging both worlds. Reviewers praise the hook and pacing and its gentle treatment of loneliness, comparable in shape to Narnia 67 - solid children's portal fantasy that is 'not bad' but written for and pitched at readers well below the higher-things bar this reader wants.

YA portal fantasy opener from a Swedish mentalist-turned-novelist. Reviews describe the plot as jumping between many odd events, the world staying strange and illogical for all 300 pages, and characters nobody warms to - exactly the shape-one confusion this reader scored 30 three separate times (Gunslinger, Colour of Magic, Guards! Guards!). Book 1 of a trilogy that mostly raises questions it does not answer.

This is a second-person Fighting Fantasy gamebook -- you are the adventurer, and the path branches on your choices -- so there is no authored protagonist with wants and flaws to root for; the character-and-motive rules this reader weighs heaviest simply have nothing to grip. Reception calls this specific entry 'very average' and lacking originality, and fan reviewers steer newcomers to other titles in the line first, which confirms there is no strong idea to fall back on either. That combination -- a form that suspends the character tests and no idea to name -- is exactly what the low band is for.

t: Skandar a kostliva kletba (Skandar and the Skeleton Curse)
why: No review specific to this fourth volume was found within budget, so this is carried on the same author-level pattern as the rest of the series (convenient plotting and flimsy worldbuilding flagged in books 1-2) - the axis:ideas doubt Gate 4 asks about, said honestly rather than argued from this book's own text. The unicorn-elemental magic is an invented mechanical system, incidentally clearing occult, though this was not a dedicated check at this exit gate.

t: Skandar a prizracny jezdec (Skandar and the Phantom Rider)
why: This is a middle-grade unicorn-academy series; a critical reader who found book 1 'incompetently written' calls this second volume 'an improvement... but not by much', and a separate review of book 1 flags 'the CONVENIENCE of so many plot points' and worldbuilding 'flimsier than its predecessors' - exactly the axis:ideas doubt Gate 4 asks about, closer to Divergent's 58 (borrowed ideas assembled without cohering) than a worked-through premise. A more positive review calls it well-paced with real character growth, so the range keeps both readings in play rather than picking one. The unicorn-elemental bond is an invented, mechanical system (a blood bond conferring power, no invocation or real-world occult source), incidentally clearing the occult question, though this was not a dedicated check at this exit gate.

t: Skandar a souteze Chaosu (Skandar and the Chaos Trials)
why: No review specific to this third volume was found within budget, so this is carried on the author-level pattern established for the series: books 1 and 2 are described as built on convenient, flimsy worldbuilding, which is the axis:ideas doubt Gate 4 asks about, and nothing found for this volume rebuts it - said honestly rather than argued from this book's own text. The unicorn-elemental magic is an invented mechanical system, incidentally clearing occult, though this was not a dedicated check at this exit gate.

Enne's search for her missing mother and Levi's ambition to escape his debts both give the book real, stated wants, the axis that tops this reader's log - but reviewers flag the lineage-based Shadow Card/orb magic system as underexplained ('names given, no definitions'), the same declare-and-fail-to-carry-through problem that cost Harry Potter and Divergent in this log, so it is carried as a risk rather than folded into the number. The missing-mother thread is an investigation, but the book's satisfaction is the heist/underworld intrigue around it (reviewers compare it repeatedly to Six of Crows), not a whodunit - flagged, not vetoed. Lineage magic (cards, orbs) reads mechanistic rather than invocation-based, so it clears the occult test.

A 16-author horror anthology built around one shared setting (Halloween) rather than a single worked idea has no axis:ideas to lean on, the same gap that keeps most short-story collections under the line. The short-idea-driven suspension removes the usual character-and-motive penalties but adds nothing on its own, and with a different author and premise every ten pages there is no protagonist to carry across the book either. Several stories draw on real Halloween/Dia de los Muertos folk-ritual material, which would need a story-by-story check this exit does not require -- axis:occult is left unexamined.

t: Svetla na obloze (A Shiver of Snow and Sky)
why: Two clear POVs from early on (Osa braving the wilderness, Ivar preparing the village) means the opening is legible rather than confusing. But the premise -- a goddess signaling omens through sky-lights, a plague, an ice dragon, a low-key romance -- is a familiar YA fantasy assembly rather than a worked idea, and reviewers call it original mainly by comparison to a generic base. That lands it with the standard adventure-fantasy tier rather than the ones the log credits for an actual idea, like Labyrint sveta 70 or Animal Farm 78.

t: Terry Pratchett (Terry Pratchett: The Spirit of Fantasy)
why: A literary biography of Pratchett, but reviewers consistently say it barely functions as one: nearly half the book is a bibliography anyone could compile from Amazon listings, the analysis is called 'sub-A level' opinion journalism rather than real criticism, and one review is titled outright 'is Terrible.' This reader's rule for the form is that it earns nothing by itself - only examining what is actually true does that (Qureshi 91 versus Anne Frank 40) - and the record here is of padding and undisciplined tangents rather than insight into Pratchett.

Mira, a war refugee posing as a marriageable lady to earn her way to freedom, uncovers a conspiracy to start a war while acting as an informal spy partner - the plot runs on what she wants and why, the axis that tops this reader's log (Mockingjay 91; Pride and Prejudice 75 shows romance-as-subject itself costs nothing). Kept out of the A band by being commercial YA adventure-romance rather than a book that works its ideas out with real depth - risk that the political intrigue is thinner than the character motivation once read in full. The task line's axis:occult signal is not supported by anything in the plot (an espionage/marriage-market drama with no magic found in research); treated as a lexicon false positive.

This is book five of an ongoing vampire-town series and reviewers of this specific installment are unusually split: 'a lacklustre effort compared to earlier offerings,' a tornado subplot that 'one does have to wonder at what purpose it served,' against other readers calling it 'the best book in the series.' The declared-rules test this reader applies -- an author must carry through what he sets up -- is exactly what the weaker reviews fault: a plotline (the storm) introduced without payoff and 'a lot left unexplained.' That keeps it capped near the competent-genre-entry line rather than the Old Man's War 87 tier a consistent vampire-politics setup could reach.

No review specific to this fourth volume was found within budget, so this is carried on the same author-level pattern as the rest of the series (a promising premise that independent readers repeatedly report as thin-plotted and unmemorable in its lead) - said honestly rather than argued from this volume's own text. C-low exit precedes the occult gate, so axis:occult is unexamined here (kept in deps).

An explicit short-story collection, old and new texts tied together only by a recurring hero or group rather than one throughline premise - axis:short-idea-driven suspends the character-and-emotion rules but supplies no axis:ideas to lean on instead, the same shape that sinks a literary collection at Gate 4. The nearest read-log analogue is Unfinished Tales 69 (fragmented, pieces not logically connected), but without Tolkien's established pull and with the wider series already flagged for thin narrative momentum, so the lower band applies rather than the default. C-low exit precedes the occult gate, so axis:occult is unexamined here (kept in deps).

War carries the same maximum-heat romantasy handling reviewers give the whole series (5-pepper rating consistent across sources), but with a more worked-through arc than a pure captivity plot: War is written with private tenderness against his public brutality, and Miriam actively teaches him what love means rather than merely surviving him - closer to the motives-over-action axis the log rewards most (Mockingjay 91, Speaker for the Dead 90). That keeps War a little ahead of a book with only captivity to offer, but the same heavy sexual-content volume/explicitness that sinks Ready Player One 55 and The Witcher 53 still caps it well under the 68 line. Opening is a single concrete scene (Jerusalem's fall, War claiming Miriam as his 'wife'), not multi-thread confusion. No on-page real-world occult rite found; one reviewer specifically praises the book's neutral, non-ritualistic treatment of religion (no ceremonies, no prayer calls shown). leanedOn axis:sexual-content, not axis:protagonist, because the character work here is comparatively strong and isn't what would cap the score.

t: Ve stinu Vlci kralovny (In the Shadow of the Wolf Queen)
why: A middle-grade fantasy (Orion Children's Books, illustrated, recommended from age 9) with a genuine idea worth naming - power-lust is literally poisoning the land, forcing an 'unlikely heroine' to confront what the Wolf Queen's rule costs - which is the axis the log rewards most (Animal Farm 78, Labyrint sveta 70). That places it above a book with nothing to think about, but the child register and MG audience cap it in the Narnia 67 / Ranger's Apprentice 74 band rather than higher. The opening is one concrete situation - an earthquake, then a sister's disappearance - not the multi-thread confusion that sank Guards! Guards! and The Colour of Magic. No occult concern found: geomancy is framed as nature-based and invented (ley lines, listening to trees), not witchcraft, seance or a real-world pantheon, and no on-page rite was found. leanedOn axis:childrens because that is what sets the ceiling here, not the idea, which is present but modest for the band.

Acclaimed Czech literary novel built on a family legend (a worm under a garden that must be fed, one grandson bound to inherit the duty), told through fragmented, multi-typeface narrators and an ending the author leaves deliberately open. Reviewers split exactly on this reader's most punished trait: one calls the fragmented, self-aware-plot-hole structure 'originalni, ne-li genialni,' another says the same thing produces 'zmatek' (confusion) and misunderstanding. This reader has scored three separate confusing, multi-thread openings 30 (Gunslinger, Colour of Magic, Guards! Guards!), so the risk is real enough to keep this under the line rather than lean up on the strong critical reception.

An illustrated picture-book-length story: a girl helps an injured ice dragon heal so spring can come. Reviews are warm but even a favorable one admits the story 'felt like something read before, just without the dragons' - a single kindness moral without an idea of its own, unlike Little Prince 82, which clears the childrens bar because it carries one. The reader-profile explicitly bands a picture book in the 30s-40s.

Opens on a concrete dramatic escape before filling in the backstory - the single-situation shape this log rewards in Hitchhiker's Guide - and the ending is repeatedly singled out as the book's strongest part, one reviewer finishing standing up with a hand on the light switch. Isarell is described as brave and capable with a clear want (survive, earn her place), the protagonist axis this reader weights most. The recurring complaint across reviews is an overloaded middle stretch - training chapters thick with faction names and rules that several reviewers say slow the read - a density cost distinct from the opening, which is separately praised as immersive.

t: Zmije a vlk (The Serpent and the Wolf)
why: Vaasa's magic is built as a trauma metaphor - an animal-shaped power she cannot control after her mother's death - which is a real idea, and reviewers single out the coven/magic system as genuinely intricate, the kind of worked-through worldbuilding Old Man's War and Project Hail Mary score high on. Vaasa has a clear want (survive, control her power) and real agency, the protagonist axis this reader weights most. But the author's own content warning lists explicit sex, and reader-submitted warnings call it graphic and recurring rather than occasional - closer to the sustained volume that sank Witcher and Ready Player One than to Old Man's War's single chapter, even without those two books' crudeness. That one axis is what keeps this under the line despite the rest working.

t: Artemis Fowl a atlantsky komplex (Artemis Fowl and the Atlantis Complex)
why: The positive case is one real idea: a boy-genius criminal's obsessive guilt breaking him into a gentle, romantic alter ego, so the plot turns on what he wants and who he is. But reviews describe this one as one action scene after another with the genius's planning missing, which removes what made the lead interesting, and the register is a younger-readers fantasy (Ranger's Apprentice 74, Narnia 67 pay a little). The occult deduction is moderate, about minus 5: a rune-curse enslaving two leads is staged, but fairy magic in this series is largely tech-like with invented rites, so graded not vetoed. It is a late sequel that assumes the reader knows its cast (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70). Leaned on the childrens register and a single idea, with the lead's rootability as the open risk.

Positive case: a clear premise worked as consequences (gods lose immortality for twelve hours every hundred years and anyone can kill them, chapters counted in hours), a closing question whether changing history always improves it, and readers praising characters with their own wants; it is a standalone. Occult under the new rule: the pantheon is invented (goddess of life, death-god the Rider, goddess of wisdom) but priesthood, temple hierarchy, god-given marks and prayer are central to the 1932 leads, so graded heavy (-10); the central act is killing gods, not sacrificing people, and no human sacrifice was found. Deductions: two timelines with six friends in the future thread and several 1932 viewpoints (multi-pov, and an opening that must establish two eras), readers call the second half weaker and the future lead immature (Divergent 58 and Ballad 65: a thin or unrootable lead outweighs the premise). The number sits ten points under where it would without the rites. Leaned on the idea because the lead evidence is mixed.

A fairy-tale grief story (survivor's guilt, addiction to power, a family that blames the wrong twin) with a nameable idea and motives that drive the plot, which supports the high 60s as it did for Animal Farm 78. Deductions stack: a children's-book register with a boy lead (Narnia 67, Ranger's Apprentice 74 pay a little); a reviewer finds the lead spineless, and the Ballad 65 and Oliver Twist 57 anchors both punish a lead who is acted upon rather than wanting; a prophecy that the 'wrong boy' will save her, graded on handling and costing little; and the occult grade. The mother is a witch who binds the dead twin's soul to the living one with the magic she guards, which resembles soul-binding necromancy and keeps the Source test open, so I grade moderate and keep occult as a risk. Leaned on ideas and motives because the worldbuilding is archetypal and the lead is the shaky axis.

Positive case: one premise worked out in consequences, a past that resists change and punishes the traveller each time, carried by a single first-person lead with flaws to overcome whose choices cost him what he loves. The love story is the emotional engine and romance as the central subject costs nothing (Pride and Prejudice 75); whether to change history leaves ideas behind, the axis shared with Project Hail Mary 92 and Speaker for the Dead 90. The opening is concrete (a teacher, a diner, a task), so the confusion that sank The Gunslinger 30 does not apply. Deductions: the time-travel logic is described as only 'almost coherent', and this reader verifies declared rules (Divergent 58, Mortal Engines 55); the book runs over 800 pages with a slow start and long stretches of ordinary years, so density is a risk even though length is not; the closing sequence of resets may drag as The Martian 82 did; sexual content is incidental to the romance. The assassination plot is stalking and surveillance, not a whodunnit, so the detective gate does not fire. Leaned on ideas and motives. Discovery (axis:discovery, 2026-10-24): a man arriving in a time he knows only from history books, who must learn how it pushes back to do what he came for, and finds out what changing it costs, the arrival case the reader named beside Project Hail Mary 92; partial, because the period itself is known, so +2.

t: Dcera kosti a dymu (Daughter of Smoke and Bone)
why: Positive case: a lead whose own past is the open question (a positive in this log), a Prague opening that is easy to read, and a war between angels and chimaera that turns on hatred across a divide, with a Romeo-and-Juliet romance as the book's subject (romance as the central subject costs nothing in Pride and Prejudice 75). Occult re-decided: Brimstone's wishes and resurrection run on teeth and pain, and souls are gleaned into thuribles and put into made bodies; this is an invented currency-and-pain system, not drawn from real grimoires or real gods, so it is an invented system's raising of the dead, graded heavy (-10), though the necromantic resemblance is real and a stricter reading would veto. Further deductions: insta-love and an age gap between a seventeen-year-old and a fifty-year-old, a young-adult register and lush prose, and a reported slog in the last third (Narnia 67 and Ranger's Apprentice 74 for register). The number sits ten points under where it would without the rites. Leaned on the lead and motives rather than worldbuilding. Since 2026-10-24 the open past credited above is priced as axis:discovery, once: partial, with the romance as the subject; the number holds.

t: Divka, ktera upijela mesic (The Girl Who Drank the Moon)
why: A fable about a society kept obedient by a manufactured fear (an annual infant 'sacrifice' to a witch who in fact rescues the babies), with several viewpoint characters who each want something different and a lie that unravels through those wants. That is the motives-over-action axis that tops Mockingjay 91, and the idea (fear and sorrow as instruments of rule) is nameable, as with Animal Farm 78. Deductions: a Newbery middle-grade register with a 13-year-old lead, which costs a little as Narnia 67 and Ranger's Apprentice 74 do; and the occult grade. Xan is explicitly a witch, the exact objection recorded on Harry Potter 51, but her magic is invented (starlight and moonlight fed to a child, no spells, no invocation, no devotion, no grimoire), so I grade it light to moderate rather than veto; the staged 'sacrifice' is an abandonment and nobody is killed. Leaned on motives and ideas, not worldbuilding, since the setting is a fairy-tale frame. The opening is one concrete scene (a baby left in the forest) though several POVs follow quickly. Occult and childrens are the axes that could pull it under the line.

t: Dny krve a hvezdneho trpytu (Days of Blood and Starlight)
why: A direct continuation that assumes the lead, world and war already established, so axis:sequels applies (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70). The lead now builds resurrected bodies for a warlord's army on the page throughout: an invented system's raising of the dead, graded heavy (-10), repeated and central to how she is useful. The war is bleak and the lead's complicity in the warlord's cause tests whether she is worth rooting for (Ballad 65, where nobody was rootable), and extra viewpoints split page time. Positive case: motives of the hurt and the hated are the whole book, and the lead stays driven by wants she can state. The number sits ten points under where it would without the rites, less a little for sequel decline. Leaned on the protagonist because the direction of her travel decides it.

A premise worked out through its consequences (a scarce resource, an engineered religious myth that comes true, a messiah plot examined rather than celebrated), told through what Jessica, Paul and the great houses want. That is the axis behind Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90, and second-order consequences are what lifted Project Hail Mary 92. Prophecy is graded on handling, and here the legend is manufactured and then examined, which the profile treats as fine unless played as cynicism, so I price a small risk on axis:faith. Occult: the Bene Gesserit and Fremen rites (the Water of Life, spice-agony initiation, the gom jabbar test) are invented and staged; the training itself reads as mechanism, and no human sacrifice is staged in any source I found, so this grades moderate, about minus 5, not veto. Remaining deductions are the opening, a cold start full of invented terms (Caladan, Bene Gesserit, Mentat) with an omniscient hop between heads that can read as shape two, and a teenage lead, small. Leaned on ideas and motives rather than worldbuilding, because Artemis 69 showed worldbuilding alone does not hold a number.

t: Jmeno vetru (The Name of the Wind)
why: Positive case: a first-person lead whose own past is the open question (a hidden legend inside an innkeeper), with page time on what he wants and why: revenge on the killers of his troupe, music, the University. That is the shape the Licanius 93 lead earned a large over-run on. The sympathy system is operated like engineering with declared rules and costs, so it is the free kind, and the stated idea (a legend seen from backstage, the gap between story and truth) is nameable. Deductions: reviewers split on whether the lead is a prodigy at everything with competence that stops feeling earned; the middle is a long school sequence, so density is a real risk; the fae episode is a fairly explicit encounter, treated poetically, at small volume; the naming of wind and elements sits close to word-magic but is invented. The opening is a framed prologue then a clear childhood start, so no filter fires. Leaned on the protagonist and motives; unearned competence is held as the risk rather than a lean because Artemis 69 shows a thin lead outranks good worldbuilding and Old Man's War 87 shows the reader rewards characters not rescued by luck. Since 2026-10-24 the open-past lead credited above is priced as axis:discovery, which forfeits the lift when the answer is not written: the central questions, the killers of his troupe and how the legend fell, wait on a final volume still unpublished at last check. So the credit comes off, two points, and the axis joins the risks; if that volume appears, the lift returns.

Positive case: a long, character-led epic that returns to a king grown old, with grief, succession and the cost of earlier victories, and Norn viewpoint chapters praised for making a dying people sympathetic; motives is the axis that tops the log, and a starred review says the setup pays off (Licanius 96 for a long world that makes sense). Occult graded heavy (-10): the Norn queen's sorcery, scrying with Witnesses and the quest to call up a dead prince's spirit are invented but performed and central, and raising the dead is the heavy line; no staged human sacrifice found, and the Aedonite church is faith background. Deductions: reviewers count more than fifteen viewpoints and describe a very slow build that only fires in the last quarter (story density, as with Lord of the Rings 84, thin story over many pages), and the opening must introduce a large cast (axis:opening, a shape-one risk). The number sits ten points under where it would without the rites. Leaned on motives and worldbuilding; the opening is the risk that could collapse it.

The positive case is a grieving, loyal fighter whose want is clear from the first pages (find who killed his closest friend), in a world whose idea (what mortals owe to and can do without gods, and what a miracle costs) is carried through a whole sequence of books and reviewed as a satisfying close. Motives and an idea to think about are the axes that carry it, as with Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90. Deductions: it is a sequel that assumes the reader knows its cast and world, and sequels in this log are not safe bets (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70); the same author produced Caropisci 67, where a hierofant rite, a same-sex thread and a sex-contrast warning each cost; the clue-following hunt for the killers has a mystery shape, a flag not a veto, since the satisfaction is the revelation about the world and not whodunit; and gods and miracles are a graded occult question I could not settle from reviews. The opening and any staged rite were not read from the text, so confidence stays medium.

Exit at the below-the-line gate on one fact: this is the closing book of an eight-book saga that starts in medias res without recap and assumes everything before it, so the number is carried by axis:sequels, and the price is seven unread books whose first one many readers call confusing with unexplained terms, a shape-two opening mitigable only by looking it up first. The case for higher is real: Czech psychotronic SF with an idea (a world formatted by competing factions, a church and Lucas) and a well-received finale that closes all lines (78 percent), but it is long (about 600 pages, 36 audio hours) and the ending is not one clean close. Occult is unexamined beyond the blurb: Lucas brings and demands sacrifices and a church of Akkutlixov is a faction; the earlier record claims a staged human-sacrifice mourning rite which I could not confirm. C-low carries an unexamined occult status.

No positive case rests on this book alone: it is a late sequel in a very long series where leads, world and stakes are assumed, so a reader coming in cold risks the opening confusion the log punishes hardest (Gunslinger 30, Guards! Guards! 30), and sequels fall even from loved starts (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70). The antagonists raise the dead as an army, an invented system but priced heavy at -10 for raising the dead on the page. Reviews report repetitive action and an all-purpose 'occult powers' explanation, the declared-capability-without-consequences breach the worldbuilding rule punishes. Violence and the series' torture material are not objections in themselves, but its sexual content is unexamined.

Positive case: an outsider lead with a concrete problem on page one (fifteen, tailless, unable to bind the Might, the Rite approaching), and a book that questions blind faith and xenophobia inside its own rules; motives and what characters want is the axis that tops the log (Mockingjay 91). A hunted, flawed lead is rootable, unlike Ballad 65. Occult re-decided under the new rule: the Seer is an invented figure, the Council rules in his name and the Rite blessing is a staged ceremony the plot turns on, and the heroine's origin includes an attempted infant sacrifice in backstory, so the rite is central and graded heavy (-10) rather than vetoed; no human sacrifice is staged on the page in anything found. Other deductions: teen lead and young-adult register a little (Ranger's Apprentice 74), and several live plot lines by the end of the opening (Guards! Guards! 30 is the cost if they start illegibly). Leaned on the lead and motives, not worldbuilding: a reviewer finds the world under-explained, and Artemis 69 shows strong worldbuilding rescues nothing. The range sits ten points under where it would without the rites. Discovery (axis:discovery, 2026-10-24): where she comes from and what the Council hides are central, she has to find out to survive, and her origin answers the world's secret, the lead's past and the world at once as in Stín věcí ztracených 93; central, so +4.

Positive case: a built resource economy where drake blood grants abilities by colour and dose, a mechanical system with declared costs and no rites, and a colonial-trade conflict that is a nameable idea. Against that, three threads start within the first chapters (a thief in the interior, a syndicate spy, a naval officer), and reviewers describe them as loosely connected, with the main conflict unclear until about page 94 and the naval thread nearly detached. That is the shape-one opening risk, which the log prices hardest: Guards! Guards! 30 and The Gunslinger 30. A single rootable lead is what the log rewards (Sunrise on the Reaping 87, Licanius 93), and this book spreads that over three. Occult is the free mechanism kind. Leaned on worldbuilding, the weakest lean per Artemis 69, so the range sits in the 60s and the risks are the opening and differentiation.

t: Oko sveta (The Eye of the World)
why: Positive case: a concrete, legible start in a farm village, a lead who is an ordinary boy pulled into a hunt, friendship and heroism themes, and a power with declared rules; The Lord of the Rings 84 shows this heroic-journey shape clears the propose line on ideas and friendship alone. Deductions: reviewers describe the story as slow and meandering with heavy infodumps and a close structural echo of Tolkien, which is the exact cancellation the Lord of the Rings 84 note records (thin story for the pages); the prologue drops into an unexplained action (shape two of the opening filter, mitigable by reading the premise first); the party splits into several threads after the midpoint. The One Power is channelled by trained women in an order the blurb itself calls sorceresses, inside a good-versus-Dark-One frame; it reads as a declared-rules system rather than invocation, so the occult deduction is held at light, but resemblance to witchcraft is the risk. Prophecy is a chosen-one thread, graded on handling, and costs nothing here. Leaned on motives and worldbuilding rather than the protagonist, because the leads are an ensemble still undifferentiated in this first book; range kept wide and under the 70s peak on density.

Exit at the below-the-line gate on one search: readers describe fast, action-heavy dark fantasy with gore and pieces on a chessboard, 'pure fantasy, too obvious', with mostly criminal characters, and I cannot name an idea it leaves behind, so axis:ideas is the doubt that carries the number (action with no character revelation is dead weight in this log; Catching Fire 83 lost points for arena for its own sake). The assassin lead may be rootable but nothing sourced says so. Occult is unexamined beyond the blurb: a priest receiving visions from his goddess, plus demons and sorcerers, were reported; invented rites would be graded and a Source-style system would veto. C-low carries an unexamined occult status. Being a late series volume adds a small sequels cost.

Positive case: a single lead followed from boyhood, left at an order of warrior-monks, with the book spent on loyalty, brotherhood and what he is made to do to keep his ideals, framed by a scribe interviewing the man now condemned as a villain. That frame makes who he is and why the open question, the open-past lead the Licanius 93 note singles out. The opening is clear: one frame scene, then one child at one gate. Deductions: the faith and the gift are invented, but a forgotten order that dabbled in 'the Dark' is a possible source of staged rites that I could not verify, so occult is a risk, graded light to moderate if it fires; a lead who excels at everything martial invites the unearned-competence question, and one dissenting review says the characters are thin; the book is violent, which costs nothing, and has a single sexual scene with some detail, small volume. Faith is a thread rather than the subject. Leaned on protagonist and motives, since a rootable lead beats worldbuilding when they compete. Since 2026-10-24 the open-past frame credited above is priced as axis:discovery, once: partial, since he tells his own story and the need belongs to the scribe; the number holds.

A direct continuation: leads, history and enemies are assumed, so it is a continuation that assumes its cast and history, and sequels are not safe in this log (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70; Osudove nebe set aside as 'just continuation'). Positive case: the same character-led epic whose strength is motives and a kingdom under strain, which is what the top of the log scores on (Licanius 96). Occult graded heavy (-10): the Norn queen's necromantic sorcery, including resurrection and scrying, is performed on the page rather than referenced; no staged human sacrifice found. Deductions: very large cast, a slow-density middle that a thin plot over many pages costs (Lord of the Rings 84), and a magic-caused plague adds bleakness. The number sits ten points under where it would without the rites. Leaned on motives; sequel decline is the risk. Not researched beyond the annotation and shared author-level reception.

A fan-service prequel whose appeal is the origin of an order the reader may already know; its threads (a healer who survives a near-death drug and founds a school, a vengeful descendant who joins to rebuild her family, an emperor suspicious of the school) do follow from their wants. But the register is plain and expository, reviewers call it long and simple in prose, and many courts and subplots run at once, the shape-one multi-plot opening that scored 30 in this log. A lead driven by revenge who grows ruthless is the Ballad 65 objection (no one to root for, sliding toward evil). The initiation drug rite is staged and graded moderate, about minus 5, since the powers read as drug and breeding mechanism with no invocation. Leaned on protagonist and the multi-thread structure and not on worldbuilding, because declared systems add obligation, not bonus. It is also a sequel-type entry whose context lives elsewhere.

t: Shannarovy magicke elfeiny (The Elfstones of Shannara)
why: A tight quest with one concrete starting situation and a lead pair who each carry something to overcome: a reluctant Healer and an elf who ran from her duty and must face it. That sits near The Hobbit 84 for easy adventure with friendship, and avoids the thin story over many pages that held The Lord of the Rings to 84. The deduction is the climax and its premise: the tree's renewal is a rite performed on the page, a seed carried to a sacred fire, tended by a consecrated order, and Amberle becomes the tree. Invented system, so it grades heavy (-10) as a rite central to the plot; her sacrifice is a voluntary transformation rather than a killing, which is a judgement call and the main uncertainty. Ideas are moderate (duty, choice) and the young-adult register costs a little, as Narnia 67 and Ranger's Apprentice 74 did.

A continuation: the lead, her world and the stakes are assumed rather than re-established, so it is a continuation that assumes its cast and history, unreachable cold, and carries axis:sequels (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70; Osudove nebe set aside as 'just continuation'). Positive case: reviewers single out the lead's growth and her commitment to healing as the strongest element, which is the rootable-and-interesting axis that beats worldbuilding in this log, and the alternating two-viewpoint structure with chapter cliffhangers is easy to follow. Occult graded heavy (-10) for the same system: a worshipped Seer, a priestly Council and stone-circle portals, with the power bound on the page; nothing found that stages a human sacrifice. The number sits ten points under where a strong middle book would without the rites, less a little for sequel-dependence and the dark turn. Leaned on the protagonist; the opening is a risk because one reviewer abandoned a third of the way in and the book starts mid-conflict.

The positive case is the lead: a boy told he houses a dark lord's soul, who must work out what he is and decide not to be that, which is the arc the top-scoring series in the log was loved for, and the pages go on what he fears and wants. The deductions stack. It is a sequel that assumes a world and cast already established (Hitchhiker's sequels 70 after 83). It is middle-grade in register, closer to Narnia 67 and Ranger's Apprentice 74 than to The Hobbit 84, in a school-of-magic setting of the kind that held Harry Potter to 51 on worldbuilding. The central act is an invented system's raising of the dead on the page (the lead gives part of his soul to revive a friend, first tried on dead animals), which grades heavy at -10. Leaned on protagonist and motives, not worldbuilding, which this reader has not rewarded.

A plot-driven quest with a concrete start: assassins strike at a royal wedding, the bride is poisoned and the prince sets out to find the one cure. That is a legible opening and a goal a reader can hold, in the register of The Hobbit 84 and Count of Monte Cristo 75. Against it: this is a sequel whose lead and world are assumed rather than re-established, and sequels are not safe bets in this log (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70). The antagonist's power is an invented but heavy necromancy, assassins that rise after death and a serpent priesthood, and the rule prices raising the dead at heavy, about -10. It is action first with little of the motive interiority that tops the log, so the number leans on the sequel and occult costs rather than on a strong positive.

The positive case is companionable quest fantasy with friendships and clear wants, easy to read, near The Hobbit 84 and Ranger's Apprentice 74 on that count. But the ideas are thin, as with Ranger's Apprentice, and three novels in one binding is a lot of pages for a story that reviews describe as inventing reasons for the hero not to use his weapon, the thin-story-over-many-pages penalty. Occult is the main deduction: spells are formalised prayers to named Styric gods, performed constantly by the heroes and central to how their power works, with a Church modelled on real medieval orders alongside. The gods are invented so Source passes, and I found no staged human sacrifice, but repeated devotion-based rites grade heavy, about minus 10. It is also a sequel that assumes a large cast and invented terms, so a cold start would be shape two.

Positive case: a single first-person narrator, an outlaw turned soldier writing his life down, told through what he wants and whom he becomes loyal to. Reviewers compare it to Robin Hood and The Count of Monte Cristo 75, and a revenge-and-loyalty engine suits the motives axis that tops the log. One viewpoint keeps the opening legible. Deductions: a visionary noblewoman at the centre of a Martyr-based faith is a real faith thread that may become the subject; her visions of a demonic apocalypse are a prophecy-handling question graded on reverence, and the faith is invented, so only a light to moderate occult deduction if rites appear, with magic reported as minimal; reviewers call the worldbuilding sparse and the religious plot slow in places, so density is a risk; the narrator is violent, which costs nothing, and sexual content is flagged but not described. Leaned on protagonist and motives; kept below the Licanius range because the lead is a roguish type with an unproven interior and the revenge strand is reported to fizzle.

t: Zlobryne a sirotci (The Ogress and the Orphans)
why: A short fable of a town that loses its library and its neighbourliness and trusts a charming liar, with a nameable idea (division and a collected 'fund' of fear) and three orphan leads who each want something.
