It is a real idea, but this is an illustrated middle-grade fable: the register sits toward a children's book (somewhere around Narnia 67 or below), and reviewers call it didactic, repetitive and slow, with the missing child arriving only at the midpoint, which is the story-density complaint the log punishes. No occult rite was found: crows that speak, benign dragons and a mayor who is more than he seems, with nothing staged. The prior occult reject on the task line quotes spellwork that does not describe this book. Leaned on ideas over character, since the cast is archetypal.

Exit at the below-the-line gate on one source: a post-nuclear action adventure that reviewers of the series praise for an inexperienced young marksman lead rather than an invincible fighter, and for pace once outside violence arrives; but I cannot name an idea beyond survival action, so axis:ideas carries the doubt (Catching Fire 83 shows arena-for-its-own-sake costs). The annotation points at a later chapter of a six-part story about a novice priestess and the sheriff. Occult graded and unexamined at this exit: the Church of the Nuclear Goddess has a priestesshood, a seven-truth doctrine and prayers, an invented faith that is light to moderate at most, and no human sacrifice was found. Being a late series volume carries axis:sequels, and sexual references were not checked.

The idea is real and nameable: the same appetite for power preys on the weak in six eras, and the nesting is more than a gimmick for the reader who finishes it. The cost is stacked. Six narrators in six registers means the opening drops the reader into one story and interrupts it for the next, a multi-line start that this reader has failed on (Colour of Magic 30, Guards! Guards! 30), though it is sequential and not simultaneous. One story carries a composer's young protege in an affair with the composer's married wife, an infidelity subplot treated neutrally, which the infidelity axis caps in the middle of the range on its own; another carries a same-sex relationship of a lead and fairly explicit sex. A thriller strand is investigation-shaped but is a flag. Leaned on ideas and the infidelity cap; opening and multi-POV are the risks that could drag it lower.

Ideas and motives carry it: the book is a long argument about what a messiah and a prescient golden path cost, driven by what the regent, the twins, the mother and the Preacher each want and fear. That is the page-time-on-motives axis that tops Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90, and prophecy is graded on handling, with foreknowledge questioned seriously inside its own rules, which the Licanius series scored very high for. Against it: a sequel that depends on its predecessors, and sequels are not safe bets in this log (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70). It drops the reader into a court, a religion and invented terms already established, which is the opening shape two that is only mitigable by reading the premise first, with several POVs live at once. One lead slides into evil, the Ballad 65 failure, though another lead is a clear rooting interest. Invented rites and faith (Muad'Dib religion, ancestral memory, sandtrout bonding) are mechanical-ish and graded about moderate. Leaned on ideas and motives, not on worldbuilding, since declared systems add obligation and no bonus.

t: Hra se sklenenymi perlami (The Glass Bead Game)
why: The idea is nameable and the book is built on it: a scholarly order sealed inside pure intellect, and whether a good life must leave it. The lead, Knecht, is a rootable, flawed man whose own motives and doubt are the story, the axis that tops the log. Against that stands density: the book opens with a lengthy essay-like introduction to the history of the Game and then a biography, thin on incident, the pattern of drawn-out description with little story that this reader marks down, though The Silmarillion 80 shows a mythic, plotless, dense book can still land. Occult is the open risk: Knecht studies Chinese wisdom under a Taoist hermit who teaches the I Ching; I could not confirm a staged consultation, so it is graded here and not rejected, and the Source test would veto if one is found on the page. Leaned on ideas and protagonist; density and occult are what could drop it.

A fortress-siege novel with a clear historical stake and the highest reader ratings in its cycle, so the momentum case is real, the kind that kept Monte Cristo 75 moving. Against it: reviewers say the lead is on the page for only a small share of the book, which is spread across the Turkish camp, the defenders and intrigues, working against the motives-over-action preference and against one rootable lead (Artemis 69 shows a thin lead outranks good worldbuilding); some found it too bloody and the camp intrigues tiresome; it is a sequel, and sequels are not safe in this log (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70). Leaned on momentum and density. Occult is only partly examined: a treacherous baroness supplies some magic, and the cycle's witch and demon material is the Source-test concern.

t: Jatka c. 5, aneb, Krizova vyprava deti - povinny tanec se smrti (Slaughterhouse-Five)
why: The idea is nameable and worked through: time-unstuck Billy and the Tralfamadorian view that every moment exists permanently turn war, fate and free will into a concrete argument, and the book leaves that behind. Short and idea-driven, so the character rules are suspended but earn nothing, as with Animal Farm 78 where bleakness did not sink an idea-led short book. The opening is legible because the premise is stated outright in the opening pages of the story (time-jumps explained at once), unlike the unexplained fan-out of Colour of Magic 30 and Guards! Guards! 30. Deductions: Billy is acted upon rather than wanting anything, the failure that put Oliver Twist at 57 and Promena at 58, and the bleakness of the bombing arrives with a fatalist shrug. Sexual content is small (the zoo pairing) and played lightly; religion is mocked in passing, a small faith-satire risk after Ja, robot 55. Leaned on ideas because that is what carries a short book; protagonist and bleakness are the risks that sank the two comparable passive-lead books. Occult not examined beyond the blurb.

t: Jez se stala sluncem (She Who Became the Sun)
why: The positive case is a book entirely about what its leads want and what they will pay for it, with fate and ambition as the working argument, and fate questioned seriously is something this reader has scored very high. The cost is the same-sex romance: both principal leads carry one (a marriage between two women, and a general's anguished desire for a man), which reviewers describe as central threads though the book is not a romance novel, so it is graded and not the premise. The nearest measurement, Caropisci 67, lost about thirteen points to a protagonist's same-sex relationship plus other causes, off a base near 80. A ruthless lead who kills and manipulates and a villain-adjacent second POV recall the Ballad 65 failure, though the arc is ambition and not a fall. Sexual content is reported as sparse. Gate checks: no mystery plot, no affair premise. Leaned on motives and the romance deduction; protagonist rootability is the risk that could push it under the range.

t: Kroniky Zapadniho pobrezi (Annals of the Western Shore (Gifts, Voices, Powers))
why: Three linked novels whose ideas are concrete: inherited gifts that are dangerous to their owners, the burning of books and the tension between a people who revere the written word and a conquering faith that forbids it, and slavery seen from inside. Each lead is a young person defined by a gift he or she does not want to use as it was meant, so motives and flaws are the page time, close to what carried Sunrise on the Reaping 87. Deductions: young leads and a register aimed at younger readers, a small pushback as with Ranger's Apprentice 74 and Narnia 67; a lead who foresees things before they happen, graded on handling; and an invented deity of the dead invoked in the worlds' religion, which grades lightly unless a staged rite turns up. The gifts are hereditary powers and not invoked rituals, so no Source concern is established. Leaned on ideas and protagonist, not on worldbuilding.

t: --o psu nemluve (To Say Nothing of the Dog)
why: A comic time-travel farce whose declared rule (the continuum repairs itself, and incongruities are tracked) is the engine of every complication, in the comic-SF register that Hitchhiker's Guide 83 and Mort 83 show carries no penalty with this reader. Positive case: a clean light romance, no sexual content to speak of, and consequences of the premise actually worked out. Deductions: the opening is confusing by design because the narrator is time-lagged, and reviewers report feeling lost for fifty to sixty pages; this reader abandoned two comic books at 30 on a confusing start, though that was many plot lines at once, not one muddled narrator, and the same genre scored 83 on Mort. There is also an investigation-shaped quest (a missing object and a trail) that is a flag, not the book's satisfaction. Leaned on worldbuilding self-consistency (rules add obligation, not bonus) and the momentum of the farce; the opening is the risk that fires hardest.

The positive case is a father who failed his twelve-year-old son after his wife's death, loses him, and has to put that right while a fortress faces an overwhelming Ottoman army: a lead with a flaw to work against and a want that drives the plot, the motive-first axis that tops the log (Mockingjay 91, Speaker for the Dead 90). The setting is a real war, not an invented world, so worldbuilding consistency is barely at stake. Deductions: readers compare the lead to Geralt and call him near superhuman while the Turks are written as fools, the lazy-stereotype cost that held Ranger's Apprentice at 74; brutality and blood are not an objection, but the Witcher comparison raises a sexual-content question that was not established (The Witcher 53). The fantasy is described as light and tied to local superstition, with reviewers split on whether it is there at all; if it is witchcraft in the real-folklore mould it vetoes, and that was not checked. The number rests on motives rather than protagonist, because the father-son arc is stated in the blurb while the lead's depth is only inferred from reviews. Over-the-top competence and simple plotting cap it below the high 70s.

Ideas are the strongest card: a cosmos governed by dark-forest logic, deterrence and dimensional weapons, each consequence of the declared premise followed out to the end of the universe, the same axis that tops Project Hail Mary 92 where second-order consequences were explored. Deductions: the lead is reported as intelligent but passive, with the plot moving because she fails, the acted-upon, not-rooted failure behind Oliver Twist 57 and Promena 58; the bleakness is sustained and ends at cosmic scale (1984 60), mild but real; the book is a sequel that assumes its lead and premise, and sequels are not safe bets (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70). Declared hard-SF rules add obligation, not bonus (Ja, robot 55), so worldbuilding is a lean only where consistent. Reviewers also report slower pacing and an uneven ending. Leaned on ideas, not on the lead, because the lead is the weak point.

A siege and field-battle novel on a concrete historical situation, and reviewers agree the fantasy is minimal, used for atmosphere around a military-historical story. The positive case is plot momentum and period detail, the quality that carried Count of Monte Cristo 75. Pulling it down: reviewers call the lead and the other heroes bland, and a flat lead holds a number back as it did for Artemis 69 despite strong worldbuilding; it is a sequel, and sequels are not safe in this log (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70); and readers name it the shortest and weakest of its cycle. Leaned on momentum and density rather than worldbuilding because the lead is thin. Occult is only partly examined: the cycle carries kabbalistic marks and black magic, and this volume has a wolf baroness, with no scene-level evidence either way.

The positive case is the lead: an unprepared, unwanted young emperor who is kind, flawed and visibly working to understand a court that despises him, which is the interesting and rootable protagonist that put Sunrise on the Reaping 87 22 above Ballad 65, and the whole book is page time on what the courtiers want and why. The lead's own past is the open question, which this reader counts as a positive. Deductions: reviewers report heavy invented names and honorifics (a glossary exists), slow etiquette-laden pacing and a weak sense of drive, the exact complaint he made about Pocitani hvezd 85 (no pull to keep reading). Invented faith with prayers and ceremonies appears, incidental and doing little, so a light occult grade is already priced in. A plot about who caused the airship crash is a flag, not the book's satisfaction, since the pull is court survival. Leaned on protagonist and motives, not worldbuilding, which owes more the more precisely it is declared. Since 2026-10-24 the open past credited above is priced as axis:discovery, once: partial, since the court rather than the past is the spine; the number holds.

Satire with a stated target and a fast adventure plot is the whole positive case; no named idea beyond lampoon holds up to what this reader asks of an idea. The narrator is the villain Gris, a saboteur who tells the story of the hero from inside his skull, and a lead who is a villain is the Ballad 65 failure with no redemptive arc to rescue it. Reviewers describe repeated crude sex, assault and ridicule of homosexuality across the series; that is the crudeness dimension that docked Artemis 69 at small volume and, at volume, Ready Player One 55 and The Witcher 53. The plot is not mainly sexual, so no filter fires, but the share in this book was not verified (the worst episodes are reported from elsewhere in the series). It is also a continuation that assumes its cast and setup, and sequels are not safe bets (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70). Leaned on protagonist and crudeness; ideas is the risk that could take it lower still. This is a D-full verdict resting on one search, so confidence stays medium.

t: Perla Petrohradu (The Jewel of St Petersburg)
why: Infidelity no longer applies: the heroine is promised to a count by her parents and loves someone else, which is an arranged betrothal and not an engagement for that axis. Nothing else vetoes: the opening is a single clear action scene (escape, then the family home blown up), no occult was reported, and it is not a detective book. The positive case is real: a driven heroine who wants a nursing vocation over the marriage market, plus momentum a reviewer calls page-turning, which is the kind of want-and-why reading that lifted Pride and Prejudice to 75 with romance as the whole subject. Held at the line, not above it, because I would list axis:ideas under risks: a romance saga set against the 1910 unrest with no idea named that it leaves behind, which is the weak side of Monte Cristo 75 and Quo Vadis 66 and Exodus 68. Reviewers also call the plot at times unbelievable and the lovers too perfect with no convincing obstacle, so the protagonist may be flat, the Artemis 69 pattern. Love scenes are called overdone; explicitness and volume are unmeasured and could cost as Ready Player One 55 did. Leaned on ideas and protagonist, not worldbuilding. Spent 2 sources against a budget of 1 at this gate.

t: Vsemi dary obdarovana (The Girl with All the Gifts)
why: Positive case: the opening is one concrete situation seen almost entirely through Melanie (cell, wheelchair, classroom), and the book's drive is what she is and what the world really is, with the fungal mechanism declared and then paid off in the ending. That is the axis that earned Stin veci ztracenych 93 (uncovering who the lead is while it is still open), and the lead is a child with a real inner life who wants things, and the motives of Justineau, Caldwell and Parks collide over her, which is the axis that tops Mockingjay 91. The idea is nameable: what makes a person human, and whether the successor deserves the world. Deductions: the viewpoint rotates among five characters, which is graded here and not a bar because the opening is not split (Hunger Games 89 is the single-POV baseline it does not match); the ending ends humanity as it was, a sustained bleak thread, mild on this reader (1984 60 was too depressing, Animal Farm 78 was fine because it left something to think about); a child lead is a small pushback only, and Ender's Game 87 shows the distance can cost. Occult is clean: the plague is a fungus operated as biology, no rite. Sexual content is negligible. Violence and cannibalism are not objections. Leaned on the protagonist and ideas rather than worldbuilding, since Artemis 69 shows strong worldbuilding cannot carry a thin lead; the lead here is not thin. Rootability is the live doubt: Melanie kills and eats, and chooses the ending, but the direction of travel is a lead learning what she is and deciding what to do about it, not sliding into evil as in Ballad 65. Since 2026-10-24 the uncovering credited above is priced as axis:discovery, central with all three conditions met; it was already in the number, so the number holds.

A nameable idea: a plane lands twice with duplicate passengers, with the simulation hypothesis as the nearest answer, and a Goncourt-winning ensemble. Held under the line on the ensemble: an assassin, an editor, a pilot, a writer and a singer mean many threads to track, reviewers call the characters uneven and the ending divisive, a withheld or playful answer being a risk rather than a lift. One thread is an affair between an editor and an older architect; the architect's marital status was not established, so it is graded as a neutral subplot and held in the risks. The first chapter on the hitman is described as excellent, so the opening is not the exposure.

A literary-historical study of four ex-communist books: reviewers call it well researched, engrossing and well written. Held under the line because it is a second-hand study of books rather than the first-person examination that earned Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75, the form earns nothing by itself, and an academic book on books risks the thin-story-over-many-pages penalty. Genre has no non-fiction value, nearest chosen.

The idea can be named: the piano was not invented but found again, set around Cristofori at the Medici court. But it is a short self-published novel of about 121 pages with no reviews, and a historical frame with a philosophical conceit rarely pays more than the lead and the working-out of the idea allow (Quo Vadis 66, Exodus 68). One source, per the C exit.

Exit at the cheap gate. The idea is nameable (many adults mask autism and pay for it), but it is a self-help and advocacy book with a how-to section: reviewers call it disorganised and repetitive and say the exercises are generic. Personal story earns nothing by itself for this reader, and the same form gave both his top non-fiction and an outright DNF. Leaned on ideas, with a thin supply of them across a whole book.

An account of one organisation, its founder's materials and its mythology of alien civilisations, with local cases. The reader's record on faith as a subject in its own right is cautionary, and the form earns only what it examines (Seeking Allah 91 examined; Diary of a Young Girl 40 did not). Here the idea beyond exposition is thin and the book is about 94 pages from a small publisher with no reviews found, so it more likely lands under the line. Occult (the group's beliefs are discussed, not enacted) is unexamined, per the C exit.

t: Chladna ruka v moji dlani (Cold Hand in Mine)
why: Literary fiction in a short-story collection: the compound penalty case. The stories are deliberately unexplained, with reviewers noting little resolution and no account of what happened, so there is no single idea the reader can name and nothing for the ideas axis to lean on; the short-form suspension of character rules removes penalties but adds nothing. A collection is read from the front and put down on its weakest early stories (I, Robot 55). Occult status of the ghostly material and the sexual content some stories dwell on are unexamined, per the C exit.

The lead is a security android that freed itself and narrates in first person, so most page time is on what it wants and why (the Mockingjay 91 axis), and a trusting companion robot gives it someone to measure itself against, a companion plot of the kind Project Hail Mary 92 was praised for. The idea left behind is what a made person owes and is owed. Held under the top because it is a sequel and sequels are not safe bets in this log (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70), and because it picks up an arc already under way, so a cold reader may lack context. Leaned on protagonist and motives; no sexual content or occult to speak of.

Exit at the cheap gate. A documentary reconstruction of the 1949 event and the secret police's torture of the priest, built from interrogation protocols and testimonies and, by the publisher's own description, without drawing a conclusion. That gives a compilation of sources with no through-line of wants and no idea beyond the facts, and it carries an investigation shape and bleakness. Leaned on density. The reader's testimony rule (earns only by examining what is true) is met only in part when no conclusion is reached. Occult not examined: the miracle is a Catholic claim, kept in deps.

A first-person narrator whose voice and sympathy reviewers praise, a boy becoming the man history will call a monster: the positive case is interior time on what Hadrian wants and why, the axis behind Speaker for the Dead 90, with the direction of travel left open in this book rather than a lead already sliding into evil as in The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65. Deductions: reviewers describe a slow, place-dwelling opening quarter and a memoir frame that removes jeopardy, which is the heavy-description-with-little-story penalty (The Lord of the Rings 84 shows it costs a few points, not a band); an invented church (the Chantry) and mystics enter as graded faith and rite material I could not size from sources, so a light to moderate occult deduction is held in the risks; a series start, and series are not safe bets in this log (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70). Leaned on protagonist and motives, not on worldbuilding, because declared systems owe consistency rather than earn credit (Ja, robot 55).

t: Cizincem v Olondrii (A Stranger in Olondria)
why: A merchant's son raised on Olondria's books arrives and is haunted by a ghost: an idea about reading and oral culture is nameable, but reviewers describe the first third as rhapsody on culture, architecture and literature, a book read for themes rather than plot, which is the heavy-description-with-little-story penalty. Occult is unexamined and is a real exposure here: sources describe a haunting and an Olondrian faith that treats ghosts as angels and those who speak with them as saints, which sits close to the seance resemblance test. Occult status is therefore unexamined at this exit; axis:occult stays in deps.

Four retired soldiers cross a silent, devastated Europe asking what is left when the system that shaped them is gone. The number depends on whether four similar men are told apart by what each wants, which is the axis that tops the log; the idea itself is broad and unproven and bleakness is a mild discount. One source, no reviews, per the C exit.

t: Dvoreni Bristol Keatsove (The Courting of Bristol Keats)
why: Fae romantasy: a rescue quest wrapped around a slow-burn courtship and a dangerous bargain with a fae king. I would list axis:ideas under risks, since nothing nameable is left behind; reviewers call much of it filler padded by the king withholding things. Open-door sex scenes exist but late and sparse, reported as moderate, so sexual content is graded and not the plot, though it prices a few points. Fae folklore, not real occult practice, and unexamined beyond that. Leaned on axis:ideas, so doubt on it carries the number.

A book of ideas: economic thought traced through Gilgamesh, the Old Testament, Aristotle, Descartes and Komensky, with the thesis that economics is bound up with ethics and storytelling. That is the thing the log rewards most in non-fiction, a book that leaves ideas behind. Reviewers praise readability for non-economists, but critics say the old texts are translated too quickly into modern terms, and one reader found it erudite but slow in places. So density and a loose, allegorical method are risks, and so is the amount of scripture used as source material, which could read as faith as a subject. Leaned on ideas only.

A sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70); it continues the lead's training with no opening of its own. I would list axis:ideas under risks: a dragon-rider apprenticeship with ability handed to the lead rather than earned (axis:unearned-competence is the second doubt). Magic runs on spoken words in an ancient language, which resembles spellcasting, and fortune-telling by knucklebones exists in the series, so occult is unexamined at this exit and stays in deps. Leaned on axis:ideas.

A book whose whole point is to check beliefs against the data, the same examining-what-is-true rigour that put Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 at the top of the non-fiction. One nameable idea with ten applications (instincts that make us misread the world), and it leaves the reader thinking differently, as The Little Prince 82 does for a very different book. Personal stories keep it moving. Held down only because the ten-part structure repeats itself and a reviewer says Rosling does not always apply his own rule. Leaned on ideas.

The idea is strong (a for-profit prison gladiator league and what it says about the real system, with footnotes citing real cases), but the love story between the two leads is described by several independent reviews as the heart of the book and one of its central arcs. Premise versus thread is genuinely unclear, since the premise is the league and the romance is its human engine, so I graded it and did not reject; the prominence is well above the thread-level case measured in Caropisci 67, which lost about thirteen points with other causes. Further deductions: sustained bleakness (Havran 40 and 1984 60 show the reader's tolerance is limited), and rotating omniscient viewpoints around a main character. Single-source note that one lead is not monogamous; infidelity not examined further.

A history of genetics told through the people who made it, which gives the motives rule something to work on: Mendel, the eugenicists, Watson and Crick each want something. It leaves ideas behind (heredity, what can and should be edited) and its family thread gives a human spine, though memoir form earns nothing on its own. Held down because reviewers say the later chapters on gene editing become technical, and the eugenics chapters are bleak, though bleakness is a mild cost. Leaned on ideas and motives, not on the family thread.

t: Hardcore historie (The End Is Always Near)
why: Carlin writes history as people deciding under pressure: Bronze Age collapse, the fall of Rome and nuclear near-misses, so page time goes to what people wanted and feared, the motives rule. His voice is a strong draw. Held down because it is deliberately loosely connected pieces with no single argument, so the idea left behind is thinner than in a book built on one question, and reviewers say he does not test his ancient sources. Pieces read from the front are also exposed to a weak early one. Leaned on motives; Animal Farm 78 shows that a short idea carries only when it is pointed.

t: Hleda se autor bestselleru 2015 – Sci-fi a fantasy pribehy (Seeking a Bestseller Author 2015 - Sci-fi and Fantasy Stories)
why: A multi-author contest anthology of five short stories chosen from over two hundred entries: no single idea to name, the order is an editor's, and nothing earns patience when the first story is weak (I, Robot 55). Slight collection, so the low band. Leaned on axis:ideas, because no idea is nameable for the collection as a whole.

A short allegory with an idea nameable in a phrase: fear delivered as a state service, installed in a home like cable television. Political and social satire costs nothing here (Animal Farm 78 is the anchor: short, idea-driven, bleak but giving something to think about). The opening is one concrete situation from the first line, a doorbell and a mother hiding her son, so no confusion. Held to the low 70s because it is a menacing two-hander with little to root for, and because the short form only suspends the character rules, it never adds points. Leaned on ideas and the short-idea-driven suspension, not on character. No occult or sexual content found in the plot summaries; sustained bleakness and a thin lead are the risks.

One idea followed to its consequences: a truth drug and a state that holds a citizen's thoughts to be its property, tested first on a marriage. An idea left behind is the axis that carries Animal Farm 78 and Speaker for the Dead 90. Deductions: sustained bleakness, with 1984 60 ('too depressing') the nearest anchor, softened because the narrator's own doubt is the engine rather than pure misery; a narrator who starts as a loyal functionary and reports a colleague is a rootability risk of the kind that sank The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65, though the direction of travel is toward doubt; a jealousy thread about a wife suspected of an affair that sources say is not actually an affair, so graded as a condemned subplot, a few points. Leaned on ideas, not worldbuilding, since the state is a sketch and the lead is the thin spot (the Artemis 69 lesson). Occult is not in play: the drug is chemistry.

Strong on the axes that top the log: a mother and a daughter with opposed motives, neither wholly wrong (the Speaker for the Dead 90 kind of page time), and a history of the world that explains the catastrophes the earlier story left open. The magic is a physical resource with stated rules, so the occult escape holds. Held down by sustained bleakness (mild), by narration that mixes second person, first-person history and third person across timelines, and by being a sequel that depends entirely on what came before, so a cold start would meet the opening bar. Same-sex relationships among the cast and the treatment of men were not examined and are risks. Leaned on worldbuilding and motives.

t: Kniha dennich modliteb (A Book of Common Prayer)
why: Literary fiction narrated at secondhand by a dying observer, told out of sequence and mostly about a woman's life elsewhere, so the lead is reconstructed rather than lived with and reads passive. Charlotte's affairs, with relatives of the narrator and around her marriage, are at least a neutral-framed subplot, the 45-55 cell of the infidelity grid; whether it reaches premise level could not be settled from summaries, so it is graded, not rejected. Spare, detached prose and a violent end add bleakness. The FBI search for the daughter is a backdrop, not a whodunnit. C-low exit; occult not examined.

First-contact SF about two minds learning to understand each other, which is the axis Speaker for the Dead 90 scores on. But the reviews I read converge on the lead as passive and bland and on two plots (a whistleblower father and the alien) that do not cohere, which hits the protagonist axis that beats worldbuilding (Artemis 69). It ends setting up a sequel. Exit at C-low after two sources, one over budget. Leaned on protagonist.

Exit at the cheap gate. The idea is real and nameable (infinity may not exist, and one solution may dissolve its paradoxes), so ideas are not the doubt. The doubt is density: a 384-page philosophy-of-mathematics-and-physics treatise whose own readers call it original but very demanding, and one reviewer calls it a treatise that could be interesting but is not. With no characters or story to carry the pages, it is a thin read per page for this reader. Leaned on density. Occult not examined.

An essay-length argument that humanity must change itself to leave its cradle, drawing on several fields. The question is nameable, but the annotation says outright that it is a challenge rather than fiction, no reviews exist and the author is a thinker working across fields rather than an established scientist, so I doubt the idea is worked out the way the Weir books work theirs. One source, per the C exit; philosophy classification suggests a thesis book more than a rigorous one.

A real idea with consequences: if the father of machine learning had been taken by the Soviets, AI would have shaped a different world, and the plot asks what follows when the machines stop. The Finlandia nomination and good reviews suggest the book holds together, and consequences worked through are what made Project Hail Mary 92 work. But the time levels are hard to follow in the first third, per reviewers, the lead is called paler than the side characters, and rules add obligation, not bonus. Leaned on ideas; those three are the risks. Opening shape known only from reviews.

One unknown pursued across a life, from a scene where a fourteen-year-old watches his parents killed by ball lightning, to an invented physics: the uncovering with a need behind it that lifted Project Hail Mary 92 (partial here: a phenomenon, not a world or his own past). Deductions: a common reader complaint is flat characters with the science overshadowing them, and a thin lead outranks strong ideas in this log (Artemis 69); the invented physics binds the author to its consequences, the test that broke Mortal Engines 55 and Divergent 58; weapons research and deaths add mild bleakness. Leaned on ideas and discovery, with protagonist and worldbuilding as the risks.

t: Liska Bystrouska – Sto let od zrodu legendy (The Cunning Little Vixen)
why: A humorous Czech classic whose lead is rootable and wants something plain, a free life over a safe one in the hut, carried by voice and wit the way Saturnin 78 is carried, with the little-fable register that cost nothing in The Little Prince 82. The opening is one concrete situation (the forester brings a cub home). No occult or sexual content in the plot accounts. Held to the low 70s: episodic and written to accompany drawings, so story density is thin, it sits toward a children's book (Narnia 67 and Ranger's Apprentice 74 pay a little), and the idea is simple rather than worked out. Leaned on the protagonist, not on worldbuilding.

A quest to a life-giving spring told with interleaved side tales in the manner of the Arabian Nights, with orcs as heroes before they became symbols of evil. The one idea I can name is that reversal, which is slight, and an episodic frame risks the story density and the thin-plot-over-many-pages problem that held LOTR 84 flat. The one review found says the author's youth shows. Magic is mentioned in the annotation and its kind (mechanism or rite) is unexamined, per the C exit. Leaned on ideas because the reversal is what could earn anything.

A slum boy sold to the sorcerer who rules a city built on a dead god's corpse: a vivid, Dickensian world. Held under the line on the protagonist: reviewers describe Nathan as moved and manipulated by others rather than wanting something, the Oliver Twist 57 shape (acted upon), plus cartoonish villains, noticeable pacing problems, a grotesque register and a depraved master. Sexual material (the mother's prostitution, the master's depravity) was not sized. Occult was not examined: magic fed by a god's corpse is an invented system, so this C exit carries an unexamined occult status; axis:occult stays in deps.

t: Muz, ktery rozumel hadi reci (Mees, kes teadis ussisonu)
why: The positive case is real: a last man of a vanishing way of life, an idea (a world lost to conversion) that the book follows through, and reviewers praise the humour. Against that, three deductions compound. Occult: the forest folk live by Estonian folk belief with spirits that demand sacrifices and a priest figure, close enough to real mythology that resemblance counts under the source test; I found no confirmation of a human sacrifice staged on the page, so it is graded, not vetoed, and the doubt stays open. Faith: reviewers describe both the pagans and the Christians as targets of satire, and religion played as ridicule is what sank I, Robot 55. Sexual content: the book is known for bear and snake seduction and a knight-and-village-girl episode, crude in tone (Artemis 69 for crudeness). Violence is not an objection. Leaned on occult and faith, the two that carry the number; the lead being a likeable outsider does not offset them.

A banking dynasty in an alternate Renaissance city, and a kind heir who must learn to read intentions: the page time goes to what people want and hide, the axis behind The Count of Monte Cristo 75 and Mockingjay 91. Davico is handed a fault to work against (too trusting for the role), which reads as a positive on rootability. Deductions: reviewers call it a slow burn with a long stretch of adolescent preoccupation, and the dragon eye is the only fantasy element for much of the book, so worldbuilding adds little; reviewers also flag sexual content as explicit and at times uncensored, which compounds on volume and explicitness (Ready Player One 55, Artemis 69), plus a slave trade and a purchased mistress as backdrop. Occult is inferred, not sourced: the dragon eye is the only supernatural object and I did not establish whether a rite is staged or how the church figures, hence medium. Leaned on motives and protagonist, not worldbuilding.

A family saga of two rival clans over jade, where the power is operated like technology: only the Kekonese can use it, after academy training, with tolerance, addiction and immunity as stated rules, which is the mechanism escape and costs nothing on occult. The number rests on motives and loyalties, with siblings who each want different things, the axis behind Golden Son 92 and Mockingjay 91. Deductions: several live viewpoints to track, a gangster protagonist family whose rootability depends on direction of travel, a graded religious or ancestral layer around jade held light (about two points), and a gay cousin handled lightly in this book, the light end of the same-sex axis (Caropisci 67 lost about thirteen with other causes). Sexual content was not sized from sources and is inferred low. Leaned on motives and protagonist, not on worldbuilding.

A stranger arrives at an inn and the first half is the village working him out: one concrete situation, easy to follow. The idea, what invisibility actually costs the man who has it, is thought through the way Project Hail Mary 92 thinks through its premise. What holds it down is the lead: Griffin slides into cruelty and a plan of terror, the Ballad 65 objection in a short book, with no one to root for. Leaned on protagonist for the cap and ideas for the floor, not on worldbuilding. The village-as-puzzle first half is mystery-shaped but not a whodunnit, so it is a flag and not a veto.

Exit at the cheap gate. The idea is nameable: outrunning light would let an observer see the past, wrapped in an 1877 antiwar frame, and that keeps it off the floor the way the allegory of Labyrint sveta 70 sat on its idea. But a short 19th-century romaneto with a long catalogue of battles and archaic prose is a thin story spread over many pages, and the lead is a vehicle for the idea rather than someone who wants anything the reader can root for; Promena 58 is the anchor for a short idea book whose lead is passive. Leaned on density, not ideas. Occult not examined (dream and conjuring frame), kept in deps.

Positive case: Alexandra Bergson takes charge of a failing farm at a young age and builds it into something lasting, a lead who wants something and is worth rooting for, and the book is about what the land and the family cost. Pride and Prejudice 75 and Little Women 79 show that a character-led classic with no big idea can clear the line. Infidelity: Marie and Emil's affair in a second strand ends in tragedy; it is a subplot beside Alexandra's story, not the premise, but the doubt is real and the framing is sympathetic, so a few points are priced in. Risk is heavy pastoral description with slow story. Leaned on protagonist and motives.

t: Odlisni (Different: Gender Through the Eyes of a Primatologist)
why: Positive: decades of watching primates, with chimpanzee and bonobo politics told as animals wanting and scheming, which is the motives rule applied to apes. The idea is nameable: sex differences exist and still justify no inequality. Held down because reviewers say the step from apes to humans is the weakest part and the sex and gender terms are used loosely, which this reader checks. Sexual behaviour of primates is discussed frankly but as science, not as plot and not crudely; a small deduction. Leaned on motives, not on the thesis.

A life that is mostly about what a man wants and what he owes: Oppenheimer builds the bomb, then faces the moral consequences, which is the motives-over-action axis, with a lead worth following who is neither a villain nor flat. The book leaves ideas behind about science, responsibility and politics. Priced in: his affairs and his wife leaving her first marriage are an incidental thread in a long political-moral biography, not the premise, and not approved; a small deduction. Density is the main risk at this length. Leaned on motives; Speaker for the Dead 90 is the anchor for the pull of understanding a person over action.

An AI-run city, a wilderness made by genetic engineering and a heroine who finds the population is being deliberately reduced: a recognisable dystopian shape, and the question that decides it is whether the system holds together under thought, as in Divergent 58 where it did not. I could not find reviews, so the number rests on the annotation only and I would list ideas and protagonist as risks; one source, per the C exit. Leaned on worldbuilding because the book is built on it.

t: Pad domu Usheru a jine povidky (The Fall of the House of Usher and Other Tales)
why: Literary fiction and a short-story collection, the two penalties that compound: it is read from the front and put down on its weakest early story (I, Robot 55). Poe's narrators are observers of decay with nobody to root for, bleakness is the whole register, and the content is atmosphere more than an idea left behind. Not verse, so Havran 40 is not the anchor. Leaned on protagonist. C-low exit: occult is unexamined (the contents of this edition were not established and some Poe tales turn on the dead returning), kept in deps.

t: Povidky z druhe kapsy (Tales from the Other Pocket)
why: A collection of 24 crime-themed tales built around guilt, justice and how hard the truth is to pin down. The idea is real, but a collection has no single premise to carry it, and a collection is read from the front and put down on its weak early pieces, as I, Robot 55 was. The tales are not pure whodunnits, so the detective bar is a risk and not a veto. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source; occult not examined, axis:occult kept in deps.

One young soldier and one decision, and the page time goes on why he crosses and what it costs him: reviewers stress he is not moved by advantage, by fear of execution or by sympathy for the other side, and that the dialogues turn on patriotism, honour, conscience and morality. That is the reader's heaviest axis (motives over action, Mockingjay 91) with a nameable idea behind it. Held below the top because a lead who is carried along rather than driving events sank Metamorphosis 58 on rootability, the war setting brings some bleakness (1984 60, mild axis), and historical novels in the log land in the high 60s (Exodus 68, Quo Vadis 66). Leaned on motives and ideas rather than the historical frame, which earned nothing alone. Opening shape inferred from reviews (single lead, one situation), not read; occult not a factor.

t: Proc se stroje uci (Why Machines Learn)
why: Non-fiction that explains machine learning through the actual mathematics, so it examines what is actually true and why, the quality that earns Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and the problem-solving of The Martian 82. Deductions: the form earns nothing by itself and the log has no technical-nonfiction anchor; reviewers say it carries more equations than most popular science (linear algebra, calculus, probability), which is a density risk for a book with no characters, and one reader found the last decade of deep learning covered superficially. Leaned on ideas; density held as a risk. Genre has no non-fiction value in the closed set, so the nearest was chosen.

The idea is nameable: an app that broadcasts words into the subconscious, first tested on a partner and then on a house of neighbours, with corporate control as the worry. But the text is about 54 pages with a rotating cast of residents, so there is little room to work the idea through or to give a lead the interiority that carries the reader's top scores; Little Prince 82 shows short work can pay, but only on a worked idea. One source, per the C exit.

An idea you can name: what part of a mind survives being moved into another animal's body and memory, with reviewers praising Damira's scent-based mammoth memory and the shift between human and mammoth voices. Damira is a skilled scientist with a task, the rootable kind, and the book is about understanding a non-human mind, the axis behind Speaker for the Dead 90. Short-idea-driven form suspends penalties but adds nothing. Deductions: several viewpoints and two timelines packed into about 110 pages, with reviewers saying the secondary viewpoints lack room, and a poaching-and-extinction darkness that is mild bleakness. Leaned on ideas and protagonist, not on worldbuilding.

Exit at the cheap gate. The idea is nameable: bioethics should anticipate biotechnology instead of arriving as a fire brigade after the fact. But it is a roughly 480-page academic study that began as a habilitation thesis, with no story, no characters and an abstract conceptual frame, so thin per page for this reader. Leaned on density; nothing in the log supports an academic monograph as a read. Occult not examined.

t: Rozhovor s Ufonem (Interview with an Alien)
why: A fictional dialogue of sketches and ideas with an unbiased alien about things humans take for granted. The idea is nameable (an outsider questions our unexamined concepts) but the book is self-published, 226 pages, with no characters or story to carry it and no independent review found, so the doubt is whether the thinking holds up under the reader's own test. Short-form suspension removes penalties and adds nothing. Leaned on axis:ideas, the only thing that could lift it.

A political dystopia in the Orwell line, short (about 190 pages) and austere. The nearest anchors pull both ways: Animal Farm 78 for short political allegory that leaves an idea, 1984 60 for sustained bleakness ('too depressing'); this exit stays under the line on the bleakness anchor with a doubt about how much story there is beyond the setting. Only publisher copy and endorsements were found, no independent review, so the opening, the lead and the plot are unsourced. Occult is not examined; the blurb names exile for 'sodomy' and whether a same-sex thread is central is not established.

A collection of fifteen essays and speeches from 1976-84, read from the front with no single thread, so there is no one idea to lean on and the collection penalty applies. The ideas are real (difference as a source of action and coalition) but are advocacy rather than a test of what is plausible, which is what lifted the Qureshi memoir 91; the form earns nothing by itself. Leaned on ideas only; at a C exit the sexuality and sex-portrayal content is unexamined.

Each short chapter takes a food and uses its history to show an economic idea. Held under the line on the idea: reviewers say the economics is a minority of each chapter, the links can be tenuous and the author has an obvious agenda, so the idea would sit in risks, and the form earns nothing by itself. Positive: accessible, memorable, often with multiple views per chapter. Genre has no non-fiction value, nearest chosen.

The positive case is the same one that put Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 on top of the non-fiction in the log: it examines what is actually true and tests belief against evidence. The idea is nameable and has consequences: forecasting skill is measurable, a few amateurs beat professionals, and the habits can be learned. Reviewers say it reads like a story built around the tournament, with case studies such as the bin Laden raid. Deductions: no lead with wants, so the motives rule has little to lean on, and some reviewers find it padded; a few points off for density. Leaned on ideas, not on momentum.

t: Svet ve stinu demonu (The Demon-Haunted World)
why: The book is about how to tell a plausible claim from an implausible one, which is exactly what lifted Seeking Allah 91: honest examination of what is believable. It leaves a method behind (the baloney detection kit: independent confirmation, falsifiability, Occam's razor), the strongest form of the ideas axis. Occult is the topic being debunked, not a system the book operates or stages, so it does not trip the source or depiction tests; flagged because the filter word appears. Deductions: some readers find Sagan sharp on religion through the ages, a risk for the faith axis though it is argument, not satire, and a chapter or two on abduction claims may run long. Leaned on ideas only.

One idea with consequences, that insects underpin everything and their collapse threatens food and ecosystems, argued from thirty years of research and an obvious love of the animals. The book ends on what farmers, gardeners and politicians can do, which softens sustained bleakness (a mild cost in any case). Held down because reviewers say the enthusiasm sometimes drowns the science, the data are patchy and much will not be new to nature readers. Leaned on ideas.

Literary fiction and a collection of eight stories, the weakest combination in the log: no single premise to carry it, and a collection is read from the front and put down on its early pieces, as I, Robot 55 was. The idea is nameable (the two faces of a person, people in a situation with no way out), so it sits near the line rather than far below it. Bleakness is mild. Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source; occult not examined, axis:occult kept in deps.

Epic fantasy: a chosen-heir quest with an ensemble band. The chosen-one handling is not itself the problem, but I would list axis:ideas under risks, and reviewers report five viewpoints at once, heavy exposition and a convoluted plot, which is the opening and multi-POV trouble the log punishes (three books at 30). It is also the start of a series. Occult not examined (an undead army opens the book), kept in deps. Leaned on ideas and multi-pov, so doubt on both carries the number.

Popular science built on one counterintuitive question: if self-deception is universal, what is it for? That leaves a nameable idea behind, and the form earns only what it examines, as Seeking Allah 91 did by testing what is plausible. Reviewers praise hard data paired with stories, though one reader found the book split between a fascinating catalogue and a looser argument that deception is good for us. Held below the top for that looseness, for anecdote padding (axis:density) and because religion appears as one example of a useful belief, which could tip into faith as a subject. Leaned on ideas, not on prose or topic.

t: Valka svetu - War of the worlds (The War of the Worlds)
why: The idea is strong and nameable: humans meet a species that treats them as they treat other animals, and the invasion moves fast, so ideas and momentum carry it like the short idea-driven books the log likes (Animal Farm 78, Little Prince 82). Held down by a narrator who watches rather than wants anything and gives no one to root for the way Hunger Games 89 does, by sustained bleakness, and above all because this is a 104-page simplified bilingual language-learning edition, a retelling and not the novel, so the juvenile register is a risk. The curate episode is a serious treatment of belief, not ridicule. Leaned on ideas and momentum because the narrator is thin.

t: Vize tela a krve (Visions of Flesh and Blood)
why: A companion guide (diary, research notes, original short stories and artwork) to two romantasy series, not a novel, and it advances no storyline. No idea to name and no character to follow, in a collection-shaped form, so the low band. The sexual content of the parent series was not examined at this exit. Leaned on axis:ideas.

A modern retelling for readers from ten, illustrated, of a pirate adventure about a mad inventor and a world-destroying explosive: a different book from the original, and it sits toward a children's book (Narnia 67 pays a little, a picture book far more). The idea (the inventor's responsibility for what he makes) is real but not worked out, and the cast is thin adventure types. Not a whodunnit: the blurb's detective is a hero, flagged not vetoed. Leaned on axis:childrens.

t: Zalm pro divostrojne (A Psalm for the Wild-Built)
why: A nameable idea: when robots left and people have all they want, what do people actually need, put to a tea monk by the first robot seen in centuries. The companionship of two very different minds is what lifted Project Hail Mary 92 over The Martian 82, and this is the same shape in miniature. Deductions: reviewers say the first third is setup and the story is low-stakes, and a missing drive to keep reading is the exact complaint recorded on The Calculating Stars 85; Dex is a burnt-out monk with a fault to work against, which helps. The monks' invented gentle faith is incidental and does no rite work, a light deduction at most. Leaned on ideas and motives, not worldbuilding; momentum is held as a risk instead of widening the range.

Epic fantasy with no idea I can name beyond a quest to avenge a master, a dual timeline 350 years apart that taxes the opening, and a plot one reviewer calls mystery-shaped (flagged, not a whodunnit veto: the shape is a run from sects and monsters). The blurb also names sects and blood magic, so occult is unexamined at this exit and stays in deps. Reviews are mixed (a 3 of 5 among positives). Leaned on axis:ideas.

Two timelines: a nameless inventor's diary about a tachyon gate that sends people back in time, and a quasi-medieval society living off the remains of ours and reverse-engineering its relics. That is a nameable idea, and the cause-and-effect between inventor and ruins is what the reader tests hardest (Divergent 58). One reader review says the idea is very good but the book drags, many ideas are only hinted and the ending comes suddenly. Risks: time-travel consistency, two threads at the start and pace. Leaned on ideas, not on the world, which has little room to be built in about 250 pages.

t: Zrozeni Evropanu (A Short History of Humanity)
why: A real idea with consequences: DNA from ancient bones rewrites who our ancestors were, a story of migration, mixing and replacement told without kings or religion. It is short (256 pages), reviewers call it clear and engaging, and reader ratings are high. Held down for the lack of a lead with wants and because readers say some ideological framing at the start and end is a distraction; part of the history is hypothetical by necessity. Leaned on ideas; The Silmarillion 80 shows he can enjoy a sweep of peoples without a single protagonist.

The positive case is a captain who lives outside normal time and a silent child with an impossible gift: a companion plot with self-sacrifice in it, as Project Hail Mary 92 was praised for, in a time-dilation setting whose consequences the opening chapter already shows as a self-contained story. Held down by structure: viewpoints shift repeatedly, three sharply different sections, and reviewers say later crew members blur, the multi-POV risk, plus mild bleakness. The captain's relationships and the amount of sexual content were not established and are carried as risks. Leaned on ideas and protagonist, not worldbuilding alone, after Artemis 69.

t: Bozsky imperator Duny (God Emperor of Dune)
why: The positive case is ideas and motives: most of the book is the ruler explaining why he holds absolute power and what he steers humanity toward, the understanding-over-action page time that tops the log (Speaker for the Dead 90). Held down by reviews describing it as slow, talky and disjointed with little suspense, a lead whose loss of humanity saps sympathy (the Ballad 65 objection, with direction of travel a risk), a messianic-religion theme to be judged on reverence, and an opening that assumes history and characters it does not re-establish, which is the shape-two opening risk. Prescience here is drug-induced and mechanical, so occult would grade rather than veto, but was not examined at length. Leaned on ideas and motives.

t: Cesta kolem Mesice (Autour de la Lune)
why: Three men in a projectile circle the Moon, and the book is its physics and its consequences: escape velocity, trajectory, air supply, splashdown. That is the problem-solving the reader liked in The Martian 82, in a single closed situation with a clear start, and it is plain adventure with no content filter anywhere. Against it: reviewers say it is talk more than action and the three stereotypes are boring, so little time goes on motives (the log's top axis); it is a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70); and Verne's own science errors may break the rules he lays down, the way I, Robot 55 did. Kept below Count of Monte Cristo 75 and Hobbit 84. Leaned on ideas.

t: 13 a 1/2 zivota kapitana Modreho Medveda (The 13 1/2 Lives of Captain Bluebear)
why: Stopped at the C-low gate on one source. A comic picaresque of about 700 pages that reviewers consistently call episodic, with no overarching quest and digressions that wear after about 500 pages: story thin for the page count, the density penalty that held The Lord of the Rings to 84 despite its ideas. Comic register itself costs nothing (Hitchhiker's Guide 83), and the invention is praised, but I cannot name an idea the book leaves behind, and it sits toward the children's end (some reviewers recommend it for slightly older children). Leaned on density; occult unexamined at this exit, keep axis:occult in deps.

t: 2084 - Konec sveta (2084: The End of the World)
why: A clear idea: a state that rules by erasing memory and enforcing one belief, an allegory aimed at religious totalitarianism, as Animal Farm 78 was for political. But 1984 60 is the direct anchor: the reader called it too depressing, and this follows that template. Reviewers call the lead too thin to carry the book, the plot episodic and driven by luck, and the author's reflections hard to absorb. Religion is the target, so the treatment of blind faith may land as the satire he disliked in I, Robot 55, though a serious critique of a regime is graded on the thread-versus-subject test. The quest for the border is a journey, not a whodunit, so investigation is a flag only. Leaned on ideas.

A hacker shielding dissidents from a surveillance state, with a clear opening and an idea worth carrying away: code as metaphor, and what a book of djinn lore does to the logic of computing. Alif has a real stake and real flaws, and the Muslim faith thread is serious and sympathetic, the interest that Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus at 91 showed. Not a detective story. Held back by the djinn world, drawn from real Islamic belief and so a resemblance risk on occult even though the magic is presented as code and metaphor and not an invoked rite, and by a faith thread that could drift toward the subject itself. Leaned on ideas and protagonist; no rite found.

The idea is rare and actually worked through: aliens who cannot say anything untrue, similes that must be acted out to be spoken, a language that addicts and a crisis that forces them to learn to lie. That is the consequence-driven idea the log rewards (Speaker for the Dead 90, understanding an alien culture). Avice narrates with a real arc, from weary to determined. Deductions: dense invented vocabulary, a narrator who loops through her past, and reviewers noting terms like immerser go undescribed, a legible-opening risk; some secondary characters drop out. Leaned on ideas and motives; the opening is the risk so confidence stays medium.

Early exit at C. A nested dream-within-dream structure told by an unreliable storyteller means the idea dissolves into a puzzle box, and Balian is a spy dragged from one episode to the next rather than someone with a want to follow; Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 score on page time spent on motives, which this book withholds by design. The opening reviewers describe (reality and dream indistinguishable) is the confusion that sank The Colour of Magic 30 and The Gunslinger 30, though here it is deliberate. Occult status unexamined: dream-illness, alchemy and Sufi lore may be drawn from real practice. Stopped at one source, so medium.

t: Babylon, neboli, Nutnost nasili (Babel, or the Necessity of Violence)
why: One clear idea on which the world is built: magic that comes from what is lost in translation, run through enchanted silver bars, so language study and empire are the plot. Silver-working looks like technology rather than a rite, the escape in the occult rule, though only its daily use and not the whole system was sourced. The lead and the friendships are the positive case, and the book leaves arguments behind. Held down: reviewers call some characters mouthpieces and the plot predictable, the argument about empire is one-sided (a small sex-portrayal risk is unexamined), the ending is reported bleak, and romance is reported as minor so same-sex is at most a light mention. Leaned on ideas and worldbuilding, the same axes that earned Project Hail Mary 92.

Folk-tale shapes (kings, dragons, knights) filled with robots, each with a point to make about technology, so the idea carries it and the character rules are suspended without earning anything. It sits further toward the fable than the comic-SF register that worked in Hitchhiker's Guide at 83, so the children's register costs a little, and as a collection it is read from the front and stopped on the weakest early story, as I, Robot at 55 was. Several of the fables are deliberately archaic and parodic, which may read as satire of belief. No rite found.

One clear opening, a bounty hunter in a dying world who wants a real animal, and an idea you can name and keep thinking about: what separates a person from a machine if empathy can be faked and a believer can be deceived. Deckard wants things and has flaws, so the lean is ideas and motives, the same kind of pull as Speaker for the Dead at 90. Hunting androids is not a whodunnit. The deductions: a single hotel scene with an android while he is married, treated neutrally and incidental to the book (a few points), a sustained bleak, decaying setting (mild), and an invented empathy religion that is shown in rite-like use and later exposed as a fraud, which could read as ridicule of belief like I, Robot at 55; held to risks rather than a heavier cut.

The idea is nameable and followed through three stages: a clinic that rebuilds the past for dementia, then healthy people moving in, then nations voting on which past to return to, a social allegory in the vein of Animal Farm 78 where the satire costs nothing. Literary fiction, so the base rate sits under the line: the narrator is an unnamed author alter ego who mostly assists and observes (passive, nothing to root for, as in Oliver Twist 57), the form is essayistic and fragmentary with little momentum, and a reviewer calls it weird. Ideas carry it; protagonist and density are the doubts.

An idea can be named (a ten-year rerun that takes away free will), but reviewers say the book uses it as an excuse to ramble through the author's memories and his alter ego's story summaries, about half autobiography, loose and disjointed, with no plot a reader follows. The log gives no credit to memoir form alone (Diary of a Young Girl 40) and a book with no line of events fails the motives and momentum the reader values most. Stopped at the cheap gate on one source. axis:occult not examined at this exit.

t: Chvalozpev na Leibowitze (A Canticle for Leibowitz)
why: A canonical book that actually carries an idea: knowledge kept, lost and misused again in cycles, with faith set against science, and what it leaves behind is the reason to read. It opens on one concrete situation, a novice finding a fallout shelter. Three parts centuries apart follow different leads, so the character rules do not apply in the usual way; The Silmarillion 80 shows the reader can score well with no single protagonist and dense mythic material. Deductions: faith is the main subject rather than a thread (a monastic order), a real risk for this reader though Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 shows serious faith is not a barrier, and the bleak run (cruelty, euthanasia). The monks' religion is real-world Catholic practice, not occult. Leaned on ideas.

In 1912 Europe is replaced overnight by an alien continent, and a 1920 expedition has to understand what happened to it; the unknown is central, survival depends on it, and the answer, when it comes, recasts the setting (Project Hail Mary 92 anchors the pull of an open unknown the lead must work out), and the idea is nameable: a world reconstructed and unaware of it. Hugo-nominated. Deductions: a second lead is a psychic, which touches the occult Source test through resemblance and I could not establish whether it is mechanism or practice; a creationist expedition and a surge of religion make faith a thread to grade; two leads mean a small POV load; reviewers split on characters and style. Leaned on ideas and discovery. Medium because occult unresolved.

First-person lead with a clear want (who killed her mother) thrown into a succession struggle inside a society ruled by enslaved gods gives a motive-driven court story and ideas about faith and power. Deductions: the central relationship with an eons-old god is sexual and prominent (reviewers call the scenes over the top, with consent questions), which costs on volume and explicitness without being the plot; an invented religious system with gods, bargains and a succession ceremony at the climax grades as a heavy occult deduction (system is invented, staged human sacrifice not established); retrospective narration opens with terms the reader does not yet have, a mild shape-two risk; the cast of men and gods is mixed so the sex-portrayal contrast is small. Leaned on motives and ideas; Yeine's first-person interior carries it.

A longevity society that treats children as a crime and trains them as servants has a clear moral idea, but reviewers say it arrives as one exposition block, the technology is otherwise today's, and the claim that crime vanished when people live forever does not hold. A brainwashed lead who has to unlearn her indoctrination is a fault to work against, but a lead acted upon is the Oliver Twist 57 failure mode, and YA register costs a little. Exited at the cheap gate; occult unexamined.

A society that cures love as a disease has a thin logic: reviewers note no biological basis, cured people still feel every other emotion, and outlawing love solves everything, which is the kind of premise that collapses under thought (Divergent 58). Praise for the social texture and propaganda is real but is worldbuilding polish, not an idea that holds. YA register and teen lead cost a little; the romance as central subject is free (Pride and Prejudice 75). Exited at the cheap gate; occult unexamined.

Gate 4 exit on one source. An unnamed civilian is lost in a bureaucratic military labyrinth and handed a mission nobody can explain: the idea of a totalitarian system sealed inside its own absurdity is real, but the lead is acted upon rather than wanting anything, the failure that left Promena at 58 and Oliver Twist at 57, and the bleakness is total, as with 1984 at 60. Occult status unexamined because this is a C-low exit.

The idea is excellent and worked through: calories as currency, bioengineered plague and the politics of a seed bank in a flooded Bangkok. The plot is the ministries, the corporation and the refugees, not sex, so the sexual-content filter does not fire, but the grading does: reviewers agree there are two extended graphic scenes of Emiko's sexual humiliation, with recurring abuse, so volume, explicitness and crudeness all cost, the Ready Player One 55 dimension. The book is also sustained bleakness and the cast is several POVs without a plainly rootable lead (a manipulative foreigner, a victim, a bitter refugee). Leaned on ideas only; with the content and the lead weaknesses that cannot hold a high range.

Two short late-career Challenger pieces: the idea is nameable (the Earth as a single living creature, a machine that takes matter apart and puts it back) but both are told as farce, so the idea is a gag rather than something the story keeps thinking about. A two-story form suspends the character tests without adding points, as the Little Prince 82 and Animal Farm 78 earn their scores on a real idea, which these do not quite have. Challenger is a bombastic, hard-to-warm-to lead and the account is relayed by a bystander. Exited at the cheap gate; occult status is unexamined at one source.

t: Dr. Krvemsta, aneb, Jak se nam vedlo po bombe
why: Gate 4 exit on one source. A post-nuclear community and a telekinetic mechanic who rises through manipulation, with an ensemble of several strands (a satellite disc jockey, a disgraced physicist, a TV repairman) and no single lead to root for; the strongest character is a villain, the Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes at 65 problem, and the bleakness is sustained. The psychic powers are mutations, not rites, but occult is not examined at a C-low exit.

Lessa, the last of a ruined line, schemes to reclaim her hold and is swept into a weyr of dragonriders defending a planet from falling spores. Her revenge and the weyr's survival give clear wants, and the world has a plausible hard cause (a wandering planet, colonists, spores) that the book builds a society around, which the reader checks. Deductions: the central mating-flight scene is widely criticised on consent grounds, which is a sexual-treatment cost (volume small, treatment dated and uncomfortable; Artemis 69 shows treatment alone can dock a lot); the male weyrleader dynamic invites a sex-portrayal check, unmeasured; the book is classic and thin on thinking beyond the survival story. Leaned on motives and momentum, not worldbuilding. Dragon telepathy is an invented bond, treated as non-occult by mechanism.

One declared physical idea, a life form on a neutron star living a hundred times faster than us, and every consequence (their history, technology and the human observers as gods in a day) is followed through, which is the pleasure of the thought-through worldbuilding praised in Project Hail Mary 92 and the alien-culture interest of Speaker for the Dead 90. But the log's strongest lesson is that a thin lead outranks strong worldbuilding (Artemis 69 against Project Hail Mary 92), and critics consistently call the human crew cardboard and the cheela functional; that caps it below the A band. Sourced reviews agree the cheela are more alive than the humans. No occult, no sex. Ideas carry it; character differentiation is the doubt.

A society in which violence is banned and rank, property and law are decided inside a fantasy computer game, with a 14-year-old whose exiled father pulls him into beating the system. The idea is nameable and Kirkus describes the economy and legal system as built into the game, so the world is the point; one concrete starting situation, single lead, constant momentum, like the Hunger Games 89 formula in miniature. Deductions: it is young-adult in register (Ranger's Apprentice 74 paid a little), a teen lead is a small life-phase cost, reviewers call the friends thinly drawn and one says it reads like a tabletop game, and a society run through a game owes consequence-by-consequence consistency the reader will check (Mortal Engines 55). Leaned on ideas and momentum.

A pressure-cooker society is the idea: a sealed, overcrowded planet where humans and frog-like aliens are kept in want, to see what such pressure breeds, and the book works out what the survivors become. That is the same kind of consequences-first worldbuilding the reader rewards (Old Man's War 87). Held down because many reviewers find the plot hard to follow, with wheels-within-wheels intrigue, many factions, and a courtroom ending built on an unfamiliar legal system, so the opening and density could bite. The agent is a trained superman, so competence may be unearned; body-switching sex is reported without detail. Leaned on axis:ideas and worldbuilding. No staged rite found.

The idea is strong and nameable: a first-contact expedition to a hostile, silent civilisation and what human assumptions do to the attempt, the same kind of reasoning about an alien culture that tops Speaker for the Dead at 90, with a priest aboard giving belief a serious, non-satirical thread. Held below that by a very long prologue on Titan before the main story, a cast of scientists with little to root for, a lead whose identity is itself an open question (only partial discovery lift), and a bleak ending. Leaned on ideas, not protagonist, because the lead is not what carries it. No occult rite found in the summaries.

A clear, concrete start, a riot at a congress in a hotel and a drugged escape through the sewers, and one idea that is genuinely left behind: a society managing perception with chemistry instead of solving anything. Held down because reviewers disagree on how much of the book is hallucination, so the reader may be tracking realities that cannot be trusted, the lead is a comic narrator mostly carried along, and the satire of drugged utopias asks little of the lead's wants. Leaned on ideas, not protagonist. No rite or occult found.

A strong, specific idea: poor people gamble their lives on abandoned alien ships whose controls they cannot read, and every flight is a lottery between riches and death. The unknown is central and the need is plain (escape poverty); the discovery lift is partial because the central question is left open. Narrator Robinette is flawed on purpose and is analysed throughout, so there is interior life. Risks: reviewers call the therapy chapters, about a third of the book, either the best part or tedious, and dated Freudian; the lead's guilt and cowardice make him hard to like; one review reports a brief same-sex episode and the book has frank sexual content at moderate volume; the ending is bleak. The opening is two timelines but one narrator voice. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:worldbuilding, not on the lead. No staged rite found.

A competent satirical novel with one idea (loneliness answered by artificial extended families) and a distinctive narrator, the last president of a collapsed America. Reviews are mixed to negative and the author rated it a D himself; the world is a loose comic collapse (plague, tiny invaders) rather than a consistent system, the twins' erotic closeness is the book's central theme though not its plot, and the tone is bleak. Probably sits just under the line. Leaned on axis:protagonist: an odd, flawed narrator with real interiority. Stopped at the cheap gate; axis:occult not examined.

t: Hlubina na nebi (A Deepness in the Sky)
why: Two human civilisations and an alien one, each with a precisely built logic, meeting around a star that goes dark on a long cycle: the book is the consequences of those declared things followed to the end, the same pleasure Project Hail Mary 92 gave and the alien-culture understanding Speaker for the Dead 90 rewards. Ideas (mind-control technology versus free trade, deception) carry it. Deductions: the opening has to carry two fleets and a prologue before any one thread is legible (shape one risk, as in the cold starts that sank Guards! Guards! 30), reviewers say it lacks one emotional centre, and the long middle is slow. Rules add obligation not bonus, so I stay below the top of the log. No occult, little sex; mechanism only.

Positive case: Holly Sykes is a lead worth following across sixty years, and a hidden war about souls and mortality gives ideas to think about, the axis Speaker for the Dead 90 and Project Hail Mary 92 score on. Deductions: the soul system (rebirth, mind-possession, immortals who murder psychic children to drink their souls) is invented but its rites are staged and central, a heavy occult grading of about ten points; whether the soul-decanting counts as staged human sacrifice is a doubt that could turn it into a veto, and I did not reject on it. Six sections, six narrators and decades risks the tracking cost of Guards! Guards! 30, although Holly's opening section is single-POV and legible. One narrator section is a manipulative seducer who is hard to root for (Ballad 65 mould), and the sex is not trivial in volume (Ready Player One 55). Leaned on ideas and motives, not worldbuilding, given the Artemis 69 lesson.

t: Horka Linka z Hadonose (The Ophiuchi Hotline)
why: Stopped at the C-low gate on one source. Ideas are dense (cloning, mind recordings, humanity evicted from Earth) and well praised, but reviewers say the plot does not live up to them, loses focus toward an abrupt ending, and the makers of the signal the book hangs on are left unexplained, which the reader checks. Casual sex and gender change are described as just part of life; that is the volume question the reader prices heavily (Ready Player One 55, The Witcher 53), and I did not measure it. A complex multi-thread opening is a further risk (Guards! Guards! 30). Leaned on ideas. Occult unexamined at this exit; keep axis:occult in deps.

A single three-day battle seen through its commanders and foot soldiers, with page time on what the characters want and what the fighting does to them; the nameable idea is the hollowness of heroism and glory. Violence and swearing are not objections, and the characters are strongly individual, so Red Rising 95 and Golden Son 92 (morally grey, violent, interior) are the anchors. Deductions: reviewers say many POVs overwhelm the first half, which is the several-lines-at-once opening risk (Guards! Guards! 30); several of the biggest voices are cynical and not rootable (Ballad 65 on a lead sliding the wrong way), though a veteran sergeant is the traditional way in; bleakness graded mild; sexual crudeness is likely and unmeasured; a wizard order in the wider world may carry rites, unexamined. Leaned on motives and ideas.

Fast, suspenseful survival story where reviewers call the lead the real hero and AIDAN one of the more interesting artificial minds, shown with its own motives and horrors in the second half; that is motives over action, the axis that tops Mockingjay 91. YA register and teen leads cost a little (Hunger Games 89 shows it is small), and an ex-couple romance is central but not the plot. Leaned on the lead and the AI as an idea.
