Risk: the dossier format takes getting used to and some find the chat banter too high-school, so the opening could miss; documents are collective rather than several voices, so character differentiation is the weaker leg.

Each story carries a nameable idea (children and a machine nursery, racism reversed on Mars, the last night of the world), and a frame of one tattooed man ties them as a fix-up, the least exposed collection form. The anchor for collections is Ja, robot 55, read from the front and dropped on weak early stories: the opening story here has children turning on their parents with nobody to root for, the same trap, so the range is not set by the best stories. The frame device (a future witch inking tattoos) is at most a light invented-frame occult touch; religion appears in a couple of stories and may not sit well if treated as satire. Short form suspends character penalties but adds no points, so the number rests on the ideas alone.

Gate 4 exit on one source. A society of former psychiatric patients organised into clans by diagnosis is a real idea, but the story is driven by a disintegrating marriage and a lead who is depressed, resigned and plotting to murder his wife by remote control, hard to root for in the way Promena at 58 and Ballad at 65 were, spread across a large cast. No affair was confirmed in summaries, so infidelity is unexamined; occult unexamined at a C-low exit.

t: Kniha ztracenych veci (The Book of Lost Things)
why: A grieving 12-year-old falls into a land made of twisted fairy tales and has to find his way home; the unknown world, the need to cross it and an open outcome fit the discovery shape (partial), and the idea left behind is nameable: stories as the way a child grows past grief. Motives are strong (his grief and resentment are the engine). Deductions: a child lead is a small life-phase cost (Narnia 67 paid a little, Hobbit 84 nothing) and this is explicitly a dark book for adults, so register is not the children's problem; sexual innuendo and a wolf-human tale appear but reviewers describe them as implied, not explicit, and the villain is a devil-like trickster in an invented tale world, which I weigh as a small occult risk rather than a veto. Leaned on ideas and discovery. Confidence medium: opening and occult inferred from reviews, not sourced to text.

An unknown to explore with a reason to explore it: a sea of crossing rails, giant mole-hunting trains and a salvaged photograph that points to what the world is. The opening is one concrete situation, Sham's first mole hunt, and he then has to find out what the Shroakes' parents sought. Moby Dick played with trains is fun and the ideas about the world are the draw. Deductions: young adult register (small, as Ranger's Apprentice 74 and Narnia 67), and reviewers say things happen to Sham until his kidnapping, so the lead is passive early. Leaned on discovery and ideas; the lead is the risk.

The idea is first-rate and fully worked out: a society that engineers contentment by conditioning, drugs and caste breeding, tested by an outsider raised on Shakespeare. It sits beside 1984 60 and Animal Farm 78, and Animal Farm shows satire with an idea can reach the high 70s; but 1984 60 was dropped as too depressing and this ends in the Savage's suicide, so bleakness is not mild here. Bernard is petty and John is a tragic figure, so the lead is a risk (Metamorphosis 58 fired on passivity), the hatchery opening is exposition-led rather than a person, and a society organised around promiscuity brings a recurring and finally explicit sexual theme. Leaned on ideas.

One nameable idea: an inventor of a total explosive and what he owes the world once powers bid for it. That is why it is not an early exit. But reviewers describe a deliberately delirious, dreamlike narrative, with the first chapters written as the hero's concussion fever and a plot that meanders through allegorical encounters; this reader abandoned The Gunslinger and the Discworld openings for an unclear start, though here it is one man's fever and not several plot lines. Gradual bleakness and a lead carried by events add to it. Leaned on axis:ideas; the opening and momentum are the risks and the range is wide on that account. No occult or affair premise found; romantic entanglements are episodes in the fever.

A boy with a secret in a world that purges what is not norm: a lead who is easy to root for, a clear want from the first pages (keep the secret, keep the people he loves) and an idea that stays with you, what a closed society does to those it fears. The telepathy is a mutation presented as a natural trait, not a rite, so occult is clear. Short and tightly plotted, which fits the log's liking for ideas that carry. Deductions: a child lead narrating (Ender's Game 87 lost a little on this, not a tier), some bleakness, and the religion is a harsh fundamentalism that the book condemns seriously rather than ridiculing, which is a thread-versus-subject question, not satire; a closing speech reviewers find uneasy is the faith risk. Protagonist and ideas carry it.

Comic robot fairy tales in which each story is built on one precise idea and carried to its absurd consequence, so ideas carry the number and the short-idea-driven suspension removes character penalties without adding points. The leads are two recurring comic constructors who are easy to follow and need no rooting for in the Ballad sense. The register is closest to Hitchhiker's Guide at 83 and Saturnin at 78, but it sits toward fable and fairy tale, a small children's-register cost, and as a collection it is read from the front and put down on the weakest early story, as I, Robot at 55 was, so the range stays modest and wide. No occult found.

One nameable idea carries it: a forest in which the minds of people near it give legends bodily form. The lead has to explore an unknown place that took his father, his brother and now a woman he loves, and the answer arrives within the book, the exploring-under-necessity shape of Project Hail Mary 92 in a very different key. Held down because reviewers call the characters one-note and the lead conventional, the book is atmospheric and descriptive, and the figures are Celtic and Arthurian legends so the occult question was not fully settled (the mechanism is invented and no rite turned up in the sources, hence a risk and not a veto). The relationship with a mythago woman is the emotional core, not the plot, and it is a rivalry with his brother, not an affair in a marriage. Leaned on ideas and discovery.

t: Letopisy z hlubin veku (Chronicles of Ancient Darkness)
why: Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. A twelve-year-old lead and a survival adventure written for ages 9-12 sit toward the children's end (Ranger's Apprentice 74 and Narnia 67 are the anchors for the cost), with not much to think about beyond loyalty and survival. Occult is unexamined at this exit and it is the real question: the clan mages, soul-eaters and spirit world look animist, so axis:occult stays in deps and is the first thing to check if this is ever revisited.

One idea carries it, seen from outside: what being human is, through a being who has to learn it in order to finish a task. The unknown is the whole world around him and the need to understand it is real (his mission depends on it), which is the shape of the discovery Project Hail Mary 92 was loved for. The lead has a clear direction of travel toward the people he was sent to harm, the arc that makes a lead worth rooting for as in Speaker for the Dead 90, and the comic outsider's view of Earth sits near Hitchhiker's Guide 83. The opening is one concrete situation, a naked arrival in Cambridge. Deductions are small: a sentimental, idealistic register that can thin the ideas, and the bleak stretch around the real professor's family. Leaned on ideas and discovery, not on the lead alone. No occult found: the aliens' abilities are technology. Some sexual references reported as incidental; volume not established.

Hard-SF collection with a strong idea per story (a common ancestor search, free will as an implant, diving a black hole), so ideas hold, but a collection is read from the front and put down on its weakest early stories (Ja, robot 55), and the English edition opens with a covert-assassination story and has a private-detective story and cult material among the ten, so the early stories carry the number. The suspension of character rules does not cover rootability, which fired on the first story of that anchor. Density risk from the maths-heavy telling. Exited at the cheap gate; occult unexamined.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. The lead is the doubt: reviewers agree Quentin is selfish, passive and sexually entitled, the not-worth-rooting-for failure that put Ballad 65 and Oliver Twist 57 under the line, and the book is heavy on sex and drink. The infidelity is outside the marriage-or-engagement scope of the axis, so graded as sexual content, not infidelity. The school magic is learned technique, not a rite, but occult is unexamined at this exit; axis:occult stays in deps. A nameable idea (wanting a fantasy world and finding it empty) keeps it near the line, not far below.

Fast near-future story with a real idea behind it (how surveillance and cryptography work and what they cost), told by a clever teen who has to outwit a security state; problem-solving and a point worth thinking about is the Weir-style axis (Project Hail Mary 92, The Martian 82). Costs: reviewers say the exposition stops the story, the book is polemic and the villains one-sided, and a team of teens beating a government is a competence-given-not-earned risk. The lead is described as a self-flattering teenage fantasy. Sexual content was not sourced and is left unexamined beyond the mandatory axis. Teen lead is a small pushback.

A short, fast book around one clean idea: a man is rebuilt as a cyborg to survive on Mars, and what that does to him and his marriage, with the project's science explained as it goes. A lead who is changed by events and has something to lose is worth rooting for. Deductions: the wife's affair with a member of the project team is a subplot, not the premise, and reviews present it as painful and messy rather than approving, which still prices as a subplot at the neutral-to-condemned end; some reviewers find the marriage thread and the characters flat. Bleakness is moderate. Leaned on axis:ideas, with axis:infidelity the reason the low end is as low as it is. No occult found.

Victorian London with time travel through H. G. Wells as the connecting figure; each of three parts gives its own lead a strong want (saving a lover, reaching a loved one in the future, defending Wells's own life), and reviewers say time travel is presented so it is never confusing or ridiculous. Costs: it is three separate narratives so the reader re-adjusts at each part, the last is called hard to follow and the author likes to wrong-foot the reader, and its third part is a murder-plot with an investigation that touches the mystery bar. Leaned on the idea of time paradoxes and on motives; opening and the mystery strand could pull it below.

The idea is clear and held to: a society run by machines in which function decides identity, and the book is the consequences, with social satire that costs nothing in the log (Animal Farm 78 is the anchor). Deductions: Paul is a passive lead drifting between sides (the Metamorphosis 58 and Oliver Twist 57 pattern), the arc is bleak and the revolt fails, and a wife's affair is a thread in his marriage that Vonnegut presents without a verdict, which is a subplot-level neutral treatment but not the premise, so a few points rather than the table's 45-55. A minister character is satirised, a small faith risk. Idea carries the number, protagonist is the doubt.

t: Mesto snicich knih (Die Stadt der Traumenden Buecher)
why: A young writer follows a masterpiece manuscript to a city built on books and down into the labyrinth beneath it, with an invented, detailed and cozy world and a love of reading as the idea; reviewers call it among the best books about books. Costs: written in a whimsical, almost young-adult register (Hobbit 84 shows that costs nothing, Narnia 67 a little), described as long-winded, and the narrator is an egotist who does not learn much. A world of whimsy owes less self-consistency, so the worldbuilding lean is moderate. Occult not found; inferred rather than sourced, since the magic is an invented life force. Leaned on worldbuilding and the book-love idea.

t: Most pres reku Kwai (The Bridge over the River Kwai)
why: The book is built on what two men want and why: Nicholson and Saito are both ruled by false pride and a letter-of-the-law sense of duty, and the novel works out where that leads, which is the page time on motives that tops Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90. The idea (duty and pride turning into collaboration) is nameable and the narration is a concise psychological study. Historical fiction has been read without complaint (Exodus 68, The Count of Monte Cristo 75), so the ceiling is held there rather than above it. Nicholson is a satirised military snob, not an obvious lead to root for, and the camp setting is grim. No occult, no detective, sex incidental. How the commando strand cuts in against the camp strand early on is inferred, not sourced, hence medium.

Stopped at the C-low gate on one source. A nameable idea exists (two civilizations, one ant and one human, failing to notice each other), but the human strand is a cellar-disappearances thread with a lead whom reviewers describe as a vehicle rather than a person, which is the axis carrying the number: a flat lead, the failure that cost Oliver Twist 57. Two interleaved storylines plus encyclopedia excerpts also risk the several-plot-lines opening that sank Guards! Guards! 30, although the ant strand is reportedly the draw. A cellar mystery is a detective-shaped flag, not a veto. Occult status is unexamined (C-low exit); keep axis:occult in deps. Medium confidence because I stopped.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. The idea is nameable (what makes a life human) but I would put worldbuilding in risks: critics' main objection is that the clones never run or resist and the world gives no reason, and the reader checks whether an author honours what he sets up. Kathy is a quiet, acquiescent narrator, the passive-lead shape that cost Metamorphosis 58 and Oliver Twist 57, and the bleakness is total. Occult unexamined at this exit; axis:occult stays in deps.

A starship lands on a dead-looking planet to find out what happened to its sister ship, and the answer, self-replicating machines that evolved by selection into a swarm, is worked out step by step from the evidence: the unknown-world exploration with a real need behind it that earned the lift for Project Hail Mary at 92. One concrete starting situation and a navigator who serves as the reader's eyes. Reviewers call the crew flat at the start, and the ending is a defeat; those are the risks. Leaned on ideas and discovery, not protagonist. No rite or occult found.

First-person coming-of-age of Mia Havero, who is tested by a month of survival on a colony world and, in the process, questions what her closed Ship society taught her about the 'mudeaters'. The positive case is motives and a lead who changes her mind, the same inside-the-lead reading that carried Ender's Game 87, plus a nameable idea: how a culture that calls other humans less than human holds together. Deductions: a 14-year-old narrator is a small life-phase and register cost (Ender's Game was marked down when the child read as a child from the inside), and the Ship society must survive the self-consistency test the reader applies to Mortal Engines 55 and Divergent 58. Leaned on motives and ideas, not worldbuilding, since a thin lead would sink strong setting (Artemis 69). Opening is a single narrator and one situation, so no opening objection found, but not verified past snippets.

t: Ocean na konci cesty (The Ocean at the End of the Lane)
why: A short, strange novel with one nameable idea: a grown man remembering what was real in his childhood and what adults never see. Its pull is atmosphere more than a system you can reason about, and the lead is a passive seven-year-old narrator acted upon rather than wanting much, the Oliver Twist 57 risk. Occult is the main uncertainty: the Hempstock women are timeless, witch-like figures, and the magic is folklore, not an engineered mechanism; the sources show no staged rite or human sacrifice, so it is graded and not vetoed, a few points off. The father's affair with the creature is a subplot, shown as horror and so condemned, a few points; it includes a scene where he tries to drown the boy, which is bleak. Leaned on ideas, with occult and bleakness as the risks.

A short satire on the Soviet space programme as propaganda: the idea is nameable (a state substituting imagined achievements for real ones), and political satire costs nothing (Animal Farm 78); the form suspends character penalties and adds none. Deductions: reviewers call it as much horror as satire, so bleakness arrives early and fully (1984 60), and Omon is acted upon by the machine rather than driving events, the passive-lead failure behind Promena 58 and Oliver Twist 57. Leaned on ideas. Opening unverified past review summaries. Occult not examined beyond blurb.

One idea, named: a discovery made with good intentions becomes a catastrophe once ignorance and politics get hold of it, a satire of scientific and political naivety. Satire aimed at politics and society costs nothing, as Animal Farm 78 shows, and a short idea-driven book has the character rules suspended, though that adds no points. The ceiling stays below Animal Farm because the lead scientist is a cold, hard-to-warm-to figure and the book is bleak and ends badly for him, the Metamorphosis 58 pattern of a passive, hard-to-root-for lead. Leaned on ideas; no religion satire or occult found.

Gate 4 exit on one source. The premise has an idea (a time-shifting drug) but the centre is an unhappy marriage between a doctor and an addicted wife, with a lead who leaves, is manipulated and drifts, the passive lead of Promena at 58, in a bleak, chaotic world. Infidelity was not found in the summaries and so is unexamined; occult unexamined as well at a C-low exit.

Stopped at the C-low gate on one source. The idea is nameable (what it is like to be the hunter who sees humans as meat), but the number rides on the lead, an alien who drugs and delivers male hitchhikers: the not-rootable-lead problem that held Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes to 65, even though reviewers say Faber wins real sympathy for her, so the range could be higher on a full read. Bleakness and horror are sustained; the lure involves sexual expectation, a small content risk. Leaned on protagonist. Occult unexamined at this exit; keep axis:occult in deps.

t: Podobenstvi o rozsevaci (Parable of the Sower)
why: A first-person journal from a lead with a clear want, to survive and build something, and a real flaw-and-gift in hyperempathy, so the protagonist and motives axes that top the log are present from the first pages (Hunger Games 89 is the shape). The collapse of the setting is consistent and the book leaves an idea behind. Deductions: Earthseed is a belief system the lead founds and the book gives it space with italic verses, so faith runs close to a subject in its own right, not just a thread; reviewers also call the voice flat for a hyperempath; the road is sustained bleakness (mild in the log, as in 1984 60); a young lead is a small pushback. Earthseed is an invented philosophy with no rite, so occult is clear. Protagonist carries it, faith is the doubt.

A named, concrete idea: an alien species whose life cycle turns breeders into fierce protectors, and what that does to a human changed by it. Reviewers call the Pak a fascinating invention and the two protector characters the best thing in it. Held down because it is two novellas split by a 200-year jump, the second built around a different lead, so the lead may not stay someone to root for through the whole book (the Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 failure), and reviewers call it disjointed. Leaned on ideas; exploring is not the engine here, and the cast risk is the more likely failure.

The idea is a megastructure and an expedition that has to learn what it is: an unknown world, a need to understand it to get home, and aliens (a cowardly puppeteer, a warrior kzin) whose logic drives the plot. That is the exploring-under-necessity shape Project Hail Mary 92 scores on, plus the alien-culture interest of Speaker for the Dead 90. Held below those because reviewers describe the only viewpoint lead as weak and the second human as there for luck and sex, so the lead could read as thin as in Artemis 69; the 1970 treatment of women may touch the sex-portrayal axis. Sexual content looks small. Leaned on ideas and discovery, not on the protagonist, which is the weak spot.

t: Prvnich patnact zivotu Harryho Augusta (The First Fifteen Lives of Harry August)
why: A time-loop idea followed to its consequences: a man reborn with all his memories who, with others like him, must decide what to do with that knowledge. Foreknowledge and a closed time loop is what the top-scoring Licanius books at 92-96 were liked for, and what a lead wants and does with that power is the motives axis. A friend-turned-antagonist gives a clear want. Held down: the time-jumping how-we-got-here structure is called bewildering by one reviewer and slow at the start by another, so the opening could cost, and one reviewer found the first half stronger than the second. No occult found in the sources (Kalachakra is a label, not a rite). Leaned on ideas and motives.

One precise idea: a scientist remakes a creature and the result, entitled and amoral, shows the folly of engineering human nature. It opens in a stray dog's voice, a distinct and concrete starting situation, and the cast is sharply drawn (professor, dog-turned-man, his assistant). Political satire costs nothing here (Animal Farm 78). Held under that book because the professor is arrogant rather than warm, so the rooting interest is split. Leaned on ideas; no occult found.

Exited at the below-the-line gate on one source. The book is an oral history of a war told from many narrators whose voices reviewers say are indistinguishable, so page time goes to events across the world, not what particular people want (the set-piece dead weight the log punishes; Golden Son 92 lost points just for leaning on action). Many short threads from the first chapters is the opening shape-one risk. A competent action SF, with the machine-uprising idea familiar. Occult not applicable at this exit but left in deps.

A contemporary novel with a nameable idea: how brands and pattern-seeking shape meaning after the 2001 attacks, with a lead whose private wound, a missing father, is the real engine. Cayce is distinctive and interior, and a quest for the maker of mysterious clips is a search for a person, not a culprit, so it is flagged as investigation-shaped, not the detective filter. Held down: reviewers split on pace and call the ending an anti-climax, the style is dense with brand detail, and as with Kafka's Metamorphosis 58 a withdrawn lead may be hard to root for. Leaned on ideas and the protagonist.

t: S pokorou a nadeji (To Be Taught, If Fortunate)
why: A first-person astronaut surveys four worlds with a crew of four and the book is about what exploring costs and means, with the somaforming idea carrying real consequences (bodies adapted to each world, Earth changing while they sleep). That is the thinking-about-it plus unknown-to-explore shape of Project Hail Mary 92, and the premise-and-ideas appeal of Pocitani hvezd 85. Same caveat as Pocitani hvezd: reviewers call it quiet and unhurried with little interpersonal drama and an abrupt ending, so drive is the soft spot. Ariadne's voice is reflective and a lead worth rooting for. Short form suspends character penalties but adds no points; the lift comes from the named idea. Crew relationships were not established from sources, so a same-sex thread is carried as a modest risk. No occult, no sex plot.

Positive case: a founding cyberpunk space opera of an idea per sentence, with two post-human factions (Shapers and Mechanists) whose rivalry is worked out across a whole solar system. Against it: reviewers say the narration keeps the reader at a distance, Lindsay is not a hero to cheer for and motivations are called unclear, and the book is dense and sometimes confusing; the reader's top axes are motives and a rootable lead, and Artemis 69 shows strong worldbuilding does not rescue a thin lead. Fractured episodes across decades also risk the multi-line opening that sank Guards! Guards! 30. Capped below 75 on that basis. Leaned on worldbuilding and ideas, with the protagonist as the named collapse risk.

A half-dragon lead with something to hide and a real fault to work against, in a world where dragons are given their own way of thinking and the treaty between the species creates real consequences: the protagonist and worldbuilding axes both carry. The murder at the centre is a mystery-shaped thread, not a whodunit in the filter's sense, since the stakes are the treaty and her secret; flagged, not vetoed. Saints and grotesques are an invented church and the dragons' mental discipline is mechanism-like, light at most. A betrothed prince is a love-triangle thread, an arranged betrothal and no affair, so no infidelity. YA register, a little juvenile (Ranger's Apprentice 74 is the nearest cost), and a sequel is needed for the full resolution.

t: Sireny z Titanu (The Sirens of Titan)
why: Strong idea: the richest man on Earth is made the plaything of a man who sees all time, and the book argues about free will and purpose in a way that stays with you. Held down by three things the log prices. The invented Church of God the Utterly Indifferent is religion played as satire, which this reader disliked outright (Ja, robot 55). The lead is stripped of memory and moved like a piece, so he is acted upon rather than wanting anything, the failure behind Oliver Twist 57. And the ending is bleak, with a sexual-assault scene reported in one review. A foreknowledge plot is graded on handling and costs nothing by itself (Licanius 92-96). Leaned on axis:ideas; axis:worldbuilding is the lift.

t: Snidane sampionu, aneb, Sbohem modre pondeli! (Breakfast of Champions)
why: Early exit at C. A plotless, digressive satire narrated by the author, with deliberately grotesque felt-tip drawings; the two leads are a failing writer and a man going mad, neither one to root for, and the long-awaited meeting is described as anticlimactic. The crudeness penalty (Artemis 69, Ready Player One 55) applies to the crude drawings and sexual references, and the digressions are the thin-story cost. The satire has a nameable idea (people as machines, free will), which keeps it from the lower band, and Animal Farm 78 shows social satire costs nothing, so this stays near the line. Leaned on the protagonist axis. One source, so medium.

Positives: it opens on one concrete situation (the pizza deliverer), moves fast and is dense with ideas about language, information and virtual space. Deductions: the central conceit retells ancient religion (Asherah, Enki, nam-shub, Pentecostalism) as an information virus and plays it as satire, and religion played for ridicule is disliked outright (Ja, robot 55); the Sumerian deities are real names but used as history-as-virus, not worship, so I grade it as a faith risk and not an occult veto (resemblance counted, low severity). Crude sexual references and a 15-year-old courier in harassment scenes add the sexual-content cost (Ready Player One 55 is the nearest kind). The protagonist is a comic hero with little interiority. Ideas and momentum carry it.

One concrete opening, a psychologist arriving at a station in disarray, and an idea that stays: contact with an intelligence that cannot be understood, and what its visitors reveal about the people they are made from. Kelvin wants to understand and has his own guilt to face, a lead with an inner life, and the motives-over-action emphasis fits what Speaker for the Dead at 90 did. Risks: long stretches of invented scholarship and description with little story, and the central question is deliberately never answered, which is a risk and not a lift. The visitor relationship is romantic, not a sexual plot. No occult rite.

After a pandemic ends the old world, a travelling troupe plays Shakespeare to scattered settlements, and the book keeps tying the survivors back to a famous actor who died on stage as it began. One concrete opening, and what stays behind is nameable: what in a civilisation is worth carrying on (art, memory), reasoned through character motives. Deductions: it moves between timelines and several people, so POV load and a restless structure are the main risk, and one reviewer found it dull; the reader said of Pocitani hvezd 85 that thought-provoking premises can still leave him without drive to continue. Bleakness is graded mildly. A prophet-led cult is a faith thread, serious in treatment rather than satire. The actor's marriages are backstory, not the premise, but I did not verify framing. Leaned on ideas and motives, not worldbuilding.

t: Stroje jako ja a lide jako vy (Machines Like Me)
why: The idea is precise and the book is its consequences: an android that cannot lie meets the white lies human relationships run on, the kind of examined-what-is-true thinking Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and Project Hail Mary 92 reward. The deductions are real. Charlie is a drifting, petty narrator, so the lead is a risk on rootability as in Ballad 65; reviewers say the philosophical passages drag, which is the thin-story-over-pages cost; there is a love triangle with sex and a rape backstory, volume uncertain. Infidelity does not apply: Charlie and Miranda are unmarried and unengaged, so the triangle is ordinary relationship drama, and it is not a sex plot. Leaned on ideas alone since the lead is thin, per the Artemis 69 lesson.

t: Svaty Leibowitz a vladkyne divokych koni (Saint Leibowitz and the Wild Horse Woman)
why: A sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log (Catching Fire 83, Hitchhiker's sequels 70). Reviewers describe it as lesser in scope than its predecessor, with politics and war councils that drag, and the central thread is a monk's crisis of faith between his vows and a nomad goddess, so faith is the subject rather than a thread. The positive case is a lead who wants something and a world with real ideas about church and empire. It was finished by another writer from an unfinished draft, a fact reviewers raise. The nomad goddess visions could read as occult; not established in the sources used, so left as a risk. Leaned on ideas.

Gate 4 exit on one source. The idea is real (a man who sees exactly one year ahead, and what that does to free will), but the lead is a carnival fortune teller who rises into a demagogue and is trapped by his own foresight, an arc of sliding into authoritarian cynicism with nobody to root for, the Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes at 65 failure, and the subplots add several strands. Seer power is a mutation, not a rite, but resemblance to divination was not examined in a C-low exit.

t: Tovarna na Absolutno (The Absolute at Large)
why: The idea is real and nameable: an engine that burns matter releases God, as an uncontrolled spiritual essence, into the world, and every faith and nation reads it its own way. But the whole thing is satire of religion and religious war (reviewers name the modern church, idolatry and religious fanaticism as targets), and religion played for ridicule is the one satire this reader marks down, anchored by Ja, robot 55, unlike political satire (Animal Farm 78). Episodic, no lead to root for, and Czech readers call the development uneven after a good initial idea. Leaned on axis:faith as the deduction and axis:ideas as the lift. Occult not found: the Absolute is a physics-like device, not an invoked rite.

An ice-hauler crew sent after a moon that has left its orbit is a hard-SF set-up with an unknown the crew must explore under real pressure, and the central captain-versus-chief-engineer conflict is a motives-driven rift, which is the axis that tops Mockingjay 91. Reviewers split on the characters (some call them dire), the ideas and science are consistently praised, and the book is open-ended with no sequel, so discovery without a full answer is a risk rather than a lift. Thin leads outrank good worldbuilding in this log (Artemis 69), so the number is held in the 70s at most. Leaned on ideas and motives; a far-future frame story is a minor opening note.

Gate 4 exit on one source. The subject is Gnostic theology itself, a mystical visionary working out God and reality, which is the theology-as-subject the reader avoids; the lead is a mentally unstable seeker with an attempted suicide and failed rescues, little plot by reviewers' account, and an experience that can be read as both belief and delusion. The idea of a Gnostic cosmos is nameable, so it stays in the default band. Occult unexamined: real religious and Gnostic sources are the risk that this exit leaves open.

t: Valka s Mloky (War with the Newts)
why: The idea is nameable and carried through: an intelligent animal species is taught tools and traded as cheap labour, and the consequences of that exploitation are followed to a war. Political and social satire costs nothing in this log (Animal Farm 78), and an allegory with a clear idea cleared the line (Labyrint sveta 70). Held below the top of the A band because there is no single lead (the book moves between a captain, a doorman, reports and newspaper clippings), the reader wants a protagonist to root for, and reviewers call the opening slow. Leaned on axis:ideas, not on character, since the characters are not what the book is built from. Opening starts on one concrete situation (a captain and the newts off an island), so no opening bar; no occult found.

A sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's sequels 83 to 70, Catching Fire 83 and Ender's Shadow 79 all landed lower. The lead's arc and the station plot are assumed, not restated, so the reader enters a story already underway, which is the shape-two risk for a book picked up cold. Case for it: the central idea (identity of a mind in one body, and what justice means for an empire built on annexing people) is carried through to its resolution, and the blurb points to motives and a station crisis rather than set-piece action, the axis that tops the log. Held to the mid-70s at best on the sequel penalty.

The idea is strong and nameable: a mind once spread across a warship and thousands of bodies reduced to one body, and what identity and loyalty mean then. Breq's want is clear (finish her mission after a betrayal) and she is interesting, with motives driving the page time, the axis that tops the log (Mockingjay 91). A revenge quest with an unknown to uncover is close to what Licanius 96 rewarded. Deductions: reviewers widely report a disorienting opening (two timelines and an all-feminine pronoun convention with unfamiliar terms), which is a shape-two opening risk and mitigable by knowing the premise first; the universal 'she' is not a competence contrast so sex-portrayal is expected to be none. Occult not found in sources checked (Radch religion appears as an imperial custom). Leaned on ideas and protagonist; opening held as the risk.

The slowing Earth is a backdrop for an eleven-year-old's adolescence, not a world whose consequences are followed, and reviewers say the cause is unexplained and the physics ignored (Mortal Engines 55 was dropped on exactly that kind of logic). A meandering, quiet story spread over many pages with a child narrator and steady melancholy costs on density, life-phase and bleakness, though a pleasant, lyrical voice earns something. Leaned on worldbuilding: the number is carried by how much the premise is followed through, which is thin. Exited at the cheap gate; occult unexamined.

The lead, Maris, wants one thing, to fly, and the book is what that want costs her and what she does with it; motives and a lead worth rooting for are the axes that top Mockingjay 91 and Red Rising 95. A world with one scarce, inherited resource (the salvaged wings) behaves as declared, and a fix-up that follows one life lets each part pay for the one before. Reviewers praise how she grows into a leader. The idea is tradition against merit, followed over her life. Held below the top: three linked novellas across decades may lose pull in the third part, flying is a smaller part than expected, and the later part turns to disputes and losses. Leaned on protagonist and motives, not on worldbuilding, since Artemis 69 shows a thin lead outweighs a good world.

A man who ages in centuries and a society that sells him a new life every eight years: the idea (living in the present versus being trapped by memory and grief) is nameable and gets worked through, which is what holds this above thin books in the 60s. Tom has an interior life, a fault to overcome (he is bound to his past) and a clear want, so the lead is both interesting and worth rooting for in the way Ender's Game 87 was. Deductions: reviewers split on the abrupt flashbacks mid-scene, which is the reader's confusing-opening risk, and some call it thoughtful but thin, a risk on how much story fills the pages. The accused-witch episode is history shown from the victim's side, not occult practice. Leaned on ideas and protagonist; the timeline structure is a risk, so the range is wide and confidence medium.

A civilisation on the verge of leaving the physical universe, a murdered high command and a retired officer pulled into it is a strong frame, and the Minds are praised as the best characters. Against that: reviewers say the lead is a witness without agency who matters because she once knew someone (Artemis 69 shows a thin lead outranks good worldbuilding), threads meander to unsatisfying ends, and the religious-ascension material is read as a gentle send-up of rapture tropes, which this reader dislikes when played for ridicule (Ja, robot 55). Opening reads as intriguing rather than confusing in reviews, but the book is dense with asides and long sentences. Leaned on ideas and worldbuilding; the lead and religion treatment could drag it below the range.

The open question is exactly the one Project Hail Mary at 92 rewarded: a lead who does not understand his world, a need to find out (small glitches grow into danger), and an outcome open until an answer arrives that fits what came before. Ragle Gumm is an ordinary man with his own past as the unknown, so the lift is taken once under discovery and not again under the protagonist. Ideas about what a person is when his reality is manufactured add the second pillar. Risks: a quiet, domestic start with several relatives and neighbours to place. No occult found.

Stopped at the C-low gate on one source. An 11-story collection, and the log's only collection, Ja robot 55, shows how one is read: from the front, put down on the weakest early story, never averaged. The ideas in the best-known pieces are real and nameable, which is why the number is not lower, but short idea-driven prose only suspends character penalties and adds nothing, and the first story of Ja robot failed on a lead nobody could root for. The table of contents varies between editions, so I cannot say which stories open this Czech printing. Occult unexamined at this exit; keep axis:occult in deps.

A real idea with consequences argued at length: a starship crew must build a conscious machine to survive, and nobody knows what consciousness is. The reader scored the same kind of thing high in Project Hail Mary 92 and Speaker for the Dead 90. Held down because reviewers call it one of the author's densest books, clumsy and early, with POV changing many times on a page and intrigue over withheld secrets, which sits close to the confusing-opening bar. The artificial mind develops a faith and the book argues about making God, a serious treatment but a heavy thread. Crew are expendable clones, so rooting is harder. Leaned on axis:ideas; opening and multi-pov in risks. No staged rite found.

t: Vzpominka zvana Rise (A Memory Called Empire)
why: A newcomer in an unfamiliar empire with a copy of a dead man's memories in her head, fifteen years out of date: identity and what an empire does to a culture it absorbs are real ideas, and the imago is an implant operated like technology, not a rite. Close in spirit to recovering a past in Licanius 93. Two things pull it down. Reviewers disagree whether it is at core a murder mystery; who killed him is not the main satisfaction (politics and identity are), so this is a flag, not a veto, but it sits near the detective bar. And the lead has a slow-burn relationship with another woman, a thread among others, the middle of the graded range and not premise level, as in Caropisci 67. Leaned on ideas and worldbuilding.

A grisly satire of debt where a repo man cannot pay for his own artificial heart has a simple, dated idea, and reviewers call the worldbuilding light and the structure a back-and-forth through time with a first half mostly backstory. The lead is a repossessor of organs, a hard man to root for (Ballad 65 on a lead who is hard to back), and crass scenes plus repeated material about his ex-wives suggest a sexual-content cost (Artemis 69, Ready Player One 55) and possibly a marriage thread I did not examine. Exited at the cheap gate; occult unexamined.

Memory as identity and a time mechanism whose consequences are followed through is the same kind of foreknowledge-and-loops material that tops the log (the Licanius volumes 92-96), and reviewers single out the pace as never slipping, which is the Hunger Games 89 strength. Deductions: reviewers call the characters serviceable vehicles for the concept and the ending hand-wavy, and a declared mechanism adds obligation rather than credit (Ja, robot 55), so the number is held below the Licanius level. Two lines of story to track (a cop and a scientist) is a small multi-POV exposure, not a confusing opening. Leaned on axis:ideas and momentum rather than the leads, because the lead evidence is thin; no occult element found, inferred from blurb and reviews rather than a text source.

Stopped at the C-low gate on one source. The book is a war and artefact-hunt story, with a noir voice rather than a whodunit (so the detective filter does not fire here), and the idea of consciousness stored and re-sleeved is nameable. But the number rides on a mercenary lead whom reviewers call brutal and unlikeable, with explicit sexuality and violence in the mix: the not-rootable lead (Ballad 65) and the volume and crudeness costs (Ready Player One 55, Artemis 69). Leaned on protagonist. Occult unexamined at this exit; keep axis:occult in deps.

A parallel-world Neanderthal society meeting ours gives a rich contrast-of-cultures idea, and reviewers say this book is chiefly about the relationship between a Neanderthal physicist and a human geneticist, with a justice-system thread on how his world would treat the crime she suffered. Motives and ideas carry it. Held down because it is a sequel that cannot be read without the lead and premise already in hand, and sequels are not safe bets in this log (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70); because the focus on a love story is a sexual-relationship question to grade, with a rape subplot and a Neanderthal social order reportedly built on sex-segregation and bonded same-sex pairs; and because Mary's religious faith is a recurring debate topic, a thread to grade (serious treatment, so not the satire problem of Ja robot 55). Infidelity status is unverified: I did not establish whether either lead is bonded to someone else.

Exited at C: the idea is nameable (what remains of a person when authority erases memory), but reviewers report that no explanation is ever given for the island's rules, that the narrator is passive and accepts them, and that the ending resolves nothing. A passive lead and a withheld answer are the Metamorphosis 58 pattern, and an unexplained rule system is the self-consistency bar this reader checks (Mortal Engines 55). Occult status unexamined at this exit; axis:occult stays in deps. Leaned on worldbuilding, the axis I doubt.

Exited at C: a competent young-adult war survival story with a rootable lead in Mahlia and a distinctive augmented soldier, but no worked-out idea I would defend as the draw, and sustained bleakness (reviewers call it the author's darkest, with child soldiers). Violence is not an objection; bleakness is a mild one. Occult status was not examined at this exit; axis:occult stays in deps. Leaned on the lead because her warmth against the grim setting is what carries the number.

t: Pustina zvana mir (A Desolation Called Peace)
why: First contact with aliens who do not understand individual personhood, approached through language and negotiation: a nameable idea and an unknown the leads must work out. But a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's 83 to 70, Catching Fire 83 after The Hunger Games 89. It assumes its lead, the empire and the imago from earlier in the series, so it cannot be read cold. It adds several viewpoints (reviewers name three new ones plus alien interludes); the two leads' relationship is restarted and developed as a main thread, the middle of the graded range as in Caropisci 67; and some reviewers found the alien mystery telegraphed. Leaned on ideas only.

Told almost entirely as interview transcripts with an unnamed interviewer, so what characters want and why is filtered and recounted after the fact, which is the reverse of the interiority this reader rewards (Red Rising 95, Mockingjay 91). Reviewers cite emotional distance, jargon monologues and recounted action, and a love triangle matters to the story. There is a nameable idea (a buried alien machine) but the central mystery is left unanswered at the end of this book, so I would list axis:ideas under risks and exit at the cheap gate. Occult unexamined at one source.

t: Za modrym horizontem udalosti (Beyond the Blue Event Horizon)
why: The idea carries on: a huge alien food factory and a device that reaches into human minds, with the physics laid out. But it is a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70, Speaker for the Dead 90 to Ender saga 81), and reviewers say it trades the character study for setting and info-dumps. The lead is a guilt-ridden, wealthy man whose own inner life is no longer the point. Leaned on axis:ideas and worldbuilding; opening and sequels in risks because a start that leans on prior events could be unclear. No staged rite found.

The ecological idea is plain (an overcrowded world kills the insects, and a hive intelligence answers back) but reviewers call the book the weakest of the author's, with flat, stereotyped characters, dated sexism, a stalling middle and an abrupt end. Leaned on axis:protagonist: no lead with a flaw to overcome has been named. Stopped at the cheap gate on one source; occult unexamined.

Five loosely linked parts across about nine hundred pages, one of them a catalogue of murdered women told like police files. Reviewers note the main threads are left unresolved, which is an answer withheld, and the detective element is a frame rather than the satisfaction, so it is not the detective veto. Long and dense, multi-strand, with sustained bleakness and sexual content. The ideas are real but spread thin over the length, and the log shows no appetite for fragmentary work (Unfinished Tales 69). Carried by axis:density; occult and infidelity not examined at this exit.

Historical novel on a real murder case. The detective signal is not a veto: the book is a psychiatric portrait whose central question (guilt) is left open, and an answer withheld is a cost. The lead is a servant narrating her life, largely acted upon, which is where Oliver Twist 57 landed. Occult is only partly examined: the climax stages a hypnotic trance in which a dead friend's voice appears to take over, read by spectators as possession and by doctors as a split personality, and the book never settles it. Not rejected because the supernatural reading is one disputed interpretation rather than a rite the book endorses, but it is the main collapse risk. Carried by axis:protagonist.

Literary fiction, one source. The book is a black satire of two men, a composer and an editor, who are both shown as heartless and hypocritical; reviewers say many readers disliked the unlikeable characters and the ending. That is the Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 failure, no one to root for, with a downward direction of travel. The euthanasia pact is a nameable idea but a reviewer says it is not what the book revolves around. A dead woman's former lovers drive the setup; affairs are backstory, not premise. Number rests on the protagonist; occult not examined and kept in deps.

A historical novel with real ideas (court and Church exploiting the people who build their monuments) and a love story at its centre. But it carries Saramago's long unbroken paragraphs with no quotation marks, heavy description and digression, a heavy anticlerical satire of Church and king that this reader marks down when religion is played for ridicule (I, Robot 55), and a visionary heroine who sees inside people and gathers human wills to power a flying machine, which resembles an occult seer closely enough that it cannot be cleared unchecked. Stopped at one source. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

t: Bezbarvy Cukuru Tazaki a jeho leta putovani (Colorless Tsukuru Tazaki and His Years of Pilgrimage)
why: The positive case is motives: a man cut off by his closest friends sets out years later to learn why, and each friend's answer is a conversation about what people wanted and hid. One lead, one concrete starting situation. Discovery lifts it only partly: the unknown is his own past and the need is real, but reviewers agree that a friend's murder, her accuser's motive and one disappearance are never resolved, so the answer does not fit everything before it. Costs: the lead begins withdrawn after the loss, with thoughts of suicide in the blurb (mild bleakness), and the novel is reported to carry dream sequences with erotic content that volume and explicitness were not measured on; whether any same-sex element rises above a dream was not checked. The inquiry into a friend's death is a strand, not the book's satisfaction. Motives and protagonist carry the number.

t: Carodejka z Florencie (The Enchantress of Florence)
why: A historical-fantasy literary novel, one source. The idea is nameable (East and West mixing, a story told to a ruler that may or may not be true), but the Historical Novel Society says the story ultimately amounts to little and that the humour too often becomes schoolboy sexual fantasy, which touches both volume and crudeness, the Ready Player One 55 failure. BookBrowse says the frequent non-linear sections undermine the clearer narrative, so the opening risk is live. The enchantress has reputed powers of sorcery and the court holds an imaginary queen, a resemblance to real practice that is unexamined here and kept as a live risk. Number rests on the thin idea.

A short literary novella, one source. The idea is nameable (rationalism against mystical conviction, read through a couple who split over one encounter), but the narrator who reconstructs his in-laws' story is an observer rather than a lead with a want. Faith is the subject of the argument between husband and wife, not a thread, and one critic found the closing section inconsistent with the collage of verdicts before it. Short idea-driven form suspends character penalties but adds nothing. Occult not examined at this exit (the title encounter is framed as a spiritual event) and kept in deps.

t: Cesta do hlubin noci (Journey to the End of the Night)
why: A picaresque through the war, colonial Africa, America and Paris, with a vivid, cynical narrator and one nameable idea: no belief survives contact with war and poverty. But Bardamu is a misanthrope who wants nothing beyond getting through, so there is no one to root for (Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65, Oliver Twist 57), the whole book is bleak, and the coarse register reaches the sexual references, where crudeness cost Artemis 69. Stopped at one source. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

Exited at the below-the-line gate, stopping early so a fuller read is still open. The idea is real and nameable: a boy who treats the camps as a new reality to adapt to, so that survival has nothing to do with fate. Against it, the narrator is a naive teenager with a flat, dispassionate voice and the camp setting is unrelieved, the shape that sank the Diary of a Young Girl 40 although this is a novel. Leaned on ideas. Occult not examined at this gate.

t: Cosi divneho v me hlave, aneb, Zivot, dobrodruzstvi a sny prodavace bozy Mevluta Karatase a jeho pratel jakoz i obrazek zivota v Istanbulu mezi lety 1969 a 2012, zachyceny ocima rady lidi (A Strangeness in My Mind)
why: Literary fiction on a large scale: forty years of a street vendor's life in Istanbul, narrated by an omniscient voice interrupted by many relatives who contradict each other. The book needs a family tree and an index of characters, which says how many lines a reader tracks, and reviewers report the elopement thread is dropped for two hundred pages and that the adolescent years drag. Mevlut is an everyman, which is not a fault in itself, so the lean is the protagonist, with the city's change as the theme, but a thin story over many pages is the density penalty. Occult not examined at this exit.

A sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's 83 to 70. Reviewers say the plot retells and relies on an older story and wonder whether it works for a reader who has not read it, the no-context opening shape that is only mitigable by reading up first. The retired narrator is called back to account for an old operation, an inquiry-shaped plot to be flagged rather than a veto. The idea, what a service owes the people it used, is real. The sequels axis carries the number. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

A coming-of-age with a nameable idea, individuation, and a mentor who reinterprets old stories. Against it: the lead is a boy acted upon for much of the book, the book is a spiritual-psychological argument rather than a plot, and it builds on Abraxas, a real gnostic deity, with a mentor who interprets dreams. If the book treats that as worship rather than symbol, the occult Source test would veto it, and that is the live risk. Faith as the subject rather than a thread also costs. Ideas carry the number. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

A Dickens retelling in Appalachia with a strong first-person voice and a real idea, that the opioid epidemic was a system failure and not a personal one. But Demon spends most of the book acted upon by foster homes, school and addiction, the Oliver Twist 57 shape, and reviewers say it can feel relentless, which hits bleakness hard. Sexual content with teenagers and drug use is graded and unexamined. The voice is why it does not sit lower. Stopped at one source. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

A long magic-realist literary novel, one source. The idea is nameable (one boy's life as the history of independent India), and the opening is an iconic single-narrator hook, but it moves back to a grandfather's story before the narrator is born, and reviewers list dense style, non-linear plot and a crowd of characters. Several risks are live: fortune-telling and telepathy might resemble real practice, not settled at this exit, plus religion and politics played for satire, which the Ja, robot 55 note says he dislikes where the object is religion. Number rests on the idea, which is strong but not worked out like a system. Unexamined occult status carried in deps.

t: Dobreho cloveka tezko najdes (A Good Man Is Hard to Find)
why: Exited at the below-the-line gate on form: literary fiction in story form, where the log reads a collection from the front and puts it down on the weakest early stories (Ja, robot 55). Positive case: each story turns on a nameable idea about grace arriving through violence. Against it, the faith content is the subject of the stories and the endings are bleak. Leaned on ideas. Occult not examined at this gate.

A literary short-story collection, which is the Ja, robot 55 exposure: read from the front and put down on the weakest early story, so the range cannot be set by the most canonical pieces. No single idea to lean on across a collection, so the idea axis carries a modest number; the short form suspends character penalties but adds no credit. Quiet domestic realism with the hidden-relationship and infidelity themes this author returns to often, graded as subplot or incidental, never premise. Thin sources were available for this title; the range rests on the author's pattern and the catalogue annotation. Occult not examined at this exit and kept in deps.

Exited at the below-the-line gate. Positive case: a family chronicle where what each generation wants from marriage and from itself is the whole book. Against it, the prose is lyrical, repetitive description with little story, a main character's relationship with a woman teacher is a heavy graded thread, and sexual relationships fill much of the later part. Density and the same-sex thread together sit under the propose line. Leaned on motives. Occult not examined at this gate.

A 213-page satire: a scholar finds a scroll that undermines Christianity, and the book skewers both publishing and the faith's reaction. Religion played for satire is disliked outright (Ja, robot 55), and the hook is exactly that treatment, not a serious weighing of belief. The lead is an egotist, which leaves rootability in doubt; reviews call the second half predictable. The idea itself is nameable, which is why this sits at the line rather than below it. Occult unexamined at this exit; it also retells the Prometheus myth.

Gothic horror in collection form with no single idea; narrators are unstable and hard to root for and the mood is sustained dread, which is the unrootable-lead objection that opened Ja, robot 55, with mild bleakness besides. Collections are read from the front. Poe's mix includes mesmerism and Ligeia-type tales, so the occult filter is unexamined at this exit, and the Dupin stories sit at the detective filter. Havran 40 was a verse and occult case, not a verdict on his prose. A slimmer bilingual selection.

A composer narrator who loves from the sidelines and loses the woman to his friend: unrequited and resigned, a lead acted upon rather than acting, which cost Oliver Twist 57 and The Metamorphosis 58. The idea, that art grows out of suffering, is nameable but not tested hard. Summaries describe an arc ending in peaceful resignation, so little drive. The friend's marriage is reported as ill-matched; whether infidelity occurs was not examined. The volume also carries a set of stories. Protagonist carries the number. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

Exited at the below-the-line gate. Positive case: a strong, nameable idea about guilt, dignity and a changing South Africa. Against it, the lead pressures a student into sex in the opening section, a rootability problem close to the one that sank Ballad 65, and a violent assault comes later. The affair is not within a marriage and the plot is the aftermath, not the sex, so no filter fires. Leaned on ideas. Occult not examined at this gate.

t: Henderson, kral deste (Henderson the Rain King)
why: A comic first-person quest: a restless millionaire goes to Africa because an inner voice keeps saying 'I want', and the book is about what he actually wants. The voice is the draw, a flawed but likeable lead in the Saturnin 78 line of voice over idea. But the second half stages invented-tribe rain rites and a king's lion-spirit belief that are central to what happens to him, a graded occult cost left unexamined here, and the story is thin and picaresque. Stopped at one source.

t: Hluk a vrava (The Sound and the Fury)
why: Four narrators with unmistakably different minds, and a family's decline as the thing left behind. But the book opens in the mind of a disabled man who does not separate past from present, jumping between about sixteen moments with no markers; that is shape two of the opening filter (no context to read it), mitigable by reading the family first. It is also bleak, with no one to root for among the Compsons, and Caddy's sexual history drives the decline. Leaned on axis:character-differentiation.

A botched political kidnapping in Argentina has a nameable idea (what a man owes to people he is tangled with by accident), but Plarr's affair with the consul's wife is a major thread that gives the characters their shape and the hut confrontation its charge. I read it as a subplot and not the premise, because the kidnapping drives the plot, and I could not settle that from the one source I used, so the doubt is stated here. A neutral infidelity subplot with a sexual thread beside it, a defrocked-priest strand of faith and a bleak ending put the number below the line. Leaned on axis:ideas; occult not examined (exit at C).

A memoir of a city and a childhood, organised as a cabinet of curiosities, not a story: family memories, history and long descriptions of apartments and interiors. The memoir form earns nothing by itself (Diary of a Young Girl 40 against Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91), and what earns there is weighing what is true, which this is not. Huzun, a collective melancholy, is the nameable idea, but the shape is description with little story and sustained mild bleakness, so the number is held under the line. Occult not examined.

The idea holds and can be named in a phrase: who is allowed to remember German victims, and what happens when the subject is left to others. Against that, the narrator is a reporter who moves back and forth between the ship's history, his mother and his estranged son, and reviewers say the characters are unappealing and the structure keeps readers at arm's length. A real idea with a thin, distant lead lands just under the line, as Oliver Twist 57 did on a lead who is acted upon. Ideas carry the number. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

t: Jama a kyvadlo & jine povidky (The Pit and the Pendulum and Other Tales)
why: Gothic horror in collection form with no single idea; narrators are unstable and hard to root for and the mood is sustained dread, which is the unrootable-lead objection that opened Ja, robot 55, with mild bleakness besides. Collections are read from the front. Poe's mix includes mesmerism and Ligeia-type tales, so the occult filter is unexamined at this exit, and the Dupin stories sit at the detective filter. Havran 40 was a verse and occult case, not a verdict on his prose. Twenty-seven stories in a single selection.

t: Jeden den Ivana Denisovice a jine povidky (One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich and other stories)
why: Literary fiction in a story collection, so it exits at C. The idea is nameable (what a person keeps of himself under total deprivation) and Shukhov is a lead to root for, but a collection is read from the front and put down on its weakest early piece, as with Ja, robot 55, and the sustained bleakness is a mild cost (1984 60). Number is carried by axis:ideas; occult not examined at this exit.

t: Jeden den Ivana Denisovice a jine prozy (One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich and other prose)
why: Literary fiction in a collection, so it exits at C. The idea holds (dignity kept under deprivation) and the lead is rootable, but a collection is judged on its weakest early piece (Ja, robot 55) and the bleakness is a mild cost (1984 60). Carried by axis:ideas; occult not examined at this exit.

A memoir of years under police protection after a death sentence for a novel. The positive case is that it examines what actually happened and shows how a hunted man and a threatened community lived, the same two things that carried Seeking Allah 91 and Son of Hamas 75, and the Boston Globe calls the fatwa years gripping and often hilarious. Cautions: the memoir form earns nothing by itself (Anne Frank 40 shows the other outcome), it is long and covers his whole life, the third-person conceit divides critics, and marriages and relationships may enter the telling at incidental to subplot level (not verified from sources). The signal 'detective' is police protection, not a mystery. Faith is the subject of the conflict but from a free-speech angle, not theology. Occult not an issue. Opening structure not sourced.

t: Kaddis za nenarozene dite (Kaddish for a Child Not Born)
why: Exited at the below-the-line gate. A single bitter monologue with almost no plot, no chapters and a repeated refusal as its refrain; the idea (a life offered as a kaddish for a child never born) is nameable, but there is little for the reader's weight on what characters do and want, and density and bleakness stack. Leaned on ideas. Occult not examined at this gate.

t: Kapitan a nepritel (The Captain and the Enemy)
why: A volume of three novellas and long stories, so a collection read from the front with no single idea to lean on. The story built on a post-war Vienna investigation is mystery-shaped, flagged and not vetoed. The author's strength is flawed characters in moral trouble. Leaned on axis:protagonist; occult not examined (exit at C).

Exited at the below-the-line gate. Positive case: a father-and-son story with a nameable idea, the quiet sacrifices of a teacher as his son sees them, mirrored in myth. Against it, the narration alternates between realism and Greek myth, so the opening may confuse, and density is a concern. Gods appear as a literary parallel and are not worshipped, so occult is a flag only. Leaned on ideas. Opening structure was not established.

Literary fiction, a novel, so no automatic exit; I exit at C because the childhood strand has a lead who is largely acted upon (Oliver Twist 57) in a mostly interior, memory-driven plot, and the bullying is sustained bleakness. Infidelity is a graded subplot, not the premise: the lead takes up with a teacher who is seeing other students and later divorces a husband who keeps having affairs, framed as damaging, so it costs a few points rather than the neutral-subplot level. The idea (how girlhood cruelty shapes a woman) is nameable. Carried by axis:protagonist; occult not examined.

A large-cast novel of ideas: two families and their circle in 1920s London, many threads running at once, the Guards! Guards! 30 shape of several plot lines to track with no single concrete situation to be invested in. Affairs run through several threads, treated neutrally, and the sex-obsessed characters add a graded cost. A murder thread is present but is not the point of the book. The idea of the novel, characters as counterpoint voices, is real but does not offset the opening. Stopped at one source, so the opening and the infidelity prominence are inferred, not read.

t: Krejci z Panamy (The Tailor of Panama)
why: The idea is worked through: a tailor blackmailed into spying invents intelligence, the invention is passed up the chain and reaches the point of an invasion, so one lie's consequences are the book. Harry Pendel is a flawed, sympathetic liar with a hidden past, a lead with something to overcome. Reviewers call it darkly comic. Costs: the corrupt officer's backstory is a compromising affair, so sexual content and an infidelity thread at incidental level are possible and were not read; the satire is cynical about the powerful. Ideas and protagonist carry the number.

t: Kulicka a jine povidky (Boule de Suif and Other Stories)
why: Literary fiction in collection form: a selection built around the title novella of a prostitute travelling through the Franco-Prussian war, which has a real idea (respectable hypocrisy) but is a single piece, and the rest has no shared idea. Collections are read from the front and put down on weak early pieces (Ja, robot 55). Maupassant is cynical about peasants and the bourgeoisie and most of these tales treat love and adultery, so infidelity and sexual content are open risks. Occult unexamined at this exit.

t: Laska dobre zeny (The Love of a Good Woman)
why: A literary short-story collection, which is the Ja, robot 55 exposure: read from the front and put down on the weakest early story, so the range cannot be set by the most canonical pieces. No single idea to lean on across a collection, so the idea axis carries a modest number; the short form suspends character penalties but adds no credit. Quiet domestic realism with the hidden-relationship and infidelity themes this author returns to often, graded as subplot or incidental, never premise. The long title novella is shaped around a drowned optometrist and what a dying woman may know, a mystery-shaped piece within an eligible book; flagged, not a veto. Occult not examined at this exit and kept in deps.

t: Lionel Aspo (Lionel Asbo: State of England)
why: Exited at the below-the-line gate. Positive case: the nephew Des is a decent, intelligent lead worth rooting for, and the satire of tabloid England is a nameable idea. Against it, the book runs on a violent, unrootable uncle and a crude comic register with a sexual thread (Des and his grandmother) that costs on crudeness as Artemis 69 did, and reviewers report little real plot. Leaned on the protagonist axis, because Des carries the book the way a good lead decided Sunrise on the Reaping over Ballad. Occult not examined at this gate.

The idea is nameable: a society anaesthetised against what is done in its name, shown through a pupil who plans to burn his dachshund in public. But the narration is a choppy, cubist jump between the dentist's chair and the classroom, readers call it hard to get used to and disjointed, and the lead is a teacher described as tragicomic while the pupil's protest is hard to root for. A lead who is acted upon is the same risk that cut Oliver Twist to 57. Protagonist carries the number. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

A chess prodigy whose obsession swallows his life is a nameable idea and the inner life is the whole book, which the reader values (Red Rising 95). But Luzhin is a socially helpless, passive man sliding toward collapse, the same lead shape that cost Promena 58, and the arc is bleak. The positive case is real, so it sits just under the line rather than far below. Leaned on axis:protagonist; occult not examined (exit at C). The one source was a page on a film adaptation of the book, hence medium confidence.

t: Malir pomijiveho sveta (An Artist of the Floating World)
why: One narrator and one concrete starting situation (an old painter, his house, his younger daughter's marriage talks), so the opening is clear. The book is almost entirely what a man wants to believe about himself and what he did, which is the motives axis that tops the log (Mockingjay 91, Speaker for the Dead 90), and it holds an idea he must face: an artist's responsibility for the cause he served. The direction of travel is toward honesty about the past, the arc the Licanius 96 lead was liked for, not a slide into evil. Capped by a quiet, slow telling and a lead who is partly self-deceiving (Oliver Twist 57 shows what a passive lead costs). No occult; the marriage talks are an arranged match, not infidelity. Carried by ideas and motives; momentum and protagonist are the collapse risks.

A Blitz-era spy thriller whose lead carries guilt for a mercy killing and is pulled into a Nazi cell through a charity-fete cake. The pull is the lead's inner state and the pace. Two costs: a fortune-teller at the fete and a staged seance are plot devices, both a fake by the spies, and I could not settle from one source whether the reader would treat that as occult by resemblance, so it is unexamined here; and once he is accused of a murder it takes on investigation shape. Leaned on axis:protagonist.

Literary fiction novel, so the exit is at the C line on one source. The idea is nameable (fiction as Cold War propaganda, a handler deceiving the writer she loves), but reviewers call it a cynical book about the art of fiction and say the narrator has no compelling voice. Serena is passive, carried by lovers and by MI5, which is the Oliver Twist 57 failure mode for a lead who is acted upon. Several affairs and sex scenes are on the page at modest volume; none is the plot. Number rests on the idea holding up; occult not examined at this exit and kept in deps.

t: Moc a slava (The Power and the Glory)
why: A hunted whisky priest, the last in a Mexican state that has outlawed the church, is a flawed man who knows it, and his direction of travel is toward doing the right thing at cost, the arc the reader rooted for. What he wants and why fills the book, set against a lieutenant sincere in his own faith in the state, a pairing that leaves ideas behind about worth and ideology. Risks: Catholic faith is the subject and not only a thread, bleakness runs throughout, and he has a child from a past lapse. Leaned on axis:protagonist and axis:motives; occult is not engaged since this is Christian devotion and not a rite. The opening was not sourced, so confidence is medium.

A collection of domestic stories about marriages and relationships with no single idea to hold them, so axis:ideas carries a low number, and the form suspends the character rules without adding anything. Several stories turn on a spouse's infidelity (title story, Salt Garden, Uglypuss), which this reader grades heavily. A collection is read from the front and dropped on its weakest early piece (Ja, robot 55). Occult not examined at this exit.

Exited at the below-the-line gate. The idea is nameable (a man whose attempt to deny faith mirrors it), but belief is the entire subject, not a thread inside a story, and the treatment is grotesque and close to satire of preachers, the combination Ja, robot 55 was abandoned partly for. Hazel is hard to root for and the book is bleak. Leaned on the faith axis. Occult not examined at this gate; a minor character with a mild psychic gift is noted for later.

t: Nas clovek v Havane (Our Man in Havana)
why: The annotation calls it a detective story, but it is a spy comedy with no whodunnit: the reader knows who is lying from the start. The idea is carried through its consequences: a vacuum-cleaner salesman invents agents for his daughter's sake, and an intelligence service that believes him is forced to act on the lies until they start to come true. Wormold is a decent, ordinary man and a devoted father, easy to root for, and the comic register with a serious turn sits with Hitchhiker's Guide 83 and Saturnin 78. Risk: the comedy turns tragic and a friend is killed. Leaned on axis:ideas and axis:protagonist. Confidence is medium because the opening is not sourced.

Exited at the below-the-line gate. Positive case: a nameable idea, what the camps and a shared love do to two brothers across fifty years, in a short novel. Against it, the gulag setting is relentlessly bleak, and the narrator is a hard man who tells of raping his way through Germany, which puts rootability in doubt as it did for Ballad 65. Leaned on ideas; bleakness is only a mild discount in this log so it stays a risk rather than the carrier. Occult not examined at this gate.

t: Nekdy proste prsi (Some Rain Must Fall and Other Stories)
why: Literary fiction and a collection of about fifteen stories, so two penalties compound: a collection has no single idea to lean on and is read from the front, stopping on the weakest early piece as in Ja, robot 55. Some stories are inventive (a god finding Earth in a dump), and the title story is about a substitute teacher after a tragedy, but the mix includes love in a sex shop and critical moments of ordinary lives, so sexual content and bleakness are open risks. Occult not examined at this exit.

A 535-page novel built on dream logic: a pianist arrives in an unnamed city for a concert he cannot remember agreeing to, underground passages and walls appear as needed, and reviewers describe circular conversations and little forward motion with a passive, self-absorbed lead. This reader abandoned Mortal Engines 55 over a world that did not obey its own logic and left Divergent 58 on a society that did not cohere, so a world that is incoherent on purpose is a heavy risk even when intended. The idea (an artist's failure to be present to those who need him) is nameable. Carried by axis:worldbuilding; occult not examined at this exit. A number below the C band is plausible, but the gate allows only this band at one source.

Opens on one concrete, vivid scene, a runaway balloon at a picnic, with a single first-person narrator, which is the starting shape this reader wants (the opposite of the Gunslinger 30 failure). The positive case is the idea: a science writer who explains everything by Darwinian reasoning cannot explain another man's delusional love, so the book keeps testing what rational explanation can and cannot cover, the kind of thinking he rewarded in Speaker for the Dead 90 and Project Hail Mary 92. Deductions: the stalker plot is a thriller, not a detection, so the detective gate does not fire, but reviewers say naming the syndrome drains the energy and the twists get absurd; the narrator is partly unreliable, so rootability is open. Sex is minor. Occult not an issue by premise (the stalker's religion is fanaticism, not rites). Leaned on the opening and the idea, not the protagonist.

Two stories, with an idea in each (an ageing libertine reckoning, a priest led astray), so something can be named, but short idea-driven form only suspends penalties and adds none. A collection is read from the front, so the first story decides, and one story is about a libertine's career, so sexual content could grade; whether the plot is mainly sexual was not examined. A priest as lead adds a faith risk. Ideas carry the number. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

t: Odlesky zapadu slunce a jine povidky (Details of a Sunset and Other Stories)
why: A literary short-story collection about childhood memory and Berlin exile. That pair compounds: a collection has no single idea to lean on, and Ja, robot 55 shows a collection is read from the front and dropped on its weakest early story, so the best stories cannot set the range. A competent author, so it sits just under the line. Leaned on axis:ideas, doubtful across a collection; occult not examined (exit at C).

The ideas are plentiful and nameable: a society engineered for individual flourishing, set against the oil-seeking outside world. But a large share of the book is dialogue lectures on Mahayana Buddhism, yoga and a mind-opening mushroom medicine, so religion and practice are the subject itself rather than a thread, and the story is thin for its length. Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 was loved for examining what is plausible, not for theology as such. The openly discussed sexual practices of the islanders add a graded cost. Stopped at one source. Occult status unexamined at this exit. The mushroom rite is of real-tradition flavour, so that check matters.
