A salvage diver finds a wrecked plane with a passenger missing and is soon questioned by agents, but reviewers say it is not a conventional mystery and the tenth passenger is never resolved, so it is a flag, not a veto. Dense, language-first writing with a second thread (his sister's) interleaved raises an opening-clarity risk that I did not source. The lead is a grieving, mostly passive man (Promena 58). Carried by axis:protagonist; occult not examined at this exit.

Exited at the below-the-line gate. The narrator is a drunk, porn-and-prostitute-fuelled advertising man, so sexual content is high on volume and crudeness, the combination that sank Ready Player One 55 and The Witcher 53; the plot is a film-financing satire and not a sexual plot, so it stays graded and is not rejected. A betrayal of him by his fiancee with another man runs as a subplot, not the premise. The satire of 1980s money culture is a real idea, but crudeness decides the range. Leaned on the sexual-treatment axis. Occult not examined at this gate.

t: Pi a jeho zivot (Life of Pi)
why: The positive case is strong. One narrator, one concrete situation, and a long survival at sea with a tiger as an unwilling companion, which answers the loneliness that held The Martian 82 down, as Rocky did in Project Hail Mary 92. The idea is nameable and stays with you: which story do you choose to believe, and what that choice says. The teenager is resourceful and has the flaw of a boy who loves all faiths, so he is rootable. Deductions: Part One is a slow set of zoo and religion chapters, faith is a large thread and edges toward a subject (Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 shows serious faith is not the problem, but theology as a subject is), the survival has stretches of bleakness, and a teen surviving 227 days invites an unearned-competence question. Pi's devotion is to real religions, treated sincerely and not as occultism or satire, so I graded it under faith and not occult. Leaned on ideas and momentum, not worldbuilding. Opening sourced, occult inferred from summaries, hence medium.

A narrator reincarnated across every era from the Stone Age on, a modern pregnancy as frame and a feminist trial of a magic fish: three layers running at once, the several-lines-at-once opening shape that scored 30 three times (Guards! Guards!, The Colour of Magic, The Gunslinger). He is described as lover to the cooks of every age, so sexual volume across a long novel is likely high, the dimension that sank Ready Player One 55 and The Witcher 53, though that is inferred from summaries and not checked. Reviewers also call it overlong and dense. There is an idea (history seen from the kitchen, who ruled whom) but the form around it is the problem, hence the lower of the two bands. Sexual volume and density carry the number; occult status of the magic fish is unexamined at this exit.

The idea is a school system that crushes a gifted boy, and it is legible. The lead is acted upon rather than wanting anything, the failure behind Oliver Twist 57, and the book is steadily bleak (1984 60 on 'too depressing'). The volume pairs the novel with a set of stories, and a collection is read from the front. Protagonist carries the number. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

t: Portugalske velehory (The High Mountains of Portugal)
why: Three linked novellas about grief and belief across eighty years, with a chimpanzee threaded through all of them. Faith is the subject rather than a thread, the form is a linked collection read from the front (I, Robot 55), reviewers split on whether the opening story is tedious, and the middle one is built on Agatha Christie-style autopsy riddles. Stopped at one source. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

t: Pozvani na popravu (Invitation to a Beheading)
why: There is a nameable idea: one man who will not conform in a world of hollow people, played as a Kafkaesque cell drama. But Cincinnatus is passive in the external plot and the whole book is waiting under dread, the shape that sank Promena 58 (passive lead, bleakness from the first page). The annotation itself compares it to Kafka. The idea carries it to the edge of the line; the lead and the mood keep it under. Leaned on axis:ideas; occult not examined (exit at C).

Memoir earns nothing by itself: the same form produced Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and The Diary of a Young Girl 40, so what earns is examining what is actually true. The book does name an idea, how far memory can be trusted when it blends with fiction, but reviewers describe a concealing-revealing style and an intrusive onion metaphor stretched over roughly 480 pages, the thin-story-over-many-pages shape that costs. Competent, probably just under the line. Memoir form carries the number. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

t: Pribehy vasne a lhostejnosti (Stories of Passion and Indifference)
why: Literary fiction in collection form: a selection of four novellas written 1922-1929, studies of passion. Zweig's psychology of motives is a real strength, but a collection is read from the front and put down on its weakest early piece (Ja, robot 55), and each novella has to find its own idea, so I would list ideas as the doubt and exit at the line. Several of these novellas centre on love affairs and desire, so infidelity and sexual content are left unexamined at this exit. Occult status also unexamined at this exit; keep axis:occult findable.

A lyrical memoir of an emigre's childhood and youth built from stand-alone essays, driven by memory and reflection with no plot. The form earns nothing by itself in this log (Diary of a Young Girl 40 against Seeking Allah 91), and what earned in the good one was examining what is true plus insight into a group; here the pull is the beauty of the recollection, so heavy description with little story is the risk. Leaned on the memoir form being carried by prose; occult not examined (exit at C).

A short experimental novel about how objects hold the memory of people, an idea I can name, but its lead strangles his wife while sleepwalking and the telling is ambiguous about who narrates and where it leads, which fails the rootable-lead test (Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65). The detective signal is a crime motif, not a whodunnit. Occult is unexamined: the narrators may be the dead, which one source did not settle. Leaned on axis:ideas.

An unfinished autobiographical novel, one source. The positive case is real: a forty-year-old looks for the father he never knew and finds his poor Algerian childhood and a mother who stands for love, and critics praise its vividness. But it is a draft found in the wreckage of the author's car, the childhood sections are the most complete, and it is a quiet, sense-heavy book with little plot, so the description-over-story risk is live. The lead is ordinary rather than flat, which costs nothing. Occult not examined; kept in deps.

A short, light, funny historical tale: an elephant and his Indian keeper walk from Lisbon to Vienna in 1551, and the keeper's bond with the animal is its warmth. Reviewers call it light with little driving tension, and say its musings on race, religion and place are touched but never developed. Saramago's no-quotation-mark paragraphs and church episodes played ironically cost something with this reader (I, Robot 55 for religion as ridicule). No idea beyond the irony of power can be named. Stopped at one source. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

A memoir-like novel of a dying philosophy professor and the friend who narrates him; the book is conversation about philosophy, friendship and mortality, so story is thin for its length and the memoir form earns nothing by itself (Diary of a Young Girl 40 against Seeking Allah 91). The idea is diffuse, conversation rather than a worked proposition, so it sits under risk. The professor's partner relationships are in the background and not the plot. Stopped at one source. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

t: Setkani v Telgte (The Meeting at Telgte)
why: One clear question, whether writing can act on politics in a ruined country, lifts it above a string of anecdotes. But the cast is twenty-odd real baroque poets arriving at once, so the reader tracks many names before any is distinct, and reviewers describe name-dropping and heavy rhetoric, one calling it a book for linguists and poets. Short idea-driven form suspends the character rules but adds no points, so a real idea with a crowded opening lands just under the line. Ideas carry the number. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

t: Slecna Fifi a jine povidky (Mademoiselle Fifi and Other Stories)
why: Literary fiction and a large collection of about forty stories from war and Norman village life: some good ones, but a collection of that size has no single idea to lean on and is read from the front, stopping on early weak pieces (Ja, robot 55). Reviewers describe the 1882 stories as cruel and cynical, with the title story little more than an anecdote. Maupassant is cynical about peasants and the bourgeoisie and most of these tales treat love and adultery, so infidelity and sexual content are open risks. Occult unexamined at this exit.

t: Smrt na uver (Death on the Installment Plan)
why: A grotesque, comic autobiographical picaresque of a poor Parisian boyhood, framed by a doctor's fever. The boy is a resentful, put-upon lead without a goal the reader can back, so it sits with Oliver Twist 57 for the protagonist who is acted upon, and the sustained squalor and coarse register add bleakness and crudeness costs. A nameable idea is thin beyond the comedy of misery. Stopped at one source. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

t: Souostrovi Gulag 3 (The Gulag Archipelago, Parts V-VII)
why: A testimony-and-investigation text covering the camps, exile and the aftermath of Stalin's death. What it examines (what actually happened and how a system sustained itself) is real, but it is the closing third of a larger work read cold, long and repetitive by a reviewer's account, and the memoir form earns nothing by itself (Diary of a Young Girl 40 against Seeking Allah 91). Bleakness is sustained. Carried by axis:density; occult not examined at this exit.

t: Spion, ktery prisel z chladu (The Spy Who Came in from the Cold)
why: It opens on one concrete situation, a man waiting nine hours at the Berlin Wall for an agent who does not arrive, then hands the lead one task with an obvious motive: ruin the man who destroyed his network. Burnt-out, bitter and loyal, Leamas is interesting, and the plan is a long deception whose reveals can be expected to fit what came before, the quality Golden Son 92 was loved for. The idea, what a state may ask of one person, is real and stays after the last page. Costs: the ending is bleak (1984 60 'too depressing', though Animal Farm 78 shows bleakness with an idea behind it is survivable), and a late interrogation section is investigation-shaped, though the satisfaction is the con rather than a culprit. Motives and ideas carry the number; the protagonist is not leaned on since the lead is deliberately closed-off. No occult element in a spy thriller.

The idea is nameable and strong: colonial 'civilising' as cover for plunder, and what unchecked power does to the man holding it. But the narrator Marlow is mostly an observer of Kurtz's decline, the prose is dense and descriptive for a thin line of action, and the mood is relentlessly grim. The Metamorphosis 58 shows what a short, bleak, passive-lead idea book can cost this reader even with a real idea. Stopped at one source. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

One setting and one form, transcripts of seven psychiatric interviews, so the opening is concrete and followable. The positive case is real: a young mathematics prodigy argues about the foundations of mathematics, the nature of mind and whether anything holds the universe together, ideas-first like Speaker for the Dead 90 and Seeking Allah 91 in what they examine. Costs: sustained and deepening bleakness (1984 60), a lead whose illness and despair make her hard to root for (Promena 58), and substantial talk of an incestuous desire for her brother, which is a theme rather than the plot, so graded on explicitness and crudeness rather than vetoed. No occult practice; hallucinated figures are symptoms. Carried by axis:ideas; the three risks could pull it below the range.

The idea is real and nameable, that one person contains many selves. The lead is a suicidal, passive intellectual and the bleakness is there from the start, which is what cut The Metamorphosis to 58 (a passive lead, bleakness arriving at once). Summaries also describe casual drugs and sexual relationships as the route out, and an extended hallucinatory theatre sequence. Competent but probably under the line. Ideas carry the number; the occult question about the theatre sequence is unexamined at this exit.

Reviewers call it essentially 470 pages of episodic encounters with more than a hundred named characters and no continuous plot, which is the thin-story-spread-over-many-pages penalty, plus dense description and a drifting lead. Crude sexual episodes appear among its comic set pieces (Artemis 69 shows what crudeness costs even at small volume). The idea (a man's search for salvation among outcasts) is nameable. Carried by axis:density; occult not examined at this exit.

t: Svedomi proti nasili (The Right to Heresy: Castellio against Calvin)
why: A nonfiction polemic with one idea stated in a phrase: conscience against enforced doctrine, told as a lone scholar against a theocratic ruler. Zweig writes it as narrative about what Castellio and Calvin each want and why, which is the motives axis that tops the log (Mockingjay 91, Speaker for the Dead 90), and an underdog lead is easy to root for. Same logic as Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91: it earns where it weighs what is plausible and true, but reviewers call it openly partisan and unsourced, so that rigour is only partly there. Deductions: religious conflict is the whole subject (the faith axis is for a thread, not theology), a one-sided portrait, dated polemical prose, and the bleak ending of the Servetus case. No occult: real church history, no rites or divination. Leaned on ideas and motives, not on the memoir form, which earns nothing alone (Diary of a Young Girl 40).

Exited at the below-the-line gate. Positive case: motives dominate, with a young man pulled between a possessive mother and two women, and the cost of that bond is a nameable idea. But a long thread has Paul as the lover of a married, separated woman and then befriending her husband, treated neutrally, which the infidelity table puts at 45-55 for a neutral subplot, and Paul is passive and drifting as he loses everything he leans on. It is not the premise, so no reject. Leaned on motives. Occult not examined at this gate.

A literary novel whose idea is real (an embassy-ordered provocation and its human cost), but nobody in it is worth rooting for: Verloc is a lazy, passive double agent, Winnie is passive until the end, and the anarchists are ineffectual. That is the Oliver Twist 57 and Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65 failure, a lead acted upon or no one to root for, and the bleakness is immediate as in 1984 60. The ironic distance and dense narration add little. Stopped at one source on the C exit. Occult status unexamined at this exit. The police inquiry is a background thread, not a whodunnit.

A sprawling ensemble novel about two families, a used-record store and fathers who abandon sons and struggle back, which is a motives story at heart. Reviewers describe an omniscient narrator, a twelve-page single-sentence chapter running through many minds, and a cast a reader tracks from the start, which is the opening and multi-POV risk. One lead's serial cheating is why his wife throws him out, a condemned subplot beside the main threads, and his illegitimate teenage son is part of the plot. The positive case is the motives of fathers and sons. Occult not examined at this exit.

A diary-form novel about a war-game champion who stays at a Catalan hotel after a friend vanishes at sea. The lead is obsessive and insular and drifts; reviewers call it claustrophobic and too long, with many threads left undeveloped and an ending that does not repay what precedes it. An illicit attraction to the married hotel owner is part of the story but does not run the book, so it is graded rather than a veto. The idea (a game as a way to replay history) is nameable. Carried by axis:protagonist; occult not examined.

t: Uz davno ti chci neco rict a jine povidky (Something I've Been Meaning to Tell You)
why: A literary short-story collection, which is the Ja, robot 55 exposure: read from the front and put down on the weakest early story, so the range cannot be set by the most canonical pieces. No single idea to lean on across a collection, so the idea axis carries a modest number; the short form suspends character penalties but adds no credit. Quiet domestic realism with the hidden-relationship and infidelity themes this author returns to often, graded as subplot or incidental, never premise. This is a Czech selection of her stories rather than a single original collection. Occult not examined at this exit and kept in deps.

t: Valka na konci sveta (The War of the End of the World)
why: A huge-cast historical novel of the Canudos rebellion in 1890s Brazil, with a real idea (fanaticism and ideology on both sides feeding a massacre). But it follows many characters across both camps at once, the shape that sank Guards! Guards! 30, and a messianic preacher's millenarian movement is the subject, so faith is central. The idea is strong enough to keep it from falling further. Stopped at one source, so the opening is inferred, not read. Occult status unexamined at this exit.

A literary short-story collection, which is the Ja, robot 55 exposure: read from the front and put down on the weakest early story, so the range cannot be set by the most canonical pieces. No single idea to lean on across a collection, so the idea axis carries a modest number; the short form suspends character penalties but adds no credit. Quiet domestic realism with the hidden-relationship and infidelity themes this author returns to often, graded as subplot or incidental, never premise. The title story is an unsolved disappearance of a girl on a hike, a mystery-shaped piece that refuses an answer; flagged, not a veto. Occult not examined at this exit and kept in deps.

t: Vybledla krajina s kopci (A Pale View of Hills)
why: Literary fiction, a novel, so no automatic exit, but I would put axis:ideas near risks: reviewers agree the central question (how far the narrator's memory of a friend is her own story) is deliberately left unanswered, and an answer withheld is a cost rather than a lift. The lead is a grieving, unreliable narrator in a quiet, dreamlike telling, and a daughter's suicide makes it bleak (Promena 58 for a passive lead plus immediate bleakness). The detective signal is a false hit: nothing is investigated. Carried by axis:protagonist; occult not examined at this exit.

A short novella: a narrator recounts a poet-pilot who turns out to be a killer, then a later search for him. The idea (what art costs the lives it uses) is nameable, but the narrator is a passive observer, the telling is full of digressions, the tone is bleak, and the closing investigation is detective-shaped though the man's identity is known throughout, so it is a flag rather than a veto. Short and idea-driven, but the suspension earns nothing here (Promena 58). Carried by axis:motives; occult not examined at this exit.

Literary fiction in three linked novellas across three eras, with Whitman's verse running through all of them. The linking idea (the same characters and a china bowl returning in a ghost story, a post-attack thriller and a far-future android tale) is nameable, but critical reception is mixed and one reviewer calls it a precious literary exercise, and three genres means three openings to survive. The first part is a ghost story in which a boy speaks Whitman's words, which I did not examine against the occult filter, and the second is a hotline-investigation thriller; the Whitman recitation also touches the verse penalty (Havran 40). Exit at the line on the doubt that the idea carries three separate stories.

Private notebooks: fragments, trial passages, travel notes and reading notes, with no story, no continuous protagonist and no single idea to work out. The ideas are real (the absurd, revolt, the Mediterranean), but scattered and peripheral rather than examined, which is the Unfinished Tales 69 complaint of pieces not aligned, and the memoir-form rule says the form earns nothing by itself. Sources cover this volume directly: Kirkus says the themes appear more peripherally than profoundly. Occult not examined; kept in deps.

Private notebooks: fragments, trial passages, travel notes and reading notes, with no story, no continuous protagonist and no single idea to work out. The ideas are real (the absurd, revolt, the Mediterranean), but scattered and peripheral rather than examined, which is the Unfinished Tales 69 complaint of pieces not aligned, and the memoir-form rule says the form earns nothing by itself. Judged from the sources on the notebooks of the 1930s; same form, and no annotation. Occult not examined; kept in deps.

Private notebooks: fragments, trial passages, travel notes and reading notes, with no story, no continuous protagonist and no single idea to work out. The ideas are real (the absurd, revolt, the Mediterranean), but scattered and peripheral rather than examined, which is the Unfinished Tales 69 complaint of pieces not aligned, and the memoir-form rule says the form earns nothing by itself. Judged from the sources on the notebooks of the 1930s; same form, later years, and no annotation. Occult not examined; kept in deps.

A comic campus novel in which the lead's wife leaves over his serial infidelities and he is carrying on an affair with his chancellor's wife, who is pregnant by him. It is a major subplot rather than the whole book, and it is framed with comic neutrality, which puts it in the neutral-subplot band of the infidelity grading rather than a reject; the lead is also an irresponsible drug-using professor, which tests rootability. A crime subplot with a stolen jacket and an editor who pursues a student add further content. Leaned on infidelity because it decides the number, not on any idea.

Exited at the below-the-line gate. Positive case: nearly all page time goes to what two couples want from each other and why, the axis that tops the log, and the argument over love versus independence is a nameable idea. Against it, the book is talk-heavy and discursive, the relationships carry a lot of sexual material, and an intense male friendship with a physical edge sits beside them. It stays graded because the plot is the couples' lives, not sex alone. Leaned on motives. Occult not examined at this gate.

t: Zivot a doba Michaela K. (Life & Times of Michael K)
why: Exited at the below-the-line gate. Positive case: the idea is clear, a man who wants only to be left alone to grow things while every institution tries to hold him. Against it, K is deliberately passive and near-wordless, the same shape that made Gregor hard to root for in Metamorphosis 58, and the bleakness is constant. Leaned on ideas, which is why it is not lower. Occult not examined at this gate.

One nameable idea carries it: what donating a dead child's heart means, laid out as a single day of choices made by the parents, doctors and coordinators. The positive case is that the parents' decision is a motives problem and the medical protocol is explained, not left vague, which fits the weight the log puts on motives over action (Mockingjay 91). Deductions: reviewers describe shifting viewpoints and page-long sentences, with some of the book tedious to them, so multi-POV and density are live; the death of a young person makes it bleak, though bleakness costs little. No occult and no detective frame. Leaned on ideas and motives, not on protagonist, because it has two co-leads and an ensemble.

t: Zradce mezi nami (Our Kind of Traitor)
why: It opens on one concrete situation: a couple on holiday in Antigua befriended by a Russian money-launderer who asks them to carry his offer to British intelligence. Ordinary people drawn into an affair they do not control gives motives (what the Russian wants for his family, what the service wants from him), and the idea, a financial system kept afloat on dirty money and who is treated as expendable, is real. Against it, reception was mixed, and the lead is an academic whose flaws are not established in the sources read; ordinary is not flat, but drive is the risk. Motives and ideas carry the number. Infidelity and sexual content were not checked beyond the plot summaries, which show neither.

t: Co ti svira hrdlo (The Thing Around Your Neck)
why: Gate 4 exit at C: a literary collection of twelve stories, read from the front, with reviews calling the quality uneven and some endings weak (the Ja, robot 55 exposure). The idea is nameable, two cultures failing to understand each other, so ideas carry it. Occult unexamined (C-low); one story is reported to touch on attraction between women, at low prominence in a collection.

What carries it is motives: three sons who each want something different from a father everyone has reason to hate, with the trial putting every motive on display. That is the axis that tops the log (Mockingjay 91, Speaker for the Dead 90), the idea content is as large as in any book read, and Alyosha is a lead who wants something and is worth rooting for. It comes in under the top because the faith material is a subject in its own right (Zosima's life, the Grand Inquisitor, faith against atheism), which the reader marks down as theology; because it is very long and digressive (Les Miserables 71 is the density anchor); and because the opening spends its time on family history and a crowd of characters, though the narrator is clear and the meeting at the monastery is one concrete situation. The murder trial is not a whodunit: the satisfaction is moral and psychological, so it is a flag, not the detective filter. Occult not at issue (Ivan's devil is a hallucination, not a practice).

t: Druhy sesit smesnych lasek (Druhy sesit smesnych lasek)
why: Gate 4 exit at C: a literary short-story collection of three stories (The Golden Apple of Eternal Desire, The Herald, The Hitchhiking Game), read from the front with no single premise carrying them (Ja, robot 55). The idea is nameable, love and desire as roles and games, so ideas lead. The stories are about seduction and erotic game-playing, so the sexual-content and infidelity axes will cost something not priced here. Occult unexamined (C-low).

A failing actor and his formidable teacher make a real friendship, and the book leaves a nameable idea: what the empire's turn to Christianity cost, and whether history went wrong there. That carries the number. Against it: the middle is a long essay on Julian the Apostate in which the narrator's voice drops out (the LA Review of Books and Houle both say so), so for a long stretch it is argument rather than character, and the faith question is the subject of that essay, not a thread, which the reader marks down as a subject in itself. Motives are mostly the narrator's guilt and loyalty, so there is less to lean on than in Pride and Prejudice 75. Occult not examined beyond the summaries.

A retired doctor hunts for the one stuffed parrot that sat on Flaubert's desk, and the idea underneath is nameable and real: how little a biography can establish about a life, and a narrator using scholarship to avoid his own grief. Motives carry the number, since Braithwaite wants something other than what he says, which is the interiority that tops the log (Mockingjay 91, Speaker for the Dead 90). Held below the line by thin plot: the book is a chain of essays, a chronology and an exam paper, so momentum behaves like Oliver Twist 57 or Promena 58, where the lead is observed more than he drives anything. The narrator's wife's adultery is backstory revealed late, condemned and incidental, a small cost only. Did not lean on ideas alone, because ideas without a lead who pulls the reader forward is the Artemis 69 lesson. Occult not examined beyond the summaries; nothing suggests it.

A volume of three works, read from the front. The Gambler has a nameable idea, the psychology of the addiction, but its lead slides into the vice he describes, the not-rootable direction of travel (Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65). The Eternal Husband is a psychological duel whose engine is a dead wife's affair with the man now facing her widower: infidelity is the premise of that one novella, but as it is one of three works and not the whole book I graded it as a subplot-level cost instead of rejecting, with the doubt stated. The third piece is a satire. Ideas lead the number; collection exposure, a lead drifting into ruin and the affair at the heart of the middle work pull it down. Occult not examined.

t: Kniha smichu a zapomneni (The Book of Laughter and Forgetting)
why: Ideas are the strong suit: forgetting of persons, of a nation's history and of one's own past, with Tamina's wish to recover her diaries as the thread. That leads the number. It is held down because it is seven loosely related parts in variations, held together by theme and geography, so the reader meets new people at each turn, like a collection read from the front (Ja, robot 55); and because reviews describe plentiful, explicit and taboo-less sex, including a threesome arranged around an affair and a rape scene on the children's island, which hits volume, explicitness and crudeness together (Ready Player One 55, Artemis 69) and carries an infidelity thread of neutral framing. The sex is not the plot, so it grades and does not reject. Occult unexamined.

A girl narrator raised in poverty by a failed-genius stepfather, then taken in by an aristocratic family. What carries the number is a narrator with a strong inner life and a pull to the story, unlike Oliver Twist 57, whose lead never wanted anything. What costs: the surviving text ends where Dostoevsky was arrested, so there is no resolved idea and no payoff; a child's inner life (Diary of a Young Girl 40, though that was testimony); heavy bleakness in the first part; and the heart of the second part is the narrator's passionate love for another girl, which commentators read as erotic, graded as a main thread of the fragment and not a premise, with the doubt stated in flags. Occult not examined.

t: Pohlednout do slunce (Staring at the Sun)
why: Gate 4 exit at C: I doubt the idea holds as one thing. Reviews describe a short life-story in three parts that drifts into philosophical rumination, Kirkus says it is not truly a novel, and readers split on the last third. What carries the number is an ordinary woman seen from inside, which the log says never to dock (ordinary is not flat), but there is no worked-out premise to add to it, so it sits just under the line, like Oliver Twist 57 where the lead is lived-through more than driving. Occult unexamined (C-low); nothing suggests any.

One clear starting situation (a brother skips communion) and one first-person narrator, so the opening is clean. Motives lead: why a pious, generous public man is violent at home, and what the aunt's household gives the children, with a real idea about religious fanaticism against lived faith. Held down by two things the log prices: a passive narrator who is acted upon (Oliver Twist 57, Promena 58) though she finds her voice, and sustained, graphic domestic violence from the start rather than gradual (Promena 58). Faith is a thread and critical of one form of it, not satire. Papa-Nnukwu's traditional Igbo religion appears as respectful background and is graded light, not as occult practice. Teen lead and a sexual-awakening crush are minor.

Gate 4 exit at C, as a judgment call: a 90-page glossary of Kundera's key words (kitsch, irony, the comic), an essay on aesthetics and existence, and texts on specific novels. The ideas are real, so ideas carry the number, but there is no narrative or character, so nothing earns patience (short-idea-driven suspends penalties and adds nothing), and the glossary leans on knowledge of his novels. Occult unexamined (C-low); nothing suggests any.

Gate 4 exit at C: literary fiction and a story collection, the shape where the log's only collection (Ja, robot 55) was read from the front and left after the weakest early pieces. One nameable idea, old age and death seen from eleven angles, so ideas carry the number, but reviewers call the stories uneven and say the shared theme repeats, so no story pays for the next. Occult unexamined (C-low); nothing in the reviews suggests any.

A five-day spa-town farce with several intertwined plots and a nameable theme in how people treat each other's wants. What decides the number is infidelity: a married trumpeter's one-night affair with a nurse who says she is pregnant by him drives the main thread, with a second extramarital relationship and a fertility scheme beside it. Per the Wikipedia summary this is one of several intertwined threads, so I could not call it the sole premise and graded it as a neutral-framed subplot (45-55 on the infidelity table) without rejecting, with the doubt stated; a death with a police finding touches the detective flag. Ideas lift it. Several simultaneous plots at the start are the shape-one opening risk (Colour of Magic 30). Occult not examined.

Gate 4 exit at C: a roughly 80-page grief memoir in 30 short reflections on her father's sudden death. I would put ideas under risks, since it is an elegy and not an examination of what is true, and the memoir form earns nothing by itself (Diary of a Young Girl 40 against Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91); what carries it is the portrait of her father's life through the Biafran war and his career, the part that examines something. Bleakness is the subject but mild by the log. Occult unexamined (C-low).

t: Zapisky z mrtveho domu (Notes from the House of the Dead)
why: A fictional narrator, a nobleman imprisoned for his wife's murder, tells prison life in Siberia from Dostoevsky's own camp years, and the idea is nameable: what a person needs to stay human when freedom is taken, and what the prison shows about the people in it. That carries the number. But reviewers agree it is episodic and rambling, with a quiet observer-narrator who documents more than he drives anything (the Oliver Twist 57 shape: acted upon, not wanting), a gallery of sketches that never coalesce into a drama, and the memoir form earns nothing by itself (Diary of a Young Girl 40 against Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91). Bleakness is mild and partly offset by the humour and sympathy reviewers report. Occult not examined beyond the summaries.

Exited at the below-the-line gate. Positive case: an old preacher's letter to his son with a likeable, reflective narrator and real ideas about grace and forgiveness. Against it, faith is the entire subject and not a thread, the plot is thin for its length, and the form is a slow reflective letter, so density is a risk. Leaned on ideas. Occult not examined at this gate.

t: 24 tvari Billyho Milligana (Slovak edition, Lindeni 2023) (The Minds of Billy Milligan)
why: A reconstruction of one case of dissociative identity disorder and a criminal trial. The form earns nothing by itself: The Diary of a Young Girl 40 shows testimony that did not work, and Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 worked because it examines what is plausible, which is the doubtful part here, as the diagnosis itself is contested and reviews call the style clinical and technical. The subject is rape charges and child abuse, which is bleak, with a central figure hard to root for. An idea exists (identity) but I would list it as a risk, so this exits at the cheap gate on one source, medium confidence, occult unexamined.

Alien first contact told partly from the aliens' side, with their senses and culture reasoned out, which is what Speaker for the Dead 90 earns on and Project Hail Mary 92 earns on in a different form. An alien scholar viewpoint is singled out by reviewers as the best element. Costs: human characters reviewers call serviceable, a slow middle, a formal register, and the Sholen's sexually charged dominance culture which is texture rather than plot. The opening drops into an alien POV, so opening and multi-POV are the risks. Leaned on worldbuilding and ideas, tempered because the human leads are only serviceable.

First-person testimony with real insight into how a child soldier in Sierra Leone experienced the war, and the arc of rehabilitation is the direction of travel (recovery rather than a slide into evil, unlike the Ballad 65 objection). The idea left behind is how war and drugs wipe out a child's identity and how it can be partly rebuilt. Held down because it is a child lead (life-phase and teen-lead costs are small), the bleakness is heavy and the prose is plain, the narrative has confusing time shifts, parts of the account are publicly disputed, and the form earns nothing alone (Anne Frank 40). Violence is not an objection. Leaned on the form's insight; the lead's rootability and bleakness stay in risks.

The Felix thread has a nameable idea, a survival personality that keeps a soldier going and what armor means for the soul, and a lead with real inner life. But reviewers say the pirate thread takes more than half the book, runs slower and has wooden dialogue, so the middle drags in story density, and the two-thread structure is confusing on a first read, which costs more than the drop-onto-Banshee opening gives. Leaned on the idea and lead; the risks are the structure and the pacing.

One wounded veteran alone on a remote warning station with an alien pet, a rock and uninvited guests; reviewers praise the portrayal of PTSD and isolation and say the sarcasm keeps it out of misery. The Martian 82 lost points because sustained loneliness is not a theme worth enjoying, so the solitary setting costs a little, and an unreliable narrator makes real events less certain. It is five linked serialised stories, which reads episodic though an arc is less exposed than a loose collection. Reviewers fault a quick romance and a heavy-handed anti-war message. Leaned on the lead and on ideas; bleakness is held as a risk.

A soldier bred for war, given a borrowed consciousness, has to find out whose mind is in his head and what he wants to do with it. That is the 'learns what he was and decides who to be' arc the Licanius books were loved for, and Scalzi's consequences-of-the-premise worldbuilding is what Old Man's War 87 scored on. Reviews describe more action and a spy-thriller strand, which costs a little because Golden Son 92 lost points to action chapters. Sexual content is brief and frank in the Old Man's War mould (small volume). A sequel is a mild risk (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70), but this one follows a new lead and restarts its own premise. No rite appears in the plot summaries; occult not examined further. Leaned on ideas (consciousness, bred soldiers with no choice) and the protagonist, not on worldbuilding, which reviewers fault for convenient tech.

A world of ice around a dying sun, with four peoples whose inherited gifts are explained by where they came from, is the strongest element in every review I saw, and a girl sold to a convent of fighting nuns wants to belong and to survive; friendship among the novices is the human core, as friendship was for The Hobbit 84. Deductions: the opening has several POVs in chapters one and two before Nona's story settles (shape one, but the situation, a hanging and a rescue, is concrete); reviewers call the pace slow for most of the book and secondary characters minimal; Nona is exceptionally gifted, a mild unearned-competence risk; the convent is almost all women and the antagonists mostly men, a sex-portrayal risk that I could not measure; bleakness mild. The convent's faith rites are invented and incidental (light). Leaned on worldbuilding and motives, since the protagonist is too uneven in reviews to carry it.

A schoolteacher on honeymoon loses his wife at the foot of an enormous tower and ascends through its ringdoms to find her; the opening is one concrete situation, he wants one thing, and the Tower works as a society whose levels each cohere around a different logic, an idea whose consequences are followed, the axis behind Project Hail Mary 92. Senlin is pompous and naive at the start and changes, the direction-of-travel arc the log rewards. Deductions: reviewers call the first half slow and the wife thin; the Tower's physical logic is fantastical and the satire may press on worldbuilding self-consistency; bleakness moderate; some brothel-like and sexual settings, mostly implied. Not an affair: the marriage is the engine. Leaned on ideas and the protagonist.

Page time goes on what the leads want and why: a slave who still tries to protect his crew, a warlord who distrusts his own visions, a young scholar scheming to rescue her family. Each carries a flaw the story makes him or her work against, which is the protagonist test Mockingjay 91 and Red Rising 95 both pass, and the warlord's thread is the learn-who-you-were arc the Licanius books were liked for. Occult: surgebinding runs on spren bonds and spoken oaths, an invented system with a Vorin devotary religion beside it; no real-world occult found and no staged human sacrifice, priced as a light-to-moderate staged rite (-2 to -5). Deductions: the opening is a prologue assassination then a five-year jump with rotating viewpoints and invented terms (reviewers report feeling lost at first); a very long book where the story can run thin against the page count, the LOTR 84 pushback; the slave years are bleak, mildly. Leans on protagonist and motives, not worldbuilding, per Artemis 69.

A serious first-contact book about environmental ethics, with a lead reviewers find one of the more interesting in SF: a hardened cop commanding the team. The ideas are the lift, in the way of Speaker for the Dead 90. Costs: the opening takes 50 to 100 pages of generic SF set-up, aliens called single-note, and a cast where the scientists are venal while the military are decent, with a view that humans are bad. Action is kept to a minimum. Leaned on ideas and protagonist.

Understanding an alien culture through one man's mistakes is the engine that tops Speaker for the Dead 90: a human translator who has to learn what loyalty and trust mean to a species that does not share the human version. Motives and interior reasoning are the whole page time. Deductions: reviewers agree the book is slow and dense, the prose rarely states Bren's conclusions, and the lead has little agency until late, so density and the opening are the risks; the series is also unfinished, which holds the open questions back. Leaned on the ideas and motives, not the pace.

The same cast through a siege war, with a fifth viewpoint added. The positive case is people with different wants colliding, which scored Red Rising 95. Costs: a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70); reviewers call it the bleakest of the books with long fights and sex scenes that add little (action-forward is the exact reason Golden Son 92 lost ground); one explicit scene and references to rape are reported, volume and explicitness graded as real costs here (Ready Player One 55 for the kind, Witcher 53 for the volume); and the deposed-heir lead is a Ballad 65 risk if the descent is hard to root for. Estimate widened accordingly. Medium: sourced from reviews, not text.

Positive case is a closed society examined seriously: descendants of two stranded founders waiting for rescue on a lightless planet, with a leader who breaks that waiting. The idea carries real thought about how a founder population drifts, and the leads have to explore the dark. Costs: reviewers report free and often public sex, incest as a theme and a few graphic scenes, so volume and explicitness both cost (Ready Player One 55, The Witcher 53 sank on volume); a reduced dialect that wears on some readers; sustained bleakness; and a society that slides into oppression. Leaned on ideas and discovery. Not a sex-as-plot book, so graded not rejected.

A hero revived after a century finds a fleet that fights by legend and not by sense: a lead who learns how the world changed and decides what kind of man to be, the arc Light of All That Falls 96 was liked for. The unknown he has to understand is central and the need to explore it is survival, so discovery adds a little. Reviewers read it as a character study of legend versus man. Deductions: supporting characters are foils, the battles are technical, and the central situation does not close in this book, a series risk (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70). Leaned on the lead and the uncovering.

Three generations of one family through a century of Chinese history, so it gives deep insight into how another society experienced warlords, Communism and the Cultural Revolution, and it asks what a regime does to the motives of ordinary people. That examined-truth side is what the log rewards in Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75; the lead changes by section but each section has its own clear want. Held down by length (about 530 pages) and context digressions that could read as heavy description, sustained political bleakness, and a changing lead. Concubinage and foot-binding appear as historical context, not as a plot about sex, and nothing in the form touches the hard filters. Leaned on the form plus the idea that a state can be a character.

A fast, tactical career story on a nameable idea: splintered human cultures bred for different strengths and a mercenary people with a code of honour. Reviewers call the lead close to a superman who wins by being different, with thin interior life and an episodic structure, which hits both protagonist and unearned competence; that is the Artemis 69 lesson, where a strong world cannot rescue a thin lead. Reviews also flag dated gender handling, which could touch the contrast axis. Leaned on the ideas and pace.

A mining ship crewed by a family and a rival corporate vessel, three storylines running toward a first contact the reader knows is coming. The case is people with competing ambitions in a believable asteroid-mining economy, the motives-first axis that tops the log. Against it: three separate threads from the first chapters, one reviewed as never syncing with the others, and a slow, 'wonky' stretch before the aliens appear; no idea carries the long wait the way Speaker for the Dead 90 does, so the number sits near the line rather than above. Mechanically hard-SF with no occult. Opening structure from reviews only, so medium.

A huntress in underground New York tunnels is paired with an outsider and exiled to the surface; first-person, constant action, and a lead who is capable and has a want, in the single-voice shape of The Hunger Games 89. Deductions: reviewers say the world is thin (how does the enclave live on rats and mushrooms, how did the world end) and the main characters flat after the first half, with a romance and love-triangle thread; the idea content is slight, the Ranger's Apprentice 74 shape of easy and light on thought; YA register; mild bleakness. Leaned on momentum and protagonist, with worldbuilding as the risk.

Ender governing a young colony, with power struggles on the voyage and in the colony and a reunion with his sister: page time on what the people want and why, the axis that tops the log and that Speaker for the Dead 90 scores on. The lead is the one the reader has rooted for since Ender's Game 87, now older, though Ender reads as a boy from the inside and that cost 3 points once. Reviewers call it idea-oriented rather than action, with an episodic, almost short-story structure, a slow letters-and-discussion opening, one implausible climax, and a lead written as close to a saint. That is a momentum risk, not a filter. A sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Ender saga #3-5 81 settled 9 under Speaker. Faith is not the subject and sexual content is not an issue (a timid shipboard romance). Opening not sourced from text, medium.

An unknown the lead has to explore with a real need behind it: a hollow asteroid with chambers that cannot fit inside it, and a mathematician recruited because her work bears on what is found. Reviewers rank the concept very high (Baxter puts it past Rama) and the idea carries the number, in the way Project Hail Mary 92 lifts on worked consequences. Discovery is partial since part of the answer lands in a sequel, so it is priced as a partial lift. Risks are density and a Cold War political layer with several POVs, and a lead whose interior life is less developed than the setting; Kirkus calls it less than fully persuasive. Leaned on ideas and discovery, not on protagonist.

Tavi, a fifteen-year-old with no furycraft in a world where everyone has it, has to be clever instead, and that gives a lead with a flaw to work against and a reason to root for him, the arc Hunger Games 89 and Ender's Game 87 rest on. A war with the Marat is told through several storylines that each want something, and the finale pays back what was set up. Deductions: reviewers find the start hard to follow because each chapter brings a new POV and place (opening shape one, though the threads resolve to a clear war by the first act); the furies are invented spirits called through skill, closer to mechanism than rite, so occult costs at most light; some romantic and sexual content in adult threads, modest. Reviewers also call it formulaic. Leaned on protagonist and momentum, not worldbuilding, since the system is under-explained per reviewers.

t: Gregor a mesto pod mestem (Gregor the Overlander)
why: An eleven-year-old pulled into a hidden world for the sake of his missing father and his little sister; his wants are clear and he is rootable, the Collins protagonist craft behind The Hunger Games 89 and Sunrise on the Reaping 87. It opens on one concrete situation in a laundry room and moves quickly. Deductions: it is clearly a children's book, aimed younger than the Hunger Games, so axis:childrens costs a little in line with Narnia 67 and Ranger's Apprentice 74, with a child lead and a small life-phase pushback; a verse prophecy is the plot's hook and is graded on handling, and reviews call it weak. Leaned on the lead and motives, not on worldbuilding, which is colourful rather than rigorous.

t: Grisa: Svetlo a stiny (Shadow and Bone)
why: A Russian-flavoured empire split by a dark Fold, a charismatic antagonist whose motives and hold on the lead are the best-drawn thing in reviews, and fast first-person narration; the small-science magic is technology-like. Deductions weigh more: the lead is the classic overlooked chosen one with power handed to her, and reviewers call her development stagnant, the Divergent 58 Mary Sue objection; the world is explained thinly and the Fold's logic is not carried through; prophecy and saint-religion are played straight (graded light); a romance triangle in a YA register costs a little. Leaned on motives and worldbuilding, with the lead flagged as the risk, because protagonist beats worldbuilding when they compete (Artemis 69).

Teenage survivors of a burning colony ship must govern themselves on a hostile planet, which gives it a real social question, but reviews say the strong start is not matched later, the lead turns bland, and exploration and development are thin. Teen leads cost little, but a young-adult register sits some way toward a children's book (Ranger's Apprentice 74). The lead is gay by design of the colony, a trait that may bring a same-sex thread, graded at the light-to-middle end until sourced. Reviewers also suspect the colony AI, a mystery strand flagged but not a veto. Leaned on motives and the lead; the range is low for the thin follow-through.

A sustained thesis: hallucination is common, has physical causes, and does not mean madness, covered across blindness, migraine, grief, sleep and drugs. That is a nameable idea and it examines what is real and plausible, the rigour Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 scored on, and it is the best-recommended of the author's books in reviews. Against it: reviewers find the physical brain descriptions heavy going and it reads as a catalogue of types rather than one story; and it discusses ghosts, hags and visions as medical events rather than practice, so occult is a light check rather than a bar. A case-collection form earns nothing by itself. Medium; the opening is a topic survey, not confusing.

A sequel, and sequels are not safe bets here (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70), but this is a payoff entry: reviewers describe answers to mysteries laid across the trilogy, and the reader rewards reveals that are consistent with all that came before (Golden Son 92, Licanius 96). A lead's crisis of faith is a serious treatment of belief, a thread rather than the subject, so the satire cost does not apply. Occult: power transfer by spiking victims with metal runs mechanically, but it is killing for power and a priesthood-like order uses it, so I grade it moderate (-5) rather than clear; no real-world occult and no sacrifice to a deity staged. Deductions: a long, heavy book with the end of the world looming (bleakness), and some self-doubt that reviewers found repetitive. Leans on motives and ideas.

The idea is real and nameable: citizenship earned by service, argued through the moral-philosophy classroom scenes and the army that follows from it. That is the Old Man's War 87 kind of worldbuilding, where the society and the soldiers follow from one premise, and it leaves a debate behind. Deductions: the lead narrates his own training with little inner life, and much of the middle is lectures and procedure, so story density is thin, the Lord of the Rings 84 complaint of sparseness. The opening drops into a drop-capsule raid but it is one concrete raid and followable, so it is not a confusing opening. No occult, no sexual content. Leaned on the ideas and the world, not on the lead, who is ordinary rather than flat; if the lectures dominate, the range falls.

A sentient prison that is a whole world, and a lead with no memory of life before it who finds a key that lets him talk to someone Outside: an unknown he must explore out of need, with the answer open, which is the shape that lifted Project Hail Mary 92 and the Licanius series. Two alternating settings are legible from the start (one lead inside, one outside), so the opening should hold. Held down because the leads read as ordinary rather than vivid in reviews, the outside society keeps archaic living for reasons that must hold up under thought (Mortal Engines 55 was dropped on exactly that kind of logic), it is YA with teen leads (Hunger Games 89 shows this is cheap), and a legendary escaper is revered in-world (graded on reverence, light). Leaned on discovery and momentum rather than worldbuilding, because Artemis 69 shows strong worldbuilding does not carry a thin lead. Arranged betrothal is not an engagement, so infidelity does not apply; an invented faith ceremony would be light at most.

The same world and its war-hero lead, now followed through four viewpoints: a Red girl, a Gray ex-soldier, the deposed heir of the old order and the lead himself. More page time inside people who want different things is the axis that scored Red Rising 95 and Golden Son 92. Costs: four threads from the opening is shape one of the opening bar for a book that is a new start with new leads; the deposed-heir thread has the Ballad 65 objection if he slides toward evil on the page (reviewers split on him); strong language and sexual references are reported (volume mild-moderate, graded). A sequel, and sequels are not safe bets (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70). Medium: opening and heir arc from reviews only.

Two threads: a trapper on a small island trying to modernise his people before invaders from the stars arrive, and a dragon captain building a crew of mismatched misfits. The positive case is the idea (how a traditional people prepares for exploitation, read by reviewers as anti-colonial) and a crew of different people that bind, the friendship note that lifts Project Hail Mary 92. Against it: two parallel threads with heavy invented terminology are an opening risk of the shape that sank Guards! Guards! 30, a reviewer found one thread's chapters tedious and jargon-heavy, and the book is a continuation that assumes earlier Cosmere reading; sequels are not safe bets in this log (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70). Investiture and aviar bonding are mechanical, not a rite, so occult costs nothing. I lean on the idea and on the crew's differentiation, not on worldbuilding, since the jargon is the complaint. Opening and occult only inferred from reviews, so medium.

A sequel, and sequels are not safe bets here (Catching Fire 83, Hitchhiker's 83 to 70). It is a finale, so the case is that questions the series has raised get answers consistent with what came before, and the lead's arc is toward being a leader worth following, not toward evil, which keeps the Ballad 65 objection away. Deductions: a close ally is at the centre of the plot, so the mood is darker than the opening of the series (mild bleakness), the young-adult register, and heavy dependence on the story so far. Leans on protagonist and motives.

Single first-person narrator, an unwanted royal bastard raised among stable hands and trained as a king's assassin; the page time goes on what Fitz wants (belonging, a father's regard, his animal bond) and why, which is the axis that tops Mockingjay 91 and Red Rising 95. He is acted on early, but he wants things and grows, so the Oliver Twist 57 failure (a lead who wants nothing) does not apply. The opening is one concrete situation, a child delivered to a castle. Wit (animal bond) and Skill (mind link) are invented, rule-bound abilities with no invocation or priesthood, so occult costs at most light. Deductions: reviewers agree it is slow and interior, with little dialogue, which touches the log's complaint about thin story over many pages; bleakness is mild and gradual. Leaned on the protagonist and motives, not worldbuilding, given the Artemis 69 lesson. Occult and sexual content are inferred from reviews, not read.

A single first-person narrator in a wrecked, parched world sets out to rescue her kidnapped twin; the want is one clear thing from the first chapter and the book moves fast, the shape of The Hunger Games 89. Saba is brash and flawed, which gives her something to overcome. Deductions: the dialect narration without quotation marks is a hurdle that reviewers split on; the world is called thin and underexplained, which the log would press on if the logic does not hold (Mortal Engines 55); the world is bleak and violent; a YA register. Leaned on momentum and protagonist, and put worldbuilding in risks rather than lean on it.

The same cast, now four viewpoints, with readers saying Lysander's eyes give real insight into the world: that is the motives-and-interiority axis that scored Red Rising 95. Costs: a sequel, and sequels are not safe bets (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70); the series is war-forward and Golden Son 92 lost ground for it; sexual content was not sourced for this one, so the series register (some explicit scenes, strong language) is assumed and graded; and the heir lead is a Ballad 65 risk if the descent is unrootable. Medium: only reviewer comments found.

Part Auschwitz testimony, part therapist's casebook, built on one idea she states and tests: that you can choose how you hold what happened to you. That idea is nameable and the memoir does examine it against real cases, which is what separated Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 from the Anne Frank 40 DNF. The camp narrator is a teenager (a small life-phase push-back) but she is a rootable adult in the therapy frame. Held down because readers report the patient chapters are less engaging than the camp chapters, the self-help register can be didactic, and the camp section is bleak (mild). Sexual content is incidental case material rather than a thread, and faith is not the subject. Leaned on form plus the single idea.

A sequel, and sequels are not safe bets here (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70), but the strongest thread is the one the log rewards most: a warlord learns what he was and decides not to be that man again, the arc the top-scoring Licanius series was liked for, and the not-rootable failure of Ballad 65 does not apply because the direction of travel is toward being better. Motives dominate the pages, and the world's history and the enemy's reasons come out in a way that is consistent with what came before. Occult: surgebinding runs on spren bonds and spoken oaths, an invented system with a Vorin devotary religion beside it; no real-world occult found and no staged human sacrifice, priced as a light-to-moderate staged rite (-2 to -5). Deductions: many viewpoints, a very long book (the LOTR 84 thin-story pushback if the middle sags), some bleakness; read cold it would hit the opening objection. Leans on protagonist and motives.

t: Mesic je drsna milenka (The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress)
why: A premise worked out in its consequences: a penal colony on the Moon, a self-aware computer as the revolution's engine, and the logistics of throwing rocks at Earth. Mike as a companion to the narrator is the draw Rocky was in Project Hail Mary 92, and the page time is on what the conspirators want and how a revolution is run, the motives axis. The world is declared precisely and mostly honours it, which adds obligation rather than bonus given Ja, robot 55. Deductions: the narration is a clipped dialect that drops articles and the middle is political talk, so density and the opening are the real risks, though it opens on one concrete situation, a technician and his computer. Line marriage and free habits are background and not explicit, and capable men and women both appear, so no one-sided contrast. No occult. Leaned on ideas and world, not on the lead.

The positive case is a world reasoned out from its physics: a massive spinning planet with crushing gravity, and a trader captain who solves problems by reason on a long journey. Worldbuilding that is thought through is what lifts Project Hail Mary 92, and The Hobbit 84 shows a plain adventure with no downsides can reach the 80s. Costs: reviewers call the aliens too human and the culture thin, the pacing is not a page-turner, and the author later admitted a gravity figure was off. Leaned on worldbuilding and ideas.

A narrator who lives inside a closed religious community and shows what each person around her wants and why, which gives the insight into how another group experiences the world that earned Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75. A clear want (protect her children) and a lead who is both interesting and worth rooting for. The plot is escape and a custody fight, not sexual behaviour, and plural marriage within the sect is not infidelity at premise level, so no hard filter fires. Held down by a coerced marriage and household dynamics that bring sexual content as context (volume and explicitness not established), sustained domestic bleakness, and a religious setting that is the subject of the narrative rather than only a thread. Leaned on form and motives.

t: Musicophilia (Musicophilia: Tales of Music and the Brain)
why: Case histories of how music works on the brain, from musical hallucination to losing the ability to hear it. The idea is nameable (music is wired deeply into the brain), but reviews say it is many anecdotes with too little analysis, and it turns dense when it moves into neurology. A collection is read from the front and put down on its weakest early pieces, never averaged, and a case-study form earns nothing by itself as the memoir form shows (Diary of a Young Girl 40 against Seeking Allah 91). Stopped at the cheap gate. Medium.

A Chinese house-church preacher's account of persecution and imprisonment, with a rootable lead and a real insight into how a persecuted group lives. But faith is the entire subject of the book, not a thread, and the reader dislikes faith as the whole story; the account asks the reader to accept miracle claims (a 74-day fast, an escape from a maximum-security prison) that are disputed by other Chinese believers, so it does not do the examined-plausibility work that earned Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91. The memoir form earns nothing alone (Anne Frank 40). Sustained torture and imprisonment add mild bleakness. Prayer here is Christian and not an occult rite. Leaned on protagonist only; memoir form and the idea are the open doubts and stay in risks.

A researched biography, not a first-person memoir, of an Olympic runner turned bomber crewman who survives weeks on a raft and then Japanese prison camps. The case is a lead who is flawed and then rootable (a delinquent youth who finds discipline), page time on endurance and what keeps men going, and companionship in the raft section, which Martian 82 shows beats solo survival. The form earns nothing alone, but the book examines what people actually did under extreme pressure. Held down by sustained brutality in the camps (bleakness is a mild objection) and by a late religious conversion that is a thread, not the subject, so the cost is small unless it dominates the close. Leaned on protagonist and the examined-truth side of the form; Anne Frank 40 is not a fit since the lead is an adult man whose inner arc is shown.

The positive case is a clear angle: human-alien first contact told from the insect side, with a lead who wants to bridge two xenophobic species. Reviewers find the lead likeable and the plot tight. Cost: readers say the aliens behave too much like humans and one calls the writing juvenile, so the idea is real but thin, and the register sits closer to a children's adventure (Ranger's Apprentice 74 pays a little for that). Leaned on the protagonist; the ideas are modest, so they are not the lift Speaker for the Dead 90 gets.

A priest-translator in a post-climate-collapse world is hired to decode forbidden texts, which gives a nameable question about what a world rebuilt on rejecting its past owes it. Reviews call the worldbuilding stunning but the book dense, with undefined-gender pronouns that confuse, and describe the lead as smarmy and passive until a late twist, a rootability risk (Ballad 65). A priesthood and its faith are central, graded on the faith thread test, and any rites in the invented religion were not sourced. Leaned on worldbuilding and ideas; the lead and faith are held as risks.

A tight single first-person voice with a clear want from the first page: revenge on the Epic who killed his father, and a plan that has to work. That is the Hunger Games 89 shape, one narrator and constant drive, and the lead has real flaws (obsessive, socially clumsy, terrible metaphors) he works against. The idea is nameable: what power does to people, and how an invulnerable tyrant's weakness can be reasoned out from patterns. Deductions: a young-adult register, a little toward children's (Ranger's Apprentice 74); the origin of the powers is unexplained, so the world owes an answer later; the weakness-deducing thread is investigation-shaped but the satisfaction is the plan, not whodunnit. Leans on protagonist and momentum, not on worldbuilding.

t: Ohen nad Hlubinou (A Fire Upon the Deep)
why: A galaxy where physics changes by region, a pack-minded alien species whose individuals think as a group, and a refugee crisis tied to a ship's accident: a world with consequences that are followed through, the axis Project Hail Mary 92 and Speaker for the Dead 90 both score on. Reviewers say the prologue is nearly incomprehensible with neologisms, which is shape two of the opening and mitigable by reading about it first, and the rotating strands mean tracking two worlds early. Aliens are praised and human leads described as weaker (Artemis 69 warns against leaning on worldbuilding when the lead is thin), so the number leans on ideas. No occult or mystery strand surfaced in the reviews.

A sequel, and sequels are not safe bets here (Catching Fire 83 against Hunger Games 89, Hitchhiker's 83 to 70). The same single narrator carries it, and the book moves his want from revenge to a harder question about whether the people he fights can be saved, which is motives rather than set pieces. The Catching Fire 83 warning applies: a setting built for its own sake would cost, so the new city must serve that question. Deductions: young-adult register, the origin of the powers still unexplained here (and a sequel does not count towards an answer), and a weakness-deducing thread shaped like an investigation. Leans on protagonist and motives.

A naval officer sent to a dead-end posting turns it around; the world is consistent about tactics and politics and the pace is steady. The risks are named in reviews: Honor is a flawless, misunderstood commander proven right, the unearned-competence axis, and the passages explaining space-battle tactics weigh on story density, like the thin-story-over-many-pages complaint on Lord of the Rings 84. Little in the way of ideas beyond duty. A series entry, and sequels are not safe bets in this log: Hitchhiker's 83 to 70. Leaned on the world and momentum, not on the lead.

A farm girl runs from an arranged marriage and earns her place in a mercenary company through training and campaigns; her wants and her growth from recruit to soldier are the substance, so the number rides on a lead whose competence is earned, the Ender's Game 87 kind of training from the inside. Deductions: reviewers say the main story only appears well past the midpoint, so the opening stretch is episodic and density is a risk. An attempted rape by an officer is shown through its aftermath, handled off the page, which costs a little at low volume and low explicitness; there is no other sexual content. Faith and a minor magic element are light here. Leaned on the lead, not on ideas, which are modest.

t: Pastwatch: The Redemption of Christopher Columbus
why: Future historians who can look at the past decide to intervene at the voyage of Columbus, with the book alternating between them and Columbus himself. It is a single idea followed through: whether history should be changed and what would have happened otherwise, the thinking-it-through axis Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 score on, and it gets human motives for Columbus and the interveners. Costs: reviews argue the book stacks the deck toward its own conclusion and defends the colonial outcome against a worse alternative, and it mentions Mexica human sacrifice as the thing the interveners want to stop, plus an invented religion built to wean peoples off it. I could not establish from sources whether a sacrifice is staged on the page, so occult and faith stay in risks; if a real-god sacrifice is staged it fails the Source test. Two storylines that merge, not a confusing opening. Confidence medium.

A boy who can see the paths people walked in the past, and who learns his father hid where they came from, in a world where the rules of time-travel get argued about seriously. The idea (time, paradox and what a gift of seeing the past can do) is the case, and the lead and his own origin are an open unknown he has to explore, which earns the discovery lift. Against it: reviewers split on whether the time-paradox dialogue is fascinating or confusing and call the book long and idea-heavy, there are two alternating storylines, and a teen lead costs a little (Ranger's Apprentice 74). The abilities are a mechanism of the world with no rite or invocation, so occult costs nothing. I lean on ideas and discovery, not on the lead, whose rootability is unsourced. Medium.

Strong first-person voice and real emotional weight, with a colony built on a prophet's faith that the planet is where God lives. The lead is sympathetic and her inner life is shown, which suits the profile. Costs are high: it is a story of grief and breakdown, so sustained bleakness (mild per the log, but constant here), faith as a major thread rather than a side one, a central secret withheld until late, and an ending reviewers call poor. Leaned on protagonist and ideas; the withheld answer earns no discovery credit.

A short, brisk story with a lead who has a flaw to work against: a lawman trying to quit the frontier, and the guilt that drove him, with a clownish friend as foil. The metal-powers system is mechanism and costs nothing, and the setting asks what guns, trains and metalworking do to a magic world, consistent but light. A courtship by contract is not an engagement, so no infidelity question. Reviewers praise the action pace and the cast. Deductions: the idea is thin compared with the best of the log (a short work, so character rules relax but nothing is added), part of the story is a hunt for a gang, an investigation-shaped thread I grade as adventure rather than whodunnit, and some knowledge of the setting's history helps. Leans on protagonist and momentum.

John Perry and Jane Sagan lead a colony whose real situation has been hidden from them, so the book is governance, loyalty and manipulation more than battle, the motives-over-action direction that Mockingjay 91 was liked for. Reviews call it quick and thoughtful but lower in density and average next to the rest of the series, and a sequel is not a safe bet in this log (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70). The narrator is the lead who carried Old Man's War 87, rootable but with less snark. Leaned on motives and the colony's logic holding together; the thinner plot is the doubt, so the range sits below the Old Man's War 87 level.

A sequel, and sequels are not safe bets here (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70), but this one moves its weight to what the leads want: a young ruler who believes in fairness trying to govern a city under siege, a street-raised heroine deciding whom to trust, and a faith-keeper cataloguing the world's religions. The idea is real and nameable, how a decent person builds a new order out of an old tyranny, the ideas-and-motives profile of Speaker for the Dead 90. Metal-fuelled powers with declared rules and no invocation, devotion or priesthood are the mechanism escape and cost nothing. The heroine is engaged while a rival pursues her; I judge it a subplot that is not the engine of the plot and not approved, a point or two at most (doubt stated). Deductions: slow siege and politics in the middle, and dependence on knowing the earlier story. Leans on motives and ideas.

t: Prey: Immigration, Islam, and the Erosion of Women's Rights
why: Gate 4 exit, one source. A polemic about sexual violence and migration in Europe with policy proposals; reviewers split on whether its anecdotes represent the whole and rate it mixed overall. It is argument rather than the first-person testimony that lifted Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91, and the sustained subject is grim. The idea is nameable but the book risks reading as one-sided. Occult and opening not examined.

t: Prezit (Alive: The Story of the Andes Survivors)
why: A reconstruction from interviews of seventy-two days in the Andes, centred on a nameable moral problem: what a group will decide and justify when survival is at stake. Group survival with self-sacrifice and companionship is the shape the reader prefers to solo survival (Martian 82: loneliness a theme not worth enjoying). Held down by a cast of dozens, many of them introduced in the opening chapters, so differentiation and the opening are real risks; by sustained bleakness, mild; by Catholic justification that runs through the survivors' decisions (a thread, not the book's subject, graded lightly); and by reviewers noting the cannibalism gets heavy emphasis. Cannibalism and violence are not objections. Leaned on the idea and motives.

A coup has already happened when the book opens, and its question (what is Kresimir's promise, and what will the coup cost) is carried by three POVs who each want something different: Tamas, his son Taniel, and the investigator Adamat. Powder mages work like technology (snorted powder, declared limits), so that system costs nothing, the Allomancy escape. Motives of rebels and a general who has betrayed his king are the strong part, and the political consequences of the coup are followed through. Deductions: it opens in medias res on an event already underway with invented terms (opening shape two, mitigable with the premise read first), and there are three live threads by chapter two. Adamat's thread is an investigation but a subplot, not the book's satisfaction, so it is a flag and not the detective filter. Reviewers call the women thinly written, a small sex-portrayal risk; Ka-poel's blood magic is described only lightly in the sources I saw, so occult is unexamined beyond mechanism. Leaned on motives and worldbuilding rather than the leads, who are not strongly distinguished in reviews.

Cazaril, a broken ex-soldier back from slavery and trying to protect a young princess, is the positive case: an interesting, rootable lead whose direction of travel is toward doing right, the axis of Light of All That Falls 96. Deductions are heavy. The magic is an invented religion of five gods with saints, prayers, miracles and a death-magic rite that Cazaril stages on the page to kill another man, central to the plot and the curse, so I price a heavy graded occult deduction. The gods are invented and not a real pantheon, so it is not a Source veto, but a deliberate rite that kills a person leans toward the human-sacrifice line and I could not settle that, which is why the range is wide and confidence is medium. Faith is the book's subject and the curse and prophecy lean on it; the treatment is serious, not satire. Early bleakness is mild. Leaned on the lead and motives, which carry the book regardless of theology.

The idea is nameable and worked through: a planet whose life answers human violence with more violence, so the settlers' fear feeds the spiral, and the way out follows from that. It opens on one concrete situation, a gambler with a deadly bet. Deductions: a pulp-era lead reviewers call impossibly capable with a psi gift that is not explained, dated dialogue, and a moral that one reviewer calls heavy-handed. Leaned on ideas and momentum; short and idea-driven, so the character rules are suspended but nothing is added, and the idea is not as deep as The Little Prince 82.

A teen lead with a real want (to be chosen for a gift he cannot have) and a magic that is geometry and chalk-drawing with duelling rules a reader can follow, so mechanism and no cost. The idea is a magic that is drawn, not cast. Deductions: the main thread is the hunt for whoever is making students disappear and the culprit is a hidden figure the story reveals, so detective is a real risk; I judge it adventure-with-mystery rather than a pure whodunnit, doubt stated; a teen school story sits toward children's (Narnia 67, Ranger's Apprentice 74); the gift conferred through an invented ceremony is a light staged rite (-2). Leans on protagonist and ideas.

A sequel, and sequels are not safe bets here (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70).
