The positive case is that a good share of the pages goes to a scholar-queen working out how the world's spirit-powered technology behaves, a singer trying to leave the wrong side, and a soldier fighting depression: what they want and why, plus an idea the reader can hold on to. That is the motives-and-ideas profile of Speaker for the Dead 90. Occult: surgebinding runs on spren bonds and spoken oaths, an invented system with a Vorin devotary religion beside it; no real-world occult found and no staged human sacrifice, priced as a light-to-moderate staged rite (-2 to -5). Deductions: sustained, heavy bleakness in the soldier's thread (mild by the log's convention, but pronounced here), a very long book with many viewpoints, and a rootability risk if the depression thread dominates. Leans on motives and ideas, not on worldbuilding.

Gate 4 exit, one source. A short cyberpunk contract-killer thriller of about 56,000 words, and reviewers describe weak characterization, underdeveloped worldbuilding and a rushed pace. The idea (the ultra-rich living almost forever) is nameable but not obviously worked through at that length, and a corporate hired killer is a rootability worry (Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes 65). The author's record in this log is on epic fantasy, which does not carry to a short thriller. Occult and opening not examined.

A real thesis: sign language is a full language and Deaf people are a culture, not a disability, told through the history of deaf education and the Gallaudet student protest. It both examines what is true and gives insight into how another group experiences the world, the two things that lifted Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75. Against it: reviewers call it the most technical of the author's books, with heavy terminology and endnotes that fill much of the volume, and history-of-education stretches have no characters to follow. Idea carries it; character does not. Medium; opening and density from reviews.

The idea is clear: colonists on a planet with a sentient bamboo that bends their biology and behaviour, and a society adapting its origin myths over generations. The need to understand the planet is real for each generation, so axis:discovery is a partial lift, as with Speaker for the Dead 90 where understanding another mind is the engine. Cost is the structure: seven sections, each with a new POV, so reviewers say you barely meet a colonist before the jump, and some find the plant too human. Leaned on ideas and discovery; the lead rotation is the risk.

A short, plainly written survival account built on one decision with a moral edge: a climber cut his partner's rope, and each man's reasoning is laid out in alternating sections, so it examines what each of them wanted and why instead of only what happened. That motives-first telling plus a companion structure (two men, not one in isolation) is the shape the reader prefers; Martian 82 lost marks for dragging on and for solitary survival, which the second half partly repeats. Held down by sustained physical suffering (bleakness, mild) and climbing jargon that thins the story in places. The delirium near the end is not occult. Leaned on momentum and the moral idea of cutting the rope.

A war journal told by one man, so the opening is a single followable thread: a young man who loses family to an alien strike and is pushed into the infantry. Positive case is motives and a lead with a reason to fight, the same shape as Old Man's War 87 (a soldier's view of a war and what it does to him). Held below that book because reviewers describe a recognisable military-SF template with some plot holes, so axis:ideas is thin and worldbuilding may not hold under thought. Leaned on the protagonist and momentum, not on worldbuilding, given the Artemis 69 lesson. Sequels are not safe bets in this log (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70), but this is judged on its own.

A sequel, and sequels are not safe bets in this log (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70, Catching Fire 83 against Hunger Games 89); but the Licanius books rose from 93 to 96 across a series when each entry deepened its leads. Here the weight sits on what the leads are hiding and what each will choose: one lead's own past is an open question that gets opened up, the loyalty between the warlord and his sons and soldiers is tested, and the oaths the leads must speak are about becoming someone, which is motives rather than action. Occult: surgebinding runs on spren bonds and spoken oaths, an invented system with a Vorin devotary religion beside it; no real-world occult found and no staged human sacrifice, priced as a light-to-moderate staged rite (-2 to -5). Deductions: many viewpoints and a very long book, so density carries some risk; bleakness continues at a mild level. Read cold it would hit the opening objection, so it is only proposable as a continuation. Leans on protagonist and motives.

A soldier left for dead wakes on a prison ship with a memory chip in her flesh, and what the chips record is the story's engine; reviewers praise the memory idea and brisk pace. Characters are described as sketchy, the religious-war strand settled poorly, and Scur is not an easy lead to like (Ballad 65). A novella with an arc rather than a collection, so collection exposure is small. Leaned on the idea and the lead's drive; faith and bleakness are held as risks.

A hunted wanderer stranded on a planet where the sun itself kills, with a town about to be besieged by a tyrant: the deadly sun forces the whole society into permanent motion, so the setting has consequences to follow, and the lead's real question is whether to stop running to help people who never can. That motive question and the world carry the number, the same pull Red Rising 95 and Old Man's War 87 had, but the book is action-forward and Golden Son 92 lost ground for that exact reason. Investiture is run like technology (declared surges, no rite, no priesthood), so occult costs nothing; no stage rite found. The opening drops the reader mid-flight on Canticle with a lead who keeps alluding to a past the book never explains and which is rooted in another series, which is shape two of the opening bar (the Foundryside 67 case, mitigable by reading the premise first) and is held as a risk, not applied. Reviews call it the most action-packed of the standalones and one calls the vague back-references repetitive; Hitchhiker's 83 to 70 is the reason a book that leans on its siblings is not priced up. Opening and protagonist not sourced beyond reviews, so medium.

A tower of shifting rooms and trials where survivors gain a magical attunement, and a young man who climbs it to find his missing brother; the magic is a heavily rule-bound system (attunements, mage ranks), operated like technology, so it costs nothing on occult (the Allomancy escape). The reader learns it as Corin does. Deductions: rules add obligation, not bonus (the I, Robot 55 lesson), and reviewers say the system is sometimes inconsistent and explained in repeated detail; the lead's decisions are called uneven and the prose plain, with a YA feel; a goddess at the top of the tower is a small faith note. Leaned on worldbuilding and momentum, keeping the thin-lead risk (Artemis 69) in view.

A vertical city whose levels run on different technologies, with zones that migrate across the land, is a strong nameable idea, and the lead is a renegade engineered angel hiding among ordinary people, so what he is and why the zones shift are open questions he has to answer to survive. Reviewers call the setting as well drawn as any Reynolds creation, but the plot is thin, the pace slows after the city, and the zone idea is not fully thought through, which is the self-consistency obligation the book sets for itself. Leaned on worldbuilding and ideas, with a thin lead the main risk (Artemis 69).

A named idea worked through in detail: a cloud that proves intelligent and has to be understood as it approaches, written by a working astronomer with the equations in. Reviewers say the plotting is masterly and Dawkins ranks it very high. The need to understand is real and the answer fits what came before, so discovery is a partial lift. Costs: a cast reviewers call stereotyped, stretches of scientific jargon, a detached tone while disasters unfold, and a 1950s register. Leaned on ideas and discovery; the characters are the weak side, so they are not leaned on.

t: The Girl of Fire and Thorns
why: Elisa starts as an overlooked, anxious princess given a divine stone she does not understand, and grows into a leader who earns her authority; direction of travel, not past, is what the log prices (the arc behind Mockingjay 91). Her want and fear drive every chapter in a single first-person voice. Deductions: faith is on nearly every page per reviewers (praying, priests, scripture), serious rather than satire, so this is the thread-versus-subject test and it presses near the subject end; the Godstone and chosen-one framing is a prophecy graded on reverence, treated seriously; teen lead and YA register are small pushbacks; some romance, little explicit. Occult: an invented faith with its own scripture; no staged sacrifice, so graded light, not vetoed. Leaned on protagonist and motives, not worldbuilding.

Opens on one concrete scene (a seventeen-year-old crossing an iced river into China) and the narrator stays the single lead throughout, so there is no confusing opening. The form gives real insight into how people inside North Korea experience everyday life and indoctrination, in a plain, brisk voice, and the narrator is both interesting and rootable, with a want that keeps changing and growing (survive, then bring out her family). That insight into another group is what earned Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91, though the form alone earns nothing (Anne Frank 40). Held down only by the hardship of the road, which is less sustained than in prison-camp accounts. Leaned on the form and protagonist; no occult content, and Christian helpers appear as an incidental thread.

A light, quick comic-action book with a clear hook: an unfit everyman hosts an alien who has shaped history through past hosts, and he must train to survive. The lead starts with flaws to overcome, which the profile counts as a plus, and Tao's chapter openers about past lives carry history without a dump. Cost: reviewers call the plot predictable and the training long, so the idea is a setup for an action plot rather than a thought you take away; the comic register fits Hitchhiker's 83 but not its ideas. Leaned on momentum and protagonist; unearned competence is held off by the training arc.

A single device, a stasis bubble, is pushed through to its consequences: a world policed by whoever controls it. Reviewers call the idea brilliant and the pace good but the plot thin and pulp-like, with a brittle nuclear allegory. Four decades old and ensemble-led, so there is no single rootable lead (Artemis 69, Ballad 65). Leaned on ideas as the one nameable carrier; the weakness is character.

Space opera where two flawed leads want things and the empire's politics follow from a conquered-and-ruling species, with a cast drawn from many species. The lead who grew up after her family was destroyed is the draw; reviewers say she is handled well and the direction is not a slide into evil so far. Costs: slow pacing, around a quarter of the book in her backstory flashbacks, a secret that is telegraphed, and physics that does not hold (RogerBW). Leaned on protagonist and motives, as with Golden Son 92 where each lead wants something different. Rooting risk exists since one lead is described as ruthless.

Near-future military SF with a hook he can name: a squad linked by implants and a lead who survives a strike through an unexplained foresight, with a hidden force behind the war. Reactor calls the opening flawless and the single-POV soldier is followable at once, as in Red Rising 95 where a hard world is seen through one man. Costs: three loosely connected parts, a squad of mostly surnames, a lead one reviewer calls a little lacking in personality, and an open central question the book leaves unresolved, so only a partial lift. Leaned on momentum and ideas.

Same author and a lead the reader would be invested in, in the register that took Licanius to 93, 92 and 96: a hidden past, consequences that cohere, characters who question what they have been told. Reviews call it among the best sequels of the year and say it answers questions while opening more. Three rotating first-person strands in three realms replace a single viewpoint and one reviewer found a strand slow, so multi-POV is the main risk, and a sequel's drop (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70) cannot be ruled out. How the Will is conferred was not established from sources and is held as an occult risk, along with an open central question in an unfinished series. Leaned on the lead and the ideas, which carried Licanius; not on worldbuilding.

A woman everyone forgets the moment she leaves, who uses it to steal, and an app that offers perfection: a nameable idea about identity and loneliness, and a lead whose situation is the interest. Reviewers call the idea fine and the language superb at times, but the book long and slow for its story, more literary than SF, and the plot gets odd once it turns to the app. Leaned on ideas and the protagonist; density is the risk (Les Miserables 71). Sexual and relationship content not sourced.

A mother and son in a Japan-like clan, each a POV, each torn between duty and what they actually want; reviewers single out Misaki, an adult woman in a hard marriage, as the standout, and the book works on honour, patriarchy and war, so it leaves ideas behind (the motives-over-action axis of Speaker for the Dead 90). Deductions: content warnings agree on war, rape, spousal abuse, suicide and child death, a heavy bleakness load that the log treats as a mild discount, and a sexual-content load that is more about violence than about explicit scenes; the ending reportedly lands hard; the slow opening builds a village and a cast; clan power is a bending-style technique (mechanical), so occult costs nothing. Leaned on motives and ideas, not worldbuilding. Range widened downward for the content load.

Ellie narrates in one voice as teenagers return from a camping trip to an invaded country and have to decide what they are willing to do; reviewers describe her as a pragmatic young woman whose moral compass is tested, so what the characters want and what it costs them is the page time, as in Mockingjay 91. The idea is real: what killing in defence does to a person. Deductions: the first fifty pages are slow per reviewers, teen leads and a YA register are small pushbacks, the romance subplot is called awkward. Leaned on motives and protagonist; the lack of a worked-out high concept is why the range stays under the 80s.

A competent, fast space adventure with a likeable lead who relies on common sense and training, but I cannot name an idea beyond trade and family business that the book leaves behind, and reviews call some situations contrived and the lead a little stereotyped. With no idea to lean on I would list axis:ideas as a risk, so this exits at the cheap gate on one source: a recorded, revisable number, medium confidence. Axis:occult is not examined.

A swordsman fights to carry out a dead king's last orders while his two friends, a duellist and an archer, argue and joke through the danger; the loyalty and banter between three distinct men carries it, the friendship the reader prized in The Hobbit 84 and The Lord of the Rings 84. Falcio's want (honour toward a king he failed) is stated and his grief gives him a flaw to work against. Deductions: reviewers find the plot fight after fight with predictable twists and thin description; the saints are invented and real in-world, and rites are incidental at most (light); bleakness is moderate (grief, cruelty); a who-did-it thread in the backstory is a flag, not the book's satisfaction. Leaned on motives and the trio, not worldbuilding, which reviewers call light.

A seventeen-year-old who fails the military academy entrance and then improvises his way into command of a mercenary fleet. Miles is interesting and rootable at once, with a visible flaw (he cannot stop digging the hole deeper) and strong wants that drive every chapter, the motives-over-action axis that tops Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90. The book opens on one concrete situation and moves fast, and the comic tone keeps the invented militaries easy to follow. Deductions: a teen lead (small), a series position that still stands alone, and the chance that his string of successes reads as luck turned into skill. Leaned on the lead, not the world.

A YA dystopia with a nameable idea: a society that makes everyone pretty at sixteen and what that hides. The lead is single-POV and makes choices under pressure, close to The Hunger Games 89 in shape. Costs: a teen lead and a young register (small each, as with Ranger's Apprentice 74), a reviewer's complaint that a boy rather than reasoning drives a key choice, and a worry that the society does not cohere under thought, which is what sank Divergent 58. Leaned on ideas and momentum, not on worldbuilding.

Lindon is a teenager who cannot use his clan's power and gets ahead by cleverness and cheek, with a spirit companion for friendship; he is rootable and has a clear want (to be allowed to matter), and it moves fast. The power system is a mechanical, rule-bound one (madra), with no invocation, devotion or real-world religion, so occult costs nothing. Deductions: short and action-led (294 pages), reviewers say it is not a deep character piece and the secondary cast is thin, so there is not much to leave behind as an idea; that places it near Ranger's Apprentice 74 (easy, little to think about) rather than near The Hobbit 84, whose friendship and ideas carried it. A young lead and a YA register are small pushbacks. Leaned on protagonist and momentum, and widened the range downward instead of exiting early.

A journalist's reconstruction of one man's life from birth inside a North Korean prison camp, which gives genuine insight into how a very different world feels from within and what a person raised without any notion of trust or love wants. The idea it leaves behind is concrete: what a mind is when no other world was ever described to it. Short and plain in prose. Held back by relentless, sustained bleakness with little relief (a mild objection, and 1984 60 was called too depressing), by a narrator whose own role in the worst events makes rooting for him complicated, and by the fact that the account was later revised by Shin himself. Leaned on the form's insight and idea; the form earns nothing alone (Anne Frank 40 is the cautionary case) so the range stays below the top memoir results.

A clear want carries it: a middle-aged Dutch watchmaker's daughter hides Jews in her home and then survives Ravensbruck with her sister. The lead is rootable and her motives are laid open page by page, which is the axis that tops the log. Held down because faith is the spine of the book, not a thread, and the reader dislikes theology and devotional treatment as a subject in its own right; reviewers also call it sanitised and hagiographic, so the examined-truth side that earned Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 is weak. The memoir form earns nothing alone (Anne Frank 40). Camp bleakness is present but softened. Leaned on protagonist and motives; no occult, since prayer here is Christian and a normal faith, not a rite.

One premise declared exactly and worked out to the end: relativistic time dilation turns a short war into centuries, so the lead returns each time to a stranger Earth, the consequence-driven world of Old Man's War 87. The ideas about the futility and alienation of war are central and leave something behind. The lead is an everyman with one clear want, to get home, and ordinary is not flat. Deductions: early mandatory sex between soldiers and later enforced homosexuality are world features with some on-page scenes; that is a graded sexual-content cost at modest volume, like the single chapter that registered in Old Man's War, and the same-sex element is society-level, not the lead's own romance. Bleakness is mild. Leaned on ideas and world.

First contact with consequences: a mission to a world the crew do not understand and a survivor whose fate is the open question, an uncovering shaped like Project Hail Mary 92 and a culture-understanding axis like Speaker for the Dead 90. The lead, a Jesuit linguist, is interesting and rootable; reviewers praise the interleaved structure, which gives one concrete starting situation. Deductions are real: faith is the book's subject, not a thread, though the treatment is serious, which the Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 case suggests is survivable; bleakness is heavy; sexual violence against the lead is a central and distressing element, graded on explicitness and volume. The outcome is open until late and the story continues, so discovery is partial. Leaned on ideas and the uncovering.

A standalone fantasy built on two sisters who each have a flaw to work against: one sheltered and spirited, one dutiful and sure of herself, both changing in ways the story follows; a god who does not believe in himself carries ideas about faith and what people owe to symbols. Breath-and-colour magic has declared rules and no invocation, the mechanism escape. The arranged marriage is not an engagement for the infidelity test. Deductions: four viewpoints by the early chapters, a religion at the centre whose treatment is serious but includes a sceptical god, a wedding-night scene with nudity that is not explicit and fades to black, and some crude mercenary banter at small volume. Leans on protagonist and motives, not on the magic system.

First-person memoir that does what Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 did: gives real insight into how a group the reader does not know sees the world (a survivalist family in rural Idaho) while the narrator examines what is true and how she knows it, with her own journals and memory questioned on the page. Education as a long idea (what it costs to see differently) and a lead whose want is clear and who is both interesting and rootable. Held down by sustained family violence and emotional abuse (bleakness, mild), the religious background of the family (a thread, treated seriously, not satire, so graded lightly), and the family's public dispute of parts of the account. Leaned on the examined-truth form and protagonist, because the Anne Frank 40 failure was a child's inner life, which this narrator outgrows quickly.

A sequel, and sequels are not safe bets here (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70, Catching Fire 83 against Hunger Games 89). It is a finale, so the case is the lead's final arc and what she is loyal to: a young pilot with real flaws, worn by a long war, and a flight of friends who matter to her. Kirkus calls it a grand finale and praises her growth. Cytonic powers are invented and operate by stated rules, and I found no rite. Deductions: reviewers report a slow first half in which the lead is adrift, the story leans on several prior books and connected novellas so the opening is hard cold, the tone is darker with the deaths of allies, and the young-adult register. Leans on protagonist and motives.

t: Vzpominky na Zemi (The Memory of Earth)
why: A city run by a failing guardian machine that starts speaking to a family and sends them out: what a machine that keeps a people safe owes them and what it takes to obey it when you do not understand the order, with brothers whose bitterness over one younger brother's favour is the human engine. That is motives and a nameable idea, the Speaker for the Dead 90 axis. Costs: faith is a large thread (the book follows the shape of the Book of Mormon opening) so it is tested against the thread-versus-subject line, the temple rites staged on the page (women hallucinating in a sacred lake, men cutting themselves with barbed rings) are an invented system and graded light to moderate, included in the range; a messianic chosen-younger-son arc is graded on reverence. Reviews call reception mixed; sex is talked about in the series but not explicit. Opening structure not sourced from text; medium.

A sequel, and sequels are not safe bets here (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70). It closes the saga's first arc, so long-threaded questions about the leads and their world get answers, which is the payoff the reader values when the answers fit everything before. Occult: surgebinding runs on spren bonds and spoken oaths, an invented system with a Vorin devotary religion beside it; no real-world occult found and no staged human sacrifice, priced as a light-to-moderate staged rite (-2 to -5). Same-sex romance: a romance between two secondary leads is reported as one thread among many viewpoints, not the premise; priced at the middle-light end of the graded range (about -5 to -8), with Foundryside 67 as the only measurement and a weak one. Deductions: the largest book of the saga with the largest cast, a thin-story risk across so many pages, and some bleakness. If the romance proves more prominent than reported it is the item that would collapse the range.

t: Z podruci islamu: otazka integrace muslimu do zapadni spolecnosti (Nomad)
why: A personal account from someone raised Muslim in Africa and Europe, mixing family history with a case about integration. What earned Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and Son of Hamas 75 was insight into how another group experiences the world plus examination of what is plausible, and this offers both. The memoir form earns nothing alone, and reviewers call her condemnations sweeping and her view of Muslim women Eurocentric, so the argument may read as polemic. Religion is the subject here, not a thread, which is a faith risk. Leaned on ideas and the testimony; opening not sourced.

Faster-than-light travel that is failing, in an empire built so that no world can survive alone, is a strong idea whose consequences drive the plot. Against it, reviewers agree one viewpoint character swears constantly, is introduced in a sex scene and later uses sex to extract secrets: crudeness at small to moderate volume (Artemis 69 was docked for that kind, Ready Player One 55 for volume). Several rotating viewpoints and repeated stops to explain the Flow add friction. Leaned on ideas and worldbuilding; the crudeness and multi-POV are held as risks, and the range sits below Old Man's War 87.

A clever girl in single-voice narration enters a lethal selection for a university, and every stage forces her to decide whom to trust; it moves quickly and keeps the want (get in, stay alive) in view, close to the tight single-POV shape of The Hunger Games 89. Deductions: reviewers see the survival stage as close to that book and the world as a textbook dystopia, thinly built; a society that kills many of the candidates it wants as leaders invites the Divergent 58 objection, that the premise comes apart when thought through; YA register. Leaned on momentum and motives, with worldbuilding as the risk.

Stories of people who lose sight, reading or recognition of faces and adapt, with the author's own eye cancer added; the idea (the brain's flexibility after loss) is nameable but thin across essays that readers call long and repetitive. A collection is read from the front and put down on its weakest early pieces, and the memoir-and-case form earns nothing by itself (Diary of a Young Girl 40 against Seeking Allah 91). Stopped at the cheap gate. Medium.

A sequel, and sequels are not safe bets here (Hitchhiker's 83 to 70, Catching Fire 83 against Hunger Games 89). It concludes a four-book story, so the case is a payoff for a cast the reader already knows: a lawman who has to decide whether to accept a higher purpose, a quick-witted friend, a thoughtful investigator and a wife whose fussy exterior hides depth. The marriage is stable, so no infidelity question. A rocky relationship with God is a thread, treated seriously rather than as satire. Deductions: the book enters a story in progress and the lead's arc is built on three prior books, which is the shape-two opening problem (mitigable only by reading them first); the plot grows cosmic, which reviewers say is mostly for invested readers. Leans on motives and protagonist.

A testimony that gives insight into how another group experiences the world, the quality that carried Son of Hamas 75: a Palestinian Christian boy in a Galilean village in 1947-48, then a priest working for reconciliation in Israel. It starts on one concrete situation, a family and village on the eve of partition, and the idea is nameable, answering injustice without hatred. A lead who acts and wants things, and a father reviewers single out. Deductions: a priest's story so faith is a real thread (serious and devotional, not satire, graded on thread versus subject), recollections not independently verified in the sources, a very idealized father, and displacement bleakness (mild). Exodus 68 is the nearest historical benchmark; this one sits above it for the personal, bottom-up viewpoint. Leaned on ideas and protagonist. No occult subject found; medium confidence as the opening is sourced but the rest inferred.

Exited at the cheap gate. A nineteen-year-old's account of living with a remote tribe in Colombia, which has real adventure, but the reader values what is actually true and plausible, and the book's events were doubted by readers and criticised by anthropologists, so the account cannot be trusted to hold up under thought (Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 scored on that rigour, the Diary of a Young Girl 40 shows form alone earns nothing). The idea is thin. A young lead and a mission-conversion theme count against it. Default range; leaned on ideas. Occult not examined past the summaries, as tribal beliefs are depicted.

Two women, friends, share a cell and an account, so there is companionship rather than the isolation that cost The Martian 82. It gives a view into how Iran's courts and Evin prison work, the sort of insight Son of Hamas 75 scored on. Deductions: 259 days of prison, a death sentence and strong faith content (sustained bleakness and faith as the main subject), a reader who doubted inconsistencies and an agenda, and little weighing of what is true. Memoir form earns nothing alone. Leaned on motives and protagonist, not ideas. Occult not examined.

A canonical novel with a nameable idea: how a divided society destroys people on both sides of the colour line and what reconciliation could cost. Kumalo, an elderly country parson looking for his lost son, is a lead worth rooting for, and the book is about what he and a bereaved white father want and why, the motives axis that tops the log (Mockingjay 91). Same shape as Animal Farm 78, serious ideas in short form, without Metamorphosis 58 style passivity because Kumalo acts throughout. Deductions: sustained sorrow (1984 60 was too depressing; here it is a gradual, compassionate bleakness, so mild), a sparse biblical cadence and landscape passages that can read as description over story, and a clergyman lead so faith is a real thread (serious, not satire, so graded on thread versus subject). A murder and trial occur but the culprit is never the question, so not the detective filter. Leaned on ideas and protagonist; no occult source found.

Epic fantasy with a concrete first scene (children, a bridge, one arriving rider), so the opening is legible, and reviewers credit a poetic, character-rich telling. The case rests on a lead who wants things and is shown through strategy and friendship, the character axis Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 score on. Deductions: a very young lead and a gentle, sometimes juvenile register (Narnia 67 and Ranger's Apprentice 74 pay a little for this), a long academy section reviewers found a jarring shift, and reviewers split on whether Aedan's brilliance is earned, which touches unearned competence. Invented world with no occult source found in the snippets; the moral framework is faith-flavoured but a thread rather than the subject. Leaned on protagonist and worldbuilding, not ideas, because no distinct idea is reported. Occult and the whole-system conferral check were not run beyond snippets, so confidence is medium.

The engineering and economics of asteroid mining are taken seriously and drive the plot, in the Project Hail Mary 92 and The Martian 82 vein, and the mission moves fast. But the cast is large, reviewers call the characters thin and the lead an action-hero figure, and the thriller form puts action over motives, the opposite of this reader's top axis (Mockingjay 91). Artemis 69 is the warning that good technical worldbuilding does not rescue a thin lead. No occult or sexual content was found in reviews.

The idea is nameable: an anthropologist from a collapsed spacefaring civilisation is taken for a sorcerer by a girl from a medieval world, and the book is two people failing and then learning to understand each other. That is the understanding-an-alien-culture axis of Speaker for the Dead 90, with Nyr's inner life as the interest. A sorcerer who is really a scientist is the mechanism escape for occult, so nothing drawn from real practice is staged. Held below the Speaker range because it is a novella, reviewers call the plot thin and the twist obvious, and Nyr's detached, depressed voice leans toward bleakness. Two viewpoints alternate but each is clear from the start.

The motives axis of Speaker for the Dead 90 applies: why did a people kill the men who came to them, and how do the killers become family? One passage retells the 1956 killings from the Waodani side. Reviewers praise the author's honesty about his own failings and his reflection on the line between helping and creating dependence, a real idea. Deductions: a missionary-family story so faith runs as a strong thread, Publishers Weekly calls the writing not accomplished, and the book is partly told in shifts of time that cost momentum. Memoir form earns nothing alone. Leaned on motives and ideas. Occult not examined past tribal beliefs.

t: Endurance: Neuveritelne putovani Shackletonovy Kralovske transantarkticke expedice (Endurance: Shackleton's Incredible Voyage)
why: Twenty-eight men survive on ice, in boats and on an island through will and leadership, so the strength is a group working together and a leader whose choices the book explains, the companionship and self-sacrifice the profile rewards over solo survival (Project Hail Mary 92, The Martian 82 for problem-solving). The motives of the leader and the crew are the point, and reviewers praise the matter-of-fact, gripping telling and an opening on the ship being crushed. The idea: what keeps people alive and together under pressure. Deductions: sustained hardship (mild), and one reviewer found the start slow while others praise it; some unit confusion mentioned. No occult source found; no sex plot. Leaned on motives and momentum.

t: I Dared to Call Him Father
why: Exited at the cheap gate. A first-person conversion account of a Pakistani Muslim woman, and the form earns nothing by itself. What would earn is insight into how a Muslim woman in Pakistan lives and what conversion costs her, which the reader valued in Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91. But that book scored on weighing what is plausible and believable, and this one is built on dreams and visions taken at face value with no examination of their plausibility, which is what the Diary of a Young Girl 40 shows a testimony can lack. I would doubt the ideas axis holds, so the range is the default one. Faith is the whole subject rather than a thread. Occult not examined past the dream-and-vision frame (visions in a Christian frame, not practice from real occultism); kept in deps. Leaned on ideas.

t: In the Presence of My Enemies
why: A single-lead captivity account with a husband and a fellow captive beside her for the whole of it, so the sustained solitude that The Martian 82 was marked down for is replaced by companionship, which the profile prefers. The motives of her captors, some recruited from villages by force, get real attention, and the book reports faith under doubt rather than argument. Deductions: 376 days of hunger, fear and killing (sustained bleakness, mild cost), faith as the lead's way of coping so a strong thread, and thin reflection on what is true beyond her own report. Memoir form earns nothing alone. Leaned on motives and protagonist. Occult not examined beyond the summaries.

A scientist hears a message from the stars and the book follows what it could mean to people, governments and faiths; it is first contact as ideas, the axis Speaker for the Dead 90 and Project Hail Mary 92 score on, and Ellie is a lead with a clear want and real flaws. Held in the mid-70s to mid-80s because the fiction is dry in places and most characters mouth viewpoints (reviewers say so), and the religion thread is a serious subject rather than a background thread, so it is tested against the faith rule; it is not satire. Sexual content is minimal as far as reviews show and was not checked in the text.

Two thieves, one practical and cold and the other warm and optimistic, whose friendship and banter reviewers call the book's best feature, give the companionship this reader values (The Hobbit 84, Ranger's Apprentice 74). It is an easy adventure in a low-magic world that clears the hard filters, but it is idea-light, reviewers call the pacing uneven, and the women are described as damsels. An investigation-shaped subplot about who killed the king is a flag, since the thieves are framed and the book is a caper, not a whodunit. Magic is minor and wizard-based, not drawn from real practice.

t: Lokynka ze Smaragdoveho more (Tress of the Emerald Sea)
why: A fairytale about a shy girl who sails a sea of spores to rescue the boy she loves; the spore ecology is the standout and behaves like physics, so it is mechanism, not occult. Tress has a clear want and earns what she gains, which keeps her in the rootable lane. The cozy fairy-tale register sits toward the children's side (The Hobbit 84 costs nothing, Ranger's Apprentice 74 a little), the idea content is light, and the narrator's voice divides readers. Hoid narrating needs no wider Cosmere knowledge.

The Apollo 13 emergency is engineered problem-solving on a real clock with a crew and a ground team working together, the thing that gave Project Hail Mary 92 its engineering interest and The Martian 82 its pull, without isolation. Deductions: the book moves among Lovell, his wife and mission control with looping chronology, many names and dense jargon (reviewers say it is explained, though some found the balance too technical), and the narration is third person; I found no source on the exact opening so that risk is inferred. Leaned on ideas and motives, with opening, multiple viewpoints and density as the risks. No occult.

A robot scavenger with a history, in a post-human world where machines fight over their own freedom and mortality, has a voice that reviewers say keeps the bleakness bearable, and what a free machine owes itself is a nameable idea. The lead is rootable. Held to the middle because a world of machines has to hold up under its own power-and-parts logic, which is what Mortal Engines 55 and Divergent 58 were marked down on, the flashback-heavy structure confused some reviewers, and the sustained bleakness is a mild cost (1984 60 shows its upper limit). Sexual content and any faith thread were not found in reviews and not checked in the text.

A memoir that earns by insight into how another group sees the world, the thing Son of Hamas 75 and Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 scored on: a mixed-race boy under apartheid, with language as the survival skill and a mother who is the book's real engine. It opens on one concrete scene, the mother throwing him from a moving minibus, and the humour and the ideas (race, language, belonging) carry it. Deductions: his mother's church life is played partly for comedy (graded on whether that is satire on religion, not taken as such here), domestic violence late in the book is bleak though mild in cost, and the comic register may carry crude references to teenage sex (volume and crudeness not checked in any source). Leaned on ideas and protagonist; confidence medium because the sexual content and occult were not sourced.

The nearest anchor is Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91: an honest first-person account of an intellectual, here an atheist English professor, weighing what is believable and what is not, and reviewers call it more eyewitness testimony than apologetics. That earns on ideas. But the profile bars theology and apologetics as a subject in its own right and the author later teaches apologetics, so the book may drift toward argument; a subject match with a 91 is not a reason to lift it. The later Catholic conversion section is described by one reader as emotional and loosely argued. Deductions: faith as the whole subject, memoir form earning nothing alone, and a lead whose interior life is the plot. Leaned on ideas; confidence medium because the share of argument against narrative was inferred from reviews.

A fast first-person adventure reviewers compare to a thriller: a Dutch former soldier who found faith, then smuggles Bibles past Iron Curtain borders. The lead is a flawed, risk-seeking man who changes, and the book offers a view of life in 1950s Eastern Europe, the sort of insight that gave Exodus 68 its place. Deductions: the book is devotional and presents border escapes as divine provision with no weighing of what is plausible, so the memoir form earns little (Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 scored on exactly that weighing), faith is the subject, and few lasting ideas are reported. Leaned on protagonist and momentum. Reviews are all from sympathetic church sources, hence medium.

The best match here is Speaker for the Dead 90: an outsider tries to understand an alien culture by what moves its people. The Sawi prize treachery, and the author must find out why before he can live among them; the peace-child custom is the nameable idea. A missionary lead who is out of his depth and has to learn. Deductions: the book exists to argue a redemptive-analogy thesis, so faith runs from thread toward subject (graded, not satire), and one reader found the claims overstated. The occult risk: the ethnography describes animist beliefs and a real ritual practised by the people, not by the lead, so occult is examined only lightly and stays in risks. Cannibalism and killing are described, and violence is not an objection. Leaned on motives and ideas.

A bioform war dog, a bear, a swarm of bees and a lizard-soldier are bred to follow orders, and the book is Rex's slow discovery of what he wants and whether obeying was ever his choice. That is motives over action, the axis Mockingjay 91 and Speaker for the Dead 90 score on, and what counts as a person is a real idea. Rex's direction of travel is toward moral independence, so he is rootable (the Sunrise on the Reaping 87 arc, not Ballad 65), and the pack members think very differently from one another. Held below those books because there are several viewpoints to track and the war setting carries some bleakness, which costs only mildly in this log. No occult or sexual content was found in reviews.

An elderly colonist who refuses evacuation and finds she is not alone on the planet is a distinctive, rootable lead with a clear want, and the contact is seen through ordinary patience and motives, the Speaker for the Dead 90 axis, not through scientists and set pieces. Held down because the lead's age is far from the reader's (a small life-phase pushback), reviewers call the second half formulaic and the aliens thinly developed, and a quiet low-tension story gives the ideas less to do than a larger first contact. Occult and sexual content were not found in reviews.

Two stranded humans must cross a hostile moon to survive while the novel alternates with the alien species living there, a first-contact problem about two kinds of perception that cannot share a world; Project Hail Mary 92 shows how much this reader gets from a companion and an alien mind. Mai and Juna are a pair, not a lone survivor, which the log prefers (The Martian 82 lost ground to sustained loneliness). Held down because reviewers say most of the book is a slow crossing and that the opening and closing sections carry too many characters, and the corporate-dystopia backdrop adds some bleakness. No occult or sexual content was found in reviews. Opening structure is inferred from review descriptions, not the text.

First-person narration by an autistic man offered an experimental cure gives a lead worth rooting for from page one and a real question, what is lost if a mind is changed; The Little Prince 82 and Animal Farm 78 show ideas carrying a short book, and here the idea has a full novel to unfold in. This reader's top scores go to interior life and motives (Red Rising 95, Speaker for the Dead 90), which a single close narrator supplies. Held below the top because reviewers say it never becomes a page-turner and runs long for its plot, and the stalker subplot reads as cliche. Faith appears as a sincere thread, not a subject. Sexual content was not found to be significant.

A girl raised inside a militarised fascist station decides to take humanity's revenge into her own hands, and the book is a radicalisation seen from inside; that is motives over action (Mockingjay 91), and the idea is nameable. Held low because Kyr is deliberately unlikeable at the start, so the rooting is earned late if at all (Ballad 65 lost 22 on exactly that), reviewers call the first half hard going, and the society's eugenics and homophobia make the tone heavy. A same-sex dynamic is present but off-page and not a romance plot, so it grades at the light end, not at the veto; the breeding programme is a society fact, and how much is shown was not established. Occult not found.

A scholar deported to a penal research colony has to decode an alien ecosystem to survive, and the book is mostly the consequences of that biology; that is the unknown-world-with-a-need shape of Project Hail Mary 92, and reviewers single out the worldbuilding. It lands below that book because the lead is a sardonic, selectively unreliable narrator whose cowardice may not be worth rooting for (the Ballad 65 failure mode), and because the colony is a totalitarian prison in the register of 1984 60, which this reader found too depressing. Occult is not at issue: this is invented evolutionary biology. Sexual content was not found in reviews and was not checked in the text.

A huge library and two leads whose stories converge on one mystery give the book a real idea (what a library is for) and a lead, Livira, whose growth from naive refugee to librarian is the engine, the direction-of-travel arc this reader liked in Licanius. Held to the middle because two viewpoints on different timelines must be tracked, reviewers call the pacing meandering and the romance thin, and the author's grim streak adds some bleakness. Occult, sexual content and the worldbuilding logic were not established beyond review summaries, so confidence stays medium. The mystery is about the library's past, not a culprit, so detective does not fire.

t: The Boy Who Harnessed the Wind
why: A boy with a clear want and a problem he must solve with what he can find, the problem-solving and humour that earned The Martian 82, here with a family around him instead of solitude and without the dragged ending reported for that book. He is rootable and interesting: neighbours call him mad. The idea is nameable: what curiosity and a library book can do against famine. Deductions: the 2001-2002 famine is a long bleak stretch (mild cost), and the village world includes magic and witchcraft beliefs that the summaries only touch on, so the occult item stays in risks as an unchecked depiction, not practice by the lead. Leaned on ideas and protagonist; medium confidence as the opening was not sourced.

A boy cut off from his village's technology wanders a world he does not understand and has to work out what it is, the unknown-world-plus-need shape that tops the log in Project Hail Mary 92. The contest between three characters over how to live with technology is a nameable idea. Held below that book because it is a novella with a young lead, one reviewer found Handry one-dimensional, and short work earns nothing from the short-idea-driven suspension; Ranger's Apprentice 74 prices an easy, younger register. The fantasy-looking surface is technology underneath, so no rite is staged and occult costs nothing; that is inferred from reviews, not the text, hence medium confidence.

Exited at the cheap gate. A missionary's account of his research among persecuted Christians, built from interviews and reflection on one question, whether faith is worth the cost. That is an idea, but it is theology and exhortation as a subject in its own right, which the profile excludes, and the same form produced both Seeking Allah, Finding Jesus 91 and the Diary of a Young Girl 40 DNF, so the form earns nothing. The persecution stories bring sustained bleakness (mild cost). I would doubt that ideas hold for this reader, so the default range. Leaned on ideas; faith and memoir form are the risks. Occult not examined.
